Nothing Beats Adavosertib on Wee1 Docking: the Top Five Sit Inside One Molecule's 0.44 kcal/mol Reproducibility Gap

Wee1 kinase guards the G2/M checkpoint by phosphorylating CDK1 at Tyr15, and TP53-mutant cancers — which have lost the G1/S checkpoint — depend on it, making Wee1 inhibition a synthetic-lethal strategy.

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-27 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #126 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Wee1; adavosertib; AZD1775; G2/M checkpoint; TP53; synthetic lethality; myelosuppression; molecular docking; ChEMBL; Pakistan

Abstract

Wee1 kinase guards the G2/M checkpoint by phosphorylating CDK1 at Tyr15, and TP53-mutant cancers — which have lost the G1/S checkpoint — depend on it, making Wee1 inhibition a synthetic-lethal strategy. Adavosertib (AZD1775/MK-1775) is the first-in-class Wee1 inhibitor, but its single-agent response rate is 3.8% and its dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression. We asked whether any published Wee1 inhibitor beats adavosertib on docking to the Wee1 kinase domain. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P30291 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL5491, 60 bioactivities → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen) we docked adavosertib and four ChEMBL Wee1 actives with AutoDock Vina on PDB 8BJU, a 1.53 Å Wee1–inhibitor complex. Nothing beats adavosertib by any meaningful margin: the whole top five spans 0.45 kcal/mol (−11.07 to −10.62 kcal/mol), and adavosertib docked twice — once as the query and once as its duplicate ChEMBL record — differs by 0.44 kcal/mol from itself. Docking cannot distinguish these five compounds at all. By measurement the leads are ~10-fold more potent than adavosertib (IC50 0.2–0.3 nM vs Kd 3.2 nM), but two of them are PAINS-clean while adavosertib itself carries the anil_di_alk PAINS alert — and a more potent Wee1 inhibitor may simply be more myelosuppressive, since the 8BJU paper's own title reports that Wee1 inhibition correlates with myelosuppression. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head kinase assay plus a bone-marrow progenitor assay: if a lead does not confirm below 1 nM, or if its potency gain comes with equal myelosuppression, the lead is refuted as a therapeutic advance. No pipeline failure occurred on this target — the structure, the centre and the target all verified — which makes the null docking result a property of the compounds, not of the method.

1. Introduction

The cell cycle has two checkpoints that matter for cancer therapy, and TP53-mutant tumours have already lost one of them. Wee1 is a nuclear serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) at the inhibitory Tyr15 residue, holding the CDK1–cyclin B complex inactive and pausing the cell at the G2/M boundary until DNA damage is repaired. In a TP53-mutant cell the G1/S checkpoint is gone, so the tumour relies almost entirely on Wee1-mediated G2 arrest; remove Wee1 and the cell enters mitosis with broken DNA, collapsing replication forks and fragmenting chromosomes — mitotic catastrophe. That is synthetic lethality: the drug kills the cancer cell not because the target is cancer-specific, but because the cancer has already discarded its backup.

Adavosertib (AZD1775, MK-1775) is the first-in-class ATP-competitive Wee1 inhibitor, and its clinical record is a study in a narrow therapeutic index. In a phase Ib trial (175 mg twice daily, days 1–3 and 8–10 of a 21-day cycle) the overall response rate was 3.8% with a disease control rate of 63.8%, and the commonest toxicities were diarrhoea (56.3%), nausea (42.5%) and fatigue (36.3%) (Bauer et al., Target Oncol 2023). A phase I once-daily study set the recommended phase II dose at 300 mg (days 1–5 and 8–12) and saw 6 confirmed partial responses in 42 patients (14%, four ovarian, two endometrial), with grade 4 haematologic toxicity as the dose-limiting event and CCNE1 (cyclin E1) overexpression emerging as a candidate predictive biomarker (Clin Cancer Res 2021;27:3834). In TP53-mutated uterine carcinosarcoma the response rate was 22.2% with median progression-free survival of 2.7 months, and the trial was terminated early after the sponsor discontinued monotherapy development. The structural basis is known: the Wee1–adavosertib complex (PDB 5V5Y, 1.90 Å, Zhu et al., J Med Chem 2017) — which also showed that adavosertib is an equally potent inhibitor of polo-like kinase PLK1, an off-target that complicates every claim about its selectivity. And the class limit is stated in the title of the newest structure paper: selective Wee1 inhibitors show antitumour activity in vitro that correlates with myelosuppression (ACS Med Chem Lett 2023; PDB 8BJU).

The gap this paper attacks is therefore not "find a more potent Wee1 inhibitor" — potency exists — but whether docking can rank the potent ones, and whether a more potent molecule is even the right goal when the dose-limiting toxicity tracks the same target.

Falsifiable question. Does any published ChEMBL Wee1 inhibitor beat adavosertib on docking to the Wee1 kinase domain, by more than the method's own reproducibility? Falsifier: a head-to-head kinase assay in which no lead confirms below 1 nM, or a progenitor assay in which the most potent lead suppresses bone-marrow progenitors at the same concentration as adavosertib — either result refutes the lead as a therapeutic advance. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking (adavosertib re-docked into a Wee1–inhibitor complex, same grid, same protocol, plus its duplicate-record re-dock as an internal reproducibility control) — association only beyond that, since no experiment was run and docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-27: the adavosertib phase Ib study (Bauer et al., Target Oncol 2023;18); the once-daily phase I study (Clin Cancer Res 2021;27:3834); the TP53-mutated uterine carcinosarcoma phase 2 report (ORR 22.2%, mPFS 2.7 months, early termination); the Wee1 structure–function paper (Zhu et al., J Med Chem 2017;60:7863–7875, doi:10.1021/acs.jmedchem.7b00996, PMID 28792760; PDB 5V5Y); and the selective-Wee1-inhibitor paper (ACS Med Chem Lett 2023; PDB 8BJU). Measured IC50/Kd values for adavosertib and the four leads were retrieved live from the ChEMBL API on 2026-11-27 (target CHEMBL5491). The classical-canon sweep is in §4.3: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses swellings and tumours (waram) and their surgical treatment, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of tumours — neither describes a kinase or an inhibitor, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and la darar (no harm), not on a classical source about this target.

2.2 Target identification

No failure occurred on this target, and the absence of failure is stated because the previous two papers in this run both needed corrections. The target was specified directly by its reviewed accession: UniProt P30291 (WEE1_HUMAN, gene WEE1, 646 aa). ChEMBL target by accession returned CHEMBL5491, "Wee1-like protein kinase", single protein, Homo sapiens, with 60 bioactivities. Adavosertib was verified against PubChem (C27H32N8O2, MW 500.61, logP 2.89, 2 H-bond donors, 8 acceptors, TPSA 104.34 Å², 7 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation, PAINS alert — see §2.4). The similarity screen against the 60 ChEMBL Wee1 actives returned 25 leads; the top four by composite score were docked alongside adavosertib.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking ran on PDB 8BJU (1.53 Å, human Wee1 kinase in complex with inhibitor QT9, an adavosertib analogue; ACS Med Chem Lett 2023). The grid centre [−14.10, −11.12, 19.32] is the centroid of the co-crystallised QT9 ligand (42 atoms, verified against the PDB file — the only non-water HETATM group), computed by dock._ligand_center. All five ligands were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 at that centre (box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses). Two structural facts must be stated: 8BJU is a Wee1–inhibitor complex, so the grid is ligand-validated (unlike the apo structures in Papers #124–125); and the QT9 inhibitor is an adavosertib analogue, so the pocket is the adavosertib pocket — the docking tests fit into adavosertib's own site, which favours adavosertib-like molecules and is a bias, not a neutral test.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to adavosertib and all four leads. The result is reported, not hidden: adavosertib carries the alert anil_di_alk_A(478) — the dialkyl-aniline substructure (its 4-(4-methylpiperazin-1-yl)aniline moiety) — and so do its duplicate record CHEMBL1976040 and CHEMBL6172478, which share the same anilino group. CHEMBL5761564 and CHEMBL6065998 are PAINS-clean. A PAINS alert is a screening flag, not a verdict: adavosertib is a clinically tested drug that carries it, which shows the filter's limits — but it also means the anilino group is a known assay-interference risk, and the validation assay in §4.5 includes the detergent and redox controls that would expose it. The two PAINS-clean leads are therefore the more interesting compounds on this axis, not the more potent ones.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking scores are not activity: Vina's noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, the structure is a single inhibitor-bound conformation, and no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. The leads' IC50s (0.2–0.3 nM) and adavosertib's Kd (3.2 nM) come from different assay formats (kinase activity vs binding) and different documents, so the "~10-fold" comparison is order-of-magnitude, not head-to-head. Adavosertib's own potency varies by assay (Kd 3.2 nM recombinant, 12 nM Kinobeads). No experimental data were generated in this study.

All five docked into the same grid (8BJU, QT9 centre [−14.10, −11.12, 19.32], box 22.5 Å). The "best" lead beats adavosertib by 0.45 kcal/mol — a quarter of Vina's noise band, and therefore not a win.

3.2 The same molecule, docked twice, spans the whole ranking

The table contains an internal control that the pipeline did not plan: CHEMBL1976040 is adavosertib itself under a duplicate ChEMBL record (identical formula C27H32N8O2, identical descriptors to the last decimal, Tanimoto similarity 1.0 to the query). It docked at −11.06 kcal/mol; adavosertib as the query docked at −10.62 kcal/mol. The same molecule, docked twice by the same protocol, differs by 0.44 kcal/mol — Vina's stochasticity on this target, measured directly. The entire top-five spread is 0.45 kcal/mol. The ranking is therefore indistinguishable from noise: the "best" lead and the reference differ by less than the method differs from itself. This is the paper's result, and it is a null result: docking cannot rank these five Wee1 inhibitors, and no lead is declared. The measured data tell a different, cleaner story — the three non-adavosertib leads are 0.2–0.3 nM against adavosertib's 3.2 nM Kd, roughly 10-fold more potent — but that story comes from the assays, not from the docking, and it is the assays that must confirm it.

3.3 The duplicate-record correction

CHEMBL1976040 and the query are the same molecule, and the paper treats them as such: the 0.3 nM-class potency belongs to adavosertib, not to a new lead, and the "−11.06 kcal/mol lead" is adavosertib re-docked. A paper that reported "CHEMBL1976040 beats adavosertib" without checking the structures would be reporting a database artefact as a discovery — the same error Paper #118 caught for tenapanor. The check took one RDKit comparison and it is stated here, not buried.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

Zhu et al. (2017) solved the Wee1–adavosertib structure but reported no docking scores, and no published Vina scores exist for these four ChEMBL compounds on 8BJU. The compounds have no common names. This paper's docking table therefore stands alone as a Vina ranking, and §3.2 is the statement that the ranking is noise.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was "what beats adavosertib?" and the honest answer is that docking cannot answer it for this target — and that the question itself may be wrong. Adavosertib's problem was never potency: at 3.2 nM it is already potent, and the leads at 0.2–0.3 nM are only 10-fold better. Its problem is the therapeutic index: single-agent response 3.8%, dose-limiting myelosuppression, and a sponsor that discontinued monotherapy development. A 10-fold more potent Wee1 inhibitor that suppresses bone marrow 10-fold more strongly is not an advance; it is the same drug with a smaller dose. The 8BJU paper's title says the quiet part aloud — Wee1 inhibition correlates with myelosuppression — because Wee1 also guards the G2/M checkpoint in healthy haematopoietic progenitors. The reframe is therefore from "find a more potent Wee1 inhibitor" to "find a Wee1 inhibitor with a wider index, or a biomarker that picks the patients who respond": TP53 mutation plus CCNE1 overexpression, the two markers the phase I study flagged, are the selection tools, and the leads' value depends on whether they spare progenitors, not on whether they dock 0.45 kcal/mol better.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three corrections guard the headline. First, the 0.45 kcal/mol margin is inside the method's own 0.44 kcal/mol reproducibility gap — it is not a win by any definition. Second, the reference drug carries a PAINS alert, so the docking scores for the anilino compounds (including adavosertib itself) carry an assay-interference caveat that the two PAINS-clean leads do not. Third, the measured 10-fold potency gap is across assay formats (IC50 vs Kd) and documents, so it is order-of-magnitude. What is solid is the validation: the grid is ligand-anchored on a 1.53 Å inhibitor complex, the target and structure both verified, and the duplicate-molecule control quantifies the noise — which is exactly why the null result is trustworthy rather than a failure to look. The memorable number is 0.44 kcal/mol — the same molecule docked twice differs by as much as the whole top five — because it is the number that kills the ranking.

4.3 Mechanism — and the classical canon

Wee1 phosphorylates CDK1 at Tyr15, holding the CDK1–cyclin B complex inactive; adavosertib competes with ATP, Tyr15 phosphorylation falls, CDK1 activates early, and the TP53-deficient cell enters mitosis with unrepaired breaks — mitotic catastrophe. Test for each link: (i) a biochemical kinase assay measures Wee1 inhibition directly, against the published 3.2 nM Kd; (ii) a pY15-CDK1 Western blot in TP53-mutant cells measures target engagement in cells, against the phase I study's paired-biopsy readout; (iii) a colony-forming-unit assay on healthy bone-marrow progenitors measures the myelosuppression that defines the index, against adavosertib as the comparator. The classical canon knows the disease, not the kinase: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses swellings and tumours (waram) and their surgical treatment, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of tumours — but neither describes a cell-cycle checkpoint, so the principle carried forward is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) joined to la darar (no harm): a drug whose benefit is measured in months and whose harm is measured in bone marrow must be selected by a biomarker, not prescribed to all comers, because the harm is certain and the benefit is not.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL6065998 inhibits recombinant Wee1 with an IC50 below 1 nM in a head-to-head kinase assay on the same day as adavosertib. Falsifier: IC50 above 1 nM, which would refute the ChEMBL record and remove the lead.
  2. CHEMBL6065998 suppresses healthy bone-marrow progenitor colony formation at a concentration at least 10-fold higher than its Wee1 IC50 (a therapeutic index of 10). Falsifier: suppression within 3-fold of the IC50, which would show the potency gain buys no safety.
  3. In TP53-mutant, CCNE1-overexpressing ovarian cancer cells, CHEMBL5761564 reduces pY15-CDK1 by at least 50% at its IC50 and induces γ-H2AX accumulation. Falsifier: no pY15 reduction at the IC50, which would show the compound does not engage the target in cells.
  4. Adavosertib's PAINS alert (anil_di_alk_A(478)) does not produce aggregation artefacts in the kinase assay (detergent control changes the IC50 by less than 2-fold). Falsifier: a detergent-sensitive IC50, which would suggest the published potency is partly artefactual.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): biochemical kinase assay — recombinant Wee1, CHEMBL6065998, CHEMBL5761564 and adavosertib on one plate, n=3, with detergent and redox controls to expose PAINS artefacts; readout IC50. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): cellular target engagement — pY15-CDK1 Western blot and γ-H2AX in TP53-mutant ovarian cancer cells (CCNE1-overexpressing), plus a colony-forming-unit assay on healthy bone-marrow progenitors for the same compounds; readout pY15 reduction and progenitor IC50. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): if a compound passes stages 1–2 — Wee1 IC50 below 1 nM and a progenitor index of at least 10 — a TP53-mutant xenograft pilot against adavosertib; if none passes, publish the negative result with the ChEMBL table as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed before stages 1–2 pass.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only, on a single inhibitor-bound conformation; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol and the measured same-molecule reproducibility gap is 0.44 kcal/mol, so no ranking is claimed.
  2. The leads' IC50s and adavosertib's Kd come from different assay formats and documents; the "~10-fold" gap is order-of-magnitude, not head-to-head.
  3. The pocket is adavosertib's own site (QT9 is an adavosertib analogue), so the docking favours adavosertib-like molecules — a bias, not a neutral test.
  4. Adavosertib's PLK1 off-target activity (equally potent, Zhu et al. 2017) is not modelled here; a lead's selectivity against PLK1 is untested.
  5. No experimental data were generated in this study; all potencies are retrieved, not measured.
  6. No Pakistani data exist on TP53 or CCNE1 frequencies in ovarian or endometrial cancer, and no local study reports Wee1-inhibitor outcomes, so the policy section recommends testing infrastructure, not a drug decision.
  7. The classical-canon sweep did not re-read the Canon or Kitab al-Hawi in full; the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and la darar as principles, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections.

6. Conclusion

Nothing beats adavosertib on Wee1 docking: the top five span 0.45 kcal/mol, and adavosertib docked twice differs from itself by 0.44 kcal/mol, so the ranking is noise and no lead is declared. By measurement the leads are ~10-fold more potent (IC50 0.2–0.3 nM vs Kd 3.2 nM), and two of them are PAINS-clean where adavosertib carries the anil_di_alk alert — but a more potent Wee1 inhibitor may simply be more myelosuppressive, and the therapeutic index, not the potency, is the bottleneck. The next step is the cheap, decisive test: one kinase assay plus one bone-marrow progenitor assay, not a bigger docking screen.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, with the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital and the Aga Khan University Hospital oncology departments as the technical arms. Decision: whether to spend anything on a Wee1 programme for ovarian and endometrial cancer, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund a docking screen or import a Wee1 inhibitor on a docking score — this paper shows the docking ranking is noise, and the class's dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression; instead, fund TP53 and CCNE1 testing in ovarian and endometrial cancer, so the patients who respond (TP53-mutant, CCNE1-overexpressing) are identified before any drug is considered. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if local testing shows CCNE1 overexpression is common in Pakistani ovarian cancer and a lead confirms a progenitor index above 10, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that lead; if CCNE1 overexpression is rare, or if the progenitor assay shows no index, drop the programme — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to la darar: where a biomarker can distinguish the patient who benefits from the patient who is only harmed, running the test is the obligation; prescribing a myelosuppressive drug without it would violate it. The evidence here is thin — retrieved potencies and a null docking result — so the recommendation is "build the testing", not "do the policy".

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-27 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #123 (daily paper run)

Keywords: THR-β; resmetirom; MASH; MASLD; sobetirome; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; fatty liver; Pakistan

Abstract

Thyroid hormone receptor beta (THR-β) is the target of resmetirom, the first drug approved for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) — FDA accelerated approval 14 March 2024 — and the question is whether any earlier or related agonist binds the receptor better, and whether docking can tell the potent agonists from the weak ones. Five compounds — resmetirom, sobetirome (GC-1), KB141 and two resmetirom-series analogues from the same Kelly et al. 2014 assay — were docked with standardised AutoDock Vina into the ligand-binding pocket of the 2.55 Å human TR-β structure 3IMY, same box and exhaustiveness, with the pocket centre taken from the co-crystallised sobetirome. No compound beats resmetirom beyond Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise: the best, resmetirom's own N-methyl analogue (EC50 40 nM), leads by 0.06 kcal/mol (−11.19 vs −11.13), and the most potent compound in the set, sobetirome (EC50 18 nM), ranks only third at −10.77. Worse, the docking order does not track potency at all: a 510-fold EC50 spread (18 nM to 9,170 nM) is compressed into 0.93 kcal/mol of docking score, Spearman rho 0.2 (n = 5). The falsifier is a recombinant THR-β reporter assay: if the N-methyl analogue's EC50 is not better than resmetirom's 210 nM on the same plate, the docking lead is noise — and the assay, not the dock, must decide, because this study shows the dock cannot rank THR-β agonists.

1. Introduction

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects 32.4% of the world's population (95% CI 29.9–34.9; Riazi et al., Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022), up from 25.5% in or before 2005 to 37.8% in 2016 or later, and a second meta-analysis puts the global figure at 30.05% (95% CI 27.88–32.32), rising 50.4% between 1990–2006 and 2016–2019 (Younossi et al., Hepatology 2023). In Pakistan the pooled prevalence is 29.82% (95% CI 21.39–39.01%) in the general population and 58.47% (95% CI 54.23–62.64%) in people with diabetes (systematic review and meta-analysis of 34 studies, 12,995 participants, Scientific Reports 2024); an earlier Pakistani cohort found 14.8% overall and 19.9% above age 40 (Ghani et al., Pak J Med Sci 2017). The disease that matters is not the fat but the fibrosis: MASH with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis (stages F2–F3) progresses to cirrhosis, and until 2024 it had no approved drug at all.

Resmetirom (MGL-3196, Rezdiffra) changed that. It is an oral, liver-directed, THR-β-selective agonist: in the discovery paper it activated THR-β with EC50 0.21 μM and THR-α with EC50 3.74 μM, 28-fold selective (Kelly et al., J Med Chem 2014). The mechanism is the one thyroid hormone itself uses in the liver — increased mitochondrial function and fatty-acid β-oxidation, reduced de novo lipogenesis — with the cardiac and bone effects of unselective thyroid hormone avoided by keeping the action on the β receptor and in the liver. In the phase 3 MAESTRO-NASH trial (966 patients with biopsy-confirmed MASH and F1B–F3 fibrosis, randomised 1:1:1 to resmetirom 80 mg, 100 mg or placebo; Harrison et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:497–509, NCT03900429), NASH resolution with no worsening of fibrosis was achieved in 25.9% (80 mg) and 29.9% (100 mg) of patients versus 9.7% on placebo (p < 0.001 for both), and fibrosis improved by at least one stage with no worsening of the NAFLD activity score in 24.2% and 25.9% versus 14.2% on placebo (p < 0.001 for both). LDL cholesterol fell 13.6% and 16.3% from baseline at week 24 versus a 0.1% rise on placebo. The FDA granted accelerated approval on 14 March 2024 — the first drug ever approved for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis — with full approval contingent on the ongoing 54-month outcomes phase of MAESTRO-NASH.

Two facts make resmetirom worth a hard look rather than a celebration. First, the absolute benefit is modest: roughly 2 in 10 treated patients gain NASH resolution over placebo, and roughly 1 in 10 gain fibrosis improvement — more than 70% of treated patients reached neither primary endpoint at 52 weeks. Second, it is no longer alone: semaglutide (Wegovy 2.4 mg) received FDA accelerated approval for the same indication on 15 August 2025 on the ESSENCE trial, where MASH resolution was 62.9% versus 34.3% on placebo and fibrosis improvement 36.8% versus 22.4% — cross-trial numbers, not a head-to-head comparison, but the gap is large enough that any THR-β programme must now justify itself against a GLP-1 drug that resolves MASH in nearly two-thirds of patients. And the price decides who gets either: resmetirom launched at a US wholesale acquisition cost of $47,400 per year, and a 2026 cost-effectiveness model put its incremental cost-effectiveness ratio at $273,445 per quality-adjusted life year — above the $100,000/QALY benchmark, needing a 61% price cut to about $23,007 per year to meet it — while the same model costed semaglutide at $16,188 per year (Abdeen et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2026).

The gap this paper attacks is narrower and prior to all of that: does any known THR-β agonist actually bind the receptor better than resmetirom, and can docking distinguish the strong agonists from the weak ones? The ChEMBL record for human THR-β holds 878 EC50/IC50 activities, and the discovery paper that produced resmetirom tested 22 analogues in a single recombinant assay with a 510-fold potency spread — a clean, same-assay rank test. If docking cannot rank that set, then no docking-based claim about a "better resmetirom" deserves belief, and the drug question for Pakistan becomes one of price and patient-finding, not of molecular optimisation.

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL-recorded THR-β agonists out-score resmetirom in the TR-β ligand-binding pocket (3IMY) by more than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and does the docking order match the same-assay EC50 order? Falsifier: (a) no compound beats resmetirom beyond noise, or (b) the docking order fails to track EC50 (Spearman rho near zero). Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the co-crystallised sobetirome defines the pocket centre on 3IMY, resmetirom and four comparators docked on the same structure with the same box and exhaustiveness — association only beyond that, since docking scores are not EC50, and the pocket was solved with sobetirome, not resmetirom.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-27: the MAESTRO-NASH phase 3 trial (Harrison et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:497–509, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2309000, NCT03900429); the resmetirom discovery paper (Kelly et al., J Med Chem 2014;57:3912–3923, PMID 24712661, doi:10.1021/jm4019299 — EC50 THR-β 0.21 μM, THR-α 3.74 μM, 28-fold selective); the resmetirom phase 2 trial (Harrison et al., Lancet 2019;394:2012–24); the TR-β structure with sobetirome (Bleicher et al., BMC Struct Biol 2008;8:1, PMID 18237438, doi:10.1186/1472-6807-8-1 — PDB 3IMY, 2.55 Å); the global prevalence meta-analyses (Riazi et al., Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022;7:851–861; Younossi et al., Hepatology 2023;77:1335–1347); the Pakistan prevalence meta-analysis (Scientific Reports 2024, doi:10.1038/s41598-024-70481-9) and the Ghani et al. 2017 Pakistani cohort (Pak J Med Sci 2017;33:121–126); the semaglutide MASH approval and ESSENCE results (FDA accelerated approval 15 August 2025; Rinella et al., Nat Med 2025, doi:10.1038/s41591-025-04130-7); the resmetirom cost-effectiveness model (Abdeen et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2026;28:8378–8389, doi:10.1111/dom.71020); the molecular-dynamics study of MGL-3196 binding (ACS Omega 2024;9:20957–20965, doi:10.1021/acsomega.4c00089); the resmetirom off-target nuclear-receptor study (Sci Rep 2026, doi:10.1038/s41598-026-37494-y); and the next-generation THR-β agonist ALG-055009 (Vandyck et al., J Med Chem 2024;67:14840–14851, doi:10.1021/acs.jmedchem.4c01029). The classical-canon sweep: Ibn Sina's Canon treats diseases of the liver at length (Book III) without a receptor concept; the principle carried is hifz al-nafs, with the honest note that no classical source addresses THR-β.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB P10828 (thyroid hormone receptor beta, Homo sapiens, 461 aa) → ChEMBL target CHEMBL1947 (Thyroid hormone receptor beta, SINGLE PROTEIN, human), whose only component is P10828 — verified by accession, not by text search. The sibling CHEMBL2111462 (Thyroid hormone receptor, PROTEIN COMPLEX, 2 components) was not used. CHEMBL1947 holds 878 EC50/IC50 activities. The docking set was deliberately taken from ONE assay — ChEMBL assay CHEMBL3266217, "agonist activity at recombinant His6-tagged THR-beta expressed in Escherichia coli", document CHEMBL3259553 (Kelly et al. 2014), 22 molecules — so that all five EC50s come from the same paper, the same assay and the same laboratory, and the rank test is a fair same-assay comparison. The potency spread in the assay is 18 → 9,170 nM, about 510-fold. The five compounds: resmetirom (reference; PubChem CID 15981237, C17H12Cl2N6O4, MW 435.2, verified live against PubChem); sobetirome (GC-1, the literature standard; CID 9862248, C20H24O4, MW 328.4, verified live); CHEMBL41036 (KB141 — identity verified by InChIKey; PubChem CID 9863447, C17H16Cl2O4); CHEMBL3261333 (resmetirom N-methyl analogue, no PubChem CID); and CHEMBL3261329 (a weak sulfoxide-anchored analogue, no PubChem CID). Earlier THR-β agonists sobetirome and eprotirome (KB2115) never reached approval; VK2809 (MB07811, a HepDirect prodrug) and ALG-055009 are the other clinical-stage THR-β agonists, but neither has a published EC50 in the Kelly assay, so neither enters the rank test — no potency is borrowed across assays.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Primary structure: 3IMY, the 2.55 Å X-ray structure of the human TR-β ligand-binding domain in complex with sobetirome (GC-1) (Bleicher et al., BMC Struct Biol 2008;8:1), grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised sobetirome (residue B72, chain A, 24 heavy atoms), verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center — the largest drug-like HETATM group in the file, ahead of three S-(dimethylarsenic)cysteine modified residues (9 atoms each), which are crystallisation artefacts, not the drug site. Two corrections from the structure search are recorded because they change what can be claimed: first, 1NAX does NOT hold GC-1, as is sometimes assumed — its ligand IH5 is KB141 (PubChem CID 9863447, C17H16Cl2O4), verified from the 1NAX PDB file; second, no resmetirom-bound TR-β structure has been deposited — an RCSB full-text search for "resmetirom" returns no entries, and the published molecular-dynamics study of MGL-3196 binding starts from 3GWS (T3-bound) and 1N46 (an MGL-3196-precursor-bound structure) and mutates the ligand in silico. Resmetirom was therefore docked into a sobetirome-shaped pocket, and the pocket-shape bias that follows is a stated limitation, not a hidden one. All five compounds were docked with the same box, centre and exhaustiveness.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all five compounds. All are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all five compounds (molecular weight, logP, H-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations). No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran a kNN read-across at low maximum similarity (0.28–0.51), which is not safety data; it is omitted rather than presented. The safety facts that matter — resmetirom's diarrhoea (27.0% at 80 mg, 33.4% at 100 mg vs 15.6% placebo) and nausea (22.0% and 18.9% vs 12.5%) from MAESTRO-NASH, with serious adverse events similar across arms (10.9% and 12.7% vs 11.5%) — are discussed in §4.2 from the trial, not from a read-across.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ EC50. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published EC50s and the published structure. The EC50s are assay-dependent: the same compound, resmetirom, is reported at EC50 0.21 μM in the Kelly et al. functional assay and at 8.8 ± 0.8 μM in a 2026 reporter-gene assay (Sci Rep 2026) — a 40-fold difference between laboratories — which is why this study takes all five potencies from one assay and why its rank test is conditional on that assay. Sobetirome is the self-dock control (3IMY was solved with it bound), so its score is the closest thing to a validated control in this set — and it still ranks third.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) EC50, Kelly assay (nM) PAINS
CHEMBL3261333 (resmetirom N-methyl analogue) −11.19 −11.19, −10.70, −7.50 40 Clean
Resmetirom (reference) −11.13 −11.13, −10.55, −9.70 210 Clean
Sobetirome (GC-1, comparator) −10.77 −10.77, −9.62, −8.87 18 Clean
CHEMBL41036 (KB141) −9.85 −9.85, −9.66, −9.06 23 Clean
CHEMBL3261329 (sulfoxide anchor) −9.84 −9.84, −9.81, −8.38 9,170 Clean

No compound beats resmetirom beyond noise. The best, CHEMBL3261333, leads by 0.06 kcal/mol — one-twentieth of Vina's noise floor — and its lead rests on two poses, its third being −7.50, a 3.69 kcal/mol drop that says the compound does not sit in the pocket consistently. Resmetirom itself is well converged (spread 1.43 kcal/mol across three poses, top two within 0.58). Sobetirome, the most potent compound in the set by 12-fold over resmetirom, scores 0.36 kcal/mol worse than resmetirom. The bottom of the table is the most informative part: KB141 (EC50 23 nM) and the sulfoxide analogue (EC50 9,170 nM) — a 400-fold potency difference between those two alone — score −9.85 and −9.84, a 0.01 kcal/mol difference. The docking cannot see the difference between a 23 nM agonist and a 9,170 nM one.

3.2 The rank test fails

Across the five compounds, Spearman rho between log10 EC50 and docking score is 0.2 (n = 5) — no rank correlation. The full 510-fold potency range (18 nM to 9,170 nM) is compressed into 0.93 kcal/mol of docking score between the most potent (sobetirome, −10.77) and the weakest (sulfoxide, −9.84) compounds — less than Vina's noise. The total spread across all five scores is 1.35 kcal/mol (−11.19 to −9.84), also inside noise. In other words, on this target, with this structure and this protocol, the docking score carries no information about potency. That is not a failed run: the run executed cleanly on all five compounds, the structure and centre are audited, the potencies are single-assay, and the method still fails. The failure is the finding.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published docking study of resmetirom on 3IMY was found in the searches for this paper, so there is no published docking table to compare against — which is itself notable, because resmetirom is the only approved drug in the class and its binding mode has been studied by molecular dynamics (ACS Omega 2024), not by a published Vina screen. The comparison that exists is against the published EC50 values from the single Kelly assay, and it is reported in §3.1 in full — and for once the honest answer is that the comparison fails. The one partial validation is the pose behaviour: resmetirom and sobetirome are the two best-converged compounds (their top two poses within 0.58 and 1.15 kcal/mol), which is what a working method should show for real binders — but convergence without ranking is not a result a drug programme can use.

3.4 The value problem: the drug that wins the pocket loses the value race

The docking table says resmetirom is not beaten. The clinic and the price say something else. In MAESTRO-NASH, resmetirom resolved MASH in 29.9% of patients at the 100 mg dose versus 9.7% on placebo — a 20.2-percentage-point absolute gain. In ESSENCE, semaglutide resolved MASH in 62.9% versus 34.3% on placebo — a 28.6-point gain, in a different trial, at 72 weeks rather than 52, so this is a cross-trial comparison and not a head-to-head claim. But the direction is consistent across both endpoints: semaglutide's fibrosis improvement (36.8% vs 22.4%) also exceeds resmetirom's (25.9% vs 14.2%). And the cost model is unambiguous: at US prices, resmetirom costs $59,269 per year against semaglutide's $16,188 in the Abdeen et al. model, with an ICER of $273,445 per QALY for resmetirom — the drug that was first to approval is the worst value of the three MASH drugs modelled, and it needs a 61% price cut to meet a $100,000/QALY threshold. For Pakistan, where the pooled MASLD prevalence is 29.8% and 58.5% among people with diabetes, the implication is stark: the binding question is settled (resmetirom is not beaten in the pocket), the value question is settled against it at current prices, and the unanswered question is who, in Pakistan, actually has F2–F3 fibrosis — because no Pakistani study reports MASH prevalence by liver biopsy or by fibrosis stage.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the question changes from "which agonist?" to "can docking rank agonists at all?"

The paper set out to find whether any ChEMBL THR-β agonist binds the receptor better than resmetirom. The answer is no — not beyond noise, not by 0.06 kcal/mol. But the more useful answer is the second one: the docking cannot rank this set at all. A 510-fold potency spread collapses into 0.93 kcal/mol, the most potent compound ranks third, and a 9,170 nM compound ties a 23 nM compound to within 0.01 kcal/mol. The question therefore changes: the finding is not "CHEMBL3261333 wins" but "Vina on 3IMY cannot distinguish a 23 nM agonist from a 9,170 nM one — and any future claim of a better resmetirom from docking alone should be treated as noise until an assay says otherwise". That is a useful negative, and it is the paper's actual contribution: it closes a door (docking-first optimisation of THR-β agonists) and names the experiment that decides what is behind the next one.

4.2 Why the negative result must not be over-read — or under-read

Four reasons not to over-read it. First, the pocket: 3IMY was solved with sobetirome, a smaller ligand (MW 328) than resmetirom (MW 435), so the pocket shape favours sobetirome-like ligands — yet sobetirome still ranked third, which cuts both ways: the bias should have helped it and did not. Second, the assay: all five EC50s come from one 2014 recombinant assay, and another laboratory reports resmetirom's EC50 40-fold higher (8.8 μM vs 0.21 μM), so the rank test is conditional on the Kelly assay being right. Third, the set: five compounds from one paper is a small rank test, and a larger set might show a weak correlation that five points cannot. Fourth, the method: Vina's scoring function is the thing that failed — a different protocol (Glide, MM-GBSA rescoring, free-energy perturbation) might recover the order, and this paper does not test those. And one reason not to under-read it: the failure is specific and quantified (rho 0.2, 510-fold → 0.93 kcal/mol), not a vague "docking is hard" — it is a measured null that the next THR-β docking paper must beat, and the falsifier for that is stated in §4.4.

The clinical caveat belongs here too. Resmetirom's benefit in MAESTRO-NASH is real but modest — 29.9% resolution, 25.9% fibrosis improvement — and its harms are mostly gastrointestinal (diarrhoea in a third of patients at 100 mg, nausea in nearly a fifth), with serious adverse events no more frequent than placebo. The drug's problem is not safety or efficacy; it is that a competitor resolves MASH in nearly twice as many patients in its own trial and costs roughly a quarter as much per year in the US model. A docking table that ranks resmetirom first has ranked binding, not benefit — and the compound that wins the pocket may still be the wrong drug to buy.

4.3 Mechanism

THR-β is a nuclear receptor: in the liver it binds thyroid hormone response elements as a heterodimer with RXR and, when agonist-bound, recruits coactivators that switch on the genes for mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty-acid β-oxidation, lipophagy and cholesterol catabolism, while suppressing de novo lipogenesis. In MASH, hepatic THR-β signalling is reduced, mitochondrial function falls, β-oxidation slows, and fat accumulates until fibrosis follows. Resmetirom restores the signal: it is 28-fold selective for THR-β over THR-α in the Kelly functional assay, so the liver gets the metabolic signal while the heart — where THR-α dominates — is largely spared the tachycardia and bone loss that made unselective thyroid hormone unusable as a chronic therapy; and it concentrates in the liver at roughly four times the serum level, adding tissue selectivity to receptor selectivity. The 3IMY structure (Bleicher et al. 2008) shows how the selectivity is built: sobetirome's binding mode in the TR-β pocket, and the pocket residues that differ between the α and β isoforms. The mechanistic question is therefore not "which compound binds tightest" but "which binding mode gives liver THR-β activation without THR-α activation" — and a docking score, which does not know which isoform it is scoring against, cannot answer that. Test for each link: (i) a recombinant THR-β/THR-α reporter assay measures EC50 and selectivity directly against the published values; (ii) a hepatocyte assay measures fatty-acid oxidation and lipogenesis genes, separating receptor activation from functional effect; (iii) a cardiomyocyte counterscreen measures the THR-α activity that decides whether an agonist is liver-safe at all.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring compound on 3IMY, CHEMBL3261333, has an EC50 within 3-fold of its published 40 nM in the same recombinant assay. Falsifier: EC50 more than 3-fold worse than published. (Status after this study: untested — and the docking gives no reason to prefer it over resmetirom, since its 0.06 kcal/mol lead is noise; the assay would be testing the published potency, not a docking prediction.)
  2. Sobetirome out-scores resmetirom on a resmetirom-shaped pocket, if one existed. Falsifier: it does not, which would show pocket bias — not the ligand — decides the ranking. (Status after this study: untestable today, because no resmetirom-bound TR-β structure has been deposited; the structure is the missing experiment.)
  3. No docking protocol (Vina, Glide, or MM-GBSA rescoring) recovers the EC50 order (rho > 0.7) on this five-compound set. Falsifier: a rescoring protocol does recover it, which would show the failure is Vina's scoring function, not the pocket. (Status after this study: the hypothesis stands for Vina — rho 0.2 — and the rescoring experiment is the cheapest way to kill or confirm it.)

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): recombinant THR-β and THR-α reporter assay for the five compounds, same plate, n = 3, with resmetirom's published EC50 (210 nM in the Kelly assay) as the control; readout EC50 and the β/α selectivity ratio. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): hepatocyte assay for the best two compounds from stage 1, measuring fatty-acid oxidation rate and lipogenesis-gene expression, with resmetirom as the control. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — EC50 better than resmetirom's and a hepatocyte effect — a cardiomyocyte counterscreen for that compound to measure the THR-α risk; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every margin in the table — the largest gap (resmetirom vs the sulfoxide analogue, 1.29 kcal/mol) is inside noise — and the only interpretable number is the compression itself: 510-fold of potency into 0.93 kcal/mol.
  2. No resmetirom-bound TR-β structure exists, so resmetirom was docked into a sobetirome-shaped pocket (3IMY, 2.55 Å, sobetirome MW 328 vs resmetirom MW 435); pocket bias favours sobetirome-like ligands, yet sobetirome still ranked third.
  3. All five EC50s come from one 2014 assay, and another laboratory reports resmetirom's EC50 40-fold higher (8.8 μM vs 0.21 μM), so the rank test is conditional on the Kelly assay; the docking is the only like-for-like comparison in this study, and it fails.
  4. Five compounds is a small rank test; a larger set might show a weak correlation that five points cannot, and other scoring protocols (Glide, MM-GBSA, free-energy perturbation) were not tested.
  5. The Tox21 read-across was run and is omitted (maximum similarity 0.28–0.51 — not safety data); the safety discussion rests on the MAESTRO-NASH trial, not on this computation.
  6. No published Pakistani study reports MASH prevalence by liver biopsy or fibrosis stage, so the clinical picture is global; the Pakistani numbers in this paper are burden numbers, not response numbers.
  7. The semaglutide comparison is cross-trial, not head-to-head (ESSENCE 72 weeks vs MAESTRO-NASH 52 weeks, different populations), and the cost figures are US prices — no Pakistan pricing or cost-effectiveness assessment exists.
  8. The classical-canon sweep found no THR-β-relevant text: the Canon describes liver disease without a receptor concept, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs, maslaha and 'adl as principles, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

No ChEMBL THR-β agonist out-scores resmetirom in the TR-β pocket beyond Vina's noise — the best, its own N-methyl analogue, leads by 0.06 kcal/mol — and the docking cannot rank the set at all: a 510-fold EC50 spread (18 nM to 9,170 nM) collapses into 0.93 kcal/mol, Spearman rho 0.2. The most potent compound, sobetirome, ranks third on the very structure solved with it bound. The next step is a recombinant THR-β reporter assay on the same five compounds, with a cardiomyocyte counterscreen for any compound that passes — the experiment that decides whether the best pocket binder is a drug, and whether docking deserves any role in the next THR-β programme. Until that assay exists, no docking-based claim of a better resmetirom should be believed.

7. Policy implications

Decision-makers: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations & Coordination, with the provincial health departments and the hepatology units that run liver clinics. Decision: whether to spend anything on a THR-β agonist programme or on resmetirom procurement, and what must exist first. Exact change: (1) do not fund a THR-β agonist discovery programme on docking evidence — this study shows docking cannot rank THR-β agonists, and resmetirom is not beaten in the pocket anyway; (2) fund instead a MASH fibrosis-staging survey using non-invasive scores (FIB-4, transient elastography) in the diabetic population, so Pakistan's own F2–F3 population is counted rather than assumed from the global 30% and the Pakistani 29.8% prevalence figures; (3) commission a Pakistan cost-effectiveness model comparing resmetirom against semaglutide at negotiated prices before any formulary decision — at US prices resmetirom costs $47,400 a year at launch with an ICER of $273,445 per QALY against semaglutide's $16,188 a year in the same model, and no Pakistan pricing exists at all. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the survey shows advanced fibrosis above 10% in diabetics and a local model shows an ICER below the local threshold at an achievable price, move to a procurement assessment; if the survey shows the burden is mostly simple steatosis, keep the money on diabetes control and weight management — do not proceed to any THR-β drug programme on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) joined to 'adl (justice, Qur'an 4:135) and maslaha (public interest): where the drug costs $47,400 a year, resolves MASH in 3 of 10 patients, and the patients who need it have not been identified, spending on the drug before spending on the test would put the benefit where the poor cannot reach it and violate all three. The evidence here is thin — docking only, and a negative at that — so the recommendation is "run the survey", not "do the policy".

A Tideglusib Analogue Out-Docks Berberine on Sortase A by 0.60 kcal/mol — but Vina Cannot Rank the Measured Potencies

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) caused more than 100,000 deaths attributable to antimicrobial resistance in 2019, yet no approved drug targets sortase A (SrtA), the transpeptidase that anchors virulence factors to the staphylococcal cell wall.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-27 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #124 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: sortase A; SrtA; Staphylococcus aureus; MRSA; anti-virulence; berberine; tideglusib; molecular docking; ChEMBL; Pakistan

Abstract

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) caused more than 100,000 deaths attributable to antimicrobial resistance in 2019, yet no approved drug targets sortase A (SrtA), the transpeptidase that anchors virulence factors to the staphylococcal cell wall. We asked whether any published SrtA inhibitor beats berberine — the best-known plant-derived SrtA inhibitor (IC50 ~26 µM) — on docking to the SrtA active site. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q9S446 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL5362, 54 bioactivities → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen) we docked berberine and four ChEMBL SrtA actives with AutoDock Vina on PDB 1T2O at the catalytic-triad centre. A tideglusib analogue, CHEMBL4646173, out-docked berberine by 0.60 kcal/mol (−7.36 vs −6.76 kcal/mol), but the docking ranking inverts the measured ranking: the most potent measured compound, CHEMBL5269466 (IC50 160 nM), docks only third (−6.67 kcal/mol), while berberine — the weakest measured compound at ~26 µM — docks second. Vina cannot rank this set. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head FRET assay of all five compounds on the same day: if CHEMBL5269466 does not confirm below 1 µM, or if CHEMBL4646173 does not confirm below 5 µM, the docking ranking is refuted and the lead list re-opens. Two pipeline failures were caught and corrected before any number was reported: the first automated run resolved the target to the wrong protein (SraP, not SrtA), and the second docked 22.1 Å from the catalytic site on a selenomethionine residue — both runs are preserved in the data files, and neither contributes a number to this paper.

1. Introduction

Resistance has outrun the antibiotic pipeline, and the arithmetic is now measured rather than warned about: bacterial antimicrobial resistance caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths directly attributable to resistance in 2019, with 4.95 million deaths associated with it, and meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus alone caused more than 100,000 attributable deaths — the single deadliest pathogen–drug combination in the analysis (Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, Lancet 2022;399:629–655). S. aureus was the second-leading pathogen for resistance-attributable deaths. Every new antibiotic that kills bacteria selects for resistance to itself; the field's response has been to look for targets that disarm rather than kill.

Sortase A is the cleanest version of that idea. SrtA is a 206-amino-acid membrane cysteine transpeptidase (UniProt Q9S446, gene srtA) that recognises the LPXTG sorting signal on surface proteins, cleaves after threonine, and anchors the protein to peptidoglycan. The anchored proteins are the pathogen's toolkit: adhesins that bind host tissue, immune-evasion proteins, and the machinery of biofilm formation. A bacterium without SrtA still grows — sortase is not essential and is not itself a virulence factor — but it cannot display its virulence factors, so it adheres poorly, forms weak biofilms, and is cleared more easily. That is the anti-virulence proposition: an inhibitor should attenuate infection without the bactericidal selection pressure that breeds resistance. It is also the proposition's weakness: because SrtA inhibition is not directly bactericidal, it is harder to screen (no MIC readout), harder to dose (attenuation, not killing), and — as of the most recent review — no approved drug targets SrtA (Hintzen et al., Chemistry 2024).

The published inhibitors fall into three generations. The first is the 2009 high-throughput screen of ~30,000 compounds (Suree et al., Bioorg Med Chem 2009;17:7174–7185), which produced pyridazinone and pyrazolethione analogues with sub-micromolar IC50 values — the most potent SrtA inhibitors reported, and still the benchmark. The second is the natural-product literature: berberine chloride, the isoquinoline alkaloid of Coptis chinensis, inhibits S. aureus sortase with an IC50 of 8.7 µg/mL (~26 µM), and the flavonoids myricetin, quercetin and curcumin inhibit in the 13–16 µg/mL range (Kim et al. 2004, and subsequent reviews). The third, most recent generation is repurposing and peptidomimetics: tideglusib analogues inhibit SrtA in the 0.9–12.6 µM range (J Med Chem 2020), and the peptidomimetic BzLPRDSar blocks biofilm formation in multidrug-resistant S. aureus (Microbiol Spectr 2026). A 2026 review in Open Biology concludes the target is promising but unproven in humans, with the open questions being selectivity across sortase homologues and whether attenuation translates into clinical benefit.

Falsifiable question. Does any published ChEMBL SrtA inhibitor beat berberine on docking to the SrtA active site, and does the docking ranking agree with the measured potencies? Falsifier: a head-to-head FRET assay in which the best docker fails to confirm below 5 µM, or the best measured compound (CHEMBL5269466, 160 nM) fails to confirm below 1 µM — either result refutes the ranking this paper reports. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking (berberine as the published reference, same structure, same grid, same protocol) — association only beyond that, since no experiment was run and docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-27: the global AMR burden analysis (Lancet 2022;399:629–655, doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(21)02724-0); the Suree et al. 2009 HTS and SAR paper (Bioorg Med Chem 2009;17:7174–7185, doi:10.1016/j.bmc.2009.08.067, PMID 19781950); the berberine sortase work (Kim et al. 2004, IC50 8.7 µg/mL); the tideglusib-analogue paper (J Med Chem 2020, doi:10.1021/acs.jmedchem.0c00803); the SrtA chemical-biology review (J Med Chem 2021, doi:10.1021/acs.jmedchem.1c00386); the complete-assessment review (Hintzen et al., Chemistry 2024, doi:10.1002/chem.202401103); the peptidomimetic study (Microbiol Spectr 2026, doi:10.1128/spectrum.02327-25, PMID 41773879); the 2026 Open Biology review (Open Biol 2026;16(9):250415, doi:10.1098/rsob.250415, PMID 42710897); and the SrtA structure paper (Zong et al., J Biol Chem 2004; PDB 1T2O). Measured IC50s for the four ChEMBL leads were retrieved live from the ChEMBL API on 2026-11-27 (target CHEMBL5362). The classical-canon sweep is in §4.3: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, Book II (materia medica), records barberry (Berberis spp., the berberine source) among medicinal plants, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of wound infection — neither describes sortase or an inhibitor, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and la darar, not on a classical source about this target.

2.2 Target identification — and the two failures that were caught

The pipeline resolves the target in two steps (UniProtKB text search, then ChEMBL target by accession), and both steps failed on the first attempt — which is why this section is written in full rather than summarised. Failure 1 (wrong protein). The query "Staphylococcus aureus sortase A" resolved to UniProt Q2FUW1 — SraP, a serine-rich adhesin for platelets, not sortase — and ChEMBL then returned CHEMBL2074, human maltase-glucoamylase. The 26 "leads" from that run were iminosugar glucosidase inhibitors (Tanimoto similarity to berberine 0.07–0.11), and the docking ran on PDB 4M00, which is the SraP ligand-binding region, not SrtA. Every number from that run is invalid for the SrtA question; the run is preserved as dock-HP-113-2026-11-27-WRONG-TARGET-SraP.json as the record of the failure, and contributes nothing to this paper. Correction. The target was re-specified by its reviewed accession: UniProt Q9S446 (gene srtA, 206 aa, Staphylococcus aureus). ChEMBL target by accession then returned CHEMBL5362, "Sortase A", single protein, S. aureus, with 54 bioactivities. Berberine was verified against PubChem (C20H18NO4+, MW 336.37, logP 3.1, 0 H-bond donors, 4 acceptors, TPSA 40.8 Å², 2 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean). The similarity screen against the 54 ChEMBL SrtA actives returned 25 leads; the top four by composite score were docked alongside berberine.

2.3 Molecular docking — and the grid-centre failure

Failure 2 (wrong grid centre). The re-run docked on PDB 1T2O (Zong et al. 2004, 2.3 Å, Se-SrtA C184A) — the correct protein — but the pipeline's centre picker landed on a selenomethionine residue. 1T2O contains no drug-like ligand, so the picker's fallback took the first HETATM group with ≥6 atoms, which is MSE141 of chain A. The grid centre (−22.31, −31.38, −5.00) is the exact centroid of MSE141 and sits 22.1 Å from the catalytic Ala184 Cα. The scores from that run (−8.57 to −7.11 kcal/mol) are systematically ~1 kcal/mol stronger than the corrected scores and measure binding near a methionine, not inhibition. They are reported here only as the failure record, in §3.3. Correction. The grid was re-centred on the catalytic triad: the centroid of all 26 atoms of His120, Ala184 (the Cys184→Ala mutation in this structure) and Arg197 in chain A, giving [−39.89, −18.59, −0.79]. All five ligands were re-docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 at that centre (box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses). The re-dock is the only docking result this paper reports. Two limits of the structure must be stated: 1T2O is the C184A mutant, so the catalytic thiol that covalent inhibitors would engage is absent; and it is an apo structure with no inhibitor bound, so the pocket is the substrate-binding site as defined by the triad, not a ligand-validated site.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to berberine and all four ChEMBL leads. All five are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide. (Berberine's isoquinoline core is a known assay-interference risk in some formats, but it carries no PAINS alert under the RDKit filter used here; the FRET validation in §4.5 includes the redox and detergent controls that would expose such an artefact.)

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking scores are not activity: Vina's noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, the structure is a C184A apo mutant, and no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. The ChEMBL IC50s are compared across records, not within one experiment — CHEMBL4646173, CHEMBL4637697 and CHEMBL4645185 each carry two ChEMBL records differing up to 10-fold (e.g. 1,200 vs 12,600 nM), which is assay-to-assay spread, not a measurement. Berberine's ~26 µM is converted from the published 8.7 µg/mL using MW 336.37. No experimental data were generated in this study.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (corrected centre)

CHEMBL5269466 CHEMBL5269466 −6.67 −6.67, −6.58, −6.52 160 nM 530.58 4.65 88.2 clean

All five docked into the same grid (1T2O, catalytic-triad centre [−39.89, −18.59, −0.79], box 22.5 Å). CHEMBL4646173 beats berberine by 0.60 kcal/mol — inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the "win" is not established by docking alone. The three tideglusib analogues are the J Med Chem 2020 series; CHEMBL5269466 is the most potent measured SrtA inhibitor in this set (160 nM, ChEMBL record from the J Med Chem 2021 review).

3.2 The ranking inversion — the real result

The docking ranking and the measured ranking disagree at every position that matters. By measurement: CHEMBL5269466 (160 nM) > CHEMBL4645185 (900 nM) > CHEMBL4646173 ≈ CHEMBL4637697 (1,200 nM) > berberine (~26,000 nM). By docking: CHEMBL4646173 (−7.36) > berberine (−6.76) > CHEMBL5269466 (−6.67) > CHEMBL4645185 (−6.35) > CHEMBL4637697 (−6.07). The best measured compound docks third; the worst measured compound docks second; the best docker is third by measurement. Berberine's −6.76 kcal/mol would imply low-micromolar binding, but its measured IC50 is ~26 µM — docking over-ranks it by roughly an order of magnitude. CHEMBL5269466's −6.67 kcal/mol would imply low-micromolar binding, but its measured IC50 is 160 nM — docking under-ranks it by roughly an order of magnitude. A paper that reported only the docking table would conclude that berberine is a near-lead and CHEMBL5269466 is unremarkable; the measured data say the opposite. This is the same failure mode this series found for HIV-1 protease inhibitors (Paper #121): rigid docking on an apo, mutated structure cannot rank congeneric and non-congeneric inhibitors together, and a docking "win" of 0.60 kcal/mol inside a ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band is not a win at all. The docking result is therefore reported as a negative: Vina cannot rank these SrtA inhibitors, and no lead is declared on docking.

3.3 The wrong-centre run, for the record

The uncorrected run (grid on MSE141, 22.1 Å from the catalytic site) returned CHEMBL5269466 −8.57, CHEMBL4646173 −8.10, berberine −7.94, CHEMBL4637697 −7.39, CHEMBL4645185 −7.11 kcal/mol — every score ~0.7–1.9 kcal/mol stronger than the corrected run, with a different rank order (CHEMBL5269466 first, not third). Had the centre error gone uncaught, this paper would have reported a false −8.57 kcal/mol "lead" and a false ranking. The correction cost one re-dock; the lesson is the standing one for this pipeline (AGENTS.md, 2026-11-11): never trust an auto-picked grid centre on a ligand-free structure — verify it against the catalytic residues, and report the check.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

Suree et al. (2009) docked their pyridazinone leads by induced-fit docking into the solution structure of the covalent SrtA–LPAT complex and reported poses consistent with sub-micromolar IC50s — but with a different method (induced-fit, not rigid Vina), a different structure, and no Vina scores to compare against, so no numerical comparison is possible. No published Vina scores exist for berberine or the tideglusib analogues on 1T2O. This paper's docking table therefore stands alone as a Vina ranking, and §3.2 is the statement that the ranking fails against measurement.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was "what beats berberine?" and the honest answer is that docking cannot answer it for this target. The measured data already answer it: CHEMBL5269466 at 160 nM is ~160-fold more potent than berberine, and the tideglusib analogues at 0.9–1.2 µM are ~20-fold more potent. The field does not need a better docker; it needs the measured compounds tested in the assay that matters — biofilm inhibition in live S. aureus — because SrtA inhibition is attenuation, and attenuation is only meaningful if the bacterium actually fails to adhere and form biofilm. The reframe is therefore from "find a better score" to "test the best measured compound in the functional assay": CHEMBL5269466 has never, to our knowledge, been reported in a biofilm assay, and that is the gap, not the docking table.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three corrections guard the headline. First, the 0.60 kcal/mol margin for CHEMBL4646173 over berberine is inside Vina noise — it is not a win. Second, the docking ranking is inverted against measurement, so even a larger margin would need assay confirmation. Third, the measured IC50s themselves carry up to 10-fold record-to-record spread (CHEMBL4646173: 1,200 vs 12,600 nM), so the "1,200 nM" figures are order-of-magnitude, not precise. What is solid is the direction: three tideglusib analogues and one 160 nM compound are all far more potent than berberine by measurement, and all five are PAINS-clean and drug-like (MW 300–531, 0–1 Lipinski violations). The memorable number is the distance: 22.1 Å — the grid was centred on the wrong residue, and the uncorrected scores were inflated by ~1 kcal/mol. A pipeline that does not check its grid centre will manufacture leads.

4.3 Mechanism — and the classical canon

SrtA cleaves the LPXTG sorting signal between threonine and glycine and transfers the cleaved protein to peptidoglycan via its catalytic Cys184–His120–Arg197 triad; an inhibitor that occupies that pocket blocks anchoring of every LPXTG protein at once — adhesins, immune-evasion factors, biofilm proteins — which is why one target can attenuate many virulence functions. Test for each link: (i) the FRET assay with the Abz-LPETG–Dnp substrate measures catalytic inhibition directly, against the published IC50s; (ii) a fibrinogen/fibronectin adhesion assay measures whether anchoring actually fails in live bacteria; (iii) a crystal-violet biofilm assay measures the functional consequence, against the BzLPRDSar peptidomimetic as the positive control. The classical canon knows the disease, not the enzyme: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025), Book II, records barberry (Berberis spp., the berberine source) among medicinal plants, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records clinical observation of wound infection — but neither describes sortase, so the principle carried forward is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, defined by Al-Ghazali in Al-Mustasfa and systematised by Al-Shatibi in Al-Muwafaqat) joined to la darar (no harm) and stewardship (khilafah): a drug that disarms rather than kills imposes less selection pressure for resistance, which is harm-avoidance extended to the next patient, not just this one. The Canon was not re-read in full for this paper; the berberine–SrtA link is modern (Kim et al. 2004), not a classical claim.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL5269466 inhibits S. aureus SrtA with an IC50 below 1 µM in the FRET assay on the same day as berberine. Falsifier: IC50 above 1 µM, which would refute the ChEMBL record and remove the lead.
  2. CHEMBL4646173 inhibits SrtA with an IC50 below 5 µM in the same assay. Falsifier: IC50 above 5 µM, which would refute its docking "win" over berberine.
  3. CHEMBL5269466 at its IC50 reduces S. aureus biofilm formation by at least 50% in a crystal-violet assay without reducing bacterial growth (OD600 unchanged). Falsifier: no biofilm reduction at the IC50, or growth inhibition at the same concentration — either would show the compound is not a functional anti-virulence lead.
  4. Berberine's FRET IC50 reproduces within 3-fold of the published ~26 µM under the same conditions. Falsifier: an IC50 below 5 µM, which would suggest the published value was an artefact of assay conditions.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): FRET assay — recombinant SrtA catalytic domain (residues 60–206), Abz-LPETG–Dnp substrate, all five compounds on one plate, n=3, with berberine as the reference and the Suree pyridazinone series as the positive control if obtainable; redox and detergent controls to expose aggregation artefacts; readout IC50. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): adhesion assay (fibrinogen binding) and crystal-violet biofilm assay for the two best compounds from Stage 1, with growth curves (OD600) to confirm the effect is anti-virulence, not antibacterial; readout percentage biofilm reduction at the IC50. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): if a compound passes stages 1–2 — IC50 below 1 µM and ≥50% biofilm reduction without growth inhibition — a Galleria mellonella infection model against the ML346 precedent; if none passes, publish the negative result with the ChEMBL table as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed before stages 1–2 pass.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only, on a C184A apo mutant structure with no inhibitor bound; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol and the docking ranking is inverted against measurement, so no lead is declared on docking.
  2. The measured IC50s are retrieved across ChEMBL records, not within one experiment; three compounds carry duplicate records differing up to 10-fold.
  3. Berberine's ~26 µM is converted from a published 8.7 µg/mL; the original assay used a different SrtA construct than the ChEMBL records for the other compounds.
  4. No experimental data were generated in this study; all potencies are retrieved, not measured.
  5. The Suree et al. pyridazinone series — the most potent published SrtA inhibitors (sub-micromolar) — were not docked here, because the pipeline's lead set is drawn from ChEMBL SrtA actives and those compounds' ChEMBL records were not in the top-ranked set; the comparison against the strongest incumbent is therefore incomplete and is the first item in the validation plan.
  6. No Pakistani MRSA isolate data exist for SrtA: no local study reports SrtA sequence variation or sortase-inhibitor susceptibility in Pakistani MRSA, so the policy section recommends measurement, not a drug decision.
  7. The classical-canon sweep did not re-read the Canon or Kitab al-Hawi in full; the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and la darar as principles, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections.

6. Conclusion

A tideglusib analogue, CHEMBL4646173, out-docks berberine on sortase A by 0.60 kcal/mol (−7.36 vs −6.76 kcal/mol), but the margin is inside Vina noise and the docking ranking inverts the measured ranking — the 160 nM lead CHEMBL5269466 docks third, and berberine, the weakest measured compound at ~26 µM, docks second. Vina cannot rank these sortase A inhibitors, and no lead is declared on docking. The measured data already point to the better compounds, and the next step is the cheap, decisive test: one head-to-head FRET assay plus one biofilm assay, not a bigger docking screen.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, with the National Institute of Health and university microbiology departments as the technical arms. Decision: whether to spend anything on an anti-virulence programme for MRSA, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund a docking screen or import a sortase inhibitor on a docking score — this paper shows a docking ranking can invert the measured ranking, and a grid-centre error of 22.1 Å inflated scores by ~1 kcal/mol; instead, fund one measurement first: a head-to-head FRET assay of the four ChEMBL compounds plus berberine against the SrtA catalytic domain, run in a Pakistani university lab, with the biofilm assay as the second gate. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the assay confirms CHEMBL5269466 below 1 µM with ≥50% biofilm reduction and no growth inhibition, move to a lead-optimisation assessment for that compound; if the assay refutes the ChEMBL potencies, drop the list and re-open the Suree pyridazinone series — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to la darar and stewardship (khilafah): where a measurement can distinguish a drug that disarms the pathogen from one that merely scores well, running the measurement is the obligation; prescribing on a docking score would risk the next patient's resistance. The evidence here is thin — retrieved potencies and a failed docking ranking — so the recommendation is "run the assay", not "do the policy".
