Docking Cannot Distinguish the Only Known GlgE Inhibitor from Its Own Substrate — a 0.59 kcal/mol Spread on the Emulated *M. tuberculosis* Site

GlgE is the maltosyltransferase of the trehalose-to-α-glucan pathway of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Its inactivation kills the bacterium by self-poisoning: maltose-1-phosphate (M1P) accumulates to toxic levels through a self-amplifying feedback loop (Kalscheuer et al., 2010).

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI research assistant) Date: 27 November 2026 | Paper #128 (Health track; topic HP-118)

Keywords: GlgE; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; maltose-1-phosphate; α-maltose-C-phosphonate; molecular docking; drug resistance; tuberculosis; Pakistan

Abstract

GlgE is the maltosyltransferase of the trehalose-to-α-glucan pathway of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Its inactivation kills the bacterium by self-poisoning: maltose-1-phosphate (M1P) accumulates to toxic levels through a self-amplifying feedback loop (Kalscheuer et al., 2010). No GlgE inhibitor has reached the clinic, and only one measured inhibitor potency exists in the published literature — α-maltose-C-phosphonate (MCP), IC50 230 ± 24 µM (Veleti et al., 2014). We asked whether AutoDock Vina docking at the GlgE M1P site can rank MCP above its own substrate and above an untested oxocarbenium mimic. ChEMBL holds a GlgE target entry (CHEMBL3112377) with zero bioactivities, so no measured series exists to learn from. No Mtb GlgE structure could be docked at a validated site: the Mtb maltose complex (PDB 4U33, 3.29 Å) carries six maltose copies with no identifiable donor-site centroid. We therefore docked on the inhibitor-bound surrogate used by the structural literature itself — Streptomyces coelicolor GlgEI-V279S, engineered to emulate the Mtb M1P site (PDB 4U31, 1.85 Å; Lindenberger et al., 2015) — at the MCP centroid. The oxocarbenium mimic DDGIM scored best (−7.72 kcal/mol), MCP second (−7.56), and the substrate M1P third (−7.13): a total spread of 0.59 kcal/mol, roughly one-third of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Docking therefore cannot rank the only measured GlgE inhibitor against its substrate or an untested mimic, and all three ligands are non-permeable (TPSA 172–236 Å², logP ≈ −5, Veber fail). The falsifiable claim is that any future GlgE docking study that reports a ranking from a spread under 1 kcal/mol without measured potencies is reporting noise. The field's bottleneck is not computation but chemistry: one measured potency in fifteen years, and no whole-cell data. Pakistan — ~670,000 TB cases in 2024, 6.3% of the global burden — should fund MCP optimisation as a national drug-discovery line with a hard go/no-go on a sub-10 µM analogue.

Introduction

Tuberculosis killed an estimated 1.23 million people in 2024, with 10.7 million falling ill (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025). Pakistan recorded an estimated 670,000 cases in 2024 — 6.3% of the global burden, the fifth-highest national burden — and roughly 12,000 new multidrug-/rifampicin-resistant (MDR/RR-TB) cases emerge each year; resistance is present in ~2.3% of new cases and ~4.6% of previously treated cases, and nearly 40% of resistant cases are already pre-XDR. New drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid, pretomanid) have improved MDR-TB outcomes, but every one of them targets a mechanism the bacterium has already learned to evade, and none is a GlgE inhibitor. A target with a genuinely new killing mechanism is therefore worth pursuing — and GlgE is the most mechanistically distinctive validated target in Mtb that no drug touches.

The GlgE pathway converts trehalose to cytosolic α-glucan in four steps: trehalose is isomerised to maltose by TreS, phosphorylated to maltose-1-phosphate (M1P) by the maltokinase Pep2, transferred by GlgE (Rv1327c; UniProt P9WQ17; 701 amino acids; glycoside hydrolase family GH13_3, double-displacement retaining mechanism), and branched by GlgB. Kalscheuer et al. (2010) showed that inactivating GlgE kills Mtb rapidly in vitro and in mice, not by starving the cell of glucan but by self-poisoning: M1P accumulates, and a self-amplifying feedback loop upregulates the trehalose-forming enzymes, making more of the poison. The same study found a synthetic-lethal interaction with the glucosyltransferase Rv3032, so a GlgE inhibitor combined with an Rv3032 inhibitor would be, in the authors' words, extremely potent. GlgE has no human orthologue, so on-target human toxicity is in principle avoidable.

Fifteen years after that validation, the medicinal chemistry of GlgE is almost empty. The only published inhibitor with a measured potency is MCP, a non-hydrolysable C-phosphonate mimic of M1P, IC50 230 ± 24 µM against Mtb GlgE in a coupled phosphate-release assay (Veleti et al., 2014). A second first-generation compound, DDGIM (2,5-dideoxy-3-O-α-D-glucopyranosyl-2,5-imino-D-mannitol), an oxocarbenium-transition-state mimic, has a crystal structure but no published potency (Lindenberger et al., 2015). No ChEMBL bioactivity exists for GlgE at all. This paper asks a narrow, falsifiable question: can Vina docking at the GlgE M1P site rank MCP above its substrate M1P and the untested mimic DDGIM by more than the method's own noise? If it cannot, then the many docking-only GlgE papers in the literature are ranking noise, and the field should stop screening and start synthesising.

Methods

Target and structures. Mtb GlgE is UniProt P9WQ17 (GLGE_MYCTU, Rv1327c, 701 aa). The LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → Vina) was run with --target P9WQ17 --ref maltose-1-phosphate: it confirmed the accession but found ChEMBL target CHEMBL3112377 with zero bioactivities and no PDB entry for the accession, so no docking was performed by the pipeline. We then verified structures manually against RCSB. PDB 4U33 ("Structure of Mtb GlgE bound to maltose", 3.29 Å) exists, but its asymmetric unit contains six maltose copies across six chains with no identifiable donor-site centroid, so it was not docked. PDB 4U3C (Mtb GlgE with maltohexaose, 3.98 Å) was likewise not used. Docking was performed on PDB 4U31, "Sco GlgEI-V279S in Complex with maltose-C-phosphonate" (1.85 Å), the structure in which the V279S variant was engineered specifically to emulate the Mtb GlgE M1P binding site (Lindenberger et al., 2015). The grid centre was the MCP residue (GPM, chain C) centroid, [24.84, −31.26, 281.44], box 22.5 Å. This is a surrogate-site docking, not Mtb-native docking, and every score below carries that caveat.

Ligands. Three compounds: (i) M1P, the natural substrate (PubChem CID 167489, isomeric SMILES, full stereochemistry); (ii) MCP, the only known inhibitor (SMILES extracted from the 4U31 crystal structure — GPM chain C residue 1 plus the adjoining GLC residue — via RDKit, with the phosphonate valence corrected to CP(=O)(O)O; formula C13H25O13P); (iii) DDGIM (SMILES extracted from PDB 4U2Y, RZM chain A residue 701, via RDKit; formula C12H23NO9). Descriptors and PAINS alerts were computed with RDKit. Docking used AutoDock Vina (exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses), the same protocol as the other papers in this series.

Literature. Targeted searches of PubMed, RCSB, PubChem and the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 (Pakistan figures via its press coverage). No data, PMIDs, DOIs or citations were invented; every number traces to a source named here or to a computation in the accompanying JSON (hidden_files/dock-HP-118-2026-11-27-redock.json).

Results

There is no measured GlgE series to dock against. ChEMBL target CHEMBL3112377 (GlgE) holds zero bioactivities, and the pipeline's similarity screen therefore returned only the query compound. The entire published, measured GlgE inhibitor record is a single compound, MCP, at 230 ± 24 µM. No whole-cell (MIC) data for any GlgE inhibitor was found.

Docking on the emulated site cannot rank the three ligands. Vina best scores (top-3 poses in parentheses): DDGIM −7.72 (−7.72, −7.50, −6.81), MCP −7.56 (−7.56, −7.29, −6.47), M1P −7.13 (−7.13, −6.94, −6.73) kcal/mol. The total spread is 0.59 kcal/mol; MCP beats its own substrate by only 0.43 kcal/mol, and the untested mimic DDGIM beats the only measured inhibitor by 0.16 kcal/mol. All three spreads sit far inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the pose-to-pose spread within a single ligand (up to 1.09 kcal/mol for MCP) exceeds the spread between ligands. Docking therefore reports no ranking at all: the measured inhibitor, its substrate, and an untested mimic are indistinguishable.

All three ligands are non-permeable. M1P: MW 422.28, logP −5.28, HBD 9, HBA 12, TPSA 236.06 Å², 2 Lipinski violations, Veber fail. MCP: MW 420.30, logP −5.17, HBD 9, HBA 11, TPSA 226.83 Å², 2 violations, Veber fail. DDGIM: MW 325.31, logP −5.14, HBD 8, HBA 10, TPSA 172.10 Å², 1 violation, Veber fail. All three are PAINS-clean. These are sugar phosphates and a sugar mimic: highly polar, charged at physiological pH, and — as the M1P pathway itself implies — they cannot cross the mycobacterial cell envelope without a transporter or a prodrug strategy. MCP's 230 µM enzymatic potency is therefore a starting point, not a lead: it is 230-fold weaker than a 1 µM lead threshold, before permeability is even considered.

The structural literature is rich; the chemistry is not. Experimental GlgE structures exist for both species: Mtb GlgE with maltose (4U33, 3.29 Å) and with maltohexaose (4U3C, 3.98 Å); Sco GlgEI-V279S with MCP (4U31, 1.85 Å) and with the DDGIM azasugar (4U2Y, 2.48 Å); Sco GlgE apo (3ZSS, 1.8 Å) and with M1P bound (4CN1, 2.55 Å) (Lindenberger et al., 2015). A homology model of Mtb GlgE with three binding cavities (primary plus two secondary sites) was published before any Mtb structure existed (Sengupta et al., 2014). The binding site is therefore well characterised — the gap is that only one compound has ever been measured against it.

Discussion

The honest reading of this paper is a negative result with a constructive edge. The negative: Vina cannot rank GlgE ligands at the emulated Mtb site — the only measured inhibitor scores within noise of its own substrate, and an untested mimic scores best. Any study that reports a GlgE "lead" from a docking spread under 1 kcal/mol without measured potency is reporting the scoring function's noise, and the literature contains several such studies (including virtual screens against the pre-2015 homology model). The constructive edge: the experiment that would settle the question is cheap and defined — synthesise MCP analogues, measure IC50s against recombinant Mtb GlgE (the Veleti coupled assay), and only then dock. One measured series of ten compounds would do more for this target than another hundred docking runs.

Three facts should shape that chemistry. First, the self-poisoning mechanism means a GlgE inhibitor does not need to starve the cell; it needs only to block the enzyme long enough for M1P to reach toxic levels, and the feedback loop then amplifies the damage — so partial, reversible inhibition may be cidal, unlike most antibiotic targets where partial inhibition is merely static. Second, the escape route is known in advance: loss of GlgE function can be suppressed by upstream mutations that abolish M1P synthesis, so a GlgE inhibitor used alone invites resistance, and combination with an Rv3032 inhibitor (the synthetic-lethal partner) or with a standard regimen should be planned from the start, not after resistance appears. Third, permeability is the real barrier: every ligand in this study fails Veber, and the mycobacterial envelope is the hardest in bacteriology. MCP optimisation must therefore be prodrug-first (e.g., masked phosphonate) or transporter-targeted, or the programme will repeat the fate of many polar antibacterials — potent in the tube, inert in the cell.

For Pakistan, the stakes are concrete. With ~670,000 cases a year and ~12,000 new MDR/RR-TB cases, a new-mechanism drug that kills by self-poisoning — and that no current resistance mechanism touches — is worth a national chemistry effort. The cost of that effort is small beside the cost of the disease: one medicinal-chemistry group, one recombinant-enzyme assay, and a defined go/no-go.

One memorable number: 230 µM — the best measured GlgE inhibitor in the world is 230 times weaker than a 1 µM lead, and it is the only measured GlgE inhibitor in the world.

Limitations

  1. Surrogate structure. All docking is on Sco GlgEI-V279S (4U31), not Mtb GlgE. The V279S variant was designed to emulate the Mtb M1P site, but residue-level differences remain, and scores are site-emulation, not Mtb-native. The Mtb structure 4U33 could not be docked at a validated centroid.
  2. No measured series. Only one published IC50 exists (MCP, 230 µM). With a single point, no docking–potency correlation can be computed; the ranking claim is a null result, not a validated failure.
  3. Vina noise. The 0.59 kcal/mol spread is far below the method's ±1–2 kcal/mol error. No pose was inspected against the crystal MCP pose (no RMSD self-dock validation was possible for M1P/DDGIM, which have no Mtb co-crystal).
  4. SMILES provenance. MCP and DDGIM SMILES were extracted from crystal coordinates via RDKit; the MCP phosphonate valence was corrected by hand from [PH](O)(O)O to CP(=O)(O)O. Connectivity is correct; protonation at pH 7.4 was left to the standard prep.
  5. No whole-cell data. No MIC, no macrophage-infection, and no animal data exists for any GlgE inhibitor. Enzymatic IC50 is not antibacterial activity.
  6. Resistance escape. Upstream mutations abolishing M1P synthesis can suppress GlgE loss; monotherapy would select for them.
  7. No laboratory verification. This is a computational and literature study only. Nothing here is a drug, a dose, or a treatment recommendation.

Conclusion

GlgE remains one of the best-validated and least-exploited TB targets: genetically essential, cidal by self-poisoning, synthetically lethal with Rv3032, and without a human orthologue. But fifteen years after validation, the field has one measured inhibitor (MCP, 230 µM), no whole-cell data, and — as shown here — a docking method that cannot distinguish that inhibitor from its own substrate. The next step is not more screening. It is synthesis: MCP analogues, measured IC50s, a prodrug strategy for the mycobacterial envelope, and a hard go/no-go. Until a sub-10 µM analogue with whole-cell activity exists, GlgE is a validated target with no lead — and that is a precise, actionable statement of where the field stands.

§7 Policy implications

  • Decision-maker: Pakistan National TB Control Programme (NTP) and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP), with the Ministry of National Health Services.
  • Decision: Fund a dedicated GlgE medicinal-chemistry work package — one chemistry group plus the recombinant-enzyme assay — inside the NTP research budget, rather than funding another docking-only screen.
  • Exact change: Allocate ring-fenced funding for MCP analogue synthesis and IC50 measurement, with a published go/no-go: a sub-10 µM analogue with whole-cell (MIC) activity by 2028, or the line is stopped and the funds reallocated to scaling up bedaquiline/pretomanid regimens.
  • Reverse-if-Z: If no analogue reaches sub-10 µM with whole-cell activity, or if upstream escape mutations arise at high frequency in the first resistance screen, stop the GlgE line and reallocate — the target is validated but undruggable on the evidence, and the money is better spent on regimens that work today.
  • Islamic principle: Hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) and la darar wa la dirar (no harm, no reciprocated harm): a drug that turns the pathogen's own metabolism into its poison uses the enemy's strength against it without harming the host, which has no GlgE — the precise form of proportionate, life-preserving stewardship that the Islamic canon on antimicrobial stewardship requires (literature-map seed #11, AMR). Stewardship also forbids spending public funds on unmeasured claims: the go/no-go above is the administrative form of that principle.

Docking Cannot Distinguish Sinefungin from Its Own Cofactor on Dengue NS5 MTase — a 0.14 kcal/mol Spread Against a 60-Fold Potency Gap

Dengue cases in Pakistan rose every year from 21,016 in 2023 to 33,394 laboratory-confirmed cases in 2025, and there is still no approved dengue antiviral.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-27 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #127 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: dengue; NS5; methyltransferase; sinefungin; S-adenosylmethionine; cap methylation; molecular docking; Pakistan

Abstract

Dengue cases in Pakistan rose every year from 21,016 in 2023 to 33,394 laboratory-confirmed cases in 2025, and there is still no approved dengue antiviral. The NS5 methyltransferase (MTase) — the N-terminal domain that builds the viral RNA cap — is the most druggable dengue target, and sinefungin, a natural S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) analogue, is its best-known inhibitor (IC50 30–41 nM). We asked whether docking can distinguish sinefungin from the molecules it must beat: the reaction product S-adenosyl-homocysteine (SAH) and the natural cofactor SAM itself. Using the LeadForge pipeline for target verification and a corrected re-dock with AutoDock Vina on PDB 1L9K, the dengue virus type 2 (DENV2) MTase domain in complex with SAH, sinefungin docked at −7.95 kcal/mol, SAH at −7.84 and SAM at −7.81 — a spread of 0.14 kcal/mol, against measured differences of 6-fold in binding (Kd 136 vs 826 nM) and 12–60-fold in inhibition. Docking cannot see the difference between the drug and its own cofactor. All three molecules also fail the Veber permeability rule (TPSA 183–209 Å²), which matches the literature record: sinefungin is non-cell-permeable and has made no progress as a drug. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head MTase assay plus a human-MTase counter-screen: if a sinefungin analogue does not beat SAH by at least 10-fold on both N7 and 2′-O activity while sparing a human MTase, the SAM-site strategy is refuted for this scaffold. Two pipeline failures were caught and corrected: the automated run retrieved NS3-protease inhibitors as "MTase leads" and docked them on 7K93 — a DENV2 NS1–antibody structure, not NS5 — and neither run contributes a number to this paper.

1. Introduction

Dengue is the fastest-growing mosquito-borne disease in Pakistan's recent surveillance, and the numbers are measured, not projected: the National Institute of Health (NIH) recorded 21,016 cases in 2023, 24,182 in 2024 and 33,394 laboratory-confirmed cases in 2025, after 48,906 cases and 183 deaths in 2021 and 41,746 cases and 62 deaths in 2022. DENV-2 has been the predominant serotype throughout 2021–2025 (78.4% of confirmed infections), with DENV-1 second (21.4%) and transmission peaking in the post-monsoon months of September and October (Umair et al., PLoS One 2026). Globally there were 13 million cases and 10,000 fatalities in 2024. There is no approved direct-acting dengue antiviral: care is supportive, case management aims to keep the fatality rate below 1%, and the vaccines carry serostatus restrictions. A drug is the missing piece, and NS5 is the target most often named for it.

NS5 is a two-domain protein: a C-terminal RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and an N-terminal methyltransferase (residues 1–296) that builds the type 1 RNA cap, m7GpppNm, in two steps — N7 methylation of the guanine, then 2′-O methylation of the first transcribed nucleotide. The N7 step precedes the 2′-O step and runs at 2.4-fold higher catalytic efficiency, and the two methylations are processive, without enzyme–RNA dissociation. The cap protects the viral RNA from host exonucleases and is required for translation, so blocking it should stop the virus — and the MTase domain is conserved across all four serotypes, which is why one inhibitor could in principle cover DENV-1 to DENV-4. The domain has two pockets: the SAM-binding site, where the methyl donor binds, and a GTP-binding site implicated in guanylyltransferase activity.

The literature's inhibitors cluster at the SAM site, and the best of them is sinefungin, a natural SAM analogue in which a carbon and an amine replace the methylated sulfur. Against long viral RNA substrates it inhibits N7 methylation at 30 nM and 2′-O at 41 nM, roughly 60- and 12-fold more potent than SAH (Chung et al., Antiviral Res 2010); its binding affinity for the free DENV MTase is 136 nM against SAM's 826 nM (Brecher et al. 2014). But sinefungin is a broad-spectrum MTase inhibitor — the SAM site is conserved in human methyltransferases too — and it is non-cell-permeable, so it has made no progress as a drug. The most advanced SAH-derived analogue, Compound 10 (Lim et al., J Biol Chem 2011), reaches 0.82 µM (N7) and 0.17 µM (2′-O) with hydrophobic extensions from the adenine N6 position aimed at selectivity. The GTP pocket has its own inhibitors (BG-323, 7.5 µM; aurintricarboxylic acid, 2 µM), and the nucleoside route has produced clinical disappointments: NITD-008 failed on toxicity, balapiravir failed for lack of efficacy in phase II.

Falsifiable question. Can docking on the DENV2 MTase SAM site distinguish sinefungin from SAH and SAM, by more than the method's own noise? Falsifier: a head-to-head MTase assay in which sinefungin does not beat SAH by at least 10-fold on both activities, or a human-MTase counter-screen in which it inhibits a human MTase within 10-fold of the viral one — either result refutes the SAM-site strategy for this scaffold. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking (SAH re-docked into its own co-crystal structure, same grid, same protocol) — association only beyond that, since no experiment was run and docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-27: the Pakistan dengue burden series (NIH surveillance via Dawn, March 2026 advisory: 21,016 in 2023, 24,182 in 2024, 33,394 in 2025); the serotype surveillance study (Umair et al., PLoS One 2026; DENV-2 78.4%); the Pakistan burden review (Int J Surg 2025, doi:10.1097/MS9.0000000000004072; 13 million cases, 10,000 deaths globally in 2024); the MTase kinetics papers (Chung et al., Antiviral Res 2010 — sinefungin 30/41 nM, SAH 1.77/0.49 µM; Egloff et al., J Gen Virol 2010 — 2′-O characterisation, SAH 0.34 µM, sinefungin 0.63 µM on short substrates; Lim et al., J Biol Chem 2011 — Compound 10, 0.82/0.17 µM; PDB 3P97); the sinefungin binding study (Brecher et al. 2014 — Kd 136 vs 826 nM); the NS5 drug-discovery review (sinefungin, SAH, GMP, BG-323, aurintricarboxylic acid, 4-HPR, ivermectin, NITD-008, balapiravir table); and the MTase structure paper (Egloff et al., EMBO J 2002; PDB 1L9K). The classical-canon sweep is in §4.3: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses epidemic fevers, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Judari wa al-Hasba (c. 910) first distinguished smallpox from measles — neither describes dengue or a methyltransferase, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and maslaha (public interest), not on a classical source about this target.

2.2 Target identification — and the two failures that were caught

Failure 1 (wrong target level). Dengue NS5 has no single-protein ChEMBL target: ChEMBL holds only organism-level dengue entries. The pipeline resolved the DENV2 polyprotein (UniProt P29990, 3,391 aa) and its ChEMBL target CHEMBL5980, "Genome polyprotein", whose 36 bioactivities mix NS3-protease, whole-virus and other assays. The top "lead", CHEMBL4862353, is an NS3-protease inhibitor (IC50 290 nM in a fluorogenic NS3 assay) — not an MTase inhibitor — and the other leads' similarities to sinefungin are 0.10–0.13, i.e. unrelated. Failure 2 (wrong protein). The pipeline then docked on PDB 7K93 — DENV2 NS1 in complex with a neutralising antibody scFv (Science 2021), 2.89 Å — not NS5 at all. The scores from that run (leads −6.82 to −6.33, sinefungin −5.76 kcal/mol) are invalid for the MTase question; they are preserved in dock-HP-145-2026-11-27.json as the failure record and contribute nothing. Correction. The docking was re-run by hand on the verified MTase structure with the three SAM-site ligands that carry published MTase data — sinefungin, SAH and SAM — and no pipeline lead was carried over, because none of them is an MTase inhibitor.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking ran on PDB 1L9K (Egloff et al., EMBO J 2002): the DENV2 NS5 MTase domain in complex with SAH, 2.4 Å. The grid centre [15.28, −42.04, 0.78] is the centroid of the co-crystallised SAH (26 atoms, verified against the PDB file), computed by dock._ligand_center. Sinefungin (SMILES from the pipeline's PubChem verification), SAH (PubChem CID 439155) and SAM (PubChem CID 34755) were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 at that centre (box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses). Two limits must be stated: 1L9K is DENV2 only, so serotype coverage is inferred from MTase conservation, not tested; and SAM's sulfonium charge produced RDKit UFFTYPER warnings during ligand preparation, so the SAM score carries a preparation caveat that the other two do not. The GTP pocket was not docked: GMP and BG-323 bind there, not at the SAM site, and docking them into the SAM grid would be the same category of error as Failure 2.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to sinefungin, SAH and SAM. All three are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking scores are not activity: Vina's noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, the structure is a single SAH-bound conformation, and no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. The measured IC50s come from different assay formats (long viral RNA vs short capped oligonucleotides) and differ accordingly — sinefungin reads 30–41 nM on long substrates and 0.63 µM on short ones — so cross-study comparisons are order-of-magnitude. No experimental data were generated in this study.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (corrected structure)

Compound Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured MTase potency MW (Da) logP TPSA (Å²) Veber PAINS
Sinefungin (reference) −7.95 −7.95, −7.84, −7.67 IC50 30 nM (N7), 41 nM (2′-O); Kd 136 nM 381.39 −2.06 208.7 fail clean
SAH (product) −7.84 −7.84, −7.82, −7.51 IC50 1.77 µM (N7), 0.49 µM (2′-O); 0.34 µM (short substrate) 384.42 −1.44 182.6 fail clean
SAM (cofactor) −7.81 −7.81, −7.71, −7.53 Kd 826 nM 398.45 −3.26 185.5 fail clean

All three docked into the same grid (1L9K, SAH centre [15.28, −42.04, 0.78], box 22.5 Å). SAH's self-dock (−7.84 kcal/mol, poses within 0.33 kcal/mol) is the protocol validation: the co-crystallised ligand re-docks tightly into its own site. Sinefungin beats SAM by 0.14 kcal/mol and SAH by 0.11 kcal/mol — both far inside Vina noise.

3.2 The 0.14 kcal/mol spread against a 60-fold potency gap

By measurement, sinefungin is 6-fold tighter than SAM (Kd 136 vs 826 nM) and 12–60-fold more potent than SAH as an inhibitor (30–41 nM vs 0.49–1.77 µM). By docking, the three are indistinguishable: −7.95, −7.84, −7.81 kcal/mol, a spread of 0.14 kcal/mol — one-fourteenth of Vina's noise band. The reason is visible in the chemistry: all three share the adenosine core and differ only at the sulfur — SAM's methylated sulfonium, SAH's thioether, sinefungin's carbon-amine — and rigid docking scores the shared adenosine anchor, not the substituent that determines potency. A paper that reported only this docking table would conclude that sinefungin, SAH and SAM are equivalent binders; the measured data say they differ by up to 60-fold. Docking cannot rank SAM-site ligands on this target, and no lead is declared on docking. The same failure mode appeared in Paper #126 (Wee1), where the whole top five fit inside one molecule's reproducibility gap — but here the gap is sharper, because the comparison includes the natural cofactor itself.

3.3 The permeability problem is the real result

All three molecules fail the Veber rule: TPSA 183–209 Å² (limit 140) with 7 rotatable bonds each, and logP from −1.44 to −3.26. These are not drugs; they are reagents. The literature agrees: sinefungin and SAH are both recorded as "no progress, compound non-cell permeable". The most advanced SAH analogue, Compound 10, improves potency (0.82 µM N7, 0.17 µM 2′-O) but the review records no permeability data for it either. The docking table therefore confirms the literature's verdict rather than challenging it: the SAM site gives potency, and the same polarity that binds the site prevents the molecule from reaching it inside a cell.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina scores exist for sinefungin, SAH or SAM on 1L9K. The 3P97 structure (DENV3 MTase + SAM, 1.7 Å, Lim et al. 2011) is the closest published comparator, but its paper reports inhibitor design, not Vina scores, so no numerical comparison is possible. This paper's docking table stands alone, and §3.2 is the statement of what it cannot support.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was "can docking distinguish sinefungin from its cofactor?" and the answer is no — which reframes the whole target. The SAM site is a solved problem in potency (30 nM exists) and an unsolved problem in selectivity and permeability: the site is conserved in human methyltransferases, so sinefungin inhibits them too, and the molecules that bind it are too polar to enter cells. The field's own literature already moved past the SAM site for exactly these reasons: the GTP/cap-binding pocket offers a flavivirus-specific site (BG-323, aurintricarboxylic acid), and N6-extended SAH analogues aim for selectivity through a hydrophobic extension the human enzymes do not accommodate. The reframe is therefore from "find a better SAM-site binder" to "leave the SAM site": the next lead should be judged on a human-MTase counter-screen and on cell permeability first, and on MTase potency second — the reverse of the usual order.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three corrections guard the headline. First, the 0.14 kcal/mol spread is one-fourteenth of Vina noise — it is not a ranking. Second, the measured 60-fold gap is itself assay-dependent (sinefungin reads 30 nM on long RNA and 630 nM on short substrates), so the exact fold is uncertain even though the direction is not. Third, the SAM score carries a ligand-preparation caveat (UFFTYPER charge warnings on the sulfonium), so even the −7.81 figure is softer than the other two. What is solid is the validation: SAH re-docks into its own site at −7.84 kcal/mol, so the protocol reproduces a known binder — and the permeability verdict (TPSA 183–209 Å²) is a computed property, not a score, so it does not depend on Vina at all. The memorable number is 0.14 kcal/mol — the docking spread between a 30 nM drug lead and the cofactor it must beat — because it is the number that shows docking is blind on this target.

4.3 Mechanism — and the classical canon

NS5 MTase transfers a methyl group from SAM to the viral RNA cap: N7 methylation first, then 2′-O, processively, without releasing the RNA. Sinefungin occupies the SAM site with an amine mimicking SAM's charged sulfur, but cannot donate a methyl group, so it blocks both methylations. Test for each link: (i) a biochemical MTase assay with long capped RNA measures N7 and 2′-O inhibition separately, against sinefungin's 30/41 nM; (ii) a human-MTase counter-screen (e.g. human RNMT) measures selectivity, against the requirement of at least 10-fold viral preference; (iii) a DENV replicon assay measures antiviral activity in cells, against the permeability prediction that sinefungin fails it. The classical canon knows the disease pattern, not the virus: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses epidemic fevers, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Judari wa al-Hasba (c. 910) first distinguished smallpox from measles by clinical observation — but neither describes dengue or a methyltransferase, so the principle carried forward is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) joined to maslaha (public interest): for a disease whose proven interventions are vector control and case management, the public-interest obligation is the surveillance and the mosquito control that already work, not a drug that is a decade away.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Sinefungin inhibits DENV2 MTase N7 activity with an IC50 below 100 nM on long capped RNA in a head-to-head assay with SAH. Falsifier: IC50 above 100 nM, which would refute the published 30 nM figure under these conditions.
  2. A sinefungin analogue with an N6 hydrophobic extension inhibits DENV2 MTase below 100 nM while sparing human RNMT by at least 10-fold. Falsifier: no selectivity at 10-fold, which would show the extension does not buy what the literature claims.
  3. Sinefungin shows no antiviral activity below 10 µM in a DENV replicon assay, consistent with its non-permeability. Falsifier: activity below 1 µM, which would reopen the SAM-site strategy.
  4. A GTP-pocket inhibitor (BG-323 class) inhibits DENV2 MTase 2′-O activity without inhibiting human RNMT at the same concentration. Falsifier: equal inhibition of the human enzyme, which would show the GTP pocket is no more selective than the SAM site.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): biochemical MTase assay — recombinant DENV2 MTase domain, long capped RNA substrate, sinefungin, SAH, SAM and Compound 10 on one plate, N7 and 2′-O readouts separately, n=3; readout IC50 for each activity. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): human-MTase counter-screen (human RNMT) for the same compounds, plus a Caco-2 or PAMPA permeability assay; readout selectivity ratio and permeability. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): if a compound passes stages 1–2 — MTase IC50 below 100 nM, selectivity above 10-fold, and measurable permeability — a DENV replicon assay in cells; if none passes, publish the negative result with the MTase table as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed before stages 1–2 pass.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only, on a single SAH-bound DENV2 structure; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol and the three-ligand spread is 0.14 kcal/mol, so no ranking is claimed.
  2. The measured IC50s come from different assay formats (long RNA vs short oligonucleotides) and differ up to 20-fold for the same compound; cross-study comparisons are order-of-magnitude.
  3. No GTP-pocket docking was run: the second pocket's inhibitors were not tested by this paper's computation.
  4. Serotype coverage is inferred from MTase conservation, not tested: the docking is DENV2 only, and DENV-1/3/4 MTase structures were not compared.
  5. Compound 10, the literature's most advanced SAH analogue, was not docked (no verified SMILES retrieved in this run) and is discussed from the literature only.
  6. No experimental data were generated in this study; all potencies are retrieved, not measured.
  7. No Pakistani study reports NS5 sequence variation in local DENV-2 isolates, so the policy section recommends surveillance, not a drug decision.
  8. The classical-canon sweep did not re-read the Canon or Kitab al-Hawi in full; the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and maslaha as principles, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections.

6. Conclusion

Sinefungin, SAH and SAM dock within 0.14 kcal/mol of each other on the dengue NS5 methyltransferase (−7.95, −7.84, −7.81 kcal/mol), while their measured potencies differ by up to 60-fold — docking cannot distinguish the drug lead from its own cofactor on this target. All three fail the Veber permeability rule, matching the literature record that sinefungin is non-cell-permeable and has made no progress. The next step is not a better SAM-site binder but a selectivity and permeability test: one MTase assay plus one human-MTase counter-screen, not a bigger docking screen.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Ministry of National Health Services and the National Institute of Health (NIH), Islamabad, with provincial dengue control programmes as the implementing arms. Decision: whether to spend anything on a dengue drug programme, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund a docking screen or a SAM-site lead programme — this paper shows docking cannot rank SAM-site ligands, and the literature shows the site's inhibitors are non-permeable and non-selective; instead, fund two things that already work: (i) DENV serotype surveillance through the NIH, so the DENV-2 dominance (78.4%) and any serotype switch are tracked in real time; and (ii) vector control and standardised case management, which is the intervention that keeps the fatality rate below 1%. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a GTP-pocket or N6-extended lead confirms below 100 nM with 10-fold selectivity over a human MTase and measurable permeability, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that lead; if surveillance shows a serotype switch away from DENV-2, re-open the target question on the new dominant serotype's sequence — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to maslaha: where the proven intervention is surveillance and mosquito control, spending on it is the obligation, and spending on a drug a decade away while cases rise every year would violate it. The evidence here is thin — retrieved potencies and a null docking result — so the recommendation is "run the surveillance and the counter-screen", not "do the policy".

A 0.20 nM Kinome Hit Out-Docks Imatinib on c-KIT by 1.65 kcal/mol — but Docking Shuffles Four Near-Identical Binders

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) are driven by activating KIT mutations in 75–80% of cases, and imatinib turned this chemo-refractory sarcoma into a chronic disease — until secondary mutations (exon 13/14 gatekeeper, exon 17 activation-loop) defeat it.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-27 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #125 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: c-KIT; GIST; imatinib; tyrosine kinase inhibitor; drug resistance; D816V; molecular docking; ChEMBL; Pakistan

Abstract

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) are driven by activating KIT mutations in 75–80% of cases, and imatinib turned this chemo-refractory sarcoma into a chronic disease — until secondary mutations (exon 13/14 gatekeeper, exon 17 activation-loop) defeat it. We asked whether any published KIT inhibitor beats imatinib on docking to the c-KIT kinase domain. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P10721 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL1936, 24 bioactivities → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen) we docked imatinib and four sub-nanomolar ChEMBL KIT binders with AutoDock Vina on PDB 1T46, the c-Kit–imatinib complex. CHEMBL273187 out-docked imatinib by 1.65 kcal/mol (−12.04 vs −10.39 kcal/mol) and is ~500-fold more potent by measurement (Ki 0.20 nM vs imatinib IC50 100 nM against wild-type KIT). But docking shuffles the four leads: the most potent measured binder, CHEMBL404366 (Ki 0.16 nM), docks worst (−9.91 kcal/mol), so docking confirms the direction (leads ≫ imatinib) and fails on the order. Docking on wild-type 1T46 also says nothing about the real clinical gap — the D816V activation-loop mutant, against which imatinib's IC50 rises 100-fold to 10,000 nM. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head kinase assay of CHEMBL273187 against wild-type KIT and the D816V mutant: if it does not confirm below 5 nM on wild-type, or if it loses more than 10-fold on D816V, the lead is refuted. Two pipeline failures were caught and corrected: the first run resolved the target to a pig protein and a human glucosidase, and the second docked on 2VIF — a SOCS6 SH2 domain, not the KIT kinase — and neither run contributes a number to this paper.

1. Introduction

GIST is the most common mesenchymal neoplasm of the gastrointestinal tract (0.4–2 cases per 100,000 people per year), arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal and driven by activating mutations in KIT (75–80%, mostly exon 11) or PDGFRA (5–10%). Before imatinib it was a chemo-refractory sarcoma; after imatinib it became the proof of concept that a small-molecule kinase inhibitor could turn a sarcoma into a chronic disease. Adjuvant imatinib 400 mg daily for 3 years (SSG XVIII trial) improves recurrence-free and overall survival in high-risk disease, and metastatic disease reaches ~50–60% 5-year overall survival on imatinib. The drug is a type-II inhibitor: it binds the DFG-out, inactive conformation of the kinase, which the juxtamembrane domain normally stabilises — and exon 11 mutations, the commonest driver (60–70% of GIST), release that autoinhibitory clamp, which is why they respond best (70–80% response).

Resistance is a ladder, and the tumour climbs it one secondary mutation at a time. Two structural neighbourhoods dominate: the ATP-binding pocket (exon 13/14 — V654A, T670I), which sterically blocks imatinib while leaving the kinase functional, and the activation loop (exon 17/18 — D816, D820, N822K), which stabilises the active DFG-in conformation that a type-II inhibitor cannot bind at all. The salvage ladder was built to cover these slices: sunitinib (second line, ATP-pocket mutants), regorafenib (third line, activation-loop mutants), ripretinib (fourth line, switch-control, broad coverage, INVICTUS trial), and avapritinib (a type-I inhibitor, the only drug effective against PDGFRA D842V, which is intrinsically imatinib-resistant from day one). Exon 9 mutations need double-dose imatinib (800 mg/day). Mutation testing is therefore mandatory before treatment (NCCN 2022): the genotype decides the drug and the dose.

The gap this paper attacks is narrow and honest. The ChEMBL KIT record holds sub-nanomolar binders from kinome profiling that have never been tested against the resistance mutants. If one of them binds wild-type KIT far better than imatinib and — crucially — retains binding on D816V, it would be a candidate for the exon-17 gap that currently has no type-II answer. Docking on the wild-type structure can only answer the first half of that question.

Falsifiable question. Does any published ChEMBL KIT binder beat imatinib on docking to the wild-type c-KIT kinase domain, and does the docking ranking agree with the measured potencies? Falsifier: a head-to-head kinase assay in which CHEMBL273187 fails to confirm below 5 nM on wild-type KIT, or loses more than 10-fold on the D816V mutant — either result refutes the lead. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking (imatinib re-docked into its own co-crystal structure, same grid, same protocol) — association only beyond that, since no experiment was run and docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-27: the GIST mutation-directed therapy guideline (KIT 75–80%, exon 11 60–70%, SSG XVIII, INVICTUS, NCCN 2022 sequencing mandate); the KIT resistance-ladder review (V654A/T670I, D816/D820/N822K, sunitinib/regorafenib/ripretinib/avapritinib lines); the 1T46 structure paper (Mol et al., J Biol Chem 2004;279:31655–31663, doi:10.1074/jbc.M403319200, PMID 15123710); the V654A resistance paper (Mol Cancer Ther 2005;4:2008–2015, ~2.25 kcal/mol destabilisation); and the SOCS6 structure paper (J Biol Chem 2011; PDB 2VIF). Measured Ki/IC50 values for imatinib and the four leads were retrieved live from the ChEMBL API on 2026-11-27 (target CHEMBL1936). The classical-canon sweep is in §4.3: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses swellings and tumours (waram) and their surgical treatment at length, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of tumours — neither describes a kinase or an inhibitor, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and adl (justice in access), not on a classical source about this target.

2.2 Target identification — and the two failures that were caught

Failure 1 (wrong species, wrong target). The query "KIT proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase" resolved to UniProt Q2HWD6 (Sus scrofa, pig), and ChEMBL then returned CHEMBL2074, human maltase-glucoamylase — the same fallback mis-resolution this pipeline produced for sortase A in Paper #124. The 26 "leads" from that run were glucosidase inhibitors, and no PDB was found. Every number from that run is invalid; it is preserved as dock-HP-129-2026-11-27-WRONG-TARGET-pig.json and contributes nothing. Correction. The target was re-specified by its reviewed accession: UniProt P10721 (KIT_HUMAN, gene KIT, 976 aa). ChEMBL target by accession then returned CHEMBL1936, "Mast/stem cell growth factor receptor Kit", single protein, Homo sapiens, with 24 bioactivities. Imatinib was verified against PubChem (C29H31N7O, MW 493.62, logP 4.59, 2 H-bond donors, 7 acceptors, TPSA 86.28 Å², 7 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean). The similarity screen returned 24 leads; the top-ranked set was docked.

2.3 Molecular docking — and the wrong-structure failure

Failure 2 (wrong protein). The re-run docked on PDB 2VIF, which the pipeline picked because the entry contains a c-KIT phosphopeptide and therefore maps to P10721. But 2VIF is the crystal structure of the SOCS6 SH2 domain in complex with that peptide (J Biol Chem 2011, 1.45 Å) — the kinase domain is not in the structure at all. The scores from that run (imatinib −8.45, leads −7.11 to −6.72 kcal/mol) measure binding to SOCS6, not KIT inhibition, and are reported here only as the failure record. Correction. The docking was re-run on PDB 1T46 (Mol et al. 2004): the c-Kit kinase domain in complex with imatinib (STI-571), 1.6 Å for the complex, with the co-crystallised imatinib as the grid anchor. The centre is the STI ligand centroid [26.18, 26.06, 40.36] from dock._ligand_center (37 atoms, verified against the PDB file). All five ligands were re-docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 at that centre (box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses). One lead could not be docked at all: CHEMBL5416410 (rank 2, similarity 0.272) has a two-fragment salt SMILES, and the RDKit ligand preparation refuses multi-fragment molecules; it was replaced by rank-6 CHEMBL272938 so the set stays at five ligands, and the exclusion is stated here, not hidden. Two limits must be stated: 1T46 is the DFG-out inactive conformation, so it can only test type-II binding; and it is wild-type KIT, so it cannot test the D816V or V654A mutants — the resistance question needs mutant structures or assays, not this docking.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to imatinib and all four docked leads. All five are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking scores are not activity: Vina's noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, the structure is a single wild-type inactive conformation, and no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. The four leads' Ki values (0.16–0.32 nM) come from one kinome-profiling panel (ChEMBL document CHEMBL1201862) and are not head-to-head with imatinib's IC50 values, which come from several different assays (100–400 nM wild-type across records; Kd 830 nM). A Ki and an IC50 are not the same measurement, so the "~500-fold" comparison is order-of-magnitude, not precise. No experimental data were generated in this study.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (corrected structure)

Compound ChEMBL ID Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured KIT potency MW (Da) logP TPSA (Å²) PAINS

CHEMBL272938 CHEMBL272938 −10.78 −10.78, −10.32, −9.43 Ki 0.32 nM 358.41 4.16 108.7 clean
Imatinib (reference) CHEMBL941 −10.39 −10.39, −10.38, −10.35 IC50 100 nM (WT); 10,000 nM (D816V) 493.62 4.59 86.3 clean
CHEMBL402846 CHEMBL402846 −9.96 −9.96, −9.88, −9.76 Ki 0.32 nM 390.42 4.31 97.9 clean
CHEMBL404366 CHEMBL404366 −9.91 −9.91, −9.67, −9.58 Ki 0.16 nM 392.85 4.51 97.9 clean

All five docked into the same grid (1T46, STI centre [26.18, 26.06, 40.36], box 22.5 Å). CHEMBL273187 beats imatinib by 1.65 kcal/mol — at the edge of Vina's noise band, so the margin alone is not proof, but it is the largest margin in this paper's set and it points the same way as the measurement. Imatinib's self-dock (−10.39 kcal/mol, poses within 0.04 kcal/mol) is the protocol validation: the co-crystallised ligand re-docks tightly into its own site.

3.2 The direction is right; the order is shuffled

By measurement, the four leads are all sub-nanomolar (Ki 0.16–0.32 nM) against imatinib's 100 nM wild-type IC50 — a ~300–600-fold potency gap, measured in the same kinome panel for the leads. Docking agrees on the big claim: the best lead beats imatinib by 1.65 kcal/mol, and three of the four leads are within 0.4 kcal/mol of imatinib or better. But docking shuffles the order among the leads: the most potent measured binder, CHEMBL404366 (Ki 0.16 nM), docks worst (−9.91 kcal/mol), while CHEMBL273187 (Ki 0.20 nM) docks best (−12.04 kcal/mol). The measured spread among the leads is 2-fold; the docking spread is 2.1 kcal/mol — Vina exaggerates differences between near-identical binders and cannot order them. The honest reading is therefore two-part: (i) the leads are genuinely far more potent than imatinib by measurement, and docking does not contradict that; (ii) no ranking among the four leads is supported by this docking, and CHEMBL273187's first place is a hypothesis, not a finding.

3.3 The resistance gap docking cannot touch

The clinically important number in the table is not a docking score: imatinib's IC50 rises from 100 nM on wild-type KIT to 10,000 nM on the D816V mutant (ChEMBL, same assay series) — a 100-fold loss, and 5,000 nM in the Ba/F3 D816V cell line against 400 nM wild-type. D816V stabilises the DFG-in active conformation, which a type-II inhibitor cannot bind at all; no docking on the DFG-out 1T46 structure can test whether CHEMBL273187 or any lead overcomes it. The V654A gatekeeper mutation likewise abrogates imatinib binding (Mol Cancer Ther 2005; estimated ~2.25 kcal/mol destabilisation). A lead that only beats imatinib on wild-type KIT is a better imatinib, not a resistance answer — and a better imatinib is not what GIST needs, since imatinib already works on wild-type disease. The value of CHEMBL273187 therefore depends entirely on the mutant assay proposed in §4.5.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

Mol et al. (2004) solved the structure but reported no docking scores. No published Vina scores exist for these four ChEMBL compounds on 1T46, and the compounds have no common names — they are kinome-panel screening hits, not developed drugs. This paper's docking table therefore stands alone as a Vina ranking, and §3.2 is the statement of what it can and cannot support.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was "what beats imatinib?" and the measured data answer it more strongly than the docking: four sub-nanomolar binders against a 100 nM drug. But the reframe is that beating imatinib on wild-type KIT is the wrong contest. Imatinib already controls wild-type and exon-11 disease; the patients who die are the ones whose tumours acquire exon 13/14 or exon 17 mutations, and the salvage ladder (sunitinib, regorafenib, ripretinib, avapritinib) exists precisely because imatinib cannot cover them. A new lead matters only if it covers a resistance slice — D816V above all, since it defeats every type-II inhibitor by conformation. The paper's contribution is therefore not "CHEMBL273187 beats imatinib" but the testable claim in §4.4: a sub-nanomolar binder with a different chemotype (MW 376, no imatinib scaffold) that should be assayed against D816V first, not last.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three corrections guard the headline. First, the 1.65 kcal/mol margin sits at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — it is suggestive, not established. Second, the docking order among the four leads contradicts their measured order, so the table cannot rank them. Third, the "~500-fold" potency gap compares a Ki (kinome panel) with an IC50 (several assays, 100–400 nM) — the gap is real in direction and order-of-magnitude, but the exact fold is assay-dependent, and imatinib's own Kd is 830 nM in one record. What is solid is the validation: imatinib re-docks into its own site at −10.39 kcal/mol with near-identical poses, so the protocol can reproduce a known binder — and the leads' sub-nanomolar Ki values are measured, not computed. The memorable number is the resistance gap: 100-fold — imatinib's IC50 from 100 nM to 10,000 nM on D816V — because that number, not any docking score, is the reason a new KIT inhibitor is needed.

4.3 Mechanism — and the classical canon

KIT is a type-III receptor tyrosine kinase: stem-cell factor binding dimerises the receptor, the juxtamembrane region is displaced, and the kinase phosphorylates PI3K, RAS–MAPK and STAT pathways that drive survival and proliferation. Imatinib occupies the ATP pocket of the DFG-out inactive conformation, displacing the juxtamembrane domain's autoinhibitory grip. Test for each link: (i) a biochemical kinase assay measures inhibition of wild-type and D816V KIT directly, against imatinib's 100 nM / 10,000 nM; (ii) a Ba/F3 cell-viability assay measures the same in cells, against imatinib's 400 nM / 5,000 nM; (iii) a GIST cell-line panel (exon-11 vs exon-17 genotypes) measures whether the compound kills the resistant genotype, against ripretinib as the positive control. The classical canon knows the disease, not the kinase: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses swellings and tumours (waram) and their surgical treatment, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of tumours — but neither describes a receptor or an inhibitor, so the principle carried forward is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) joined to adl (justice): the drug exists, but the test that decides who gets which drug — KIT/PDGFRA sequencing — is the access gap, and justice in this case means the test, not the tablet.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL273187 inhibits wild-type KIT with an IC50 below 5 nM in a biochemical kinase assay on the same day as imatinib. Falsifier: IC50 above 5 nM, which would refute the docking "win".
  2. CHEMBL273187 inhibits the D816V mutant with an IC50 within 10-fold of its wild-type value. Falsifier: a loss greater than 10-fold, which would show it is another type-II binder defeated by the same conformation as imatinib.
  3. CHEMBL404366 — the most potent measured binder (Ki 0.16 nM) and the worst docker — inhibits wild-type KIT below 5 nM. Falsifier: IC50 above 5 nM, which would suggest the kinome-panel Ki does not reproduce.
  4. In Ba/F3 cells, CHEMBL273187 kills D816V-expressing cells at a concentration within 10-fold of its wild-type value. Falsifier: no killing below 1 µM, which would end the resistance claim regardless of the biochemical result.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): biochemical kinase assay — wild-type KIT and D816V KIT, CHEMBL273187, CHEMBL404366 and imatinib on one plate, n=3, with the published 100 nM / 10,000 nM imatinib values as the controls; readout IC50 for both genotypes. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): Ba/F3 cell-viability assay for the same three compounds on wild-type and D816V lines, with ripretinib as the positive control for the mutant; readout GI50. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): if a compound passes stages 1–2 — wild-type IC50 below 5 nM and D816V loss under 10-fold — a GIST cell-line panel (exon-11 vs exon-17 genotypes) and a selectivity screen against the closest kinases (PDGFRA, FLT3, ABL); if none passes, publish the negative result with the ChEMBL table as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed before stages 1–2 pass.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only, on a single wild-type DFG-out structure; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol and the docking order among the leads contradicts their measured order, so no ranking among the leads is claimed.
  2. The leads' Ki values come from one kinome-profiling panel and are compared with imatinib IC50s from several different assays; the "~500-fold" gap is order-of-magnitude, not a head-to-head measurement.
  3. No mutant structure or mutant docking was run: the D816V question — the actual clinical gap — is entirely untested by this paper's computation.
  4. The four leads have no common names, no published pharmacology beyond the kinome panel, and no selectivity data reported here; CHEMBL5416410, the second-ranked lead, could not be docked at all (two-fragment salt SMILES).
  5. No experimental data were generated in this study; all potencies are retrieved, not measured.
  6. No Pakistani GIST data exist: no national registry, no published incidence, and no local study of KIT mutation frequencies or imatinib outcomes in Pakistan, so the policy section recommends testing infrastructure, not a drug decision.
  7. The classical-canon sweep did not re-read the Canon or Kitab al-Hawi in full; the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and adl as principles, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections.

6. Conclusion

CHEMBL273187 out-docks imatinib on wild-type c-KIT by 1.65 kcal/mol (−12.04 vs −10.39 kcal/mol) and is ~500-fold more potent by measurement (Ki 0.20 nM vs imatinib IC50 100 nM), with imatinib's tight self-dock validating the protocol. But docking shuffles the four sub-nanomolar leads — the most potent measured binder docks worst — so no ranking among them is claimed, and docking on wild-type 1T46 cannot test the D816V resistance mutant, where imatinib loses 100-fold. The next step is the cheap, decisive test: one kinase assay on wild-type and D816V KIT, not a bigger docking screen.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, with the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital and the Aga Khan University Hospital oncology departments as the technical arms. Decision: whether to spend anything on GIST care beyond generic imatinib, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not spend on a new KIT inhibitor or a docking programme — instead, make KIT/PDGFRA sequencing available at public oncology centres before the first imatinib prescription, so exon-9 patients receive 800 mg/day instead of 400 mg, PDGFRA D842V patients receive avapritinib instead of futile imatinib, and exon-17 patients are routed to the salvage ladder instead of failing imatinib for months. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a Pakistani GIST registry shows fewer than 5% non-exon-11 genotypes, narrow the sequencing programme to referral centres; if it shows a high D842V or exon-17 share, expand sequencing to all tertiary oncology units and negotiate avapritinib access — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to adl (justice): the test that decides the drug is the access gap, and a patient who receives the wrong dose for the wrong genotype because the test was unavailable has been denied both. The evidence here is thin — retrieved potencies and a wild-type docking table — so the recommendation is "build the testing", not "do the policy".

Direct SCD1 Inhibitors Out-Score Aramchol by 3.87 kcal/mol in the SCD1 Tunnel — the Day's Only Docking Win Beyond Noise, and the Skin-Eye Risk Still Decides Whether It Matters

Stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) makes the monounsaturated fatty acids that fill a fatty liver, and aramchol — the most clinically advanced SCD1 modulator — works by downregulating SCD1 expression, not by binding its active site, while direct active-site inhibitors were abandoned for skin and eye toxicity.
