AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-26 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #122 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: SCD1; aramchol; A939572; MASH; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; fatty liver; Pakistan

Abstract

Stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) makes the monounsaturated fatty acids that fill a fatty liver, and aramchol — the most clinically advanced SCD1 modulator — works by downregulating SCD1 expression, not by binding its active site, while direct active-site inhibitors were abandoned for skin and eye toxicity. Five compounds — aramchol, three ChEMBL direct inhibitors (CHEMBL594289, CHEMBL595247, CHEMBL594084) and the literature standard A939572 — were docked with standardised AutoDock Vina into the substrate tunnel of the 3.25 Å human SCD1 structure 4ZYO, same box and exhaustiveness. The direct inhibitors out-scored aramchol by 2.79–3.87 kcal/mol: CHEMBL594289 best at −11.02 kcal/mol against aramchol's −7.15, a lead beyond Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and the only such lead in today's five papers. The docking order also matches the published IC50 order exactly (0.068, 0.48, 0.56, 37 nM), the only paper today where the method validates against experiment. The win still does not make the direct inhibitors better drugs: complete SCD1 inhibition causes sebaceous gland atrophy and dry eye, and aramchol's partial inhibition is precisely what avoids it. Pose consistency was tight for A939572 and aramchol (three-pose spreads 0.26 and 0.48 kcal/mol) and reasonable for the two leaders, whose top two poses converge; CHEMBL594084's third place rests on a single pose, its third being a +4.96 kcal/mol clash, so its honest score is about −8.8, below A939572. The falsifier is a recombinant SCD1 desaturation assay: if CHEMBL594289's IC50 is not better than A939572's 37 nM on the same plate, the docking lead is a tunnel artefact.

1. Introduction

Stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1, UniProt O00767, 359 aa) catalyses the rate-limiting step in monounsaturated fatty acid synthesis — inserting a cis double bond at the Δ9 position of palmitoyl- and stearoyl-CoA — and its product, oleate, is the substrate for the triglycerides that fill a fatty liver. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease affects 13% of people in Africa and up to 32% in Latin America and the Middle East, and in Pakistan NAFLD frequency is reported at 15–29% (highest above age 40), inside a chronic liver disease burden of 2–29%. Aramchol (3β-arachidyl-amido cholanoic acid), a fatty acid–bile acid conjugate, is the most clinically advanced SCD1 modulator: it partially inhibits hepatic SCD1 (70–83% inhibition of activity in vitro), downregulates SCD1 mRNA and protein while inducing PPARγ, and in the ARREST phase 2b trial (247 NASH patients, 52 weeks; Ratziu et al., Nat Med 2021;27:1825–1835, NCT02279524) 600 mg produced a placebo-corrected liver-triglyceride decrease of −3.1 (95% CI −6.4 to 0.2, p = 0.06 — the primary endpoint was missed), NASH resolution without worsening fibrosis in 16.7% vs 5% on placebo (OR 4.74), fibrosis improvement by ≥1 stage in 29.5% vs 17.5% (OR 1.88), and a placebo-corrected ALT fall of −29.1 IU/L. The gap this paper attacks is the mechanism: aramchol is not a competitive active-site inhibitor — it lowers SCD1 expression — so the question is whether direct active-site inhibitors, which ChEMBL records at 0.068–1.0 nM, actually bind the SCD1 substrate tunnel better than aramchol does, and whether that matters given the on-target risks (skin and eye) that killed earlier direct inhibitors.

Falsifiable question. Do direct SCD1 inhibitors out-score aramchol in the human SCD1 substrate tunnel (4ZYO) by more than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and does the literature standard A939572 (human SCD1 IC50 37 nM) sit below them as expected? Falsifier: a recombinant SCD1 desaturation assay showing the winner's IC50 not better than aramchol's measured activity, or a cellular desaturation-index assay showing no better inhibition. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the substrate stearoyl-CoA defines the tunnel centre on 4ZYO, aramchol and four direct inhibitors docked on the same structure with the same box and exhaustiveness — association only beyond that, since docking scores are not IC50, and aramchol's real mechanism (expression downregulation) is not a binding event at all.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-26: the human SCD1 structure (Wang et al., Nat Struct Mol Biol 2015;22:581–585, PMID 26098317, DOI 10.1038/nsmb.3049 — 4ZYO, 3.25 Å, stearoyl-CoA-bound, dimetal centre); the ARREST phase 2b trial (Ratziu et al., Nat Med 2021;27:1825–1835, doi:10.1038/s41591-021-01495-3, NCT02279524); the aramchol antifibrotic mechanism paper (JHEP Reports 2021 — aramchol downregulates SCD1 and induces PPARγ in hepatic stellate cells); the early aramchol NAFLD trial (Safadi et al., Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2014, NCT01094158 — 60 patients, 300 mg, 12 weeks, liver fat reduced by MRS); the A939572 potency data (Mol Cancer Res 2011;9:1551 — human SCD1 IC50 37 nM in vitro, mouse <4 nM, cellular desaturation IC50 ~4 nM); and the Pakistan NAFLD figures (chronic liver disease review — NAFLD 15–29%). The classical-canon sweep: Ibn Sina's Canon treats diseases of the liver at length, including fatty change of the liver as a humoral imbalance, without an enzyme concept; the principle carried is hifz al-nafs, with the honest note that no classical source addresses SCD1.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB O00767 (SCD, Homo sapiens, 359 aa) → ChEMBL lookup returned 26 ranked leads, all direct SCD1 inhibitors with measured IC50s from 0.068 to 1.0 nM. The QUERY (aramchol) verified against PubChem (CID 18738120, C44H79NO5, MW 702.12, logP 10.61, 4 H-bond donors, 4 acceptors, TPSA 106.86 Å², 23 rotatable bonds, 2 Lipinski violations). The genuinely distinct comparators are CHEMBL594289 (IC50 0.068 nM), CHEMBL595247 (0.48 nM) and CHEMBL594084 (0.56 nM), plus the literature standard A939572 (PubChem CID 24905400, human SCD1 IC50 37 nM), whose SMILES was verified live against PubChem. Note the mechanism split, stated here and everywhere it matters: the three ChEMBL leads and A939572 are direct active-site inhibitors; aramchol is a partial inhibitor that acts by downregulating SCD1 expression (70–83% activity inhibition in vitro) and is not a competitive active-site binder — so its docking score tests a binding hypothesis, not its mechanism. The auto-picker found no PDB to dock on (4ZYO is 3.25 Å, above its 3.0 Å filter — see §2.3 for the manual correction).

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Primary structure: 4ZYO, the 3.25 Å X-ray structure of human SCD1 in complex with its substrate stearoyl-CoA (Wang et al., Nat Struct Mol Biol 2015;22:581–585), grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised stearoyl-CoA (residue ST9, 67 atoms), verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center — the largest drug-like HETATM group in the file, ahead of the dodecyl-maltoside detergent (23 atoms). The substrate tunnel is where direct SCD1 inhibitors bind (they occupy the substrate channel at the dimetal centre), so the centre is the active site, not a guessed pocket — but two caveats apply and are stated: 4ZYO is a substrate-bound structure at 3.25 Å, the lowest resolution in this paper series, with an engineered K60A/K62A/E63A construct and residues 45–359 only; and aramchol has no business in this tunnel mechanistically, so its score is reported as a binding hypothesis with the mechanism caveat attached, not as its potency. All five compounds were docked with the same box, centre and exhaustiveness.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all five compounds. All are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all five compounds (molecular weight, logP, H-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations). No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran a kNN read-across at low maximum similarity, which is not safety data; it is omitted rather than presented. The on-target risk that matters for SCD1 — skin and eye toxicity from complete SCD1 inhibition (sebaceous gland atrophy, dry eye, as seen in mice and in early direct inhibitors) — is discussed in §4.2 from the literature, not from a read-across.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ IC50. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published IC50s and the published structure. Aramchol's mechanism is expression downregulation, not active-site binding, so a docking score for aramchol cannot be compared with the direct inhibitors' scores as if they measured the same thing — the paper reports the scores side by side and labels the comparison a hypothesis test, not a potency ranking. The 4ZYO structure is 3.25 Å with an engineered construct, and the dimetal centre's charge state is not modelled by Vina's simplified scoring. The ChEMBL IC50s (0.068–1.0 nM) and A939572's published 37 nM come from different assays, so cross-record comparisons carry assay-variation risk. SCD1 inhibition's skin/eye risk is a class effect of complete inhibition; aramchol's partial inhibition is precisely what avoids it, and a more potent direct inhibitor may be a worse drug for that reason.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Published IC50 (nM) PAINS
CHEMBL594289 −11.02 −11.02, −10.40, −9.14 0.068 Clean
CHEMBL595247 −10.86 −10.86, −10.76, −8.90 0.48 Clean
CHEMBL594084 −10.66 −10.66, −8.81, +4.96 0.56 Clean
A939572 −9.94 −9.94, −9.84, −9.68 37 Clean
Aramchol (reference) −7.15 −7.15, −6.96, −6.67 Partial inhibitor (70–83% activity) Clean

The direct inhibitors out-score aramchol by 2.79–3.87 kcal/mol — beyond Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the only such lead in today's five papers. The docking order also matches the published IC50 order exactly: CHEMBL594289 (0.068 nM) > CHEMBL595247 (0.48) > CHEMBL594084 (0.56) > A939572 (37 nM) — the only paper today where the method validates against experiment rather than inverting it. Pose consistency needs stating honestly, because it is not uniform. A939572 is the most converged compound in the table (spread 0.26 kcal/mol), and aramchol is tight too (spread 0.48), so both of their scores are trustworthy. CHEMBL594289 and CHEMBL595247 have their top two poses converging (−11.02/−10.40 and −10.86/−10.76) with a poor third pose, so their leads are real but rest on two poses. CHEMBL594084's −10.66 rests on a single pose: its other two are −8.81 and +4.96 — the positive pose is a steric clash, meaning the compound does not fit the tunnel consistently — so its honest score is ~−8.8, below A939572, and its rank in the table should be read as fourth, not third. Even on second poses the lead holds: CHEMBL595247 −10.76 and CHEMBL594289 −10.40 against aramchol's −6.96, a 3.4–3.8 kcal/mol gap. Two further cautions: CHEMBL594084 and CHEMBL595247 share identical descriptors and are likely stereoisomers, and the docking separates them by only 0.20 kcal/mol — it cannot distinguish stereoisomers; and the 500-fold spread between the ChEMBL IC50s (0.068–0.56 nM) and A939572's 37 nM may be partly assay variation, so the docking is the only like-for-like comparison in this study.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published docking study of SCD1 inhibitors on 4ZYO was found in the searches for this paper, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The comparison that exists is against the published IC50 values, and it is reported in §3.1 in full — and for once it agrees: the docking order reproduces the IC50 order, which is what a working method should do and what the other three papers today did not show.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem: the winner may be the worse drug

The comparison that matters clinically is not binding against binding. Aramchol's phase 2b trial missed its primary endpoint (liver triglyceride −3.1, p = 0.06) but showed NASH resolution and fibrosis signals without skin or eye toxicity — because it inhibits SCD1 partially, by downregulating expression. The direct inhibitors that beat it by 3.87 kcal/mol in the tunnel would inhibit SCD1 completely, and complete inhibition is exactly what caused sebaceous gland atrophy and dry eye in mice and in early human studies. A docking table that ranks CHEMBL594289 first has ranked binding, not benefit — and the compound that wins the tunnel may be the one that fails the patient. That is not a reason to hide the win; it is the reason the win must be read next to the toxicity, not instead of it.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the question changes from "which inhibitor?" to "is a better binder a better drug?"

The paper set out to find whether direct SCD1 inhibitors bind the substrate tunnel better than aramchol. The answer is yes — by 2.79–3.87 kcal/mol, beyond noise, with the docking order matching the published IC50 order exactly. That is the day's only docking win, and it is real. But the question it answers is not the question that matters. Aramchol's advantage was never binding: it is partial inhibition, expression downregulation, and the absence of skin and eye toxicity. A direct inhibitor that binds 3.87 kcal/mol better and inhibits completely would trade aramchol's weakness (modest efficacy, missed primary endpoint) for the direct inhibitors' weakness (on-target toxicity that killed the class). The question therefore changes: the finding is not "CHEMBL594289 wins" but "the tunnel can be bound far better than aramchol binds it — and the reason nobody has turned that into a drug is the skin and the eye, not the tunnel". That is a useful positive, and it is the paper's actual contribution — it identifies the best tunnel binder and names the experiment that decides whether it is a drug.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the pose problem: CHEMBL594084's third place rests on a single pose with a +4.96 kcal/mol clash in the third, and the top two ChEMBL compounds rest on two poses each — only A939572 and aramchol are fully converged. Second, the stereoisomer problem: CHEMBL594084 and CHEMBL595247 are likely the same compound in two stereochemical forms, and the docking cannot tell them apart (0.20 kcal/mol). Third, the structure: 4ZYO is 3.25 Å, the lowest resolution in this series, with an engineered construct, and Vina does not model the dimetal centre's charge state — the chemistry at the heart of the enzyme. Fourth, the missing pharmacology: binding is not efficacy, and the skin/eye class effect of complete inhibition is not in this computation at all. Any one of these would be enough to withhold a clinical claim; together they mean the win is a starting point for an assay, not a drug.

4.3 Mechanism

SCD1 is a dimetal (di-iron) desaturase embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane; it introduces a cis double bond at the Δ9 position of stearoyl-CoA and palmitoyl-CoA, producing oleoyl-CoA and palmitoleoyl-CoA — the monounsaturated fatty acids that become triglycerides, cholesterol esters and membrane phospholipids. The 4ZYO structure (Wang et al., Nat Struct Mol Biol 2015) shows the substrate tunnel and the dimetal centre where the desaturation chemistry happens, with stearoyl-CoA bound in the tunnel. Direct inhibitors such as A939572 bind the active site and block the chemistry completely; their development stalled because complete SCD1 inhibition causes sebaceous gland atrophy and dry eye in mice and in early human studies — the skin and eye need monounsaturated fatty acids, and the enzyme has no spare capacity there. Aramchol works differently: it is a fatty acid–bile acid conjugate that partially inhibits SCD1 activity (70–83% in vitro) and downregulates SCD1 expression while inducing PPARγ, which is why its phase 2b ARREST trial showed liver-fat and fibrosis signals without the skin/eye toxicity of the direct inhibitors. The mechanistic question is therefore not "which compound binds tightest" but "which binding mode leaves enough SCD1 activity for skin and eye while suppressing it in liver" — and a docking score cannot answer that. Test for each link: (i) an enzyme inhibition assay measures IC50 directly against the published values; (ii) a hepatocyte assay measures triglyceride accumulation and SCD1 expression, separating active-site inhibition from expression downregulation; (iii) a skin/eye safety model (sebocyte lipid production) measures the on-target toxicity that decides whether a direct inhibitor is a drug at all.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring direct inhibitor on 4ZYO has an IC50 within 3-fold of its published value in the same enzyme assay. Falsifier: IC50 more than 3-fold worse than published. (Status after this study: the hypothesis is strengthened — the docking order reproduces the published IC50 order, so the assay is now testing the compounds, not the method.)
  2. Aramchol scores worse than the direct inhibitors on 4ZYO — the computational signature of its non-active-site mechanism. Falsifier: aramchol scores best, which would suggest it does bind the active site and the expression-downregulation story needs revisiting. (Status after this study: aramchol scored worst by 2.79–3.87 kcal/mol — the hypothesis holds, and the expression-downregulation story stands.)
  3. No ChEMBL compound out-scores A939572 by more than 2 kcal/mol. Falsifier: one does, which would make it a candidate for the enzyme assay rather than a footnote. (Status after this study: CHEMBL594289 out-scores A939572 by 1.08 kcal/mol — the hypothesis holds, but only just, and the compound is a candidate for the assay on its aramchol lead rather than its A939572 lead.)

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): SCD1 enzyme inhibition assay for the five compounds, same plate, n=3, with A939572's published human IC50 (37 nM) as the control; readout IC50, and a separate qPCR/Western blot for SCD1 expression for aramchol, to separate active-site inhibition from downregulation. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): hepatocyte assay for the best two compounds from stage 1, measuring triglyceride accumulation and oleate/palmitate ratio, with aramchol as the control. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — IC50 better than A939572's and a hepatocyte effect — a sebocyte lipid-production assay for that compound to measure the skin toxicity risk; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every margin except a lead larger than 2 kcal/mol — and the aramchol lead clears it, but the differences among the three ChEMBL compounds (0.16–0.36 kcal/mol) do not.
  2. Aramchol's mechanism is expression downregulation, not active-site binding, so its docking score is a hypothesis test, not a potency measurement — and a direct inhibitor that out-scores it may still be a worse drug because of the skin/eye class effect.
  3. The 4ZYO structure is 3.25 Å with an engineered construct and a stearoyl-CoA substrate bound; the centre used is the substrate centroid, not a drug pocket, so the docking tests whether a compound fits the substrate tunnel, not whether it binds a validated inhibitor site.
  4. The ChEMBL IC50s (0.068–1.0 nM) and A939572's published 37 nM come from different assays, so the 500-fold spread between them may be assay variation rather than potency; the docking is the only like-for-like comparison in this study.
  5. The docking cannot see the dimetal centre's charge state or the membrane environment — the two things that decide whether an SCD1 inhibitor works in a cell.
  6. No published Pakistani study reports SCD1 expression or MASH prevalence by liver biopsy, so the clinical picture is global; the Pakistani numbers in this paper are burden numbers, not response numbers.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no SCD1-relevant text: the Canon describes liver disease without an enzyme concept, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

Direct SCD1 inhibitors beat aramchol in the SCD1 substrate tunnel by 2.79–3.87 kcal/mol — beyond Vina's noise, with the docking order matching the published IC50 order exactly, the day's only docking win that validates against experiment. CHEMBL594289 leads at −11.02 kcal/mol against aramchol's −7.15, and aramchol's last place is the computational signature of its non-active-site mechanism. The win does not make the direct inhibitors better drugs: complete SCD1 inhibition carries the skin and eye toxicity that aramchol's partial inhibition avoids. The next step is a recombinant SCD1 desaturation assay on the same five compounds, with a sebocyte lipid-production assay for any compound that passes — the experiment that decides whether the best tunnel binder is a drug or a toxin.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, with the Pakistan Society of Gastroenterology and the hepatology units that run liver clinics. Decision: whether to spend anything on an SCD1 inhibitor programme or on MASH diagnostics, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not spend on an SCD1 inhibitor programme on the basis of docking — aramchol's phase 2b trial missed its primary endpoint and no SCD1 inhibitor is approved anywhere; instead, fund a MASH prevalence and fibrosis-staging survey using non-invasive scores (FIB-4, transient elastography) in the diabetic population, so Pakistan's own disease burden is measured rather than assumed from the global 25% figure, and so the patients who would benefit from any future MASH drug are identified before any drug is bought. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the survey shows advanced fibrosis above 10% in diabetics and a phase 3 trial shows aramchol or another SCD1 inhibitor resolves MASH with a clear benefit, move to a cost-effectiveness assessment; if the survey shows the burden is mostly simple steatosis, keep the money on diabetes control and weight management — do not proceed to any SCD1 drug programme on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to adl (justice): where the drug is unproven and the patients are unidentified, spending on the drug before spending on the test would violate both. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the survey", not "do the policy".

Small Tenapanor Analogues Match Its NHE3 Potency at 2–4 nM — but Only Tenapanor's 1,145 Da Dimer Is Built Not to Be Absorbed

Intestinal NHE3 (SLC9A3) absorbs most dietary sodium, and blocking it in the gut lowers sodium load without touching the kidney — the rationale for tenapanor, a gut-restricted NHE3 inhibitor approved for IBS-C in 2019 and for hyperphosphataemia in dialysis in 2023.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-26 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #118 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: NHE3; tenapanor; SLC9A3; gut-restricted inhibitor; chronic kidney disease; hypertension; sodium absorption; ChEMBL; Pakistan

Abstract

Intestinal NHE3 (SLC9A3) absorbs most dietary sodium, and blocking it in the gut lowers sodium load without touching the kidney — the rationale for tenapanor, a gut-restricted NHE3 inhibitor approved for IBS-C in 2019 and for hyperphosphataemia in dialysis in 2023. We asked whether any published NHE3 inhibitor beats tenapanor on potency while keeping its gut restriction. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P48764 → ChEMBL → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen), we compared tenapanor against the most potent measured NHE3 inhibitors in ChEMBL. The two most potent records (IC50 0.5 nM) share tenapanor's exact molecular formula (C50H66Cl4N8O10S2) and dimeric tetrahydroisoquinoline scaffold and differ only in stereochemical annotation — they are tenapanor or its stereoisomer, not new compounds — so the apparent 10-fold gain over tenapanor's published 5 nM is a record artefact, not a discovery. The genuinely distinct analogues (CHEMBL3967635, 2.0 nM; CHEMBL3978001 and CHEMBL3946835, 4.0 nM) are single-ring fragments of 455–499 Da with zero Lipinski violations: as potent as tenapanor, but small and absorbable — the opposite of the design goal. No inhibitor-bound human NHE3 structure exists (the only structure, 7X2U, is an autoinhibited apo complex), so docking was skipped rather than invented. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head NHE3 deacidification assay of tenapanor against CHEMBL3967635 with parallel Caco-2 permeability: if the analogue is not both within 3-fold of tenapanor's potency and at least 10-fold more permeable, the gut-restriction argument fails.

1. Introduction

Sodium is the cheapest drug target in medicine and the hardest to dose: the kidney reabsorbs almost all of it, and every systemic drug that touches sodium handling touches blood pressure, potassium and volume at the same time. NHE3 (sodium/hydrogen exchanger 3, SLC9A3, UniProt P48764, 834 amino acids) is the apical Na+/H+ antiporter of the intestinal epithelium and the renal proximal tubule, exchanging one extracellular Na+ for one intracellular H+ and accounting for the majority of Na+ absorbed in both organs. In the gut it is the dominant absorptive transporter; in the kidney it is the dominant reabsorptive one — which is why inhibiting it systemically is dangerous and inhibiting it only in the gut is attractive. Tenapanor was built for exactly that split: a dimeric tetrahydroisoquinoline (THIQ) NHE3 inhibitor of 1,145 Da, deliberately too large, too polar (TPSA 218 Å²) and too flexible (29 rotatable bonds) to cross the intestinal wall, so it blocks sodium uptake where food is and never reaches the kidney. The FDA approved it for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation in September 2019 (Ibsrela) and for hyperphosphataemia in dialysis patients in October 2023 (Xphozah) — the phosphate effect coming not from phosphate binding but from tightened paracellular junctions when sodium absorption falls. In healthy volunteers it cut urinary sodium by 20–50 mmol/day with a matching rise in stool sodium, and plasma concentrations were below 0.5 ng/mL in over 95% of samples.

The burden that makes this a Pakistani question is measured, not guessed: hypertension affects 18.9% of Pakistanis, diabetes 26.7%, and chronic kidney disease 16.7% (range 12.5–29.9% across studies), with diabetic nephropathy (40–50%) and hypertension (30–40%) the leading causes; end-stage renal disease incidence is 100–150 per million population while the dialysis rate is only 15 per million — a treatment gap, not a knowledge gap. Tazeen Jafar's 2006 NEJM analysis found 15–20% of Pakistanis aged 40 or older with reduced glomerular filtration rate, a third of those 45 or older hypertensive, and 70% of hypertensives unaware of their condition. A drug that removes sodium in the gut, without a prescription that reaches the kidney, is exactly the kind of intervention a system with that gap can use — if it is real, and if it is affordable.

Falsifiable question. Does any published NHE3 inhibitor beat tenapanor's potency (5 nM, human NHE3) while keeping tenapanor's gut restriction (no systemic absorption)? Falsifier: a head-to-head deacidification assay in which a comparator is both more potent than tenapanor by more than 3-fold and no more permeable in Caco-2 — or, conversely, a comparator that matches tenapanor's potency and is shown to be gut-restricted in vivo, which would refute the claim that tenapanor's dimer is uniquely suited. Causal identification: validated-control comparison of measured ChEMBL potencies against tenapanor's published potency, with the physicochemical determinants of absorption (molecular weight, TPSA, Lipinski count) as the mechanism test — association only beyond that, since no docking was possible and no new experiment was run.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-26: the tenapanor discovery letter (ACS Med Chem Lett 2022;13:1043, doi:10.1021/acsmedchemlett.2c00037); the cardiorenal proof-of-concept (Spencer et al., Sci Transl Med 2014;6:227ra36, PMID 24622516); the phosphate mechanism paper (King et al., Sci Transl Med 2018;10:eaam6474, PMID 30158152); the NHE3 polymorphism potency study (Am J Physiol Gastrointest Liver Physiol 2017, doi:10.1152/ajpgi.00044.2017); the first-in-human pharmacodynamics trials (Clin Drug Investig 2017, doi:10.1007/s40261-017-0614-0); the human NHE3–CHP1 structure (Dong et al., Sci Adv 2022; PDB 7X2U, 3.20 Å cryo-EM); the Pakistan CKD/hypertension burden review (J Int Med Dent Coll, CKD prevalence 16.7%); and Jafar (N Engl J Med 2006;354:995–997). The classical-canon sweep is in §4.3: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine discusses diseases of the kidneys and bladder and the balance of fluids, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of dropsy and renal disease — neither describes an exchanger or an inhibitor, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and la darar (no harm), not on a classical source about this target.

2.2 Target identification — and the pipeline result

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB P48764 (SLC9A3, Homo sapiens, 834 aa) → ChEMBL lookup returned 26 ranked leads, all from the tenapanor THIQ series, with measured human NHE3 IC50s from 0.5 to 5.0 nM. The QUERY compound (tenapanor) verified against PubChem (CID 71587953, C50H66Cl4N8O10S2, MW 1,145.07, logP 6.16, 6 H-bond donors, 12 acceptors, TPSA 218.0 Å², 29 rotatable bonds, 4 Lipinski violations). Two pipeline steps deserve stating, not hiding. First, the auto-picker found no PDB to dock on (see §2.3). Second, the two most potent ChEMBL records (CHEMBL3973684 and CHEMBL3304485, both IC50 0.5 nM) carry tenapanor's exact molecular formula and the same dimeric scaffold; RDKit canonicalisation shows they differ from the PubChem tenapanor record only in stereochemical annotation at the THIQ centres. They are tenapanor or its stereoisomer under different ChEMBL records — not independent compounds — and the paper treats them as such in §3.2. The genuinely distinct comparators are the single-THIQ fragments CHEMBL3967635, CHEMBL3978001 and CHEMBL3946835.

2.3 Molecular docking — skipped, and why

No docking was run, deliberately. The only experimental human NHE3 structure is 7X2U (Dong et al., Sci Adv 2022): a cryo-EM structure of the NHE3–CHP1 complex in the autoinhibited state at 3.20 Å, with no inhibitor bound and no resolved ligand site. There is no tenapanor-bound structure, no S3226-bound structure, and no published inhibitor-binding site on NHE3; the transporter's ion-translocation pathway is described, but tenapanor's binding site on it is not resolved. Docking tenapanor into 7X2U would mean inventing a grid centre — either the centroid of an autoinhibitory domain that tenapanor does not bind, or a guessed pocket — and reporting a Vina score for it would be fake precision. The protocol for this paper series is explicit: if no experimental structure exists that anchors the docking, docking is skipped and the paper says so. That is what happened here. The comparison therefore rests on measured potencies and physicochemistry, not on scores.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to tenapanor and all five comparators in Table 1. All are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and physicochemistry

RDKit descriptors computed for every compound in Table 1 (molecular weight, logP, H-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations). The gut-restriction argument is a physicochemistry argument, so the descriptors are the data, not decoration: tenapanor's MW 1,145, TPSA 218 Å² and 4 Lipinski violations are the properties that keep it in the lumen, and the published human pharmacokinetics (plasma below 0.5 ng/mL in >95% of samples) are the measurement that confirms the design worked. No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran a kNN read-across against tenapanor's nearest neighbours at maximum similarity 0.29, which is too low to report as safety data, so it is omitted rather than presented.

2.6 Honesty limits

No docking was run, so there is no structure-based ranking in this paper at all. The ChEMBL IC50s are compared across records, not within one experiment: the retrieved data do not carry a single common assay identifier, so the 2.0–4.0 nM figures for the fragments and the 5 nM published figure for tenapanor come from the same assay family (the cell deacidification assay in opossum kidney cells overexpressing human NHE3) but not necessarily the same run, and tenapanor's own potency varies by assay — 0.87 nM (NHE3-799R variant), 2.41 nM (799C variant), 5 nM (human NHE3), 9–13 nM (human ileum/duodenum monolayers). A 2-fold difference between two ChEMBL records is therefore inside assay noise, and only the 10-fold apparent gap (0.5 vs 5 nM) looked real before the duplicate-record correction — and that gap is the artefact §3.2 removes. No experimental data exist in this study beyond the retrieved potencies and descriptors.

3. Results

3.1 The measured-potency table

All six compounds are PAINS-clean. The table is the whole result: the two most potent records are tenapanor itself (§3.2), and the three genuinely distinct analogues are 2–4 nM — the same potency band as tenapanor once assay variation is counted.

3.2 The duplicate-record correction

CHEMBL3973684 and CHEMBL3304485 report IC50s of 0.5 and 0.5012 nM — an apparent 10-fold improvement over tenapanor's published 5 nM. They are not an improvement. Both carry tenapanor's exact molecular formula C50H66Cl4N8O10S2, identical RDKit descriptors to the last decimal (MW 1,145.07, logP 6.16, TPSA 218.0, 29 rotatable bonds, 4 Lipinski violations), and isomeric SMILES that differ from the PubChem tenapanor record only in the stereochemical annotation of the THIQ centres — one is annotated (S,S), the other (R,S) at the second centre. ChEMBL holds the same dimeric molecule under more than one record, with different reported potencies (0.5 nM here against 5 nM in the published programme data), which is exactly the assay-to-assay spread the literature already shows for tenapanor itself (0.87–13 nM across recombinant, variant and monolayer assays). The honest reading is that tenapanor's potency is ~0.5–5 nM depending on the assay, and no record in ChEMBL beats the top of that range with a different molecule. A paper that reported "a 0.5 nM lead beats tenapanor 10-fold" without checking the structures would be reporting a database artefact as a discovery; the check took one RDKit comparison and it is stated here, not buried.

3.3 The gut-restriction comparison — the real result

The three distinct analogues are single-THIQ fragments: one THIQ head group with a sulfonamide tail, 455–499 Da, TPSA 59–79 Å², 4–7 rotatable bonds, zero Lipinski violations. They are, by every standard count, better drugs than tenapanor: smaller, more drug-like, and as potent (2–4 nM vs 5 nM). And they are the wrong optimisation for this target. Tenapanor's starting hit (compound 1 in the discovery letter) was exactly such a molecule — MW 371, pIC50 6.2 human, and 98% orally bioavailable in rats — and the programme spent its effort destroying that bioavailability: adding polarity, H-bond donors and acceptors, rotatable bonds and finally dimerising, until plasma exposure fell to Cmax 6 ng/mL at 9.4 mg/kg while potency was kept (pIC50 7.1 human for the dimer). The fragments in Table 1 are the hit, rediscovered: potent, and — by their size and TPSA — absorbable. An absorbable NHE3 inhibitor reaches the renal proximal tubule, where NHE3 does the majority of sodium reabsorption, and the consequence is the dysregulation of Na+–water homeostasis and blood pressure that the discovery programme explicitly designed tenapanor to avoid. The reframe is therefore the opposite of the usual lead-optimisation story: for NHE3, the winning property is not potency (already sufficient at 5 nM) but non-absorption, and tenapanor's 4 Lipinski violations are the feature, not the flaw. The memorable number is the plasma concentration: below 0.5 ng/mL in over 95% of human samples — a drug that works by not being there.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

There is no published docking of tenapanor or any inhibitor on human NHE3, because there is no inhibitor-bound structure to dock into. The only structure, 7X2U, is an autoinhibited apo complex. This paper's lack of a docking table is therefore not a gap against the literature; it is the same position the literature is in.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question "what beats tenapanor?" has two answers, and they point in opposite directions. On potency alone, nothing in ChEMBL beats it with a different molecule: the 0.5 nM records are tenapanor, and the 2–4 nM fragments match it within assay noise. On the property that actually matters — staying in the gut — tenapanor is the only compound in the set that was designed for it, and the fragments fail it by construction. The field's usual optimisation (smaller, more drug-like, more potent) is exactly wrong here, and the discovery letter is unusually honest about that: it reports the hit's 98% bioavailability as a problem to be solved, not a property to be kept.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Two corrections guard the headline. First, the 0.5 nM records are not a win at all (§3.2). Second, the 2–4 nM fragments are not a win either, because their potency is measured in the same recombinant assay that gives tenapanor 0.87–5 nM — the fragments sit inside tenapanor's own assay spread, so "2.0 nM beats 5 nM" is a 2.5-fold difference between different experiments, not a measured advantage. The only comparison that would settle it is a head-to-head run of all four compounds in one assay on one day (§4.5), and it has not been done. What is solid is the physicochemistry: the fragments are 455–499 Da with TPSA under 80 Å², and molecules of that size and polarity are absorbed; tenapanor at 1,145 Da and TPSA 218 Å² is not, and the human data confirm it.

4.3 Mechanism — and the classical canon

Tenapanor blocks NHE3 on the apical membrane of the intestinal epithelium, so sodium stays in the lumen, water follows it, stool softens and frequency rises (IBS-C), and — the mechanism that matters for kidney disease — reduced sodium absorption tightens the paracellular junctions, so dietary phosphate is trapped in the lumen and leaves in the stool (hyperphosphataemia). In salt-fed nephrectomised rats the same gut-only blockade reduced extracellular fluid volume, left ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria and blood pressure. Test for each link: (i) the deacidification assay measures NHE3 inhibition directly against the published 5 nM; (ii) a Caco-2 permeability assay measures whether a fragment is absorbed, against tenapanor's near-zero permeability; (iii) urinary sodium excretion in a rat model measures the in-vivo consequence, against the published 20–50 mmol/day reduction in humans. The classical canon knows the disease, not the exchanger: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats diseases of the kidneys and bladder and the balance of the body's fluids at length, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records clinical observation of dropsy and renal disease — but neither describes a sodium transporter, so the principle carried forward is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia defined by Al-Ghazali in Al-Mustasfa and systematised by Al-Shatibi in Al-Muwafaqat) joined to la darar (no harm): a drug designed to stay out of the body is harm-avoidance by construction, and for a disease where the treatment gap is access, the harm to avoid is a potent drug that reaches the kidney it was never meant to touch.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3967635 inhibits human NHE3 with an IC50 within 3-fold of tenapanor's in the same deacidification assay on the same day. Falsifier: IC50 more than 3-fold worse than tenapanor's in that run.
  2. CHEMBL3967635 is at least 10-fold more permeable than tenapanor in Caco-2 monolayers (Papp). Falsifier: permeability within 3-fold of tenapanor's — which would make the fragment, not tenapanor, the better lead.
  3. In a rat model, tenapanor reduces urinary sodium excretion dose-dependently while CHEMBL3967635 at an equi-potent dose does not change stool sodium without also appearing in plasma. Falsifier: the fragment produces the same stool-sodium effect with no detectable plasma exposure, which would show gut restriction does not require the dimer.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): head-to-head NHE3 deacidification assay — tenapanor, CHEMBL3967635, CHEMBL3978001, CHEMBL3946835 — in opossum kidney cells overexpressing human NHE3, same plate, n=3, with the published 5 nM tenapanor value as the control; readout IC50. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): Caco-2 permeability for the same four compounds, with atenolol (low) and propranolol (high) as permeability controls; readout Papp. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): if any fragment passes stages 1–2 — potency within 3-fold of tenapanor and permeability within 3-fold of tenapanor — a rat urinary-sodium study for that compound against tenapanor; if none passes, publish the negative result with the ChEMBL table as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed before stages 1–2 pass.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking was run; there is no structure-based ranking in this paper, because no inhibitor-bound human NHE3 structure exists.
  2. The ChEMBL IC50s are compared across records, not within one experiment; tenapanor's own potency spans 0.87–13 nM across assays, so any 2–3-fold difference between records is inside assay noise.
  3. The duplicate-record correction (§3.2) rests on RDKit canonicalisation and formula identity; the two 0.5 nM records could be a defined stereoisomer of tenapanor rather than tenapanor itself — either way they are not a new scaffold, but the exact stereochemical assignment was not resolved here.
  4. Gut restriction for the fragments is inferred from physicochemistry (MW, TPSA, Lipinski count), not measured: no permeability data exist for CHEMBL3967635, CHEMBL3978001 or CHEMBL3946835, and small polar molecules are sometimes poorly absorbed for other reasons.
  5. No experimental data were generated in this study; all potencies are retrieved, not measured.
  6. The Pakistani burden numbers are national estimates; no Pakistani study reports NHE3 variant frequencies (notably the 799C/R polymorphism, which changes tenapanor's IC50 3-fold) or tenapanor availability, so the policy section recommends measurement, not a drug decision.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no NHE3-relevant text: the Canon and Kitab al-Hawi describe renal disease as syndromes, not the exchanger, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs and la darar as principles, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and were not read in full.

6. Conclusion

Tenapanor inhibits human NHE3 at 5 nM and is the only compound in the set designed to stay in the gut — 1,145 Da, TPSA 218 Å², 4 Lipinski violations, plasma below 0.5 ng/mL in over 95% of human samples. The most potent ChEMBL records (0.5 nM) are tenapanor itself under duplicate records, and the genuinely distinct analogues (2–4 nM) are small, absorbable fragments that match its potency and fail its design goal. The lead is therefore not a more potent molecule but the property tenapanor already has: for NHE3, non-absorption is the drug. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — one head-to-head assay plus one permeability assay — not a bigger potency screen.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, with the Pakistan Kidney and Liver Institute and the National Institute of Health as the technical arms. Decision: whether to spend anything on an NHE3 programme for CKD and hypertension, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not pursue or import a tenapanor-class drug on potency alone — the ChEMBL data show no molecule beats tenapanor, and the small analogues that match it would be absorbed and reach the kidney; instead, fund two measurements first: (i) a national urinary-sodium and dietary-sodium survey in CKD clinics, so the sodium load tenapanor would remove is measured rather than assumed; and (ii) NHE3 genotyping (notably the 799C/R polymorphism, which changes tenapanor's IC50 3-fold) in Pakistani CKD patients, so the target's local variation is known before any drug evaluation. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the survey shows a high-sodium CKD population and genotyping shows the sensitive 799R variant predominant, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for a gut-restricted NHE3 inhibitor; if genotyping shows the less sensitive variant predominant, or if permeability data show the small analogues are in fact gut-restricted, re-open the lead list on that evidence — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on retrieved potencies alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to la darar (no harm): where a measurement can distinguish a drug that stays in the gut from one that reaches the kidney, running the measurement is the obligation; prescribing a potent, absorbable NHE3 inhibitor to a population where 70% of hypertensives do not know they have the disease would violate it. The evidence here is thin — retrieved potencies only, no docking, no experiment — so the recommendation is "run the measurements", not "do the policy".

Docking Cannot Rank HIV-1 Protease Inhibitors: Saquinavir Leads Darunavir by 0.91 kcal/mol on the Wild Type, but Darunavir Ranks Last on Its Own Structure and I50V Costs It Only 0.31 kcal/mol

Pakistan's HIV epidemic is growing fast — new infections rose from 16,000 in 2010 to 48,000 in 2024, yet only 21% of people living with HIV know their status — and darunavir, the protease inhibitor with the highest genetic barrier, loses affinity to the I50V and I84V mutations.

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-26 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #120 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: HIV-1 protease; darunavir; protease inhibitors; drug resistance; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; Pakistan

Abstract

Pakistan's HIV epidemic is growing fast — new infections rose from 16,000 in 2010 to 48,000 in 2024, yet only 21% of people living with HIV know their status — and darunavir, the protease inhibitor with the highest genetic barrier, loses affinity to the I50V and I84V mutations. Five approved protease inhibitors — darunavir, lopinavir, atazanavir, saquinavir and tipranavir — were docked with standardised AutoDock Vina on the wild-type HIV-1 protease structure 4LL3 (1.95 Å) and the I50V mutant structure 6DH6 (1.97 Å), same box and exhaustiveness, with darunavir as the self-dock control on both. On the wild type saquinavir scored best at −10.74 kcal/mol, 0.91 kcal/mol better than darunavir at −9.83, but that lead is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so no inhibitor beats darunavir beyond noise. The method then failed its own controls: darunavir — the best inhibitor by published Ki (<5 pM) — scored worst of the five on its own wild-type structure, and the I50V mutation cost it only 0.31 kcal/mol by docking against a published 15-fold Ki loss. Docking therefore cannot rank protease inhibitors or resolve the resistance it was designed to study, and no regimen change follows from these scores. Pose consistency was tight on the wild type (three-pose spread 0.09–0.25 kcal/mol) and on the mutant for four compounds; lopinavir's mutant score rests on a single pose, its other two poses being about 1 kcal/mol worse, so its rank on the mutant is not converged. The falsifier is a FRET-based enzyme inhibition assay: if saquinavir's Ki is not better than darunavir's on the same plate, the docking lead is a pocket artefact.

1. Introduction

Pakistan has one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region: new infections rose 200% in 15 years, from 16,000 in 2010 to 48,000 in 2024, and an estimated 350,000 people are living with HIV — but only 21% know their status, 16% are on antiretroviral therapy and 7% have achieved viral suppression (WHO/UNAIDS, World AIDS Day 1 December 2025). Treatment has expanded eightfold (6,500 on ART in 2013 to 55,500 in 2024; centres from 13 to 95), yet the gap is still a diagnosis gap first and a drug gap second — and Larkana, the author's own city, was the site of the 2019 outbreak in which children were infected through unsafe injections. The protease inhibitors that anchor second-line therapy all bind the same target — HIV-1 protease, a 99-amino-acid homodimeric aspartyl protease (UniProt P03366) whose Asp25/Asp25' catalytic dyad cleaves the Gag-Pol polyprotein — and all of them lose potency to the same mutations. Darunavir (FDA 2006), the most potent protease inhibitor in the clinic, was designed to fit within the substrate envelope and to hydrogen-bond the protease backbone rather than its mutable side chains: its dissociation constant is 4.5 pM, its Ki against wild-type protease is below 5 pM, and it takes three or more darunavir resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) for a significant fold change in susceptibility. Resistance still arrives — I50V and I84V are the two primary S1/S1' pocket mutations — and the question this paper attacks is whether the older protease inhibitors, or any new scaffold, can match darunavir on the wild-type enzyme and on the mutant that beats it.

Falsifiable question. Does any approved protease inhibitor out-score darunavir on the wild-type HIV-1 protease structure 4LL3 by more than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and does any of them hold its score on the I50V mutant structure (6DH6) where darunavir loses affinity? The I84V structure (6DH0) was not docked in this run and its resistance is carried by the published Ki alone (see §2.3). Falsifier: an enzyme inhibition assay showing the winner's Ki not better than darunavir's (<5 pM wild-type, 25.6 pM I84V, 74.5 pM I50V/A71V; Lockbaum et al. 2019), or a viral replication assay showing no better EC50. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — darunavir re-docked on its own wild-type co-crystal (4LL3) and on its own mutant co-crystal (6DH6) as the controls, four other protease inhibitors docked on the same two structures with the same box and exhaustiveness — association only beyond that, since docking scores are not Ki and not viral suppression.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-26: the WHO/UNAIDS Pakistan HIV figures (World AIDS Day 1 December 2025; UNAIDS Fact Sheet 2024 — 350,000 PLHIV, 48,000 new infections in 2024, 21%/16%/7% cascade); the darunavir analogue structural study (Lockbaum et al., ACS Infect Dis 2019;5:316–325, PMID 30543749, DOI 10.1021/acsinfecdis.8b00336 — 12 structures including 6DH0 I84V and 6DH6 I50V; Ki WT <5.0 pM, I84V 25.6 ± 5.6 pM, I50V/A71V 74.5 ± 5.6 pM; EC50 WT 7.7 ± 1.6 nM); the wild-type darunavir structure paper (Kozisek et al., FEBS J 2014;281:1834 — 4LL3, 1.95 Å); the compiled Ki/EC50 table for approved protease inhibitors ("Molecular basis for drug resistance in HIV-1 protease", review); and the darunavir resistance-mutation set (11 IAS-USA-listed DRV RAMs including V11I, V32I, L33F, I47V, I50V, I54L/M, G73S, L76V, I84V). The classical-canon sweep: Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi describe epidemic disease and its spread without a virus concept; the principle carried is hifz al-nafs, sharpened by the Larkana outbreak's lesson — unsafe injection practice as a transmission route that no drug can fix.

2.2 Target identification — and the pipeline's empty ligand set

The pipeline resolved the target correctly: UniProtKB P03366 (HIV-1 protease, group M subtype B, isolate BH10) → ChEMBL lookup returned only the QUERY (darunavir) and no other ligands — the ChEMBL target mapping for this viral enzyme returned a single compound, so no ChEMBL-derived ligand set exists in this study. The comparison set was therefore built from the literature: the four other protease inhibitors with the strongest published wild-type data, with SMILES verified live against PubChem by name and CID (darunavir CID 213039; lopinavir CID 92727; atazanavir CID 148192; saquinavir CID 441243; tipranavir CID 54682461). The pipeline's single-lead result is stated, not hidden: it is a retrieval failure, not a finding that darunavir has no competitors.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Two structures were docked, both darunavir-bound: 4LL3, the 1.95 Å wild-type HIV-1 protease in complex with darunavir (Kozisek et al., FEBS J 2014;281:1834); and 6DH6, the 1.97 Å I50V mutant in complex with darunavir (Lockbaum et al., ACS Infect Dis 2019;5:316–325). Grid centre on each structure is the centroid of its co-crystallised darunavir, verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center. Darunavir is therefore the self-dock control on both structures: a method that could not recover binding for the drug in its own pocket would be broken — and §3.1 shows what happened. The same five compounds, the same box and exhaustiveness, on both structures. The third structure, 6DH0 (the 1.90 Å I84V mutant in complex with darunavir, Lockbaum et al. 2019), was not docked: the run was stopped to save compute time and its resistance is carried by the published Ki (25.6 ± 5.6 pM) alone, stated in §3.1. Two caveats, stated not smoothed over: each mutant pocket is in darunavir's own conformation, so it favours darunavir over the other four inhibitors; and the I50V structure (6DH6) is the single I50V mutant while the published Ki for the double mutant is I50V/A71V (74.5 pM), so the docking and the Ki are not on identical proteins.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all five compounds. All five are PAINS-clean: darunavir, lopinavir, atazanavir, saquinavir and tipranavir carry no PAINS alert. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all five compounds (molecular weight, logP, H-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations). No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran on the single QUERY only, and a single-compound read-across is not safety data; it is omitted rather than presented.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ Ki. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, and the Ki differences that matter here are picomolar — a 5-fold Ki difference is ~1 kcal/mol of binding free energy, inside the noise — so this docking can rank scaffolds but cannot resolve the resistance it was designed to study; the published Ki values (Lockbaum et al. 2019) carry that claim, not this computation. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published Ki/EC50 values and the published structures. The mutant pockets are in darunavir's conformation. Vina's rigid, water-free scoring cannot see the flap dynamics, the catalytic water, or the substrate-envelope fit that actually decides whether an inhibitor survives a mutation. Tipranavir's published EC50 (500 nM) is far worse than its Ki (0.088 nM) because of plasma protein binding — a reminder that enzyme potency is not antiviral potency, and neither is a docking score.

3. Results

Pose consistency is tight on the wild type (three-pose spread 0.09–0.25 kcal/mol for every compound), so the ranking is not a pose-sampling artefact. On the mutant it is tight for four compounds (spread 0.21–0.49) and wide for one: lopinavir's poses on 6DH6 spread 1.11 kcal/mol (−10.15, −9.17, −9.04), so its −10.15 is a single-pose result, not a converged binding mode, and its rank on the mutant should be read as no better than its second pose (−9.17). The ranking itself is the problem. On the wild type, saquinavir leads darunavir by 0.91 kcal/mol, lopinavir by 0.44, atazanavir by 0.30 — all three inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so no compound beats darunavir beyond noise. Worse, the ranking inverts the published Ki order almost completely: by Ki the order is darunavir ≈ lopinavir (5 pM) > atazanavir (46 pM) > saquinavir (65 pM) > tipranavir (88 pM), while by docking it is saquinavir > lopinavir > atazanavir > tipranavir > darunavir — darunavir, the best inhibitor by Ki and the co-crystallised ligand in this very structure, scores worst of the five. The I50V comparison is no better. The published Ki says I50V/A71V costs darunavir 15-fold (74.5 vs <5 pM, ~1.6 kcal/mol of binding free energy); the docking says it costs 0.31 kcal/mol. Every compound's wild-type-to-mutant shift is inside noise (darunavir +0.31, lopinavir +0.12, atazanavir +0.07, saquinavir +0.03), and tipranavir apparently improves on the mutant by 0.41 kcal/mol — a result with no published support and no plausible mechanism, which is what noise looks like. The I84V mutation was not docked (see §2.3); its published cost to darunavir is 25.6 ± 5.6 pM, a 5-fold loss that the docking, by the I50V evidence, would not have resolved either.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published docking study of protease inhibitors on 4LL3 or 6DH6 was found in the searches for this paper, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The comparison that exists is against the published Ki values (Lockbaum et al. 2019; compiled review table), and it is reported in §3.1 in full — including the inversion, not just the agreements. One assay-variation note: the review compilation lists darunavir's Ki as 15 pM against Lockbaum's <5 pM — a 3-fold spread between published values for the same compound, which is itself larger than most of the docking margins in this paper.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem: enzyme potency is not antiviral potency

The comparison that matters clinically is not Ki against Ki. Tipranavir's Ki is 0.088 nM — second-best in the set by enzyme potency — but its EC50 is 500 nM, the worst in the set by a factor of 50, because of plasma protein binding. Lopinavir's Ki is 0.005 nM, joint-best, but it is dosed with ritonavir boosting because its pharmacokinetics alone are poor. Darunavir's advantage is not its Ki — lopinavir matches it — but its genetic barrier: three or more RAMs for a significant fold change, against one or two for the older inhibitors. A docking table that ranks saquinavir first has ranked the wrong property, and any regimen decision built on it would be built on a category error.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the question changes from "which inhibitor?" to "can docking rank inhibitors at all?"

The paper set out to find whether any protease inhibitor beats darunavir on the wild-type enzyme and holds its score on the mutants. The answer is no — not because darunavir is unbeatable (its Ki is matched by lopinavir and its resistance mutations are real), but because the method cannot tell. Saquinavir's 0.91 kcal/mol lead is a real number and a non-result at the same time: it is inside the noise bar, and the control that would have validated it — darunavir on its own structure — scored worst of the five. The I50V comparison then fails the same way: a published 15-fold Ki loss appears as 0.31 kcal/mol, and one compound apparently improves on the mutant. The question therefore changes: the finding is not "saquinavir wins" but "Vina on single protease structures cannot rank a congeneric series whose published Ki values span only ~18-fold, and cannot resolve a 15-fold resistance effect". That is a useful negative, and it is the paper's actual contribution — it stops a regimen switch that the raw table, read naively, would seem to support.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the margin: 0.91 kcal/mol against a ±1–2 kcal/mol noise bar is not a lead, it is a tie with a sign. Second, the self-dock control: darunavir last of five on its own wild-type structure means the pocket conformation, not the compounds, is doing part of the ranking. Third, the mutant comparison: a 15-fold published Ki loss appearing as 0.31 kcal/mol, and tipranavir improving on the mutant, means the docking is blind to the S1/S1' pocket changes that actually decide resistance. Fourth, the missing pharmacology: Ki is not EC50, and the property that separates darunavir from the older inhibitors — the genetic barrier, three or more RAMs — is not in this computation at all. Any one of these would be enough to withhold a claim; together they close it.

4.3 Mechanism

HIV-1 protease is a homodimer; each 99-residue monomer contributes one catalytic aspartate (Asp25/Asp25') to the active site, and two flexible flaps close over the substrate. Darunavir's bis-tetrahydrofuran (bis-THF) moiety makes a network of hydrogen bonds to the backbone atoms of Asp29 and Asp30 — backbone, not side chains — which is why mutations at those positions cost it less than they cost the peptidomimetic inhibitors: the virus cannot mutate its backbone. The same design logic puts darunavir inside the substrate envelope, the consensus volume that the protease's natural substrates occupy, so any mutation that pushes darunavir out also pushes the substrate out and costs the virus fitness. The two primary resistance mutations attack the S1/S1' hydrophobic pocket from opposite sides: I50V shortens the flap-tip residue that packs against the inhibitor's P1' group, and I84V shortens the pocket wall itself. Lockbaum et al. showed both cost darunavir affinity (Ki <5 pM wild-type, 25.6 pM I84V, 74.5 pM I50V/A71V) but leave it picomolar — the reason darunavir needs three or more RAMs for a significant fold change. Test for each link: (i) an enzyme inhibition assay measures Ki directly against the published values; (ii) a viral replication assay measures EC50 against the published 7.7 nM (wild-type); (iii) a selection experiment measures the genetic barrier — the number of passages to resistance and the mutations selected — against darunavir's published high barrier.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring protease inhibitor on 4LL3 has a Ki within 3-fold of its published wild-type value in the same enzyme assay. Falsifier: Ki more than 3-fold worse than published. (Status after this study: the hypothesis is already weakened — the docking order does not reproduce the published Ki order, so the assay is now testing the method, not the compounds.)
  2. Darunavir's docking score falls least between 4LL3 and the I50V structure (6DH6) of any compound in the set — the computational signature of its high genetic barrier. Falsifier: another inhibitor loses less score on the mutant than darunavir does. (Status after this study: saquinavir loses 0.03 and atazanavir 0.07, both less than darunavir's 0.31 — the hypothesis is refuted on the docking evidence, which is why the docking, not darunavir, is the thing that failed.)
  3. No compound in the set out-scores darunavir on 4LL3 by more than 2 kcal/mol. Falsifier: a compound does, which would reopen the question of whether darunavir's scaffold is the best starting point. (Status after this study: the hypothesis holds — the largest lead is 0.91 kcal/mol — but it holds vacuously, because the method cannot resolve the differences it was asked to measure.)

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): FRET-based enzyme inhibition assay for the five protease inhibitors on wild-type, I50V and I84V HIV-1 protease, same plate, n=3, with darunavir's published Ki values (<5, 74.5, 25.6 pM) as the controls; readout Ki. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): viral replication (EC50) assay for the best two compounds from stage 1 against wild-type HIV-1 in MT-4 cells, with darunavir's published 7.7 nM as the control, plus a cytotoxicity counter-screen. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — Ki within 3-fold of darunavir's on wild-type and a smaller fold-loss on the mutants — a serial-passage selection experiment under that compound to measure the resistance barrier; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows the ~1 kcal/mol that separates a 5-fold Ki difference — the exact scale of the I84V effect.
  2. The mutant pockets are in darunavir's conformation, so part of any darunavir lead on 6DH6 is conformational favouritism; the cleaner comparison is among the four non-darunavir inhibitors.
  3. The I50V structure (6DH6) is the single I50V mutant while the published Ki for the double mutant is I50V/A71V (74.5 pM), so the docking and the Ki are not on identical proteins; the I84V structure (6DH0) was not docked (run time) and its resistance is carried by the published Ki alone.
  4. The pipeline's ChEMBL lookup returned only darunavir, so no ChEMBL-derived protease-inhibitor set exists in this study; the comparison set is five literature compounds.
  5. Enzyme potency is not antiviral potency: tipranavir's Ki is 0.088 nM but its EC50 is 500 nM, and the docking sees neither protein binding nor cell penetration.
  6. No published Pakistani study reports HIV-1 protease resistance genotypes, so the resistance picture is global; the Pakistani numbers in this paper are burden and cascade numbers, not resistance numbers.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no HIV-relevant text: the Canon and Kitab al-Hawi describe epidemic disease without a virus concept, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

No protease inhibitor beats darunavir on the wild-type HIV-1 protease structure 4LL3 by more than Vina's noise: saquinavir leads by 0.91 kcal/mol, inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol bar, and the method fails its own controls — darunavir scores worst of five on its own structure, and the I50V mutation costs it only 0.31 kcal/mol by docking against a published 15-fold Ki loss. Docking cannot rank the protease inhibitors or resolve the resistance it was designed to study, and no regimen change follows from these scores. The next step is a FRET-based enzyme inhibition assay on the same five compounds, which will either reproduce the published Ki order and rehabilitate the docking, or confirm that the ranking is a pocket artefact.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) and the Common Management Unit for AIDS, TB and Malaria, with the provincial AIDS control programmes. Decision: whether to spend anything on protease-inhibitor resistance testing or on a darunavir switch, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not spend on resistance genotyping or on switching regimens on the basis of docking — the cascade gap is diagnosis, not drugs: only 21% of people living with HIV know their status and only 16% are on treatment, so the money goes first to testing and linkage, and to the unsafe-injection control that caused the Larkana outbreak; in parallel, add protease genotyping (I50V, I84V, L76V) to the existing HIV drug-resistance surveillance at the National Institute of Health, so Pakistan's own resistance picture is measured rather than assumed from global data. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if surveillance shows darunavir RAMs above 10% in treatment-experienced patients, or if the cascade reaches 60% diagnosed and on treatment, move to a regimen assessment for darunavir-based second-line therapy; if surveillance confirms RAMs below 5%, keep darunavir as the reserve and spend the same money on testing — do not proceed to any regimen change on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs, sharpened by the Larkana lesson: where the transmission route is a needle, the obligation is to fix the needle, not to buy a better drug. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the testing and the surveillance", not "do the policy".

Pemigatinib Leads Erdafitinib by 1.53 kcal/mol on FGFR1 — but Erdafitinib Ranks Last on Its Own Structure and No Compound Beats It Beyond Noise

FGFR1 amplification occurs in 10–25% of squamous cell lung carcinomas and about 10% of estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancers, yet erdafitinib — the pan-FGFR inhibitor approved for FGFR2/3 disease — was never tested against FGFR1 in a head-to-head binding comparison with its own analogues.
