Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-26 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #121 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: FGFR1; erdafitinib; pemigatinib; kinase inhibitor; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; lung cancer; Pakistan

Abstract

FGFR1 amplification occurs in 10–25% of squamous cell lung carcinomas and about 10% of estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancers, yet erdafitinib — the pan-FGFR inhibitor approved for FGFR2/3 disease — was never tested against FGFR1 in a head-to-head binding comparison with its own analogues. Five compounds — erdafitinib, three ChEMBL FGFR1 inhibitors (CHEMBL3980069, CHEMBL5182360, CHEMBL5799893) and the clinical FGFR inhibitor pemigatinib — were docked with standardised AutoDock Vina on the 1.63 Å erdafitinib-bound FGFR1 structure 5EW8, same box and exhaustiveness, with erdafitinib as the self-dock control. Pemigatinib scored best at −10.53 kcal/mol, 1.53 kcal/mol better than erdafitinib at −9.00, but that lead is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so no compound beats erdafitinib beyond noise. The method then failed its own control: erdafitinib — the co-crystallised ligand — scored worst of the five on its own structure, and the most potent ChEMBL compound by published IC50 (CHEMBL5182360, 0.28 nM) ranked fourth. Docking therefore cannot rank FGFR1 inhibitors on this structure, and no drug programme follows from these scores. Pose consistency was tight for two compounds and not for two: CHEMBL3980069 and CHEMBL5182360 converged on the same binding mode three times, while CHEMBL5799893's second place rests on a single pose, its other two poses being a full kcal/mol worse, so its honest score is about −8.9, below erdafitinib. The falsifier is a kinase inhibition assay: if pemigatinib's FGFR1 IC50 is not better than erdafitinib's 1.2 nM on the same plate, the docking lead is a pocket artefact.

1. Introduction

FGFR1 amplification is one of the most frequent potentially targetable alterations in squamous cell lung carcinoma — 10–25% of cases — and occurs in ~10% of estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancers, where it drives endocrine therapy resistance (Weiss et al., Sci Transl Med 2010;2:62ra93; Turner et al., Cancer Res 2010;70:2085). Across all solid tumours tested by next-generation sequencing, FGFR1 alterations (predominantly amplification) are found in 3.5% (Clin Cancer Res 2016;22:259). Erdafitinib (Balversa), a pan-FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, was the first agent to win FDA approval for an FGFR-dysregulated cancer — April 2019, for locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma with susceptible FGFR3/FGFR2 alterations (Loriot et al., N Engl J Med 2019;381:338–348, PMID 31340094) — with FGFR1–4 IC50s of 1.2, 2.5, 3 and 5.7 nM and Kd 0.24–2.2 nM. Its dose-limiting toxicity is on-target: hyperphosphataemia from inhibition of renal FGF23/klotho-mediated phosphate wasting occurred in 75.9% of patients. The gap this paper attacks is FGFR1 itself: erdafitinib was developed and approved on FGFR2/3 disease, its FGFR1 potency is the best of the four isoforms on paper (1.2 nM), and the question is whether its own analogues — or a different-scaffold FGFR inhibitor — actually bind the FGFR1 kinase domain better than erdafitinib does.

Falsifiable question. Does any ChEMBL FGFR1 inhibitor or clinical FGFR inhibitor out-score erdafitinib on the erdafitinib-bound FGFR1 structure 5EW8 by more than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise? Falsifier: a kinase assay showing the winner's FGFR1 IC50 not better than erdafitinib's 1.2 nM, or a cell-viability assay on an FGFR1-amplified line (NCI-H520) showing no better growth inhibition. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — erdafitinib re-docked on its own co-crystal (5EW8) as the control, three ChEMBL analogues and pemigatinib docked on the same structure with the same box and exhaustiveness — association only beyond that, since docking scores are not IC50 and not tumour response.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-26: the FGFR1 amplification frequencies (Weiss et al., Sci Transl Med 2010;2:62ra93; Turner et al., Cancer Res 2010;70:2085; Clin Cancer Res 2016;22:259); the erdafitinib approval trial (Loriot et al., N Engl J Med 2019;381:338–348, PMID 31340094); the erdafitinib–FGFR1 structure and the FGFR mutation landscape (Patani et al., Oncotarget 2016;7:24252 — 5EW8, 1.63 Å); the RAGNAR phase 2 study of erdafitinib in FGFR-altered solid tumours; and pemigatinib's approvals (FDA 2020 for FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma; 2022 for myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with FGFR1 rearrangement). The classical-canon sweep: the Canon of Medicine describes tumours (waram) and their treatment without a kinase concept; the principle carried is hifz al-nafs, with the honest note that no classical source addresses FGFR1.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB P11362 (FGFR1, Homo sapiens) → ChEMBL lookup returned 26 ranked leads. Two records deserve stating, not hiding: CHEMBL3545376 (IC50 0.25 nM) and CHEMBL5189383 (IC50 0.2 nM) carry erdafitinib's exact descriptors (MW 446.56, logP 4.18, TPSA 77.33) — CHEMBL3545376 is erdafitinib's own ChEMBL record and CHEMBL5189383 is the same compound under another record — so they are not independent leads and are not used as comparators. The genuinely distinct comparators are CHEMBL3980069 (IC50 0.3631 nM), CHEMBL5182360 (0.28 nM) and CHEMBL5799893 (0.355 nM), plus the clinical comparator pemigatinib (PubChem CID 86705695), whose SMILES was verified live against PubChem. The QUERY (erdafitinib) verified against PubChem (CID 67462786, C25H30N6O2, MW 446.56, logP 4.18, 1 H-bond donor, 7 acceptors, TPSA 77.33 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations). The auto-picker found no PDB to dock on (its <3.0 Å X-ray filter plus the ligand-centre check skipped 5EW8 — see §2.3 for the manual correction).

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Primary structure: 5EW8, the 1.63 Å X-ray structure of the FGFR1 kinase domain in complex with erdafitinib (Patani et al., Oncotarget 2016;7:24252), grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised erdafitinib, verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center. Erdafitinib is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure. The structure shows erdafitinib bound to an inactive (αC-out, DFG-in) conformation — a type I½ inhibitor — so the pocket is in erdafitinib's conformation and favours its own scaffold; the paper states this rather than letting the headline stand alone. All five compounds were docked with the same box, centre and exhaustiveness.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all five compounds. All are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all five compounds (molecular weight, logP, H-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations). No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran a kNN read-across at low maximum similarity, which is not safety data; it is omitted rather than presented.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ IC50. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, and the ChEMBL IC50s in this set span only 0.2–0.36 nM — a 1.8-fold range that is inside both assay noise and docking noise — so this docking can rank scaffolds but cannot resolve sub-nanomolar potency differences; the published IC50s carry that claim, not this computation. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published IC50s and the published structure. The 5EW8 pocket is in erdafitinib's αC-out conformation, so it favours erdafitinib-like scaffolds over pemigatinib's. Erdafitinib's published FGFR1 IC50 (1.2 nM) and its ChEMBL records (0.2–0.25 nM) differ 5-fold — assay variation, stated in §3.2 — so no ChEMBL number is treated as the true value. FGFR-family selectivity is not measured here: a compound that scores well on FGFR1 may bind FGFR2/3/4 equally, and the hyperphosphataemia that limits erdafitinib is an FGFR1/3-mediated effect, so selectivity is the question the docking cannot answer.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Published FGFR1 IC50 (nM) PAINS
Pemigatinib −10.53 −10.53, −10.50, −9.08 Not reported in sources searched Clean
CHEMBL5799893 −9.88 −9.88, −8.91, −8.81 0.355 Clean
CHEMBL3980069 −9.59 −9.59, −9.51, −9.48 0.3631 Clean
CHEMBL5182360 −9.14 −9.14, −8.99, −8.93 0.28 Clean
Erdafitinib (reference, self-dock control) −9.00 −9.00, −8.83, −8.44 1.2 Clean

Pose consistency is tight for two compounds and not for two. CHEMBL3980069 (spread 0.11) and CHEMBL5182360 (spread 0.21) converged on the same binding mode three times, so their scores are the most trustworthy in the table. Pemigatinib's top two poses converge (−10.53, −10.50) and its third is 1.45 kcal/mol worse, so its lead is real as a docking result but rests on two poses. CHEMBL5799893's −9.88 rests on a single pose — its other two poses are −8.91 and −8.81, a full kcal/mol worse — so its honest score is ~−8.9, below erdafitinib, and its rank in the table should be read as second-to-last, not second. The ranking itself is the problem. Pemigatinib leads erdafitinib by 1.53 kcal/mol, inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so no compound beats erdafitinib beyond noise. Worse, the ranking inverts the published IC50 order: by IC50 the order is CHEMBL5182360 (0.28 nM) > CHEMBL5799893 (0.355) ≈ CHEMBL3980069 (0.363) > erdafitinib (1.2 nM), while by docking it is pemigatinib > CHEMBL5799893 > CHEMBL3980069 > CHEMBL5182360 > erdafitinib — the most potent ChEMBL compound by IC50 ranks fourth of five, and erdafitinib, the co-crystallised ligand, ranks last on its own structure. The 5-fold spread between erdafitinib's published IC50 (1.2 nM) and its own ChEMBL records (0.2–0.25 nM) is itself larger than the 1.8-fold spread across the three ChEMBL compounds, so the "more potent" ChEMBL numbers may be assay variation rather than potency — and the docking, which is the only like-for-like comparison in this study, does not reproduce them.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published docking study of FGFR inhibitors on 5EW8 was found in the searches for this paper, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The comparison that exists is against the published IC50 values, and it is reported in §3.1 in full — including the inversion, not just the agreements. One assay-variation note, stated in §2.6 and repeated here because it decides the interpretation: erdafitinib's published FGFR1 IC50 is 1.2 nM while its own ChEMBL records give 0.2–0.25 nM, so no ChEMBL IC50 in this set can be treated as the true value.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem: which erdafitinib?

The comparison that matters clinically is not IC50 against IC50. Erdafitinib's published FGFR1 IC50 (1.2 nM) and its ChEMBL records (0.2–0.25 nM) differ 5-fold for the same compound — the same assay-variation problem that makes the three ChEMBL compounds (0.28–0.36 nM) look "more potent" than erdafitinib. A ranking built on numbers that cannot agree about the reference drug is ranking assay conditions, not compounds. The same problem applies to the clinical comparison: pemigatinib was optimised for FGFR2, not FGFR1, and its FGFR1 IC50 was not reported in the sources searched — so its docking lead on FGFR1 has no published potency to be checked against, and the kinase assay in §4.5 is the first measurement that would settle it.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the question changes from "which FGFR inhibitor?" to "can docking rank kinase inhibitors at all?"

The paper set out to find whether any FGFR1 inhibitor beats erdafitinib on the FGFR1 kinase domain. The answer is no — not because erdafitinib is unbeatable (its published IC50 is the worst in the set, and its own ChEMBL records say it is 5-fold better than its label value), but because the method cannot tell. Pemigatinib's 1.53 kcal/mol lead is a real number and a non-result at the same time: it is inside the noise bar, and the control that would have validated it — erdafitinib on its own structure — scored worst of the five. The question therefore changes: the finding is not "pemigatinib wins" but "Vina on a single kinase structure cannot rank a congeneric series whose published IC50s span only ~4-fold". That is a useful negative, and it is the paper's actual contribution — it stops a drug programme that the raw table, read naively, would seem to support.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the margin: 1.53 kcal/mol against a ±1–2 kcal/mol noise bar is not a lead, it is a tie with a sign. Second, the self-dock control: erdafitinib last of five on its own structure means the pocket conformation, not the compounds, is doing part of the ranking. Third, the pose problem: CHEMBL5799893's second place rests on a single pose, and pemigatinib's lead on two — the only compound in the table whose ranking is fully converged is CHEMBL3980069, which leads erdafitinib by 0.59 kcal/mol, well inside noise. Fourth, the missing pharmacology: the docking cannot see the αC-out/DFG-in equilibrium or the gatekeeper mutations that decide clinical resistance — the two properties that separate erdafitinib from the next FGFR inhibitor. Any one of these would be enough to withhold a claim; together they close it.

4.3 Mechanism

Erdafitinib is a pan-FGFR inhibitor that binds in the ATP pocket in the αC-out/DFG-in conformation — type I½. Its pyrimidinyl-pyrazole core occupies the adenine pocket, and its dimethoxyphenyl group extends into a hydrophobic pocket that opens only when the αC helix moves out. The published biochemical profile (FGFR1 1.2 nM, FGFR2 2.5 nM, FGFR3 3 nM, FGFR4 5.7 nM; Kd 0.24–2.2 nM) reflects that binding mode, and the clinical hyperphosphataemia (75.9% of patients) is the on-target signature of FGFR inhibition of phosphate homeostasis — a pharmacodynamic marker, not a side effect to be wished away. The resistance mutations that matter clinically are gatekeeper mutations (FGFR1 V561M, FGFR3 V555M) and the molecular-brake mutations (FGFR3 N540K, FGFR1 N546K), which shift the kinase toward the active conformation that type I½ inhibitors bind poorly. Test for each link: (i) a kinase inhibition assay measures IC50 directly against the published values; (ii) a cellular assay (FGFR1-amplified lung cancer cell line) measures growth inhibition and phospho-FGFR suppression; (iii) a gatekeeper-mutant kinase assay measures the fold-loss in potency, which is the property that decides whether a compound survives resistance.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring compound on 5EW8 has an IC50 within 3-fold of its published value in the same kinase assay. Falsifier: IC50 more than 3-fold worse than published. (Status after this study: the hypothesis is already weakened — the docking order does not reproduce the published IC50 order, so the assay is now testing the method, not the compounds.)
  2. Erdafitinib out-scores pemigatinib on 5EW8 — the computational signature of erdafitinib's broader FGFR profile, since pemigatinib was optimised for FGFR2. Falsifier: pemigatinib scores better, which would suggest the FGFR1 pocket does not discriminate the two drugs. (Status after this study: pemigatinib scored better by 1.53 kcal/mol — the hypothesis is refuted, and the FGFR1 pocket does not discriminate the two drugs by docking.)
  3. No ChEMBL compound out-scores erdafitinib by more than 2 kcal/mol. Falsifier: one does, which would make it a candidate for the kinase assay rather than a footnote. (Status after this study: the hypothesis holds — the largest ChEMBL lead is 0.88 kcal/mol — but it holds vacuously, because the method cannot resolve the differences it was asked to measure.)

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): kinase inhibition assay for the five compounds on FGFR1, FGFR2 and FGFR3, same plate, n=3, with erdafitinib's published IC50 values (1.2, 2.5, 3 nM) as the controls; readout IC50. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): cellular assay for the best two compounds from stage 1 on an FGFR1-amplified lung cancer cell line, measuring growth inhibition and phospho-FGFR suppression, with erdafitinib as the control. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — IC50 within 3-fold of erdafitinib's on FGFR1 and a cellular effect — a gatekeeper-mutant (V561M) kinase assay for that compound; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every margin except a lead larger than 2 kcal/mol.
  2. The 5EW8 pocket is in erdafitinib's conformation, so part of any erdafitinib lead is conformational favouritism; the cleaner comparison is among the four non-erdafitinib compounds.
  3. The three ChEMBL compounds have no recorded assay type in the pipeline output, so their IC50 values (0.28–0.36 nM) may not be comparable to erdafitinib's published values; a "more potent" ChEMBL compound may simply have been assayed differently.
  4. The pipeline returned erdafitinib itself as its own "lead" (CHEMBL3545376, 0.25 nM) and a duplicate record (CHEMBL5189383, 0.2 nM, identical descriptors), so no ChEMBL-derived independent FGFR1 ligand set exists in this study beyond the three compounds used.
  5. The docking cannot see the αC-out/DFG-in equilibrium or the gatekeeper mutations that decide clinical resistance — the two properties that separate erdafitinib from the next FGFR inhibitor.
  6. No published Pakistani study reports FGFR1 amplification frequencies in lung or breast cancer, so the clinical picture is global; the Pakistani numbers in this paper are burden numbers, not response numbers.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no FGFR-relevant text: the Canon describes cancer without a kinase concept, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

No FGFR1 inhibitor beats erdafitinib on the FGFR1 structure 5EW8 by more than Vina's noise: pemigatinib leads by 1.53 kcal/mol, inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol bar, and the method fails its own control — erdafitinib scores worst of five on its own structure, and the most potent ChEMBL compound by published IC50 ranks fourth. Docking cannot rank the FGFR1 inhibitors, and no drug programme follows from these scores. The next step is a kinase inhibition assay on the same five compounds, which will either reproduce the published IC50 order and rehabilitate the docking, or confirm that the ranking is a pocket artefact.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, with the provincial cancer institutes that run oncology services. Decision: whether to spend anything on FGFR testing or on an erdafitinib programme, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not spend on an erdafitinib programme on the basis of docking — the drug is not on Pakistan's essential medicines list and its cost is far beyond public procurement; instead, fund a molecular-testing survey for FGFR alterations in lung and breast cancer at the provincial cancer institutes, so Pakistan's own alteration frequencies are measured rather than assumed from the global 10–25% figures, and so the patients who would benefit from an FGFR inhibitor are identified before any drug is bought. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the survey shows FGFR1 amplification above 10% in squamous lung carcinoma and a cost-effectiveness analysis shows an FGFR inhibitor is affordable at a negotiated price, move to a procurement assessment; if the survey shows alteration rates below 5%, keep the money on testing for the commoner targets (EGFR, HER2) — do not proceed to any FGFR drug programme on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to adl (justice): where the drug is unaffordable and the patients are unidentified, spending on the drug before spending on the test would violate both. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the testing survey", not "do the policy".

Telmisartan Leads Losartan by 1.52 kcal/mol on AT1R — but Docking Cannot Rank the Sartans: the Self-Dock Control and the Active Metabolite Both Invert the Published Order

Hypertension affects 18.9% of Pakistanis and 70% of hypertensives do not know they have it; losartan, the first angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) blocker, is the weakest binder of its class by published rank order, and the question was whether any sartan beats it on the human AT1R structure.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-26 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #119 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: angiotensin II type 1 receptor; sartans; losartan; telmisartan; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; hypertension; Pakistan

Abstract

Hypertension affects 18.9% of Pakistanis and 70% of hypertensives do not know they have it; losartan, the first angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) blocker, is the weakest binder of its class by published rank order, and the question was whether any sartan beats it on the human AT1R structure. Six sartans — losartan, its active metabolite EXP3174, candesartan, telmisartan, valsartan and olmesartan — were docked with standardised AutoDock Vina on the 2.8 Å olmesartan-bound AT1R structure 4ZUD, same box and exhaustiveness, with olmesartan as the self-dock control. Telmisartan scored best at −10.57 kcal/mol, 1.52 kcal/mol better than losartan at −9.05, but that lead is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the answer to the falsifiable question is no: no sartan beats losartan beyond noise. The method then failed its own controls: olmesartan, the co-crystallised ligand, scored only fourth (−8.90), and EXP3174 — 10–40 times more potent than losartan in published assays — scored worse than losartan (−8.68). Docking therefore cannot rank sartans on this structure, and no procurement or prescribing switch follows from these scores. Pose consistency was tight for every compound (three-pose spread 0.12–0.22 kcal/mol), so the ranking is not a sampling artefact; it is a scoring-function failure, and the same failure would apply to any procurement ranking built on these scores. The falsifier is a radioligand binding assay: if telmisartan's Ki is not better than losartan's by more than 3-fold on the same plate, the docking lead is a pocket artefact.

1. Introduction

Hypertension affects 18.9% of Pakistanis, diabetes 26.7%, and chronic kidney disease 16.7% (range 12.5–29.9%), with hypertension the cause of 30–40% of CKD; end-stage renal disease incidence is 100–150 per million while the dialysis rate is only 15 per million. Tazeen Jafar (N Engl J Med 2006;354:995–997) found 15–20% of Pakistanis aged 40+ with reduced GFR, a third of those 45+ hypertensive, and 70% of hypertensives unaware. The angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R, AGTR1, UniProt P30556, 359 aa) is the GPCR through which angiotensin II raises blood pressure, retains sodium and drives aldosterone — and the sartans (ARBs) that block it are the most prescribed antihypertensive class in the world. Losartan, the first ARB (FDA 1995), is a surmountable, competitive antagonist whose active metabolite EXP3174 is 10–40 times more potent by weight; the FDA label records ~1,000-fold selectivity for AT1 over AT2. The rank order of sartan binding affinity (candesartan 1, telmisartan 10, EXP3174 10, losartan 50, eprosartan 100; PMID 10579749) makes losartan the weakest binder of the class — which is the gap this paper attacks: do newer or unexploited scaffolds actually bind the AT1R pocket better than losartan, on losartan's own terms, i.e. in the same structure with the same protocol?

Falsifiable question. Does any sartan or sartan-like scaffold out-score losartan on the human AT1R structure 4ZUD by more than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise? Falsifier: a radioligand binding assay showing the winner's Ki not better than losartan's, or a functional assay showing no greater rightward shift of the angiotensin II dose–response curve. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — olmesartan re-docked on its own co-crystal (4ZUD) as the control, losartan and four other sartans docked on the same structure with the same box and exhaustiveness — association only beyond that, since docking scores are not affinity and not blood pressure.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-26: the AT1R structures (Zhang et al., Cell 2015;161:833–844, PMID 25913193, DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2015.04.011 — 4YAY, 2.9 Å, ZD7155; and Zhang et al., J Biol Chem 2015;290:29127 — 4ZUD, 2.8 Å, olmesartan); the sartan pharmacology review (PMID 10579749 — rank order of affinities, surmountable vs insurmountable antagonism); the losartan FDA label (1000-fold AT1/AT2 selectivity; EXP3174 10–40× more potent; ~33% bioavailability; CYP2C9/3A4); the Pakistan burden review (CKD 16.7%, hypertension 18.9%); and Jafar (NEJM 2006;354:995–997). The classical-canon sweep: Ibn Sina's Canon treats hypertension's symptoms (headache, palpitation, renal disease) without a receptor concept; the principle carried is hifz al-nafs.

2.2 Target identification — and the pipeline failure that had to be corrected

The pipeline resolved the target WRONG on the first run: UniProtKB Q9WVK0 (Mus musculus, type-1 angiotensin II receptor-associated protein, AGTRAP, 161 aa) — a negative regulator of AT1R signalling, not the receptor itself — and its ChEMBL lookup returned silicon-containing glucosidase inhibitors, not sartans. The mismatch is stated, not hidden: the pipeline's target search matched "angiotensin II type 1 receptor" to the associated protein, and its 26 ranked "leads" are not used anywhere in this paper. The comparison set was therefore built from the literature: the six sartans with the strongest published AT1R data, with SMILES verified live against PubChem by name and CID (losartan CID 3961; EXP3174 CID 108185; candesartan CID 2541; telmisartan CID 65999; valsartan CID 60846; olmesartan CID 158781). The correct target is human AT1R, UniProt P30556.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Primary structure: 4ZUD, the 2.8 Å X-ray structure of human AT1R in complex with olmesartan (Zhang et al., J Biol Chem 2015;290:29127), grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised olmesartan, verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center. Olmesartan is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover binding for the drug in its own pocket would be broken. Losartan has no co-crystal with AT1R, so it is docked into the olmesartan pocket — the standard cross-docking setup, with the caveat stated in §2.6 that the pocket is in olmesartan's conformation and favours its own ligand. All six compounds were docked with the same box, centre and exhaustiveness.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all six compounds. All six are PAINS-clean: losartan, EXP3174, candesartan, telmisartan, valsartan and olmesartan carry no PAINS alert. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all six compounds (molecular weight, logP, H-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations). No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran against the wrong target (AGTRAP), and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ affinity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published affinities and the published structure. The 4ZUD pocket is in olmesartan's conformation, so it favours olmesartan over the other five sartans. Vina's rigid, water-free scoring cannot see the GPCR's membrane environment, the sodium ion site, or the receptor's active/inactive conformational equilibrium — the three things that decide whether an antagonist works in a cell. Losartan's measured affinity is the lowest of the class by rank order, but affinity is not blood pressure: losartan's metabolite, its insurmountable-vs-surmountable kinetics and its duration of action are not in this computation.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Target (PDB) Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
Telmisartan AT1R (4ZUD) −10.57 −10.57, −10.53, −10.44 Clean
Candesartan AT1R (4ZUD) −9.53 −9.53, −9.44, −9.32 Clean
Losartan (reference) AT1R (4ZUD) −9.05 −9.05, −9.00, −8.86 Clean
Olmesartan (self-dock control) AT1R (4ZUD) −8.90 −8.90, −8.78, −8.68 Clean
EXP3174 (losartan metabolite) AT1R (4ZUD) −8.68 −8.68, −8.52, −8.48 Clean
Valsartan AT1R (4ZUD) −7.79 −7.79, −7.77, −7.67 Clean

Pose consistency is tight for every compound: the spread across the three poses is 0.12–0.22 kcal/mol, so the ranking is not a pose-sampling artefact — each compound converged on the same binding mode three times. The ranking itself is the problem. Telmisartan leads losartan by 1.52 kcal/mol, candesartan by 0.48 kcal/mol, and both margins are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise: neither clears the bar the falsifiable question set. The two controls then fail in opposite directions. Olmesartan — the drug co-crystallised in this very pocket, the self-dock control — scores fourth of six at −8.90, worse than losartan, candesartan and telmisartan; a scoring function that cannot rank its own ligand first cannot be trusted to rank the class. EXP3174 — losartan's active metabolite, 10–40 times more potent than losartan by weight in published assays — scores fifth at −8.68, 0.37 kcal/mol worse than its own parent. The published rank order is candesartan 1, telmisartan 10, EXP3174 10, losartan 50; the docking order is telmisartan 1, candesartan 2, losartan 3, olmesartan 4, EXP3174 5, valsartan 6. The docking reproduces the top two in the right order and then inverts the rest. The honest reading is that Vina on 4ZUD separates the strong binders from the weak ones (valsartan last, −7.79, 1.26 kcal/mol behind losartan) but cannot resolve the differences that matter — the 5-fold gap between candesartan and losartan, and the 10–40-fold gap between EXP3174 and losartan, are both invisible to it.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published docking study of sartans on 4ZUD was found in the searches for this paper, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The comparison that exists is against the published affinity rank order (PMID 10579749), and it is reported in §3.1 in full — including the two inversions, not just the agreements.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem: which losartan?

The comparison that matters clinically is not losartan-the-molecule against telmisartan-the-molecule. In a patient, losartan is a prodrug: most of its effect comes from EXP3174, which is 10–40 times more potent. Docking the parent alone therefore understates the drug by an order of magnitude, and docking the metabolite alone overstates nothing — it scores worse than the parent here, which is the opposite of the published pharmacology. Any ranking that treats "losartan" as one molecule is ranking the wrong thing, and any procurement decision built on such a ranking would be built on a category error. The same problem applies to the other sartans in a smaller way: candesartan is dosed as the prodrug candesartan cilexetil, and telmisartan's long half-life (24 h) and high volume of distribution are properties no docking score can see.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the question changes from "which sartan?" to "can docking rank sartans at all?"

The paper set out to find whether any sartan beats losartan on AT1R. The answer is no — not because losartan is the best binder (it is not, by published affinity), but because the method cannot tell. Telmisartan's 1.52 kcal/mol lead is a real number and a non-result at the same time: it is inside the noise bar, and the two controls that would have validated it both failed. The question therefore changes: the finding is not "telmisartan wins" but "Vina on a single GPCR structure cannot rank a congeneric series whose published affinities span only ~50-fold". That is a useful negative, and it is the paper's actual contribution — it stops a procurement or prescribing switch that the raw table, read naively, would seem to support.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the margin: 1.52 kcal/mol against a ±1–2 kcal/mol noise bar is not a lead, it is a tie with a sign. Second, the self-dock control: olmesartan fourth of six on its own structure means the pocket conformation, not the compounds, is doing part of the ranking. Third, the metabolite inversion: EXP3174 scoring worse than losartan contradicts 10–40-fold published potency, which means the scoring function is blind to the carboxylate interaction that makes the metabolite potent — the very interaction the 4YAY structure shows matters (Arg167). Fourth, the missing pharmacology: affinity is not blood pressure, and the properties that separate losartan from the insurmountable sartans — dissociation kinetics, the active metabolite, duration of action — are not in this computation at all. Any one of these would be enough to withhold a claim; together they close it.

4.3 Mechanism

Sartans bind the orthosteric pocket of AT1R, where angiotensin II would bind. The 4YAY structure (Zhang et al., Cell 2015) showed the binding mode for the class: the biphenyl-tetrazole moiety sits deep in the pocket, with the tetrazole making an ionic interaction with Arg167, and Trp84 and Tyr35 contributing π–π and hydrogen-bond contacts. Losartan carries the same biphenyl-tetrazole on an imidazole core with a hydroxymethyl group; its active metabolite EXP3174 replaces that group with a carboxylate, which strengthens the ionic interaction — the structural reason EXP3174 is 10–40 times more potent by weight. The pharmacological split that matters clinically is kinetic, not thermodynamic: losartan is a surmountable antagonist (parallel rightward shift of the angiotensin II curve, fast dissociation), while candesartan, telmisartan, irbesartan, valsartan and EXP3174 are insurmountable (they depress the maximal response, slow dissociation). Test for each link: (i) a radioligand binding assay measures Ki directly against the published rank order; (ii) a functional assay (angiotensin II dose–response in rabbit aorta or calcium flux in AT1R-expressing cells) measures surmountable vs insurmountable behaviour; (iii) a washout experiment measures dissociation half-life, which is the property that separates losartan from the rest of the class.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring sartan on 4ZUD has a Ki within 3-fold of its published rank-order value in the same radioligand binding assay. Falsifier: Ki more than 3-fold worse than published. (Status after this study: the hypothesis is already weakened — the docking order does not reproduce the published order, so the assay is now testing the method, not the compounds.)
  2. The docking winner's advantage over losartan (if any) survives the functional assay: it produces a greater rightward shift of the angiotensin II dose–response curve than losartan at equal concentration. Falsifier: no greater shift, which would show the docking advantage is a pocket artefact.
  3. Olmesartan's self-dock score predicts its rank: if olmesartan does not score best or near-best on its own structure, the method — not the compounds — is the problem, and the ranking is discarded. Falsifier: olmesartan scores worst on 4ZUD. (Status after this study: olmesartan scored fourth of six — the hypothesis is refuted, and the ranking is discarded as a potency claim.)

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): radioligand binding assay for the six sartans on AT1R-expressing membranes, same plate, n=3, with losartan and candesartan as the low/high-affinity anchors; readout Ki. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): functional calcium-flux assay for the best two compounds from stage 1 against losartan, measuring the angiotensin II dose–response shift and the insurmountable/surmountable pattern; readout EC50 shift and maximal-response depression. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — Ki better than losartan by more than 3-fold and a greater functional shift — a dissociation-kinetics (washout) experiment for that compound; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every margin except a lead larger than 2 kcal/mol.
  2. The 4ZUD pocket is in olmesartan's conformation, so part of any olmesartan lead is conformational favouritism; the cleaner comparison is among the five non-olmesartan sartans.
  3. Losartan has no co-crystal with AT1R, so it is cross-docked into the olmesartan pocket — the standard setup, but a cross-dock, not a self-dock.
  4. The pipeline's target resolution failed (AGTRAP, mouse) and its ligand set was discarded; the comparison set is six literature compounds, and no ChEMBL-derived AT1R ligand set exists in this study.
  5. Affinity is not blood pressure: the docking cannot see dissociation kinetics, the active metabolite, or duration of action — the three properties that separate losartan from the insurmountable sartans clinically.
  6. No published Pakistani study reports AT1R variant frequencies or sartan response rates, so the clinical picture is global; the Pakistani numbers in this paper are burden numbers, not response numbers.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no AT1R-relevant text: the Canon describes hypertension's symptoms without a receptor concept, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

No sartan beats losartan on the human AT1R structure 4ZUD by more than Vina's noise: telmisartan leads by 1.52 kcal/mol, inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol bar, and the method fails its own controls — olmesartan scores fourth on its own structure and EXP3174 scores worse than its parent despite being 10–40 times more potent. Docking cannot rank the sartans, and no switch from losartan follows from these scores. The next step is a radioligand binding assay on the same six compounds, which will either reproduce the published rank order and rehabilitate the docking, or confirm that the ranking is a pocket artefact.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, with the provincial health departments that run primary care. Decision: whether to spend anything switching antihypertensive procurement from losartan to a newer sartan, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not switch procurement on the basis of affinity rankings — losartan is the cheapest sartan, the most widely available, and the only one whose active metabolite is 10–40 times more potent than the parent, which partly closes its affinity gap in vivo; instead, fund a blood-pressure measurement and control-rate survey in primary care, because the binding question is settled and the delivery question is not — only about a third of Pakistani adults have ever had their blood pressure measured and 70% of hypertensives do not know they have the disease. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the survey shows control rates above 50% on losartan and a head-to-head trial shows a newer sartan controls blood pressure better by more than 5 mmHg systolic at equal cost, move to a procurement assessment for that sartan; if the survey confirms the measurement gap, keep the money on screening and losartan supply — do not proceed to any drug switch on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs joined to adl (justice): where the effective drug is already cheap and the gap is that people are never measured, spending on the newer drug before spending on measurement would violate both. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the survey", not "do the policy".

AMG-517 Beats Capsaicin by 2.19 kcal/mol in the Human TRPV1 Vanilloid Pocket — but It Is the Antagonist That Failed in Phase I for Hyperthermia Past 40 °C

Chronic pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide — about 619 million people lived with low back pain in 2020 — yet the analgesic ladder runs from NSAIDs that fail in neuropathic pain to opioids that carry dependence liability.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-25 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #115 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: TRPV1; capsaicin; chronic pain; molecular docking; SB-705498; AMG-517; hyperthermia; vanilloid pocket; Pakistan

Abstract

Chronic pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide — about 619 million people lived with low back pain in 2020 — yet the analgesic ladder runs from NSAIDs that fail in neuropathic pain to opioids that carry dependence liability. TRPV1, the capsaicin receptor on pain-sensing nerve endings, is the non-opioid target: capsaicin itself works only topically, as the 8% patch, while every systemic TRPV1 antagonist that reached humans failed — AMG-517 for hyperthermia past 40 °C. We asked whether known antagonists and ChEMBL similarity leads bind the human TRPV1 vanilloid pocket more strongly than re-docked capsaicin. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q8NER1 → ChEMBL CHEMBL4794 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked ten compounds on 8GFA, the 2.29 Å human TRPV1 structure with the antagonist SB-366791, centred exactly on its co-crystallised ligand (centre audit by direct PDB computation — the pipeline's own centre picker lands on a phospholipid 18.4 Å from the pocket). Capsaicin re-docked at −8.26 kcal/mol and SB-366791 self-docked at −9.36 kcal/mol, validating the protocol. AMG-517 scored best at −10.45 kcal/mol, ahead of capsaicin by 2.19, beyond Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; SB-705498 scored −9.91 and three pipeline leads scored −9.65 to −9.73, all ahead of capsaicin but inside noise. The honest limit: the best binder is the drug that failed in Phase I for fever, the ranking rests on a single antagonist-bound structure, resiniferatoxin failed to dock, and a docking score cannot tell an agonist from an antagonist. The falsifiable next step is a calcium-flux assay of AMG-517 and SB-705498 against capsaicin-evoked human TRPV1 activation, with proton-mode selectivity and core-temperature monitoring: if AMG-517's IC50 is not within 3-fold of SB-705498's published 3 nM, or if it blocks the proton mode as potently as the capsaicin mode, the docking ranking is refuted as a drug lead.

1. Introduction

Chronic pain is the largest single cause of disability on earth. The Global Burden of Disease 2021 analysis counted about 619 million people living with low back pain in 2020 — the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide — and projects about 843 million cases by 2050. In Pakistan, where most pain care is paid for out of pocket, the standard analgesic ladder runs from paracetamol and NSAIDs, which fail in neuropathic pain and injure stomach and kidney with chronic use, to opioids, which carry dependence liability. A non-opioid target that works peripherally, without reaching the brain's reward circuits, is the gap this paper attacks.

That target is transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1; gene TRPV1, chromosome 17p13.2; UniProt Q8NER1; 839 amino acids): a non-selective, calcium-permeant cation channel in the free nerve endings of primary pain-sensing Aδ and C fibres. It is a polymodal integrator — opened by noxious heat above about 42 °C, by protons, and by vanilloids — and it mediates inflammatory pain and hyperalgesia. Its genetics and pharmacology are unusually clean for a pain target: the channel was cloned as the capsaicin receptor (Hayes et al., Pain 2000;88:205–215; PMID 11050376), and its activation by capsaicin is selective — capsaicin does not activate the homologous TRPV2–6 channels.

The reference drug of this paper is capsaicin itself — and the paper states its route plainly, because the route is the point. Capsaicin is a TOPICAL drug, not an oral systemic one. It activates TRPV1 with an EC50 of approximately 700 nM, and the 8% cutaneous patch (Qutenza) works by a paradox: a single 60-minute application over-activates the channel until the nerve ending desensitises, giving months of relief. In the pivotal trials a single application cut pain by 22.8–32.3% against 10.7–25.0% for control patches, with 34–47% of patients reaching a 30% response against 18–36% on control, and retreatment every 90 days (EMA product information; Backonja et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7:1106–1112 — 402 patients with postherpetic neuralgia, −29.6% against −19.9% at weeks 2–8, 42% against 32% responders). Only about 1% of the applied capsaicin is absorbed into the skin. The drug's weakness is therefore not efficacy but reach: it treats the patch area and nothing else, it burns on application, and it cannot help pain that is widespread, deep, or central.

The obvious next step — a systemic TRPV1 antagonist, a pill that blocks the channel everywhere — failed in humans for a reason docking cannot see but this paper must report. AMG-517, a potent (IC50 < 10 nM), selective, orally bioavailable antagonist, produced marked, reversible, plasma-concentration-dependent hyperthermia in Phase I, and after molar extraction it caused long-lasting hyperthermia with body temperature surpassing 40 °C (Gavva et al., Pain 2008;136:202–210; PMID 18337008). The authors' conclusion was unhedged: TRPV1-selective antagonists like AMG-517 cannot be developed for systemic use as stand-alone agents. The mechanism was worked out in rats in the same programme: the drug constricted tail skin vessels and increased thermogenesis — TRPV1 tonically restrains both. The field's response was mode selectivity: Garami et al. (J Neurosci 2010;30:1435–1440) showed across eight antagonists that hyperthermia tracks blockade of the proton mode of TRPV1 activation (sensitivity 0.43–0.65), not the heat mode (0.00–0.01) — so an antagonist that spares proton activation might be fever-free. SB-705498, the GSK antagonist that reached Phase II (migraine, cough, dental pain), embodied the test: in a first-in-human study it was safe and well tolerated at single oral doses up to 400 mg, reduced the capsaicin-evoked flare area (p = 0.0047) and raised the heat pain threshold by 1.3 °C (Chizh et al., Pain 2007;132:132–141; PMID 17659837). It was not developed further for pain.

The structural ground truth is now good. The first TRPV1 structures came from single-particle cryo-EM: the apo rat channel at 3.4 Å (Liao et al., Nature 2013;504:107–112; PMID 24305160) and the capsaicin- and resiniferatoxin-bound states at 4.2 and 3.8 Å (Cao et al., Nature 2013;504:113–118; PMID 24305161) — but capsaicin itself was never modelled as a ligand in those entries, only a small density near segments S3–S4. The atomic mechanism came from computation validated by mutagenesis: capsaicin binds "tail-up, head-down", its vanillyl and amide groups anchoring to the S4–S5 linker and pulling it to stabilise the open state (Yang et al., Nat Chem Biol 2015;11:518–524). The structure used here is the newest and best: human TRPV1 in complex with the antagonist SB-366791 at 2.29 Å (Neuberger et al., Nat Commun 2023;14:2451; PMID 37117175), the first human TRPV1 structure with a drug-like antagonist modelled in the vanilloid pocket.

The classical medical canon knows pain, not the channel — and it cannot know capsaicin at all: Capsicum is a New World plant, unknown in the Old World before 1492, so no text of Ibn Sina or Al-Razi can contain it. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes pain (waja') and its remedies as syndromes, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records clinical observation of pain treatments — but neither describes a capsaicin-like drug, and this paper does not pretend otherwise. The principle carried forward is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7): a painkiller that drives body temperature past 40 °C fails the first test of a medicine.

Falsifiable question. Do known TRPV1 antagonists and ChEMBL similarity leads bind the human TRPV1 vanilloid pocket (PDB 8GFA) more strongly than re-docked capsaicin, and does any of them combine a better docking score with a clean PAINS profile and a mode-selective rationale for avoiding hyperthermia? Falsifier: a calcium-flux assay showing the best-scoring compound's IC50 more than 3-fold worse than SB-705498's published 3 nM (capsaicin mode), or a thermoregulation study showing hyperthermia at analgesic exposure, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the co-crystallised antagonist SB-366791 re-docked on its own structure (8GFA) — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and not analgesia.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-25: the TRPV1 cloning paper (Hayes et al., Pain 2000;88:205–215; PMID 11050376); the first cryo-EM structures (Liao et al., Nature 2013;504:107–112; PMID 24305160; Cao et al., Nature 2013;504:113–118; PMID 24305161); the nanodisc structures (Gao et al., Nature 2016;534:347–351); the capsaicin binding mechanism (Yang et al., Nat Chem Biol 2015;11:518–524; doi:10.1038/nchembio.1835); the capsaicin/resiniferatoxin binding-mode analysis (Elokely et al., PNAS 2016;113:E137–E145); the human SB-366791 structure (Neuberger et al., Nat Commun 2023;14:2451; PMID 37117175); the AMG-517 hyperthermia report (Gavva et al., Pain 2008;136:202–210; PMID 18337008); the mode-selectivity analysis (Garami et al., J Neurosci 2010;30:1435–1440); the SB-705498 first-in-human study (Chizh et al., Pain 2007;132:132–141; PMID 17659837); the capsaicin analogue review (Fattori et al., Molecules 2016;21:966; doi:10.3390/molecules21080966); the Qutenza pivotal data (Backonja et al., Lancet Neurol 2008;7:1106–1112; EMA product information); the low-back-pain burden (GBD 2021, via BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2025); and the UniProtKB record for Q8NER1. The daily digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/ is stale (last 2026-11-14) and was not used.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB Q8NER1 (transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily V member 1, Homo sapiens, 839 amino acids) → ChEMBL target CHEMBL4794 → 41 known ligands with measured bioactivity → 25 similarity-screened leads → 26 ranked compounds (25 leads + the QUERY). The top five pipeline leads were taken forward. One identification from the sweep: CHEMBL17976, the pipeline's second lead, IS resiniferatoxin — the ultra-potent TRPV1 agonist, several thousand-fold more potent than capsaicin — so it is docked once, under its common name, not twice.

2.3 Molecular docking

Ten compounds were docked on PDB 8GFA (human TRPV1 in complex with SB-366791, 2.29 Å) using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised SB-366791 (residue ZEI, chain A, seqnum 1202), [105.36, 80.97, 88.36], computed directly from the PDB file. The tetramer has four equivalent vanilloid pockets, one per subunit; subunit A is used, exactly as the IRAK4 papers used one pocket.

Centre audit — the pipeline's own centre was wrong, and this paper caught it. The pipeline's run_docking.py reported no_pdb_found, because its find_pdb_for_uniprot accepts only X-ray structures below 3.0 Å and every TRPV1 structure is cryo-EM — a filter limitation, not an absence of structure. Worse, calling dock._ligand_center on 8GFA returns [92.49, 85.19, 76.00], which is the centroid of POV A 1201 — a phospholipid, not the drug site. POV is not in dock._LIPIDS, so the picker takes the largest HETATM group (POV, 134 atoms) over the drug (ZEI, 34 atoms); the lipid centroid sits about 18.4 Å from the vanilloid pocket, so a box centred there would miss the pocket. The correction script (health-papers-agent/dock_trpv1_8gfa_correction.py) centres on the ZEI centroid instead, verified against the RCSB chemical-component record (ZEI = SB-366791, C16H14ClNO2, PubChem CID 667594, ChEMBL CHEMBL122413). SB-366791 is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover strong binding for the drug in its own pocket would be broken.

Membrane caveat, stated not smoothed over. TRPV1 is a membrane channel and the vanilloid pocket is a lipid-facing site: in the apo nanodisc structures a phosphatidylinositol lipid occupies the capsaicin site, and capsaicin is thought to displace it. Vina docks into a rigid, water-free, membrane-free pocket — it cannot model lipid displacement, the membrane, or the channel's gating. A docking score here measures fit to the antagonist-bound closed conformation; it cannot tell an agonist from an antagonist, and 8GFA's closed conformation may favour antagonists over agonists. The scores are compared only as binding, never as analgesic potency.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all ten compounds. Nine are PAINS-clean. One is not: capsazepine carries a catechol_A(92) alert — the catechol is a known redox-cycling and assay-interference motif, and it changes the validation design (see §4.3). No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper.

2.5 ADMET and drug-likeness read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all ten compounds. Capsaicin: MW 305.42, logP 3.79, 2 hydrogen-bond donors, 3 acceptors, TPSA 58.56 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations — the smallest compound in the set and the most drug-like by the standard counts, which is consistent with its being the only compound here that is actually a medicine (topically). SB-366791: MW 287.75, logP 4.00, HBD 1, HBA 2, TPSA 38.33 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations — the smallest compound of all. SB-705498: MW 429.24, logP 4.26, HBD 2, HBA 3, TPSA 57.26 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations. AMG-517: MW 430.41, logP 5.52, HBD 1, HBA 6, TPSA 77.00 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 1 violation (logP > 5) — the poor water solubility that the literature records as one reason it stopped. Capsazepine: MW 376.91, logP 3.62, HBD 3, HBA 3, TPSA 55.73 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations, plus the catechol PAINS alert. The pipeline leads are the largest and least drug-like: CHEMBL3681230 (MW 516.36, 1 violation), resiniferatoxin (MW 628.72, 1 violation), CHEMBL4242293 (MW 475.34, logP 5.08, 1 violation) and CHEMBL3407765 (MW 519.97, 1 violation) — size is a confounder for their scores, and the paper says so in §3.1 and §4.2 rather than letting any headline stand alone. No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran only on the QUERY, and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity, and for this target docking ≠ function: an agonist and an antagonist can score identically in the same pocket while doing opposite things to the channel. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published potencies and trial results. The five pipeline leads have no published TRPV1 potency at all — they are similarity hits against ChEMBL actives, not measured inhibitors. The structure used (8GFA, SB-366791-bound, 2.29 Å) holds the channel in the antagonist-bound closed conformation, which favours antagonists. Capsaicin was never modelled as a ligand in any TRPV1 structure, so there is no capsaicin-bound human structure to cross-check against.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

AMG-517 scores best at −10.45 kcal/mol, ahead of capsaicin by 2.19 kcal/mol — the only gap in the table larger than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — with tight pose consistency (−10.45, −9.61, −9.49). SB-705498 follows at −9.91 kcal/mol, 1.65 ahead of capsaicin, inside noise, with only two poses returned (−9.91, −9.66). The three pipeline leads cluster at −9.65 to −9.73 kcal/mol, 1.39–1.47 ahead of capsaicin, all inside noise; two of the three have very tight poses (CHEMBL3407765: −9.73, −9.70, −9.57; CHEMBL4242293: −9.67, −9.54, −9.52), but the third does not — CHEMBL228451's poses spread from −9.65 to −2.36, so its best score is a single-pose outlier and the honest reading is its median pose, −7.85, which would put it behind capsaicin. The self-dock control works: SB-366791 re-docks at −9.36 kcal/mol on its own structure with moderate pose consistency (−9.36, −8.67, −8.63), so the protocol recovers strong binding for the drug in its own pocket — but the co-crystallised drug does not win on its own structure, coming sixth of nine. Capsaicin re-docks at −8.26 kcal/mol with tight poses (−8.26, −8.12, −7.80): the reference drug is consistent, and it is beaten by six of the nine compounds that docked. CHEMBL3681230, the pipeline's top-ranked similarity lead, loses to capsaicin by 0.10 kcal/mol — inside noise, but a loss all the same, and the largest pipeline lead by molecular weight (516.36). Capsazepine is the worst compound in the set at −6.74 kcal/mol, 1.52 behind capsaicin, with very tight poses (−6.74, −6.70, −6.66) — consistently bad, not noisily bad — and it carries the set's only PAINS alert. Resiniferatoxin, the ultra-potent agonist and the pipeline's second lead, failed to dock: the Vina subprocess returned an error (truncated in the log), and it was not retried — the largest ligand in the set (628.72 Da) under heavy CPU contention, and a compound whose score cannot change the paper's conclusion, since it is an agonist and the question is about antagonist leads.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of these ten compounds on 8GFA was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (compounds vs re-docked capsaicin on the same structure, same protocol). The published ground truth is the binding mechanism, not a docking table: capsaicin's "tail-up, head-down" pose with its pull on the S4–S5 linker (Yang et al. 2015) and the refined capsaicin/resiniferatoxin binding modes (Elokely et al. 2016). Against the published potencies, the docking order is consistent only within noise: SB-705498's published IC50 is 3 nM in the capsaicin mode and AMG-517's is < 10 nM, so the two antagonists are in the same single-digit-nanomolar range — and their docking gap, 0.54 kcal/mol in AMG-517's favour, is inside Vina's noise, so docking cannot separate them either. The published potency order the docking could not test is the agonist one: resiniferatoxin is several thousand-fold more potent than capsaicin (Fattori et al. 2016), but it failed to dock, so the paper cannot say whether the ultra-potent agonist would also have been the best binder. The decisive published fact is not a potency number but a clinical one: AMG-517, the best binder here by more than noise, produced hyperthermia past 40 °C in Phase I and was stopped — a drug that binds the pocket best and harms the patient most. The docking order cannot explain that; the thermoregulation data can.

3.3 The standardisation problem: what the patch proves and what it does not

The Qutenza data are the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. A single 60-minute application of an 8% capsaicin patch cuts pain by about a quarter to a third for up to three months — but only where the patch sits, only in peripheral neuropathic pain, and only after an application that burns. The drug that "wins" this docking table, whatever it is, would still have to beat that bar in a human: a systemic drug must match a topical drug's efficacy without the topical drug's locality, and must do it without raising body temperature. No docking score measures either half of that bar. The honest reading of the table is therefore narrow: it ranks pocket fit in one closed conformation, and the winner is a candidate for the calcium-flux assay, not a candidate for a patient.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since AMG-517 stopped. Before the hyperthermia data, the question was "can an antagonist out-bind capsaicin in the vanilloid pocket?" — now it is "can any antagonist bind the pocket well AND spare the proton mode that drives fever?" AMG-517 answers the first half and fails the second: it is the best binder in this table by more than noise, and it is the drug that raised body temperature past 40 °C. The benchmark is therefore a screen with a two-part bar: beat −8.26 kcal/mol against capsaicin, and show a capsaicin-over-proton selectivity ratio above 3 in patch-clamp, with no hyperthermia at analgesic exposure. This paper supplies the first half of the bar and shows the second half is where the pipeline must go next: SB-705498, which reached Phase II with human target-engagement data and no hyperthermia reported at 400 mg, is the template for what a successor must look like — not the best binder, but the best binder with a human safety record.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the winner is the clinically failed drug: AMG-517's 2.19 kcal/mol lead over capsaicin is real by docking standards and irrelevant by clinical standards, because the same compound was stopped in Phase I for hyperthermia past 40 °C — a docking table that ranks a failed drug first is a ranking of pocket fit, not of medicines. Second, every margin except AMG-517's lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, including SB-705498's 1.65 and the three pipeline leads' 1.39–1.47, so the table cannot rank compounds second through sixth at all. Third, the pose consistency check undermines one of the three leads: CHEMBL228451's poses spread 7.29 kcal/mol (−9.65 to −2.36), so its headline score is a single pose, not a reproducible binding mode, and its median pose would rank it behind capsaicin. Fourth, the set is confounded by size and by conformation: two of the three pipeline leads ahead of capsaicin carry a Lipinski violation (CHEMBL3407765, MW 519.97; CHEMBL4242293, logP 5.08 — CHEMBL228451, MW 405.59, is the exception with none), the largest pipeline lead (CHEMBL3681230, MW 516.36) loses to capsaicin, and the whole ranking was computed in the antagonist-bound closed conformation, which favours antagonists over the two agonists in the set. A fifth reason is specific to this target: the pocket is lipid-facing, a phosphatidylinositol occupies it in the apo state, and Vina has no membrane — so the score measures fit to a dry, rigid pocket that does not exist in a neuron.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Only one compound in the set carries a PAINS alert — capsazepine, catechol_A(92). The catechol is a classic redox-cycling motif: in a calcium-flux assay it can generate reactive oxygen species and produce apparent channel effects that have nothing to do with TRPV1 binding. The honest handling is not to delete capsazepine from the table — it is the field's first antagonist and belongs in the comparison — but to design the validation so the alert is tested, not assumed away: run the flux assay with and without a reducing agent (e.g. dithiothreitol) and with a reactive-oxygen scavenger, and require the IC50 to survive both. A compound whose apparent potency disappears under redox control was never a TRPV1 ligand. The nine PAINS-clean compounds need no such control, which is itself a result: the screen did not have to hide anything.

4.4 Mechanism

Capsaicin binds "tail-up, head-down" in the vanilloid pocket between transmembrane segments S3–S4 and the S4–S5 linker: the vanillyl and amide groups anchor to the channel while the aliphatic tail samples conformations, and the bound agonist pulls the S4–S5 linker to stabilise the open state (Yang et al., Nat Chem Biol 2015). Antagonists occupy the same pocket and stabilise the closed state instead — SB-366791 in 8GFA sits where the vanillyl group would sit, blocking the pull. Test for each link: (i) a calcium-flux (FLIPR) assay measures IC50 against capsaicin-evoked activation directly, with SB-705498's published 3 nM as the comparator; (ii) whole-cell patch-clamp measures whether the compound blocks capsaicin-, acid- and heat-evoked currents separately — the three modes must be reported apart, because hyperthermia tracks the proton mode, not the heat mode (Garami et al. 2010); (iii) a capsaicin-evoked flare assay in human skin, as in Chizh et al. 2007, measures target engagement in people, with core temperature monitored throughout as the safety readout.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring compound inhibits capsaicin-evoked calcium flux in human TRPV1 with an IC50 within 3-fold of SB-705498's published 3 nM. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than SB-705498.
  2. The best-scoring compound is mode-selective: it blocks capsaicin-evoked activation more potently than proton-evoked activation (IC50 ratio > 3), the profile Garami et al. associate with freedom from hyperthermia. Falsifier: proton-mode IC50 equal to or better than capsaicin-mode IC50.
  3. The best-scoring compound raises no hyperthermia signal: in the human flare assay, core temperature does not rise above 38 °C at the tested exposure. Falsifier: any temperature above 38 °C attributable to the drug.
  4. Capsazepine's apparent potency survives redox control (dithiothreitol and a reactive-oxygen scavenger do not shift its IC50). Falsifier: the IC50 shifts more than 3-fold under redox control, which would show the catechol, not TRPV1 binding, produced the signal.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): calcium-flux assay for the ten compounds against capsaicin-evoked human TRPV1 activation — SB-705498 as the positive control, capsazepine with and without redox controls, readout IC50, n = 3. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): whole-cell patch-clamp for the best compound from stage 1, reporting capsaicin-, acid- and heat-mode IC50s separately, with SB-705498 as the comparator. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — IC50 within 3-fold of SB-705498 and a capsaicin-over-proton selectivity ratio above 3 — a human capsaicin-evoked flare study with continuous core-temperature monitoring; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every margin smaller than that.
  2. Docking cannot distinguish an agonist from an antagonist: capsaicin and resiniferatoxin activate the channel, the other eight compounds are meant to block it, and a better score for an agonist is not a better analgesic.
  3. The structure is the antagonist-bound closed conformation (8GFA, SB-366791-bound, 2.29 Å), which may favour antagonists over agonists — the agonist scores are therefore a lower bound, not a ranking.
  4. The vanilloid pocket is lipid-facing and Vina has no membrane, no explicit lipid and no gating: in the apo structures a phosphatidylinositol lipid occupies the capsaicin site, and docking cannot model its displacement.
  5. The five pipeline leads have no published TRPV1 potency; they are similarity hits against ChEMBL actives, and four of them carry a Lipinski violation, so part of any lead may be size.
  6. Capsazepine carries a catechol PAINS alert; its score must survive redox control before it means anything.
  7. No capsaicin-bound human structure exists to cross-check against — capsaicin was never modelled as a ligand in any TRPV1 structure, only as a small density — so the reference drug has no self-dock control of its own; SB-366791 is the control instead.
  8. The classical-canon sweep found no capsaicin-relevant text: Capsicum is a New World plant, unknown to Ibn Sina and Al-Razi, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this drug. The full Kitab al-Hawi exists in English only in selections (see the literature map's gap list); the 23 volumes were not read.
  9. No Pakistan-specific data exist on TRPV1-targeted pain care: no registry of neuropathic-pain prevalence, no Qutenza availability or price data for Pakistan, and no local hyperthermia-monitoring protocol for any systemic TRPV1 drug.
  10. The ranking rests on a single structure (8GFA); no cross-structure check was run, and resiniferatoxin failed to dock (Vina subprocess error, truncated in the log — the largest ligand in the set at 628.72 Da) and was not retried, so the published potency order (resiniferatoxin far above capsaicin) could not be tested by docking.

6. Conclusion

Capsaicin, the only TRPV1 drug that is actually a medicine — topically, as the 8% patch — re-docks at −8.26 kcal/mol on the 2.29 Å human structure 8GFA with no PAINS alert, and six of the nine compounds that docked beat it. AMG-517 scores best at −10.45 kcal/mol, ahead by 2.19 kcal/mol, the only gap in the paper larger than the noise; SB-705498 and three pipeline leads follow at −9.91 to −9.65 kcal/mol, all inside noise. The docking verdict is a warning, not a lead: the best binder is the antagonist that failed in Phase I for hyperthermia past 40 °C, the ranking rests on a single antagonist-bound structure, resiniferatoxin failed to dock, and one lead's headline score is a single-pose outlier. The next screen must be a calcium-flux assay plus mode-separated patch-clamp with core-temperature monitoring, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same pocket that binds AMG-517 at −10.45 kcal/mol is the pocket whose blockade drove body temperature past 40 °C, and only a mode-selective assay can tell whether a successor keeps the binding without the fever. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a flux assay for AMG-517 and SB-705498 against capsaicin-evoked human TRPV1, reporting the proton mode apart — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the provincial pain-management programmes, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to spend anything on TRPV1 drugs in Pakistan, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund or fast-track any systemic TRPV1 antagonist evaluation — no systemic antagonist is approved anywhere, the only one that reached humans raised body temperature past 40 °C, and Pakistan has no registry of the neuropathic-pain patients such a drug would treat. Instead, (a) ask DRAP to assess the 8% capsaicin patch for formulary inclusion for postherpetic neuralgia and painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, with a price and availability audit — a single 60-minute application giving up to three months of relief is exactly the kind of low-frequency, non-opioid treatment a cash-constrained system can deliver; and (b) require any future systemic TRPV1 trial in Pakistan to include a written thermoregulation protocol (continuous core-temperature monitoring, a stopping rule at 38.5 °C, and acetaminophen on standby, as the AMG-517 programme used) before ethics approval. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a mode-selective antagonist — one that spares proton-mode activation — completes a Phase I trial with no hyperthermia signal at analgesic exposure, and the patch audit shows the topical route cannot reach the patients who need it, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that compound; if the patch audit shows the 8% patch is unavailable or unaffordable in Pakistan, redirect the same money to securing its supply rather than to any new systemic drug; do not proceed to any systemic evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia: Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; systematised by Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat): a painkiller that drives body temperature past 40 °C violates the preservation of life it is meant to serve, and the Qur'anic command "do not throw yourselves into destruction" (Qur'an 2:195) sets the safety bar before the efficacy bar. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".
