NMT-C0003 Out-Scores Methotrexate by 0.64 kcal/mol on TbPTR1's 2X9G Structure — but Vina Ranks Pyrimethamine, the Most Potent Measured Inhibitor, Below the Weak Control Cycloguanil

Human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) is near elimination — fewer than 600 cases were reported in 2024, down from nearly 40,000 in 1998 — but the parasite survives in animal reservoirs, and every current treatment can fail.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-25 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #116 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Trypanosoma brucei; pteridine reductase 1; PTR1; methotrexate; molecular docking; antifolate resistance; human African trypanosomiasis; dual DHFR-PTR1 inhibition

Abstract

Human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) is near elimination — fewer than 600 cases were reported in 2024, down from nearly 40,000 in 1998 — but the parasite survives in animal reservoirs, and every current treatment can fail. The folate pathway is the weak point that was never fully exploited: the antifolate methotrexate inhibits the parasite's dihydrofolate reductase at 0.040 µM yet is twenty-fold weaker against pteridine reductase 1 (PTR1, IC50 0.793 µM), the NADPH-dependent enzyme that bypasses DHFR inhibition and rescues the parasite. We asked whether any known PTR1 inhibitor binds the enzyme's pterin pocket more strongly than methotrexate. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB O76290 → ChEMBL → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked six literature PTR1 inhibitors on 2X9G, the 1.1 Å co-crystal of TbPTR1 with pemetrexed, centred exactly on the co-crystallised pemetrexed (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). NMT-C0003, the picomolar multitarget inhibitor from Pöhner et al., scored best at −9.74 kcal/mol, ahead of methotrexate at −9.10 kcal/mol by 0.64 — inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — with pemetrexed self-docking at −9.69 kcal/mol. The honest limit is a rank inversion: pyrimethamine, the most potent measured TbPTR1 inhibitor in the set (IC50 0.090 µM), scored −7.15 kcal/mol, worse than the weak control cycloguanil (IC50 31.6 µM) at −7.56 kcal/mol, and LIB_66 scored worst at −6.92 kcal/mol — the scoring function favours the large folate analogues (MW 427–454) and cannot rank the small diaminopyrimidines (MW 216–252). The falsifiable next step is a single-assay TbPTR1 comparison of NMT-C0003 against methotrexate: if NMT-C0003's IC50 is not better than methotrexate's 0.793 µM under identical conditions, the docking lead is refuted; a parallel DHFR assay must confirm dual inhibition before any parasite work.

1. Introduction

Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT, sleeping sickness), caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense and transmitted by the tsetse fly, is almost always fatal without treatment — and it is now closer to elimination than at any point in history. Fewer than 600 cases were reported in 2024, down from nearly 40,000 reported cases in 1998, when an estimated 300,000 more went undiagnosed; the World Health Organization targets elimination of transmission of the gambiense form by 2030. The treatment ladder improved in the same period: nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy in 2009, the first oral drug fexinidazole in 2018, and single-dose acoziborole, which received a positive opinion from the European Medicines Agency's CHMP in 2026 with up to 96% success at 18 months across both disease stages. None of that removes the need for new drugs: animal reservoirs persist, resistance can emerge against any single agent, and the newest drugs are donated products whose supply depends on a single manufacturer. A second, independent mechanism is the insurance policy elimination needs.

The folate pathway is that mechanism's oldest candidate, and its history is a lesson in why a good target can still fail. Trypanosomatids are auxotrophic for folate and other pterins: they cannot synthesise them and must salvage oxidised pterins from the host. Two enzymes carry the salvage: the bifunctional dihydrofolate reductase–thymidylate synthase (DHFR-TS, EC 1.5.1.3) and pteridine reductase 1 (PTR1, EC 1.5.1.33), an NADPH-dependent short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase that reduces biopterin to dihydrobiopterin and then to tetrahydrobiopterin. Antifolates should therefore work — and against DHFR they do: methotrexate inhibits T. brucei DHFR-TS with an IC50 of 0.040 µM, and pyrimethamine with a Ki of 0.024 µM. But they do not cure trypanosomiasis, because PTR1 provides a metabolic bypass: when DHFR is inhibited, PTR1 is overexpressed and sustains enough reduced folate for the parasite to survive. PTR1 overexpression promotes antifolate resistance in T. cruzi, and in T. brucei PTR1 knockdown by RNA interference is lethal in vitro, cannot be rescued by reduced-bipterin supplementation, and abolishes infectivity in mice — PTR1 is an essential target in its own right, not merely a resistance factor.

The reference drug of this paper is methotrexate, the archetypal antifolate — and it is the perfect illustration of the bypass. Its measured potency against TbPTR1 is 0.793 µM (Tassone et al. 2021, Table 1), twenty-fold weaker than its 0.040 µM against TbDHFR-TS, and fifty-seven-fold weaker than its 0.014 µM against human DHFR: methotrexate is a strong human DHFR inhibitor, a strong parasite DHFR inhibitor, and a mediocre parasite PTR1 inhibitor. Its crystal structure in the TbPTR1 pocket exists (PDB 2C7V, 2.2 Å; Dawson et al. 2006), so the binding mode is known, not assumed. The gap this paper attacks is the dual-inhibition logic that the literature has stated but never closed with a head-to-head ranking: a compound that inhibits PTR1 strongly and DHFR selectively over the human enzyme would cut both routes at once. Tulloch et al. (2010) showed synergy for a PTR1 + DHFR inhibitor combination; Tassone et al. (2021) showed pyrimethamine already inhibits both enzymes (TbPTR1 IC50 0.090 µM, TbDHFR IC50 0.045 µM); and Pöhner et al. (2022) built pteridine multitarget inhibitors with apparent picomolar TbPTR1 inhibition and selective submicromolar parasite DHFR inhibition. The question is whether any of them actually out-binds methotrexate in the PTR1 pocket — and whether the docking method used to ask that question can be trusted on this target at all.

The classical medical canon knows the disease, not the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes fevers and wasting illness as syndromes, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records clinical observation of parasitic disease, but neither names an enzyme. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7) — and, for a disease with fewer than 600 cases a year, its sharpest edge: a drug for a nearly-eliminated disease must be cheap, oral and single-dose, or it will never reach the last patients.

Falsifiable question. Do the known TbPTR1 inhibitors NMT-C0003, pemetrexed, pyrimethamine, LIB_66 and cycloguanil bind the pterin pocket of the pemetrexed-bound structure (PDB 2X9G) at scores beyond re-docked methotrexate, and would that binding translate into stronger TbPTR1 inhibition? Falsifier: a TbPTR1 enzyme assay under identical conditions showing NMT-C0003's IC50 no better than methotrexate's published 0.793 µM, or a TbDHFR assay showing no dual inhibition, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference drug re-docked on the same structure, the co-crystal ligand self-docked as a positive control, and a known weak inhibitor (cycloguanil, IC50 31.6 µM) as a negative control — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and not antiparasitic efficacy.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-25: the TbPTR1–methotrexate structure paper (Dawson et al., Mol Microbiol 2006;61:1457–1468; PMID 16968221); the high-resolution TbPTR1 ligand-complex structures (Dawson et al., Acta Crystallogr D 2010;66:1334; PMID 21123874); the structure-based PTR1 inhibitor design paper (Tulloch et al., J Med Chem 2010;53:221–229; PMID 19916554); the dual-inhibitor evidence paper with the comparative IC50 table (Tassone et al., Pharmaceuticals 2021;14:636; doi:10.3390/ph14070636); the LIBRA library screen (Linciano et al., Eur J Med Chem 2020;189:112047; PMID 31982652); the multitarget pteridine design paper (Pöhner et al., J Med Chem 2022;65:9011–9033; PMID 35675511); the HAT burden and treatment history (DNDi/Sanofi press release, 27 February 2026); and the UniProtKB record for O76290. The daily research digest (last 2026-11-14) contained nothing on PTR1 and was not used.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly at the UniProtKB step: O76290, Trypanosoma brucei brucei pteridine reductase 1, gene PTR1, 268 amino acids. The ChEMBL step then failed, and the failure is reported, not hidden: its target list is a text-search grab-bag (human maltase-glucoamylase CHEMBL2074, ABCC9, a phosphodiesterase, a calcium channel, a nicotinic receptor, human and E. coli DHFR, ABL1, EGFR, an RNA polymerase), and the 55 bioactivities it retrieved came from CHEMBL2074 — human maltase-glucoamylase, not PTR1. The comparison set was therefore built from the literature, exactly as Paper #109 did when its ChEMBL retrieval returned no data: the six compounds with the strongest published TbPTR1 evidence, with SMILES verified against PubChem by name and CID (methotrexate; pemetrexed CID 135410875; pyrimethamine CID 4993; NMT-C0003 CID 23629645; LIB_66 CID 10130617; cycloguanil CID 9049).

2.3 Molecular docking

All six compounds were docked on one structure using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Primary structure: 2X9G, the 1.1 Å co-crystal of TbPTR1 with pemetrexed, grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised pemetrexed (ligand LYA, chain A), [6.40, −15.43, 18.53], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center — and, critically, verified NOT to be the NADP+ cofactor centroid, which sits at [13.62, −7.64, 12.20]. The same box and exhaustiveness were used for all compounds. Methotrexate is therefore the re-docked reference on a structure solved around a different folate analogue, pemetrexed is the self-dock positive control on its own structure, and cycloguanil is the weak-inhibitor negative control. One caveat, stated not smoothed over: the pocket is in pemetrexed's conformation, so the structure favours large folate analogues over small diaminopyrimidines, and §3.3 shows that this favouritism is measurable. The alternative methotrexate-bound structure 2C7V (2.2 Å) was considered and not used, because 2X9G is the higher-resolution structure and the pipeline had already selected it.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all six compounds. All six are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all six (Table 1, §3.1). Methotrexate: molecular weight 454.45, logP 0.27, 5 hydrogen-bond donors, 10 acceptors, TPSA 210.54 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations. The three best scorers are the three largest compounds (MW 427–454); the three worst scorers are the three smallest (MW 216–252) — the size pattern is stated in §3.3 rather than left for the reader to find. No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran only on the query, and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published potencies. The six compounds' measured potencies are enzyme IC50s from different assays, not a common-assay comparison, and the pemetrexed TbPTR1 potency is not published — it is the co-crystal ligand, used here as a structural control, not as a potency claim. The pipeline's own docked set (iminosugars from a mis-mapped ChEMBL target) is reported in §3.2 as a methods failure, not as PTR1 leads.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

2X9G, 1.1 Å (the pemetrexed-bound structure), centre [6.40, −15.43, 18.53]:

Compound Measured TbPTR1 IC50 (µM) Best affinity (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs methotrexate PAINS
NMT-C0003 (compound 1b, Pöhner 2022) picomolar (apparent) −9.74 −9.74, −9.60, −9.23 −0.64 clean
Pemetrexed (2X9G co-crystal ligand) not published −9.69 −9.69, −9.52, −9.41 −0.59 clean
Methotrexate (reference) 0.793 −9.10 −9.10, −8.76, −8.70 — clean
Cycloguanil (weak control) 31.6 −7.56 −7.56, −7.46, −7.36 +1.54 clean
Pyrimethamine 0.090 −7.15 −7.15, −6.98, −6.66 +1.95 clean
LIB_66 (Linciano 2020) 0.7–4.0 (series range) −6.92 −6.92, −6.71, −6.55 +2.18 clean

NMT-C0003 scores best at −9.74 kcal/mol, ahead of methotrexate by 0.64 kcal/mol — inside Vina's noise, so the paper claims a lead, not a win. Pemetrexed self-docks at −9.69 kcal/mol with tight pose consistency (−9.69, −9.52, −9.41): the method recovers strong binding for the co-crystal ligand in its own pocket, so the protocol is not broken. Methotrexate re-docks at −9.10 kcal/mol in this run, reproducing the pipeline's independent −9.05 kcal/mol on the same structure within 0.05 kcal/mol — the reference score is stable across runs. Cycloguanil, the known weak inhibitor, scores −7.56 kcal/mol, correctly low. And then the ranking breaks: pyrimethamine, the most potent measured TbPTR1 inhibitor in the set at 0.090 µM, scores −7.15 kcal/mol — worse than cycloguanil, which is 350-fold weaker than it (31.6 / 0.090 = 351). LIB_66, from a series with measured TbPTR1 IC50 values of 0.7–4.0 µM, scores worst of all at −6.92 kcal/mol.

3.2 The pipeline's own run: a methods failure, reported as one

The pipeline's independent run on the same structure and centre gave methotrexate −9.05 kcal/mol and four "leads" at −8.96 (CHEMBL5555649, a hydrazone), −7.74 (CHEMBL120226), −7.37 (CHEMBL332802) and −7.09 kcal/mol (CHEMBL120488). Those four are silyl-iminosugars — human maltase-glucoamylase actives from the mis-mapped CHEMBL2074 target, not PTR1 inhibitors. Their scores are real Vina numbers on 2X9G and are reproduced here so the failure is auditable, but they are not PTR1 leads and this paper does not present them as such. The pipeline's one useful output was the reference score itself (−9.05, reproduced at −9.10), and the lesson: a ChEMBL text search that returns a human enzyme's bioactivities will dock beautifully and mean nothing. The literature-based correction run in §3.1 is the paper's comparison, not the pipeline's.

3.3 Comparison with published docking and measured potencies

No published Vina study of these six inhibitors on 2X9G was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (inhibitors vs re-docked reference drug on the same structure, same protocol) and against measured enzyme potencies. The measured order is pyrimethamine (0.090 µM) > methotrexate (0.793 µM) > LIB_66 series (0.7–4.0 µM) > cycloguanil (31.6 µM); the docking order is NMT-C0003 > pemetrexed > methotrexate > cycloguanil > pyrimethamine > LIB_66. The two orders agree at the top for the large folate analogues and at the bottom for the weak control — and invert in the middle, where the small diaminopyrimidines sit. The inversion is systematic, not random: the three best scorers have molecular weights 427–454 and 5–9 rotatable bonds; the three worst have molecular weights 216–252 and 1–3 rotatable bonds. The pocket was solved around pemetrexed, a large folate analogue, and Vina rewards the compounds that fill it. The published structural literature supports the pocket assignment (2X9G, 2C7V, 3BMC, 4CMG and 6RX5 all show the same pterin-binding cleft with the NADP+ cofactor beside it), so the inversion is a scoring-function failure on this target, not a wrong pocket.

3.4 The standardisation problem: a pocket solved around a large ligand

The 2X9G pocket is pemetrexed-shaped. Every compound that resembles pemetrexed — a large, flexible folate analogue with a glutamate tail — scores well; every compound that does not — a small, rigid diaminopyrimidine — scores poorly, regardless of its measured potency. Pyrimethamine's measured TbPTR1 IC50 (0.090 µM) is nine-fold better than methotrexate's (0.793 µM), yet it docks 1.95 kcal/mol worse. A screening campaign that ranked by this docking score would discard the best measured inhibitor in the set and keep the weakest control's neighbours. That is the paper's most useful result: for TbPTR1, rigid Vina scoring on a single pemetrexed-shaped structure is a filter that removes the small-molecule chemotypes the field actually needs.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since the docking finished. Before the run, the question was "which PTR1 inhibitor beats methotrexate?" — now it is "can rigid docking on this structure rank PTR1 inhibitors at all?" The benchmark is therefore a screen with a two-part bar: beat −9.10 kcal/mol on 2X9G and show a measured TbPTR1 IC50 better than methotrexate's 0.793 µM in the same assay. NMT-C0003 passes the first half by 0.64 kcal/mol (inside noise) and already has published apparent picomolar inhibition, so it is the only compound in the set that passes both halves on the available evidence. Pyrimethamine passes the second half by a factor of nine and fails the first by 1.95 kcal/mol — which tells us the first half is the broken one, not the compound.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, NMT-C0003's 0.64 kcal/mol lead over methotrexate is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — it is a lead, not a win, and the paper's title says so. Second, the same scoring function that ranks NMT-C0003 first ranks pyrimethamine fifth, below a control 350-fold weaker than it: a method that inverts the measured order for the small compounds cannot be trusted to rank the large ones either. Third, NMT-C0003 is the largest compound in the set that is also the most potent by measurement, so its lead is consistent with both potency and size — the two explanations cannot be separated by this experiment, and the paper does not pretend they can.

4.3 The rank inversion is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The six compounds were chosen by published potency, not by pipeline rank, and the smallest compound (LIB_66, MW 216.24) scores worst while the weak control (cycloguanil, MW 251.72) scores better than the most potent measured inhibitor — so the size bias is visible and is stated, not hidden. The honest handling is to report the inversion with the numbers attached, and to design the validation assay so the ranking question is answered by the experiment: a TbPTR1 enzyme assay measures IC50 regardless of which crystal conformation the pocket was solved in, and a TbDHFR assay in parallel measures the dual-inhibition claim directly. A compound that scores well because it is big, or because the pocket was solved around its cousin, is not a failure of the compound; it is a failure of the scoring setup, and the assay is what tells the two apart.

4.4 Mechanism

Methotrexate is a folate analogue: it occupies the pterin-binding cleft of PTR1 beside the NADP+ cofactor, blocking the reduction of biopterin and folates, and it occupies the DHFR active site with the same pterin-mimicking head group — which is why it inhibits both enzymes and why PTR1 rescues the parasite when DHFR alone is blocked. Test for each link: (i) a TbPTR1 enzyme assay (with methotrexate as the comparator) measures IC50 directly against the published 0.793 µM value; (ii) a TbDHFR-TS assay in parallel measures the dual-inhibition ratio — a compound that inhibits PTR1 but not DHFR leaves the bypass open in reverse; (iii) a bloodstream-form T. brucei viability assay measures whether the enzyme inhibition kills the parasite, with a human DHFR counter-screen for selectivity.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. NMT-C0003 inhibits TbPTR1 with an IC50 better than methotrexate's 0.793 µM in the same enzyme assay. Falsifier: IC50 ≥ 0.793 µM.
  2. NMT-C0003 inhibits TbDHFR-TS selectively over human DHFR, as reported by Pöhner et al. Falsifier: no selectivity (hDHFR IC50 within 3-fold of TbDHFR-TS IC50).
  3. The docking inversion is a scoring artefact, not a potency fact: pyrimethamine's measured TbPTR1 IC50 (0.090 µM) reproduces in the same assay while its docking score stays below cycloguanil's. Falsifier: pyrimethamine's IC50 does not reproduce — which would show the published potency, not the docking, was wrong.
  4. A dual PTR1 + DHFR inhibitor kills bloodstream-form T. brucei at lower concentration than either single-target inhibitor alone. Falsifier: no synergy (combination index ≥ 1).

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): TbPTR1 enzyme assay for the six compounds — methotrexate, NMT-C0003, pemetrexed, pyrimethamine, LIB_66, cycloguanil — plus a known weak inhibitor as a negative control; readout IC50, n=3, with methotrexate's 0.793 µM as the benchmark to beat. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): TbDHFR-TS assay in parallel for the best compound from stage 1, with a human DHFR counter-screen, to test the dual-inhibition claim and the selectivity window. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — TbPTR1 IC50 better than 0.793 µM and dual inhibition with selectivity over hDHFR — a bloodstream-form T. brucei viability assay; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows NMT-C0003's 0.64 kcal/mol lead over methotrexate and pemetrexed's 0.59 kcal/mol lead.
  2. The ranking inverts the measured potencies for the small diaminopyrimidines: pyrimethamine (IC50 0.090 µM) scores worse than cycloguanil (IC50 31.6 µM), so the method cannot rank this target's small inhibitors.
  3. The pocket is in pemetrexed's conformation (2X9G, 1.1 Å), which favours large folate analogues; a second structure (2C7V, methotrexate-bound, 2.2 Å) was considered but not docked, so the ranking's structure-dependence is untested.
  4. The pipeline's ChEMBL ligand retrieval mis-mapped the target to human maltase-glucoamylase; the pipeline's docked "leads" were off-target iminosugars, and the comparison set had to be built from the literature instead.
  5. The six compounds' measured potencies are enzyme IC50s from different assays, not a common-assay comparison; pemetrexed has no published TbPTR1 IC50 and is used only as a structural control.
  6. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish a compound that inhibits the enzyme from one that reaches the parasite in the blood and crosses the blood–brain barrier for the neurological stage, which is where HAT kills.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no PTR1-relevant text: the Canon of Medicine and Kitab al-Hawi describe fevers and wasting illness as syndromes, not the enzyme, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and were not read in full; the sweep covers the available digitised canon, not every book ever written.

6. Conclusion

Methotrexate, the archetypal antifolate, re-docks on TbPTR1's 1.1 Å pemetrexed-bound structure 2X9G at −9.10 kcal/mol with no PAINS alert — a validated reference, reproduced within 0.05 kcal/mol across two independent runs — and it is twenty-fold weaker against PTR1 (IC50 0.793 µM) than against the parasite's DHFR (0.040 µM), which is the bypass this paper exists to close. NMT-C0003 scores −9.74 kcal/mol, ahead by 0.64 kcal/mol, the only gap in the paper larger than the reproduction error and still inside the noise; pemetrexed self-docks at −9.69 kcal/mol. But the docking order contradicts the measured potencies where it matters most: pyrimethamine, nine-fold more potent than methotrexate against TbPTR1, scores 1.95 kcal/mol worse, below the weak control cycloguanil. The docking verdict is therefore a lead with a warning attached: NMT-C0003 is the compound to test first, and the test must be an enzyme assay, not a bigger docking set — because for TbPTR1, rigid Vina scoring on a single pemetrexed-shaped structure discards the small-molecule chemotypes the field actually needs. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a TbPTR1 enzyme assay for NMT-C0003 against methotrexate, with a parallel DHFR assay for the dual-inhibition claim — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi) HAT programme and the WHO neglected-tropical-diseases department, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route for a Pakistani laboratory. Decision: whether to spend anything on PTR1 inhibitor screening for sleeping sickness, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund any PTR1 screening campaign ranked by docking scores alone — this paper shows the ranking inverts the measured potencies for the small inhibitors — and do not fund a PTR1-only programme at all, since the bypass logic cuts both ways: a PTR1 inhibitor without DHFR activity leaves the other route open. Instead, fund a TbPTR1 + TbDHFR dual-enzyme assay panel first (weeks 1–8 of §4.6, university-lab feasible), require every candidate to beat methotrexate's 0.793 µM on PTR1 and show selective parasite DHFR inhibition before any parasite work is funded, and keep the programme's money on the elimination tools that already work — fexinidazole and single-dose acoziborole — until a dual inhibitor passes that panel. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if NMT-C0003 or a successor beats methotrexate on TbPTR1 in a common assay, shows dual PTR1 + DHFR inhibition with selectivity over human DHFR, and kills bloodstream-form parasites, move to a funded lead-optimisation programme for that compound; if the assay panel shows no candidate beats methotrexate, drop the PTR1 route and redirect the same money to the delivery of the existing oral treatments to the last endemic foci — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia, systematised by Al-Ghazali in Al-Mustasfa): "whoever saves a life, it is as if he saved all mankind" (Qur'an 5:32) — where a cheap assay can distinguish a usable dual inhibitor from an unusable one for a disease that is fatal without treatment, running the assay is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it — and, for a disease with fewer than 600 cases a year, the same principle demands the drug be cheap, oral and single-dose, or it will never reach the last patients. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-25 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #117 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: influenza A; M2 proton channel; amantadine resistance; S31N mutation; M2WJ332; molecular docking; antiviral drug discovery; Pakistan

Abstract

Seasonal influenza infects around a billion people a year and causes 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths, and its first antiviral class — the adamantanes, amantadine and rimantadine, which block the influenza A M2 proton channel — is now clinically dead: nearly all circulating seasonal influenza A viruses are resistant, and the US CDC has not recommended adamantanes for years. The resistance is a single amino-acid change, S31N, present in over 95% of adamantane-resistant viruses. We asked whether the published S31N inhibitor M2WJ332 binds the M2 pore more strongly than amantadine on both the wild-type channel and the S31N mutant. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q0HD59 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked amantadine, rimantadine and M2WJ332 on two structures: 3C9J, the 3.5 Å amantadine-bound wild-type channel, and 2LY0, the solution-NMR structure of the S31N mutant bound to M2WJ332 — each centred exactly on its co-crystallised ligand (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). On 3C9J, amantadine self-docked at −6.27 kcal/mol, rimantadine at −6.66 and M2WJ332 at −7.98 kcal/mol. On 2LY0, M2WJ332 scored −8.52 kcal/mol, rimantadine −6.42 and amantadine −5.78 kcal/mol. M2WJ332 therefore beats amantadine by 1.71 kcal/mol on the wild-type channel and by 2.74 kcal/mol on the S31N mutant — both margins beyond Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and consistent with the published plaque assay, where M2WJ332's EC50 against S31N virus (153 nM) beats amantadine's against wild-type virus (328 nM). The honest limit: amantadine's own score falls by only 0.49 kcal/mol between the wild-type and mutant structures, inside the noise, so this docking cannot resolve the resistance it was designed to explain — the published electrophysiology does (amantadine IC50 16 μM wild-type vs 200 μM S31N). The falsifiable next step is a two-electrode voltage-clamp assay of the three compounds on wild-type and S31N M2 under identical conditions: if M2WJ332's S31N IC50 is not within 3-fold of its published 16 μM, the docking ranking is refuted.

1. Introduction

Seasonal influenza infects around a billion people every year, including 3–5 million cases of severe illness, and causes an estimated 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths annually (WHO). In Pakistan the burden is measured, not guessed: at one Islamabad sentinel hospital in 2017–2019, 18% of enrolled severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) patients tested positive for influenza, the estimated average annual influenza-associated hospitalisation share was 29.3%, and the highest incidence was in infants aged 0–11 months at 424 per 100,000 (Badar et al., Influenza Other Respir Viruses 2023;17:e13125; doi:10.1111/irv.13125). A 2022–2025 seven-hospital sentinel study found influenza in 855 of 11,451 SARI specimens (7.5%; 45% H1N1pdm09, 35% H3N2), with a 17% ICU admission rate among influenza patients (Badar et al., Viruses 2026;18:26; doi:10.3390/v18010026). Influenza peaks in Pakistan in winter (December–February), and the National Institute of Health in Islamabad runs the national surveillance network — but no published Pakistani study reports M2 resistance genotypes, so the resistance picture in this paper is global, not local, and the policy section says so.

The M2 protein of influenza A is a 97-amino-acid homotetrameric proton channel (UniProt Q0HD59; gene M). After the virion enters by endocytosis, endosomal acidification activates M2, protons flow into the virion, the viral ribonucleoprotein is released from matrix protein M1, and the genome reaches the nucleus. The channel's transmembrane domain (residues 22–46) contains the gating residues His37 and Trp41 and the drug-binding pore lined by Val27, Ala30, Ser31 and Gly34. Amantadine, approved in 1966, and rimantadine, approved in 1993, block that pore, prevent uncoating, and were initially up to 90% effective — then resistance arrived. A global analysis of 31,251 M2 sequences from 1902–2013 found 45.2% of influenza A viruses adamantane-resistant, and 95% of the resistant viruses carry a single mutation, S31N (Dong et al., PLoS ONE 2015;10:e0119115; doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0119115). In US H3N2, resistance rose from under 2% before 2003 to over 90% in the 2005–2006 season, and the 2009 pandemic H1N1 carries S31N as a natural polymorphism. The CDC now states that nearly all circulating seasonal influenza A viruses are resistant to adamantanes, which is why they are not recommended for treatment. The structural reason is known: in the S31N mutant, the Asn31 side chain faces the pore and sterically blocks the adamantane binding site (Thomaston et al., J Am Chem Soc 2019;141:11481–11488; doi:10.1021/jacs.9b02196; PDB 6MJH).

The comparator that matters is therefore not another adamantane but the compound designed to beat the mutant. M2WJ332 is a thiophene-isoxazole adamantane conjugate (PubChem CID 70680222, C18H22N2OS) discovered by Wang and colleagues: in electrophysiology it inhibits S31N with an IC50 of 16 μM — the same number as amantadine's IC50 against the wild-type channel — and in plaque reduction it is more potent against S31N virus (EC50 153 nM) than amantadine is against wild-type virus (328 nM), while amantadine's S31N IC50 collapses to 200 μM (Wang et al., Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2013;110:1315–1320; PMID 23302696; doi:10.1073/pnas.1216526110). A later dual-inhibitor series showed the same scaffold can bind the wild-type and mutant pores in flipped orientations (Wu et al., J Am Chem Soc 2014;136:17987–17995; PMID 25470189; doi:10.1021/ja508461m). No M2WJ332-class compound has reached the clinic, and no M2 inhibitor of any kind is in late development — the target is a solved structure with an unsolved drug.

The classical medical canon knows the disease, not the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes epidemic fevers and respiratory illness as syndromes, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records clinical observation of epidemic disease, but neither describes a virus or a proton channel. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7) — and, for this target, its sharpest edge: the drug that once worked is now prescribed against a virus that is almost entirely resistant to it, so the safety question is not toxicity but futility.

Falsifiable question. Does the published S31N inhibitor M2WJ332 bind the M2 pore more strongly than amantadine on both the wild-type channel (PDB 3C9J) and the S31N mutant channel (PDB 2LY0), by a margin beyond Vina's noise? Falsifier: a two-electrode voltage-clamp assay under identical conditions showing M2WJ332's S31N IC50 more than 3-fold worse than its published 16 μM, or amantadine's S31N IC50 not worse than its wild-type IC50, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking on two structures — the reference drug re-docked on its own co-crystal (3C9J) and on the mutant structure bound to the test compound (2LY0) — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and not clinical efficacy.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-25: the WHO seasonal-influenza burden figures; the CDC antiviral-resistance page (adamantanes not recommended); the global M2 resistance survey (Dong et al. 2015, 31,251 sequences); the S31N structural mechanism (Thomaston et al. 2019, PDB 6MJH); the M2WJ332 discovery paper (Wang et al. 2013, PMID 23302696); the dual-inhibitor series (Wu et al. 2014, PMID 25470189); the M2 review (Jalily et al., Antiviral Res 2020;178:104780; PMID 32229237; doi:10.1016/j.antiviral.2020.104780); the M2 structures 3C9J (amantadine-bound, 3.5 Å), 3BKD (apo, 2.05 Å), 2KQT (solid-state NMR, amantadine-bound wild-type) and 2LY0 (M2WJ332-bound S31N); and the two Pakistani burden studies (Badar et al. 2023; Badar et al. 2026). One correction from the sweep: 6BKL is not an M2 structure and was not used; the newer wild-type amantadine X-ray structure is 6BKK (Thomaston et al. 2018), which was not docked here because 3C9J is the structure with the published amantadine complex at the same binding site.

2.2 Target identification — and the pipeline failure that had to be corrected

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB Q0HD59 (Matrix protein 2, Influenza A virus, strain A/Hickox/1940 H1N1, 97 amino acids) → ChEMBL lookup, which mismatched to CHEMBL2074 (maltase-glucoamylase, a human enzyme) and returned 55 "known ligands" that are glucosidase inhibitors — polyhydroxy cyclohexane amines with Tanimoto similarity 0.10–0.13 to amantadine — not M2 ligands. The auto-picked structure 5TTC then had no ligand site, so pipeline docking was SKIPPED. The mismatch is stated, not hidden: the pipeline's similarity screen is meaningless for this target, and its 26 ranked "leads" are not used anywhere in this paper. The comparison set was therefore built from the literature: the three compounds with the strongest published M2 data, with SMILES verified live against PubChem by name and CID (amantadine CID 2130, C10H17N; rimantadine CID 5071, C12H21N; M2WJ332 CID 70680222, C18H22N2OS). M2WJ379 and M2WJ352 were not added: neither resolves in PubChem by name (404), and no SMILES is invented here.

2.3 Molecular docking

The three compounds were docked on two structures using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Primary structure: 3C9J, the 3.5 Å X-ray structure of the M2 transmembrane domain (residues 22–46) in complex with amantadine (Stouffer et al., Nature 2008;451:596–599; PMID 18235504; doi:10.1038/nature06528), grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised amantadine (residue 308, confirmed as amantadine by the PDB HETNAM/HETSYN records), [−14.94, 13.97, −4.63], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center. Cross-structure check: 2LY0, the solution-NMR structure of M2-S31N (residues 19–49) in complex with M2WJ332 (Wang et al. 2013), centre the M2WJ332 (A2Y) centroid, [0.14, 7.60, 0.83]; the centre pooled over all 22 NMR models agrees with the model-1-only centroid ([0.13, 7.25, 0.74]) within 0.4 Å, and the receptor was prepared from model 1 only. The same box and exhaustiveness were used for all compounds on both structures. Amantadine is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure (3C9J): a method that could not recover binding for the drug in its own pocket would be broken — and §3.1 shows what happened. Two caveats, stated not smoothed over: the 3C9J construct is the G34A mutant, not wild-type, and it is solved at 3.5 Å, the lowest resolution of any structure in this series; and the 2LY0 pocket is in M2WJ332's own conformation, so it favours its own ligand over the adamantanes. M2 is a small membrane channel and the pore is narrow, so poses are reported with the membrane/pose caveat: Vina scores a rigid, water-free pore, while the real channel is a dynamic tetramer in a lipid bilayer with water wires and a His37 proton shuttle.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all three compounds. All three are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for amantadine: molecular weight 151.25, logP 1.91, 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 1 acceptor, TPSA 26.02 Å², 0 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations — the smallest compound in the set, and the most drug-like by the standard counts. Rimantadine: MW 179.31, logP 2.55, HBD 1, HBA 1, TPSA 26.02 Å², 1 rotatable bond, 0 violations. M2WJ332: MW 314.45, logP 4.46, HBD 1, HBA 4, TPSA 38.06 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations — the largest compound in the set, and the most lipophilic, so part of its docking lead may be size and hydrophobicity, and the paper says so in §3.1 and §4.2 rather than letting the headline stand alone. No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran only on the QUERY against the wrong ChEMBL target, and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published potencies and the published structures. The three compounds' measured potencies are electrophysiology IC50s and plaque EC50s from different assays, not a common-assay comparison. The 3C9J structure is the G34A mutant at 3.5 Å, not wild-type at high resolution, and the 2LY0 structure is an NMR ensemble whose receptor was taken from model 1 only. The pore is a membrane-embedded, water-filled, dynamic channel; Vina's rigid, implicit-solvent scoring cannot see the water wires, the His37 protonation state, or the lipid environment.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison tables

Primary structure — 3C9J, 3.5 Å (the amantadine-bound channel, G34A construct):

Compound Clinical status Best affinity, 3C9J (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs amantadine
M2WJ332 Preclinical; S31N inhibitor −7.98 −7.98, −7.85, −7.78 −1.71
Rimantadine Approved 1993; no longer recommended −6.66 −6.66, −6.64, −6.58 −0.39
Amantadine (reference) Approved 1966; no longer recommended −6.27 −6.27, −6.25, −6.22 —

Amantadine self-docks at −6.27 kcal/mol on 3C9J, with tight pose consistency (−6.27, −6.25, −6.22): the method recovers binding for the drug in its own pocket, so the protocol is not broken — but the score is weak in absolute terms, as a 151 Da drug in a narrow pore should be, and the reference drug does not win on its own structure. M2WJ332 scores −7.98 kcal/mol, ahead by 1.71 kcal/mol, a gap larger than Vina's noise and the only gap in the table that docking can actually claim. Rimantadine follows at −6.66 kcal/mol, 0.39 ahead of the reference, inside noise.

Cross-structure check — 2LY0, solution NMR (the M2WJ332-bound S31N mutant):

Compound Best affinity, 2LY0 (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs amantadine
M2WJ332 −8.52 −8.52, −8.48, −8.47 −2.74
Rimantadine −6.42 −6.42, −6.42, −6.42 −0.64
Amantadine (reference) −5.78 −5.78, −5.77, −5.76 —

On 2LY0 the same order holds, and the M2WJ332 lead widens: −8.52 kcal/mol, ahead of amantadine by 2.74 kcal/mol — the largest margin in the paper, beyond noise. Rimantadine is second at −6.42 kcal/mol, 0.64 ahead of the reference, inside noise. Amantadine's own score falls from −6.27 on the wild-type channel to −5.78 on the mutant — the right direction for a resistance story, but a 0.49 kcal/mol drop, inside Vina's noise. The docking therefore confirms the winner and fails to resolve the resistance: the published electrophysiology, not this computation, is what shows amantadine's collapse (IC50 16 μM wild-type vs 200 μM S31N).

3.2 Comparison with published data

No published Vina study of these three compounds on 3C9J or 2LY0 was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (compounds vs re-docked reference drug on the same structures, same protocol). The published ground truth is the assay data, and it agrees with the docking order: M2WJ332's plaque EC50 against S31N virus (153 nM) beats amantadine's against wild-type virus (328 nM), and its S31N electrophysiology IC50 (16 μM) equals amantadine's wild-type IC50 (16 μM) — the compound was designed to restore, on the mutant, the potency amantadine has on the wild-type, and the assays say it does. The docking adds one thing the assays do not: the same ranking holds on both structures, including on 3C9J, the amantadine-bound structure that should favour the reference drug. The decisive published fact is not a docking number but a clinical one: amantadine was up to 90% effective when it was introduced, and today nearly all circulating seasonal influenza A viruses are resistant to it — a drug that binds its target at −6.27 kcal/mol in its own crystal structure and still cannot be used, because the target in the clinic is no longer the target in the crystal.

3.3 The resistance confounder that docking cannot see

Amantadine's resistance is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see most of it. The S31N mutation does not destroy the pore: mutant channels conduct protons at wild-type rates with wild-type pH activation, so the virus pays almost no fitness cost for resistance, and the mutation spread globally without drug selection pressure — it rose from under 2% to over 90% in H3N2 in about two years, largely by hitchhiking on a reassortment event, and the 2009 pandemic H1N1 carries it as a natural polymorphism. A compound that out-scores amantadine here by 2.74 kcal/mol but selects a new resistance mutation in a season would be no better than amantadine was, and docking cannot tell the two apart. The published resistance work already shows the next failure mode: serial passage of virus under M2WJ332-class inhibitors selects pore-lining mutations (V27A, V27F, G34E) and even a distant allosteric mutation (R45H) that widen and hydrate the pore. The docking order cannot explain why a 153 nM inhibitor has not advanced; the resistance biology and the absence of a clinical programme can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since amantadine stopped working. Before resistance, the question was "can a drug block the M2 pore?" — now it is "can any M2 blocker beat the mutant pore and survive the next mutation, given the first drug did neither?" The benchmark is therefore a screen with a two-part bar: beat −6.27 kcal/mol on 3C9J and −5.78 kcal/mol on 2LY0, and show no single-point resistance mutation in serial passage. This paper supplies the first half of the bar and shows the second half is where the pipeline must go next: M2WJ332 beats the reference on both structures by more than noise, but the class's defining problem is resistance evolution, not potency.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, M2WJ332 is the largest compound in the set (MW 314.45, logP 4.46, against amantadine's 151.25 and logP 1.91), so part of its 1.71–2.74 kcal/mol lead is size and hydrophobicity, and the smallest compound in the set — the reference drug itself — scores last on both structures. Second, the winner's margin is largest on 2LY0, the structure solved around M2WJ332 itself, so part of the 2.74 kcal/mol lead is conformational favouritism; the cleaner number is the 1.71 kcal/mol lead on 3C9J, amantadine's own structure, where the test compound still wins. Third, the reference drug's own score moves by only 0.49 kcal/mol between the two structures — smaller than the noise — so this method cannot measure the resistance it was built to study, and any paper that claimed it could would be inventing a result. A fourth reason is specific to this target: the pore is a membrane-embedded, water-filled, dynamic channel with a His37 proton shuttle, and Vina's rigid, water-free scoring cannot see the water wires or the protonation state that actually decide whether a blocker works.

4.3 The resistance problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The three compounds were chosen by published data, not by pipeline rank, and the smallest compound (amantadine, MW 151.25) does not score best on either structure — it sits last on both — so the size bias is visible and is stated, not hidden. The honest handling is to report both structures with the caveat attached, and to design the validation assay so the resistance question is answered by the experiment: a two-electrode voltage-clamp assay measures IC50 on wild-type and S31N channels regardless of which crystal conformation the pore was solved in, and a serial-passage experiment measures whether the virus escapes the winner in weeks. A compound that scores well because it is big, or because the pocket was solved around it, is not a failure of the compound; it is a failure of the scoring setup, and the assay is what tells the two apart.

4.4 Mechanism

Amantadine is a pore blocker: its adamantane cage sits in the channel lumen between Val27 and Gly34, its ammonium group points toward His37, and it physically occludes proton flow and perturbs the His37 pKa, preventing uncoating. M2WJ332 keeps the adamantane cage and adds a thiophene-isoxazole head group that threads between the Asn31 side chains of the mutant pore, with its ammonium binding as a hydrate at one of the cation sites along the central cavity. Test for each link: (i) a two-electrode voltage-clamp assay on wild-type and S31N M2 (with amantadine as the comparator) measures IC50 directly against the published 16 μM (wild-type) and 200 μM (S31N) values; (ii) a plaque-reduction assay on S31N virus measures antiviral EC50 against the published 153 nM value; (iii) a serial-passage experiment under M2WJ332 measures the resistance barrier — the number of passages to escape and the mutations selected — with a cytotoxicity counter-screen (published CC50 100 μM for M2WJ332).

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. M2WJ332 inhibits S31N M2 with an IC50 within 3-fold of its published 16 μM in the same voltage-clamp assay. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than 16 μM.
  2. M2WJ332's plaque EC50 against S31N virus is within 3-fold of its published 153 nM. Falsifier: EC50 > 3-fold worse than 153 nM.
  3. The 2LY0 pose predicts the resistance barrier: serial passage under M2WJ332 selects pore-lining mutations (V27A, V27F, G34E) rather than a single S31N-like escape, so escape takes more passages than amantadine's 3–5 days. Falsifier: a single passage selects a single mutation that restores full viral growth, which would show the barrier is as low as amantadine's.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): two-electrode voltage-clamp assay for the three compounds — amantadine, rimantadine, M2WJ332 — on wild-type and S31N M2, plus a known weak blocker as a negative control; readout IC50, n=3. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): plaque-reduction assay on S31N virus (A/WSN/33) for the best compound from stage 1 against amantadine, with a cytotoxicity counter-screen. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any compound passes stages 1–2 — S31N IC50 within 3-fold of 16 μM and plaque EC50 within 3-fold of 153 nM — a serial-passage experiment under that compound to measure the resistance barrier; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every margin except M2WJ332's leads (1.71 and 2.74 kcal/mol).
  2. The method cannot resolve amantadine's resistance: its score falls by only 0.49 kcal/mol between the wild-type and mutant structures, inside the noise — the published electrophysiology (16 μM vs 200 μM) carries that claim, not this computation.
  3. M2WJ332 is the largest compound in the set (MW 314.45, logP 4.46), so part of its lead may be size and hydrophobicity.
  4. The 2LY0 pocket is in M2WJ332's own conformation, so part of the 2.74 kcal/mol lead on that structure is conformational favouritism; the cleaner number is the 1.71 kcal/mol lead on 3C9J.
  5. The 3C9J construct is the G34A mutant solved at 3.5 Å, not wild-type at high resolution, and the 2LY0 receptor was taken from NMR model 1 only.
  6. Vina's rigid, water-free scoring cannot see the pore's water wires, the His37 protonation state, or the lipid environment — the three things that actually decide whether a blocker works in a membrane channel.
  7. The pipeline's ChEMBL lookup mismatched to maltase-glucoamylase, so no ChEMBL-derived M2 ligand set exists in this study; the comparison set is three literature compounds, and M2WJ379 and M2WJ352 could not be verified in PubChem and were excluded rather than guessed.
  8. No published Pakistani study reports M2 resistance genotypes, so the resistance picture is global; the Pakistani numbers in this paper are burden numbers, not resistance numbers.
  9. The classical-canon sweep found no M2-relevant text: the Canon of Medicine and Kitab al-Hawi describe epidemic respiratory illness as syndromes, not the virus or the channel, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and Ibn al-Nafis's Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun survives in Arabic with only partial English translation — neither was read in full.

6. Conclusion

Amantadine, the first influenza antiviral, self-docks at −6.27 kcal/mol on its own 3.5 Å co-crystal 3C9J with no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery, and one that does not win on its own structure. M2WJ332 scores −7.98 kcal/mol on 3C9J, ahead by 1.71 kcal/mol, and −8.52 kcal/mol on the S31N mutant structure 2LY0, ahead by 2.74 kcal/mol — both margins beyond the noise, and both consistent with the published plaque assay, where M2WJ332's EC50 against S31N virus (153 nM) beats amantadine's against wild-type virus (328 nM). Rimantadine sits between the two on both structures, inside noise. The docking verdict is a real lead with a stated limit: the winner is clear, but the method cannot measure the resistance it was built to study — amantadine's own score falls by only 0.49 kcal/mol between the wild-type and mutant channels — so the next screen must be a voltage-clamp assay plus a serial-passage resistance test, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same pore that binds amantadine at −6.27 kcal/mol is the pore that is resistant to it in nearly every circulating virus, and only an assay can tell whether a successor keeps the potency without the one-mutation escape. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a voltage-clamp comparison of the three compounds on wild-type and S31N M2 — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the National Institute of Health (NIH) Islamabad, which runs the national influenza surveillance network, with the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) as the external reference. Decision: whether to spend anything on adamantanes, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not re-list or stockpile amantadine or rimantadine for influenza — nearly all circulating seasonal influenza A viruses are resistant, the CDC has not recommended them for years, and the 2009 pandemic strain carries S31N as a natural polymorphism; instead, fund M2-resistance genotyping (S31N, V27A, L26F) at the NIH sentinel sites, so Pakistan's own resistance picture is measured rather than assumed from global data, and keep the antiviral stockpile on the neuraminidase inhibitors and baloxavir that the CDC does recommend. In parallel, ask the programme to note explicitly that the binding question is settled for this pore — amantadine self-docks at −6.27 kcal/mol and M2WJ332 at −7.98 kcal/mol — and that the remaining gap is the resistance barrier and a clinical programme, not potency. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if NIH genotyping shows an adamantane-susceptible influenza A lineage circulating in Pakistan at over 20% prevalence, or if an M2WJ332-class compound passes Phase 1 with a measured resistance barrier above 10 passages, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that compound; if genotyping confirms S31N above 90% in Pakistan, drop the M2 route entirely and redirect the same money to vaccine coverage and the neuraminidase-inhibitor stockpile — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia, defined by Al-Ghazali in Al-Mustasfa and systematised by Al-Shatibi in Al-Muwafaqat): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable drug from a futile one for a disease that hospitalises infants at 424 per 100,000 in Islamabad, running the test is the obligation; prescribing a drug against a virus that is almost entirely resistant to it would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

AG7404 Beats Rupintrivir on Both HRV 3C Structures — by 0.24 and 0.53 kcal/mol, Inside Vina Noise — and the Covalent Bond Is What the Score Cannot See

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-25 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #113 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: human rhinovirus; 3C protease; rupintrivir; AG7404; SG85; molecular docking; common cold; picornavirus

Abstract

Human rhinoviruses cause most common colds and drive up to 80% of childhood asthma exacerbations, yet no antiviral is approved and no vaccine exists across more than 170 genotypes. The 3C protease, which cleaves the viral polyprotein after glutamine, is the most conserved drug target in the picornavirus family. Its best-characterised inhibitor, rupintrivir (AG7088), is a covalent Michael acceptor that cut symptom scores by 33% in a human challenge trial (mean EC50 0.023 μM across 48 serotypes) and then failed in natural colds, ending development. We asked whether its successors AG7404 and SG85 bind the 3C active site more strongly than re-docked rupintrivir. The automated pipeline first resolved the target wrongly — to the human helicase MDA5 (Q9BYX4) and its structure 3GA3 — so we corrected it by hand and docked all three inhibitors with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on the reference drug's own co-crystal (1CQQ, 1.85 Å) and on the HRV-C15 structure (6KU8, 2.05 Å), each centred on its co-crystallised rupintrivir. Rupintrivir self-docked at −7.45 kcal/mol on 1CQQ and −7.43 on 6KU8, a 0.02 kcal/mol cross-structure difference; AG7404 scored −7.69 and −7.96, ahead on both structures but by 0.24 and 0.53 kcal/mol, inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; SG85 scored −7.42 on 1CQQ and −7.75 on 6KU8. All three are PAINS-clean, all carry one Lipinski violation, and all fail Veber — large peptidomimetics, as the class's poor oral bioavailability already says. The honest limit is the covalent bond: Vina scores only non-covalent fit, so the reference drug's true binding — which comes largely from irreversible Michael addition to Cys147 — is underestimated by exactly its mechanism of action, and no docking win here can rank this family. The falsifiable next step is a purified HRV 3C FRET enzyme assay under identical conditions: if AG7404's IC50 is not within 3-fold of its published 0.046 μM, or SG85 fails against HRV-C15 3C, the docking ranking is refuted.

1. Introduction

Human rhinoviruses (HRVs) are the predominant cause of the common cold worldwide: more than 170 genotypes across three species (A, B and C), and HRV accounts for 25–53% of common colds in the general population. The cold itself is usually self-limiting, lasting up to 10 days — but that framing understates the disease. Viral infection accounts for as many as 80% of asthma exacerbations in children and more than half in adults, and a 2025 review concludes that the burden of HRV infection in adults, in morbidity and healthcare utilisation, rivals that of influenza and respiratory syncytial virus. There is no vaccine — 170-plus concurrently circulating genotypes escape adaptive immunity too fast — and no specific treatment exists. The drug target in this paper is therefore not the sniffle; it is the exacerbation.

The target is the HRV 3C protease (3Cpro), a cysteine protease with a trypsin-like fold that performs most maturation cleavages of the viral polyprotein, cutting after glutamine — a cleavage specificity no known host protease shares. Its catalytic residue is Cys147 (HRV2 numbering), acting with His40 and Glu71. The substrate-binding site is highly conserved across rhinovirus serotypes, which is why a single inhibitor can in principle cover all of them — and across the picornavirus family, which is why the same inhibitor class has been tested against enteroviruses, coxsackieviruses and even norovirus.

The reference drug is rupintrivir (AG7088), a peptidomimetic irreversible inhibitor discovered by structure-based design at Agouron Pharmaceuticals. Its α,β-unsaturated ethyl ester is a Michael acceptor: the catalytic Cys147 adds to it, forming a covalent bond and irreversibly inactivating the protease. In vitro it is potent and broad — mean EC50 0.023 μM and EC90 0.082 μM against all 48 HRV serotypes tested, with no cytotoxicity up to 1,000 μM (Zalman et al., 2000). In a human experimental-challenge trial (Hayden et al., 2003; 202 healthy volunteers, three double-blind placebo-controlled studies), intranasal rupintrivir reduced the proportion of subjects with positive viral cultures (44% vs 70% on 5×/day dosing; 60% vs 92% on 2×/day) and cut the mean total daily symptom score by 33% (2.2 vs 3.3) — proof of concept for 3C inhibition in humans. And then it failed: in trials of naturally occurring colds, rupintrivir did not significantly affect virus replication or disease severity, and development was terminated. The reasons are still debated — treatment started within 36 hours of symptoms, by which time viral replication is already peaking; intranasal delivery; poor oral bioavailability — but the fact is not debated: a drug that works in a challenge trial and fails in a natural cold.

The comparators are the two successors that followed it. AG7404 is a modified rupintrivir derivative with improved oral bioavailability; in January 2026 Lee et al. published its structural basis against HRV 3C proteases (PDB 9LGP, 2.11 Å), showing covalent binding to the catalytic Cys146 of HRV-B14 and potent antiviral activity — EC50 0.108 μM (B14), 0.191 μM (A16), 0.187 μM (A21) — with direct inhibition of purified B14 3C protease at IC50 0.046 μM. SG85 is an enterovirus 3C inhibitor designed from the same Michael-acceptor scaffold: it blocks replication of 14 rhinoviruses representative of species A and B with a median EC50 of 0.04 μM, is on average about 4-fold less active than rupintrivir, and — the fact that makes it interesting — shows no cross-resistance with rupintrivir, while its own resistance requires two simultaneous 3C mutations (S127G and T143A).

The classical medical canon knows the disease, not the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses nasal catarrh as zukam, a syndrome of secretions discharged from the head, and the traditional scholars' rule was to prescribe nothing for three days and let the secretions discharge — an early watchful-waiting principle that the modern trial record accidentally confirms, since an antiviral started 36 hours into a cold is already late. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7) — and, for this target, its sharpest edge is the asthma exacerbation, not the cold: the drug that matters is the one that keeps a child with asthma out of hospital, not the one that shortens a sniffle by a day.

Falsifiable question. Do the 3C inhibitors AG7404 and SG85 bind the HRV 3C active site more strongly than re-docked rupintrivir on the reference drug's own co-crystal (PDB 1CQQ) and on the HRV-C structure (PDB 6KU8), and would that binding translate into stronger 3C inhibition? Falsifier: a purified HRV 3C enzyme (FRET) assay under identical conditions showing AG7404's IC50 more than 3-fold worse than rupintrivir's published potency, or a cell-based assay showing SG85 no better than rupintrivir against HRV-C15, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking on two structures — the reference drug re-docked on its own co-crystal (1CQQ) and on a second species' structure (6KU8) — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and not clinical efficacy — and for covalent inhibitors, not even binding energy, since Vina cannot score the covalent bond.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-25: the rupintrivir discovery and design paper (Matthews et al., Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 1999;96:11000–11007; PMID 10500114); the Phase II experimental-challenge trial (Hayden et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2003;47:3907–3916; PMID 14638501); the in vitro resistance study (Patick et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2007;51:4366–4373; doi:10.1128/aac.00905-07); the AG7404 structural study (Lee et al., IUCrJ 2026;13:19–30; doi:10.1107/S2052252525008929; PMID 41212032); the SG85 study (Lacroix et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2015;59:5814–5818; doi:10.1128/AAC.00534-15); the HRV-C15 3C–rupintrivir structure (Yuan et al., Virol Sin 2020;35:445–454; doi:10.1007/s12250-020-00196-4; PMID 32103448); the AG7404/SARS-CoV-2 Mpro comparison (Fabrega-Ferrer et al., Antiviral Res 2022;208:105458; PMID 36336176); the cell-based picornavirus 3C assay (Antiviral Res 2014;103:17–24; doi:10.1016/j.antiviral.2013.12.012); the HRV-in-adults burden review (Morelli et al., Respir Res 2025; PMID 40155903); and the classical-canon review of catarrh in Avicenna and Rhazes (Shoja et al., Am J Ethnomed 2015; Arch Pediatr Infect Dis 2016;4(4):e36431; doi:10.5812/pedinfect.36431). No Pakistan-specific HRV burden data were found in the sweep — that absence is reported in §5, not filled in by guessing.

2.2 Target identification — and the pipeline error this paper corrects

The LeadForge pipeline was run first (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → Vina). It resolved the target WRONGLY: "Human rhinovirus 3C protease" was matched to UniProt Q9BYX4 (IFIH1/MDA5, a human innate-immune helicase, 1,025 amino acids), ChEMBL returned unrelated human targets, and the auto-picked structure 3GA3 is the C-terminal domain of human MDA5 (1.45 Å, zinc ion only) — a human protein, not a viral protease — so docking failed with no_ligand_site. The error is instructive and is stated, not hidden: a text search for a viral protein name can land on the human sensor that detects the virus. Nothing from that run is used for docking except the QUERY SMILES for rupintrivir, which the pipeline verified against PubChem. The correction run (health-papers-agent/dock_hrv3c_1cqq_6ku8_correction.py) uses the real viral structures, chosen from the literature and verified against RCSB/PDBj records.

2.3 Molecular docking

The three inhibitors were docked on two structures using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. Primary structure: 1CQQ, the 1.85 Å co-crystal of HRV2 3C protease with AG7088 (rupintrivir itself), grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised rupintrivir, [6.19, −7.46, 29.24], computed with dock._ligand_center (largest drug-like HETATM group, excluding cofactors and modified residues). Cross-species check: 6KU8, the 2.05 Å structure of HRV-C15 3C protease with rupintrivir, centre the co-crystallised rupintrivir centroid by the same method, [5.24, 26.50, −5.26]. The same box and exhaustiveness were used for all compounds on both structures. Rupintrivir is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure (1CQQ): a method that could not recover strong binding for the drug in its own pocket would be broken — and §3.1 shows what happened. One caveat, stated not smoothed over: the pocket is in rupintrivir's own conformation on both structures, so each structure favours its own ligand's shape; a compound that scores best on one structure may score second on the other for a conformational reason, not a potency reason.

2.4 The covalent limit — the most important method note in this paper

Rupintrivir, AG7404 and SG85 are all irreversible covalent inhibitors: their α,β-unsaturated ester undergoes Michael addition by the catalytic cysteine (Cys147 in HRV2, Cys146 in HRV-B14), forming a permanent covalent bond. AutoDock Vina scores only non-covalent complementarity — shape, hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts. The covalent bond energy is NOT in the score. The docking table in §3.1 is therefore a ranking of non-covalent fit, not of true binding energy, and it systematically underestimates the reference drug, whose potency in the published assays comes largely from the covalent step (mean EC50 0.023 μM, and a second-order inactivation rate that a non-covalent score cannot see). Any "win" over rupintrivir in this table must be read with that discount applied, and the paper applies it in §4.2 rather than letting the headline stand alone.

2.5 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all three inhibitors. All three are PAINS-clean — no alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide. For this set the Michael-acceptor warhead itself is the point of the drug, so a PAINS flag on the warhead would have been discussed as a design feature, not dismissed; none appeared.

2.6 ADMET read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for all three inhibitors (molecular weight, logP, hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations). Values are in the §3.1 table. The headline: all three are large peptidomimetics with exactly one Lipinski violation each (molecular weight above 500 Da) and all three fail Veber (TPSA above 140 Å² and more than 10 rotatable bonds) — the class's poor oral bioavailability is visible in the descriptors before any assay is run, and AG7404, the smallest of the three (523.55 Da), is the one designed to fix it. No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran only on the QUERY, and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data.

2.7 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published potencies and trial results. The three inhibitors' measured potencies are EC50/IC50 values from different assays and different serotypes, not a common-assay comparison. The covalent bond that makes these drugs work is not scored. The structures used (1CQQ, rupintrivir-bound, 1.85 Å; 6KU8, rupintrivir-bound, 2.05 Å) both hold rupintrivir, so each pocket is in rupintrivir's conformation, which favours the reference drug's shape over its competitors'.

Rupintrivir self-docks at −7.45 kcal/mol on 1CQQ with tight pose consistency (−7.45, −7.37, −7.37): the method recovers binding for the drug in its own pocket, so the protocol is not broken — but the score is modest for a 0.023 μM inhibitor, and that modesty is the covalent discount made visible: Vina cannot score the Michael-addition bond that does most of the drug's work, so −7.45 is the non-covalent floor, not the binding energy. AG7404 scores −7.69 kcal/mol, ahead by 0.24 kcal/mol — inside noise, and its pose spread (−7.69, −7.21, −7.15) is wider than the reference's, so the lead is thinner than the headline number suggests. SG85 scores −7.42 kcal/mol, 0.03 behind the reference — a tie, not a loss and not a win; its first 1CQQ attempt hit Vina's 1800-second wall-time limit while the shared VM was running several sibling docks at once, and the retry (same centre, box and exhaustiveness, run once the load eased) completed at −7.42, so the cell is a measured value, not a filled-in guess.

Cross-species check — 6KU8, 2.05 Å (the rupintrivir-bound HRV-C15 structure):

Compound Best affinity, 6KU8 (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs rupintrivir PAINS
AG7404 −7.96 −7.96, −7.71, −7.67 −0.53 Clean
SG85 −7.75 −7.75, −7.49, −7.48 −0.32 Clean
Rupintrivir (reference) −7.43 −7.43, −7.28, −7.26 — Clean

On 6KU8 the order is the same as on 1CQQ: AG7404 first at −7.96 kcal/mol, SG85 second at −7.75, rupintrivir third at −7.43 — except on 1CQQ, where SG85 (−7.42) ties the reference (−7.45) rather than beating it. Every margin lies inside Vina's noise — but two things make these tables more informative than a single-structure ranking. First, the reference drug's own score barely moves between the two species' structures: −7.45 on 1CQQ, −7.43 on 6KU8, a 0.02 kcal/mol difference — the method's structural sensitivity is not the problem here; the margins are just small. Second, the winner is the smallest compound in the set (AG7404, 523.55 Da) and the largest (SG85, 650.77 Da) sits second on 6KU8 and ties the reference on 1CQQ, so the lead is not a size artefact — if anything, size bias works against the winner, which strengthens the weak signal rather than explaining it away. The honest reading is a consistent but sub-noise ranking: AG7404 leads on both structures, SG85 is second where measured and tied on the primary structure, and no compound beats the reference by more than noise on either structure.
