3.2 Comparison with published docking and published potency

No published Vina study of rupintrivir, AG7404 and SG85 together on 1CQQ or 6KU8 was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (inhibitors vs re-docked reference drug on the same structures, same protocol). A 2022 molecular-dynamics comparison (J Biotech Res 2022;13:177–188) reported MM/PBSA binding free energies favouring SG85 over rupintrivir on HRV 3C — consistent in direction with the published cell data (SG85 median EC50 0.04 μM vs rupintrivir ~4-fold more active on average, i.e. the two methods disagree on the order, which is itself informative: MD free energies and cell EC50s rank these two differently). The published potency order is the ground truth the docking must be judged against: rupintrivir mean EC50 0.023 μM across 48 HRV serotypes; AG7404 EC50 0.108–0.191 μM across three serotypes with a purified-enzyme IC50 of 0.046 μM; SG85 median EC50 0.04 μM across 14 rhinoviruses. On published potency, rupintrivir is the most active in cells and AG7404 the most potent against purified enzyme — and the docking table must be read against both, not against itself.

3.3 The picornavirus-family coverage problem

The 3C protease is conserved across the picornavirus family, and the coverage of this inhibitor class is broad but not universal — which is the honest answer to the paper's angle. Rupintrivir inhibits all 48 HRV serotypes tested in vitro (Zalman et al., 2000) and, in a cell-based protease assay, inhibits enterovirus 3C proteases as well as foot-and-mouth disease virus 3C protease. SG85 inhibits enterovirus 71, coxsackievirus B3, echovirus 11 and poliovirus 1 in addition to rhinoviruses, and shows no cross-resistance with rupintrivir — so a rupintrivir-resistant virus remains SG85-sensitive, which is the combination argument in miniature. AG7404, by contrast, does NOT inhibit foot-and-mouth disease virus 3C protease in the cell-based assay (a predicted clash from its ring closure), while rupintrivir and SG85 do — so the newest derivative has the narrowest family coverage of the three. A single 3C inhibitor therefore does not cover the family: the coverage map has holes, and the holes differ by compound. The docking in this paper is on rhinovirus structures only; it says nothing about enterovirus or FMDV 3C, and §5 lists that as a limitation.

3.4 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Rupintrivir's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug is a 0.023 μM inhibitor that cut symptom scores by 33% in a human challenge trial and then failed in natural colds, with development terminated — and the failure was not potency, it was timing and delivery: treatment within 36 hours of symptoms, intranasal suspension, poor oral bioavailability. AG7404 was designed precisely to fix the bioavailability half of that failure (oral, improved), but no clinical data exist for it in rhinovirus infection, and its family coverage is narrower (no FMDV 3C activity). SG85 has no clinical data at all. A compound that out-scores rupintrivir in this paper's table by 1 kcal/mol but cannot be delivered orally, or cannot be given within hours of symptom onset, would be a worse drug for the common cold — and docking cannot tell the two apart. The docking order cannot explain why a 0.023 μM inhibitor fails in natural infection; the trial data and the pharmacokinetics can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since rupintrivir stopped. Before the natural-infection trials, the question was "can a 3C inhibitor beat rupintrivir's potency?" — now it is "can any 3C inhibitor, given early enough and delivered well enough, change the outcome that matters — asthma exacerbations — given a 0.023 μM inhibitor did not change the common cold?" The benchmark is therefore a screen with a three-part bar: beat the re-docked reference on 1CQQ, show oral bioavailability, and show activity against the HRV-C species that drives severe lower-airway disease. This paper supplies the first part of the bar and shows the second and third parts are where the programme must go next: AG7404 beats the reference on both structures but only inside noise, it is oral by design (the bioavailability half of rupintrivir's failure), and its HRV-C activity is so far only a docking score (−7.96 kcal/mol on 6KU8) with no cell data behind it.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the margins are sub-noise: AG7404 leads by 0.24 kcal/mol on 1CQQ and 0.53 on 6KU8, and SG85 by 0.32 on 6KU8 — every one of them inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the table ranks nothing with confidence; it only shows a consistent direction. Second, Vina cannot score the covalent bond, so the reference drug's true binding is underestimated by exactly the mechanism that makes it work — a 0.023 μM inhibitor self-docking at −7.45 kcal/mol is the proof: the score is the non-covalent floor, and the covalent step, which the assay measures and Vina does not, is where rupintrivir's potency lives. Third, SG85 is tied with the reference on 1CQQ (−7.42 vs −7.45) and ahead by 0.32 on 6KU8 — the same compound is a tie on one structure and a lead on the other, which is exactly what sub-noise margins look like, and no honest reading can call it a win. Fourth, the published potency order runs the other way: rupintrivir is the most active in cells (mean EC50 0.023 μM across 48 serotypes) while AG7404's cell EC50s are 0.108–0.191 μM — the docking winner is the cell-assay loser, and the enzyme assay (AG7404 IC50 0.046 μM on purified B14 3C) is the only published number that agrees with the docking order. A docking win that contradicts the cell data and agrees only with the enzyme data is a hypothesis about the pocket, not a finding about the drug.

4.3 The covalent problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The three inhibitors were chosen by published data, not by pipeline rank, and all three carry the same Michael-acceptor warhead — so the covalent discount applies to the whole set, not to one compound, and the ranking within the set is still informative about non-covalent fit even though the absolute numbers understate binding. The honest handling is to report both structures with the caveat attached, and to design the validation assay so the ranking question is answered by the experiment: a purified-enzyme FRET assay measures IC50 regardless of which crystal conformation the pocket was solved in, and it captures the covalent inactivation rate (k_inact/K_I) that Vina cannot see. A compound that scores well because it is big, or because the pocket was solved around its competitor, is not a failure of the compound; it is a failure of the scoring setup, and the assay is what tells the two apart.

4.4 Mechanism

Rupintrivir, AG7404 and SG85 are all peptidomimetic Michael acceptors: the P1 glutamine-mimicking lactam sits in the S1 pocket, the P2/P3 groups fill their subsites, and the α,β-unsaturated ester is attacked by the catalytic cysteine (Cys147 HRV2 / Cys146 HRV-B14), forming a covalent bond and irreversibly inactivating the protease, which blocks polyprotein processing and so blocks viral replication. Test for each link: (i) a purified HRV 3C FRET enzyme assay (with rupintrivir as the comparator) measures IC50 and the covalent inactivation rate k_inact/K_I directly against the published values; (ii) a cell-based cytopathic-effect assay across HRV-A, -B and -C serotypes measures antiviral EC50 — a fall in enzyme activity without a fall in viral replication would break the claimed mechanism and point to delivery or permeability; (iii) a resistance-selection passage measures whether the compound selects the known rupintrivir mutations or new ones, and whether SG85 retains activity against the rupintrivir-resistant virus (the no-cross-resistance claim, tested rather than cited).

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. AG7404 inhibits purified HRV-B14 3C protease with an IC50 within 3-fold of the published 0.046 μM in the same FRET assay. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than 0.046 μM.
  2. SG85 inhibits HRV-C15 3C protease in the enzyme assay and HRV-C15 replication in cells at an EC50 within 3-fold of its published median 0.04 μM. Falsifier: EC50 > 3-fold worse, which would show the HRV-C pocket (with its half-closed S2 subsite) rejects it.
  3. The docking ranking predicts the enzyme ranking: the compound that scores best on 1CQQ has the lowest IC50. Falsifier: the docking winner's IC50 is worse than the reference drug's, which would show the non-covalent score does not rank this covalent family.
  4. SG85 retains activity against a rupintrivir-resistant HRV (selected by serial passage), confirming no cross-resistance in this system. Falsifier: the resistant virus is equally resistant to SG85.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): purified HRV 3C FRET enzyme assay for the three inhibitors — rupintrivir, AG7404, SG85 — plus a known weak inhibitor as a negative control; readout IC50 and k_inact/K_I, n=3, on HRV-B14 3C and HRV-C15 3C. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): cell-based cytopathic-effect assay for the best compound from stage 1 against rupintrivir across HRV-A, -B and -C serotypes, with a cytotoxicity counter-screen. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any inhibitor passes stages 1–2 — IC50 within 3-fold of the published value and EC50 matching rupintrivir on at least two species — a resistance-selection passage to test the cross-resistance claim; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows small margins.
  2. The covalent bond that makes these drugs work is not scored by Vina — the reference drug's true binding is underestimated by exactly its mechanism of action.
  3. SG85's first 1CQQ dock hit Vina's 1800 s wall-time limit under shared-CPU contention; the retry (same centre, box and exhaustiveness) completed at −7.42 kcal/mol, so the table is complete — but the timeout is a warning that this VM cannot reliably dock the largest ligands when several papers run at once.
  4. Both structures hold rupintrivir, so each pocket is in rupintrivir's conformation, which favours the reference drug's shape over its competitors'.
  5. The pipeline's target resolution was wrong (human IFIH1/MDA5, structure 3GA3) and had to be corrected by hand; the correction is documented in §2.2, but it means the automated pipeline cannot be trusted for viral targets without a manual structure audit.
  6. The three inhibitors' measured potencies are EC50/IC50 values from different assays and different serotypes, not a common-assay comparison.
  7. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the 0.023 μM potency the class achieves from the natural-infection failure that stopped it, nor the delivery and timing problem that a better score does not fix.
  8. Docking was on rhinovirus structures only; the picornavirus-family coverage claims (enterovirus, FMDV, norovirus) rest on published assays, not on this paper's computation — and AG7404's FMDV gap is published, not computed here.
  9. No Pakistan-specific HRV burden data were found; the paper reports the global numbers and does not invent local ones.
  10. The classical-canon sweep found the disease (catarrh, zukam) but not the target: the Canon of Medicine describes coryza as a syndrome, not a protease, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and Ibn al-Nafis's Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun survives as an Arabic manuscript with only partial English translation — neither was fully read, and the sweep covers the available digitised canon only.

6. Conclusion

Rupintrivir (AG7088), the covalent 3C inhibitor with a 0.023 μM mean EC50 that cut symptom scores by 33% in a human challenge trial and then failed in natural colds, self-docks at −7.45 kcal/mol on its own 1.85 Å co-crystal 1CQQ and −7.43 kcal/mol on the HRV-C15 structure 6KU8, with no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery, and a modest score that shows Vina cannot see the covalent bond that does the drug's work. AG7404 scores −7.69 and −7.96 kcal/mol, ahead on both structures by 0.24 and 0.53 kcal/mol, inside noise; SG85 scores −7.42 on 1CQQ — tied with the reference — and −7.75 on 6KU8. The docking verdict is a consistent but sub-noise ranking that contradicts the cell-assay potency order and agrees only with the purified-enzyme data — and it is useful precisely as one: this covalent family cannot be ranked by rigid non-covalent scoring, the reference drug's win is absent even on its own co-crystal, and the next screen must be a purified 3C enzyme assay measuring the covalent inactivation rate, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same pocket that binds rupintrivir at −7.45 kcal/mol is the pocket whose blockade failed in natural infection, and only an enzyme assay plus a cell assay can tell whether a successor keeps the potency without the delivery failure. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a 3C FRET enzyme assay for the three inhibitors against rupintrivir — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the National Institute of Health (NIH) Islamabad, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to spend anything on a rhinovirus 3C-inhibitor programme in Pakistan, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund any rupintrivir-repurposing or 3C-inhibitor evaluation for the common cold — no 3C inhibitor is approved, the only clinical data show a challenge-trial win and a natural-infection failure, and Pakistan has no published HRV burden data at all. Instead, fund two cheap things first: (a) a one-season HRV surveillance study in Larkana and Karachi clinics, typing HRV-A/B/C in cold and asthma-exacerbation cases, so the patients who could benefit from any 3C inhibitor are counted before any drug is discussed; and (b) a purified 3C enzyme assay capability at one university lab, so the docking rankings in papers like this one can be tested for the price of reagents rather than debated. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the surveillance shows HRV-C drives a defined share of asthma exacerbations in Pakistan, and an inhibitor shows an IC50 within 3-fold of rupintrivir's published potency against HRV-C15 3C with oral bioavailability, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that compound; if the surveillance shows HRV is a minor contributor to exacerbations, drop the 3C route and redirect the same money to the respiratory diseases Pakistan's patients actually carry — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia; Qur'an 5:32 — "whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely"): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable inhibitor from an unusable one for a virus that drives asthma exacerbations, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it — and the classical rule, that nothing be prescribed for catarrh for three days while secretions discharge, is the same principle in older language: do not intervene until you know what you are treating. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-25 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #114 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: EZH2; tazemetostat; PRC2; molecular docking; follicular lymphoma; drug resistance; H3K27me3; Pakistan

Abstract

EZH2 is the catalytic subunit of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, which silences genes by methylating histone H3 at lysine 27; gain-of-function mutations (Y641, A677G, A687V) drive B-cell lymphoma, and the SAM-competitive inhibitor tazemetostat was the first EZH2 drug approved — until Ipsen withdrew it worldwide on 9 March 2026, after the SYMPHONY-1 trial found new blood cancers in 5.7% of treated patients against none in the control arm. We asked whether four ChEMBL EZH2 inhibitors with sub-nanomolar measured potencies bind the SAM pocket more strongly than tazemetostat. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q15910, ChEMBL CHEMBL2189110, AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked the four leads and tazemetostat on two inhibitor-bound PRC2 structures: 5WG6 (3.90 Å, GSK126-bound) and 5IJ7 (2.62 Å, pyridone-bound). The pipeline's first auto-picked structure, 5U5T, was EED, not EZH2, and was rejected by centre audit; a planned 5HYN cross-check failed at receptor preparation and was replaced by 5IJ7. Tazemetostat re-docked at −11.52 kcal/mol on 5WG6 and −12.12 on 5IJ7. One lead, CHEMBL5562984 (measured EZH2 IC50 0.45 nM), beat it on both structures: −12.58 on 5WG6 and −13.74 on 5IJ7, margins of 1.06 and 1.62 kcal/mol, with tight pose consistency on 5IJ7; the other three leads tied or lost, and one flipped from tied to a clear loss between structures. All six compounds are PAINS-clean. The honest limit: the winning margin sits at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, the winner is the largest compound in the set, and no docking score can address the second-malignancy risk that ended tazemetostat. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay EZH2 comparison of CHEMBL5562984 against tazemetostat plus a W113C/Y111D mutant panel: if its IC50 is not within 3-fold of tazemetostat's Ki of 2.5 nM, or it fails the resistance mutants, the claim is refuted.

1. Introduction

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is the third most common cancer in Pakistan: the International Agency for Research on Cancer's GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates put NHL at 10,066 new cases and 5,242 deaths in Pakistan in 2024, behind only breast and colorectal cancer. The subtype mix differs from the West: a 548-case Pakistani series (Saleem et al., Cureus 2023) found diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in 58.94% of B-cell NHL and follicular lymphoma (FL) in only 4.01%. That matters for this paper, because the drug at its centre was approved for FL — a small slice of Pakistan's lymphoma burden — and DLBCL is where most Pakistani patients are.

Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2; gene EZH2, chromosome 7q36.1; UniProt Q15910; 746 amino acids) is the catalytic subunit of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), which methylates lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me1/2/3) and silences target genes. Its SET domain (residues 612–727) carries the methyltransferase activity, and it works only inside PRC2, with EED and SUZ12 required for the active complex. Gain-of-function mutations in the SET domain — Y641 (Y641F/N/H/C/S, ~20% of FL and germinal-centre DLBCL), A677G (~1–3%) and A687V (~2%) — change the enzyme's substrate preference so it makes more H3K27me3, and the tumours become addicted to it. Y641 mutants need the wild-type allele to make H3K27me3; A677G works alone. The first EZH2 inhibitor to reach patients, GSK126, was the proof of concept (McCabe et al., Nature 2012;492:108–112): a SAM-competitive inhibitor that lowered H3K27me3 and shrank EZH2-mutant DLBCL xenografts.

The reference drug of this paper is tazemetostat (EPZ-6438, Tazverik), a SAM-competitive EZH2 inhibitor (Knutson et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2014;13:842–854; PMID 24563539; ChEMBL Ki 2.5 nM against wild-type EZH2, IC50 1.0 nM). It was the first-in-class EZH2 inhibitor approved by the US FDA: accelerated approval on 23 January 2020 for metastatic or locally advanced epithelioid sarcoma not eligible for complete resection, on the EZH-202 basket trial (Gounder et al., Lancet Oncol 2020; objective response rate 15%, 9 of 62 patients, median progression-free survival 5.5 months), and on 18 June 2020 for relapsed or refractory FL with an EZH2 mutation after at least two prior systemic therapies, on the phase 2 trial of Morschhauser et al. (Lancet Oncol 2020;21:1433–1442; NCT01897571; objective response rate 69% in EZH2-mutant FL, 31 of 45 patients, against 35% in EZH2 wild-type, 19 of 54). The dose was 800 mg orally twice daily.

That approval no longer stands. On 9 March 2026 Ipsen voluntarily withdrew tazemetostat from all indications and all markets, after the confirmatory phase Ib/III SYMPHONY-1 trial (NCT04224493, tazemetostat plus lenalidomide and rituximab versus lenalidomide and rituximab in relapsed or refractory FL) found haematologic second primary malignancies in 18 of 318 treated patients (5.7%) against none in the control arm — mostly myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), with 3 deaths among the 18 and 14 without resolution. At accelerated approval the recognised second-malignancy risk had been 1.7%; the SYMPHONY-1 rate exceeded 5% over a median treatment duration of 15.8 months. The independent data monitoring committee recommended stopping enrolment and discontinuing the drug in all treated patients, and the FDA issued a safety alert (US FDA, 2026). The reference drug of this paper is therefore a withdrawn drug — and that changes the question this paper can ask. It is no longer "can a new compound beat tazemetostat?" but "which successor, if any, is worth pursuing now that the first-in-class drug has been withdrawn for causing the very blood cancers it was meant to treat, and does any SAM-competitive inhibitor avoid that risk?"

The successors are already in the clinic. Valemetostat (DS-3201, Ezharmia), a dual EZH1/EZH2 inhibitor, was approved in Japan in September 2022 for relapsed or refractory adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (Keam, Drugs 2022;82:1621–1627; phase 2 J201 objective response rate 48% at 200 mg once daily) — and it is the only EZH2 inhibitor still on the market anywhere. The other route around the problem is allosteric: EED inhibitors (EED226, MAK683) bind the H3K27me3 pocket of EED and shut PRC2 down without touching the EZH2 SAM pocket at all (Lingel et al., J Med Chem 2017;60:415–427).

Resistance is the second reason the question changed. SAM-competitive EZH2 inhibitors select for mutations that block drug binding without killing the enzyme: a forward-genetics screen in Pfeiffer cells found the D1-domain hotspot Y111D (and I109K), which abolished drug binding by cellular thermal shift assay and shifted the IC50 by more than 1,000-fold in the A677G background — though only 3–4-fold in the Y641F background (Gonzalvez et al., Oncotarget 2015;6(32)). Y111N, F120L and Y661D are reported in the same class. More recently, W113C — a gain-of-function mutation outside the SET domain, in the SET-activation loop — was shown to raise H3K27me3 about 3-fold, matching Y641F, and to confer resistance to both tazemetostat and valemetostat while retaining sensitivity to EED inhibitors (Chu et al., J Biol Chem 2023;299:103073; PMID 36858198). A successor that only beats tazemetostat on the wild-type pocket, and fails against Y111D or W113C, is not a successor at all.

The classical medical canon knows the disease, not the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes tumours and swellings as syndromes, but not the methyltransferase. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7) — and, for this target, its sharpest edge: the drug that was withdrawn was withdrawn because it caused new blood cancers, so the safety bar for any successor is the trial's 5.7% second-malignancy rate, not the docking score.

Falsifiable question. Do the four ChEMBL EZH2 inhibitors with the strongest measured potencies bind the SAM pocket of the GSK126-bound PRC2 structure (PDB 5WG6) at scores beyond re-docked tazemetostat, and would that binding translate into stronger EZH2 inhibition? Falsifier: an EZH2 enzyme assay under identical conditions showing a lead's IC50 more than 3-fold worse than tazemetostat's published Ki of 2.5 nM, or a cellular H3K27me3 assay showing no advantage, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking on two structures — the reference drug re-docked on the inhibitor-bound PRC2 structure (5WG6) and on a second, higher-resolution PRC2 structure (5IJ7) — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and not clinical efficacy, and not safety.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-25: the tazemetostat discovery paper (Knutson et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2014;13:842–854; PMID 24563539); the FL phase 2 trial (Morschhauser et al., Lancet Oncol 2020;21:1433–1442; PMID 33035457; NCT01897571); the epithelioid-sarcoma basket trial (Gounder et al., Lancet Oncol 2020; PMID 33035459; NCT02601950); the GSK126 proof of concept (McCabe et al., Nature 2012;492:108–112); the March 2026 withdrawal (US FDA safety alert, 2026; SYMPHONY-1, NCT04224493); valemetostat's first approval (Keam, Drugs 2022;82:1621–1627); the D1-domain resistance screen (Gonzalvez et al., Oncotarget 2015;6(32)); the W113C resistance paper (Chu et al., J Biol Chem 2023;299:103073; PMID 36858198); the GSK126-bound PRC2 structure (Bratkowski et al., Sci Rep 2018;8:9092; PDB 5WG6); the EED-binder series (Lingel et al., J Med Chem 2017;60:415–427; PMID 27992714); the EZH2 catalytic-domain structure (Antonysamy et al., PLoS One 2013; doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0083737); the Pakistan lymphoma burden (GLOBOCAN 2024 Pakistan fact sheet; Saleem et al., Cureus 2023;15:e34298; PMID 36860238); and the UniProtKB record for Q15910. ChEMBL bioactivities for the comparison set were read live from the ChEMBL API (target CHEMBL2189110) on 2026-11-25.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly: UniProtKB Q15910 (histone-lysine N-methyltransferase EZH2, Homo sapiens, 746 amino acids) → ChEMBL target CHEMBL2189110 → 56 bioactivities retrieved → 25 compounds passed the similarity screen → 26 leads ranked (25 ChEMBL compounds plus the QUERY). The top four ChEMBL leads are unnamed research compounds with measured EZH2 potencies (see §3.2); none has a preferred name in ChEMBL, so this paper identifies them by ChEMBL ID, formula and measured IC50 — never by an invented name.

2.3 Molecular docking — and the centre audit that changed the structure

The first pipeline run auto-picked PDB 5U5T (1.60 Å, first by resolution in the UniProt Q15910 cross-reference list) and began docking into it. That pick is wrong, and the run was killed before it saved anything: 5U5T is EED — the non-catalytic PRC2 subunit — in complex with an EED-binder (Lingel et al., J Med Chem 2017;60:415–427). Tazemetostat is a SAM-competitive inhibitor of the EZH2 SET domain; docking it into EED's H3K27me3 pocket answers nothing about EZH2 inhibition. The UniProt cross-reference list puts the whole EED-binder series (5U5T, 5U62, 5H14, 5H19, 7QK4, 7QJG, 7QJU) under EZH2, and the auto-pick trusts UniProt xrefs and resolution — so it lands on the wrong subunit. This is the same failure class as the TYK2/3LXP centre error of 2026-11-11: never trust an auto-picked structure without checking which subunit the ligand sits in.

The corrected structures, verified by direct inspection of the PDB files on 2026-11-25:

  • Primary — 5WG6 (Bratkowski et al., Sci Rep 2018;8:9092): human PRC2 in complex with GSK126, a SAM-competitive pyridone EZH2 inhibitor of the same chemical class as tazemetostat. Resolution 3.90 Å (stated as a limit); EZH2 is an EZH2–SUZ12 chimera, but the SET domain and the SAM pocket are EZH2's. The only drug-like HETATM is GSK126 (residue A9G, chain A, 39 atoms); the grid centre is its centroid, [−81.71, 2.47, −54.66], computed with dock._ligand_center. The <3.0 Å filter in the auto-pick is why the pipeline never reached this structure.
  • The 5HYN trap (rejected as a cross-check) (2.95 Å): human PRC2 with H3K27M peptide and SAH in the SAM pocket. A second trap lives here: dock._ligand_center(5HYN) returns [79.59, −82.35, 23.29] — the M3L trimethyllysine of the JARID2 peptide sitting in EED's pocket, ~28 Å from the SAM pocket. The correct centre is the SAH chain-A centroid, [81.25, −98.86, 2.65], computed directly from the PDB file. The isolated catalytic domain 4MI5 (2.0 Å) was rejected: Antonysamy et al. (PLoS One 2013) show its cofactor site is only partially formed, with the post-SET domain displaced.

Docking used standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. On 5WG6 the top five ChEMBL leads plus the QUERY (tazemetostat) were docked. The cross-check was planned on 5HYN, but its receptor preparation failed — RDKit's PDB parser returns None for the 5HYN file (it carries M3L trimethyllysine residues in the JARID2 peptide chains) — so the cross-check moved to 5IJ7, a better template: human PRC2 in complex with a pyridone inhibitor (Brooun et al., Nat Commun 2016;7:11384; PMID 27122193), 2.62 Å, centre the 6BN pyridone centroid [30.90, 4.98, 205.18] via dock._ligand_center, with the QUERY plus the top two leads docked. The failed 5HYN attempt is preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-127-2026-11-25-5HYN.json with ok:false for all three compounds. One duplicate was caught and handled, not hidden: ChEMBL3414621 is tazemetostat itself (ChEMBL preferred name TAZEMETOSTAT, max phase 4, first approval 2020; identical formula C34H44N4O4 and similarity 1.0 to the QUERY), so it is the reference drug's own ChEMBL record, docked as a replicate of the QUERY — not a lead, and never counted as one. The same compound is never docked twice and called two drugs.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to tazemetostat and to every lead. All six compounds are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for tazemetostat and every lead. Tazemetostat: molecular weight 572.75, logP 4.73, 2 hydrogen-bond donors, 6 acceptors, TPSA 86.90 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation (molecular weight above 500) — the reference drug is not Lipinski-clean, which matters when judging the leads by the same counts. The four leads: CHEMBL5562984 (MW 681.88, logP 4.65, HBD 2, HBA 6, TPSA 115.68 Å², 8 rotatable bonds, 1 violation — the largest compound in the set, so part of any docking lead may be size); CHEMBL5188577 (MW 614.79, logP 4.92, HBD 2, HBA 7, TPSA 96.13 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 1 violation); CHEMBL4792256 (MW 511.67, logP 4.84, HBD 3, HBA 4, TPSA 82.16 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 1 violation); CHEMBL5868146 (MW 439.51, logP 3.29, HBD 2, HBA 6, TPSA 96.80 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 0 violations — the only Lipinski pass in the set, and the smallest compound). No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran only on the QUERY, and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data. That omission matters more than usual here: the drug's withdrawal was a safety event, and no in-silico panel can speak to it.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published potencies and trial results. The four leads' measured potencies are IC50s from different assays, not a common-assay comparison. The primary structure (5WG6) is 3.90 Å — low resolution for a docking template — and holds GSK126, not tazemetostat, so the pocket is in GSK126's conformation. The withdrawal's mechanism is unknown: whether the 5.7% second-malignancy rate is on-target EZH2 biology or an off-target property of tazemetostat is not established, so docking cannot say whether a successor avoids it.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison tables

Primary structure — 5WG6, 3.90 Å (human PRC2 with GSK126):

Compound Measured EZH2 potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 5WG6 (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs tazemetostat
CHEMBL5562984 (pyridone-benzamide series) IC50 0.45 nM (WT) −12.58 −12.58, −12.02, −11.44 −1.06
Tazemetostat (QUERY, reference) Ki 2.5 nM (WT) −11.52 −11.52, −11.23, −10.74 —
Tazemetostat (ChEMBL3414621, replicate) Ki 2.5 nM (WT) −11.36 −11.36, −11.26, −11.01 +0.16
CHEMBL5188577 IC50 0.68 nM (WT); 0.47 nM (Y641F) −11.30 −11.30, −11.09, −10.80 +0.22
CHEMBL4792256 IC50 9.9 nM; Ki 0.5 nM −10.96 −10.96, −10.79, −10.70 +0.56
CHEMBL5868146 IC50 4.8 nM (A677G/Y641F) −9.80 −9.80, −9.63, −9.44 +1.72

Tazemetostat self-docks at −11.52 kcal/mol on 5WG6, with tight pose consistency (−11.52, −11.23, −10.74): the method recovers strong binding for the drug in the GSK126-shaped SAM pocket, so the protocol is not broken. Its ChEMBL record, docked as a separate run of the identical molecule, scores −11.36 kcal/mol — a 0.16 kcal/mol replicate difference that is a direct measure of Vina's run-to-run stochasticity on this structure, and it sets the bar for what counts as a real margin. Only one lead clears it: CHEMBL5562984 scores −12.58 kcal/mol, ahead by 1.06 kcal/mol against the QUERY re-dock and 1.22 kcal/mol against the ChEMBL-record replicate — at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the claim is a lead, not a proof. Its pose consistency is the loosest in the table (−12.58, −12.02, −11.44; a 1.14 kcal/mol spread), which weakens the headline further. CHEMBL5188577 follows at −11.30 kcal/mol, 0.22 behind the reference, inside noise. CHEMBL4792256 trails at −10.96 kcal/mol, 0.56 behind, inside noise. CHEMBL5868146 — the smallest compound and the only Lipinski pass — scores worst at −9.80 kcal/mol, 1.72 behind the reference, a clear loss: the most drug-like compound in the set by the standard counts is the weakest binder here, and the largest compound (CHEMBL5562984, MW 681.88) is the strongest, so size is doing visible work in this ranking and is stated, not hidden.

Cross-structure check — 5IJ7, 2.62 Å (human PRC2 with a pyridone inhibitor):

Compound Best affinity, 5IJ7 (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs tazemetostat
CHEMBL5562984 (pyridone-benzamide series) −13.74 −13.74, −13.72, −13.30 −1.62
Tazemetostat (QUERY, reference) −12.12 −12.12, −11.74, −10.96 —
CHEMBL5188577 −10.92 −10.92, −9.95, −9.75 +1.20

On 5IJ7 the reference drug scores better than on 5WG6 (−12.12 against −11.52, a 0.60 kcal/mol move) — a direct measure of this method's structural sensitivity, and larger than every margin on 5WG6 except the winner's. But the winner is the same compound on both structures: CHEMBL5562984 scores −13.74 kcal/mol, ahead by 1.62 kcal/mol, with the tightest pose consistency in the paper (−13.74, −13.72, −13.30; a 0.44 kcal/mol spread). The runner-up does not survive the change of structure: CHEMBL5188577, essentially tied with tazemetostat on 5WG6 (−11.30, 0.22 behind), falls to −10.92 on 5IJ7, 1.20 behind, with the loosest poses in the table (−10.92, −9.95, −9.75). The honest reading is therefore a split verdict: one lead wins on both structures, one lead's ranking is structure-dependent, and the reference drug's own score moves by 0.60 kcal/mol between the two — so the method can claim one lead, not a ranking.

3.2 Comparison with published data

The measured potencies, read live from ChEMBL (target CHEMBL2189110) on 2026-11-25, are the ground truth the docking must be judged against — not the other way round. Tazemetostat: Ki 2.5 nM against wild-type EZH2 (flash-plate assay), IC50 1.0 nM (biotinylated-nucleosome assay), and 20 nM for cellular H3K27me3 reduction in HeLa cells. The four leads: CHEMBL5188577, IC50 0.68 nM (wild-type EZH2), 0.47 nM (Y641F) and 0.21 nM (Y641N); CHEMBL5562984, IC50 0.45 nM (wild-type EZH2), from a 2024 Bioorganic & Medicinal Chemistry series of pyridone-benzamide EZH2 inhibitors for B-cell lymphoma (doi:10.1016/j.bmc.2024.117725); CHEMBL4792256, IC50 9.9 nM and Ki 0.5 nM; CHEMBL5868146, IC50 4.8 nM against A677G/Y641F-mutant EZH2 (from a 2020 benzofuran-derivative patent). Every lead is therefore already a sub-nanomolar or low-nanomolar EZH2 inhibitor by measurement — the docking question is only whether the ranking holds in the SAM pocket, not whether these compounds inhibit EZH2 at all. No published Vina study of these compounds on 5WG6 or 5IJ7 was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (leads vs re-docked reference drug on the same structures, same protocol).

3.3 The withdrawal confounder that docking cannot see

The decisive published fact is not a potency number but a safety one: tazemetostat's SYMPHONY-1 second-malignancy rate of 5.7% (18 of 318 patients) against 0 in the control arm, with 3 deaths and 14 patients without resolution. A lead that out-scores tazemetostat by 1.62 kcal/mol but carries the same second-malignancy risk is a worse drug, and docking cannot tell the two apart. The docking order cannot explain why a 2.5 nM inhibitor causes MDS and AML in 1 in 18 patients; only a mechanism study and a trial can. And the clinical record cuts the other way too: the same drug that caused those malignancies produced only a 15% response rate in epithelioid sarcoma and a 69% response rate in EZH2-mutant FL — real but modest efficacy, bought at a risk that ended the drug. The one lead that wins here, CHEMBL5562984, is a pyridone-benzamide from a 2024 series designed for B-cell lymphoma (Bioorg Med Chem 2024; doi:10.1016/j.bmc.2024.117725); it has no clinical data of any kind, and its second-malignancy risk is entirely unknown. The docking win is therefore a reason to test it, not a reason to prefer it.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask changed on 9 March 2026. Before the withdrawal, the question was "can an EZH2 inhibitor beat tazemetostat's potency?" — now it is "can any SAM-competitive EZH2 inhibitor be developed at all, given the first-in-class drug was withdrawn for causing blood cancers, and which successor clears the safety bar the trial set?" The benchmark is therefore a screen with a two-part bar: beat the re-docked tazemetostat score on 5WG6, and show a second-malignancy rate below the 5.7% that ended tazemetostat. This paper supplies the first half of the bar and shows the second half is where the pipeline must go next: CHEMBL5562984 beats tazemetostat on both structures tested (−12.58 against −11.52 on 5WG6, −13.74 against −12.12 on 5IJ7), the only lead to do so, with the tightest poses on the higher-resolution structure — but its margin on 5WG6 (1.06 kcal/mol) sits at the edge of Vina's noise, it is the largest compound in the set, and no docking score in this paper touches the safety question that actually ended the reference drug.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the winning margin is at the edge of the noise: 1.06 kcal/mol on 5WG6 against the QUERY re-dock (1.22 against the ChEMBL-record replicate) sits inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol band, and only the 5IJ7 margin (1.62) clears 1.5 — so the claim rests on two structures agreeing, not on either one alone. Second, CHEMBL5562984 is the largest compound in the set (MW 681.88, the only compound above 650, with 1 Lipinski violation), and the smallest compound (CHEMBL5868146, MW 439.51, the only Lipinski pass) scores worst by 1.72 kcal/mol — the ranking tracks molecular size, and the paper says so rather than letting the headline stand alone. Third, the reference drug's own score moves by 0.60 kcal/mol between the two structures, and the runner-up flips from tied to a clear loss — a scoring function whose second place depends on which crystal structure is used cannot rank this family beyond its winner. A fourth reason is specific to this target: the withdrawal. Potency never was the problem — a 2.5 nM inhibitor was withdrawn for causing blood cancers — so a docking win measures the wrong thing for the decision that matters, which is safety.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All six compounds are PAINS-clean, so there is no PAINS alert to design around in this set — which is itself a result worth stating, because the leads are large, lipophilic molecules (logP 3.29–4.92) of exactly the kind that often trip the filter. The design constraint that remains is size: the winner is the largest compound in the set, so the validation assay must be able to tell a genuine affinity gain from a size effect. The enzyme assay in §4.6 does that — a larger molecule that only fills space scores well in Vina and poorly in the assay, and the IC50 comparison against tazemetostat's Ki of 2.5 nM is the test that separates the two. The mutant panel does the rest: a compound whose advantage survives the Y641F, W113C and Y111D mutants has earned its lead; one that only wins on the wild-type pocket has not.

4.4 Mechanism

Tazemetostat is a SAM-competitive EZH2 inhibitor: it occupies the SAM pocket of the SET domain, blocks transfer of the methyl group to H3K27, and so lowers H3K27me3, de-represses PRC2 target genes (including CDKN2A), and arrests the cell cycle. Test for each link: (i) an EZH2 enzyme assay (with tazemetostat as the comparator) measures IC50 directly against the published Ki of 2.5 nM; (ii) a cellular H3K27me3 assay in EZH2-mutant lymphoma cells measures target engagement — a fall in enzyme activity without a fall in H3K27me3 would break the claimed mechanism; (iii) a mutant panel (Y641F, A677G, W113C, Y111D) measures whether the lead survives the resistance mutations that defeated tazemetostat — a lead that fails W113C or Y111D is not a successor; (iv) a long-term genotoxicity and clonal-haematopoiesis screen, because the withdrawal was a safety event and no potency assay can see it.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best lead inhibits EZH2 with an IC50 within 3-fold of tazemetostat's Ki of 2.5 nM in the same enzyme assay. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than tazemetostat.
  2. The best lead lowers H3K27me3 in EZH2-mutant lymphoma cells to the same extent as tazemetostat at matched IC50 multiples. Falsifier: H3K27me3 reduction < 50% of tazemetostat's at the same multiple.
  3. The best lead retains activity against the W113C and Y111D resistance mutants where tazemetostat fails. Falsifier: IC50 shift > 10-fold on either mutant.
  4. The best lead shows no clonal-haematopoiesis signal in a long-term haematopoietic stem-cell assay at therapeutic exposure. Falsifier: any MDS/AML-associated clonal expansion — which would show the second-malignancy risk is a class effect of SAM-competitive EZH2 inhibition, not a property of tazemetostat alone.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): EZH2 enzyme assay for tazemetostat and the four leads, plus GSK126 as a second reference; readout IC50, n=3. Before the assay, re-dock the best lead on the Y641N-mutant structure 5IJ8 (the same pyridone-bound PRC2 series as 5IJ7) — a lead whose margin collapses on the mutant structure is deprioritised before any wet-lab spending. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): cellular H3K27me3 assay in EZH2-mutant lymphoma cells for the best compound from stage 1 against tazemetostat, with a mutant panel (Y641F, A677G, W113C, Y111D) as the resistance control. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any lead passes stages 1–2 — IC50 within 3-fold of tazemetostat, H3K27me3 reduction matching it, and activity retained on at least one resistance mutant — a long-term haematopoietic stem-cell genotoxicity screen; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows small margins.
  2. The primary structure (5WG6) is 3.90 Å — low resolution for a docking template — and holds GSK126, not tazemetostat, so the pocket is in GSK126's conformation.
  3. EZH2 in 5WG6 is an EZH2–SUZ12 chimera; the SET domain is EZH2's, but the construct is not the native complex.
  4. The four leads are unnamed ChEMBL compounds with no preferred name and no clinical data; their measured potencies come from different assays, not a common-assay comparison.
  5. The reference drug was withdrawn in March 2026 for second primary malignancies, and whether that risk is on-target EZH2 biology or specific to tazemetostat is unknown — docking cannot address it, and no potency result in this paper changes it.
  6. No data on the resistance mutants: the docking was run on wild-type EZH2 only; W113C and Y111D change the pocket, and a lead that wins here may fail there. The Y641N-mutant structure 5IJ8 exists and was not docked in this run — that re-dock is the first step of the validation plan, not a result of this paper.
  7. No Pakistani EZH2-mutation frequency data exist: FL is only 4.01% of Pakistani B-cell NHL, and the fraction of Pakistani DLBCL/FL carrying EZH2 mutations has never been measured, so the eligible population in Pakistan is unknown.
  8. The planned 5HYN cross-check failed at receptor preparation (RDKit could not parse the file) and was replaced by 5IJ7; the failed attempt is preserved in the data files, but no 5HYN scores exist.
  9. The classical-canon sweep found no EZH2-relevant text: the Canon of Medicine describes tumours as syndromes, not the methyltransferase, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target. The full 23 volumes of Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and Ibn al-Nafis's Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun survives as an Arabic manuscript with only partial English translation — neither was read in full for this paper.

6. Conclusion

Tazemetostat (EPZ-6438), the first EZH2 inhibitor approved and the first withdrawn — accelerated approval in January and June 2020, voluntary withdrawal worldwide on 9 March 2026 after SYMPHONY-1 found new blood cancers in 5.7% of treated patients — re-docks at −11.52 kcal/mol on its class's co-crystal structure 5WG6 and −12.12 kcal/mol on 5IJ7, with no PAINS alert: a validated control, not a discovery. One lead, CHEMBL5562984 (measured EZH2 IC50 0.45 nM), beats it on both structures: −12.58 kcal/mol on 5WG6 and −13.74 kcal/mol on 5IJ7, margins of 1.06 and 1.62 kcal/mol, with the tightest poses on the higher-resolution structure. The other three leads tie or lose, and one flips from tied to a clear loss between structures, so the method can claim one lead, not a ranking. The docking verdict is therefore a single lead with an honest margin: this compound is worth the enzyme assay, the cellular H3K27me3 assay and the W113C/Y111D mutant panel — and worth a re-dock on the Y641N-mutant structure 5IJ8 before any of that — but no docking score in this paper addresses the second-malignancy risk that ended tazemetostat, and only a mechanism study and a trial can. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — an EZH2 enzyme assay for CHEMBL5562984 against tazemetostat — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to spend anything on EZH2 inhibitors in Pakistan, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not pursue registration, import or evaluation of tazemetostat — it was withdrawn worldwide on 9 March 2026, and no stock should be procured; do not fund any SAM-competitive EZH2-inhibitor evaluation until the second-malignancy mechanism is clarified, because the SYMPHONY-1 rate of 5.7% (18/318, 3 deaths) is the bar any successor must clear, and docking cannot clear it. Instead, fund a lymphoma registry with EZH2 mutation testing in DLBCL and FL, so the patients who could benefit from any EZH2 inhibitor are counted before any new drug is discussed — FL is only 4.01% of Pakistani B-cell NHL, and the EZH2-mutant fraction in Pakistan has never been measured — and, in parallel, ask the programme to note explicitly that the binding question is settled for this pocket — tazemetostat re-docks at −11.52 kcal/mol on 5WG6 — and that the remaining gap is safety and resistance, not potency. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a successor EZH2 inhibitor shows a Phase 2 response with a second-malignancy rate below 1% over at least 2 years of follow-up, and Pakistan's registry identifies an EZH2-mutant cohort, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that compound; if the registry shows EZH2-mutant lymphoma is rare in Pakistan, drop the EZH2 route and redirect the same money to the lymphomas Pakistan's patients actually carry — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable inhibitor from an unusable one for a disease that kills working-age adults, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it — and, for this target, the same principle sets the safety bar higher than usual, because the drug that was withdrawn was withdrawn for causing the very blood cancers it was meant to treat (Qur'an 5:32 — "whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely"; Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa, on the five necessities including hifz al-nafs). The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

BI-3406 Self-Docks at −9.07 kcal/mol on Its Own SOS1 Co-Crystal 6SCM — and Beats MRTX0902 and BAY-293 by Less Than Vina Noise

KRAS is the most commonly mutated oncogene in human cancer, present in about 25% of all tumours — 85–92% of pancreatic cancers, 40–49% of colorectal cancers and 30–35% of non-small-cell lung cancers — and direct KRAS blockade covers only some alleles.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-24 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #107 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: SOS1; KRAS; BI-3406; guanine-nucleotide exchange factor; molecular docking; MRTX0902; pancreatic cancer; non-small-cell lung cancer

Abstract

KRAS is the most commonly mutated oncogene in human cancer, present in about 25% of all tumours — 85–92% of pancreatic cancers, 40–49% of colorectal cancers and 30–35% of non-small-cell lung cancers — and direct KRAS blockade covers only some alleles. SOS1, the guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that switches KRAS from GDP-bound to GTP-bound, sits upstream of all KRAS mutants and is a feedback node that MEK inhibition reactivates, which makes it a combination target. We asked whether the newer SOS1 inhibitors MRTX0902 and BAY-293 bind the SOS1 catalytic pocket more strongly than BI-3406, the reference SOS1::KRAS interaction inhibitor. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q07889 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked BI-3406, MRTX0902 and BAY-293 on 6SCM, the 1.87 Å crystal structure of SOS1 in complex with BI-3406 itself, centred exactly on the co-crystallised BI-3406 (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). BI-3406 self-docked at −9.07 kcal/mol. MRTX0902 scored −8.10 kcal/mol and BAY-293 −8.11 kcal/mol — behind by 0.97 and 0.96 kcal/mol, just inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the two comparators are 0.01 kcal/mol apart. The honest limit: the reference drug wins on its own structure, which biases the comparison in its favour, and BI-3406 itself never entered the clinic — the clinical data belong to its analogue BI 1701963, whose Phase 1 showed limited efficacy as monotherapy (one partial response). The falsifiable next step is a single-assay SOS1::KRAS interaction comparison (IC50) of the three inhibitors under identical conditions: if MRTX0902's IC50 is not within 3-fold of BI-3406's, the dead-heat claim is refuted.

1. Introduction

KRAS is the most commonly mutated oncogene in human cancer, present in about 25% of all tumours (MD Anderson) and about 23% of all human malignancies (Curr Oncol 2025 review), and oncogenic KRAS alterations drive about one in seven human cancers. The burden concentrates in the deadliest solid tumours: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma 85–92%, colorectal cancer 40–49%, non-small-cell lung cancer 30–35% (lung adenocarcinoma 25–30%), with alleles concentrated at codons 12, 13 and 61 — G12D, G12V, G12C and G13D the most prevalent, about nine mutations accounting for about 90% of KRAS-driven cancers. KRAS G12C is about 13% of non-small-cell lung cancer and 1–3% of colorectal cancer. KRAS was called "undruggable" for about 40 years until the G12C inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib arrived in 2021 — and those cover only one allele. No Pakistan-specific KRAS-mutant registry data were found in this sweep; the burden numbers above are global, and the absence of local genotyping data is itself part of the policy question in §7.

SOS1 (Son of Sevenless homolog 1) is the guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that catalyses GDP-to-GTP exchange on KRAS, switching it from inactive (GDP-bound) to active (GTP-bound) — described as a "pacemaker" for KRAS cycling between off and on states. Receptor-tyrosine-kinase activation recruits GRB2 and SOS (facilitated by SHP2) to the plasma membrane, where SOS promotes the exchange; active KRAS-GTP drives RAF–MEK–ERK (MAPK) and PI3K–AKT–mTOR signalling. SOS1 has two KRAS-binding sites: the CDC25 catalytic site, where exchange happens, and the REM allosteric site, where a second KRAS molecule binds and modulates activation. Its homolog SOS2 can compensate when SOS1 is inhibited, which modulates inhibitor efficacy. SOS1 sits upstream of all KRAS mutants and is a feedback node: MEK inhibition reactivates the pathway through SOS1, so combined SOS1 and MEK inhibition is a therapeutic concept, and SOS1 inhibition raises the GDP-KRAS pool that G12C inhibitors need. Hence the "vertical combination" rationale: SOS1 plus MEK, SOS1 plus KRAS G12C, SOS1 plus EGFR.

The reference drug of this paper is BI-3406, a potent, selective, orally bioavailable small-molecule SOS1::KRAS interaction inhibitor from Boehringer Ingelheim (Hofmann et al., Cancer Discovery 2021;11:142–157; doi:10.1158/2159-8290.CD-20-0142; PMID 32816843). It binds the catalytic (CDC25) domain of SOS1, prevents interaction with KRAS-GDP, reduces GTP-loaded RAS, and limits proliferation of KRAS-driven cancers. Its potency on the Boehringer open-innovation profile: SOS1::KRAS interaction IC50 5 nM; pERK inhibition IC50 4 nM in KRAS-mutant NCI-H358 cells; proliferation IC50 24 nM (NCI-H358) and 36 nM (DLD-1, KRAS G13D); no activity on KRAS wild-type H520 cells (>10,000 nM); selective against SOS2 (IC50 >10 µM); no off-target hits in a 368-kinase panel at 5 µM; expected low brain penetration. In preclinical models, BI-3406 attenuates MEK-inhibitor-induced feedback reactivation, combines with the EGFR inhibitor afatinib against KRAS G13D-mutant colorectal tumour cells (Ramharter et al., J Med Chem 2021;64:6569–6580), and with KRAS G12C inhibitors enhances efficacy, limits RTK/ERK rebound, resensitises drug-tolerant persister cells and delays acquired resistance in lung adenocarcinoma models regardless of KEAP1/STK11 co-mutation status (Cancer Research 2025;85:118–133; PMID 39437166).

The critical distinction: BI-3406 itself is a preclinical probe; it did not enter the clinic. The clinical analogue is BI 1701963 (structure undisclosed), a close analogue of BI-3406, in the Phase 1 trial NCT04111458 (started 4 November 2019; KRAS-mutant advanced/metastatic solid tumours; status "Active, not recruiting"; estimated primary completion 31 March 2027). The dose-escalation results show limited efficacy as monotherapy: dose-limiting toxicities in 6 of 75 patients (8.0%) on monotherapy against 6 of 19 (31.6%) in combination with trametinib; maximum tolerated dose 800 mg monotherapy and 100 mg BI 1701963 with 1 mg trametinib in combination; one partial response on monotherapy plus stable disease in both arms (an earlier report: stable disease in 7 of 31 KRAS-mutant patients up to 18 weeks). Enrolment is reported as 71 on ClinicalTrials.gov and 94 in a later summary — the discrepancy is flagged, not resolved, and no single enrolment number is quoted as settled.

The comparators are the other clinical-stage and tool SOS1 inhibitors. MRTX0902 (Mirati/Bristol Myers Squibb) is a potent, selective, brain-penetrant, orally bioavailable phthalazine-based SOS1:KRAS disruptor (Ketcham et al., J Med Chem 2022;65:9678–9690; doi:10.1021/acs.jmedchem.2c00741; PMID 35833726), in Phase 1 (NCT05578092) alone and with adagrasib; its rationale is that disrupting SOS1:KRAS increases GDP-loaded KRAS G12C, the form adagrasib binds. BAY-293 (Bayer) is an aminoquinazoline tool inhibitor with high affinity and moderate antiproliferative activity, synergistic with the KRAS G12C inhibitor ARS853; it is a research tool, not clinically suitable, though a related compound, BAY3498264, entered clinical evaluation. RMC-5845 (Revolution Medicines) remains preclinical and IND-deferred — it is not described as clinical-stage anywhere in this paper.

The classical medical canon knows the disease family, not the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes tumours (saratān) and their treatment — the syndrome, not the protein. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do the SOS1 inhibitors MRTX0902 and BAY-293 bind the catalytic pocket of the BI-3406-bound structure (PDB 6SCM) at scores beyond re-docked BI-3406, and would that binding translate into stronger SOS1::KRAS disruption? Falsifier: a SOS1::KRAS interaction assay under identical conditions showing an IC50 for MRTX0902 more than 3-fold worse than BI-3406's, or a pERK assay in KRAS-mutant cells showing no advantage, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference drug re-docked on its own co-crystal structure, with the co-crystallised ligand as the centre — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and not clinical efficacy.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-24: the BI-3406 discovery paper (Hofmann et al., Cancer Discov 2021;11:142–157; doi:10.1158/2159-8290.CD-20-0142; PMID 32816843); the Boehringer open-innovation profile for BI-3406; the BI 1701963 Phase 1 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04111458) and its dose-escalation results; the MRTX0902 paper (Ketcham et al., J Med Chem 2022;65:9678–9690; doi:10.1021/acs.jmedchem.2c00741; PMID 35833726) and trial (NCT05578092); the afatinib combination paper (Ramharter et al., J Med Chem 2021;64:6569–6580); the KRAS G12C combination study (Cancer Res 2025;85:118–133; PMID 39437166); the SOS1 structural literature (6SFR, 6SCM, 7AVS, 5OVE, 6EPM/6EPN); the KRAS burden reviews (MD Anderson; Curr Oncol 2025;32:614); and the UniProtKB record for Q07889. No Pakistan-specific KRAS-mutant data were found.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB Q07889 (Son of sevenless homolog 1, Homo sapiens) → ChEMBL lookup returned no target record (chembl_targets empty), so no ChEMBL ligands were retrieved and the similarity screen was skipped — stated, not hidden. The comparison set was therefore built from the literature: the three SOS1 inhibitors with the strongest published data, with SMILES verified against PubChem by molecular formula (BI-3406 C23H25F3N4O3; MRTX0902 C22H24N6O; BAY-293 C25H28N4O2S).

2.3 Molecular docking

The three inhibitors were docked on 6SCM, the 1.87 Å crystal structure of SOS1 in complex with BI-3406, using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised BI-3406 (ligand L7H, 58 heavy atoms), [1.31, −31.24, −44.42], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center (the centre audit confirmed L7H is the drug-like HETATM group; the imidazole and ethylene-glycol crystallisation additives were correctly excluded); box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for all three compounds. BI-3406 is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover strong binding for the drug in its own pocket would be broken. One caveat, stated not smoothed over: the pocket is in BI-3406's own conformation, which biases the comparison in the reference drug's favour, and a MRTX0902 pose optimised for its own (non-existent) co-crystal might score differently. The docked BI-3406 is the parent SMILES as returned by PubChem; the crystal holds BI-3406 itself.

A correction is recorded here, because the pipeline's first run was wrong and the error matters. The pipeline docked BI-3406 on 6V9M at −8.88 kcal/mol, but the centre audit showed 6V9M's largest drug-like HETATM group is GNP, a GTP analogue bound to KRAS chain A — 6V9M is a SOS1-activator fragment screen (SOS1 plus KRAS–GNP complex), not an inhibitor-bound SOS1 structure, so BI-3406 was docked into the KRAS GTP pocket. That −8.88 kcal/mol score is discarded and does not appear in this paper's results. The 6SCM run reported here replaces it.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all three inhibitors. All three are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for BI-3406: molecular weight 462.47, logP 4.89, 2 hydrogen-bond donors, 7 acceptors, TPSA 91.52 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. The two comparators: MRTX0902 (MW 388.48, logP 3.52, HBD 1, HBA 7, TPSA 86.96 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations) and BAY-293 (MW 448.59, logP 5.58, HBD 2, HBA 7, TPSA 68.30 Å², 8 rotatable bonds, 1 violation). MRTX0902 is the smallest and least lipophilic of the three and the only one reported as brain-penetrant — a property the docking scores cannot see and the paper does not claim for it. No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran only on the QUERY, and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published potencies and trial results. The three inhibitors' measured potencies are interaction and cellular IC50s from different assays, not a common-assay comparison, and their binding poses are not annotated anywhere — all three are SOS1 inhibitors by pharmacology, but the pose is assumed, not shown. The structure used (6SCM) holds BI-3406, so the pocket conformation is the reference drug's own, which favours it over the other two.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (6SCM, 1.87 Å — the BI-3406-bound structure)

Compound Clinical status Best affinity, 6SCM (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs BI-3406
BI-3406 (reference) Preclinical probe; clinical analogue BI 1701963 in Phase 1 −9.07 −9.07, −9.01, −8.36 —
BAY-293 Research tool; related compound in clinic −8.11 −8.11, −8.09, −7.47 +0.96
MRTX0902 Phase 1 (NCT05578092) −8.10 −8.10, −7.63, −7.32 +0.97

BI-3406 self-docks at −9.07 kcal/mol on 6SCM, with good pose consistency (−9.07, −9.01, −8.36): the method recovers strong binding for the drug in its own pocket, so the protocol is not broken. MRTX0902 scores −8.10 kcal/mol and BAY-293 −8.11 kcal/mol — behind by 0.97 and 0.96 kcal/mol, just inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the two comparators are 0.01 kcal/mol apart. Every margin in the table lies inside the noise, so no compound can be claimed to beat any other on this evidence — including the reference drug, whose win is smaller than the noise and comes on its own structure. The honest reading is a null result on ranking, with one validated control: the method works, and the three inhibitors are indistinguishable by rigid docking on this structure.

3.2 Comparison with published data

No published Vina study of BI-3406, MRTX0902 or BAY-293 on 6SCM was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (inhibitors vs re-docked reference drug on the same structure, same protocol). The structural literature is the published ground truth for the binding mode: the 6SCM structure shows BI-3406 in the CDC25 catalytic pocket, 6SFR (1.92 Å) shows the early quinazoline hit BI-68BS in the same pocket, 7AVS shows the afatinib-combination series compound, 5OVE shows another quinazoline inhibitor at 1.85 Å, and 6EPM/6EPN show the SOS1–KRAS(G12C) protein–protein complex at 2.50 Å. The published potency order is the opposite of the docking order's implication: BI-3406's SOS1::KRAS interaction IC50 is 5 nM, and MRTX0902's published cellular data are in the same range — the assays cannot separate them either, which is consistent with the docking null result rather than a contradiction of it. The decisive published fact is not a potency number but a clinical one: the only SOS1 inhibitor with Phase 1 dose-escalation results, BI 1701963, showed limited efficacy as monotherapy — one partial response — which is why the field's rationale is now vertical combination, not single-agent SOS1 inhibition.

3.3 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

BI 1701963's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug reached its maximum tolerated dose (800 mg monotherapy) with dose-limiting toxicities in 8.0% of patients, yet produced one partial response as monotherapy and stable disease as its best result in most patients — a drug that engages its target and still does not shrink tumours alone, because SOS2 compensates and because KRAS-mutant cancers rewire around a single upstream block. The combination data point the other way: with trametinib, dose-limiting toxicities rose to 31.6% of patients, and the combination's maximum tolerated dose fell to 100 mg with 1 mg trametinib — the vertical combination that the biology demands is also the combination that the toxicity budget punishes. A compound that out-scores BI-3406 here by 0.97 kcal/mol but cannot be combined safely would be a worse drug, and docking cannot tell the two apart. The docking order cannot explain why the class works in combination models and stalls as monotherapy in patients; the feedback biology and the toxicity data can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since BI-3406 was published. Before the Phase 1 data, the question was "can a SOS1 inhibitor beat BI-3406's potency?" — now it is "can any SOS1 inhibitor be combined safely enough to matter, given monotherapy stalls?" The benchmark is therefore a screen with a two-part bar: beat −9.07 kcal/mol on 6SCM and show a combinable safety profile. This paper supplies the first half of the bar and shows the second half is where the pipeline must go next: the three inhibitors cannot be separated by docking, and the class's defining problem is combination toxicity, not potency.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, every margin in §3.1 lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — the largest gap, 0.97 kcal/mol, is less than half the noise. Second, the reference drug wins on its own co-crystal structure, which biases the comparison in its favour; a win on home ground by less than noise is not a win. Third, the two comparators are 0.01 kcal/mol apart — a scoring function that cannot separate a brain-penetrant clinical candidate (MRTX0902) from a research tool (BAY-293) by more than a hundredth of a kilocalorie cannot rank this family. A fourth reason is specific to this target: SOS2 compensation means even a perfect SOS1 binder leaves a parallel route to KRAS activation open, so the docking score measures the wrong thing — binding to one GEF, not blockade of the pathway.

4.3 The dead heat is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The three inhibitors were chosen by published data, not by pipeline rank, and the smallest and least lipophilic of them (MRTX0902, MW 388.48, logP 3.52) does not score best — it ties last — so the size bias is visible but not total in this set. The honest handling is to report the scores with the caveat attached, and to design the validation assay so the dead heat is answered by the experiment: a SOS1::KRAS interaction assay measures IC50 regardless of molecular weight, and a pERK assay in KRAS-mutant cells measures whether the inhibitor actually lowers pathway output, including through SOS2 compensation. A compound that scores well because the pocket was solved around it is not a failure of the compound; it is a failure of the scoring setup, and the assay is what tells the two apart.

4.4 Mechanism

BI-3406 binds the CDC25 catalytic domain of SOS1, prevents the SOS1::KRAS-GDP interaction, and so lowers GTP-loaded RAS and downstream RAF–MEK–ERK signalling. Test for each link: (i) a SOS1::KRAS interaction assay (with BI-3406 as the comparator) measures IC50 directly against the published 5 nM value; (ii) a pERK assay in KRAS-mutant NCI-H358 cells measures pathway output — a fall in pERK without a fall in RAS-GTP would break the claimed mechanism; (iii) a proliferation assay in KRAS-mutant versus KRAS wild-type cells measures selectivity, with SOS2 knockdown as the control for the compensation question.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. MRTX0902 disrupts the SOS1::KRAS interaction with an IC50 within 3-fold of BI-3406 in the same assay. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than BI-3406.
  2. The same compound lowers pERK in KRAS-mutant NCI-H358 cells within 3-fold of BI-3406's published 4 nM. Falsifier: pERK IC50 > 3-fold worse than BI-3406.
  3. The 6SCM pose predicts the combination profile: an inhibitor whose docked pose occupies the same CDC25 pocket as BI-3406 attenuates MEK-inhibitor feedback reactivation to the same extent. Falsifier: no attenuation of feedback reactivation in combination with trametinib.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): SOS1::KRAS interaction assay for the three inhibitors — BI-3406, MRTX0902, BAY-293 — plus a known weak binder as a negative control; readout IC50, n=3. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): pERK assay in KRAS-mutant NCI-H358 cells for the best compound from stage 1 against BI-3406, with SOS2 knockdown as the compensation control. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any inhibitor passes stages 1–2, a proliferation assay in KRAS-mutant versus KRAS wild-type cells, and a trametinib-combination arm to test feedback attenuation; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin — the largest gap is 0.97 kcal/mol.
  2. The ranking cannot separate the three inhibitors (the two comparators are 0.01 kcal/mol apart), so the set cannot test ranking at all.
  3. The reference drug wins on its own co-crystal structure (6SCM), which biases the comparison in its favour.
  4. The pipeline's first run docked BI-3406 into the KRAS GTP pocket of 6V9M (−8.88 kcal/mol); that score is discarded here, and the error is recorded in §2.3 rather than hidden.
  5. One rigid structure was used (6SCM, inhibitor-bound, 1.87 Å); the other SOS1 structures (6SFR, 7AVS, 5OVE) and the SOS1–KRAS complex (6EPM/6EPN) were not docked.
  6. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the monotherapy that stalls from the combination that the toxicity budget punishes, nor the SOS2 compensation that leaves a parallel route open.
  7. The ChEMBL ligand retrieval returned no data for this target, so the comparison set was built from the literature rather than from measured ChEMBL potencies; the three inhibitors' potencies are interaction and cellular IC50s from different assays, not a common-assay comparison.
  8. No Pakistan-specific KRAS-mutant data were found; the burden numbers are global, and the absence of local genotyping data is a limitation of the policy section, not of the docking.
  9. The classical-canon sweep found no SOS1-relevant text: the Canon of Medicine describes tumours, not proteins, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

BI-3406, the SOS1::KRAS interaction inhibitor with a 5 nM interaction IC50 and a 4 nM pERK IC50 in KRAS-mutant cells, self-docks at −9.07 kcal/mol on its own 1.87 Å co-crystal 6SCM with no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery. MRTX0902 and BAY-293 follow at −8.10 and −8.11 kcal/mol, behind by less than noise and 0.01 kcal/mol apart. The docking verdict is a null result on ranking, with one validated control, and it is useful precisely as one: this family cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring on a single structure, the reference drug's win comes on its own structure, and the next screen must be an interaction assay plus a pERK assay with a SOS2 control, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same pocket that binds BI-3406 at −9.07 kcal/mol is the pocket whose blockade stalls as monotherapy in patients and whose combination with MEK inhibition the toxicity budget punishes. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a SOS1::KRAS interaction assay for the three inhibitors against BI-3406 — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the National Cancer Control Programme, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to spend anything on SOS1 inhibitors in Pakistan, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund any SOS1-inhibitor evaluation — no SOS1 drug is approved, the only clinical data show limited monotherapy efficacy, and Pakistan has no KRAS-mutant registry, so the patients who could benefit cannot even be identified. Instead, fund KRAS genotyping capacity (next-generation sequencing) in the public cancer hospitals, starting with pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancer, so the 25%-of-tumours population is counted before any targeted drug is discussed; and, in parallel, ask the cancer programme to note explicitly that the binding question is settled for this pocket — BI-3406 self-docks at −9.07 kcal/mol — and that the remaining gap is combination safety and SOS2 compensation, not potency. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a SOS1 inhibitor shows a Phase 2 response rate above 20% in KRAS-mutant solid tumours in combination, and Pakistan's genotyping programme identifies a KRAS-mutant cohort, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that combination; if genotyping shows KRAS mutations are rarer in Pakistan's cancers than the global 25%, drop the SOS1 route and redirect the same money to the mutations Pakistan's patients actually carry — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable targeted drug from an unusable one for the most commonly mutated oncogene in human cancer, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

Etavopivat Out-Scores Mitapivat by 0.09 kcal/mol on the Mitapivat-Bound PKR Structure 8XFD — a Dead Heat Between Two Pyruvate-Kinase Activators, and a 2.74 kcal/mol Gap to the Discontinued Tebapivat
