Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-24 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #108 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: endothelin receptor type A; ETA antagonist; ambrisentan; pulmonary arterial hypertension; molecular docking; bosentan; macitentan; Pakistan

Abstract

Pulmonary arterial hypertension affects about 25 people per million and is fatal without treatment, yet no endothelin-receptor antagonist has ever been co-crystallised with its target — the first endothelin receptor type A (ETA) structures, solved by cryo-electron microscopy in 2023, hold the agonist endothelin-1, not an antagonist. We asked whether the established endothelin-receptor antagonists bosentan, macitentan, sitaxentan and zibotentan occupy the ETA pocket more strongly than ambrisentan, the most ETA-selective drug in the class. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P25101 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked the five antagonists on 8HCQ, the 3.0 Å cryo-EM structure of ETA bound to endothelin-1, centred on the endothelin-1 residues that occupy the pocket (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). Ambrisentan scored −7.37 kcal/mol — worst in the set. Bosentan scored best at −8.72 kcal/mol, followed by sitaxentan at −8.46, zibotentan at −8.34 and macitentan at −7.57 kcal/mol. The honest limit: the structure is in the active, endothelin-1-bound conformation, so these are pocket-occupancy numbers on an agonist-bound receptor, not antagonist potencies — and the ranking inverts the clinical one, since ambrisentan is the most ETA-selective drug in the set (ETA:ETB about 4,000:1) while the top scorer, bosentan, is the least selective, a dual antagonist. The falsifiable next step is a radioligand binding comparison (Ki) for ETA under identical conditions: if bosentan's Ki is not better than ambrisentan's, the pocket-occupancy ranking is refuted — and the decisive test is an antagonist-bound ETA structure, which does not yet exist.

1. Introduction

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive disease of the small pulmonary arteries — vasoconstriction, smooth-muscle proliferation and vascular remodelling that raise pulmonary vascular resistance until the right ventricle fails. Its prevalence is about 25 per million people, and the Global Burden of Disease 2021 study estimates 2.28 cases per 100,000 population. No Pakistan-specific PAH epidemiology was found in this sweep; the burden numbers above are global, and the absence of local data is itself part of the policy question in §7.

Endothelin-1 (ET-1) is a 21-amino-acid peptide and one of the most potent vasoconstrictors known. It acts through two G-protein-coupled receptors: ETA, on vascular smooth muscle, which mediates vasoconstriction and proliferation, and ETB, on endothelium, which mediates vasodilatation through nitric oxide and clears ET-1 from the circulation. In PAH, ET-1 is overexpressed, and blocking its receptors lowers pulmonary vascular resistance. The endothelin-receptor antagonists (ERAs) are one of the three pillars of PAH therapy, alongside phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and prostacyclins.

The reference drug of this paper is ambrisentan (Letairis, Gilead), approved by the FDA on 15 June 2007 for PAH. It is the most ETA-selective antagonist in the class, with an ETA:ETB selectivity of about 4,000:1. In the ARIES-1 and ARIES-2 trials (Galiè et al., Circulation 2008;117:3010–3019; PMID 18506008), ambrisentan improved six-minute walk distance by 31 and 51 metres at 5 and 10 mg (ARIES-1) and by 32 and 59 metres at 2.5 and 5 mg (ARIES-2) against placebo. Its liver warning was removed in 2011 after more than 7,800 patient-years of exposure without a hepatotoxicity signal, and its risk-evaluation programme was removed in April 2025 (verify at submission — the date rests on the sweep's check). The comparators span the class's history. Bosentan (Tracleer, Actelion) was the first ERA, approved in 2001, a dual ETA/ETB antagonist that requires monthly liver monitoring. Macitentan (Opsumit, Actelion) is a dual antagonist with improved tissue penetration; in the SERAPHIN trial (Pulido et al., N Engl J Med 2013;369:809–820; PMID 23984728) it reduced the composite of morbidity and mortality by 45% (hazard ratio 0.55). Sitaxentan (Thelin, Pfizer), a selective ETA antagonist, was withdrawn worldwide in 2010 after fatal hepatotoxicity. Zibotentan (AstraZeneca) is a highly selective ETA antagonist that was never approved, studied in cancer and in systemic sclerosis digital ulcers.

The structural gap is the paper's premise. No ETA–antagonist crystal structure exists: the structures sometimes cited for the class, 5XPR and 5GLH, are endothelin receptor type B, not ETA. The first ETA structures were solved by cryo-electron microscopy in 2023 (Ji et al., Nat Commun 2023;14:1268): 8HCQ at 3.0 Å and 8HCX at 3.5 Å, both of ETA bound to endothelin-1 in complex with Gq — the active, agonist-bound conformation. Every docking study of an ETA antagonist therefore has a choice: dock into an agonist-bound pocket, or not dock at all. This paper docks, and says plainly what the numbers are.

The classical medical canon knows the disease, not the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes breathlessness and heart failure as syndromes, but not the endothelin receptor. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do the established endothelin-receptor antagonists bosentan, macitentan, sitaxentan and zibotentan occupy the ETA pocket of the endothelin-1-bound structure (PDB 8HCQ) at scores beyond ambrisentan, and would that occupancy translate into stronger ETA antagonism? Falsifier: a radioligand binding assay for ETA under identical conditions showing bosentan's Ki no better than ambrisentan's, or an antagonist-bound ETA structure (when solved) giving a different rank order, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking is not available here — there is no antagonist-bound structure to validate against — so the identification is weaker than in the other papers in this series, and the paper says so: this is pocket-occupancy on an agonist-bound structure, association only, not a potency comparison.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-24: the first ETA structures (Ji et al., Nat Commun 2023;14:1268); the ARIES-1/2 trials (Galiè et al., Circulation 2008;117:3010–3019; PMID 18506008); the SERAPHIN trial (Pulido et al., N Engl J Med 2013;369:809–820; PMID 23984728); the FDA approval of ambrisentan (15 June 2007) and the removal of its liver warning (2011) and risk-evaluation programme (April 2025); the sitaxentan withdrawal (2010); the bosentan approval (2001); the PAH burden estimates (Global Burden of Disease 2021); and the UniProtKB record for P25101. No Pakistan-specific PAH epidemiology was found.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB P25101 (endothelin receptor type A, Homo sapiens) → ChEMBL lookup returned no target record (chembl_targets empty), so no ChEMBL ligands were retrieved and the similarity screen was skipped — stated, not hidden. No PDB structure was found by the pipeline at all (no_pdb_found), so docking was skipped in the pipeline run and the comparison set was built from the literature: the five ERAs with the strongest published data, with SMILES verified against PubChem by molecular formula (ambrisentan C22H22N2O4; bosentan C27H29N5O6S; macitentan C19H20Br2N6O4S; sitaxentan C18H15ClN2O6S2; zibotentan C19H16N6O4S).

2.3 Molecular docking

The five antagonists were docked on 8HCQ, the 3.0 Å cryo-EM structure of human ETA in complex with endothelin-1 and Gq, using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: grid centre the centroid of endothelin-1 residues 16–21, the residues that occupy the orthosteric pocket, [122.27, 115.66, 128.27], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center; box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for all five compounds. Two technical notes, stated not smoothed over. First, the receptor preparation required a documented fix: the PDB's charge annotation on ASP/GLU carboxylates breaks RDKit's sanitizer ("Explicit valence ... greater than permitted"), so columns 79–80 were blanked before parsing — coordinates and elements unchanged, standard sanitization then succeeds with proper aromaticity (845 aromatic carbons; the sanitize=False fallback perceives none and would mistype every aromatic receptor carbon in Vina). The fix is in health-papers-agent/dock_lenient.py. Second, the _prep_receptor step keeps all ATOM records, so the endothelin-1 peptide chain L (171 ATOM lines) was stripped from the cached 8HCQ.pdb before docking — it would otherwise block the pocket — and the original PDB was restored afterwards; the derived 8HCQ_rec.pdbqt in the cache is intentionally the chain-L-stripped receptor, and any future 8HCQ dock must use the stripped receptor, never the endothelin-1-occupied one. The G-protein chains (A/B/G) and the scFv (chain E) remain; they are far from the 22.5 Å box and harmless. There is no self-dock control in this paper, because no antagonist is co-crystallised with ETA: ambrisentan is the reference drug, not a validated control, and the paper's identification is weaker for it.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all five antagonists. All five are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for ambrisentan: molecular weight 378.43, logP 3.52, 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 5 acceptors, TPSA 81.54 Å², 7 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass — the smallest and most drug-like compound in the set. The four comparators: bosentan (MW 551.63, logP 4.20, HBD 2, HBA 10, TPSA 145.65 Å², 10 rotatable bonds, 1 violation), sitaxentan (MW 454.91, logP 3.96, HBD 1, HBA 8, TPSA 107.73 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 0 violations), zibotentan (MW 424.44, logP 2.71, HBD 1, HBA 9, TPSA 132.99 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 0 violations) and macitentan (MW 588.28, logP 3.57, HBD 2, HBA 8, TPSA 128.22 Å², 11 rotatable bonds, 1 violation). The largest compound in the set, macitentan, does not score best — it sits fourth — so the size bias is visible but not total. No ToxGuard read-across is reported for this set: the pipeline's Tox21 panel ran only on the QUERY, and the values are not a measurement; they are omitted rather than presented as safety data.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published trial results. The five antagonists' measured potencies are clinical walk-distance and event outcomes, not binding Ki values in a common assay, and their binding poses are not annotated anywhere — all five are ERAs by pharmacology, but the pose is assumed, not shown. The structure used (8HCQ) holds endothelin-1, the agonist, in the active conformation, so the pocket is in the agonist-bound state, not the antagonist-bound state — the scores are pocket-occupancy numbers, and the reference drug's low score may reflect a poor fit to the active conformation rather than weak antagonism.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (8HCQ, 3.0 Å — the endothelin-1-bound structure)

Compound Clinical status Best affinity, 8HCQ (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs ambrisentan
Bosentan Approved 2001; dual ETA/ETB; monthly liver monitoring −8.72 −8.72, −8.54, −8.43 −1.35
Sitaxentan Withdrawn 2010 (fatal hepatotoxicity) −8.46 −8.46, −8.40, −8.05 −1.09
Zibotentan Never approved; highly selective ETA antagonist −8.34 −8.34, −8.16, −7.97 −0.97
Macitentan Approved; SERAPHIN 45% morbidity–mortality reduction −7.57 −7.57, −7.54, −7.47 −0.20
Ambrisentan (reference) Approved 2007; most ETA-selective (4,000:1) −7.37 −7.37, −7.36, −7.36 —

Ambrisentan scores −7.37 kcal/mol on 8HCQ — worst in the set, with perfectly consistent poses (−7.37, −7.36, −7.36), so the low score is stable, not a sampling failure. Bosentan scores best at −8.72 kcal/mol, 1.35 kcal/mol ahead of the reference drug — the only gap in the table larger than Vina's noise, apart from sitaxentan's 1.09 kcal/mol gap. Macitentan sits fourth at −7.57 kcal/mol, only 0.20 kcal/mol ahead of ambrisentan. The honest reading is an inversion: the ranking on this structure is the reverse of the clinical ranking by ETA selectivity, and the drug with the best clinical selectivity scores worst.

3.2 Comparison with published data

No published Vina study of these antagonists on 8HCQ was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (antagonists vs reference drug on the same structure, same protocol). The structural literature is the published ground truth for the binding mode: the 8HCQ structure (Ji et al. 2023) shows endothelin-1 occupying the orthosteric pocket in the active conformation, and the structures sometimes cited for the class, 5XPR and 5GLH, are ETB, not ETA — they were not used. The published potency order is the reverse of the docking order: ambrisentan's ETA:ETB selectivity is about 4,000:1, zibotentan is highly selective, sitaxentan was selective, macitentan is dual, and bosentan is dual — yet the docking order is bosentan, sitaxentan, zibotentan, macitentan, ambrisentan. A scoring function that ranks the least selective drug first and the most selective drug last, on an agonist-bound structure, is measuring pocket occupancy in the active conformation, not antagonist potency. The decisive published fact is not a potency number but a structural one: no antagonist-bound ETA structure exists, so no docking study of this class can be validated against a co-crystal.

3.3 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Ambrisentan's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug improved six-minute walk distance by up to 59 metres, had its liver warning removed after more than 7,800 patient-years without a hepatotoxicity signal, and had its risk-evaluation programme removed in 2025 — the cleanest liver record in the class. Sitaxentan, the second-best scorer here, was withdrawn worldwide in 2010 for fatal hepatotoxicity. Bosentan, the best scorer, requires monthly liver monitoring. A compound that out-scores ambrisentan here by 1.35 kcal/mol but carries a hepatotoxicity risk would be a worse drug, and docking cannot tell the two apart. The docking order cannot explain why the class's most selective drug has the cleanest liver record while its second-best scorer was withdrawn for liver failure; the trial data and the pharmacovigilance record can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since the first ETA structures were solved. Before 2023, the question was "can we dock ERAs at all?" — now it is "what does docking into an agonist-bound structure actually measure?" The benchmark is therefore a screen with a two-part bar: occupy the pocket on 8HCQ and show a binding Ki that matches the occupancy. This paper supplies the first half of the bar and shows the second half is where the pipeline must go next: the occupancy ranking inverts the clinical ranking, and the class's defining problem is liver safety, not pocket occupancy.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the structure is agonist-bound, so every score in §3.1 is a pocket-occupancy number on the active conformation, not an antagonist potency — and the reference drug's low score may be a property of the conformation, not of the drug. Second, the ranking inverts the clinical selectivity order (bosentan first, ambrisentan last), which is the opposite of what a potency ranking should look like — a scoring function that inverts the known order on the only available structure cannot be trusted to rank this family. Third, the two gaps larger than noise (bosentan's 1.35 and sitaxentan's 1.09 kcal/mol) both belong to drugs with liver liabilities, while the cleanest drug in the class scores worst — the scores correlate with the liability, not with the benefit, which is the worst possible direction for a screening tool.

4.3 The inversion is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The five antagonists were chosen by clinical history, not by pipeline rank, and the largest of them (macitentan, MW 588.28) does not score best — it sits fourth — so the size bias is visible but not total in this set. The honest handling is to report the scores with the caveat attached, and to design the validation assay so the inversion is answered by the experiment: a radioligand binding assay measures Ki regardless of which conformation the receptor was solved in, and a hepatocyte toxicity assay measures the liability docking cannot see. A compound that scores well because it fits the active conformation is not a failure of the compound; it is a failure of the scoring setup, and the assay is what tells the two apart.

4.4 Mechanism

Ambrisentan is a selective ETA antagonist: it occupies the orthosteric pocket of ETA, blocks endothelin-1 binding, and so reduces smooth-muscle vasoconstriction and proliferation, lowering pulmonary vascular resistance. Test for each link: (i) a radioligand binding assay (with ambrisentan as the comparator) measures Ki directly against the published selectivity; (ii) a smooth-muscle contraction assay measures functional vasodilatation — a fall in contraction without a fall in binding would break the claimed mechanism; (iii) a hepatocyte toxicity assay measures whether the analogue reproduces the class's liver liability — a rise in ALT release is the likeliest way a "better" antagonist becomes a worse drug, because hepatotoxicity is the liability that withdrew one member of this class.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. Bosentan binds ETA with a Ki no better than ambrisentan in the same radioligand assay. Falsifier: Ki more than 3-fold better than ambrisentan, which would show the docking ranking was real.
  2. Ambrisentan's ETA:ETB selectivity (about 4,000:1) is preserved in the same assay. Falsifier: selectivity below 100:1, which would show the published selectivity does not reproduce.
  3. The 8HCQ pose predicts the safety profile: an antagonist whose docked pose makes the same deep-pocket contacts as bosentan carries the same liver liability as bosentan. Falsifier: an antagonist with those contacts shows no hepatocyte toxicity signal.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): radioligand binding assay for the five antagonists — ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan, sitaxentan, zibotentan — on recombinant human ETA and ETB; readout Ki and selectivity ratio, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): smooth-muscle contraction assay for the best compound from stage 1 against ambrisentan at matched Ki multiples. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any antagonist passes stages 1–2 — Ki within 3-fold of ambrisentan and selectivity above 100:1 — a hepatocyte toxicity assay; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows the 0.97 and 0.20 kcal/mol gaps, though not the 1.35 and 1.09 kcal/mol gaps.
  2. The ranking inverts the clinical selectivity order, so the set cannot be used to rank antagonists — the scores are pocket-occupancy numbers on an agonist-bound structure.
  3. There is no self-dock control in this paper, because no antagonist is co-crystallised with ETA; the identification is weaker than in the other papers in this series.
  4. The structure used (8HCQ) holds endothelin-1, the agonist, in the active conformation at 3.0 Å cryo-EM resolution — the pocket is in the agonist-bound state, and the lower resolution (against the 1.87–2.10 Å crystal structures in this series) adds coordinate uncertainty.
  5. One rigid structure was used (8HCQ); the other ETA structure (8HCX, 3.5 Å) was not docked, and no antagonist-bound ETA structure exists.
  6. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the haemodynamic benefit the class achieves from the hepatotoxicity that withdrew one member of it.
  7. The ChEMBL ligand retrieval returned no data for this target, and the pipeline found no PDB structure at all, so the comparison set and the structure were both chosen from the literature rather than from the pipeline.
  8. No Pakistan-specific PAH epidemiology was found; the burden numbers are global, and the absence of local data is a limitation of the policy section, not of the docking.
  9. The classical-canon sweep found no ETA-relevant text: the Canon of Medicine describes breathlessness and heart failure as syndromes, not the receptor, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

Ambrisentan, the most ETA-selective antagonist in the class (ETA:ETB about 4,000:1) and the one with the cleanest liver record, scores worst at −7.37 kcal/mol on the 3.0 Å endothelin-1-bound ETA structure 8HCQ with no PAINS alert — a pocket-occupancy number, not a potency, and not a discovery. Bosentan scores best at −8.72 kcal/mol, followed by sitaxentan at −8.46, zibotentan at −8.34 and macitentan at −7.57 kcal/mol. The docking verdict is an inversion, and it is useful precisely as one: antagonists cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring on an agonist-bound structure, the ranking reverses the clinical selectivity order, and the next screen must be a radioligand binding assay plus a hepatocyte toxicity assay, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the safety split: the same pocket that binds ambrisentan at −7.37 kcal/mol is the pocket whose blockade lowers pulmonary vascular resistance, and only a binding assay and a liver assay can tell whether a successor keeps the haemodynamic benefit without the liver cost. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a radioligand binding assay for the five antagonists against ambrisentan — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the National Pulmonary Hypertension Programme, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to spend anything on endothelin-receptor antagonists in Pakistan, and what must exist first. Exact change: do not fund any ERA procurement or evaluation — no ERA is cheap, the class's liver liabilities need monitoring capacity Pakistan's PAH services may not have, and there is no Pakistan-specific PAH epidemiology, so the patients who could benefit cannot even be counted. Instead, fund a PAH registry and echocardiography screening in high-risk groups (connective-tissue disease, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease), so the 25-per-million population is counted before any targeted drug is discussed; and, in parallel, ask the programme to note explicitly that the binding question is unsettled for this pocket — ambrisentan scores −7.37 kcal/mol on the only available ETA structure, and no antagonist-bound structure exists — and that the remaining gap is a structure, not a drug. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a PAH registry identifies a cohort and an antagonist-bound ETA structure is solved showing a candidate with a binding Ki better than ambrisentan and no liver signal, move to a drug-evaluation assessment for that candidate; if the registry shows PAH is rarer in Pakistan than the global 25 per million, drop the ERA route and redirect the same money to the pulmonary conditions Pakistan's patients actually carry — do not proceed to any drug evaluation on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable antagonist from an unusable one for a fatal disease, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

Meropenem Out-Scores Avibactam by 1.22 kcal/mol on Wild-Type OXA-48 — and the Comparison Is Meaningless, Because One Is a Substrate and the Other Is Covalent

Bacterial antimicrobial resistance directly caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths in 2019, and the OXA-48 carbapenemase — a class D serine β-lactamase widespread in Enterobacterales — is one of the enzymes that makes carbapenems, the drugs of last resort, fail.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-23 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #104 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: OXA-48; avibactam; carbapenemase; meropenem; molecular docking; ChEMBL; antimicrobial resistance; diazabicyclooctane; ceftazidime-avibactam

Abstract

Bacterial antimicrobial resistance directly caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths in 2019, and the OXA-48 carbapenemase — a class D serine β-lactamase widespread in Enterobacterales — is one of the enzymes that makes carbapenems, the drugs of last resort, fail. Avibactam, the diazabicyclooctane inhibitor paired with ceftazidime, inhibits OXA-48 by acylating its catalytic Ser70 — covalently, and only slowly reversibly. We asked whether any measured OXA-48 ligand binds the active site more strongly than avibactam. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q6XEC0 → ChEMBL CHEMBL1287604 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked avibactam and the single ChEMBL ligand with measured potency on the 2.3 Å wild-type OXA-48 structure in covalent complex with avibactam (PDB 4WMC), centred exactly on the co-crystallised avibactam (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). Avibactam re-docked, non-covalently, at −6.73 kcal/mol. The comparator, CHEMBL127 — verified as meropenem, the carbapenem substrate (Kd 850 nM) — scored −7.95 kcal/mol, "beating" avibactam by 1.22 kcal/mol. The comparison is meaningless, and the paper says so plainly: meropenem is the substrate OXA-48 hydrolyses, not an inhibitor, and avibactam's potency lives in the covalent acylation step that rigid non-covalent docking cannot model at all. A substrate out-scoring a covalent inhibitor on a non-covalent score proves the method's limit, not the substrate's superiority. The pipeline's first answer was worse still: it docked both compounds on 8PEB, a directed-evolution quintuple mutant centred on a malonate buffer ion, and those scores are discarded here as measurements of the wrong enzyme. The falsifiable next step is a nitrocefin-hydrolysis inhibition assay of avibactam against OXA-48, with the 4WMC pose as the structural hypothesis — not another docking run.

1. Introduction

The β-lactams — penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems — are the most commonly prescribed antibiotic class, and in Gram-negative bacteria the dominant resistance mechanism is production of β-lactamases that hydrolyse the four-membered β-lactam ring. The carbapenemases are the enzymes that defeat the drugs of last resort, and OXA-48, a class D serine β-lactamase, is among the most widely disseminated in Enterobacterales, the order that includes Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. OXA-48 uses a nucleophilic serine (Ser70) to hydrolyse β-lactams, with a proximal post-translationally carbamylated lysine (Lys73) proposed to act as the general base for both the acylation and deacylation steps of the reaction. It confers resistance to penicillins and moderate resistance to cephalosporins and carbapenems, and its variants — OXA-163 and OXA-405, with deletions in the β5–β6 loop neighbouring the active site — change activity towards different β-lactam classes.

Avibactam is the inhibitor that extended β-lactam therapy to OXA-48 producers. A diazabicyclooctane (DBO), not a β-lactam, it inhibits class A and class C β-lactamases and certain class D enzymes, and it does so covalently: it acylates Ser70, and the acyl-enzyme deacylates only exceptionally slowly in class D enzymes — the slow reversibility that the 4WMC structure was solved to explain. The combination ceftazidime–avibactam is the clinical product. The DBO class is not uniform against OXA-48: nacubactam is about 80-fold less potent than avibactam towards the enzyme, a difference traced to electrostatic repulsion between Arg214 on the β5–β6 active-site loop and nacubactam, but not avibactam — and the difference shrinks in OXA-163 and OXA-405, which lack Arg214. Sequence variation in the loop therefore affects reactivity towards inhibitors as well as towards β-lactam substrates, and crystallographic and mass-spectrometry data show all three enzymes support desulfation of the bound DBOs. The question this paper asks is the standard one for this series: among compounds with measured OXA-48 potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind the active site more strongly than avibactam — and can non-covalent docking even ask that question about a covalent inhibitor?

The classical medical canon knows the wound, not the enzyme: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats wounds and fevers — the syndrome, not the carbapenemase. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured OXA-48 potency bind the active site of the avibactam-bound structure (PDB 4WMC) at non-covalent scores beyond re-docked avibactam, and would that binding translate into stronger OXA-48 inhibition? Falsifier: a nitrocefin-hydrolysis inhibition assay showing an IC50 worse than the analogue's published value, or loss of potentiation of ceftazidime against an OXA-48 producer, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the inhibitor re-docked, non-covalently, on a co-crystal structure of its own target, with the co-crystallised inhibitor as the centre — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and for a covalent inhibitor they are not even a proxy for the rate-limiting step.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-23: the OXA-48/avibactam structural paper (Lahiri et al., ACS Chem Biol 2015;10:591–600; PMID 25406838; doi:10.1021/cb500703p); the DBO electrostatic study (Hoff et al., RSC Med Chem 2025;16:5441–5455; PMID 40927637; doi:10.1039/d5md00512d); the directed-evolution epistasis paper and the 8PEB structure (Frohlich et al., Nat Catal 2024;7:499–509; PMID 38828429; doi:10.1038/s41929-024-01117-4); the global antimicrobial-resistance burden analysis (Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, Lancet 2022;399:629–655); and the RCSB records for PDB 4WMC and 8PEB.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB Q6XEC0 (beta-lactamase OXA-48, Klebsiella pneumoniae) → ChEMBL CHEMBL1287604, "Beta-lactamase OXA-48", SINGLE PROTEIN, 1 bioactivity, verified live 2026-11-23. This is the correct target, the correct organism — and a comparison set of exactly one compound, which is the thin end of the series: one bioactivity cannot test ranking.

2.3 The pipeline's failure, stated not smoothed over

The pipeline's PDB picker selected 8PEB and docked avibactam at −6.27 kcal/mol and meropenem at −7.29 kcal/mol. Verified live 2026-11-23, 8PEB is OXA-48_Q5 — a directed-evolution quintuple mutant whose four mutations increase antibiotic resistance 40-fold by shifting the rate-limiting step of the catalytic cycle — and it is an apo structure: the only drug-like HETATM group in the file is a malonate buffer ion (MLI, 9 atoms), and the centre the pipeline used is that ion's centroid. The scores are therefore dockings into a mutant enzyme centred on a buffer ion, and they are discarded in full: they appear in this paper only as the artefact they are, with their file reference, so that no reader mistakes them for a result. The same structure-picker error has now bitten this series five times in two days (Papers #95, #100, #101, #103, #104), and the lesson is the same: the picked PDB entry's title, mutations and bound ligands must be verified by hand, every run.

2.4 Molecular docking — the redock on the correct structure

The benchmark structure is 4WMC: the 2.3 Å crystal structure of wild-type OXA-48 in covalent complex with avibactam (Lahiri et al., ACS Chem Biol 2015). A targeted redock script (health-papers-agent/redock_hp063_4wmc.py) docked avibactam and meropenem on 4WMC using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised avibactam (ligand NXL, chain A residue 301, 17 heavy atoms — C7H11N3O6S, matching avibactam), [42.21, 34.64, 52.56], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center. The centre audit is the decisive check here: the file holds eight OXA-48 chains, each with its own covalently bound avibactam, plus carbamylated Lys73 (KCX) and carbon-dioxide groups, and a naive group-average pick would have centred on the average of all eight avibactams — a point in empty space between chains. dock._ligand_center returned chain A's NXL centroid, which is a real binding site, and the audit names it. Box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for both compounds. Avibactam is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure — with the covalent caveat in §2.5 attached, not hidden. The docked avibactam is the parent SMILES as returned by PubChem (CID 9835049); the crystal holds the same molecule, covalently bound to Ser70, so the docked pose is the non-covalent encounter complex of the same molecule, not a metabolite.

2.5 The covalent caveat — why this docking cannot rank DBO inhibitors

Avibactam inhibits OXA-48 by acylating Ser70. The acyl-enzyme then deacylates only exceptionally slowly in class D enzymes — that slow reversibility is the drug's mechanism and the reason the 4WMC structure was solved. Rigid non-covalent Vina docking models neither the acylation step nor the deacylation rate; it scores the encounter complex before the bond forms. A non-covalent score therefore cannot rank covalent DBO inhibitors against each other, and it cannot rank an inhibitor against a substrate at all: the substrate's score measures how well it sits in the pocket before hydrolysis, and the inhibitor's score measures how well it sits in the pocket before acylation, and those are different questions with different answers. This paper reports both scores with that caveat in the table itself, not in a footnote.

2.6 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to avibactam and meropenem. Both are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.7 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for avibactam: molecular weight 265.25, logP −1.53, 2 hydrogen-bond donors, 5 acceptors, TPSA 130.24 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. Meropenem (CHEMBL127): molecular weight 383.47, logP −0.31, 3 hydrogen-bond donors, 6 acceptors, TPSA 110.18 Å², 5 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for avibactam: maximum predicted probability 0.148 (NR-AR), a weak read-across (maximum neighbour similarity 0.22), not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development — it is the profile of an already-approved drug, reported for completeness. Meropenem's Tox21 panel was measured (mode: measured), with all assays 0 except SR-MMP (not reported).

2.8 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity, and for a covalent inhibitor docking ≠ even the rate-limiting step. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics, free-energy refinement or covalent docking was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond meropenem's published Kd of 850 nM. The comparison set is a single compound — and it is a substrate, not an inhibitor — so the benchmark question is unanswerable in the form asked. One rigid structure was used (4WMC, wild-type OXA-48, 2.3 Å, eight chains in the asymmetric unit); the β5–β6 loop is flexible and adapts to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape. The docked avibactam returned only two poses, so its pose ensemble is thinner than the three-pose standard of this series.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (4WMC, 2.3 Å — the drug's own structure)

Compound Measured OXA-48 potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 4WMC (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose Margin vs avibactam
CHEMBL127 (meropenem — carbapenem SUBSTRATE) Kd 850 nM −7.95 −7.95, −7.48, −6.87 −7.48 −1.22
Avibactam (reference — COVALENT inhibitor) — (approved drug; potency is in the acylation step) −6.73 −6.73, −6.23 (2 poses only) — —

Avibactam re-docks, non-covalently, at −6.73 kcal/mol on its own structure, with only two poses returned (−6.73, −6.23): the method recovers binding for the drug in the pocket it was crystallised in, so the protocol is not broken — but the score is weak, and the pose ensemble is thin. Meropenem "beats" it at −7.95 kcal/mol, a 1.22 kcal/mol margin that lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise even before the category error is considered. The discarded pipeline scores (−6.27 for avibactam and −7.29 for meropenem on 8PEB, the quintuple mutant centred on malonate) are not in the table, because they are not measurements of wild-type OXA-48 — though it is worth noting that they show the same order, which is itself a warning: the wrong structure and the right structure agree, because both are measuring the same non-covalent encounter complex, and neither measures the covalent step.

The decisive check is the comparison with what the molecules are, and it dissolves the ranking. Meropenem is the substrate: OXA-48 hydrolyses it, and its Kd of 850 nM is a binding constant for a molecule the enzyme destroys. Avibactam is the inhibitor: its potency lives in the acylation of Ser70 and the exceptionally slow deacylation that follows, neither of which appears in a Vina score. A scoring function that ranks a substrate above a covalent inhibitor on a non-covalent score has not found a better inhibitor; it has found the limit of its own question. The honest reading of the table is therefore a null result on ranking, with a method lesson: no compound in this run can be claimed to beat avibactam, because the only comparator is not an inhibitor and the score cannot see the inhibition.

3.2 Comparison with published data

No published Vina study of avibactam or meropenem on 4WMC was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (ligands vs re-docked reference drug on the same structure, same protocol). The structural literature is the published ground truth for the binding mode: the 4WMC structure shows avibactam covalently bound to Ser70, with the carbamylated Lys73 positioned as the general base, and the asymmetric unit's eight subunits provide snapshots of different states of the inhibited enzyme — the structural evidence for the exceptionally slow reversibility. The DBO literature gives the paper its most useful context: nacubactam is about 80-fold less potent than avibactam towards OXA-48, and the difference is electrostatic repulsion with Arg214 on the β5–β6 loop — a loop-sequence effect that rigid docking on a single wild-type structure cannot see, and that disappears in the OXA-163 and OXA-405 variants that lack Arg214.

3.3 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Avibactam's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug's value is not its non-covalent affinity — it is that the acyl-enzyme it forms with OXA-48 barely deacylates, so a single molecule blocks the enzyme for far longer than a substrate occupies it, and that ceftazidime–avibactam restores activity against OXA-48 producers that no cephalosporin alone can touch. A compound that out-scores avibactam here by 1.22 kcal/mol but deacylates in seconds would be a worse drug, and docking cannot tell the two apart. The docking order cannot explain why ceftazidime–avibactam works where ceftazidime alone fails; the acylation chemistry together with the structure can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since avibactam was approved. Before approval, the question was "can a non-β-lactam inhibit a class D carbapenemase at all?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, acylates Ser70 faster and deacylates slower than avibactam?" The benchmark is therefore a screen for successors with a two-part bar: a non-covalent encounter score at least as good as −6.73 kcal/mol on 4WMC, and a covalent acylation/deacylation profile at least as good as avibactam's. This paper supplies the first half of the bar and shows the second half is where the pipeline must go next: the comparison set is a single substrate, and the score cannot see the covalent step.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the margin (1.22 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the comparator is a substrate, not an inhibitor — the ranking compares two different molecular events. Third, avibactam's potency is covalent and the score is not: the method measures the encounter complex and calls it the drug, which is like judging a lock by how well the key slides in before it turns.

4.3 The covalent problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The single-compound comparison set was chosen by pipeline rank, not by mechanism, and ChEMBL's one bioactivity for OXA-48 happened to be a substrate. The honest handling is to report the scores with the category error in the table itself, and to design the validation assay so the covalent question is answered by the experiment: a nitrocefin-hydrolysis assay measures inhibition regardless of mechanism, and a mass-spectrometry acylation assay (or a deacylation-rate measurement) would then place the covalent step. A compound that scores well non-covalently but acylates slowly is not a failure of the compound; it is a failure of the scoring function, and the assay is what tells the two apart.

4.4 Mechanism

Avibactam binds the OXA-48 active site, acylates Ser70, and deacylates only exceptionally slowly, with the carbamylated Lys73 acting as the general base; desulfation of the bound DBO is also observed. Test for each link: (i) a nitrocefin-hydrolysis inhibition assay (with avibactam as the comparator) measures IC50 directly against the published mechanism; (ii) a mass-spectrometry acylation assay measures the acyl-enzyme formation rate and the deacylation rate — the numbers that actually decide whether a DBO beats avibactam; (iii) a checkerboard MIC assay of ceftazidime plus the candidate against an OXA-48-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae measures potentiation at matched concentration, with a cytotoxicity counter-screen; (iv) the same assay on OXA-163 and OXA-405 producers measures whether the candidate kept activity where the β5–β6 loop differs.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. Avibactam inhibits OXA-48 nitrocefin hydrolysis with an IC50 within 3-fold of its published value. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than published.
  2. A candidate DBO that out-scores avibactam on 4WMC acylates Ser70 at least as fast as avibactam and deacylates no faster. Falsifier: deacylation >10-fold faster than avibactam's.
  3. The 4WMC pose predicts the loop effect: a candidate whose docked pose clashes with Arg214 loses activity against wild-type OXA-48 but keeps it against OXA-163. Falsifier: a candidate with an Arg214 clash keeps wild-type potency.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): fix the pipeline query (hand-verify PDB title, mutations and bound ligands with a centre audit; exclude mutant structures from the benchmark) and re-run the ligand retrieval for OXA-48 to build the comparison set this paper could not — five ChEMBL DBO ligands with measured potency, docked on 4WMC at the audited centre, plus nacubactam docked on 4WMC as the known 80-fold-weaker control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): nitrocefin-hydrolysis inhibition assay for avibactam against its published mechanism, plus the best-scoring candidate from stage 1, on wild-type OXA-48. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any candidate passes stages 1–2, mass-spectrometry acylation/deacylation assay plus a ceftazidime-potentiation MIC assay against an OXA-48 producer; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only, and non-covalent docking of a covalent inhibitor; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows the reported margin.
  2. The comparison set is a single compound — and it is a substrate, not an inhibitor — so the benchmark question is unanswerable in the form asked.
  3. The pipeline's first structure (8PEB) was a quintuple mutant centred on a malonate ion; the scores on it are discarded — the centre audit is what separates the two.
  4. One rigid structure was used (4WMC, wild-type OXA-48, 2.3 Å, eight chains); the β5–β6 loop is flexible, and the Arg214 loop effect was not docked.
  5. Docking was on the wild-type structure only; the OXA-163/OXA-405 variant question — the one that changes DBO potency 80-fold — was not docked, because no variant structure with a candidate ligand was in the comparison set.
  6. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the ceftazidime–avibactam combination that works from the ceftazidime that fails, because the difference is the covalent step.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no OXA-48-relevant text: the Canon of Medicine treats wounds and fevers, not enzymes, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

Avibactam, the diazabicyclooctane that acylates OXA-48's Ser70 and barely lets go, re-docks non-covalently at −6.73 kcal/mol on its own 2.3 Å structure 4WMC with a thin two-pose ensemble and no PAINS alert — a validated control, and a weak one by the only number this method can produce. Meropenem, the carbapenem substrate, "beats" it at −7.95 kcal/mol — but the margin lies inside Vina noise, the comparator is a molecule the enzyme destroys rather than one that blocks it, and avibactam's potency lives in the covalent step the score cannot see. The paper's useful result is therefore the control plus the named failure: the method works on the right structure, the question was the wrong one, and the fix — covalent docking or an acylation assay, a real inhibitor comparison set, and a hand-verified wild-type structure — is specified so the next run can ask the question this one could not. What the docking cannot do is resolve the covalent question that defines this drug: the same active site that binds avibactam at −6.73 kcal/mol is the site where Ser70 acylation and slow deacylation decide whether a DBO works, and only an acylation assay can tell whether a successor keeps avibactam's barrier. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — fix the query, build the inhibitor comparison set, and run a nitrocefin assay plus an acylation-rate measurement — not another non-covalent docking run on an unverified structure.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the National Institute of Health's antimicrobial-resistance programme, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of DBO inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise, and whether to prioritise ceftazidime–avibactam in procurement for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week pipeline-fix plus nitrocefin screen proposed in §4.6 for the five best ChEMBL DBO ligands against avibactam, with nacubactam as the known weaker control, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target on unverified structures; and, in parallel, ask the AMR programme to note explicitly that the binding question is settled for the wild-type active site — avibactam re-docks at −6.73 kcal/mol — and that the remaining gap is the covalent step and the variant loop, not the drug's non-covalent affinity: every rupee spent re-docking avibactam into a mutant enzyme is a rupee not spent measuring acylation rates. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a candidate beats avibactam's acylation rate and deacylates no faster in the mass-spectrometry assay, drop the access-only framing and fund the candidate's development; if the fixed query returns no DBO within noise of avibactam, drop this ligand set and redirect the same screen to the next DBO chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable OXA-48 inhibitor from a useless one for a resistance mechanism that defeats the drugs of last resort, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only, and a single-substrate comparison at that — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-23 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #103 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; KasA; thiolactomycin; mycolic acid; molecular docking; ChEMBL; tuberculosis; FAS-II; drug resistance

Abstract

In 2023, tuberculosis caused an estimated 10.8 million new cases and 1.25 million deaths, and Pakistan is among the eight countries accounting for two-thirds of the global burden — yet the front-line drug isoniazid is defeated by katG mutations in most resistant strains, because isoniazid must be activated before it can inhibit its target, InhA. KasA, the β-ketoacyl-ACP synthase of the FAS-II mycolic-acid pathway, is isoniazid-independent: it needs no activation, so a KasA inhibitor bypasses the commonest isoniazid-resistance route entirely. Thiolactomycin, the thiolactone natural product that first proved KasA druggable, inhibits both KasA and KasB, and overexpression of either enzyme raises resistance to it — but no KasA inhibitor has reached the clinic. We asked whether any measured KasA ligand binds the active site more strongly than thiolactomycin. The LeadForge pipeline resolved the target correctly to UniProtKB P9WQD9 (M. tuberculosis KasA, H37Rv) — and then failed twice: ChEMBL resolved to CHEMBL2074, verified live as human maltase-glucoamylase, so zero bioactivities were returned and no comparison set exists; and the pipeline's PDB picker selected 6P9K, KasA in complex with the preclinical indazole JSF-3285, not thiolactomycin — its −6.11 kcal/mol score is a docking into the JSF-3285 pocket and is reported here only as the artefact. On the correct structure, the 1.80 Å crystal structure of KasA with bound thiolactomycin (PDB 2WGE), thiolactomycin re-docked at −6.92 kcal/mol (poses −6.92, −6.88, −5.79) centred exactly on the co-crystallised ligand TLM (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). The paper's finding is therefore a validated control plus two honest negatives: the method recovers binding for the drug in its own pocket, but the score is weak — consistent with a weak, early inhibitor, not with a drug — and the "does any analogue beat thiolactomycin" question cannot be answered from ChEMBL as queried. The falsifiable next step is a KasA enzyme assay of thiolactomycin against its published mechanism, with the 2WGE pose as the structural hypothesis — not another docking run.

1. Introduction

The mycobacterial cell wall is a waxy, nearly impermeable barrier built from mycolic acids — very-long-chain α-alkyl-β-hydroxy fatty acids that make up as much as 60% of the wall and let the bacillus persist inside human macrophages. Mycobacteria make them with two fatty-acid systems: the mammalian-like FAS-I, which builds C14–C16 chains de novo, and the bacterial FAS-II, which elongates them to C54–C56. In FAS-II, the acyl carrier protein AcpM shuttles the growing chain between discrete enzymes: FabH primes, MabA and InhA process, and the β-ketoacyl-AcpM synthases KasA and KasB do the elongation — KasA the early rounds, KasB the later steps. Inhibiting cell-wall biosynthesis is fatal for the organism, which is why the pathway has been a drug target since isoniazid: but isoniazid inhibits InhA only after activation by the catalase-peroxidase KatG, and katG mutations are the commonest cause of isoniazid resistance. KasA needs no activation. A KasA inhibitor therefore bypasses the resistance route that defeats the front-line drug — the isoniazid-independent angle that defines this target.

Thiolactomycin (TLM), a thiolactone natural product, is the molecule that proved KasA druggable. It inhibits fatty-acid and mycolic-acid biosynthesis by targeting both KasA and KasB: overexpression of KasA, KasB or KasAB in Mycobacterium bovis BCG raises resistance to it in vitro and in vivo, and a multidrug-resistant clinical isolate was found highly sensitive to it — the first evidence that a KasA inhibitor could counter multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Its analogues, designed from the structure, were more potent both in vitro against fatty-acid and mycolic-acid biosynthesis and in vivo against M. tuberculosis. The first atomic view came in 2009: the crystal structures of KasA in apo form and bound to thiolactomycin, which also revealed a polyethylene-glycol molecule mimicking a fatty-acid substrate of about 40 carbons — a platform for designing thiolactomycin analogues with higher affinity. The class has since advanced past thiolactomycin itself: the indazole JSF-3285, optimised from the earlier inhibitor DG167 by a structure-based approach, gained a 30-fold increase in mouse plasma exposure, and showed substantial activity in acute and chronic mouse models of infection, with efficacious reductions in colony-forming units at doses as low as 5 mg/kg once daily orally, and improved the efficacy of isoniazid or rifampicin. It is a preclinical candidate. The question this paper asks is the standard one for this series: among compounds with measured KasA potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind the active site more strongly than thiolactomycin — and can the pipeline even ask that question correctly?

The classical medical canon knows the disease, not the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats consumption (sil) and chronic cough — the syndrome, not the enzyme. The principle carried forward here is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured M. tuberculosis KasA potency bind the active site of the thiolactomycin-bound structure (PDB 2WGE) at scores beyond re-docked thiolactomycin, and would that binding translate into stronger KasA inhibition and antimycobacterial activity? Falsifier: a KasA enzyme assay showing an IC50 worse than the analogue's published value, or a whole-cell MIC above 25 µg/mL against M. tuberculosis H37Rv, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference inhibitor re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target, with the co-crystallised inhibitor as the centre — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-23: the thiolactomycin KasA/KasB mechanism paper (J Biol Chem 2000;275:16857–16864; doi:10.1074/jbc.M000569200); the KasA crystal structures with thiolactomycin (Luckner et al., Structure 2009;17:1004–1013; doi:10.1016/j.str.2009.04.012; PMID 19604480); the JSF-3285 preclinical-candidate paper and the 6P9K structure (Inoyama et al., Cell Chem Biol 2020;27:560; PMID 32197094; doi:10.1016/j.chembiol.2020.02.007); the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 (10.8 million cases, 1.25 million deaths in 2023); and the RCSB records for PDB 2WGE and 6P9K.

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target to UniProtKB P9WQD9 (3-oxoacyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] synthase 1, KasA, Mycobacterium tuberculosis strain ATCC 25618 / H37Rv), verified live 2026-11-23. This is the correct target. What failed was the ChEMBL resolution: the pipeline selected CHEMBL2074, verified live as "Maltase-glucoamylase", SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens — a human digestive enzyme. It is the same fallback ID the pipeline returned for FtsZ in Paper #101, which suggests CHEMBL2074 is the pipeline's default when its ChEMBL search fails, not a genuine match. The standing fix for this series is now to verify the ChEMBL target's name and organism before any ligand retrieval is trusted — and to treat a repeated CHEMBL2074 as a failed search, not a result.

2.3 The pipeline's two failures, stated not smoothed over

First, ChEMBL bioactivity retrieval for the wrong target CHEMBL2074 returned zero records (step 2: no_data, count 0). No known ligands with measured potency were retrieved, so the similarity screen was skipped and the only "lead" ranked was the query compound itself, thiolactomycin (score 97.5 by the pipeline's composite). There is therefore no comparison set in this run, and the question "does any analogue beat thiolactomycin" has no computational answer here. That is a data-retrieval failure, not a finding about thiolactomycin.

Second, the pipeline's PDB picker selected 6P9K and docked thiolactomycin on it at −6.11 kcal/mol. Verified live 2026-11-23, 6P9K is the crystal structure of M. tuberculosis KasA in complex with O6G — JSF-3285, the preclinical indazole candidate. The enzyme is right; the pocket is the JSF-3285 pocket, optimised by structure-based design for a later, more potent indazole, not the thiolactomycin pocket. A −6.11 kcal/mol score for thiolactomycin in the JSF-3285 pocket is a property of the wrong ligand's pocket and is reported here only as the artefact it is, with its file reference, so that no reader mistakes it for the control. The same structure-picker error has now bitten this series four times in two days (Papers #95, #100, #101, #103), and the lesson is the same: the picked PDB entry's title and bound ligands must be verified by hand, every run.

2.4 Molecular docking — the redock on the correct structure

The benchmark structure is 2WGE: the 1.80 Å crystal structure of M. tuberculosis KasA with bound thiolactomycin (Luckner et al., Structure 2009). A targeted redock script (health-papers-agent/redock_hp093_2wge.py) docked thiolactomycin on 2WGE using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised thiolactomycin (ligand TLM, 14 heavy atoms — C11H14O2S, matching thiolactomycin), [38.10, 1.00, −6.78], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center (the centre audit confirmed TLM is the largest drug-like HETATM group in the file; the seven glycerols, the isopropyl alcohol, the sodium ion and the waters were correctly excluded); box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The receptor preparation keeps the polyethylene-glycol substrate mimic in the structure, so the long acyl-chain channel is realistic. Thiolactomycin is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover binding for the drug in the pocket it was crystallised in would be broken. The docked thiolactomycin is the parent SMILES as returned by PubChem (CID 135403829); the crystal holds the same molecule, so no prodrug/metabolite caveat applies here.

2.5 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to thiolactomycin. PAINS-clean: no alerts. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.6 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for thiolactomycin: molecular weight 210.30, logP 2.98, 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 3 acceptors, TPSA 37.3 Å², 2 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for thiolactomycin: maximum predicted probability 0.308 (SR-ARE), a weak read-across (maximum neighbour similarity 0.242), not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development — it is the profile of a natural-product starting point, reported for completeness.

2.7 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond thiolactomycin's published mechanism. There is no comparison set: ChEMBL returned zero bioactivities for the wrongly resolved target, so the benchmark question is unanswered, not answered in the negative. One rigid structure was used (2WGE, 1.80 Å); KasA's active site adapts to different chemotypes, and the long acyl-chain channel means one structure under-samples the binding landscape. The docked compound is thiolactomycin itself, not its more potent analogues or JSF-3285, which is the molecule that actually advanced to preclinical candidacy.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (2WGE, 1.80 Å — the drug's own structure)

Compound Measured potency (published) Best affinity, 2WGE (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose
Thiolactomycin (reference) KasA/KasB inhibitor (natural product; mechanism published, no single IC50 in this run) −6.92 −6.92, −6.88, −5.79 −6.88
(no comparison ligands — ChEMBL resolved to human maltase-glucoamylase, 0 bioactivities) — — — —

Thiolactomycin re-docks at −6.92 kcal/mol on its own structure, with the top two poses tight (−6.92, −6.88) and the third 1.1 kcal/mol higher: the method recovers binding for the drug in the pocket it was crystallised in, so the protocol is not broken — but the score is weak. A −6.92 kcal/mol re-dock is the weakest self-dock control in this series so far (doravirine −11.85, PC190723 −9.43, venetoclax −10.22), and it is consistent with what the literature says about thiolactomycin: a weak, early natural-product inhibitor whose value is as a starting point, not as a drug. There is no analogue to compare it against, so no "beats thiolactomycin" claim can be made in either direction. The discarded pipeline score (−6.11 kcal/mol on 6P9K, the JSF-3285 pocket) is not in the table, because it is not a measurement of this pocket — though it is worth noting that it is also weak, and that the 0.81 kcal/mol gap between the two pockets is inside Vina noise, which is itself a warning about how little either number can say about a weak binder.

3.2 Comparison with published data

No published Vina study of thiolactomycin on 2WGE was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (the inhibitor re-docked on its own structure, same protocol as Papers #1/#3). The structural literature is the published ground truth for the binding mode: the 2WGE structure shows thiolactomycin in the KasA active site, and the polyethylene-glycol molecule in the same structure mimics a fatty-acid substrate of about 40 carbons — the atomic view of the long-chain channel that makes KasA a target. The medicinal-chemistry literature gives the paper its most useful context: the thiolactomycin analogues designed from that structure were more potent in vitro and in vivo, and the indazole JSF-3285 — optimised from DG167 by a structure-based approach, with a 30-fold increase in mouse plasma exposure and efficacy at 5 mg/kg once daily in acute and chronic mouse models — is the proof that the pocket rewards optimisation. The gap between thiolactomycin's −6.92 and JSF-3285's candidacy is the gap this series exists to measure.

3.3 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Thiolactomycin's clinical story is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug's value was never its potency — it was the proof of concept: a KasA inhibitor works against a multidrug-resistant clinical isolate, and overexpression of the target raises resistance, which is the genetic proof of mechanism. And its failure was never its affinity alone — it was potency and pharmacokinetics together, which is why the class's advance is JSF-3285, a molecule optimised for exposure as much as for binding. A compound that out-scores thiolactomycin here by 1 kcal/mol but keeps its weak exposure would be no advance at all, and docking on a wild-type structure cannot tell the two apart. The docking order cannot explain why no KasA inhibitor has reached the clinic; the exposure data together with the structure can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since thiolactomycin was published. Before 2000, the question was "can KasA be inhibited at all?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, beats thiolactomycin in the active site and survives the exposure test that stopped the class?" The benchmark is therefore a screen for successors with a two-part bar: beat −6.92 kcal/mol on 2WGE and keep mouse exposure. This paper supplies the first half of the bar — and shows it is a low bar, because the reference drug is weak — and the second half is where the work is: the comparison set does not exist in ChEMBL as queried, and the structure picker chose the successor's pocket.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

There is no win to over-read. Three reasons the paper is a control plus two negatives, not a discovery. First, there is no comparison set — ChEMBL resolved to a human enzyme and returned zero bioactivities. Second, the pipeline's first structure was the JSF-3285 complex and its −6.11 kcal/mol score measured the wrong pocket, and that score must be discarded, not averaged in. Third, even the valid re-dock is weak (−6.92 kcal/mol) and a single rigid structure, and the third pose sits 1.1 kcal/mol above the best, so the pose ensemble is not tight.

4.3 The pipeline failure is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The two failures have different root causes and the same fix. The ChEMBL failure is a fallback error (CHEMBL2074 returned twice in one day for two unrelated bacterial targets); the structure failure is a bound-ligand error (the successor's complex picked over the reference's own). The fix, now standing practice for this series: verify the ChEMBL target's name and organism before ligand retrieval, treat a repeated CHEMBL2074 as a failed search, and verify the picked PDB entry's title and bound ligands by hand before any score is reported — with a centre audit that names the ligand the centre came from, as this redock does. A pipeline that docks the right drug into the wrong pocket and reports the number is worse than a pipeline that reports nothing — this paper reports the nothing, with the artefact named.

4.4 Mechanism

Thiolactomycin binds the KasA active site and blocks the condensation of the growing acyl-AcpM chain with malonyl-AcpM, halting FAS-II elongation and therefore mycolic-acid biosynthesis. Test for each link: (i) a KasA enzyme assay (condensation of acyl-AcpM with malonyl-AcpM, with thiolactomycin as the comparator) measures IC50 directly against the published mechanism; (ii) a mycolic-acid biosynthesis assay (radiolabelled acetate incorporation) measures pathway inhibition in whole cells; (iii) a whole-cell MIC assay against M. tuberculosis H37Rv and a multidrug-resistant clinical isolate measures antimycobacterial activity at matched concentration, with a cytotoxicity counter-screen; (iv) a KasA-overexpression strain measures whether a candidate kept the on-target logic — loss of activity on overexpression is the genetic proof that defines the class.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. Thiolactomycin inhibits M. tuberculosis KasA in an enzyme assay with an IC50 within 3-fold of its published mechanism. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than published.
  2. A candidate KasA inhibitor that out-scores thiolactomycin on 2WGE keeps activity against a multidrug-resistant clinical isolate within 5-fold of H37Rv. Falsifier: >10-fold loss against the resistant isolate.
  3. The 2WGE pose predicts the resistance profile: a candidate whose docked pose loses contact with the active-site residues where KasA overexpression raises resistance loses activity against the overexpression strain first. Falsifier: a candidate without those contacts keeps wild-type potency on overexpression.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): fix the pipeline query (verify ChEMBL target name and organism; treat CHEMBL2074 as a failed search; hand-verify PDB title and bound ligands with a centre audit) and re-run the ligand retrieval for M. tuberculosis KasA to build the comparison set this paper could not — five ChEMBL KasA ligands with measured potency, docked on 2WGE at the audited centre, plus JSF-3285 docked on 2WGE as the positive control the field already has. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): KasA enzyme assay for thiolactomycin against its published mechanism, plus the best-scoring candidate from stage 1, on wild-type KasA. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any candidate passes stages 1–2, MIC assay against H37Rv and a multidrug-resistant clinical isolate plus a KasA-overexpression strain; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows any margin under ~2 kcal/mol.
  2. There is no comparison set: ChEMBL resolved to human maltase-glucoamylase and returned zero bioactivities, so the benchmark question is unanswered.
  3. The pipeline's first structure (6P9K) was the JSF-3285 complex; the −6.11 kcal/mol score on it measured the successor's pocket, not thiolactomycin's own, and is discarded — the centre audit is what separates the two.
  4. One rigid structure was used (2WGE, 1.80 Å); KasA's active site and its long acyl-chain channel adapt to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  5. Docking was on the wild-type structure only; the multidrug-resistance question — the one that matters clinically — was not docked, because no resistant-strain KasA structure with a candidate ligand was in the comparison set.
  6. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the proof-of-concept activity against a multidrug-resistant isolate from the potency and exposure problems that kept the class out of the clinic.
  7. The classical-canon sweep found no KasA-relevant text: the Canon of Medicine treats consumption, not enzymes, so the Islamic-principle discussion rests on hifz al-nafs as a principle, not on a classical source about this target.

6. Conclusion

Thiolactomycin, the thiolactone natural product that first proved KasA druggable, re-docks at −6.92 kcal/mol on its own 1.80 Å structure 2WGE with tight top-two pose consistency and no PAINS alert — a validated control, and a weak one. No analogue can be claimed to beat it or lose to it: ChEMBL resolved the target to a human digestive enzyme and returned zero bioactivities, so there is no comparison set, and the pipeline's first structure was the JSF-3285 complex, whose −6.11 kcal/mol score measured the successor's pocket and is discarded as a measurement of thiolactomycin's own. The paper's useful result is therefore the control plus the two named failures, and the low bar they set: the reference drug docks at −6.92 kcal/mol, the weakest self-dock control in this series, which is exactly why the class advanced to JSF-3285 — a molecule optimised for exposure, not just for binding. What the docking cannot do is resolve the potency-and-exposure question that defines this class: the same active site that binds thiolactomycin at −6.92 kcal/mol is the site whose optimisation produced a preclinical candidate, and only a KasA enzyme assay plus a whole-cell MIC can tell whether a successor keeps the isoniazid-independent logic that made KasA interesting. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — fix the query, build the comparison set, dock JSF-3285 as the positive control, and run a KasA enzyme assay plus MIC — not another docking run on an unverified structure.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's National TB Control Programme and the DRAP registration office, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of KasA inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise, and whether to prioritise isoniazid-independent targets in procurement for drug-resistant tuberculosis. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week pipeline-fix plus enzyme screen proposed in §4.6 for the five best ChEMBL KasA ligands against thiolactomycin, with JSF-3285 as the positive control, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target on unverified structures; and, in parallel, ask the TB programme to note explicitly that the binding question is settled for the wild-type active site — thiolactomycin re-docks at −6.92 kcal/mol — and that the remaining gap is potency and exposure, not the drug's mechanism: every rupee spent re-docking thiolactomycin into the JSF-3285 pocket is a rupee not spent testing candidates against a multidrug-resistant isolate. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a candidate beats thiolactomycin's re-dock by >2 kcal/mol on 2WGE and keeps activity against a multidrug-resistant isolate within 5-fold, drop the access-only framing and fund the candidate's development; if the fixed query returns no candidate within noise of thiolactomycin, drop this ligand set and redirect the same screen to the next KasA chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable KasA inhibitor from a useless one for a disease that killed 1.25 million people in 2023, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only, and a single-compound control at that — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".
