Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-22 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #97 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: renin; aliskiren; hypertension; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; ChEMBL; renin inhibitor; drug repurposing

Abstract

Hypertension affects 1.3 billion people and one in three adults worldwide, yet four in five are not adequately treated, and the only approved direct renin inhibitor, aliskiren, failed to improve outcomes when added to ACE-inhibitor or ARB therapy in the ALTITUDE trial. We asked whether structure-based docking can rank renin inhibitors by potency, using aliskiren as the reference and the ChEMBL renin bioactivity set as the lead pool. The pipeline resolved human renin (UniProtKB P00797) to ChEMBL CHEMBL286, retrieved 54 bioactivities, and ranked 26 leads; docking ran on two structures — 2V0Z (renin co-crystallised with aliskiren, 2.2 Å) and 3K1W (renin co-crystallised with a different inhibitor, 1.50 Å). On 2V0Z, aliskiren self-docked at −8.78 kcal/mol, CHEMBL1276275 (IC50 0.039 nM) scored −10.01, 1.23 kcal/mol better, while CHEMBL3907708 (also IC50 0.039 nM) scored −8.79, 0.01 kcal/mol from aliskiren despite being about 15-fold more potent in assay. On the cross-dock structure 3K1W, aliskiren fell to −6.84 and CHEMBL3907708 to −7.51. Three further top leads, each with 17–18 rotatable bonds, could not be docked at all: their Vina runs did not converge in 9–11 minutes on this machine and were terminated without a score. Docking therefore ranks this series only partially and only on the self-dock structure, and a single Vina score is not a reliable potency predictor. The falsifier is a head-to-head renin enzymatic assay of aliskiren, CHEMBL1276275 and CHEMBL3907708 under identical conditions: if the 0.039 nM compounds do not outperform aliskiren there, the docking claim fails.

1. Introduction

Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular death. The World Health Organization's 2023 hypertension report counts 1.3 billion people living with hypertension — up from 650 million in 1990 — one in three adults, with four in five not adequately treated, and estimates 76 million deaths could be averted between 2023 and 2050 by better control. Renin, the rate-limiting enzyme of the renin–angiotensin system, is a rational target: it catalyses the first and rate-limiting step, angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and its inhibition lowers blood pressure without the bradykinin cough of ACE inhibitors.

Aliskiren is the only direct renin inhibitor ever approved (FDA, 2007; Tekturna). It inhibits human renin with a published IC50 of 0.6 nM, yet its clinical record is mixed. In the ALTITUDE trial (Parving et al., NEJM 2012), 8,561 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease received aliskiren or placebo added to an ACE inhibitor or ARB: the primary cardiovascular and renal endpoint occurred in 18.3% versus 17.1% (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.98–1.20, p = 0.12), hyperkalaemia ≥6 mmol/L occurred in 11.2% versus 7.2%, and hypotension in 12.1% versus 8.3%; the trial was stopped early in December 2011. Aliskiren is therefore not a failed drug so much as a drug whose combination use failed — and the question of whether a better renin inhibitor exists in the known chemical space remains open.

This paper tests one falsifiable hypothesis: Vina docking on the aliskiren-bound renin structure (2V0Z) ranks known renin inhibitors in the same order as their measured IC50 values. The falsifier is stated in the Abstract.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were verified on 22 November 2026: WHO Global Hypertension Report 2023 (burden figures); Parving et al., N Engl J Med 2012;367(23):2204–13 (ALTITUDE, PMID 23121378, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1208799); Rahuel et al., Chem Biol 2000 (2V0Z structure, PMID 10903938, doi:10.1016/S1074-5521(00)00134-4); Wood et al., Biochem Biophys Res Commun 2003 (aliskiren design and 0.6 nM IC50, PMID 12927720, doi:10.1016/S0006-291X(03)01351-9). ChEMBL bioactivities for renin (CHEMBL286) were retrieved live. The Islamic literature sweep found no canonical work that addresses renin: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine discusses pulse and bloodletting for blood disorders, but the renin–angiotensin system was discovered nine centuries later, so no classical source can inform the docking question; this is recorded as a limitation, not hidden.

2.2 Molecular docking

The standardised AutoDock Vina protocol of Papers #1 and #3 was used. Target: human renin, UniProtKB P00797, resolved live to ChEMBL CHEMBL286 (SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens), 54 bioactivities, 26 leads after similarity screening. Two structures were docked. 2V0Z (renin co-crystallised with aliskiren, 2.2 Å, two chains C and O): the grid centre [7.62, 46.19, 69.09] is the centroid of the co-crystallised aliskiren ligand (HETATM group C41, 39 atoms, chain C residue 1328), computed with dock._ligand_center, which excludes the NAG glycan and waters — the centre audit is mandatory after the TYK2 wrong-domain precedent. 3K1W (renin co-crystallised with inhibitor BFX, 1.50 Å): centre [3.83, 6.23, 1.46], the BFX centroid; this is a cross-dock for aliskiren, not its own structure. Box 22.5 Å on both. Best of three poses reported; the reference drug and the analogues were docked under the identical protocol on each structure. Ligands: aliskiren (PubChem CID 5493444) and ChEMBL leads with their ChEMBL activities.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All four compounds reported here are PAINS-clean.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so gaps smaller than ~1 kcal/mol cannot rank compounds. No experimental data were generated; no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. Three ligands could not be docked at all (see §3.3) and are reported as failures, not as scores.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured activity (ChEMBL) 2V0Z best affinity (kcal/mol) 2V0Z poses 3K1W best affinity (kcal/mol) PAINS
Aliskiren (reference) IC50 0.6 nM (published) −8.78 −8.78, −8.54, −8.11 −6.84 clean
CHEMBL1276275 IC50 0.039 nM −10.01 −10.01, −9.45, −9.43 not docked clean
CHEMBL3907708 IC50 0.039 nM −8.79 −8.79, −8.74, −8.45 −7.51 clean

On the self-dock structure 2V0Z, the ranking is half-right. CHEMBL1276275 scores −10.01, 1.23 kcal/mol better than aliskiren, in the direction its 15-fold potency advantage predicts — but 1.23 kcal/mol sits at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so it is suggestive, not proof. CHEMBL3907708, with the identical measured potency (IC50 0.039 nM), scores −8.79, a 0.01 kcal/mol difference from aliskiren — docking cannot distinguish a 0.039 nM inhibitor from a 0.6 nM one in this pair. On the cross-dock structure 3K1W the scores compress and fall: aliskiren −6.84, CHEMBL3907708 −7.51. The cross-dock penalty for aliskiren is 1.94 kcal/mol relative to its own structure, and the structure choice changes the answer — the same lesson as the HCV NS5B paper (#96), where the co-crystallised structure was required for a meaningful redock.

3.2 Compound properties

Compound MW logP HBD HBA Rotatable bonds TPSA (Å²) Lipinski violations Veber Tox21 max
Aliskiren 551.77 3.29 4 7 19 146.13 1 fail 0.000
CHEMBL1276275 601.79 5.23 2 7 15 81.29 2 fail 0.197
CHEMBL3907708 471.60 3.23 2 8 8 109.59 0 pass 0.274

Aliskiren is the worst drug-like of the three by the usual rules: 19 rotatable bonds, TPSA 146.13 Å², one Lipinski violation, Veber fail — consistent with its known low oral bioavailability (~2.5%). CHEMBL3907708 is the cleanest (MW 471.6, 8 rotatable bonds, zero Lipinski violations, Veber pass). CHEMBL1276275 carries two Lipinski violations (MW 601.79, logP 5.23) and would need optimisation for oral delivery even if its potency advantage is real. All three are PAINS-clean with low Tox21 kNN scores (max 0.274).

3.3 The three ligands that could not be docked

CHEMBL1276276 (IC50 0.06 nM), CHEMBL390196 (IC50 0.067 nM) and CHEMBL1761531 (IC50 0.06 nM) — ranks 3, 4 and 5 of the lead list — each carry 17–18 rotatable bonds. On 3K1W, each Vina run ran 9–11 minutes of wall time without converging on this 1.5-CPU virtual machine and was terminated; no score was recorded for them on either structure. This is a compute limit, not a property of the molecules: highly flexible peptidomimetic renin inhibitors are the hardest case for exhaustive Vina sampling, and the three undocked compounds are all sub-nanomolar in assay. Any ranking claim that ignores them is incomplete, and the paper states that plainly.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of aliskiren against these specific ChEMBL analogues on 2V0Z was found in the literature sweep; the numbers here are the first report of this comparison. The 2V0Z structure itself has been used for structure-based design since Rahuel et al. (2000), and aliskiren's 0.6 nM IC50 is the published anchor.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank renin inhibitors. The answer is: partially, and only on the right structure. The self-dock (2V0Z) produced one correct ranking (CHEMBL1276275 ahead of aliskiren, matching its potency) and one null (CHEMBL3907708 identical to aliskiren despite equal potency to CHEMBL1276275). The cross-dock (3K1W) produced lower scores for everything and no usable ranking. Structure selection is therefore not a detail — it is the result.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

CHEMBL1276275's 1.23 kcal/mol advantage over aliskiren is inside Vina's noise band. Its three poses span −10.01 to −9.43, and aliskiren's span −8.78 to −8.11; the pose ranges nearly touch. The compound also has two Lipinski violations and 15 rotatable bonds, so even a real potency advantage would need medicinal-chemistry work before it became a drug. The honest reading: CHEMBL1276275 is the most promising lead in this set and the first one to assay — nothing more.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All three compounds are PAINS-clean, so the head-to-head assay does not need the redox and aggregation controls that a PAINS-positive lead would demand. The assay's controls instead need to cover the known confounder in renin assays: substrate depletion at sub-nanomolar inhibitor concentrations, which flattens apparent IC50 differences. The validation design must use substrate concentrations well above Km and report the exact assay conditions.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL1276275 inhibits recombinant human renin with an IC50 below 0.1 nM in the same assay that gives aliskiren 0.6 nM. Settled by the head-to-head assay.
  2. CHEMBL3907708 inhibits renin with an IC50 of ~0.04 nM in the same assay, despite docking identically to aliskiren — which, if true, confirms that Vina cannot rank this pair.
  3. CHEMBL1276275's docking advantage disappears on the cross-dock structure 3K1W, confirming that the ranking is structure-dependent.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): source the three compounds (commercial, ≥95% purity) and recombinant human renin; set up a FRET-based renin activity assay with aliskiren as the internal control. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): dose–response curves for all three compounds in triplicate, same plate, same substrate concentration; report IC50 with 95% confidence intervals. Stage 3 (weeks 7–8): repeat on a second renin lot; if CHEMBL1276275's advantage holds, run a 100 ns molecular-dynamics simulation of its 2V0Z pose to check pose stability. Stage 4 (weeks 9–12): ADMET panel (solubility, microsomal stability) for the winner only.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol means the 1.23 kcal/mol gap for CHEMBL1276275 is suggestive, not conclusive.
  2. Three of the five top leads could not be docked (Vina non-convergence on 17–18 rotatable bonds); the ranking is incomplete.
  3. Single-structure analysis per compound set; no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  4. ChEMBL activities come from different assays and laboratories; the IC50 values compared here were not measured under identical conditions — the head-to-head assay is the correction.
  5. No canonical Islamic medical work addresses renin; the literature sweep covers the available digitised canon and names this gap rather than claiming a classical precedent that does not exist.
  6. Aliskiren's clinical record (ALTITUDE) concerns combination therapy in diabetic kidney disease, not monotherapy; nothing here supports a clinical recommendation.

6. Conclusion

Aliskiren self-docks at −8.78 kcal/mol on its own renin structure 2V0Z. One sub-nanomolar analogue, CHEMBL1276275, scores 1.23 kcal/mol better, and a second equally potent analogue, CHEMBL3907708, scores identically to aliskiren. Docking ranks this renin series only partially, only on the self-dock structure, and a single Vina score cannot be trusted as a potency predictor. The next step is a head-to-head renin assay of the three compounds under identical conditions.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the ORIC director and the laboratory supervisor at SMBBMU Larkana (Prof. Dr. Nadeem Baloch, ORIC), who control the university's small research budget. Decision: whether to fund the 8–12-week head-to-head renin assay proposed in §4.5 before any lead-optimisation work. Exact change: approve the assay for aliskiren, CHEMBL1276275 and CHEMBL3907708 as the next funded step, capped at the cost of three commercial compounds and one recombinant renin lot, and spend nothing on analogue synthesis until the assay returns. Reversal condition: if the assay shows CHEMBL1276275 does not outperform aliskiren, drop the lead and close this line — do not spend further on docking refinements. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, one of the maqasid al-sharia): hypertension kills silently and at scale, and a cheaper, better renin inhibitor would serve that end — but the same principle forbids spending scarce university funds on a lead that has not survived its first assay, and forbids any clinical claim before that assay exists.

Malaria caused 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths in 2023, three-quarters of the deaths in children under five in Africa, and artemisinin resistance makes new antimalarials urgent.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-22 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #98 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Plasmodium falciparum; dihydroorotate dehydrogenase; DSM265; malaria; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; ChEMBL; antimalarial

Abstract

Malaria caused 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths in 2023, three-quarters of the deaths in children under five in Africa, and artemisinin resistance makes new antimalarials urgent. DSM265, a selective Plasmodium falciparum dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (PfDHODH) inhibitor, is the reference compound for this benchmark. We asked whether Vina docking on the DSM265-bound PfDHODH structure ranks known PfDHODH inhibitors by their measured IC50 values. The pipeline resolved PfDHODH (UniProtKB Q08210) to ChEMBL CHEMBL3588732, retrieved 58 bioactivities, and ranked 26 leads; docking ran on 4RX0 (PfDHODH co-crystallised with DSM265, 2.25 Å) and on 7L01 (PfDHODH co-crystallised with a different inhibitor, DSM782, 1.6 Å). On 4RX0, DSM265 self-docked at −10.70 kcal/mol, but CHEMBL3289670 (IC50 35 nM) scored −12.16 and CHEMBL1738786 (IC50 38 nM) scored −11.86 — both weaker in assay than DSM265 (IC50 27 nM) yet better in docking, so the ranking inverts. The same molecule docked twice under different SMILES spellings scored −10.70 and −10.37 on 4RX0 and −8.22 and −7.79 on 7L01, a same-molecule reproducibility spread of 0.33–0.43 kcal/mol, and the self-dock structure scored every compound about 2.5 kcal/mol better than the cross-dock structure. Docking therefore cannot rank this PfDHODH series, and the best-pose scores are unstable across poses. The falsifier is a head-to-head PfDHODH enzymatic assay of DSM265, CHEMBL3289670 and CHEMBL1738786 under identical conditions: if the two analogues do not outperform DSM265 there, the docking ranking is refuted.

1. Introduction

The World Health Organization's World Malaria Report 2024 records 263 million malaria cases and 597,000 deaths in 2023, with children under five accounting for 76% of deaths in the African Region. Artemisinin partial resistance is now confirmed in multiple regions, and the pipeline of new antimalarials is thin. Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), the fourth enzyme of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis, is a validated target: Plasmodium falciparum cannot salvage pyrimidines and depends entirely on this pathway, while the human enzyme differs enough in its inhibitor-binding pocket to allow selectivity.

DSM265 is the flagship PfDHODH inhibitor. Phillips et al. (Sci Transl Med 2015) showed it is selective for the Plasmodium enzyme over the human enzyme, active against blood and liver stages, and that a single oral dose of 200–400 mg maintains therapeutic concentrations for more than eight days. Its measured PfDHODH IC50 in ChEMBL is 27 nM, consistent with the published value of about 33 nM. This paper tests one falsifiable hypothesis: Vina docking on the DSM265-bound PfDHODH structure (4RX0) ranks known PfDHODH inhibitors in the same order as their measured IC50 values. The falsifier is stated in the Abstract.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources verified on 22 November 2026: WHO World Malaria Report 2024 (burden figures); Phillips et al., Sci Transl Med 2015;7:296ra111 (DSM265 discovery and properties, PMID 26180101, doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aaa6645); ChEMBL bioactivities for PfDHODH (CHEMBL3588732), retrieved live. The Islamic literature sweep found no canonical work that addresses DHODH or malaria chemotherapy: Ibn Sina's Canon describes fevers and their treatment, but the parasite, the enzyme and the drug were all unknown to the classical authors, so no classical source can inform the docking question; this is recorded as a limitation, not hidden.

2.2 Molecular docking

The standardised AutoDock Vina protocol of Papers #1 and #3 was used. Target: P. falciparum DHODH, UniProtKB Q08210, resolved live to ChEMBL CHEMBL3588732 (SINGLE PROTEIN, Plasmodium falciparum isolate 3D7), 58 bioactivities, 26 leads after similarity screening. Two structures were docked. 4RX0 (PfDHODH co-crystallised with DSM265, 2.25 Å): the grid centre [−26.36, −11.70, −16.46] is the centroid of the co-crystallised DSM265 ligand (HETATM group D65, 70 atoms including alternate conformations), computed with dock._ligand_center, which excludes the FMN cofactor, the orotate substrate and waters — the centre audit is mandatory after the TYK2 wrong-domain precedent. 7L01 (PfDHODH co-crystallised with inhibitor DSM782, 1.6 Å): centre [5.00, 49.01, 2.20], the DSM782 centroid; this is a cross-dock for DSM265, not its own structure. Box 22.5 Å on both. Best of three poses reported; the reference drug and the analogues were docked under the identical protocol on each structure. Ligands: DSM265 (PubChem CID 51347395) and ChEMBL leads with their ChEMBL activities.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All five compounds reported here are PAINS-clean.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so gaps smaller than ~1 kcal/mol cannot rank compounds. No experimental data were generated; no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. The same molecule was docked twice under different SMILES spellings, which measures reproducibility rather than adding a compound.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

On the self-dock structure 4RX0, the ranking inverts. The most potent compound, DSM265 (27 nM), scores −10.70; the two least potent, CHEMBL3289670 (35 nM) and CHEMBL1738786 (38 nM), score −12.16 and −11.86 — 1.46 and 1.16 kcal/mol better than DSM265. CHEMBL1956283 (28 nM) scores −10.78, essentially tied with DSM265. Ranked by docking: CHEMBL3289670 > CHEMBL1738786 > CHEMBL1956283 ≈ DSM265. Ranked by assay: DSM265 > CHEMBL1956283 > CHEMBL3289670 > CHEMBL1738786. The two orders are reversed. The same inversion appears on the cross-dock structure 7L01, where CHEMBL3289670 again scores best (−9.61) and DSM265 worst (−8.22/−7.79).

Two further findings qualify the numbers. First, the same molecule docked twice: DSM265 entered as the PubChem query and as ChEMBL1956285 (identical connectivity, different SMILES spelling) scores −10.70 versus −10.37 on 4RX0 and −8.22 versus −7.79 on 7L01 — a same-molecule reproducibility spread of 0.33–0.43 kcal/mol, which is the floor below which score differences are meaningless. Second, the pose spreads are wide: DSM265's three 4RX0 poses span −10.70 to −7.72 (2.98 kcal/mol), and CHEMBL3289670's span −12.16 to −9.00 (3.16 kcal/mol). The best pose is an outlier in both cases, not a consensus. Third, the structure effect is large and consistent: every compound scores about 2.5 kcal/mol better on its self-dock structure 4RX0 than on the cross-dock structure 7L01 (DSM265: −10.70 vs −8.22; CHEMBL3289670: −12.16 vs −9.61).

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of DSM265 against these specific ChEMBL analogues on 4RX0 was found in the literature sweep; the numbers here are the first report of this comparison. The 4RX0 structure itself is the published DSM265 complex from Phillips et al. (2015).

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank PfDHODH inhibitors. The answer is no — not on either structure, and not even in the right direction. The most potent compound scores worst, and the two weakest score best. This is the third consecutive paper in this run (#96 HCV NS5B, #97 renin, #98 PfDHODH) in which Vina fails to rank a congeneric series by potency, and the strongest such failure yet: an outright inversion rather than a null.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

There is no win to over-read here, and that is the point. CHEMBL3289670's −12.16 is the best score in the table, but its best pose is 3.16 kcal/mol ahead of its second pose, its assay potency is 35 nM against DSM265's 27 nM, and its advantage over DSM265 (1.46 kcal/mol) is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. A reader who took −12.16 at face value would prioritise the wrong compound. The honest reading: these four compounds are all sub-40 nM PfDHODH inhibitors, docking cannot separate them, and the choice between them must be made on properties and assay data, not on Vina scores.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All five compounds are PAINS-clean, so the head-to-head assay does not need redox and aggregation controls. The assay's controls instead need to cover the known confounder in DHODH assays: the enzyme's dependence on its electron acceptor (decylubiquinone in vitro), whose concentration shifts apparent IC50 values. The validation design must fix the acceptor concentration and report it.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3289670 and CHEMBL1738786 inhibit recombinant PfDHODH with IC50 values of ~35 and ~38 nM in the same assay that gives DSM265 27 nM — i.e. the docking inversion does not reproduce in assay. Settled by the head-to-head assay.
  2. DSM265 docked twice under different SMILES spellings reproduces within 0.5 kcal/mol on any PfDHODH structure — a reproducibility check for future benchmarks.
  3. A 100 ns molecular-dynamics simulation of the CHEMBL3289670 4RX0 pose shows it leaving the pocket or rearranging, confirming that its −12.16 best pose is a scoring outlier.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): source the four compounds (commercial, ≥95% purity) and recombinant PfDHODH; set up a colorimetric DHODH activity assay (DCIP reduction) with DSM265 as the internal control and a fixed decylubiquinone concentration. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): dose–response curves for all four compounds in triplicate, same plate; report IC50 with 95% confidence intervals. Stage 3 (weeks 7–8): repeat on a second enzyme lot; if the inversion holds in assay (the analogues genuinely outperform DSM265), run a 100 ns molecular-dynamics simulation of the top pose. Stage 4 (weeks 9–12): selectivity panel against human DHODH for the winner only — selectivity is the property that made DSM265 a drug, and a PfDHODH inhibitor that also hits the human enzyme is not a lead.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol, and the best-pose scores reported here are outliers within their own pose sets.
  2. The same-molecule reproducibility spread (0.33–0.43 kcal/mol) sets a floor on meaningful differences that most of the table's gaps do not clear.
  3. Single-structure analysis per compound set; no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  4. ChEMBL activities come from different assays and laboratories; the IC50 values compared here were not measured under identical conditions — the head-to-head assay is the correction.
  5. No canonical Islamic medical work addresses DHODH or malaria chemotherapy; the literature sweep covers the available digitised canon and names this gap rather than claiming a classical precedent that does not exist.
  6. Nothing here supports a clinical recommendation; DSM265's clinical record is outside this paper's scope.

6. Conclusion

DSM265 self-docks at −10.70 kcal/mol on its own PfDHODH structure 4RX0, yet two weaker analogues score better (−12.16 and −11.86), inverting the potency ranking. The same molecule docked twice reproduces only within 0.33–0.43 kcal/mol, and the self-dock structure scores every compound about 2.5 kcal/mol better than the cross-dock structure. Vina cannot rank this PfDHODH series. The next step is a head-to-head PfDHODH assay of the four compounds under identical conditions.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the ORIC director and the laboratory supervisor at SMBBMU Larkana (Prof. Dr. Nadeem Baloch, ORIC), who control the university's small research budget. Decision: whether to fund the 8–12-week head-to-head PfDHODH assay proposed in §4.5 before any analogue prioritisation. Exact change: approve the assay for DSM265, CHEMBL3289670, CHEMBL1738786 and CHEMBL1956283 as the next funded step, capped at the cost of four commercial compounds and one recombinant PfDHODH lot, and spend nothing on analogue synthesis until the assay returns. Reversal condition: if the assay confirms the ChEMBL potencies (DSM265 best), drop the docking-based prioritisation entirely and use assay data only for future lead selection — do not spend further on Vina benchmarks of this series. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, one of the maqasid al-sharia): malaria kills 597,000 people a year, mostly children, and a better antimalarial would serve that end — but the same principle forbids spending scarce university funds on a compound chosen by a score that the paper itself shows cannot rank, and forbids any clinical claim before the assay exists.

Keywords: KRAS G12C; sotorasib; covalent inhibitor; lung cancer; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; ChEMBL; switch-II pocket

Abstract

KRAS was considered undruggable for decades until covalent inhibitors of the G12C mutant reached the clinic; sotorasib received FDA accelerated approval on 28 May 2021, with a 37.1% objective response rate in CodeBreaK 100. We asked whether Vina docking on the sotorasib-bound KRAS G12C structure ranks known KRAS G12C inhibitors by their measured potency. The pipeline resolved KRAS (UniProtKB P01116) to ChEMBL CHEMBL2189121, retrieved 51 bioactivities, and ranked 26 leads; docking ran on 6OIM (KRAS G12C covalently bound to sotorasib, 1.65 Å) and on 9IAY (GDP-KRAS in complex with a different inhibitor, 0.953 Å). On 6OIM, sotorasib self-docked at −8.71 kcal/mol and the four analogues scored −8.20 to −9.21, a 1.01 kcal/mol spread for compounds spanning 0.3–0.6 nM — docking cannot separate them. On the cross-dock structure 9IAY the spread exploded to 4.77 kcal/mol, with sotorasib worst at −7.54 and an analogue best at −12.31. The cross-dock spread is a pocket artefact, not a potency signal, and Vina cannot model the covalent bond to Cys12 that gives these drugs their potency, so every score here is a non-covalent pose score only. The falsifier is a covalent docking or free-energy calculation (or a head-to-head biochemical assay with fixed pre-incubation time) of sotorasib, CHEMBL5892737 and CHEMBL5905084 under identical conditions: if the covalent-aware ranking does not separate the 0.3 nM compound from the 0.6 nM compound, the docking approach is confirmed uninformative for this series, and future KRAS G12C work must use covalent-aware methods from the start.

1. Introduction

KRAS mutations occur in 43% of lung adenocarcinomas, and the G12C mutation accounts for about 13% of lung adenocarcinomas. For decades KRAS was called undruggable: the protein lacks a deep pocket, and its picomolar affinity for GTP seemed to rule out competitive inhibition. The breakthrough was the switch-II pocket, a shallow groove that opens only in the GDP-bound state, and the cysteine at position 12, which the G12C mutation places within reach of a covalent warhead. Sotorasib (AMG 510) exploits both: it binds the switch-II pocket and forms a covalent bond to Cys12, locking KRAS in its inactive GDP-bound state.

Sotorasib received FDA accelerated approval on 28 May 2021 for KRAS G12C-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer. In the CodeBreaK 100 phase II trial the objective response rate was 37.1%, median overall survival 12.5 months, median progression-free survival 6.8 months and median duration of response 11.1 months; the two-year analysis (Dy et al., J Clin Oncol 2023) reported a 41% response rate, 12.5 months median overall survival and 33% two-year overall survival. Resistance emerges through secondary KRAS mutations, bypass signalling and histological transformation, and newer covalent G12C inhibitors are in development. This paper tests one falsifiable hypothesis: Vina docking on the sotorasib-bound KRAS G12C structure (6OIM) ranks known KRAS G12C inhibitors in the same order as their measured potency. The falsifier is stated in the Abstract.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources verified on 22 November 2026: Hong et al., N Engl J Med 2020;383:1207–17 (first-in-human sotorasib, PMID 32955176, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1917239); Dy et al., J Clin Oncol 2023;41:3311–17 (two-year CodeBreaK 100 outcomes, PMID 37098232, doi:10.1200/JCO.22.02524); FDA accelerated approval 28 May 2021; ChEMBL bioactivities for KRAS (CHEMBL2189121), retrieved live. The Islamic literature sweep found no canonical work that addresses KRAS or covalent oncology drugs: the classical authors described tumours and their treatment, but the gene, the mutation and the drug are all modern, so no classical source can inform the docking question; this is recorded as a limitation, not hidden.

2.2 Molecular docking

The standardised AutoDock Vina protocol of Papers #1 and #3 was used. Target: human KRAS, UniProtKB P01116, resolved live to ChEMBL CHEMBL2189121 (SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens), 51 bioactivities, 26 leads after similarity screening. Two structures were docked. 6OIM (human KRAS G12C covalently bound to AMG 510/sotorasib, 1.65 Å): the grid centre [1.87, −8.26, −1.36] is the centroid of the co-crystallised sotorasib ligand (HETATM group MOV, 41 atoms), computed with dock._ligand_center, which excludes GDP, the magnesium ion and waters — the centre audit is mandatory after the TYK2 wrong-domain precedent. 9IAY (GDP-KRAS in complex with inhibitor "10", 0.953 Å): centre [21.83, −0.61, 4.76], the compound-10 centroid; this is a cross-dock for sotorasib, not its own structure. Box 22.5 Å on both. Best of three poses reported; the reference drug and the analogues were docked under the identical protocol on each structure. Ligands: sotorasib (PubChem CID 137278711) and ChEMBL leads with their ChEMBL activities. Covalent caveat: sotorasib and the four analogues are covalent G12C inhibitors whose potency comes from bond formation with Cys12. Vina does not model covalent bond formation; every score in this paper is therefore a non-covalent pose score, and the covalent contribution is invisible to the method.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All five compounds reported here are PAINS-clean.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and for covalent inhibitors it is not even a complete affinity estimate. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so gaps smaller than ~1 kcal/mol cannot rank compounds. No experimental data were generated; no covalent docking, molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.

CHEMBL5892737 Kd 0.3 nM −9.21 −9.21, −8.97, −8.82 −11.66 −11.66, −10.43, −10.07 clean
CHEMBL5905084 IC50 0.4 nM −8.20 −8.20, −8.03, −7.91 −12.31 −12.31, −11.11, −10.16 clean
CHEMBL5948638 IC50 0.5 nM −8.96 −8.96, −8.95, −8.16 −10.50 −10.50, −10.16, −9.20 clean
CHEMBL4876243 IC50 0.6 nM −8.57 −8.57, −8.49, −8.24 −10.61 −10.61, −10.28, −10.26 clean

On the self-dock structure 6OIM, the five compounds score within 1.01 kcal/mol of each other (−9.21 to −8.20) while their measured potencies span 0.3–0.6 nM. The most potent, CHEMBL5892737 (Kd 0.3 nM), scores best (−9.21), but the second-most-potent, CHEMBL5905084 (IC50 0.4 nM), scores worst (−8.20). The ranking is a null: docking cannot separate sub-nanomolar covalent inhibitors by non-covalent pose score, and the 1.01 kcal/mol spread is inside Vina's noise.

On the cross-dock structure 9IAY the picture is dramatically different — and misleading. The spread explodes to 4.77 kcal/mol: CHEMBL5905084 scores −12.31, CHEMBL5892737 −11.66, and sotorasib worst at −7.54. Sotorasib's three 9IAY poses are nearly identical (−7.54, −7.53, −7.44), which suggests Vina found only one shallow minimum for it in the compound-10 pocket. A reader who saw only the 9IAY table would conclude sotorasib is a poor binder and CHEMBL5905084 is a breakthrough — both conclusions are artefacts of the pocket, not of the molecules. The 6OIM table corrects them: on sotorasib's own structure, the five compounds are indistinguishable.

Sotorasib 560.61 4.48 1 7 5 104.45 1 pass 0.599
CHEMBL5892737 549.05 4.67 2 8 5 86.64 1 pass 0.214

All five are close analogues by properties (MW 540–589, logP 4.40–4.76, 5–6 rotatable bonds, one Lipinski violation each, Veber pass). Sotorasib's Tox21 kNN maximum of 0.599 is the highest in the set and above 0.5, the only compound in this run's five papers to cross that threshold; the analogues sit at 0.197–0.370. All are PAINS-clean.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of sotorasib against these specific ChEMBL analogues on 6OIM was found in the literature sweep; the numbers here are the first report of this comparison. The 6OIM structure itself is the published sotorasib complex. The covalent nature of these inhibitors is well established in the literature, and the non-covalent-only limitation of Vina for this series is a known methods gap, not a new finding — the new finding is how large the cross-dock artefact is (4.77 kcal/mol) relative to the true spread (1.01 kcal/mol).

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank KRAS G12C inhibitors. The answer is no, twice over. On the right structure, the scores are too close to separate (a null). On the wrong structure, the scores separate dramatically — and wrongly (an artefact). The 9IAY table is the most dangerous result in this run's five papers, because it looks like a discovery: a 4.77 kcal/mol spread with a clear winner. It is not a discovery. It is the pocket of a different inhibitor doing the ranking.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

CHEMBL5905084's −12.31 on 9IAY must not be quoted as a finding. On 6OIM it scores −8.20, the worst of the five. Its 9IAY advantage comes from fitting the compound-10 pocket, not from binding KRAS G12C better. Equally, sotorasib's −7.54 on 9IAY must not be quoted as a failure: on its own structure it scores −8.71, and its clinical efficacy is established by trial data, not by any docking score. The covalent bond to Cys12 — the source of these drugs' potency — is invisible to Vina, so the method cannot, even in principle, rank this series by affinity.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All five compounds are PAINS-clean, so the validation assay does not need redox and aggregation controls. The assay's controls instead need to cover the known confounder for covalent inhibitors: time-dependent inhibition. IC50 values for covalent drugs depend on pre-incubation time, so the validation design must fix the incubation time and report it, and must include a non-covalent control (a warhead-free analogue) to separate the covalent contribution from the pose contribution.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Covalent docking (or a free-energy calculation that includes the Cys12 bond) ranks CHEMBL5892737 (Kd 0.3 nM) ahead of CHEMBL4876243 (IC50 0.6 nM) by more than 1 kcal/mol. Settled by the covalent-aware calculation.
  2. A head-to-head biochemical assay with fixed pre-incubation time reproduces the ChEMBL potencies (0.3–0.6 nM) for all five compounds, confirming that the 6OIM null is correct and the 9IAY spread is an artefact.
  3. A warhead-free analogue of sotorasib docks at the same −8.71 on 6OIM but shows no KRAS G12C inhibition in assay, confirming that the covalent bond, not the pose, carries the potency.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): source the five compounds (commercial, ≥95% purity) and recombinant KRAS G12C (GDP-loaded); set up a nucleotide-exchange or SOS1-mediated exchange assay with sotorasib as the internal control and a fixed pre-incubation time. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): dose–response curves for all five compounds in triplicate, same plate, same incubation time; report IC50 with 95% confidence intervals. Stage 3 (weeks 7–8): repeat with a second KRAS G12C lot and a warhead-free sotorasib analogue as the non-covalent control. Stage 4 (weeks 9–12): covalent docking of the top two compounds on 6OIM to check whether the covalent-aware ranking separates them.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; Vina cannot model the covalent Cys12 bond, so every score here omits the main source of these drugs' potency.
  2. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol; the 6OIM spread (1.01 kcal/mol) is inside the noise.
  3. Single-structure analysis per compound set; no covalent docking, molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  4. ChEMBL activities come from different assays and laboratories, and covalent IC50 values depend on pre-incubation time, which was not standardised across the source assays — the head-to-head assay is the correction.
  5. No canonical Islamic medical work addresses KRAS or covalent oncology drugs; the literature sweep covers the available digitised canon and names this gap rather than claiming a classical precedent that does not exist.
  6. Nothing here supports a clinical recommendation; sotorasib's clinical record comes from the CodeBreaK trials, not from this paper.

6. Conclusion

Sotorasib self-docks at −8.71 kcal/mol on its own KRAS G12C structure 6OIM, and four sub-nanomolar analogues score within 1.01 kcal/mol of it — docking cannot rank this covalent series by non-covalent pose score. On the cross-dock structure 9IAY the spread explodes to 4.77 kcal/mol, a pocket artefact that would mislead any reader who quoted it. For covalent inhibitors, Vina's numbers are pose scores, not affinities. The next step is a covalent-aware calculation or a head-to-head assay with fixed pre-incubation time.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the ORIC director and the laboratory supervisor at SMBBMU Larkana (Prof. Dr. Nadeem Baloch, ORIC), who control the university's small research budget. Decision: whether to fund the 8–12-week head-to-head KRAS G12C assay proposed in §4.5, including a warhead-free control, before any further docking work on this series. Exact change: approve the assay for sotorasib and the four analogues as the next funded step, capped at the cost of five commercial compounds and one recombinant KRAS G12C lot, and spend nothing on further Vina benchmarks of covalent inhibitors until a covalent-aware method is in place. Reversal condition: if the assay reproduces the ChEMBL potencies and the warhead-free analogue shows no inhibition, close the Vina line for covalent series and adopt covalent docking as the standard for any future KRAS work. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, one of the maqasid al-sharia): lung cancer is a leading killer, and a better KRAS inhibitor would serve that end — but the same principle forbids spending scarce university funds on a ranking the paper itself shows is an artefact, and forbids any clinical claim before the assay exists.

Upadacitinib Re-Docks at −9.30 kcal/mol on the Tofacitinib-Bound JAK1 Structure — but the Ranking Reverses on a Second JAK1 Structure, and Docking Cannot Decide Whether Any Measured Analogue Beats It

Question. Rheumatoid arthritis is projected to affect 31.7 million people by 2050, and upadacitinib — a JAK1-selective inhibitor that beat adalimumab in the SELECT-COMPARE trial (ACR20 71% vs 63% at 12 weeks) — costs over $60,000 a year for uninsured patients.

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan. ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509. Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI research assistant). Date: 22 November 2026. Field: Health (medicinal chemistry / drug discovery). Status: Manuscript draft. Not submitted anywhere. No professor's endorsement is claimed; the Harvard / MIT / Oxford policy-shaping scholars named in the method brief are the standard this paper practises, not co-authors.

Abstract

Question. Rheumatoid arthritis is projected to affect 31.7 million people by 2050, and upadacitinib — a JAK1-selective inhibitor that beat adalimumab in the SELECT-COMPARE trial (ACR20 71% vs 63% at 12 weeks) — costs over $60,000 a year for uninsured patients. We asked whether any compound with measured JAK1 potency already in ChEMBL binds the JAK1 ATP pocket more strongly than upadacitinib. Claim. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P23458 → ChEMBL CHEMBL2835 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked upadacitinib and five ChEMBL ligands (IC50 0.011–0.031 nM) on the 1.90 Å tofacitinib-bound JAK1 structure 3EYG, centred exactly on the co-crystallised tofacitinib (centre audit via dock._ligand_center), and confirmed the result on the 1.33 Å JAK1 structure 6N7A. On 3EYG upadacitinib re-docked best at −9.30 kcal/mol, 0.39 ahead of the best analogue. On 6N7A the ranking reversed: three analogues beat upadacitinib (−9.63, −9.56 and −9.24 vs −8.41 kcal/mol), a 1.39 kcal/mol swing for the same compound between structures. Docking therefore cannot rank this series, and no analogue can be claimed to beat upadacitinib on this evidence. Tofacitinib, the pan-JAK incumbent, re-docked worse than upadacitinib on both structures (−7.87 and −8.10 kcal/mol). All five analogues share tofacitinib's pyrrolo-pyrimidine core, pass Lipinski/Veber with no PAINS alerts, and carry only low Tox21 read-across signals. Falsifier. A JAK1 binding assay showing an analogue's Kd worse than its published IC50, or an IL-6-stimulated STAT3-phosphorylation cell assay showing no advantage over upadacitinib, refutes the claim for that compound. Identification. Validated-control re-docking on two co-crystal structures; association only beyond that — docking scores are not activity. One clean number: 1.39 kcal/mol — the swing in one compound's docking score between two JAK1 structures, larger than the 0.39 kcal/mol gap it was supposed to settle.

Keywords: JAK1; upadacitinib; tofacitinib; rheumatoid arthritis; molecular docking; ChEMBL; Janus kinase; selectivity

1. Introduction

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease of progressive joint destruction and systemic inflammation. A 2026 review in Frontiers in Pharmacology puts the global burden at an estimated 31.7 million cases projected by 2050 (Wang et al., 2026). In Pakistan, where rheumatology care is concentrated in cities and biologic therapy is largely unaffordable, an effective oral pill matters more than an effective injection, because a pill is the treatment a patient can actually take — and the price of that pill decides whether it is taken at all.

The Janus kinase (JAK)–signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway integrates signals from the cytokines that drive RA: interleukin-6, interferons, and the common gamma-chain cytokines. Four JAK family members exist (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2), and they work in pairs; JAK1 partners with JAK2, JAK3 or TYK2 to transduce IL-6, interferon and IL-10-family signals, while JAK2 alone carries erythropoietin and thrombopoietin signalling — which is why sparing JAK2 is supposed to spare haemoglobin and platelets. Tofacitinib (Xeljanz, Pfizer), approved by the FDA in 2012, was the first JAK inhibitor: a pan-JAK drug that hits JAK1 and JAK3. Upadacitinib (Rinvoq, AbbVie; ABT-494), FDA-approved in 2019, was engineered for JAK1 selectivity: in biochemical assays its IC50 is 0.043–0.045 µM for JAK1 versus 0.109–0.12 µM for JAK2, and in cellular assays the gap widens to 0.014 µM versus 0.593 µM — over 40-fold selectivity for JAK1 (Paruch et al., BMC Rheumatology, 2018). In the SELECT-COMPARE trial it outperformed adalimumab, achieving ACR20 in 71% versus 63%, ACR50 in 45% versus 29% at 12 weeks, with efficacy sustained beyond five years; real-world data from the Canadian CLOSE-UP study found 63.5% of patients reaching DAS28-CRP ≤2.6 at six months (Wang et al., 2026). Its indications have since widened — psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, atopic dermatitis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, and, with phase 3 evidence in 2026, giant cell arteritis — while the class carries an FDA boxed warning for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), venous thromboembolism (VTE) and malignancy, driven by the ORAL Surveillance trial of tofacitinib: in 4,362 cardiovascular-risk-enriched RA patients, MACE occurred in 3.4% on tofacitinib versus 2.5% on a TNF inhibitor (hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 0.91–1.94) and cancers in 4.2% versus 2.9% (HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.04–2.09), with non-inferiority not shown (Ytterberg et al., N Engl J Med, 2022). Against that background, a 2025 meta-analysis of 9,547 upadacitinib-treated patients found increased risks of hepatic disorder, neutropenia, acne, herpes zoster and raised creatine phosphokinase — dose-dependent for the first three — but no significant association with MACE or VTE (Zhang et al., 2025); an integrated safety analysis of 8,632 patients over 27,164.2 patient-years reported MACE at 0–0.5 and VTE at 0–0.9 per 100 patient-years, stable over time (Advances in Therapy, 2025). The drug's problem is not efficacy or, on current evidence, a proven cardiovascular signal of its own — it is price: over $60,000 a year for uninsured patients (Wang et al., 2026).

The classical medical canon discussed joint disease centuries before JAK1 was known. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025) — Europe's medical textbook for some 500 years — treats diseases of the joints under waja' al-mafasil (joint pain), giving the first detailed account of its aetiopathogenesis in terms of altered temperament (su-e-mizaj) and morbid matter (mawad-e-fasida) accumulating in the joint spaces; Al-Razi, in Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900), treated waja' al-mafasil as an umbrella term covering conditions from gout (niqris) to sciatica (Khan et al., J Drug Deliv Ther, 2019). These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence — they know the syndrome, not the target — but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is a thousand years old in this region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §6).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured JAK1 potency bind the ATP pocket of the tofacitinib-bound JAK1 structure (PDB 3EYG) at scores beyond re-docked upadacitinib, and would that binding translate into stronger JAK1 inhibition? Falsifier: a JAK1 binding assay showing a Kd worse than the analogue's published IC50, or a cell assay (IL-6-stimulated STAT3 phosphorylation) showing no advantage over upadacitinib, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the approved drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target, confirmed on a second JAK1 structure — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 22 November 2026: the upadacitinib RA review (Wang et al., Front Pharmacol 2026;17:1776317, doi:10.3389/fphar.2026.1776317); the upadacitinib safety meta-analysis (Zhang et al., Front Pharmacol 2025;16:1598972, doi:10.3389/fphar.2025.1598972); the integrated upadacitinib safety analysis across 16 studies (Adv Ther 2025;42:5215–5237, doi:10.1007/s12325-025-03328-y); the ORAL Surveillance trial (Ytterberg et al., N Engl J Med 2022;386:316–326, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2109927); the JAK1-selectivity characterisation of upadacitinib (BMC Rheumatol 2018;2:23, doi:10.1186/s41927-018-0031-x); the 2026 review of JAK inhibitors beyond arthritis (J Clin Med 2026;15(22):8894); the alopecia-areata network meta-analysis (J Invest Dermatol 2026, doi:10.1016/j.jid.2026.10.039); the RCSB records for PDB 3EYG and 6N7A; and the Unani-medicine literature on waja' al-mafasil (Khan et al., 2019, doi:10.22270/jddt.v9i2-s.2699). The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900); Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat (d. 1388) — consulted via the literature map and modern reviews, not read in full Arabic text (see Limitations). Note on sources: the daily research digest last issued on 14 November 2026 and has not updated since, so this sweep used targeted searches on 22 November 2026 instead of the digest.

2.2 Target identification

The LeadForge pipeline resolved the target from UniProtKB: human Janus kinase 1 (JAK1), accession P23458, Homo sapiens; ChEMBL target CHEMBL2835 ("Tyrosine-protein kinase JAK1", single protein), with 58 live bioactivities retrieved. The query compound was upadacitinib, verified live against PubChem (CID 9958327; SMILES CCC1CN(CC1C2=CN=C3N2C4=C(NC=C4)N=C3)C(=O)NCC(F)(F)F; formula C17H19F3N6O; MW 380.37). A Morgan-fingerprint (Tanimoto) similarity screen against the 58 known actives returned 25 compounds; after the ADMET and safety panel, 26 leads were ranked (25 analogues plus the query) by the composite score: similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20. The top five non-query leads were taken forward to docking.

2.3 Structure selection — the auto-pick, set aside on purpose

The pipeline's PDB picker auto-selected 6N7A (1.33 Å, "Structure of the human JAK1 kinase domain with compound 39"). That structure was set aside for the primary run in favour of 3EYG, because 3EYG is the co-crystal of JAK1 with a named drug — tofacitinib (residue MI1) — in the same ATP pocket upadacitinib occupies, while "compound 39" is an unnamed tool compound. 3EYG was verified directly against the RCSB record before docking: single chain A, human JAK1 (gene JAK1), 1.90 Å resolution, deposited 20 October 2008, title "Crystal structures of JAK1 and JAK2 inhibitor complexes". No upadacitinib co-crystal is deposited, so the tofacitinib-bound structure is the closest validated control; this is stated, not hidden. The set-aside structure 6N7A was then used as the confirmation structure (§3.3) rather than discarded.

2.4 Docking centre — audited, never hand-rolled

The docking centre was computed by dock._ligand_center on the 3EYG file and audited residue by residue. The pick was MI1, chain A, residue 1, 23 heavy atoms — the co-crystallised tofacitinib — at centre [10.989, 14.186, −14.773]. The phosphotyrosine modified residue PTR (32 atoms) was correctly excluded as a non-drug-like modified residue. The same audit on 6N7A picked KEV, chain A, residue 1203, 28 atoms — the co-crystallised inhibitor "compound 39" — at centre [5.291, −24.420, 22.094] (KEV is also present in chain B, residue 1202, 28 atoms; the audit picked chain A). Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, a 22.5 Å cubic box centred on the co-crystallised ligand, exhaustiveness 8, 3 modes. Two controls were re-docked on each structure: upadacitinib (the query drug) and tofacitinib (SMILES fetched live from PubChem CID 9926791), the pan-JAK incumbent and strongest comparator.

2.5 ADMET and safety panel

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski, Veber), PAINS screen, and a ToxGuard Tox21 k-nearest-neighbour read-across panel (12 assays) were computed for every lead before docking; only leads passing the panel were ranked. Vina's scoring noise is taken as ±1–2 kcal/mol throughout: a margin inside that band is reported as "not distinguishable", never as a win.

2.6 Analysis plan (stated before results)

The plan was fixed in the run script before any score was seen: dock the top five non-query leads plus the two controls on 3EYG, then repeat all seven on 6N7A; the claim "an analogue beats upadacitinib" counts as supported only if an analogue out-scores re-docked upadacitinib by more than 1 kcal/mol on both structures. A single-structure margin, or a margin inside Vina noise, does not support the claim. The ranking was also to be checked against the published IC50s: a method that cannot reproduce the assay ordering cannot be trusted to rank new compounds.

3. Results

3.1 Pipeline output

58 ChEMBL bioactivities for JAK1 (CHEMBL2835); 25 compounds passed the similarity screen; 26 leads ranked. The five leads taken to docking all carry measured JAK1 IC50 values between 0.011 and 0.031 nM (pChEMBL 10.51–10.96) — a span of only 2.8-fold, which limits how much ranking the assay data can test. All five are close structural relatives of tofacitinib, built on the same pyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidine core with a sulfonyl side chain; none is a new chemotype, and their Tanimoto similarity to upadacitinib is low (0.21–0.24) because upadacitinib carries a different core (imidazo-pyrrolo-pyrazine).

3.2 Docking on 3EYG — upadacitinib best, by less than noise

On 3EYG, upadacitinib re-docks best at −9.30 kcal/mol. The best analogue, CHEMBL5934018, trails by 0.39 kcal/mol — inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the two are not distinguishable. Tofacitinib re-docks at −7.87, a full 1.43 kcal/mol worse than upadacitinib on the same pocket. The ranking tracks the assay ordering only loosely: the most potent ligand by assay (CHEMBL5934018, 0.011 nM) does dock best among the analogues, and the least potent (CHEMBL5777563, 0.031 nM) docks worst — but the second-most-potent ligand, CHEMBL5933670 (0.013 nM), docks second-worst at −7.69, a clear inversion.

CHEMBL3652403 −9.63 −9.63, −9.40, −8.89 −1.39

On the higher-resolution structure the ranking reverses: three analogues now beat upadacitinib, by 0.83–1.22 kcal/mol, and the compound that was third on 3EYG (CHEMBL3652403) is best on 6N7A. The swing for a single compound between the two structures reaches 1.39 kcal/mol — larger than the 0.39 kcal/mol gap the experiment was supposed to settle. By the analysis plan fixed in §2.6, the claim "an analogue beats upadacitinib" is therefore not supported: it holds on one structure and fails on the other, and the method cannot decide between them. This is the same failure mode this series found for TYK2, where one compound swung 1.84 kcal/mol between two JH2 structures. Two findings are stable across both structures and are reported as such: tofacitinib re-docks worse than upadacitinib on both (−7.87 and −8.10 vs −9.30 and −8.41), and CHEMBL5933670 and CHEMBL5777563 are the two worst-docking analogues on both.

3.4 ADMET and safety

All five analogues pass Lipinski (0 violations) and Veber, carry no PAINS alerts, and show only low Tox21 read-across signals (highest single-assay value 0.377, SR-MMP for CHEMBL3652403; all others ≤0.30). Their properties are drug-like and close to upadacitinib's own (MW 380.37, logP 2.91, HBD 2, HBA 3, TPSA 78.32 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations): MW 352–492, logP 1.36–3.34, HBD 1–2, HBA 5–7, TPSA 78.95–108.49 Å². Nothing in the ADMET panel disqualifies any of the five; equally, nothing in it distinguishes them from upadacitinib. The two largest analogues (CHEMBL3652403, MW 491.66; CHEMBL6031741, MW 455.46, ranked sixth and not docked) sit near the top of the Lipinski weight range, which is a watch-point, not a failure.

4. Discussion

Mechanism. JAK1 inhibition works by occupying the ATP-binding pocket of the JH1 kinase domain, blocking the phosphorylation of STAT proteins downstream of IL-6, interferon and common gamma-chain cytokines. Upadacitinib's advantage over tofacitinib in the clinic is selectivity, not raw JAK1 potency: tofacitinib inhibits JAK3 nearly as well as JAK1, while upadacitinib's cellular selectivity for JAK1 over JAK2 exceeds 40-fold. Docking into a single rigid JAK1 structure cannot measure selectivity — it can only measure fit to one pocket — so the 1.43 kcal/mol gap between the two drugs' re-dock scores on 3EYG is consistent with the selectivity story but does not prove it. The honest reading is narrower: upadacitinib fits the JAK1 ATP pocket at least as well as its predecessor, and no measured analogue in ChEMBL fits it demonstrably better.

Why the reversal matters. The 6N7A result is not a contradiction to be averaged away; it is the experiment's most informative output. Both structures are human JAK1 JH1 domains with an inhibitor in the same pocket, yet the ranking of seven compounds changes completely between them. The likely causes are the ones this series keeps meeting: different co-crystallised ligands leave different pocket conformations (tofacitinib in 3EYG, compound 39 in 6N7A), rigid-receptor docking cannot adapt to either, and the five analogues differ from each other by small sulfonyl-side-chain changes that Vina scores within its own noise. The consequence is practical: any paper that reports a single-structure docking "win" for a JAK1 analogue without a second-structure check is reporting noise. The TYK2 paper in this series reached the same conclusion on the same grounds, and the two together make the case that the LeadForge pipeline's docking step needs a mandatory second-structure confirmation — which this run performed — before any lead is called a lead.

The cost question. The clinical case for a cheaper JAK1 inhibitor is the strongest part of this paper and the part docking cannot answer. Upadacitinib at over $60,000 a year is out of reach for nearly every RA patient in Pakistan paying out of pocket, and the drug's own safety record — no significant MACE or VTE signal in the 2025 meta-analysis of 9,547 patients, and stable low rates over 27,164 patient-years — removes the main clinical objection to wider use, leaving price as the binding constraint. A molecule that matched upadacitinib's JAK1 binding at a fraction of the price would change who gets treated; this screen found no such molecule among measured ChEMBL ligands, but it also found three analogues (CHEMBL5934018, CHEMBL5929524, CHEMBL3652403) that cannot be excluded on docking evidence and that all pass the ADMET panel. They are the correct subjects of the falsifying assay, not the subject of a claim.

Comparison against the strongest incumbent. Upadacitinib was judged against two incumbents, not against nothing: tofacitinib, the pan-JAK predecessor it was designed to improve on (beaten on both structures, by 1.43 and 0.31 kcal/mol), and adalimumab, the TNF-inhibitor standard it beat in SELECT-COMPARE on clinical endpoints (ACR20 71% vs 63%). On the clinical evidence the drug is already the strongest incumbent in its class for RA; the docking adds only that its pocket fit is not obviously beaten by anything already measured.

5. Limitations

  1. Vina noise decides this paper. The 0.39 kcal/mol gap on 3EYG and the 1.39 kcal/mol structure-to-structure swing are both inside, or barely outside, the ±1–2 kcal/mol error of the method. Nothing here is a measured difference.
  2. One pocket, rigid, no water, no dynamics. Both structures are rigid-receptor docks with no molecular dynamics, no explicit water and no induced fit. A flexible-ligand/flexible-receptor or free-energy calculation could change the ordering again.
  3. No selectivity screen. No JAK2, JAK3 or TYK2 structure was docked, so nothing is claimed about selectivity — the property that actually distinguishes upadacitinib. A compound that binds JAK1 tightly and JAK2 tighter would be worse, not better.
  4. The potency range is too narrow to test ranking. The five assay IC50s span 0.011–0.031 nM, a 2.8-fold range. With potencies that close, even a perfect scoring function would struggle to order them, and the one clear inversion (CHEMBL5933670) may reflect assay heterogeneity rather than a docking failure. The ChEMBL IC50s come from different assays and publications, and their conditions were not harmonised in this run.
  5. No laboratory data. No compound in this study has been synthesised, assayed or tested by the author. Every number is computational or cited.
  6. Islamic canon read in part. Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi were consulted through modern reviews and the literature map, not read in full Arabic; the full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and many classical Arabic manuscripts remain undigitised (see the literature map's gap list). No Canon-listed plant was tested against JAK1 in this run, so no historical drug claim is made.
  7. Stale digest. The daily research digest last issued on 14 November 2026; the literature sweep for this paper used targeted searches on 22 November 2026 instead. A resumed digest may surface 2026 work this sweep missed.
  8. 6N7A chain choice. The confirmation centre used chain A's KEV pocket; chain B carries the same inhibitor, and a chain-B dock was not run. The 3EYG structure has a single chain, so this affects only the confirmation.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker 1 — the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) and the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations & Coordination. The exact change: open a pooled-procurement negotiation for JAK1 inhibitors, with a voluntary-licence request to the originator as the fallback, and put upadacitinib on the formulary for RA only after methotrexate failure, with mandatory tuberculosis screening and herpes-zoster vaccination before initiation — the zoster signal is the one adverse effect that is both dose-dependent and more common in Asian populations (Zhang et al., 2025). The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life: "whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely" (Qur'an 5:32); a drug priced beyond the reach of the patients who need it does not preserve life, whatever its trial results. The falsifier for this recommendation: if DRAP publishes a negotiated price that brings a month of upadacitinib within reach of a median Pakistani household income, the procurement case for an analogue programme weakens and the priority shifts to distribution.

Decision-maker 2 — the Higher Education Commission (HEC), through NRPU funding. The exact change: fund one JAK1 binding-plus-cell assay programme at a Pakistani university laboratory to test CHEMBL5934018, CHEMBL5929524 and CHEMBL3652403 head-to-head against upadacitinib (JAK1 binding, then IL-6-stimulated STAT3 phosphorylation in cells, then JAK2 counter-screen) over 8–12 weeks, and publish the result whatever it shows — including a clean negative. The Islamic principle is maslaha (public interest, Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat) and ijtihad (independent reasoning, Iqbal, The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam, 1930): a country that cannot afford the imported answer must reason its way to its own, and must publish the negative result so the next laboratory does not repeat it. The falsifier: if the binding assay shows any analogue's Kd worse than its published IC50, that analogue is dropped and the programme reports the failure.

Decision-maker 3 — the State Bank of Pakistan and the Ministry of Finance, on how the procurement is paid for. The exact change: finance any pooled JAK1 procurement through risk-sharing (musharakah) arrangements rather than interest-bearing borrowing, so the cure for a disease of the joints is not bought with a contract the law forbids (Qur'an 2:275–279; Chapra, Islam and the Economic Challenge, 1992). The principle is 'adl, justice (Qur'an 4:135): a financing structure that loads interest onto a public-health purchase taxes the sick to pay the lender.

7. Conclusion

Upadacitinib re-docks at −9.30 kcal/mol on the tofacitinib-bound JAK1 structure and is the best-scoring compound on that structure — but the best measured analogue trails by only 0.39 kcal/mol, and on a second JAK1 structure three analogues out-score it by up to 1.22 kcal/mol. Docking cannot decide whether any measured analogue beats upadacitinib, and this paper does not claim that one does. What it establishes is the shortlist that deserves the assay — CHEMBL5934018, CHEMBL5929524 and CHEMBL3652403 — the method's failure mode, and the policy question that matters more than the ranking: a drug that works and costs over $60,000 a year does not reach the patients whose joints it was made to save. The next step is a binding assay, not a better docking score.
