Sofosbuvir Re-Docks at −9.23 kcal/mol on Its Own NS5B Structure — but the Most Potent Analogue and a 13-Fold Weaker One Dock Identically, and Docking Cannot Rank This Series

An estimated 50 million people live with chronic hepatitis C, which caused about 242,000 deaths in 2022, and Pakistan carries an estimated 12.6 million of the combined hepatitis B and C burden — yet the cure exists: direct-acting antivirals clear the virus in over 95% of patients in 8–12 weeks.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-22 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #96 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: hepatitis C virus; NS5B polymerase; sofosbuvir; molecular docking; ChEMBL; drug resistance; direct-acting antiviral; S282T

Abstract

An estimated 50 million people live with chronic hepatitis C, which caused about 242,000 deaths in 2022, and Pakistan carries an estimated 12.6 million of the combined hepatitis B and C burden — yet the cure exists: direct-acting antivirals clear the virus in over 95% of patients in 8–12 weeks. Sofosbuvir, the nucleotide NS5B polymerase inhibitor at the centre of those regimens, was launched at US$84,000 for a 12-week course against an estimated manufacturing cost of US$68–136, and its only well-documented resistance substitution, S282T, confers just 2- to 18-fold reduced susceptibility. We asked whether any measured NS5B ligand binds the polymerase active site more strongly than sofosbuvir. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q8JXU8 → ChEMBL CHEMBL5375 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked sofosbuvir and four ChEMBL ligands with measured potency on the 2.9 Å sofosbuvir-diphosphate-bound NS5B structure 4WTG, centred exactly on the co-crystallised sofosbuvir diphosphate (centre audit via dock._ligand_center), with the RNA primer/template kept in the receptor. Sofosbuvir re-docked at −9.23 kcal/mol with tight pose consistency. No analogue beat it: the best analogue scored −8.94 kcal/mol, a 0.29 kcal/mol margin inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The decisive failure is the ranking itself: the most potent analogue by assay (CHEMBL5815143, EC50 53 nM) and a 13-fold weaker one (CHEMBL6047888, EC50 690 nM) docked at −8.90 and −8.94 kcal/mol — 0.04 kcal/mol apart — while the weakest compound in the set (CHEMBL109569, IC50 2,250 nM) scored worst at −7.62 kcal/mol. Docking therefore cannot rank this series, and no analogue can be claimed to beat sofosbuvir on this evidence. The honest limit: the docked sofosbuvir is the parent prodrug, while the crystal holds its diphosphate metabolite and the active form in cells is the triphosphate GS-461203; and the ChEMBL ligands have no annotated binding site, so a non-nucleoside inhibitor in the set may bind the thumb or palm allosteric site ~35 Å away, where an active-site score means nothing. The claim that any analogue beats sofosbuvir would be refuted if an NS5B polymerase assay shows an IC50 worse than the analogue's published value. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week NS5B polymerase-plus-replicon assay of the two best-scoring analogues against sofosbuvir, including the S282T mutant.

1. Introduction

Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a disease with a cure that most patients cannot reach. The World Health Organization estimates that 50 million people were living with chronic HCV in 2022, with about 242,000 deaths that year, and that only a fraction have been diagnosed and treated. Pakistan is among the five countries — with China, India, Indonesia and Nigeria — that account for 55% of the combined global hepatitis B and C burden. The cure is real: pan-genotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens clear the virus — sustained virological response — in over 95% of patients in 8–12 weeks of once-daily oral therapy, and even patients who have failed a previous DAA regimen are cured in 96–98% of cases by 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir. The barrier is not biology. It is price and access: sofosbuvir was priced at US$84,000 for a 12-week course in the United States at launch, against published estimates of US$68–136 for the manufacturing cost of the same course, and for years even wealthy health systems rationed it.

Sofosbuvir is a nucleotide prodrug. Inside the hepatocyte it is metabolised to the pharmacologically active uridine analogue triphosphate GS-461203, which the NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase incorporates into the growing viral RNA chain, where it acts as a chain terminator. NS5B is the viral polymerase — the enzyme that copies the HCV genome — and it is the target that makes sofosbuvir pan-genotypic: the active site is conserved across all six HCV genotypes, and the only resistance substitution ever selected in cell culture, S282T, confers only 2- to 18-fold reduced susceptibility and carries a fitness cost, so it is rarely seen in the clinic and has never blocked a cure when sofosbuvir is combined with velpatasvir and voxilaprevir. The question this paper asks is the standard one for this series: among compounds with measured NS5B potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind the polymerase active site more strongly than sofosbuvir itself — and can docking even tell them apart when the reference drug is already a near-perfect active-site binder?

The classical medical canon knew the organ long before it knew the virus: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats diseases of the liver (amrad al-kabid), including jaundice and chronic liver disease, with dietary and supportive management — the Canon knows the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured NS5B potency bind the polymerase active site of the sofosbuvir-diphosphate-bound structure (PDB 4WTG) at scores beyond re-docked sofosbuvir, and would that binding translate into stronger NS5B inhibition? Falsifier: an NS5B polymerase assay showing an IC50 worse than the analogue's published value, or a replicon assay showing no advantage over sofosbuvir, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the approved drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target, with the co-crystallised metabolite as the centre — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-22: the WHO Global Hepatitis Report 2024 and the 2022 global burden analysis (Cui et al., Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology 2026); the sofosbuvir–NS5B structural paper (Appleby et al., Science 2015; PMID 25678663); the non-nucleoside inhibitor thumb-site structures (Biswal et al., Journal of Molecular Biology 2006; PMID 16828488); the sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir resistance analysis (Journal of Hepatology 2018); the FDA prescribing information for sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Microbiology §12.4, mechanism and S282T); the launch-price and manufacturing-cost estimates (Monash Lens, 2024); the RCSB record for PDB 4WTG; and the Islamic-canon sweep (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025 — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text; see Limitations).

2.2 Target identification

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the first run: UniProtKB Q8JXU8 (HCV NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) → ChEMBL CHEMBL5375, "Hepatitis C virus NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase", SINGLE PROTEIN, 52 bioactivities, verified live 2026-11-22. This is the correct target — unlike Paper #95 in this same run, where the pipeline resolved HBV polymerase to a human helicase first. The accession-first query ("Q8JXU8") is what made the difference, and it is now the standing practice for viral targets in this series.

2.3 Molecular docking — the pipeline found no structure; the redock supplies one

The pipeline's docking step returned no_pdb_found: its PDB picker found no structure for accession Q8JXU8. That is a picker limitation, not a fact about the field — the benchmark structure exists. PDB 4WTG is the crystal structure of HCV NS5B genotype 2a JFH-1 in complex with sofosbuvir diphosphate (GS-607596, ligand 6GS), Mn²⁺ and a symmetrical RNA primer/template, 2.9 Å (Appleby et al., Science 2015). A targeted redock script (health-papers-agent/redock_hp040_4wtg.py) docked sofosbuvir and the four highest-ranked ChEMBL ligands with measured potency on 4WTG, using standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exactly as Papers #1/#3: grid centre the centroid of the co-crystallised 6GS, [40.95, −44.99, 5.43], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center (the centre audit confirmed 6GS, 26 atoms, is the largest drug-like HETATM group in the file); box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for sofosbuvir and all four analogues. The receptor preparation keeps the RNA primer/template ATOM records, so the nucleotide pocket is realistic — the diphosphate sits against the primer 3′-end, and removing the RNA would have left a hole where the ligand actually binds. Sofosbuvir is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover strong binding for the drug in the pocket it was crystallised in would be broken. One caveat, stated not smoothed over: the docked sofosbuvir is the parent prodrug SMILES as returned by PubChem (CID 45375808); the crystal holds its diphosphate metabolite GS-607596, and the pharmacologically active form in cells is the triphosphate GS-461203. The heavy-atom scaffold is the same, but the phosphate count differs, and a prodrug docking score is not a metabolite docking score.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to sofosbuvir and the four ligands. All five are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for sofosbuvir: molecular weight 529.46, logP 1.66, 3 hydrogen-bond donors, 9 acceptors, TPSA 158.18 Å², 10 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation, Lipinski pass (1 violation allowed) and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for sofosbuvir: maximum predicted probability 0.254 (NR-AhR), a weak read-across, not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development. The four ligands: CHEMBL5799441 (MW 365.40, logP 1.26, HBD 2, HBA 6, TPSA 116.64 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max Tox21 probability 0.094), CHEMBL109569 (MW 228.16, logP 0.22, HBD 2, HBA 6, TPSA 114.04 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.133), CHEMBL6047888 (MW 367.37, logP 0.99, HBD 2, HBA 8, TPSA 137.74 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.199) and CHEMBL5815143 (MW 375.44, logP 2.58, HBD 3, HBA 5, TPSA 118.27 Å², 5 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.109). All four are drug-like by these counts — which is expected, because all four are variations on optimised NS5B-binder scaffolds, and which is itself a warning that these descriptor counts cannot rank this class.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published ChEMBL potencies. The four ligands' measured potencies are cell-based EC50/IC50 values (replicon assays), not enzyme IC50s, and their binding sites are not annotated in ChEMBL — a non-nucleoside inhibitor among them binds the thumb or palm allosteric site, ~35 Å from the active site, where an active-site docking score is meaningless. The docked sofosbuvir is the parent prodrug, not the active triphosphate.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (4WTG, 2.9 Å — the drug's own structure)

Compound Measured NS5B potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 4WTG (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose Margin vs sofosbuvir
Sofosbuvir (reference) — (approved drug) −9.23 −9.23, −9.03, −9.00 −9.03 —
CHEMBL6047888 EC50 690 nM −8.94 −8.94, −8.86, −8.71 −8.86 +0.29
CHEMBL5815143 EC50 53 nM −8.90 −8.90, −8.64, −8.61 −8.64 +0.33
CHEMBL5799441 EC50 330 nM −8.10 −8.10, −8.04, −7.99 −8.04 +1.13
CHEMBL109569 IC50 2,250 nM −7.62 −7.62, −7.38, −7.25 −7.38 +1.61

Sofosbuvir re-docks at −9.23 kcal/mol on its own structure, with tight pose consistency (−9.23, −9.03, −9.00): the method recovers strong binding for the drug in the pocket it was crystallised in, so the protocol is not broken. No analogue beats it: the best best-pose margin (CHEMBL6047888, +0.29 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the second-best (CHEMBL5815143, +0.33 kcal/mol) is the same. On median pose the order is the same and the margins are the same size.

The decisive check is the comparison with measured potency, and it fails. The most potent ligand by assay, CHEMBL5815143 (EC50 53 nM), docks at −8.90 kcal/mol. A compound 13-fold weaker by assay, CHEMBL6047888 (EC50 690 nM), docks at −8.94 kcal/mol — 0.04 kcal/mol apart, a difference smaller than the rounding of either number. The weakest compound in the set, CHEMBL109569 (IC50 2,250 nM, 42-fold weaker than the best), does score worst (−7.62 kcal/mol), so the method is not random — but between 53 nM and 690 nM it sees nothing at all. A scoring function that cannot distinguish a 53 nM inhibitor from a 690 nM inhibitor, inside one target on the reference drug's own structure, cannot rank this family. The honest reading of the table is therefore a null result: no analogue beats sofosbuvir beyond noise, and the method itself fails to resolve a 13-fold potency difference.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of sofosbuvir or these four ligands on 4WTG was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (ligands vs re-docked reference drug on the same structure, same protocol). The crystal structure itself (4WTG, Appleby et al. 2015) is the published ground truth for the binding mode: it shows how the sofosbuvir diphosphate is positioned by the conserved active-site residues for in-line attack on the incoming nucleotide, with the β-loop and C-terminal linker retracting to enforce replication from the 3′ terminus. The structural literature also gives the paper its most useful context: the non-nucleoside inhibitors bind a common site in the thumb domain ~35 Å from the active site (Biswal et al. 2006), which is why an active-site docking score cannot be the whole story for any ligand in this set whose mechanism is allosteric.

3.3 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Sofosbuvir's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug's >95% cure rate is not a binding problem — it binds at the conserved active site of a polymerase that cannot easily mutate around it: S282T, the only resistance substitution, costs the virus fitness, confers only 2- to 18-fold reduced susceptibility, and has never blocked a cure in the SOF/VEL/VOX salvage regimen (96–98% SVR12 even in DAA-experienced patients, with baseline resistance substitutions having no impact on outcome). The reason sofosbuvir does not cure more people is not its affinity; it is that most of the 50 million people with chronic HCV have never been diagnosed, and that the drug was launched at a price — US$84,000 for 12 weeks — that rationed it even in wealthy health systems. A compound that out-scores sofosbuvir here by 0.29 kcal/mol would still face the same access problem, and the generic sofosbuvir now available in Pakistan at a fraction of the launch price is the intervention that actually changes the cure rate. The docking order cannot explain why the drug cures 95% of treated patients and reaches fewer than 15% of infected ones. That is a limitation of the question, not of the execution.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since sofosbuvir was approved. Before approval, the question was "can a nucleotide inhibitor cure hepatitis C at all?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, beats the approved drug, and by what mechanism?" The docking benchmark is therefore a screen for successors, not for proof of concept, and its bar is higher: a new compound must beat sofosbuvir on the target and then survive the clinical test that sofosbuvir has already passed — a pan-genotypic cure with a resistance barrier no other DAA class has matched. This paper's null result is useful precisely as a null: it says the next screen must be a polymerase assay plus a replicon assay, not a bigger docking set of the same scaffold.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, every margin in §3.1 lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the ranking contradicts measured potency in the decisive pair — a 53 nM compound and a 690 nM compound dock 0.04 kcal/mol apart. Third, the binding sites are not annotated: any non-nucleoside inhibitor in the set binds ~35 Å from the pocket it was docked into, so its score is a property of the wrong site.

4.3 The site-mismatch problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The four ligands were chosen by pipeline rank, not by mechanism, and ChEMBL does not annotate which NS5B site each one binds. The honest handling is to report the active-site scores with the caveat attached, and to design the validation assay so the site question is answered by the experiment: a polymerase assay measures inhibition regardless of site, and a thumb-site competition assay (or a structure) would then place the mechanism. A compound that scores poorly at the active site but inhibits the enzyme is not a failure of the compound; it is a failure of the docking site, and the assay is what tells the two apart.

4.4 Mechanism

Sofosbuvir's active metabolite GS-461203 is incorporated by NS5B into the growing viral RNA chain and terminates it. Test for each link: (i) an NS5B polymerase assay (primer-extension, with GS-461203 as the comparator) measures IC50 directly against sofosbuvir's metabolite; (ii) a replicon assay in Huh-7 cells measures EC50 against sofosbuvir at matched concentration, with a cytotoxicity counter-screen; (iii) an S282T mutant replicon measures whether the analogue kept the resistance barrier that defines the class — loss of activity against S282T is the likeliest way a "better" NS5B binder becomes a worse drug, because S282T is the substitution the virus actually selects.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring analogue binds NS5B with an IC50 within 3-fold of its published ChEMBL value in a polymerase assay. Falsifier: IC50 > 3-fold worse than published.
  2. The same analogue inhibits HCV replication in a replicon assay at least as strongly as sofosbuvir at matched concentration. Falsifier: no inhibition below 1 µM.
  3. The analogue keeps activity against the S282T mutant replicon within 5-fold of wild-type. Falsifier: >10-fold loss against S282T.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): NS5B polymerase primer-extension assay for the two candidate analogues — CHEMBL6047888 (best best-pose, −8.94) and CHEMBL5815143 (most potent by assay, EC50 53 nM) — plus sofosbuvir's active metabolite GS-461203 as control; readout IC50, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): replicon assay in Huh-7 cells for the same set, plus an S282T mutant replicon for the best compound from stage 1. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin.
  2. The ranking cannot resolve a 13-fold potency difference (53 nM vs 690 nM dock 0.04 kcal/mol apart), so the set cannot test ranking at all.
  3. The binding sites of the four ChEMBL ligands are not annotated; any non-nucleoside inhibitor among them was docked into the wrong pocket.
  4. The docked sofosbuvir is the parent prodrug; the crystal holds the diphosphate metabolite and the active form in cells is the triphosphate GS-461203.
  5. One rigid structure was used (4WTG, genotype 2a JFH-1, with engineered mutations S15G/E86Q/E87Q/C223H/V321I and a β-hairpin deletion); the NS5B active site adapts to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  6. The pipeline's PDB picker found no structure for Q8JXU8 and skipped docking; the redock had to be supplied by hand, which shows the picker's accession mapping needs independent verification every run.
  7. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the >95% of treated patients who are cured from the majority of infected people who are never diagnosed or cannot afford the drug.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on liver disease were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Sofosbuvir, the nucleotide NS5B inhibitor at the centre of the hepatitis C cure, re-docks at −9.23 kcal/mol on its own 2.9 Å structure 4WTG with tight pose consistency and no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery. No analogue beats it: the best best-pose margin (CHEMBL6047888, +0.29 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina noise, and the method fails its own positive control in the decisive pair — the most potent analogue by assay (EC50 53 nM) and a 13-fold weaker one (EC50 690 nM) dock 0.04 kcal/mol apart. The docking verdict is a null result, and it is useful precisely as one: this series cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring on a single structure, the binding sites are not annotated so some ligands may have been docked into the wrong pocket, and the next screen must be a polymerase assay plus a replicon assay, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the access split: the same drug cures over 95% of the patients who receive it while most of the 50 million infected people never receive it at all. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a polymerase assay plus a replicon assay for the best-scoring analogues against sofosbuvir, including the S282T mutant — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the National Hepatitis Control Programme, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of NS5B inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise, and whether to prioritise generic sofosbuvir procurement and case-finding over any new-molecule programme. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week polymerase-plus-replicon screen proposed in §4.6 for the two best-scoring analogues against sofosbuvir, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target; and, in parallel, ask the hepatitis programme to note explicitly that the binding question is settled — sofosbuvir's barrier to resistance is the highest in its class — and that the remaining gap is diagnosis and price, not potency: every rupee spent searching for a molecule that beats sofosbuvir by 0.29 kcal/mol is a rupee not spent finding the undiagnosed. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the best analogue beats sofosbuvir's metabolite by >10-fold in the polymerase assay and keeps activity against S282T, drop the access-only framing and fund the analogue's development; if it loses >3-fold to its published value, drop this ligand set and redirect the same screen to the next NS5B chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable NS5B inhibitor from a useless one for a disease that kills about 242,000 people a year, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

The HBV Polymerase Benchmark Cannot Run: No Experimental Structure, No ChEMBL Target — and What the Organism-Level Data Say About Tenofovir

Chronic hepatitis B infects an estimated 254 million people and killed about 1.1 million in 2022, yet only 13% of those infected have been diagnosed and 3% treated — and Pakistan alone carries an estimated 12.6 million of the combined hepatitis B and C burden.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-22 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #95 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: hepatitis B virus; HBV polymerase; tenofovir; entecavir; molecular docking; ChEMBL; drug resistance; AlphaFold

Abstract

Chronic hepatitis B infects an estimated 254 million people and killed about 1.1 million in 2022, yet only 13% of those infected have been diagnosed and 3% treated — and Pakistan alone carries an estimated 12.6 million of the combined hepatitis B and C burden. Tenofovir is the first-line nucleos(t)ide analogue, but it rarely achieves a functional cure because covalently closed circular DNA persists in hepatocytes, and long-term therapy selects resistance mutations. We asked whether any measured anti-HBV compound binds the viral polymerase more strongly than tenofovir, using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem/RDKit → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate as the reference drug. The benchmark cannot run, and this paper documents exactly why: the pipeline's first run resolved the target to the wrong protein entirely — human RNA helicase DDX3X (UniProtKB O00571) — and its corrected run resolved the true target, HBV Protein P (UniProtKB P03156, genotype D, 832 amino acids), but ChEMBL holds no single-protein HBV polymerase target, and the pipeline's fallback then silently selected an unrelated human target (ABCC9, CHEMBL1971), whose 41 bioactivities were discarded. No experimental high-resolution structure of HBV polymerase exists — the only structural record is a 14.5 Å cryo-EM density of the encapsidated enzyme — so docking was skipped rather than run on a substitute. The usable evidence is organism-level: ChEMBL target CHEMBL613497 (Hepatitis B virus) holds 3,659 potency records with pChEMBL values across 2,513 molecules, topped by entecavir (IC50 0.06 nM in dHepaRG cells) and tenofovir (EC50 0.064 nM in HepG2.2.15 cells) — but those two numbers come from different assays and the tenofovir value sits far below the published micromolar range for the same cell line, so no head-to-head ranking can be built on them. The honest limit: no docking score exists in this paper, no analogue can be claimed to beat tenofovir, and the claim that the benchmark is impossible would be refuted by the deposition of a single high-resolution HBV polymerase structure with a bound inhibitor. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week validation of an AlphaFold-based HBV polymerase model against the published deep-mutational-scanning fitness map, followed by a HepG2.2.15 antiviral assay of the best-scoring tenofovir analogues.

1. Introduction

Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is one of the largest untreated epidemics in the world. The World Health Organization's Global Hepatitis Report 2024 estimates that 254 million people were living with chronic HBV infection in 2022, that about 1.2 million people became newly infected that year, and that roughly 1.1 million died from HBV-related cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma — more deaths than tuberculosis caused in 2023. Only 13% of the 254 million had been diagnosed and only 3% had received antiviral treatment. The burden is concentrated: five countries — China (83.7 million), India (35.3 million), Indonesia (18.9 million), Nigeria (15.7 million) and Pakistan (12.6 million) — account for 55% of the combined global HBV and HCV burden. In Pakistan, where this paper's author studies pharmacy, hepatitis B is therefore not a distant problem; it is the disease in the next ward.

The drugs that exist work, and they do not cure. Tenofovir (as the disoproxil fumarate or alafenamide prodrug) and entecavir are the first-line nucleos(t)ide analogues recommended by the WHO 2024 guidelines: once inside the hepatocyte they are phosphorylated to their active diphosphate/triphosphate forms, compete with the natural substrate deoxyadenosine triphosphate for incorporation by the HBV polymerase, and terminate the growing viral DNA chain because they lack a 3′-hydroxyl group. They suppress viral replication, reduce progression of liver disease and lower hepatocellular carcinoma incidence — but they rarely achieve a functional cure, because the covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) template persists in the hepatocyte nucleus, and because long-term therapy selects resistance mutations in the polymerase: rtL180M/rtM204(I/V) for lamivudine, entecavir and telbivudine, and rtA181V/rtN236T for adefovir and tenofovir. Resistance develops very slowly for entecavir and tenofovir, which is why they remain first-line — but "very slowly" is not "never", and a patient who has taken tenofovir for a decade with detectable virus has few options left.

The question this paper asks is the standard one for this series: among compounds with measured anti-HBV potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind the HBV polymerase more strongly than tenofovir itself? The answer turns out to be that the question cannot be asked in that form yet — and the reason is not a lack of compounds but a lack of infrastructure: no target record and no structure. That negative answer is the paper. A benchmark that cannot run is worth documenting precisely, because every future HBV polymerase docking study will hit the same two walls, and because the pipeline that produced this paper hit a third wall of its own — it resolved the target to the wrong protein twice before the audit caught it.

The classical medical canon knew the organ long before it knew the virus: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats diseases of the liver (amrad al-kabid), including jaundice and chronic liver disease, with dietary and supportive management — the Canon knows the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured anti-HBV potency bind the HBV polymerase (UniProtKB P03156) more strongly than tenofovir, as measured by standardised AutoDock Vina docking on an experimental structure? Falsifier: the deposition of a single high-resolution HBV polymerase structure with a bound inhibitor, on which tenofovir re-docks and a ligand out-scores it beyond Vina noise, refutes the claim that the benchmark cannot run. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the approved drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target — is the method this series uses, and it is unavailable here; association only beyond that. The absence of a structure is a fact about the field, not a failure of this run.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-22: the WHO Global Hepatitis Report 2024 and the WHO 2024 chronic hepatitis B guidelines; the 2022 global burden analysis (Cui et al., Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology 2026); the nucleos(t)ide analogue mechanism and resistance review (Menendez-Arias et al., Current Opinion in Virology 2014; PMID 24814823); the only structural record of the enzyme (Wang et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2014; PMID 25034253); the deep mutational scanning fitness map of HBV polymerase (Yu et al., Cell 2024; PMID 38723628); the full-length homology-model study (Patil et al., Journal of Biomolecular Structure and Dynamics 2024); the ChEMBL target search and the UniProtKB records for P03156 and O00571; and the Islamic-canon sweep (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025 — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text; see Limitations).

2.2 Target identification — resolved to the wrong protein twice, caught and corrected

The pipeline's first run, on the text query "Hepatitis B virus polymerase", resolved the target to human ATP-dependent RNA helicase DDX3X (UniProtKB O00571; ChEMBL CHEMBL5553, 57 bioactivities). DDX3X is a real HBV-relevant host protein — it interacts with viral proteins — but it is not the HBV polymerase, and its 26 ranked leads are DDX3X ligands, not HBV polymerase ligands. That run is discarded in full. The error class is the same as the TYK2 wrong-domain error in this series (Paper #92): the pipeline's target search prefers human entries, and a text query that names a virus returns a human protein that the virus touches.

The corrected run used the accession directly ("P03156") and resolved the true target: HBV Protein P, UniProtKB P03156, Hepatitis B virus genotype D subtype ayw (isolate France/Tiollais/1979), 832 amino acids — a multifunctional enzyme that converts the viral RNA genome into double-stranded DNA inside cytoplasmic capsids, with DNA-directed DNA polymerase activity, RNA-directed DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase) activity, and RNase H activity, and with protein priming at the epsilon loop of the pregenomic RNA. Verify the UniProt accession, the ChEMBL target name, the PDB title, the domain and the ligand identity before any score is quoted — that audit rule, written after Paper #92, is what caught both errors here.

2.3 The ChEMBL gap — no single-protein HBV polymerase target exists

With the correct accession, the pipeline's precise lookup (ChEMBL target by UniProt accession P03156) returned zero targets, verified live 2026-11-22. A ChEMBL target search for "Hepatitis B virus polymerase" returns no single-protein HBV polymerase target either; the closest record is CHEMBL613497, "Hepatitis B virus", an ORGANISM-level target holding whole-virus and cell-based assay data. The pipeline's fallback then silently selected an unrelated human target — ATP-binding cassette sub-family C member 9 (ABCC9, CHEMBL1971) — because the gene symbol of P03156 is "P" and the fallback matches any target name containing that letter. Its 41 bioactivities and 26 ranked leads are ABCC9 ligands and are discarded with the DDX3X set. The fallback is a defect, not a feature: a one-letter gene symbol must never select a target, and this paper is the report that proves it. The two discarded runs are preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-089-2026-11-22.json (the corrected run, including the discarded ABCC9 ligand set) and disclosed here, not deleted.

2.4 Organism-level ligand data — the only usable ChEMBL evidence

Because no enzyme-level target exists, the ligand evidence was pulled directly from the organism-level target CHEMBL613497 with a dedicated script (health-papers-agent/hbv_organism_activities.py, ChEMBL API, live 2026-11-22): all EC50/IC50 activities with a pChEMBL value, 3,659 records across 2,513 molecules, ranked by pChEMBL. Molecule names for the top entries were verified against the ChEMBL molecule records. These are whole-virus and cell-based potencies (HepG2.2.15, HepG2-hNTCP, dHepaRG cells), not enzyme inhibition — the distinction is stated in every row of the table, because a cell EC50 is not a polymerase Ki and cannot be compared with one.

2.5 Molecular docking — skipped, and why no substitute was used

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3 — except that it was not run. The pipeline's docking step returned no_pdb_found: there is no experimental high-resolution structure of HBV polymerase in the Protein Data Bank. The only structural record is the 14.5 Å cryo-EM density of the encapsidated reverse transcriptase inside authentic RNA-filled cores (Wang et al. 2014; EMDB EMD-2509), which resolves a donut-shaped density, not an atomic active site. Published docking on HBV polymerase therefore uses homology models extrapolated from HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (Das et al. 2001; Chong & Chu 2002) or, more recently, full-length models built with Phyre2/Modeller (Patil et al. 2024) and AlphaFold 2 predictions (Yu et al. 2024). This paper does not dock on any of those models: a homology model is a hypothesis about the active site, and a docking score on a hypothesised pocket is a model-on-model number that cannot be falsified against a crystal structure. The reference drug was verified computationally instead: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, PubChem CID 6398764, RDKit descriptors computed live (molecular weight 635.52 as the fumarate salt, logP 2.75, 3 hydrogen-bond donors, 16 acceptors, TPSA 260.04 Å², 15 rotatable bonds, 2 Lipinski violations — expected for a prodrug salt — PAINS-clean, maximum Tox21 kNN probability 0.196).

2.6 Honesty limits

No docking score exists in this paper. No analogue can be claimed to beat tenofovir. The organism-level potencies in §3.2 are cell-based EC50/IC50 values from different assays, cell lines and readouts, and are not comparable head to head. The tenofovir value in the table conflicts with the published range for the same cell line and is flagged, not smoothed over. No experimental data were generated in this study.

3. Results

3.1 The audit table — two wrong resolutions, one correct target, no structure

Two things are visible in this table and both matter. First, the two approved drugs sit at the top of the entire ChEMBL organism-level record — entecavir and tenofovir are the most potent measured anti-HBV compounds in the database, ahead of every investigational molecule in the top eight. Second, the table is not a ranking: entecavir's 0.06 nM was measured in dHepaRG cells by extracellular viral DNA, tenofovir's 0.064 nM in HepG2.2.15 cells by viral DNA, and the HBsAg readouts measure a different endpoint again. A 0.004 nM gap between two drugs in two different assays is not a difference; it is two different experiments. The most useful row is the seventh: CHEMBL4647919 holds EC50 0.25 nM against the rtL180M/T184L/M204V triple mutant — the entecavir-resistance genotype — in HepG2.A64 cells. That is the only row in the top eight that speaks to the resistance problem at all, and its molecule is unnamed in ChEMBL.

3.3 The tenofovir value conflicts with the published range — flagged, not hidden

The tenofovir record in §3.2 (EC50 0.064 nM, HepG2.2.15, activity 20613339, assay CHEMBL4606644) sits far below the published micromolar range for tenofovir in the same cell line — the comparative literature reports tenofovir EC50 values around 1 µM in HepG2.2.15 cells, roughly four orders of magnitude higher. One of the two must be wrong for this assay, or the record carries a unit or compound-form error that ChEMBL does not flag. This paper does not resolve the conflict; it reports the record exactly as ChEMBL holds it, with its activity and assay IDs so any reader can check it, and it does not build any claim on the number. The lesson generalises: a ChEMBL pChEMBL ranking across assays is a triage list, not a league table, and a single anomalous record at the top of the list is a reason to verify, not a reason to celebrate. The entecavir record (IC50 0.06 nM, dHepaRG, activity 18775795) is consistent with entecavir's known sub-nanomolar potency and is not flagged the same way.

3.4 The resistance landscape the benchmark would have to address

The resistance mutations are the reason a successor to tenofovir is wanted at all. Lamivudine resistance (rtM204V/I, usually with rtL180M) emerges in a large fraction of patients within years; entecavir resistance requires rtL180M + rtM204V/I plus an additional change (rtT184, rtS202 or rtM250) and develops very slowly; adefovir resistance (rtA181V, rtN236T) is uncommon; tenofovir resistance is the slowest of all, with rtA181V/rtN236T the documented pattern and no single mutation conferring high-level resistance. The deep mutational scanning fitness map (Yu et al. 2024) now gives this landscape a residue-level basis: nearly every single-codon variant of the polymerase was assayed for fitness, the map identifies the conserved prolines that stall ribosomes and enforce the polymerase's cis-preference for its own pregenomic RNA, and an AlphaFold 2 model of the polymerase was used to relate the fitness map to structure. That map — not a docking score — is the best available guide to which polymerase residues a new inhibitor must engage and which mutations it must survive.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since tenofovir was approved. Before approval, the question was "can the HBV polymerase be inhibited at all?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, beats tenofovir, and on what evidence?" The benchmark protocol this series uses — re-dock the approved drug on its own co-crystal structure, then dock the analogues on the same structure — cannot run for HBV polymerase, because the structure does not exist and the target record does not exist. The paper's contribution is therefore infrastructural: it names the two missing pieces, proves they are missing with live queries rather than asserting it, and shows what evidence does exist (organism-level potencies) and what it cannot do (rank drugs across assays). A field that cannot benchmark its own reference drug cannot tell whether its docking papers are measuring binding or measuring the homology model.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

There is no win in this paper, and that is the point. Three reasons the organism-level table must not be read as a ranking: first, the assays differ in cell line (dHepaRG vs HepG2.2.15 vs HepG2-hNTCP), readout (viral DNA vs HBsAg) and duration; second, the tenofovir value conflicts with the published range for the same cell line by four orders of magnitude; third, a cell EC50 conflates polymerase inhibition with cell entry, phosphorylation, efflux and cytotoxicity, so it cannot rank polymerase binders at all. The two discarded pipeline runs are a fourth reason for caution in general: a pipeline that silently substitutes a human helicase or a human ABC transporter for a viral polymerase will produce a complete, plausible-looking ranking that survives any check that does not verify the target accession.

4.3 Mechanism

Tenofovir diphosphate competes with dATP at the polymerase active site and terminates chain elongation; entecavir triphosphate competes with dGTP and additionally impairs protein priming. Test for each link: (i) a polymerase activity assay on a purified or reconstituted HBV polymerase measures inhibition directly against tenofovir as comparator — this assay does not exist in a standardised form today, which is itself part of the infrastructure gap; (ii) a HepG2.2.15 antiviral assay measures viral DNA reduction at matched concentrations, with a cytotoxicity counter-screen (CC50) so that a potent-looking compound is not simply a toxic one; (iii) a resistance panel — wild-type plus rtL180M/rtM204V, rtA181V/rtN236T and the entecavir-resistance triple mutant — measures whether the analogue keeps activity where the approved drugs lose it, because a molecule that only beats tenofovir on wild-type virus is not a successor.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. An AlphaFold 2 model of HBV Protein P, validated against the Yu et al. deep-mutational-scanning fitness map, predicts the resistance mutations (rtM204V/I, rtA181V, rtN236T) as residues whose mutation preserves fitness while reducing inhibitor binding. Falsifier: the model places those residues outside the predicted active site.
  2. The unnamed investigational compound CHEMBL4647919 inhibits the rtL180M/T184L/M204V triple mutant in HepG2.A64 cells at an EC50 within 3-fold of its recorded 0.25 nM. Falsifier: EC50 worse than 1 nM on re-test.
  3. Tenofovir's recorded EC50 of 0.064 nM in assay CHEMBL4606644 does not reproduce in a fresh HepG2.2.15 viral-DNA assay. Falsifier: the fresh assay returns a value within 3-fold of 0.064 nM, which would force a revision of the published micromolar range instead.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): build the AlphaFold 2 model of HBV Protein P (P03156) and validate it against the published deep-mutational-scanning fitness map — the model must place the known resistance residues in or adjacent to the active site and must reproduce the fitness cost of mutating the YMDD motif. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): HepG2.2.15 antiviral assay for tenofovir, entecavir and the two best-characterised investigational compounds from §3.2, with CC50 counter-screen, n=3, same readout (viral DNA by qPCR) and same duration for all four — the first head-to-head comparison in this paper's evidence base. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): resistance-panel assay (wild-type plus the three mutant genotypes in §4.3) for the best compound from stage 2; if none beats tenofovir on the panel, publish the negative result with the organism-level data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking was run; no docking score exists in this paper. The benchmark is impossible on current infrastructure, and that is the finding, not an omission to be filled by a substitute structure.
  2. The organism-level potencies are cell-based EC50/IC50 values from different assays, cell lines and readouts; they cannot rank drugs head to head.
  3. The tenofovir EC50 of 0.064 nM conflicts with the published micromolar range for the same cell line by roughly four orders of magnitude; the conflict is unresolved.
  4. Two pipeline runs resolved the target to the wrong protein (DDX3X, then ABCC9 via a one-letter gene-symbol fallback); the audit caught both, but the episode shows the pipeline's target resolution needs independent verification every run — and the fallback must be fixed so a one-letter gene symbol can never select a target.
  5. The homology-model literature (Das et al. 2001; Chong & Chu 2002; Patil et al. 2024) and the AlphaFold model (Yu et al. 2024) were read as published summaries; no model was built or validated in this study.
  6. No data on the clinical confounder: only 13% of people with chronic HBV have been diagnosed and 3% treated, so the binding question is secondary to the access question for most patients.
  7. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on liver disease were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Tenofovir remains the reference drug for chronic hepatitis B, and this paper cannot say whether any compound beats it on the polymerase — because the benchmark cannot run. ChEMBL holds no single-protein HBV polymerase target, no experimental high-resolution structure of the enzyme exists, and the pipeline that attempted the benchmark resolved the target to the wrong protein twice (human DDX3X, then human ABCC9) before the audit caught it. What does exist is organism-level evidence: 3,659 potency records across 2,513 molecules, topped by entecavir and tenofovir themselves, with one investigational compound active at 0.25 nM against the entecavir-resistance triple mutant — but those numbers come from different assays and the tenofovir record conflicts with the published range, so no ranking can be built on them. The next step is not another docking run on a homology model; it is the cheap, decisive infrastructure work — validate an AlphaFold model of HBV Protein P against the deep-mutational-scanning fitness map, then run a single head-to-head HepG2.2.15 assay of tenofovir, entecavir and the best investigational compounds on the same readout. Until that exists, any HBV polymerase docking score should be read as a score against a hypothesis, not against the enzyme.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Higher Education Commission research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund HBV polymerase structure-and-assay infrastructure — an AlphaFold-model validation plus a standardised HepG2.2.15 assay — instead of funding another purely computational screen of a target with no structure. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week validation proposed in §4.5 for the HBV polymerase, and, in parallel, ask DRAP's registration reviewers to note that tenofovir's ChEMBL record contains a four-orders-of-magnitude discrepancy for the same cell line — a single anomalous potency record must not anchor a procurement or formulary decision without a fresh assay. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if a high-resolution HBV polymerase structure is deposited, drop the infrastructure-first recommendation and fund the docking benchmark on that structure immediately; if the fresh assay reproduces tenofovir at 0.064 nM, revise the published potency range instead of discarding the record. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable HBV drug from a useless one for a disease that kills about 1.1 million people a year — 12.6 million of them in Pakistan — running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score, or on an unverified database record, would violate it. The evidence here is thin — no docking, no enzyme assay — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-21 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #92 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: TYK2; deucravacitinib; JH2 pseudokinase; psoriasis; molecular docking; ChEMBL; allosteric inhibitor; Janus kinase

Abstract

Psoriasis affects an estimated 2–3% of the world's population, and its most effective oral drug, deucravacitinib, is the first medicine that works by binding the pseudokinase (JH2) domain of tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2) rather than the conserved ATP site — yet it clears the skin completely in only about one in seven patients, and a next-generation rival has just beaten it head to head. We asked whether any measured TYK2 ligand binds the JH2 pocket more strongly than deucravacitinib itself. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P29597 → ChEMBL CHEMBL3553 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked deucravacitinib and four ChEMBL ligands with measured potency on the 2.35 Å deucravacitinib-bound TYK2 JH2 structure 6NZP, centred exactly on the co-crystallised deucravacitinib (centre audit via dock._ligand_center), and confirmed the result on the 2.73 Å JH2 structure 6NZH. Deucravacitinib re-docked at −10.19 kcal/mol on its own structure and −10.38 kcal/mol on 6NZH. Three analogues out-scored it on best pose on 6NZP — CHEMBL5419627 at −10.62, CHEMBL4789639 at −10.50 and CHEMBL4435170 at −10.46 — but every margin (0.27–0.43 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the ranking contradicts measured potency: the most potent ligand by assay (CHEMBL5424497, Kd 0.019 nM) docks worst on both structures, while the least potent (CHEMBL5419627, Kd 0.028 nM) docks best on 6NZP. The ranking is also not stable to structure choice: on 6NZH deucravacitinib is best and CHEMBL4435170 is worst, a 1.84 kcal/mol swing for the same compound. Docking therefore cannot rank this series, and no analogue can be claimed to beat deucravacitinib on this evidence. The honest limit: the pipeline first docked the wrong domain (the JH1 ATP site, 3LXP) and that run is discarded; all five potencies span only 0.019–0.028 nM, so the set cannot test ranking at all; and no laboratory data exist for any compound in this study. The claim that any analogue beats deucravacitinib would be refuted if a TYK2 JH2 binding assay shows a Kd worse than the analogue's published value. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week JH2 binding-plus-cell assay of the best-scoring analogue against deucravacitinib.

1. Introduction

Psoriasis affects an estimated 2–3% of the world's population — tens of millions of people with a visible, stigmatising, lifelong disease — and moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis is a systemic inflammatory disease, not a skin problem: it carries increased risks of psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular disease and depression. In Pakistan, where dermatology care is concentrated in cities and biologic therapy is largely unaffordable, an effective oral pill matters more than an effective injection, because a pill is the treatment a patient can actually take.

Deucravacitinib (Sotyktu; BMS-986165, Bristol Myers Squibb) is the first drug that binds the JH2 pseudokinase domain of TYK2. TYK2 is one of the four Janus kinase (JAK) family members (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2) and signals for interleukin-12, interleukin-23 and type I interferons — the cytokines that drive psoriasis. Every JAK inhibitor approved before September 2022 engages the JH1 catalytic ATP-binding domain; deucravacitinib instead binds the JH2 regulatory pseudokinase domain, which lacks catalytic activity (its DFG-like motif is degenerate and cannot coordinate Mg²⁺-ATP productively) but allosterically regulates JH1, locking TYK2 in an inactive conformation without blocking the ATP site. The drug is also the first de novo deuterated drug ever approved by the FDA (a trideuteriomethyl group, which slows its metabolism). The FDA approved it on 9 September 2022 for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in adults, on the POETYK PSO-1 and PSO-2 trials: in PSO-1, PASI 75 at week 16 was achieved by 58.4% of patients on deucravacitinib versus 12.7% on placebo and 35.1% on apremilast, and a static Physician's Global Assessment of 0/1 by 53.6% versus 7.2% and 32.1%; in PSO-2 the figures were 53.0% versus 9.4% and 39.8%. In the long-term extension, PASI 75 was 72.1% at year 1 and 67.3% at year 5. The drug was subsequently approved for psoriatic arthritis (ACR20 54.2% versus 34.1% and 39.4% on placebo in the POETYK PsA-1 and PsA-2 trials). It is, by any measure, a good drug — and it clears the skin completely (PASI 100) in only about one in seven patients.

The pipeline behind it is now moving, and it has already overtaken it. Zasocitinib (TAK-279, Takeda), a next-generation TYK2 inhibitor, beat deucravacitinib head to head in the phase 3 LATITUDE Atlas trial reported at EADV 2026: complete skin clearance (PASI 100) at week 16 in 36.5% of patients on zasocitinib versus 13.9% on deucravacitinib, PASI 90 in 62.5% versus 34.0%, and sPGA 0 in 43.2% versus 18.5%. The question this paper asks is narrower and cheaper than a trial: among compounds with measured TYK2 potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind the JH2 pocket more strongly than deucravacitinib itself — and can docking even tell them apart when they are all sub-nanomolar?

The classical medical canon discussed diseases of the skin centuries before TYK2 was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats diseases of the skin (amrad al-jild), including scaling and itching conditions, with topical and supportive management — the Canon knows the organ and the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured TYK2 potency bind the JH2 pocket of the deucravacitinib-bound structure (PDB 6NZP) at scores beyond re-docked deucravacitinib, and would that binding translate into stronger TYK2 inhibition? Falsifier: a TYK2 JH2 binding assay showing a Kd worse than the analogue's published value, or a cell assay (IL-23-stimulated STAT3 phosphorylation) showing no advantage over deucravacitinib, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the approved drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target, confirmed on a second JH2 structure — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-21: the deucravacitinib discovery paper (Wrobleski et al., J Med Chem 2019), the POETYK PSO-1 trial (Armstrong et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2023; PMID 35820547), the POETYK PSO-2 and long-term extension data, the LATITUDE Atlas head-to-head results (Takeda, EADV 2026), the FDA approval announcement (9 September 2022), the TYK2 selective-inhibitor review (Springer, 2026), the RCSB records for PDB 6NZP, 6NZH and 3LXP, and the WHO Global report on psoriasis (2016). The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Target identification — the wrong domain, caught and corrected

The pipeline resolved the target correctly (UniProtKB P29597, human TYK2; ChEMBL CHEMBL3553, 44 bioactivities) and then docked the wrong domain. Its PDB picker chose 3LXP, the TYK2 JH1 ATP-site structure (chains 888–1182), and returned scores (−8.37 to −9.26 kcal/mol) for deucravacitinib binding a pocket it never binds. That run is discarded in full. This is the exact error the TYK2 centre audit in this series warns about: deucravacitinib binds the JH2 pseudokinase domain (6NZH/6NZP, chains 575–869), NOT the JH1 ATP site (3LXP, chains 888–1182). The correction was to dock on the JH2 structures only. The lesson is now the fourth in this series (after HIF-2α/FIH-1, HIF-2α/PHD2 and c-MET/HGF): verify the PDB title and the domain before any score is quoted.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: human TYK2, UniProtKB P29597; ChEMBL target CHEMBL3553 (verified live 2026-11-21). Primary structure: PDB 6NZP, the TYK2 JH2 domain in complex with compound-11 — which is deucravacitinib itself (ligand LB7) — 2.35 Å X-ray resolution (Wrobleski et al., J Med Chem 2019). Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised LB7, [14.04, −3.48, 28.63], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center; box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for deucravacitinib and all four analogues. Deucravacitinib is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover strong binding for a sub-nanomolar JH2 ligand would be broken.

Confirmation on a second JH2 structure. PDB 6NZH, the TYK2 JH2 domain in complex with compound_40 (ligand L9A), 2.73 Å, was docked with the same protocol (centre [13.31, −2.78, 29.74], the L9A centroid via dock._ligand_center). Deucravacitinib's score on 6NZH is a cross-dock into the compound_40 pocket. Both structures are reported; neither is hidden.

The comparison set is five compounds from the corrected P29597 ChEMBL run (26 ranked leads from 44 bioactivities): deucravacitinib itself and the four highest-ranked ligands with measured potency. Their measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements: CHEMBL4435170 Ki 0.02 nM (pChEMBL 10.70); CHEMBL5419627 Kd 0.028 nM (pChEMBL 10.55); CHEMBL4789639 Ki 0.02 nM (pChEMBL 10.70); CHEMBL5424497 Kd 0.019 nM (pChEMBL 10.72). Note the endpoint mix (Ki vs Kd) and the near-identical values: the whole set spans 0.019–0.028 nM, a 1.5-fold range. One further caveat: the docked deucravacitinib is the non-deuterated SMILES as returned by PubChem (formula C20H22N8O3, MW 422.45); the approved drug carries a trideuteriomethyl group (MW ~425.5). The heavy-atom structure is identical and docking is unaffected, but the distinction is stated, not smoothed over.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to deucravacitinib and the four ligands. All five are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for deucravacitinib (non-deuterated form): molecular weight 422.45, logP 1.73, 3 hydrogen-bond donors, 8 acceptors, TPSA 135.95 Å², 7 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for deucravacitinib: maximum predicted probability 0.256 (SR-ARE), with a maximum neighbour similarity of only 0.28 — a weak read-across, not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development. The four ligands: CHEMBL4435170 (MW 425.47, logP 1.73, HBD 3, HBA 8, TPSA 135.95 Å², 7 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max Tox21 probability 0.360, SR-MMP), CHEMBL5419627 (MW 437.46, logP 1.62, HBD 3, HBA 8, TPSA 139.19 Å², 6 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.349, NR-AhR), CHEMBL4789639 (MW 439.47, logP 3.14, HBD 3, HBA 7, TPSA 118.13 Å², 7 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.424, SR-ARE) and CHEMBL5424497 (MW 380.41, logP 1.92, HBD 4, HBA 6, TPSA 135.02 Å², 5 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.462, NR-AhR). The whole set is drug-like by these counts — which is expected, because all five are variations on optimised JH2-binder scaffolds, and which is itself a warning that these descriptor counts cannot rank this class.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published ChEMBL potencies. The five measured potency values in this paper are published ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements, and they span only 0.019–0.028 nM. The docked deucravacitinib is the non-deuterated SMILES; the approved drug is deuterated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (6NZP, 2.35 Å — the drug's own structure)

Compound Measured TYK2 potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 6NZP (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose Margin vs deucravacitinib
Deucravacitinib (reference) — (approved drug) −10.19 −10.19, −9.25, −9.02 −9.25 —
CHEMBL4435170 Ki 0.02 nM −10.46 −10.46, −9.55, −9.10 −9.55 +0.27
CHEMBL5419627 Kd 0.028 nM −10.62 −10.62, −10.40, −9.44 −10.40 +0.43
CHEMBL4789639 Ki 0.02 nM −10.50 −10.50, −10.01, −9.01 −10.01 +0.31
CHEMBL5424497 Kd 0.019 nM −9.23 −9.23, −9.17, −9.14 −9.17 −0.96

Deucravacitinib re-docks at −10.19 kcal/mol on its own structure. That is a strong self-dock control: the method recovers strong binding for a sub-nanomolar JH2 ligand in the pocket it was crystallised in, so the protocol is not broken. Three analogues out-score it on best pose, but every margin (0.27, 0.31 and 0.43 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The fourth analogue, CHEMBL5424497, scores 0.96 kcal/mol worse than deucravacitinib — also inside noise, but in the other direction. On best pose, the whole series spans 1.39 kcal/mol, from −10.62 to −9.23: the five compounds are barely distinguishable by this method.

On median pose the order changes, and that is itself the finding. On 6NZP the medians run CHEMBL5419627 (−10.40), CHEMBL4789639 (−10.01), CHEMBL4435170 (−9.55), deucravacitinib (−9.25), CHEMBL5424497 (−9.17) — a 1.23 kcal/mol spread, with CHEMBL5419627 leading deucravacitinib by 1.15 kcal/mol on medians while leading by only 0.43 on best pose. Two pose statistics, two different leaders, one conclusion: the ranking is not stable to the choice of statistic.

The decisive check is the comparison with measured potency. The most potent ligand by assay, CHEMBL5424497 (Kd 0.019 nM), docks worst on both structures (−9.23 on 6NZP, −9.09 on 6NZH). The least potent, CHEMBL5419627 (Kd 0.028 nM), docks best on 6NZP (−10.62). A scoring function that ranks the weakest binder first and the strongest binder last, inside one target family on the reference drug's own structure, cannot rank this family at all. The honest reading of the table is therefore a null result: no analogue beats deucravacitinib beyond noise, and the method itself fails its own positive control.

3.2 Confirmation on a second JH2 structure (6NZH, 2.73 Å)

Compound Measured TYK2 potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 6NZH (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose
Deucravacitinib (reference) — (approved drug) −10.38 −10.38, −9.14, −8.57 −9.14
CHEMBL4435170 Ki 0.02 nM −8.62 −8.62, −8.41, −8.25 −8.41
CHEMBL5419627 Kd 0.028 nM −9.29 −9.29, −8.61, −8.40 −8.61
CHEMBL4789639 Ki 0.02 nM −10.05 −10.05, −9.26, −8.54 −9.26
CHEMBL5424497 Kd 0.019 nM −9.09 −9.09, −8.79, −8.70 −8.79

On the compound_40 pocket, deucravacitinib is best (−10.38) and CHEMBL4435170 is worst (−8.62) — the reverse of the 6NZP order for that compound, a 1.84 kcal/mol swing for the same molecule between two structures of the same domain. CHEMBL5419627 swings by 1.33 kcal/mol. Only deucravacitinib itself (−10.38 vs −10.19) and CHEMBL5424497 (−9.09 vs −9.23) are stable across the two structures. The ranking is therefore not a property of the molecules; it is a property of the structure chosen. That is the paper's most useful finding, and it is also the reason the 3LXP run had to be discarded rather than reported: a wrong-domain docking would have produced a third, equally confident, equally meaningless ranking.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of deucravacitinib or these four ligands on 6NZP or 6NZH was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (ligands vs re-docked reference drug on the same structures, same protocol). The crystal structures themselves (6NZP for deucravacitinib, 6NZH for compound_40) are the published ground truth for the binding mode; this paper tests whether a rigid scoring function can rank compounds inside that mode. The structural literature does give the paper its most useful context: deep mutational scanning has mapped the JH2 pocket residues that govern inhibitor binding and resistance, which is why a docking ranking that ignores those residues is a weak predictor of the clinic.

3.4 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Deucravacitinib's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug's 58.4% PASI 75 response is not a binding problem — it binds at sub-nanomolar affinity — it is a biology problem: psoriasis is driven by IL-23, IL-12 and type I interferons through TYK2, but also by TNF, IL-17 and other pathways TYK2 inhibition does not touch, and the patients who do not respond are the ones whose disease is driven elsewhere. The head-to-head proof is zasocitinib: the same target, the same domain, a 36.5% complete-clearance rate against deucravacitinib's 13.9% — a difference no docking score in this paper predicts, because both drugs bind the same pocket at sub-nanomolar affinity and the difference is in pharmacokinetics, exposure and the exact JH2 conformation stabilised, none of which Vina scores. A compound that out-scores deucravacitinib here by 0.43 kcal/mol would still face the same biology, and the zasocitinib result is a standing warning that JH2 affinity does not predict clinical superiority. The docking order cannot explain why deucravacitinib works in 58% of patients and not the other 42%, and it cannot predict which patient will respond. That is a limitation of the question, not of the execution.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since deucravacitinib was approved. Before approval, the question was "can the JH2 pseudokinase be drugged at all?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, beats the approved drug, and by what mechanism?" The docking benchmark is therefore a screen for successors, not for proof of concept, and its bar is higher: a new compound must beat deucravacitinib on the target and then survive the clinical test that zasocitinib has already passed and deucravacitinib has already failed head to head. This paper's null result is useful precisely as a null: it says the next screen must be a binding assay plus a cell assay, not a bigger docking set of the same scaffold.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, every margin in §3.1 lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise unless stated otherwise. Second, the ranking contradicts measured potency — the most potent ligand docks worst on both structures. Third, the ranking is not stable to structure choice: the same compound swings by 1.84 kcal/mol between two JH2 structures. Fourth, all five potencies span only 0.019–0.028 nM, so there is no pharmacological difference for docking to explain.

4.3 The domain lesson

The discarded 3LXP run deserves a paragraph of its own, because it is the failure mode this series must keep auditing for. The pipeline resolved the target correctly and then docked the wrong domain — the JH1 ATP site instead of the JH2 pseudokinase domain — and produced a complete, plausible-looking ranking (−8.37 to −9.26 kcal/mol) that would have survived any check that did not verify the PDB title. The correction is mechanical, not judgmental: verify the UniProt accession, the ChEMBL target name, the PDB title, the domain and the ligand identity before any score is quoted, and discard and disclose the runs that fail the audit. This paper does that; the discarded run is preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-100-2026-11-21.json and disclosed in §2.2, not deleted.

4.4 Mechanism

Deucravacitinib binds the JH2 pseudokinase domain and locks the JH2–JH1 pair in an inactive conformation, preventing TYK2 activation and the downstream phosphorylation of STAT proteins in response to IL-12, IL-23 and type I interferons. Test for each link: (i) a TYK2 JH2 binding assay (TR-FRET or thermal shift) measures Kd directly against deucravacitinib as comparator; (ii) an IL-23-stimulated STAT3 phosphorylation assay in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells measures functional inhibition; (iii) a JAK1/JAK2/JAK3 counter-screen measures whether the analogue kept the selectivity that defines the class — loss of JAK selectivity is the likeliest way a "better" TYK2 binder becomes a worse drug, because JAK1/2 inhibition drives the cytopenias and infections that the JH2 mechanism was designed to avoid.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring analogue binds the TYK2 JH2 domain with a Kd within 3-fold of its published ChEMBL value in a TR-FRET binding assay. Falsifier: Kd > 3-fold worse than published.
  2. The same analogue inhibits IL-23-stimulated STAT3 phosphorylation in human PBMCs at least as strongly as deucravacitinib at matched concentration. Falsifier: no inhibition below 1 µM.
  3. The analogue keeps ≥100-fold selectivity over JAK1, JAK2 and JAK3. Falsifier: JAK inhibition within 10-fold of the TYK2 value.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): TYK2 JH2 TR-FRET binding assay for the two candidate analogues — CHEMBL5419627 (best best-pose on 6NZP, −10.62) and CHEMBL4789639 (best on medians among the analogues, −10.01) — plus deucravacitinib control; readout Kd, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): IL-23-stimulated pSTAT3 assay in human PBMCs plus a JAK1/2/3 counter-screen for the same set. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin.
  2. All five docked compounds are near-equipotent by assay (0.019–0.028 nM), so the set cannot test ranking at all.
  3. The ranking is not stable to structure choice: the same compound swings by up to 1.84 kcal/mol between two JH2 structures.
  4. The docked deucravacitinib is the non-deuterated SMILES; the approved drug is deuterated (the heavy-atom structure is identical).
  5. Two rigid structures were used; the JH2 pocket adapts to different chemotypes, so two structures still under-sample the binding landscape.
  6. The pipeline docked the wrong domain (JH1, 3LXP) before the correction; the audit caught it, but the episode shows the pipeline's structure picks need independent verification every run.
  7. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the 58% of patients who respond to deucravacitinib from the 42% who do not, and cannot predict the zasocitinib head-to-head result.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on skin disease were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Deucravacitinib, the first allosteric TYK2 JH2 inhibitor, re-docks at −10.19 kcal/mol on its own 2.35 Å structure 6NZP and −10.38 kcal/mol on the 2.73 Å JH2 structure 6NZH, with tight pose consistency and no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery. No analogue beats it: the best best-pose margin (CHEMBL5419627, +0.43 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina noise, the most consistent analogue on medians leads by 1.15 kcal/mol but is the least potent compound by measured assay, and the method fails its own positive control — the most potent ligand by measured Kd docks worst on both structures. The docking verdict is a null result, and it is useful precisely as one: this near-equipotent series cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring, the ranking is not stable to structure choice, and the next screen must be a JH2 binding assay plus a pSTAT3 cell assay, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same drug clears the skin completely in 13.9% of patients while its successor clears it in 36.5%, and no binding score explains that. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a JH2 binding assay plus an IL-23 pSTAT3 assay for the best-scoring analogue against deucravacitinib — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Higher Education Commission research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of TYK2 JH2 inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise, and whether to prepare DRAP's assessment pathway for a drug class whose successor has already beaten the approved drug head to head. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week JH2 binding-plus-pSTAT3 screen proposed in §4.6 for the two best-scoring analogues against deucravacitinib, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target; and, in parallel, ask DRAP's registration reviewers to note the LATITUDE Atlas head-to-head result explicitly in any future TYK2 dossier — approval of deucravacitinib is not evidence that it is the best drug in its class, and a successor that clears the skin in 36.5% of patients changes the cost-effectiveness question for a health system that pays out of pocket. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the best analogue loses >3-fold to its published Kd in the binding assay or fails the pSTAT3 assay, drop this ligand set and redirect the same screen to the next TYK2 chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable TYK2 inhibitor from a useless one for a disease that affects 2–3% of the world's population, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

TAM16 Re-Docks at −9.82 kcal/mol on the Pks13 Thioesterase Domain — but the Pipeline First Docked the Wrong Domain, Every Compound Carries a PAINS Alert, and the Most Potent Analogue Docks Worst

Tuberculosis caused 10.8 million cases and 1.25 million deaths worldwide in 2023, and Pakistan carries 6.3% of that burden — about 670,000 cases in 2024, the fifth-highest national total — yet no approved drug targets polyketide synthase 13 (Pks13), the enzyme that performs the final step of mycolic-acid synthesis for…
