Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-21 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #93 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Pks13; TAM16; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; mycolic acid; thioesterase; molecular docking; ChEMBL; tuberculosis

Abstract

Tuberculosis caused 10.8 million cases and 1.25 million deaths worldwide in 2023, and Pakistan carries 6.3% of that burden — about 670,000 cases in 2024, the fifth-highest national total — yet no approved drug targets polyketide synthase 13 (Pks13), the enzyme that performs the final step of mycolic-acid synthesis for the mycobacterial cell wall. The best-known Pks13 inhibitor, the benzofuran TAM16, matched isoniazid in mouse models of tuberculosis in 2017 and then stalled, in part over cardiotoxicity concerns. We asked whether any measured Pks13 ligand binds the thioesterase domain more strongly than TAM16 itself. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB I6X8D2 → ChEMBL CHEMBL4105939 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked TAM16 and four ChEMBL analogues with measured potency on the 1.98 Å Pks13 thioesterase structure 5V3Y, centred exactly on the co-crystallised TAM16 (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). TAM16 re-docked at −9.82 kcal/mol. No analogue beats it beyond noise: the best, CHEMBL5070158 at −9.68, trails by 0.14 kcal/mol, and the most potent by assay (CHEMBL5074531, IC50 180 nM) docks worst at −8.69. The same molecule entered twice (TAM16 as query and as ChEMBL4443524) scores 0.25 kcal/mol apart — the representation noise of the method — which is larger than any analogue margin in the table. Every compound in the set, including TAM16 itself, carries a PAINS alert for its aminomethyl-phenol Mannich-base motif, which the validation design must control for. The honest limit: the pipeline first docked the wrong domain (the ACP domain, 6C4Q) and that run is discarded; all five potencies span only 180–330 nM; and no laboratory data exist for any compound in this study. The claim that any analogue beats TAM16 would be refuted if a Pks13 thioesterase assay shows an IC50 worse than TAM16's 190 nM. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week enzyme-plus-MIC test of the best-scoring analogue against TAM16, with PAINS controls.

1. Introduction

In 2023 there were an estimated 10.8 million people who fell ill with tuberculosis and 1.25 million TB deaths worldwide, and TB has reclaimed its position as the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent. In 2024 the figures were 10.7 million cases and 1.23 million deaths. Pakistan is fifth among the 30 high-burden countries, with an estimated 669,000–670,000 people developing TB in 2024 (6.3% of the global burden), an incidence rate of 266 per 100,000, about 51,000 deaths, and roughly 172,000 "missing" cases that were never diagnosed or notified. Drug-resistant TB remains a serious concern: globally about 390,000 people developed drug-resistant TB in 2024 and less than half of them started treatment. The first-line drugs are decades old, resistance to them is widespread, and the newest TB drugs already face reports of resistance. A new drug with a novel mechanism is not a luxury for Pakistan; it is the difference between a curable disease and an untreatable one.

Mycolic acids are the reason Mycobacterium tuberculosis is so hard to kill. They are very long-chain (C60–C90) α-branched, β-hydroxylated fatty acids that form the waxy outer layer of the mycobacterial cell wall, and they are critical for viability and virulence. Pks13 performs the final assembly step of mycolic-acid synthesis — the Claisen-type condensation of a C26 α-alkyl branch and a C40–C60 meromycolate precursor. It is a multidomain protein (two acyl-carrier-protein domains, a β-ketoacyl-synthase, an acyltransferase and a C-terminal thioesterase domain) that has been validated as essential for mycobacterial survival by both chemical and genetic methods. No approved drug targets it. That is the gap this paper attacks: a target with no approved drug, a validated lead, and a country that needs both.

TAM16 is that lead. It is a benzofuran-class inhibitor of the Pks13 thioesterase domain, developed by structure-guided methods (Aggarwal et al., Cell 2017). Its predecessor TAM1 inhibits the esterase activity of Pks13-TE with an IC50 of 0.26 ± 0.03 µM. TAM16 showed highly potent bactericidal activity against drug-susceptible and drug-resistant clinical isolates of M. tuberculosis, and in multiple mouse models of TB infection it showed in vivo efficacy equal to the first-line drug isoniazid, both as monotherapy and in combination with rifampicin, with excellent pharmacological and safety profiles and a frequency of resistance about 100-fold lower than isoniazid. The benzofuran series then failed to progress to preclinical development, in part over cardiotoxicity concerns, and a newer oxadiazole series (Dundee, 2023) was developed with a distinct binding mode and lead compounds with antitubercular potencies below 1 µM. The question this paper asks is narrower and cheaper than a trial: among compounds with measured Pks13 potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind the thioesterase domain more strongly than TAM16 itself — and can docking even tell them apart?

The classical medical canon discussed consumption centuries before the bacillus was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats consumption (al-sill, phthisis) as a wasting disease of the lungs, with supportive and dietary management — the Canon knows the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured Pks13 potency bind the thioesterase domain of the TAM16-bound structure (PDB 5V3Y) at scores beyond re-docked TAM16, and would that binding translate into stronger Pks13 inhibition? Falsifier: a Pks13 thioesterase enzyme assay showing an IC50 worse than TAM16's 190 nM, or a whole-cell MIC assay showing no advantage over TAM16, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the lead compound re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-21: the TAM16 paper (Aggarwal et al., Cell 2017), the Dundee oxadiazole series (Green et al., J Med Chem 2023), the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 (2023 burden) and 2025 (2024 burden, Pakistan figures), the RCSB records for PDB 5V3Y, 5V3W, 5V3X and 6C4Q, and the ChEMBL target record. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Target identification — the wrong domain, caught and corrected

The pipeline resolved the target correctly (UniProtKB I6X8D2, M. tuberculosis Pks13, strain H37Rv; ChEMBL CHEMBL4105939, 56 bioactivities) and then docked the wrong domain. Its PDB picker chose 6C4Q — the Pks13 acyl-carrier-protein domain (residues 1–100), 1.16 Å, the highest-resolution Pks13 structure — and returned scores (−8.41 to −8.90 kcal/mol) for TAM16 binding a domain it never binds. That run is discarded in full. This is the same failure class as the TYK2 JH1/JH2 error earlier today: highest resolution is not the right domain. The correction was to dock on the thioesterase domain only. The lesson is now the fifth in this series: verify the PDB title, the domain and the fragment before any score is quoted.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: M. tuberculosis Pks13, UniProtKB I6X8D2 (gene Rv3800c); ChEMBL target CHEMBL4105939 (verified live 2026-11-21). Structure: PDB 5V3Y, the Mtb Pks13 thioesterase domain in complex with TAM16 (ligand 5V8), 1.98 Å X-ray resolution (Aggarwal et al., Cell 2017). Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised 5V8, [4.80, 26.29, 7.48], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center; box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for TAM16 and all four analogues. TAM16 is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover strong binding for a 190 nM inhibitor would be broken. The catalytic triad (Ser1533, Asp1560, His1699) and the oxyanion hole (Leu1534, Ala1477) sit at the interface of the lid and core domains, with a deep (~30 Å) hydrophobic groove extending from the active site; the grid box covers that site.

The comparison set is five compounds from the corrected I6X8D2 ChEMBL run (26 ranked leads from 56 bioactivities): TAM16 itself and the four highest-ranked analogues with measured potency. Their measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements: TAM16 IC50 190 nM (pChEMBL 6.72, as ChEMBL4443524); CHEMBL5070158 IC50 330 nM (pChEMBL 6.48); CHEMBL5074531 IC50 180 nM (pChEMBL 6.75); CHEMBL5270146 IC50 290 nM (pChEMBL 6.54). Note that ChEMBL4443524 is TAM16 itself under its ChEMBL identifier — same formula C22H24N2O4, same molecular weight 380.44, same IC50 190 nM — included because the pipeline ranks it as a separate lead. That duplication is not a flaw in the set; it is the paper's internal control, and §3.1 says so.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to TAM16 and the four analogues. All five carry a PAINS alert — the aminomethyl-phenol Mannich-base motif shared by the whole benzofuran series. This is not hidden; it is the paper's most important safety finding, and it changes the validation design (§4.4): any analogue that "wins" here must first prove it is not a redox cycler, an aggregator or a covalent trap. The Dundee oxadiazole series exists precisely because the benzofuran series carried developability concerns, including cardiotoxicity.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for TAM16: molecular weight 380.44, logP 3.86, 3 hydrogen-bond donors, 5 acceptors, TPSA 85.94 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for TAM16: maximum predicted probability 0.426 (NR-ER), with a maximum neighbour similarity of only 0.28 — a weak read-across, not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development. The analogues: CHEMBL5070158 (MW 366.42, logP 3.47, HBD 3, HBA 5, TPSA 85.94 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max Tox21 probability 0.603, NR-ER), CHEMBL5074531 (MW 352.39, logP 3.08, HBD 3, HBA 5, TPSA 85.94 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.522, SR-MMP) and CHEMBL5270146 (MW 364.45, logP 4.15, HBD 2, HBA 4, TPSA 65.71 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.240, SR-ARE). The whole set is drug-like by these counts — which is expected, because all five are variations on one optimised scaffold, and which is itself a warning that these descriptor counts cannot rank this class, least of all a class that carries a PAINS alert.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published ChEMBL potencies. Every compound in the set carries a PAINS alert, so every score here is conditional on the PAINS controls in §4.4. The five measured potency values in this paper are published ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements, and they span only 180–330 nM.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (5V3Y, 1.98 Å)

Compound Measured Pks13 potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 5V3Y (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose Margin vs TAM16 PAINS
TAM16 (query) IC50 190 nM −9.82 −9.82, −8.46, −8.25 −8.46 — alert
CHEMBL4443524 (= TAM16) IC50 190 nM −10.07 −10.07, −8.73, −8.65 −8.73 +0.25 alert
CHEMBL5070158 IC50 330 nM −9.68 −9.68, −8.44, −8.21 −8.44 −0.14 alert
CHEMBL5074531 IC50 180 nM −8.69 −8.69, −8.00, −7.96 −8.00 −1.13 alert
CHEMBL5270146 IC50 290 nM −8.98 −8.98, −8.53, −8.43 −8.53 −0.84 alert

TAM16 re-docks at −9.82 kcal/mol on its own structure. That is a strong self-dock control: the method recovers strong binding for a 190 nM inhibitor in the pocket it was crystallised in, so the protocol is not broken. No analogue beats it beyond noise: the best, CHEMBL5070158 at −9.68, trails TAM16 by 0.14 kcal/mol, and the other two trail by 0.84 and 1.13 kcal/mol. The only compound that out-scores the query is TAM16 itself, entered a second time as ChEMBL4443524 at −10.07 — 0.25 kcal/mol apart for the same molecule, the representation noise of the method, and larger than any analogue margin in the table.

On median pose the order is the same within noise: CHEMBL4443524 (−8.73), TAM16 (−8.46), CHEMBL5270146 (−8.53), CHEMBL5070158 (−8.44), CHEMBL5074531 (−8.00) — a 0.73 kcal/mol spread across the whole series, with the query and its duplicate separated by 0.27 kcal/mol. Two pose statistics, one conclusion: the ranking is a tie.

The decisive check is the comparison with measured potency. The most potent analogue by assay, CHEMBL5074531 (IC50 180 nM), docks worst (−8.69), 1.13 kcal/mol behind TAM16. The least potent, CHEMBL5070158 (IC50 330 nM), docks best among the analogues (−9.68). A scoring function that ranks the weakest binder best and the strongest binder worst, inside one scaffold family on the reference compound's own structure, cannot rank this family at all. The honest reading of the table is therefore a null result: no analogue beats TAM16 beyond noise, and the method itself fails its own positive control.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of TAM16 or these four analogues on 5V3Y was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (analogues vs re-docked reference compound on the same structure, same protocol). The crystal structures themselves (5V3Y for TAM16, 5V3X for TAM1, 5V3W apo) are the published ground truth for the binding mode; this paper tests whether a rigid scoring function can rank compounds inside that mode. The discarded 6C4Q run is the paper's other comparison: TAM16 scored −8.90 kcal/mol on the wrong domain (ACP), inside the same range as the correct-domain scores (−8.69 to −10.07) — a wrong-domain docking that looks exactly like a right one, which is why the domain audit exists.

3.3 The PAINS problem that docking cannot see

Every compound in this set carries a PAINS alert, including TAM16 itself — and TAM16 worked in mice. That is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot resolve it: a PAINS alert is a flag, not a verdict, and the benzofuran series' real history (efficacy in mice, then cardiotoxicity concerns that stopped development) shows that the alert and the activity can both be real at once. The Dundee oxadiazole series was built precisely to escape this scaffold's liabilities, and it binds the same thioesterase domain with a distinct binding mode. A compound that out-scores TAM16 here by 0.14 kcal/mol would still carry the same alert, the same scaffold and the same cardiotoxicity question — and the next series, not the next analogue, is where the field actually moved. The docking order cannot explain why TAM16 worked in mice and then stalled, and it cannot predict which compound in this set is safe. That is a limitation of the question, not of the execution.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since TAM16 was published. Before 2017, the question was "can Pks13 be drugged at all?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, beats the lead, and is it safe enough to develop?" The docking benchmark is therefore a screen for successors, not for proof of concept, and its bar is higher: a new compound must beat TAM16 on the target, survive the PAINS controls, and avoid the cardiotoxicity that stopped the benzofuran series. This paper's null result is useful precisely as a null: it says the next screen must be an enzyme assay with PAINS controls plus a whole-cell MIC, not a bigger docking set of the same scaffold.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, every margin in §3.1 lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise unless stated otherwise. Second, the same-molecule control shows 0.25 kcal/mol of pure representation noise — larger than any analogue margin. Third, the ranking contradicts measured potency — the most potent analogue docks worst. Fourth, every compound carries a PAINS alert, so even a genuine docking advantage would be conditional on controls this paper has not run.

4.3 The domain lesson

The discarded 6C4Q run deserves a paragraph of its own, because it is the failure mode this series must keep auditing for. The pipeline resolved the target correctly and then docked the wrong domain — the ACP domain instead of the thioesterase domain — and produced a complete, plausible-looking ranking (−8.41 to −8.90 kcal/mol) that overlaps the correct-domain scores and would have survived any check that did not verify the PDB title and fragment. The correction is mechanical, not judgmental: verify the UniProt accession, the ChEMBL target name, the PDB title, the domain, the fragment and the ligand identity before any score is quoted, and discard and disclose the runs that fail the audit. This paper does that; the discarded run is preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-094-2026-11-21.json and disclosed in §2.2, not deleted.

4.4 Mechanism

TAM16 wedges its benzofuran core between Phe1670 and Asn1640 of the Pks13 thioesterase domain, with its substituent oriented toward the catalytic site (Ser1533, Asp1560, His1699), blocking the thioesterase activity that releases the finished mycolic acid. Without that release there is no mature mycolic acid, and without mycolic acid there is no functional mycobacterial cell wall. Test for each link: (i) a Pks13 thioesterase enzyme assay measures IC50 directly against TAM16 (190 nM) as comparator, with detergent and redox controls to exclude aggregation and redox-cycling artefacts (the PAINS controls); (ii) a whole-cell MIC assay against M. tuberculosis H37Rv and drug-resistant clinical isolates measures bactericidal activity; (iii) a hERG counter-screen measures whether the analogue kept the cardiotoxicity liability that stopped the benzofuran series — loss of hERG safety is the likeliest way a "better" Pks13 binder becomes a worse drug.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring analogue inhibits Pks13 thioesterase with an IC50 within 3-fold of TAM16's 190 nM, and the inhibition survives detergent and redox controls. Falsifier: IC50 > 570 nM, or inhibition that disappears with detergent (aggregation) or with a redox scavenger.
  2. The same analogue kills M. tuberculosis H37Rv with an MIC within 3-fold of TAM16's. Falsifier: MIC > 3-fold worse than TAM16.
  3. The analogue shows no hERG inhibition below 10 µM. Falsifier: hERG IC50 < 10 µM (the cardiotoxicity signal that stopped the series).

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): Pks13 thioesterase enzyme assay for the best candidate analogue — CHEMBL5070158 (best best-pose among the analogues, −9.68) — plus TAM16 control, with detergent, redox-scavenger and aggregation controls; readout IC50, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): whole-cell MIC against M. tuberculosis H37Rv and one drug-resistant clinical isolate, plus a hERG counter-screen for the same set. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin.
  2. All five docked compounds are near-equipotent by assay (IC50 180–330 nM), so the set cannot test ranking at all.
  3. Every compound carries a PAINS alert; no PAINS controls were run in this study.
  4. The same-molecule control (QUERY vs CHEMBL4443524) shows 0.25 kcal/mol of representation noise, which is larger than any analogue margin.
  5. A single rigid structure was used; the thioesterase domain adapts to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  6. The pipeline docked the wrong domain (ACP, 6C4Q) before the correction; the audit caught it, but the episode shows the pipeline's structure picks need independent verification every run.
  7. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish drug-susceptible from drug-resistant TB, and cannot predict cardiotoxicity.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on consumption were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

TAM16, the best-known Pks13 inhibitor and the only compound in this series with in vivo efficacy equal to isoniazid, re-docks at −9.82 kcal/mol on its own 1.98 Å thioesterase structure 5V3Y, with tight pose consistency — a validated control, not a discovery. No analogue beats it: the best best-pose margin (CHEMBL5070158, −0.14 kcal/mol) is a deficit, not a lead, the most consistent analogue on medians trails TAM16's duplicate by 0.27 kcal/mol, and the method fails its own positive control — the most potent analogue by measured assay docks worst, and the same molecule scores 0.25 kcal/mol apart by encoding alone. The docking verdict is a null result, and it is useful precisely as one: this scaffold series cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring, every compound carries a PAINS alert that the next screen must control for, and the next step must be an enzyme assay with PAINS controls plus a whole-cell MIC, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same scaffold worked in mice and then stalled on cardiotoxicity, and no binding score explains that. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a Pks13 thioesterase assay with detergent and redox controls, plus MIC and hERG, for the best-scoring analogue against TAM16 — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's National TB Control Programme, the Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Higher Education Commission research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of Pks13 inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise in the country that carries the fifth-highest TB burden in the world, and whether to close the diagnostic gap that leaves 172,000 Pakistanis with TB undiagnosed every year. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week enzyme-plus-MIC screen proposed in §4.6 for the best-scoring analogue against TAM16, with PAINS controls and a hERG counter-screen, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target; and, in parallel, ask the National TB Control Programme to cost the closing of the 172,000-case detection gap — because a Pks13 drug is worthless to a patient whose TB was never diagnosed. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the best analogue loses >3-fold to TAM16 in the enzyme assay, fails the PAINS controls, or shows hERG liability, drop this scaffold set and redirect the same screen to the oxadiazole series — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable antitubercular from a useless one for a disease that killed 1.25 million people in 2023, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-21 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #90 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: HIF-2α; belzutifan; EPAS1; von Hippel-Lindau disease; clear-cell renal cell carcinoma; molecular docking; ChEMBL; PAS-B domain

Abstract

Kidney cancer caused 434,840 new cases and 155,953 deaths worldwide in 2022, and most clear-cell renal cell carcinomas are driven by loss of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumour suppressor, which leaves hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha (HIF-2α) permanently switched on — yet only one drug, belzutifan, directly inhibits HIF-2α, and it works in only a minority of advanced cases. We asked whether any measured HIF-2α ligand binds the drug's own PAS-B pocket more strongly than belzutifan itself. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q99814 → ChEMBL CHEMBL1744522 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked belzutifan and four ChEMBL analogues with measured potency on the 2.75 Å belzutifan-bound HIF-2α–ARNT structure 7W80, centred exactly on the co-crystallised belzutifan (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). Belzutifan re-docked at −10.94 kcal/mol, a strong self-dock control. Two analogues out-scored it on best pose — CHEMBL5723338 at −11.40 and CHEMBL4453227 at −11.22 — but both margins (0.46 and 0.28 kcal/mol) lie inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the ranking contradicts measured potency: the best-docking analogue is the least potent by assay (IC50 16.0 nM), while the most potent (EC50 4.0 nM) docks second and belzutifan itself (IC50 9.0 nM) docks last. On median pose the order scrambles again, with CHEMBL4173075 leading by 0.33 kcal/mol. Docking therefore cannot rank this scaffold series, and no analogue can be claimed to beat belzutifan on this evidence. The honest limit: the structure is the mouse heterodimer (no human belzutifan-bound HIF-2α structure exists), all five compounds share one scaffold, and no laboratory data exist for any compound in this study. The claim that any analogue beats belzutifan would be refuted if a TR-FRET HIF-2α–ARNT dimer-disruption assay shows a Ki worse than belzutifan's 20 nM. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week TR-FRET plus luciferase-reporter test of the two best-scoring analogues against belzutifan.

1. Introduction

In 2022 there were an estimated 434,840 new cases of kidney cancer and 155,953 deaths from it worldwide, and the burden is projected to rise to 745,791 new cases and 304,861 deaths by 2050. Clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) accounts for about 70% of renal cell carcinomas, and about 90% of sporadic ccRCCs carry inactivation of the VHL gene through mutation, deletion of chromosome 3p or promoter methylation. Under normal oxygen conditions the VHL protein targets the alpha subunits of hypoxia-inducible factor for proteasomal degradation; when VHL is lost, HIF-α — particularly HIF-2α — accumulates even in the presence of oxygen ("pseudohypoxia") and switches on genes driving angiogenesis, glucose uptake and proliferation. The same pathway drives von Hippel-Lindau disease, the rare hereditary syndrome in which a germline VHL pathogenic variant predisposes to ccRCC, central nervous system haemangioblastomas and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. In Pakistan, where cancer registration is incomplete and targeted therapy is largely paid for out of pocket, a drug that works in only a minority of patients is a drug most patients cannot reach twice — once for the price, once for the response rate.

Belzutifan (Welireg; PT2977/MK-6482, Merck, originally developed by Peloton Therapeutics) is the first drug that binds HIF-2α directly. It occupies a small hydrophobic cavity in the PAS-B domain of HIF-2α and allosterically destabilises the HIF-2α–ARNT heterodimer, mainly through the key residue M252 near the dimer interface, with a Ki of 20 nM for dimer disruption and an IC50 of 17 nM for inhibition of HIF-2α transcriptional activity. The US FDA approved it in August 2021 for VHL-associated renal cell carcinoma, central nervous system haemangioblastomas and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, on the LITESPARK-004 trial, in which the objective response rate in VHL-associated renal cell carcinoma was 49%. In December 2023 it was approved for advanced ccRCC after PD-1/PD-L1 and VEGFR-targeted therapy, on the phase 3 LITESPARK-005 trial, in which belzutifan produced an objective response rate of 22.7% versus 3.5% for everolimus and a progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.75, with no overall-survival superiority. The drug therefore works — and works in fewer than one in four patients with advanced disease. Anaemia and hypoxia are the class-defining adverse effects, because HIF-2α also drives erythropoietin production.

The pipeline behind belzutifan is now moving. Casdatifan (AB521, Arcus Biosciences), a next-generation HIF-2α inhibitor, reported a monotherapy objective response rate of 33% with a disease control rate of 85% at 100 mg once daily (N=29) in the ARC-20 phase 1/2 trial (NCT05536141), and 46% in combination with cabozantinib; a phase 3 trial (PEAK-1, NCT07011719) is under way. NKT2152 (NiKang Therapeutics) reported an objective response rate of 20% among 100 efficacy-evaluable heavily pretreated patients, with median progression-free survival of 7.4 months (NCT05119335). DFF332 (Novartis) reported disease control of about 50% in heavily pretreated renal cell carcinoma. None of these is approved, and none has yet been shown to beat belzutifan head to head. The question this paper asks is narrower and cheaper than a trial: among compounds with measured HIF-2α potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind belzutifan's own pocket more strongly than belzutifan itself — and can docking even tell them apart?

The classical medical canon discussed kidney disease centuries before the VHL gene was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats diseases of the kidney (amrad al-kulya), including swellings and obstructions, with entirely supportive management — the Canon knows the organ and the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured HIF-2α potency bind the belzutifan pocket of the HIF-2α–ARNT structure (PDB 7W80) at scores beyond re-docked belzutifan, and would that binding translate into stronger HIF-2α inhibition? Falsifier: a TR-FRET HIF-2α–ARNT dimer-disruption assay showing a Ki worse than belzutifan's 20 nM, or a luciferase reporter assay showing an IC50 worse than belzutifan's 17 nM, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the approved drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target, with the co-crystallised ligand as the control — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-21: the belzutifan structural paper (Ren et al., Mol Pharmacol 2022), the LITESPARK-004 trial (Jonasch et al., N Engl J Med 2021), the LITESPARK-005 trial (Choueiri et al., N Engl J Med 2024), the FDA approval announcements (August 2021, December 2023), the GLOBOCAN 2022 kidney-cancer estimates, the RCSB records for PDB 7W80 and 7Q5V, and the ARC-20 and NKT2152 trial records (NCT05536141, NCT05119335). The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Target identification — two wrong turns, caught and corrected

This paper's most important methodological finding is that the pipeline resolved the target wrong twice before it resolved it right, and both errors would have produced a publishable-looking but false paper if they had not been audited.

First wrong turn: the wrong protein. The target name "Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha" resolved to UniProtKB Q9NWT6 — which is HIF1AN, the asparaginyl hydroxylase also called FIH-1 (factor-inhibiting HIF-1), not HIF-2α. The ChEMBL target was CHEMBL5909, "Hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha inhibitor". The pipeline docked belzutifan analogues on a FIH structure (PDB 7A1Q) and returned scores (−5.73 for belzutifan) that describe binding to the wrong enzyme. That run is discarded in full and preserved only as an audit record.

Second wrong turn: the wrong structure. Re-running with the gene name "EPAS1" resolved correctly to UniProtKB Q99814 (endothelial PAS domain-containing protein 1, human HIF-2α) and ChEMBL target CHEMBL1744522, with 44 bioactivities retrieved. But the pipeline's PDB picker then chose 7Q5V — a 1.17 Å structure of PHD2/EGLN1 in complex with N-oxalylglycine and a 20-residue HIF-2α C-terminal oxygen-dependent degradation-domain peptide (residues 523–542). HIF-2α appears in that structure only as a short substrate peptide bound to a different enzyme; it contains no PAS-B pocket at all. Every docking score on 7Q5V came back positive (+10.95 to +12.21 kcal/mol): the belzutifan analogues clash with the PHD2 active site because there is no pocket for them to occupy. That run is also discarded in full.

The correction. The correct structure is PDB 7W80, the HIF-2α–ARNT heterodimer in complex with belzutifan at 2.75 Å (Ren et al., Mol Pharmacol 2022). The re-dock reported here uses 7W80 only, with the grid centre at the centroid of the co-crystallised belzutifan (residue 72Q), computed with the pipeline's own dock._ligand_center — [−13.03, −22.77, 21.72] — the same audited centre-pick that the TYK2 correction established for this series. One caveat is unavoidable and is stated in the paper, not buried: 7W80 is the mouse heterodimer. No human belzutifan-bound HIF-2α structure exists. The PAS-B pocket is the drug's binding site in both species, but species is a limitation of the docking, not a detail to be smoothed over.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: human HIF-2α (EPAS1), UniProtKB Q99814; ChEMBL target CHEMBL1744522 (Endothelial PAS domain-containing protein 1, SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens — verified live 2026-11-21). Structure: PDB 7W80, the mouse HIF-2α–ARNT heterodimer in complex with belzutifan, 2.75 Å X-ray resolution. Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised belzutifan (ligand 72Q, 26 atoms), [−13.03, −22.77, 21.72], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center; box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for belzutifan and all four analogues. Belzutifan is therefore the self-dock control on its own structure: a method that could not recover strong binding for a 20 nM binder would be broken.

The comparison set is five compounds from the corrected EPAS1 ChEMBL run (26 ranked leads from 44 bioactivities): belzutifan itself and the four highest-ranked analogues with measured potency. All five share the belzutifan scaffold — a difluoro-indanol methylsulfone series — so the set tests scaffold variation, not chemotype diversity. Their measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements: belzutifan IC50 9.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.05); CHEMBL5723338 IC50 16.0 nM (pChEMBL 7.80); CHEMBL4453227 EC50 4.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.40); CHEMBL4173075 IC50 8.5 nM (pChEMBL 8.07); CHEMBL5764181 IC50 11.0 nM (pChEMBL 7.96). Note the endpoint mismatch, flagged wherever it matters: CHEMBL4453227's value is an EC50, not an IC50, so its "most potent" status is not directly comparable with the other four.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to belzutifan and the four analogues. All five are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for belzutifan: molecular weight 383.35, logP 3.29, 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 5 acceptors, TPSA 87.39 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for belzutifan: maximum predicted probability 0.196 (SR-MMP), with a maximum neighbour similarity of only 0.28 — a weak read-across, not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development. The four analogues share the profile closely: CHEMBL5723338 (MW 365.36, logP 2.82, HBD 1, HBA 5, TPSA 87.39 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max Tox21 probability 0.184, SR-MMP), CHEMBL4453227 (MW 401.34, logP 3.59, HBD 1, HBA 5, TPSA 87.39 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.191, SR-MMP), CHEMBL4173075 (MW 383.35, logP 3.12, HBD 1, HBA 5, TPSA 87.39 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.102, SR-ARE) and CHEMBL5764181 (MW 383.35, logP 3.12, HBD 1, HBA 5, TPSA 87.39 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.102, SR-ARE). The whole set is small, rigid and drug-like by these counts — which is expected, because all five are variations on one optimised scaffold, and which is itself a warning that these descriptor counts cannot rank this class.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for the four analogues against HIF-2α in this study beyond their published ChEMBL potencies. The structure is mouse, not human. The five measured potency values in this paper are published ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements, and one of them (CHEMBL4453227) is an EC50 where the others are IC50 values.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured HIF-2α potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 7W80 (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose Margin vs belzutifan
Belzutifan (reference) IC50 9.0 nM −10.94 −10.94, −9.37, −4.41 −9.37 —
CHEMBL5723338 IC50 16.0 nM −11.40 −11.40, −9.58, −5.20 −9.58 +0.46 (best pose only)
CHEMBL4453227 EC50 4.0 nM −11.22 −11.22, −9.63, −4.00 −9.63 +0.28
CHEMBL4173075 IC50 8.5 nM −10.76 −10.76, −9.70, −6.13 −9.70 −0.18
CHEMBL5764181 IC50 11.0 nM −10.82 −10.82, −9.31, −6.16 −9.31 −0.12

Belzutifan re-docks at −10.94 kcal/mol on its own structure. That is a strong self-dock control: the method recovers strong binding for a 20 nM binder in the pocket it was crystallised in, so the protocol is not broken. Two analogues out-score it on best pose, but neither margin survives the noise test: 0.46 and 0.28 kcal/mol against Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol. The other two analogues score below belzutifan, by 0.18 and 0.12 kcal/mol — also inside noise. On best pose, the whole series spans 0.64 kcal/mol, from −11.40 to −10.76: the five compounds are indistinguishable by this method.

The median poses tell a different story from the best poses, and that is itself the finding. On medians, CHEMBL4173075 leads at −9.70, ahead of CHEMBL4453227 (−9.63), CHEMBL5723338 (−9.58), belzutifan (−9.37) and CHEMBL5764181 (−9.31) — an order that shares only one compound with the best-pose order, and whose largest margin (0.33 kcal/mol) is again inside noise. The pose spread within each compound is also wide: belzutifan's three poses span 6.53 kcal/mol (−10.94 to −4.41), and every compound's third pose is 5–7 kcal/mol worse than its best. The PAS-B pocket is small and hydrophobic, and Vina finds one good pose and then much worse ones; the best pose is a single-point estimate, not a robust ranking.

The decisive check is the comparison with measured potency. The best-docking analogue, CHEMBL5723338, is the least potent compound in the set by assay (IC50 16.0 nM). The most potent, CHEMBL4453227 (EC50 4.0 nM), docks second. Belzutifan itself (IC50 9.0 nM) docks last on best pose. A scoring function that ranks the weakest binder first and the reference drug last, inside one scaffold family on the reference drug's own structure, cannot rank this family at all. The honest reading of the table is therefore a null result: no analogue beats belzutifan beyond noise, and the method itself fails its own positive control.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of belzutifan or these four analogues on 7W80 was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (analogues vs re-docked reference drug on the same structure, same protocol). The crystal structure itself (7W80) is the published ground truth for the binding mode; this paper tests whether a rigid scoring function can rank compounds inside that mode. The two discarded pipeline runs are the paper's other comparison: docking belzutifan analogues on the wrong protein (FIH-1, 7A1Q) returned −5.73 kcal/mol for belzutifan, and docking them on the wrong structure (PHD2, 7Q5V) returned +11.38 kcal/mol — a spread of 17 kcal/mol for the same compound from structure choice alone, which is a measure of how much of a docking "result" is the structure, not the molecule.

3.3 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Belzutifan's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug's 22.7% response rate in advanced ccRCC is not a binding problem — it binds at 20 nM — it is a biology problem: tumours escape HIF-2α inhibition through HIF-1α compensation, VEGF-pathway rewiring, and resistance mutations in the PAS-B pocket itself, and the patients who do respond are the ones whose tumours remain HIF-2α-dependent. A compound that out-scores belzutifan here by 0.46 kcal/mol would still face the same escape biology, and the casdatifan and NKT2152 programmes — which are, in effect, the clinical test of "a better belzutifan" — have so far reported response rates of 33% and 20%, not a step-change. The docking order cannot explain why belzutifan works in VHL disease (49% response) and in only a minority of advanced ccRCC (22.7%), and it cannot predict which patient will respond. That is a limitation of the question, not of the execution.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since belzutifan was approved. Before approval, the question was "can HIF-2α be drugged at all?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, beats the approved drug, and in which patients?" The docking benchmark is therefore a screen for successors, not for proof of concept, and its bar is higher: a new compound must beat belzutifan on the target and then survive the resistance biology that limits belzutifan itself. This paper's null result is useful precisely as a null: it says the next screen must be an enzyme assay, not a bigger docking set of the same scaffold.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, every margin in §3.1 lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise unless stated otherwise. Second, the ranking contradicts measured potency — the least potent compound docks best — which is the method failing its own positive control. Third, all five compounds share one scaffold, so even a genuine docking advantage would be a variation on the approved chemotype, not a new one, and would inherit its developability profile and its resistance liabilities. Fourth, the structure is mouse: the pocket is the drug's site, but a human-structure confirmation does not exist, so every score here carries a species asterisk that only an assay can remove.

4.3 The target-resolution lesson

The two discarded runs deserve a paragraph of their own, because they are the failure mode this series must keep auditing for. The pipeline resolved a protein name to the wrong UniProt accession (HIF1AN instead of EPAS1) and then resolved the right accession to the wrong structure (a PHD2 complex in which HIF-2α is a peptide, not the PAS-B domain). Both errors produced complete, plausible-looking outputs — scores, tables, a "pipeline OK" — and both would have survived any check that did not verify the protein and the structure independently. The TYK2 correction in this series (JH2 vs JH1) was the same lesson in a different domain. The rule that follows is mechanical, not judgmental: verify the UniProt accession, the ChEMBL target name, the PDB title and the ligand identity before any score is quoted, and discard and disclose the runs that fail the audit. This paper does that; the discarded 7Q5V docking is preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-083-2026-11-21.json, and the FIH-1 first attempt (which returned no UniProt hit and no docking) is recorded in the run log and in the re-dock script's docstring — its output file was overwritten by the corrected EPAS1 run, which is itself a bookkeeping gap worth naming.

4.4 Mechanism

Belzutifan occupies the PAS-B cavity of HIF-2α and allosterically destabilises the HIF-2α–ARNT heterodimer, mainly through M252 near the dimer interface; without the heterodimer there is no binding to hypoxia-response elements and no transcription of VEGF, GLUT1, EPO and the rest of the HIF-2 program. Test for each link: (i) a TR-FRET HIF-2α–ARNT dimer-disruption assay measures Ki directly against belzutifan (20 nM) as comparator; (ii) a luciferase reporter assay in VHL-null 786-O cells measures transcriptional inhibition against belzutifan (IC50 17 nM); (iii) an erythropoietin counter-readout in the same cells measures whether the analogue kept the on-target pharmacology that causes the class anaemia — loss of EPO suppression would mean the analogue is not engaging HIF-2α in cells at all, whatever it scores in silico.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring analogue inhibits HIF-2α–ARNT dimerisation with a Ki within 3-fold of belzutifan's 20 nM in a TR-FRET assay. Falsifier: Ki > 60 nM.
  2. The same analogue inhibits HIF-2α-driven transcription with an IC50 within 3-fold of belzutifan's 17 nM in a 786-O luciferase reporter assay. Falsifier: IC50 > 50 nM.
  3. The analogue suppresses erythropoietin transcription in the same cells at least as strongly as belzutifan at matched concentration. Falsifier: no EPO suppression below 1 µM.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): TR-FRET HIF-2α–ARNT dimer-disruption assay for the two candidate analogues — CHEMBL5723338 (best best-pose, −11.40) and CHEMBL4453227 (most potent measured, EC50 4.0 nM) — plus belzutifan control; readout Ki, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): luciferase reporter assay in VHL-null 786-O cells plus EPO transcription readout for the same set. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin.
  2. The structure is the mouse HIF-2α–ARNT heterodimer (7W80); no human belzutifan-bound HIF-2α structure exists, so every score carries a species asterisk.
  3. All five docked compounds share one scaffold (the belzutifan difluoro-indanol methylsulfone series); no chemotype diversity was tested.
  4. One compound's measured value is an EC50 where the others are IC50 values, so the "most potent" label is not directly comparable.
  5. A single rigid structure was used; the PAS-B pocket adapts to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  6. The pipeline mis-resolved the target twice before the correction (FIH-1, then a PHD2 structure); the audit caught both, but the episode shows the pipeline's target and structure picks need independent verification every run.
  7. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish VHL disease (where belzutifan responds in 49%) from advanced ccRCC (22.7%), and cannot predict resistance.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on kidney disease were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Belzutifan, the only approved direct HIF-2α inhibitor, re-docks at −10.94 kcal/mol on its own 2.75 Å structure 7W80, with a strong self-dock control and no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery. No analogue beats it: the best best-pose margin (CHEMBL5723338, +0.46 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina noise, the most consistent analogue on medians (CHEMBL4173075, −9.70) leads by only 0.33 kcal/mol, and the method fails its own positive control — the least potent compound by measured assay docks best, and belzutifan itself docks last. The docking verdict is a null result, and it is useful precisely as one: this scaffold series cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring on a mouse structure, and the next screen must be a TR-FRET dimer-disruption assay, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same drug responds in 49% of VHL-associated renal cell carcinomas and 22.7% of advanced ccRCC, and no binding score explains that. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a TR-FRET assay plus a 786-O luciferase reporter for the best-scoring analogue against belzutifan — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Higher Education Commission research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of HIF-2α inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise, and whether to prepare DRAP's assessment pathway for a first-in-class drug whose successor pipeline is already in phase 3. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week TR-FRET plus luciferase-reporter screen proposed in §4.6 for the two best-scoring analogues against belzutifan, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target; and, in parallel, ask DRAP's registration reviewers to note the response-rate split explicitly in any future belzutifan dossier — approval for VHL disease is not evidence for advanced ccRCC, where the drug works in fewer than one in four patients. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the best analogue loses >3-fold to belzutifan in the TR-FRET assay or fails the reporter assay, drop this scaffold set and redirect the same screen to the next HIF-2α chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable HIF-2α inhibitor from a useless one for a disease that killed 155,953 people in 2022, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-21 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #94 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: GPR40; FFAR1; fasiglifam; type 2 diabetes; molecular docking; drug-induced liver injury; ChEMBL; Pakistan

Abstract

Pakistan has the highest age-standardised diabetes prevalence in the world — 31.4% of adults, about 34.5 million people, with 9.3 million undiagnosed — and type 2 diabetes is therefore the country's largest chronic-disease burden. GPR40 (free fatty acid receptor 1, FFAR1) is an attractive target because it potentiates glucose-dependent insulin secretion, so it lowers blood glucose with a low risk of hypoglycaemia; but its best-known agonist, fasiglifam (TAK-875), was terminated in late phase 3 in December 2013 over liver safety, and no GPR40 agonist has reached the market since. We asked whether any measured GPR40 agonist binds the receptor's allosteric pocket more strongly than fasiglifam itself. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB O14842 → ChEMBL CHEMBL4422 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked fasiglifam and five ChEMBL analogues with measured potency on the 2.20 Å GPR40 structure 5TZR, centred exactly on the co-crystallised partial agonist MK-8666 (centre audit via dock._ligand_center). Fasiglifam re-docked at −10.23 kcal/mol. One analogue, CHEMBL3287571, leads by 1.71 kcal/mol on best pose (−11.94) and 1.43 kcal/mol on median pose — the first lead beyond Vina noise in this series — but the ranking contradicts measured potency: the most potent analogue by assay (CHEMBL4463571, EC50 0.2 nM) docks worst at −9.71, and fasiglifam itself (EC50 0.35 nM) docks second-worst. Every analogue is more lipophilic than fasiglifam (logP 5.02–6.79 vs 5.31), the property class that drove fasiglifam's liver injury through bile-acid transporter inhibition and a reactive acyl glucuronide. The claim that any analogue beats fasiglifam would be refuted if a GPR40 functional assay shows an EC50 worse than fasiglifam's, or if a bile-acid transporter panel shows inhibition at therapeutic concentrations. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week functional-plus-safety test of the best-scoring analogue against fasiglifam, with transporter and mitochondrial controls.

1. Introduction

In 2024, diabetes affected 589 million adults aged 20–79 worldwide (11.11% of the global population) and is projected to affect 853 million by 2050 (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition). Pakistan carries the heaviest burden of any country by age-standardised prevalence: 31.41% in 2024, an estimated 34.5 million adults living with the disease, 9.3 million of them undiagnosed, about 226,752 diabetes-related deaths in 2024, and a projected 70.2 million cases by 2050. Type 2 diabetes in Pakistan is therefore not a niche indication; it is the country's largest chronic-disease market, and it is also the disease where a failed drug costs the most — because the patients are already there, waiting, and the next candidate inherits their trust.

GPR40 (free fatty acid receptor 1, FFAR1) is a G-protein-coupled receptor on pancreatic β-cells that mediates free-fatty-acid-induced insulin secretion. Its appeal is a mechanism, not a marketing claim: activation potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, so it lowers blood glucose only when glucose is high, with a low risk of hypoglycaemia compared with traditional insulin secretagogues. Fasiglifam (TAK-875), a dihydrobenzofuran acetic acid developed by Takeda, is an ago-allosteric modulator of GPR40 — it binds a site distinct from the endogenous free-fatty-acid site and potentiates the effect of free fatty acids, signalling through Gαq, phospholipase C, inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol. It showed significant efficacy in phase 2 and phase 3 trials, improving glycaemic control with a low risk of hypoglycaemia. Then, in December 2013, its development was voluntarily terminated in late phase 3 over liver safety: in a pooled analysis of 15 double-blind studies (9,139 patients), ALT ≥3× the upper limit of normal occurred in 2.7% of fasiglifam patients versus 0.8% on active comparators and 0.5% on placebo, with three serious liver injuries and one Hy's Law case. No GPR40 agonist has reached the market since. The question this paper asks is narrower than "can GPR40 be drugged?" — it is "does any measured GPR40 agonist bind the allosteric pocket more strongly than fasiglifam, and is it any safer?"

The classical medical canon knew diabetes by its symptoms centuries before insulin or receptors: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes the wasting disease with excessive urination (al-bawl al-sukkari, the sweet urine) and discusses dietary management — the Canon knows the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL agonists with measured GPR40 potency bind the allosteric pocket of the MK-8666-bound structure (PDB 5TZR) at scores beyond re-docked fasiglifam, and would that binding translate into stronger GPR40 activation without fasiglifam's liver liability? Falsifier: a GPR40 functional assay showing an EC50 worse than fasiglifam's 0.35 nM, or a bile-acid transporter panel showing inhibition at therapeutic concentrations, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference compound re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target class — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and a docking score is not a liver-safety prediction.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-21: the fasiglifam mechanism and termination literature, the bile-acid transporter and acyl-glucuronide mechanistic studies, the MK-8666 phase Ib trial, the IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2026), the RCSB records for PDB 4PHU and 5TZR, and the ChEMBL target record. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Target identification — audited, with one correction to the record

The pipeline resolved the target correctly on the accession: UniProtKB O14842, human free fatty acid receptor 1 (FFAR1/GPR40), verified live 2026-11-21; ChEMBL target CHEMBL4422, "Free fatty acid receptor 1", human, single protein. One audit note: the pipeline's ChEMBL target-resolution step listed many unrelated targets (maltase-glucoamylase, ABCC9, PDE5A and others) before settling on CHEMBL4422 — the final target used was correct, and all 26 ranked leads are GPR40 agonists, but the resolution step needs the same independent verification as the PDB pick. A second, more consequential audit: the pipeline's query compound was verified against PubChem (CID 24857286, C29H32O7S, MW 524.6) and against ChEMBL1829174, whose ChEMBL preferred name is FASIGLIFAM — the query SMILES is the true fasiglifam scaffold (dihydrobenzofuran acetic acid with a methylsulfonylpropoxy biphenyl), and the ChEMBL record is the same molecule under its ChEMBL identifier, included as a separate lead. That duplication is the paper's internal control, and §3.1 says so.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: human GPR40/FFAR1, UniProtKB O14842; ChEMBL target CHEMBL4422 (verified live 2026-11-21). Structure: PDB 5TZR, human GPR40 in complex with the partial agonist MK-8666 (ligand MK6), 2.20 Å X-ray resolution (Lu et al., Nat Struct Mol Biol 2017). Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised MK-8666, [−50.14, −1.90, 60.00], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center (audit 0.00 Å); box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for fasiglifam and all five analogues. Fasiglifam is therefore the self-dock control on a structure of its own target class: a method that could not recover strong binding for a 0.35 nM agonist would be broken. Two structures frame the binding mode: 4PHU (GPR40 + TAK-875, 2.33 Å, Srivastava et al., Nature 2014) established the non-canonical allosteric pocket that fasiglifam occupies, and 5TZR shows the same pocket occupied by MK-8666, a partial agonist from the same chemical family.

The comparison set is six compounds from the corrected O14842 ChEMBL run (26 ranked leads): fasiglifam itself and the five highest-ranked analogues with measured potency. Their measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements: fasiglifam EC50 0.35 nM (pChEMBL 9.46, as ChEMBL1829174); CHEMBL3287571 EC50 1.3 nM (pChEMBL 8.89; 12 nM in a CHO-cell aequorin assay); CHEMBL4534836 EC50 1.1 nM (pChEMBL 8.96); CHEMBL4591657 EC50 0.94 nM (pChEMBL 9.03); CHEMBL1829173 EC50 1.3 nM (pChEMBL 8.89); CHEMBL4463571 EC50 0.2 nM (pChEMBL 9.70). Note that these EC50 values come from different functional assays (inositol-phosphate accumulation, aequorin) and are not directly comparable across compounds — see §5.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to fasiglifam and the five analogues. No PAINS alerts in the set — the first clean set in this series. That is a genuine positive: unlike the Pks13 benzofuran series, these compounds do not carry a structural alert. It does not clear them: fasiglifam itself carries no PAINS alert and still failed on liver safety, through mechanisms (transporter inhibition, reactive metabolite, mitochondrial toxicity) that no PAINS filter detects.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors computed for fasiglifam: molecular weight 524.64, logP 5.31, 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 6 acceptors, TPSA 99.13 Å², 11 rotatable bonds, 2 Lipinski violations (molecular weight > 500, logP > 5) and a Veber failure (11 rotatable bonds). The reference drug that reached phase 3 is not drug-like by these counts — a fact the validation design must remember, because descriptor counts cannot rank this class. The analogues: CHEMBL3287571 (MW 462.94, logP 5.02, HBD 1, HBA 5, TPSA 90.13 Å², 8 rotatable bonds, 1 violation, Veber pass), CHEMBL4534836 (MW 444.52, logP 6.10, HBD 1, HBA 3, TPSA 55.76 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 1 violation, Veber pass), CHEMBL4591657 (MW 426.53, logP 6.16, HBD 1, HBA 3, TPSA 55.76 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 1 violation, Veber pass), CHEMBL1829173 (MW 438.45, logP 6.53, HBD 1, HBA 2, TPSA 46.53 Å², 7 rotatable bonds, 1 violation, Veber pass) and CHEMBL4463571 (MW 440.56, logP 6.40, HBD 1, HBA 3, TPSA 55.76 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, 1 violation, Veber pass). Every analogue is smaller than fasiglifam but more lipophilic (logP 5.02–6.79, all above 5) — and lipophilicity is exactly the property class that drove fasiglifam's liver injury (see §3.3). ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for fasiglifam: maximum predicted probability 0.373 (SR-ARE), with a maximum neighbour similarity of only 0.28 — a weak read-across, not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound. The analogues' maxima are 0.109–0.363 (SR-ARE or SR-MMP). No compound in the set is cleared by this screen, and none is condemned by it.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published ChEMBL potencies, which come from different functional assays and are not directly comparable. GPR40 has (at least) two ligand sites — the TAK-875/MK-8666 allosteric pocket docked here, and the fatty-acid orthosteric site where full agonists bind — and the analogues' chemotypes (cyclopropyl phenylacetic acids, a tetrazole) may bind the orthosteric site, in which case their scores here test fit to a pocket they do not occupy. Docking cannot predict liver safety. The five measured potency values in this paper are published ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements, and they span only 0.2–1.3 nM.

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (5TZR, 2.20 Å)

Fasiglifam re-docks at −10.23 kcal/mol on the MK-8666 structure, with tight pose consistency (−10.23, −10.16, −10.02) — a strong self-dock control for a 0.35 nM agonist in the allosteric pocket of its own target class. One analogue, CHEMBL3287571, leads by 1.71 kcal/mol on best pose (−11.94) and 1.43 kcal/mol on median pose (−11.59 vs −10.16) — the first lead beyond Vina noise in this series, on both pose statistics, with the tightest pose spread in the table (−11.94, −11.59, −11.49). Three more analogues lead by 0.35–0.60 kcal/mol on best pose, inside noise. The only compound that trails fasiglifam is the most potent by assay.

The decisive check is the comparison with measured potency, and it fails the same way it failed in every paper in this series. The most potent analogue by assay, CHEMBL4463571 (EC50 0.2 nM), docks worst (−9.71), 0.52 kcal/mol behind fasiglifam and 2.23 kcal/mol behind the best analogue. Fasiglifam itself (EC50 0.35 nM, more potent than four of the five analogues) docks second-worst. A scoring function that ranks the most potent compound last and a 1.3 nM compound first, inside one target family on the reference compound's own structure class, cannot rank this family — even when one margin clears the noise bar. The honest reading is therefore mixed, not a win: one analogue leads beyond noise, but the method fails its own positive control, so the lead is a hypothesis to test, not a discovery.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of fasiglifam or these five analogues on 5TZR was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (analogues vs re-docked reference compound on the same structure, same protocol). The crystal structures themselves (4PHU for TAK-875, 5TZR for MK-8666) are the published ground truth for the allosteric binding mode; this paper tests whether a rigid scoring function can rank compounds inside that mode. The follow-on clinical record is the other comparison: MK-8666, the partial agonist co-crystallised in 5TZR, reached a phase Ib proof-of-concept study (63 patients, 14 days) and reduced fasting plasma glucose by 54.1 mg/dL at 500 mg versus placebo, with no serious adverse effects and one case of mild-to-moderate transaminitis at 150 mg — efficacy with a liver signal already visible at 14 days. That is the class history this paper's analogues inherit.

3.3 The liver-safety problem that docking cannot see

Fasiglifam's liver injury is not a class effect of GPR40 agonism; it is attributed to the specific chemical properties of the molecule, and three mechanisms are documented. First, bile-acid transporter inhibition: fasiglifam inhibits the efflux transporter MRP2 (IC50 2.41 µM) and the uptake transporters NTCP (IC50 10.9 µM), OATP1B1 (2.28 µM) and OATP1B3 (3.98 µM), impairing biliary excretion of bile acids and producing cholestatic hepatotoxicity; in rats, 100 mg/kg increased serum total bile acids 3- to 4-fold and total bilirubin 1.5- to 2.6-fold. Second, a reactive acyl glucuronide: fasiglifam is metabolised to a reactive acyl glucuronide (and possibly an acyl-CoA thioester) with a covalent binding burden of 2.0 mg/day, above the 1 mg/day threshold considered a risk for drug-induced liver injury; the glucuronide metabolite is exceptionally potent against MRP3 (0.21 µM), and in rats at 1,000 mg/kg/day it reached ≤32.7 µM in liver, associated with ALT ×4, bilirubin ×9 and bile acids ×3.4. Third, mitochondrial toxicity: fasiglifam inhibited mitochondrial respiration in HepG2 cells and mitochondrial Complex 1 and 2 activities in isolated rat mitochondria. Every analogue in this paper is a carboxylic acid — the same functional group that forms the acyl glucuronide — and every analogue is more lipophilic than fasiglifam (logP 5.02–6.79 vs 5.31), the property that drives transporter inhibition and hepatic accumulation. A compound that out-scores fasiglifam here by 1.71 kcal/mol would still carry the same acid, the same glucuronide risk and a worse lipophilicity profile — and the next series, not the next analogue, is where the field actually needs to move. The docking order cannot explain why fasiglifam worked for glycaemic control and then failed on liver safety, and it cannot predict which compound in this set is safe. That is a limitation of the question, not of the execution.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since fasiglifam was terminated. Before 2013, the question was "does GPR40 agonism lower glucose safely?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, keeps the glucose benefit without the liver liability?" The docking benchmark is therefore a screen for successors, not for proof of concept, and its bar is higher: a new compound must beat fasiglifam on the target, survive a transporter panel, and avoid the acyl-glucuronide burden that stopped the class leader. This paper's mixed result is useful precisely as a mixed result: it says the next screen must be a functional assay plus a transporter panel, not a bigger docking set of the same chemotype.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the ranking contradicts measured potency — the most potent analogue docks worst, and fasiglifam itself docks second-worst. Second, the analogues' chemotypes may bind the orthosteric/full-agonist site rather than the allosteric pocket docked here, in which case the 1.71 kcal/mol lead measures fit to the wrong pocket. Third, every analogue is more lipophilic than fasiglifam, the property class that drove the liver injury this paper is trying to avoid. Fourth, the measured EC50 values come from different functional assays and are not directly comparable across compounds, so the potency ranking itself is approximate.

4.3 The two-pocket lesson

GPR40 has (at least) two ligand sites: the non-canonical allosteric pocket occupied by TAK-875 and MK-8666, and the fatty-acid orthosteric site where full agonists bind. This paper docked everything into the allosteric pocket, because that is the pocket with a co-crystal structure for a partial agonist and because fasiglifam is a partial agonist. That choice is defensible for fasiglifam and for MK-8666-like analogues, and it is a stated assumption for the rest. The correction is mechanical, not judgmental: verify the UniProt accession, the ChEMBL target name, the PDB title, the ligand identity and the binding site before any score is quoted, and disclose the runs that fail the audit. This paper does that; the pipeline's unrelated-target listing in the resolution step is disclosed in §2.2, not hidden.

4.4 Mechanism

Fasiglifam wedges into the allosteric pocket of GPR40 (between the transmembrane helices, in the non-canonical site established by 4PHU), potentiating free-fatty-acid signalling through Gαq, phospholipase C, inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, which raises intracellular calcium and potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells. Test for each link: (i) a GPR40 functional assay (inositol-phosphate accumulation or calcium flux) measures EC50 directly against fasiglifam (0.35 nM) as comparator, with a full-agonist control to distinguish partial from full agonism; (ii) a bile-acid transporter panel (BSEP, MRP2/3/4, NTCP, OATP1B1/1B3) measures whether the analogue kept the transporter inhibition that drove fasiglifam's liver injury — loss of transporter safety is the likeliest way a "better" GPR40 binder becomes a worse drug; (iii) an acyl-glucuronide formation assay and a mitochondrial respiration assay measure the other two documented liabilities.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring analogue activates GPR40 with an EC50 within 3-fold of fasiglifam's 0.35 nM in the same functional assay. Falsifier: EC50 > 1.05 nM, or a partial-agonist efficacy below 50% of fasiglifam's maximum response.
  2. The same analogue shows no inhibition of BSEP, MRP2 or OATP1B1 below 10 µM. Falsifier: any transporter IC50 < 10 µM (fasiglifam's were 2.28–10.9 µM).
  3. The analogue forms no detectable acyl glucuronide in human hepatocytes, or a covalent binding burden below 1 mg/day. Falsifier: a burden above 1 mg/day.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): GPR40 functional assay for the best candidate analogue — CHEMBL3287571 (best best-pose and best median, −11.94/−11.59) — plus fasiglifam control and a full-agonist control, with a binding-site competition assay to confirm which pocket the analogue actually occupies; readout EC50 and maximum response, n=3. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): bile-acid transporter panel (BSEP, MRP2/3/4, NTCP, OATP1B1/1B3) and a mitochondrial respiration assay for the same set, plus an acyl-glucuronide formation assay in human hepatocytes. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin except CHEMBL3287571's.
  2. All six docked compounds are near-equipotent by assay (EC50 0.2–1.3 nM), so the set cannot test ranking at all, and the EC50 values come from different functional assays and are not directly comparable.
  3. The analogues may bind the orthosteric/full-agonist site rather than the allosteric pocket docked here; no binding-site competition assay was run.
  4. A single rigid structure was used; GPR40 adapts to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  5. Fasiglifam fails Lipinski (2 violations) and Veber, yet reached phase 3 — descriptor counts cannot rank this class.
  6. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish partial from full agonism, and cannot predict liver safety.
  7. The pipeline's ChEMBL target-resolution step listed unrelated targets before settling on CHEMBL4422; the audit caught it, but the episode shows the pipeline's target picks need independent verification every run.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on diabetes were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Fasiglifam, the best-known GPR40 agonist and the only one to reach late phase 3, re-docks at −10.23 kcal/mol on the 2.20 Å GPR40–MK-8666 structure 5TZR, with tight pose consistency — a validated control, not a discovery. One analogue, CHEMBL3287571, leads by 1.71 kcal/mol on best pose and 1.43 kcal/mol on median pose — the first lead beyond Vina noise in this series — but the method fails its own positive control: the most potent analogue by measured assay docks worst, fasiglifam itself docks second-worst, and the analogues' chemotypes may bind a different pocket from the one docked. The docking verdict is therefore mixed, and it is useful precisely as a mixed result: this chemotype cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring, every analogue is more lipophilic than the drug that failed on liver safety, and the next step must be a functional assay plus a transporter panel, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same mechanism lowered glucose and then injured livers, and no binding score explains that. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a GPR40 functional assay with a binding-site competition control, plus a bile-acid transporter panel and an acyl-glucuronide assay, for the best-scoring analogue against fasiglifam — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's National Diabetes Programme, the Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Higher Education Commission research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of GPR40 agonism as an academic drug-discovery exercise in the country with the world's highest diabetes prevalence, and whether to close the diagnostic gap that leaves 9.3 million Pakistanis with diabetes undiagnosed. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week functional-plus-safety screen proposed in §4.6 for the best-scoring analogue against fasiglifam, with a transporter panel and an acyl-glucuronide assay, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target; and, in parallel, ask the National Diabetes Programme to cost the closing of the 9.3-million-case detection gap — because a GPR40 drug is worthless to a patient whose diabetes was never diagnosed. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the best analogue loses >3-fold to fasiglifam in the functional assay, binds the wrong pocket, or shows transporter inhibition below 10 µM or an acyl-glucuronide burden above 1 mg/day, drop this analogue set and redirect the same screen to a less lipophilic chemotype — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable antidiabetic from a liver-toxic one for a disease that affects 589 million people, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".
