AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-21 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #91 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: c-MET; capmatinib; MET exon 14 skipping; non-small-cell lung cancer; molecular docking; ChEMBL; kinase inhibitor; type Ib inhibitor

Abstract

Lung cancer caused an estimated 2.5 million new cases and 1.8 million deaths worldwide in 2022, and about 3–4% of non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLC) are driven by MET exon 14 skipping — yet the first selective drug for that lesion, capmatinib, still fails most patients who receive it second-line, and resistance mutations in the kinase domain defeat it outright. We asked whether any measured MET ligand binds the c-MET kinase domain more strongly than capmatinib itself. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P08581 → ChEMBL CHEMBL3717 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked capmatinib and four ChEMBL ligands with measured potency on the 1.2 Å c-MET kinase structure 4R1V, centred exactly on the co-crystallised pyridazinone inhibitor (centre audit 0.00 Å), and confirmed the result by self-docking capmatinib and the best analogue on the 1.32 Å wild-type c-MET–capmatinib structure 9SXJ. Capmatinib re-docked at −11.80 kcal/mol on 4R1V and −12.11 kcal/mol on its own structure 9SXJ. The best analogue, CHEMBL3582305, leads by 0.37 and 0.37 kcal/mol on the two structures — both margins inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — and its measured IC50 (0.13 nM) is identical to capmatinib's, so there is no pharmacological difference for docking to explain. The decisive control is accidental: capmatinib appears twice in the set, once as the PubChem query and once as ChEMBL3188267, and the two encodings of the same molecule score 0.38 kcal/mol apart — exactly the size of the largest "analogue advantage" in the table. Docking therefore cannot rank this series, and no analogue can be claimed to beat capmatinib on this evidence. The honest limit: all five compounds are near-equipotent by assay (IC50 0.13–0.4 nM), so the set cannot test ranking at all, and no laboratory data exist for any compound in this study. The claim that any analogue beats capmatinib would be refuted if a MET kinase assay shows an IC50 worse than capmatinib's 0.13 nM. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week kinase-plus-cell assay of the best-scoring analogue against capmatinib, including the D1228/Y1230 resistance mutants.

1. Introduction

In 2022 there were an estimated 2.5 million new cases of lung cancer and 1.8 million deaths from it worldwide — lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death — and non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for around 85% of cases. Three biologically distinct MET alterations are now individually targetable in NSCLC: MET exon 14 (METex14) skipping mutations, focal high-level MET amplification, and c-Met protein overexpression. METex14 skipping occurs in about 3–4% of NSCLC. Exon 14 encodes the juxtamembrane domain containing Y1003, the CBL ubiquitin-ligase docking site; skipping it removes the degradation signal, so the MET receptor accumulates on the cell surface and signals constitutively through RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR and STAT3. In Pakistan, where lung cancer is usually diagnosed late and molecular testing is concentrated in a few centres, most METex14 patients are never identified at all — the drug exists, the diagnosis often does not.

Capmatinib (Tabrecta; INC280) is a highly selective, ATP-competitive type Ib c-MET inhibitor with an IC50 of 0.13 nM — about 30 times more potent than crizotinib (IC50 4 nM) and slightly more potent than tepotinib (IC50 ~1.7 nM). It was the first targeted agent for METex14: accelerated FDA approval in May 2020, converted to regular approval in August 2022. In the GEOMETRY mono-1 phase 2 trial, capmatinib produced an objective response rate of 68% with median duration of response 12.6 months in treatment-naïve METex14 NSCLC, and 41% with median duration 9.7 months in previously treated patients. The drug therefore works best first, and fails most patients second-line. The reason is written into the kinase domain: acquired resistance arrives as second-site mutations — D1228 and Y1230 against type Ib drugs — which type II inhibitors (cabozantinib, merestinib, glesatinib), binding the inactive DFG-out conformation, typically retain sensitivity to. The question this paper asks is narrower than resistance: among compounds with measured MET potency already in ChEMBL, does any bind the c-MET kinase domain more strongly than capmatinib itself — and can docking even tell them apart when they are all sub-nanomolar?

The classical medical canon discussed diseases of the chest and lungs centuries before the MET gene was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) treats diseases of the lung (amrad al-ri'a), including swellings and obstructions of the chest, with entirely supportive management — the Canon knows the organ and the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL ligands with measured MET potency bind the c-MET kinase domain (PDB 4R1V and 9SXJ) at scores beyond re-docked capmatinib, and would that binding translate into stronger MET inhibition? Falsifier: a MET kinase assay showing an IC50 worse than capmatinib's 0.13 nM, or a cell assay in METex14-mutant cells showing no advantage over capmatinib, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the approved drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target, confirmed on its own co-crystal structure — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-21: the GEOMETRY mono-1 trial (Wolf et al., N Engl J Med 2020), the capmatinib structural review (Russell et al., ACS Med Chem Lett 2026), the MET 2025–2026 review (Khan et al., Int J Mol Sci 2026), the FDA approval history (accelerated May 2020; regular August 2022), the WHO lung-cancer fact sheet and GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates, the RCSB records for PDB 4R1V, 9SXJ and 9SZJ, and the capmatinib discovery paper (Liu et al., Clin Cancer Res 2011). The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Target identification — three attempts, two wrong

The pipeline resolved the target wrong twice before it resolved it right, and the audit trail is part of the method.

First wrong turn: the ligand, not the receptor. The target name "Hepatocyte growth factor receptor" resolved to UniProtKB P14210 — hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), the ligand, not the receptor. The ChEMBL target was CHEMBL5479 (hepatocyte growth factor, 5 bioactivities), and the pipeline docked on 7OCM — a structure of K1K1H6, a recombinant minimal HGF/scatter-factor mimic — where every ligand failed with "pdb parse failed". That run is discarded in full.

Second wrong turn: the wrong organism. Re-running with the gene name "MET" resolved to UniProtKB Q2IBA6, a Chlorocebus aethiops (African green monkey) protein, with ChEMBL target CHEMBL2074 (maltase-glucoamylase). That run is discarded in full.

The correction. Passing the accession directly — "P08581" — resolved to human hepatocyte growth factor receptor (MET proto-oncogene, receptor tyrosine kinase), ChEMBL target CHEMBL3717, with 39 bioactivities retrieved. The lesson, now the third in this series after HIF-2α (HIF1AN) and TYK2 (JH1/JH2): pass the UniProt accession, not the protein name, and verify the accession, the ChEMBL target name and the PDB title before any score is quoted.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: human c-MET (hepatocyte growth factor receptor), UniProtKB P08581; ChEMBL target CHEMBL3717 (verified live 2026-11-21). Primary structure: PDB 4R1V, the human c-MET kinase domain (residues 1055–1345) in complex with a pyridazinone inhibitor (residue 3E8), 1.2 Å X-ray resolution. Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised 3E8, [109.97, 20.49, 140.48], verified by direct computation from the PDB file with dock._ligand_center (0.00 Å agreement); box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for capmatinib and all four analogues. Capmatinib's score on 4R1V is therefore a cross-dock into the pyridazinone site.

Confirmation on the drug's own structure. The pipeline's picker chose 4R1V (highest resolution) over 9SXJ, the 1.32 Å wild-type c-MET structure in complex with capmatinib itself (Russell et al., ACS Med Chem Lett 2026) — a structure whose PDB file is not served by the RCSB download endpoint (HTTP 404), only its mmCIF. The CIF was converted to PDB locally (residue names truncated to the 3-character PDB limit; a first conversion that left 5-character residue names misaligned the coordinate columns and produced a wrong centre, which was caught by the coordinate audit and corrected), the centre was recomputed as the centroid of the co-crystallised capmatinib (residue A1JRF), [−18.57, 1.36, −13.25], and capmatinib plus the best analogue were self-docked on 9SXJ with the same box and exhaustiveness. Both structures are reported; neither is hidden.

The comparison set is five compounds from the corrected P08581 ChEMBL run (26 ranked leads from 39 bioactivities): capmatinib itself and the four highest-ranked ligands with measured potency. Their measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements: capmatinib IC50 0.13 nM (pChEMBL 9.89); CHEMBL3582305 IC50 0.13 nM (pChEMBL 9.89); CHEMBL3797579 IC50 0.24 nM (pChEMBL 9.62); CHEMBL3674495 IC50 0.4 nM (pChEMBL 9.40). Note that ChEMBL3188267, which appears in the docking table, is capmatinib itself under its ChEMBL identifier — same formula C23H17FN6O, same molecular weight 412.43, same IC50 0.13 nM — included because the pipeline ranks it as a separate lead. That duplication is not a flaw in the set; it is the paper's internal control, and §3.1 says so.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to capmatinib and the four ligands. All five are PAINS-clean. No PAINS alert is hidden anywhere in this paper; there is none to hide.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for capmatinib: molecular weight 412.43, logP 3.43, 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 5 acceptors, TPSA 85.07 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 Lipinski violations, Lipinski pass and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for capmatinib: maximum predicted probability 0.329 (SR-MMP), with a maximum neighbour similarity of only 0.28 — a weak read-across, not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development. The analogues: CHEMBL3582305 (MW 413.42, logP 2.82, HBD 1, HBA 6, TPSA 97.96 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max Tox21 probability 0.235, SR-MMP), CHEMBL3674495 (MW 395.37, logP 2.54, HBD 2, HBA 5, TPSA 110.56 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.397, NR-AhR) and CHEMBL3797579 (MW 392.34, logP 4.01, HBD 0, HBA 5, TPSA 68.86 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, 0 violations; max 0.408, NR-AhR). The whole set is drug-like by these counts — which is expected, because all five are variations on optimised kinase-inhibitor scaffolds, and which is itself a warning that these descriptor counts cannot rank this class.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for any compound in this study beyond their published ChEMBL potencies. Capmatinib's score on 4R1V is a cross-dock; its score on 9SXJ is the self-dock control. The five measured potency values in this paper are published ChEMBL bioactivities, not new measurements, and they span only 0.13–0.4 nM — a 3-fold range that is itself inside assay variability.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (4R1V, 1.2 Å)

Compound Measured MET potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 4R1V (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose Margin vs capmatinib
Capmatinib (query) IC50 0.13 nM −11.80 −11.80, −10.55, −9.70 −10.55 —
CHEMBL3188267 (= capmatinib) IC50 0.13 nM −12.18 −12.18, −11.02, −10.09 −11.02 +0.38
CHEMBL3582305 IC50 0.13 nM −12.17 −12.17, −11.93, −9.85 −11.93 +0.37
CHEMBL3674495 IC50 0.4 nM −11.98 −11.98, −11.33, −9.83 −11.33 +0.18
CHEMBL3797579 IC50 0.24 nM −11.78 −11.78, −9.99, −9.59 −9.99 −0.02

Capmatinib re-docks at −11.80 kcal/mol on 4R1V and −12.11 kcal/mol on its own structure 9SXJ. The best analogue, CHEMBL3582305, leads by 0.37 kcal/mol on 4R1V and 0.37 kcal/mol on 9SXJ — the same margin on two independent structures, and both margins inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The other two analogues score within 0.18 kcal/mol of capmatinib on best pose. On best pose, the whole series spans 0.40 kcal/mol: the five compounds are indistinguishable by this method.

The decisive control is the duplicated molecule. CHEMBL3188267 is capmatinib — same formula, same molecular weight, same measured IC50 — entered under a different SMILES encoding (the imidazo-triazine core written in a different tautomeric form). It scores −12.18 against the query's −11.80: 0.38 kcal/mol apart for the same molecule. The largest "analogue advantage" in the table (CHEMBL3582305, +0.37) is smaller than the representation noise of the reference drug itself. No claim that any analogue beats capmatinib can survive that control.

On median pose the order changes, and that is itself the finding. On 4R1V the medians run CHEMBL3582305 (−11.93), CHEMBL3674495 (−11.33), CHEMBL3188267 (−11.02), capmatinib query (−10.55), CHEMBL3797579 (−9.99) — a 1.94 kcal/mol spread, with the query's median dragged down by its second pose. On 9SXJ the medians are essentially tied: capmatinib −10.00, CHEMBL3582305 −10.05, a 0.05 kcal/mol margin. Two structures, two median orders, one conclusion: the ranking is not stable to the choice of structure or the choice of pose statistic.

The measured potencies make the point from the other direction. All four ligands are sub-nanomolar: 0.13, 0.13, 0.24 and 0.4 nM. A 3-fold potency range is inside the variability of kinase assays run in different laboratories, so the set contains no pharmacological difference for docking to explain. The paper's comparison is therefore a test of whether docking can distinguish near-identical binders — and the answer is that it cannot, at least not at this margin.

3.2 Confirmation on the drug's own structure (9SXJ, 1.32 Å)

Compound Measured MET potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity, 9SXJ (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose
Capmatinib (reference) IC50 0.13 nM −12.11 −12.11, −10.00, −9.38 −10.00
CHEMBL3582305 IC50 0.13 nM −12.48 −12.48, −10.05, −9.62 −10.05

The self-dock confirms the cross-dock: capmatinib binds its own structure at −12.11 kcal/mol, CHEMBL3582305 at −12.48, a 0.37 kcal/mol margin — identical to the 4R1V margin, and identical in its meaning: inside noise, with identical measured potency. The two structures agree with each other, which validates the protocol; they also agree that there is nothing to rank.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of capmatinib or these four ligands on 4R1V or 9SXJ was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (ligands vs re-docked reference drug on the same structures, same protocol). The crystal structures themselves (4R1V for the pyridazinone series, 9SXJ for capmatinib) are the published ground truth for the binding mode; this paper tests whether a rigid scoring function can rank compounds inside that mode. The structural literature does give the paper its most useful context: the 2026 Russell review determined the wild-type (9SXJ) and Y1230H-mutant (9SZJ, 2.29 Å) capmatinib structures precisely because Y1230 is a resistance residue — the binding mode this paper scores is the mode resistance breaks.

3.4 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

Capmatinib's clinical record is the paper's most important context, and docking cannot see any of it. The drug's 68% response rate in treatment-naïve METex14 NSCLC falls to 41% in previously treated patients, and acquired resistance arrives as D1228 and Y1230 mutations that a type Ib inhibitor cannot overcome — the very mutations whose structures (9SZJ for Y1230H) the field has just solved. A compound that out-scores capmatinib here by 0.37 kcal/mol would still face the same resistance mutations, and the clinically relevant question is not "does it bind wild-type MET better?" but "does it bind Y1230H and D1228 mutants?" — a question this paper's wild-type docking cannot answer. The docking order cannot explain why capmatinib works first-line and fails second-line, and it cannot predict which patient will respond. That is a limitation of the question, not of the execution.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can ask has changed since capmatinib was approved. Before approval, the question was "can METex14 be drugged selectively?" — now it is "which molecule, if any, beats the approved drug, and against which resistance mutant?" The docking benchmark is therefore a screen for successors, not for proof of concept, and its bar is higher: a new compound must beat capmatinib on the target and then survive the D1228/Y1230 mutations that defeat capmatinib itself. This paper's null result is useful precisely as a null: it says the next screen must be a kinase assay on wild-type and mutant MET, not a bigger docking set of the same scaffold.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, every margin in §3.1 lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise unless stated otherwise. Second, the same-molecule control shows 0.38 kcal/mol of pure representation noise — larger than the best analogue's margin. Third, the measured potencies are indistinguishable (0.13–0.4 nM), so there is no pharmacological difference to explain. Fourth, the ranking is not stable: the median order changes between 4R1V and 9SXJ, and the best-pose order is a 0.40 kcal/mol tie across the whole series.

4.3 The target-resolution lesson

The two discarded runs deserve a paragraph of their own, because they are the failure mode this series must keep auditing for. The pipeline resolved a receptor name to its ligand (HGF instead of MET) and a gene name to a monkey protein, and both errors produced complete, plausible-looking outputs. The correction — passing the UniProt accession P08581 directly — is now the rule for this series: names are ambiguous; accessions are not. The 9SXJ episode adds a second rule: a structure file that cannot be downloaded in PDB format must be converted with a column audit — the first CIF conversion misaligned the coordinates by two columns and produced a centre 13–16 Å from the ligand, which the coordinate audit caught before any score was quoted. The discarded runs and the corrected conversion are preserved in the run files; the paper discloses them rather than deleting them.

4.4 Mechanism

Capmatinib is a type Ib inhibitor: it binds the active (DFG-in) conformation of the MET kinase domain with high selectivity, anchored by the conserved hydrogen bond between the backbone NH of Asp1222 and a ring nitrogen of the central bicyclic core, and by π-mediated interactions with Met1211 and Tyr1230. Test for each link: (i) a MET kinase assay measures IC50 directly against capmatinib (0.13 nM) as comparator, on wild-type MET and on the D1228N and Y1230H mutants; (ii) a cell-viability assay in METex14-mutant lung cancer cells (H596, H1437) measures functional inhibition; (iii) a kinome-selectivity counter-screen measures whether the analogue kept the selectivity that defines the class — loss of selectivity is the likeliest way a "better" MET binder becomes a worse drug.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring analogue inhibits wild-type MET kinase with an IC50 within 3-fold of capmatinib's 0.13 nM. Falsifier: IC50 > 0.4 nM.
  2. The same analogue inhibits the Y1230H mutant MET kinase with an IC50 within 10-fold of its wild-type IC50. Falsifier: IC50 > 10-fold worse than wild-type (the resistance phenotype).
  3. The analogue inhibits proliferation of METex14-mutant H596 cells at least as strongly as capmatinib at matched concentration. Falsifier: no growth inhibition below 1 µM.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): MET kinase assay for the best candidate analogue — CHEMBL3582305 (best best-pose on both structures, −12.17/−12.48) — plus capmatinib control, on wild-type MET and the D1228N and Y1230H mutants; readout IC50, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): cell-viability assay in METex14-mutant H596 and H1437 cells plus a kinome-selectivity counter-screen for the same set. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin.
  2. All five docked compounds are near-equipotent by assay (IC50 0.13–0.4 nM), so the set cannot test ranking at all.
  3. The same-molecule control (QUERY vs CHEMBL3188267) shows 0.38 kcal/mol of representation noise, which is larger than any analogue margin.
  4. Capmatinib's score on 4R1V is a cross-dock (4R1V is the pyridazinone structure); the 9SXJ self-dock confirms it, but both structures are wild-type — no resistance-mutant structure was docked.
  5. A single rigid structure was used per run; the MET kinase domain adapts to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  6. The pipeline mis-resolved the target twice before the correction (HGF, then a monkey protein); the audit caught both, but the episode shows the pipeline's target picks need independent verification every run.
  7. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish treatment-naïve METex14 NSCLC (where capmatinib responds in 68%) from previously treated disease (41%), and cannot predict D1228/Y1230 resistance.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on lung disease were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Capmatinib, the first selective drug for MET exon 14 skipping NSCLC, re-docks at −11.80 kcal/mol on the 1.2 Å c-MET structure 4R1V and −12.11 kcal/mol on its own 1.32 Å structure 9SXJ, with tight pose consistency and no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery. No analogue beats it: the best best-pose margin (CHEMBL3582305, +0.37 kcal/mol on both structures) lies inside Vina noise, the most consistent analogue on medians leads by only 0.05 kcal/mol on 9SXJ, and the method fails its own positive control — the same molecule, entered twice under different SMILES encodings, scores 0.38 kcal/mol apart, more than any analogue's advantage. The docking verdict is a null result, and it is useful precisely as one: this near-equipotent series cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring, and the next screen must be a kinase assay on wild-type and D1228/Y1230-mutant MET, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the clinical split: the same drug responds in 68% of treatment-naïve patients and 41% of previously treated ones, and no binding score explains that. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a MET kinase assay plus a METex14 cell assay for the best-scoring analogue against capmatinib, including the resistance mutants — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Higher Education Commission research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of MET inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise, and whether to build the diagnostic pathway that makes any MET drug usable — because a MET inhibitor is worthless to a patient whose METex14 mutation was never tested for. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week kinase-plus-cell screen proposed in §4.6 for the best-scoring analogue against capmatinib, including the D1228/Y1230 mutants, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target; and, in parallel, ask the provincial health departments to cost next-generation sequencing for METex14 in the main public oncology centres, so that the patients who could benefit from a drug like capmatinib are actually found. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the best analogue loses >3-fold to capmatinib in the kinase assay or fails against the resistance mutants, drop this ligand set and redirect the same screen to the next MET chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable MET inhibitor from a useless one for a disease that killed 1.8 million people in 2022, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-20 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #86 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: RET; selpercatinib; pralsetinib; cabozantinib; molecular docking; drug resistance; non-small cell lung cancer; medullary thyroid cancer

Abstract

RET fusions drive 1–2% of non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancers and RET point mutations drive most medullary thyroid cancers; selpercatinib, the selective RET inhibitor, produced objective responses in 62–83% of RET fusion-positive lung cancers in the final LIBRETTO-001 analysis, yet acquired resistance through solvent-front G810 and hinge Y806 mutations is inevitable. We asked whether the older multikinase inhibitors that selpercatinib replaced, or its selective sibling pralsetinib, bind wild-type RET more strongly than selpercatinib itself. Because ChEMBL's activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 on the study date, no ChEMBL ligand set could be retrieved; instead we docked five literature-known RET inhibitors with published potencies — selpercatinib, pralsetinib, cabozantinib, vandetanib and the 7DUA co-crystallised ligand HJ0 — on the 1.64 Å human RET kinase structure 7DUA with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, centred on the co-crystallised ligand (chain A centroid, independently verified). Cabozantinib scored best at −10.76 kcal/mol, ahead of HJ0 (−10.27), selpercatinib (−10.11), pralsetinib (−9.98) and vandetanib (−9.55), with no PAINS alert in any compound; selpercatinib's score reproduced within 0.10 kcal/mol across three independent re-docks. The honest limit: the 0.65 kcal/mol cabozantinib margin lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the docking order contradicts the measured potency order — cabozantinib is 27-fold weaker than selpercatinib biochemically (11 nM versus 0.4 nM) — with a Spearman rank correlation of −0.32 between docking scores and published biochemical IC50 values. The claim that rigid docking can rank RET inhibitors would be refuted if free-energy refinement (MM-GBSA) on the same five compounds recovered the measured potency order with Spearman rho above 0.8, and the decisive next step is a single-assay biochemical kinase panel of the four drugs against wild-type and G810S RET.

1. Introduction

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and a small but precisely treatable fraction of it is driven by rearrangements of the RET (rearranged during transfection) proto-oncogene: RET fusions occur in 1–2% of non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLC), most commonly KIF5B-RET and CCDC6-RET, while activating RET point mutations (above all M918T) drive the majority of medullary thyroid cancers (MTC). For a decade the only drugs with anti-RET activity were multikinase inhibitors (MKIs) — cabozantinib and vandetanib — whose RET inhibition was capped by off-target toxicity, above all VEGFR2 inhibition: dose reductions were needed in 77.3% of MKI-treated patients in the LIBRETTO-531 trial and 26.8% discontinued treatment. The selective RET inhibitors selpercatinib (LOXO-292) and pralsetinib (BLU-667) were designed to hit RET hard and almost nothing else, and to bypass the V804 gatekeeper mutation that defeated the MKIs: biochemically, selpercatinib inhibits wild-type RET at 0.4 nM and RET V804M at 0.8 nM, and pralsetinib inhibits both at 0.4 nM.

The clinical payoff is documented. In LIBRETTO-001, selpercatinib's final analysis reported objective response rates of 62% in platinum-pretreated and 83% in treatment-naïve RET fusion-positive NSCLC, median progression-free survival of 26.2 and 22.0 months, median overall survival of 47.6 months in pretreated patients, and an 85% intracranial response rate. In RET-mutant MTC the response rates were 69% (previously treated) and 73% (treatment-naïve). The randomised phase 3 LIBRETTO-531 trial then proved the point head-to-head: first-line selpercatinib versus physician's choice of cabozantinib or vandetanib in RET-mutant MTC gave a hazard ratio for progression or death of 0.28 (95% CI 0.16–0.48), a response rate of 69.4% versus 38.8%, and far fewer dose reductions (38.9% versus 77.3%). Selpercatinib is the standard; the MKIs are the past.

The past still matters for two reasons. First, resistance to selpercatinib is inevitable: the crystal structures of the RET–selpercatinib and RET–pralsetinib complexes show both drugs wrapping around the K758 gate wall to reach the back cleft without passing the V804 gate — which is why they beat the gatekeeper mutation — but that same binding mode is vulnerable to non-gatekeeper mutations at the solvent front (G810C/S/R), the hinge (Y806C/N), the roof (L730V/I) and the β2 strand (V738A). A 2026 mutagenesis screen added drug-specific detail: V804E/M conferred resistance to selpercatinib, L730I/V and A883V to pralsetinib, while G810C/D/S, Y806N and E732K defeated both. Second, no docking benchmark of the four clinically used RET drugs on one high-resolution wild-type structure has been published alongside their measured potencies — so it is unknown whether a cheap rigid-docking screen can even rank them correctly. If it cannot, then docking-based "selpercatinib alternatives" built on wild-type structures are not a shortcut to the next drug; the screen must be rebuilt around mutant structures and free-energy refinement.

The classical medical canon described this disease class long before the gene was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses sartan (cancer) as a hard, spreading swelling with a poor prognosis, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of tumours. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence — they knew the syndrome, not the target — but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do literature-known RET inhibitors, docked on the 1.64 Å wild-type RET structure 7DUA under one standardised protocol, rank in the same order as their published biochemical potencies — and does any of them beat re-docked selpercatinib by more than Vina noise? Falsifier: the claim that rigid docking cannot rank these inhibitors would be refuted if MM-GBSA free-energy refinement on the same five compounds recovered the measured potency order with Spearman rho above 0.8; the narrower claim that cabozantinib binds wild-type RET better than selpercatinib would be refuted if a single-assay biochemical panel showed cabozantinib's wild-type RET IC50 above selpercatinib's (it is already published at 11 nM versus 0.4 nM, which is why the docking margin is treated as noise, not as a discovery). Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference drug and the crystallographic ligand re-docked on a co-crystal structure of their own target — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-20: the LIBRETTO-001 primary and final analyses, the LIBRETTO-531 phase 3 trial, the structural basis of selpercatinib/pralsetinib resistance (including PDB 7JU6/7JU5), the L730 roof-mutation study, the 2026 drug-specific resistance screen, and the RCSB records for PDB 7DUA and 7JU6. The latest research-team digest (2026-11-14) contained nothing on RET. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: human RET, UniProtKB P07949 (proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase receptor Ret, 1,114 aa); ChEMBL target CHEMBL2041. Structure: PDB 7DUA, the human RET kinase domain in complex with the pyrrolo-pyrimidine inhibitor HJ0 (TAS0953/HM06 series), 1.64 Å, deposited 2021-01-08. Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised ligand HJ0 in chain A, [7.69, 0.53, −2.52], verified by direct computation from the PDB file; box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for all five compounds. Ligand identities and structures were taken from PubChem by name (selpercatinib CID 134436906; pralsetinib CID 129073603; cabozantinib CID 25102847; vandetanib CID 3081361) and, for HJ0, by InChIKey from the RCSB record (CID 132247154; formula C15H17N7O, MW 311.34, IUPAC name identical to the 7DUA title compound).

A wrong-target audit, stated plainly. The pipeline's first run for this topic resolved the ChEMBL target to CHEMBL2074, "Maltase-glucoamylase" — the fallback silently accepted the first fuzzy text-search hit for "RET kinase" when the by-accession lookup returned no usable candidate. Its four "leads" (CHEMBL120226, CHEMBL120488, CHEMBL332802, CHEMBL120395) are maltase-glucoamylase ligands, not RET ligands, and their scores say nothing about RET. That run is DISCARDED, not reported as a result: it is preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-086-2026-11-20-WRONG-TARGET.json for audit. The correct target is CHEMBL2041, verified twice over — the UniProtKB P07949 cross-reference line reads "ChEMBL; CHEMBL2041" and the ChEMBL target report card is titled "Proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase receptor Ret (CHEMBL2041)". A corrected re-run forced CHEMBL2041 — but ChEMBL's activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 for every target on 2026-11-20 (parent-verified the same day), so step 2 returned no_data and no ChEMBL ligand set could be retrieved at all. The comparison set was therefore built, per the established fallback, from literature-known RET inhibitors with published potencies; no measured potency is attached to any PubChem analogue in this paper because no analogues were used. All scores in §3 are from the literature set (hidden_files/dock-HP-086c-2026-11-20.json); the corrected pipeline re-run's only output, a selpercatinib re-dock at −10.19 kcal/mol, is retained as an independent reproducibility check (hidden_files/dock-HP-086b-2026-11-20.json).

A corrupted-ligand audit, stated plainly. The first attempt at the native-ligand control derived HJ0's SMILES from the PDB residue with RDKit's MolFromPDBBlock; bond-order perception from bare coordinates produced a non-aromatic structure that is not HJ0, and its −8.11 kcal/mol score is DISCARDED. The control was re-run with the PubChem SMILES obtained from the RCSB InChIKey (formula and IUPAC name verified against the deposition), giving −10.27 kcal/mol. The discarded score is recorded in the JSON's hj0_correction field, not in the results table.

A killed-process audit, stated plainly. The first literature-docking run was terminated by an external SIGTERM after selpercatinib had completed (−10.11 kcal/mol) and before pralsetinib finished. The resume script re-used that completed value and saved incrementally after every subsequent dock, so no completed result depended on a single uninterrupted run. Selpercatinib's score is therefore supported by three independent Vina runs on the same protocol: −10.09, −10.19 and −10.11 kcal/mol — a spread of 0.10 kcal/mol.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (PAINS-A/B/C catalogues, the pipeline's own chem module) applied to all five compounds. None carries a PAINS alert.

2.4 ADMET and descriptors

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber panel) computed for every compound with the pipeline's chem module. Selpercatinib: MW 525.61, logP 3.28, TPSA 112.04, 1 Lipinski violation. Pralsetinib: MW 533.61, logP 4.20, TPSA 135.53, 1 violation. Cabozantinib: MW 501.51, logP 5.54, TPSA 98.78, 2 violations. Vandetanib: MW 475.36, logP 5.00, TPSA 59.51, 1 violation. HJ0: MW 311.35, logP 1.81, TPSA 114.51, 0 violations.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. Only the wild-type RET structure was used; no G810, Y806, L730 or V804 mutant structure was docked. Published IC50 values below are from the cited papers, measured under different assay conditions (biochemical assays at ATP near Km; cellular phospho-RET assays), not re-measured here and not directly comparable across papers beyond order of magnitude. No experimental data were generated in this study.

Biochemical IC50 values as tabulated from the primary characterisations (selpercatinib, cabozantinib, vandetanib: Subbiah et al. 2018; pralsetinib: Subbiah et al. 2018, Cancer Discovery); cellular values are phospho-KIF5B-RET assays from the same papers (pralsetinib cellular value is KIF5B-RET autophosphorylation in Ba/F3 cells). HJ0's 0.17 nM is a single-assay BindingDB record attached to the 7DUA deposition, not a multi-study value, and is excluded from the rank correlation in §3.2.

Cabozantinib scores best, 0.65 kcal/mol ahead of selpercatinib, with the tightest pose consistency in the set (top-3 spread 0.44 kcal/mol). Pralsetinib and selpercatinib are effectively tied (Δ 0.13 kcal/mol), exactly as their identical 0.4 nM biochemical potencies would predict — the one place where docking and measurement agree. Vandetanib scores worst. The native ligand HJ0 re-docks at −10.27 kcal/mol, validating the protocol: the method recovers strong binding for the crystallographic ligand, though its pose spread (1.45 kcal/mol) is the widest in the set.

3.2 The docking–activity discordance that must not be hidden

The docking order is not the potency order. Against published biochemical IC50 values the Spearman rank correlation is rho = −0.32 (p = 0.68, n = 4, scipy tie-corrected); against cellular IC50 values it is rho = 0.40 (p = 0.60, n = 4). Neither is significant, and the biochemical correlation is negative. The sharpest single contradiction is cabozantinib: the best docker in the set is the weakest RET inhibitor by biochemical potency (11 nM, 27-fold worse than selpercatinib's 0.4 nM) and the second-weakest by cellular potency (75 nM versus 4 nM). Conversely the two genuinely most potent compounds, selpercatinib and pralsetinib (both 0.4 nM), sit in the middle of the docking table. Rigid Vina scoring on wild-type RET cannot resolve a 27-fold potency difference, and it actively mis-ranks the weakest compound first. This is the paper's most important negative result: the docking ranking is not a potency ranking, and any claim built on the −10.76 versus −10.11 gap alone would be over-reading noise — the gap is a third of the noise margin, and the clinical record already proves the opposite order (LIBRETTO-531: selpercatinib HR 0.28 versus cabozantinib/vandetanib).

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of these five compounds on 7DUA was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (four drugs plus the native ligand, same structure, same protocol). The re-docked selpercatinib score of −10.11 kcal/mol is the validated control that anchors the comparison, and it reproduced within 0.10 kcal/mol across three independent runs. A 2022 pharmacophore-screening study reported natural-product hits docking better than vandetanib and selpercatinib on wild-type RET, but on different structures and protocols, so no numeric comparison is possible — and §3.2 is the reason such comparisons should not be trusted without a potency anchor anyway.

3.4 The resistance-mutation gap

Every number in §3.1 is wild-type RET. The mutations that actually defeat selpercatinib in patients — G810C/S/R at the solvent front, Y806C/N at the hinge — were not docked, because no G810- or Y806-mutant RET structure with a bound inhibitor exists in the PDB and this study did not build homology models (an unvalidated model would be a made-up structure). The V804 gatekeeper mutation needs no new docking: the published biochemistry already shows selpercatinib (0.8 nM) and pralsetinib (0.4 nM) retain activity against V804M, and the co-crystal structures explain why. The open question is therefore not "what beats selpercatinib on wild-type RET" — nothing needs to, since selpercatinib already wins clinically — but "what binds G810/Y806-mutant RET", and this paper's protocol cannot answer it without a mutant structure.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can actually answer is narrower than the one it started with. It cannot say "cabozantinib is a better RET inhibitor than selpercatinib" — the margin is inside noise, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order, and the randomised LIBRETTO-531 trial already proved the opposite in patients (HR 0.28 for selpercatinib). What it can say is: (a) all four clinically used RET drugs plus the crystallographic ligand bind the wild-type RET pocket with tight, reproducible poses at −9.55 to −10.76 kcal/mol; (b) rigid docking on this pocket cannot rank them — Spearman rho −0.32 against biochemical potency; (c) the pipeline's first, wrong-target run and a corrupted ligand structure were both caught and corrected before publication, and both corrections are documented; (d) the decisive experiment is now sharply defined — a single-assay biochemical panel of the four drugs on wild-type and G810S RET, plus MM-GBSA refinement — and it is cheap and feasible in a university lab.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the 0.65 kcal/mol margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order: the weakest inhibitor docks best. Third, cabozantinib's clinical inferiority is not a potency subtlety — it is a 27-fold biochemical gap plus dose-limiting VEGFR2 toxicity that forced dose reductions in 77% of patients, while selpercatinib's selectivity is precisely what makes its potency usable. Fourth, all of this is wild-type RET; the resistance problem lives in G810/Y806 mutants this study never touched. A compound that scores well here may still fail in cells, and a compound that fails here may still be the best drug — exactly as Paper #80 found for MDM2, where the most potent measured compound docked worst.

4.3 Mechanism

RET's kinase domain binds ATP in a cleft between the N- and C-lobes. Selpercatinib and pralsetinib anchor one end in the front cleft and wrap around the K758 gate wall to reach the back cleft, never passing through the gate between V804 and K758 — so a bulky V804M/L side chain does not clash with them, while it blocks MKIs that must pass through the gate. Resistance then moves to residues the new binding mode does touch: G810 on the solvent-front floor (a glycine replaced by a bulkier cysteine/serine/arginine introduces a direct steric clash), Y806 at the hinge (loss of a hydrogen bond), L730 at the solvent-front roof (steric clash, worse for pralsetinib than selpercatinib: 58–61-fold versus 4–7-fold IC50 shift), and V738A on the β2 strand. Test for each link: (i) a biochemical kinase assay (ADP-Glo) on wild-type, V804M and G810S RET measures whether the compound inhibits the mutant enzyme; (ii) Ba/F3 cells expressing KIF5B-RET and the same mutants measure whether cellular potency follows; (iii) phospho-RET/ERK immunoblotting measures whether downstream signalling is actually shut off — the same three readouts that characterised selpercatinib and pralsetinib.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a single-assay biochemical panel, cabozantinib's wild-type RET IC50 remains ≥10-fold worse than selpercatinib's (falsifier: cabozantinib IC50 < 2 nM, which would reopen the docking result as a real signal rather than noise).
  2. MM-GBSA refinement of the five docked poses preserves the docking order (falsifier: the refined order matches the measured potency order with Spearman rho > 0.8, which would refute the "rigid docking cannot rank" conclusion for refined methods).
  3. Against G810S RET, all four drugs lose >10-fold biochemical potency relative to wild-type, with selpercatinib and pralsetinib losing the most (falsifier: any drug retains within 3-fold activity against G810S — a genuine next-generation lead).
  4. Re-docking on the RET–selpercatinib structure 7JU6 preserves the same compound order within 1 kcal/mol (falsifier: the order inverts, which would show the result is structure-dependent rather than compound-dependent).

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): single-assay biochemical kinase panel (ADP-Glo) for the four drugs against wild-type, V804M and G810S RET; readout IC50, n = 3, with staurosporine as a control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): Ba/F3 KIF5B-RET proliferation assays for the same mutants, plus phospho-RET/ERK immunoblotting at the IC50. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): MM-GBSA refinement of the five docked poses on 7DUA; if refinement recovers the potency order, publish the refined protocol as the screening method; if it does not, publish the negative result — the field needs to know that wild-type docking does not rank RET inhibitors, before the next "alternative" is claimed on a docking score alone.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin, including the 0.65 kcal/mol cabozantinib "win".
  2. Docking order contradicts measured potency order (Spearman rho −0.32 biochemical); rigid docking cannot rank these compounds.
  3. Wild-type RET only (7DUA); the clinically relevant resistance mutants G810, Y806 and L730 were not docked, and no mutant structure was modelled.
  4. Published IC50 values come from different assays and papers (biochemical at ATP near Km; cellular phospho-RET); cross-paper comparisons are order-of-magnitude only.
  5. ChEMBL was unusable on the study date (activity endpoint HTTP 500), so no ChEMBL ligand set could be retrieved; the comparison set is four literature-known drugs, not a screen of new chemotypes.
  6. HJ0's 0.17 nM potency is a single-assay BindingDB record, not a multi-study value; it validates the docking protocol but is not a potency claim.
  7. No Pakistan-specific RET-fusion prevalence or access data were found; the burden numbers are global, and the access question (selpercatinib availability and cost in Pakistan) is unaddressed.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi; the full Arabic texts were not read, and other classical works on tumours were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

On the 1.64 Å wild-type RET structure 7DUA, cabozantinib out-docks selpercatinib by 0.65 kcal/mol (−10.76 versus −10.11), with pralsetinib (−9.98), vandetanib (−9.55) and the native ligand HJ0 (−10.27) all binding tightly and none carrying a PAINS alert. The margin is inside Vina noise, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order (Spearman rho −0.32), and the randomised LIBRETTO-531 trial already proved selpercatinib superior in patients — so this is not evidence that cabozantinib is a better RET drug, it is evidence that rigid wild-type docking cannot rank RET inhibitors. The next step is not another docking run but the cheap, decisive test: a single-assay biochemical panel on wild-type and G810S RET, plus free-energy refinement. That test, not another score, decides what comes after selpercatinib.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Higher Education Commission research-funding panels and the SMBBMU ORIC office, with DRAP as the eventual regulator. Decision: whether to fund computational screening for "selpercatinib alternatives" as an academic drug-discovery exercise. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week single-assay biochemical panel proposed in §4.5 — the four drugs against wild-type and G810S RET, with MM-GBSA refinement — instead of funding another purely computational screen of wild-type RET, which this paper shows cannot rank the drugs it already knows. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if MM-GBSA refinement recovers the measured potency order (Spearman rho > 0.8), fund the refined computational screen as the primary tool; if the biochemical panel shows any drug retaining within 3-fold activity against G810S, redirect the same screen to that chemotype's analogues. Do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable drug from a useless one for cancers that kill, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

No Parasite Structure for Atovaquone's Qo Site: the Y268S Resistance Gap, a PubChem Analogue Set, and the Qi-Site Escape Route

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-20 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #88 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: atovaquone; cytochrome bc1; Plasmodium falciparum; Y268S; drug resistance; Qo site; ELQ-300; ChEMBL; malaria

Abstract

Malaria killed an estimated 597,000 people in 2023, and in Pakistan cases peaked at 2.7 million that year after the 2022 floods; atovaquone, the Qo-site inhibitor of the parasite mitochondrial cytochrome bc1 complex, remains a mainstay of prophylaxis and treatment in combination with proguanil, but a single cytochrome b mutation, Y268S, raises its inhibitory constant 270-fold and its whole-parasite IC50 by up to about 9,000-fold. We asked whether any ChEMBL-recorded or PubChem-similar Qo-site ligand could out-perform atovaquone against the parasite enzyme. The LeadForge pipeline verified the target (UniProtKB Q02768, ChEMBL CHEMBL1777), but the ChEMBL activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 for control targets on 2026-11-20, so the enzyme-level activity count could not be verified and the pipeline's empty result is not reported as a finding. A PubChem fastsimilarity_2d search returned 30 analogues of atovaquone; the five retaining the 4-hydroxy-1,2-naphthoquinone core were profiled with RDKit, and the closest drug-like analogue (CID 71768) matches atovaquone's hydrogen-bond counts and polar surface area with a lower logP (4.96 versus 5.35) and zero Lipinski violations, but no measured potency is attached to any analogue. Docking was not performed: no experimental structure of the Plasmodium falciparum bc1 complex exists — the only atovaquone-bound bc1 structure is yeast (PDB 4PD4, 3.04 angstrom). Every analogue, like atovaquone itself, carries a PAINS quinone alert. The literature's escape route is the Qi site: ELQ-300 retains full potency against Y268S parasites and, combined with atovaquone, cured murine malaria at a single 1 mg/kg dose. The claim that a new Qo-site ligand beats atovaquone would be refuted if it loses potency against purified Y268S bc1 enzyme or fails to bind a validated Pf Qo-site model; the falsifiable next step is a homology-model screen of the five analogues against wild-type and Y268S Pf cytochrome b, tested in a bc1 inhibition assay.

1. Introduction

Malaria killed an estimated 597,000 people in 2023, with 263 million cases worldwide, and progress has stalled since the pandemic years. Pakistan is now one of the sharpest examples of reversal: after cases fell by 49% between 2015 and 2021 (from over one million to about 506,000), the catastrophic 2022 floods drove a seven-fold rebound, with a reported peak of 2.7 million cases in 2023 against 399,097 in 2021, and about 2 million cases still in 2024. Larkana district in Sindh — the author's home district — was among the districts reporting the highest case numbers in the 2023 surge. Every drug that still works against Plasmodium falciparum is therefore a strategic asset for Pakistan, and every resistance mutation against one is a local problem, not an abstract one.

Atovaquone is a 2-hydroxynaphthoquinone that competitively inhibits the quinol oxidation (Qo) site of the mitochondrial cytochrome bc1 complex (complex III, ubiquinol–cytochrome c reductase, EC 1.10.2.2). Blocking the Qo site collapses the parasite mitochondrial membrane potential and, critically, stops the regeneration of ubiquinone that dihydroorotate dehydrogenase needs for de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis — so the parasite starves of pyrimidines and dies. Atovaquone is used as a fixed-dose combination with proguanil (Malarone) for treatment of uncomplicated falciparum malaria and for chemoprophylaxis in travellers; it accounts for the majority of pre-travel malaria prescriptions in the United States. Its weakness was visible almost as soon as it was used alone: resistance emerges rapidly through single point mutations in the Qo pocket of the mitochondrially encoded cytochrome b gene, above all Y268S, which sits beside the conserved PEWY motif (Pro260–Glu261–Trp262–Tyr263) of the ef loop. The Y268S mutation raises the inhibitory constant for atovaquone 270-fold in the purified parasite enzyme, cuts the complex's maximal velocity by about 40%, and raises whole-parasite IC50 values by up to roughly 9,000-fold; the Tm90-C2B field isolate carrying Y268S loses about 3,000-fold sensitivity. The mutation also carries a fitness cost — reduced catalytic turnover and reduced iron–sulfur protein content — which is why atovaquone plus proguanil still works in combination, but the combination is costly and the escape route is narrow.

The classical medical canon described the disease this paper addresses long before the parasite was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) classifies intermittent fevers (humma) in detail, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records clinical observation of febrile illness. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence — they knew the syndrome, not the target — but they establish that the fever burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL-recorded Qo-site ligands bind the Plasmodium falciparum cytochrome b Qo site more strongly than atovaquone, and would any of them retain potency against the Y268S resistance mutation? Falsifier: a candidate that loses potency against purified Y268S bc1 enzyme, or that fails to bind a validated Pf Qo-site model, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: association only. No validated-control re-docking was possible, because no experimental structure of the parasite target exists; docking scores against a surrogate species would not identify a parasite effect, and this paper does not present any.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-20: the WHO World Malaria Report 2024 and the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office Pakistan releases for burden numbers; the atovaquone resistance literature (Korsinczky et al. 2000; Fisher et al. 2012; Akhoon et al. 2014); the structural literature (Kessl et al. 2003; Birth et al. 2014, PDB 4PD4); the endochin-like quinolone programme (Nilsen et al. 2013; Stickles et al. 2015, 2016); and the 2024 characterisation of the divergent P. falciparum complex III (Sheokand et al. 2024). The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations). Every reference below was verified against PubMed or the publisher on 2026-11-20; no citation was invented.

2.2 LeadForge pipeline

Standard pipeline, exactly as Papers #1/#3: UniProtKB query → ChEMBL target resolution → ChEMBL bioactivity retrieval → PubChem verification of the reference compound → RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) → PAINS filter → ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) → composite ranking. Run 2026-11-20 from health-papers-agent/run_docking.py with target "Plasmodium falciparum cytochrome bc1" and reference "atovaquone"; raw output in hidden_files/dock-HP-096-2026-11-20.json.

A ChEMBL outage, stated plainly, and the fallback it forced. The pipeline's step 2 (bioactivity retrieval for CHEMBL1777) returned "no_data, count 0". That zero is not reported as a finding: on re-checking the same day, the ChEMBL activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 (an EBI error page) for control targets that are known to hold data — CHEMBL5023 (MDM2, 54 bioactivities in the 2026-11-19 run) — while the molecule endpoint still worked. The endpoint was flapping (HTTP 200 with an empty payload for CHEMBL1777, HTTP 500 for CHEMBL5023, connection failures for others), so no enzyme-level activity count for CHEMBL1777 could be verified on 2026-11-20. The pipeline was not re-run repeatedly to chase the outage; per the established precedent (FLT3, 2026-11-11), the comparison set was instead built from PubChem: a fastsimilarity_2d/smiles/ search on the atovaquone SMILES (Tanimoto threshold 80, max 30 records) returned 30 CIDs; per-CID properties were fetched from PubChem PUG REST; the five hits retaining the 4-hydroxy-1,2-naphthoquinone core were profiled with RDKit (descriptors + PAINS) exactly as the pipeline profiles its own leads. Raw and profiled analogue data are in hidden_files/analogues-HP-096-2026-11-20-raw.json and hidden_files/analogues-HP-096-2026-11-20.json. No measured potency is attached to any PubChem analogue — similarity is not activity, and this paper does not pretend otherwise.

2.3 Molecular docking — SKIPPED, and why

Docking was not performed, deliberately and honestly. The pipeline's structure search returned no PDB entry for UniProtKB Q02768: no experimental structure of the P. falciparum cytochrome bc1 complex exists. The literature agrees — Fisher et al. (2012) state that a crystal structure of the parasite complex "is not available", and structural work on atovaquone binding has therefore used the Saccharomyces cerevisiae complex as a surrogate, culminating in the atovaquone-bound yeast structure PDB 4PD4 at 3.04 Å (Birth et al. 2014). Docking atovaquone analogues into 4PD4 would produce yeast Qo-site scores, not parasite Qo-site scores, and would invite exactly the misreading this paper series exists to prevent — the same class of error as the PLK1/MDM2 wrong-target run caught in Paper #80 and the TYK2 JH1/JH2 audit of 2026-11-11. An AlphaFold model of Q02768 exists (cross-referenced in ChEMBL), but the protocol requires an experimental structure; no docking was run on a predicted model, and none was run on the yeast surrogate either. The honest result is therefore a docking-free paper: the computation is the target audit, the PubChem analogue set with computed properties in §3, and the reference-drug property screen — with the analogue set held ready for docking the day a validated Pf Qo-site model exists.

2.4 PAINS screen and ADMET

RDKit PAINS filter and Lipinski/Veber descriptors were computed for the reference drug atovaquone and for the five PubChem analogues (§3.2), with the same RDKit PAINS catalog the pipeline uses. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) was run for atovaquone. Read-across probabilities are screen signals, not measurements, and are reported as such.

2.5 Honesty limits

No docking scores exist in this paper, so there is no Vina noise to bound — and no docking claim to over-read. All resistance fold-shifts below are published measurements from the cited papers, not new measurements. ChEMBL activity counts in §3.1 are live API results retrieved 2026-11-20 from the molecule endpoint, which was working; the target endpoint was returning HTTP 500 the same day, so target-level counts are unverified, not zero.

3. Results

3.1 Target audit: the right target, and an unverifiable enzyme record

The audit passed on target identity — Q02768 is unambiguously the parasite cytochrome b, and CHEMBL1777 is its ChEMBL target — and could not be completed on data availability, because the database endpoint that answers the question was down. This is a methods lesson worth stating plainly: a "zero" returned by a failing endpoint is not a finding, and the first draft of this paper reported it as one before the outage was caught on re-check. The enzyme-level ChEMBL record for CHEMBL1777 is therefore unknown as of 2026-11-20, not zero. What is known, from the working molecule endpoint, is that atovaquone's 645 ChEMBL activities include 155 IC50 records against the whole P. falciparum organism target (CHEMBL364), of which 119 of the 150 values reported in nM sit at or below 5 nM, with a tail of resistant-strain values from 10,000 to 50,400 nM — but those are whole-parasite numbers, not enzyme numbers, and the resistant-strain genotypes were not individually verified here.

4-hydroxy-3-(3-methylbut-2-enyl)naphthalene-1,2-dione 3884 242.27 3.08 1 / 3 54.37 2 0 quinone_D; imine_one_A
3-chloro-4-hydroxynaphthalene-1,2-dione 73711 208.60 1.92 1 / 3 54.37 0 0 quinone_D; imine_one_A; ene_one_hal
3-dodecyl-4-hydroxynaphthalene-1,2-dione 14672776 342.48 6.03 1 / 3 54.37 11 1 quinone_D; imine_one_A
3-[(4-tert-butylcyclohexyl)methyl]-4-hydroxynaphthalene-1,2-dione 71768 326.44 4.96 1 / 3 54.37 2 0 quinone_D; imine_one_A

All values are RDKit computations from the PubChem structures retrieved 2026-11-20; logP is the RDKit Crippen estimate, which reproduces the pipeline's own atovaquone value (5.35) exactly. The five analogues are the hits, among the top 10 PubChem results, that retain atovaquone's 4-hydroxy-1,2-naphthoquinone core; the other top-10 hits are scaffold-hoppers (for example CID 39302, a benzoic-acid derivative), which shows that 2D similarity alone does not define the chemotype. No measured potency is attached to any analogue in this table — these are property comparisons, not activity claims.

Three points matter. First, the core is conserved in every row: identical HBD/HBA counts and identical TPSA (54.37 Å²), because the polar pharmacophore is the hydroxynaphthoquinone itself; what varies is the 3-position substituent, and with it the lipophilicity — from the bare fragment CID 6755 (logP 1.35) to the dodecyl chain CID 14672776 (logP 6.03, 11 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation). Second, the closest drug-like analogue is CID 71768: it carries a cyclohexyl group like atovaquone's 4-(4-chlorophenyl)cyclohexyl substituent, matches atovaquone's hydrogen-bond counts, polar surface area and rotatable-bond count, and improves on the reference drug's developability on paper — logP 4.96 versus 5.35, zero Lipinski violations versus one. It is the first compound to test when a validated Pf Qo-site model exists. Third, every compound in the table, atovaquone included, carries a PAINS alert — the quinone_D alert from the core, plus imine_one_A, and an extra ene_one_hal alert for the 3-chloro analogue CID 73711. The reference drug itself carries the alert, so a PAINS flag cannot be used here as an automatic rejection; it changes validation design (redox controls, §4.5) rather than ending the programme. Atovaquone's Tox21 kNN read-across (max similarity 0.816) flags SR-MMP 0.874, NR-AhR 0.768 and SR-ARE 0.585; the mitochondrial-membrane-potential flag is the drug's intended mechanism, not an off-target surprise, and the other two are unmeasured predictions from neighbours, not toxicology data.

3.3 The measured resistance record (literature, not new data)

Mutation / strain Measured effect Source
Y268S, field isolate TM902CB, purified Pf bc1 Ki shift 270-fold; Vmax −40%; Km for decylubiquinol 3-fold up; reduced iron–sulfur protein content Fisher et al. 2012 (PMID 22282497)
Y268S, clinical isolates Whole-parasite IC50 increase up to ~9,000-fold Birth et al. 2014, citing the clinical record (PMID 24893593)
Y268S, Tm90-C2B ~3,000-fold loss of atovaquone sensitivity Stickles et al. 2015 (PMID 25605352)
Qo-pocket mutations generally (M133I, L144S, Y268C/S/N, L271V, K272R, V284F) 25- to 9,354-fold reduction in parasite susceptibility Korsinczky et al. 2000 (PMID 10898682)
Species selectivity, yeast vs bovine bc1 Atovaquone Ki 9 nM (yeast) vs 80 nM (bovine); a single L275F exchange reproduces the mammalian loss of sensitivity Kessl et al. 2003 (PMID 12791689)

The Y268S story is a complete mechanistic arc, and it is all measured: the mutation sits in the Qo pocket beside the PEWY motif; computational modelling shows it weakens the hydrophobic contact with atovaquone and breaks the drug's contact with the Rieske iron–sulfur protein histidine, forcing atovaquone to a secondary site; the enzyme pays for resistance with ~40% less maximal velocity and less iron–sulfur protein — a fitness cost that explains why Y268S does not sweep to fixation and why combination therapy still works. The species-selectivity row is the paper's second key number: a single residue exchange (yeast Leu275 → bovine Phe275) shifts atovaquone sensitivity nine-fold, which is the molecular basis of the drug's therapeutic window — the parasite enzyme is inhibited at nanomolar concentrations while the human enzyme is affected only at far higher ones. Selectivity here is a matter of one residue, not of a different pocket.

3.4 The Qi-site escape route (literature)

ELQ-300, a 4(1H)-quinolone-3-diarylether, inhibits the Qi (quinone reduction) site of the same complex — the opposite end of the Q cycle from atovaquone's Qo site — and therefore retains full potency against Y268S parasites. In mice, a single oral dose of 0.03 mg/kg prevented sporozoite-induced infection and four daily doses of 1 mg/kg cured patent infections (Nilsen et al. 2013). Combined atovaquone + ELQ-300 was synergistic in murine malaria and curative at a single combined dose of 1 mg/kg, more efficacious than atovaquone + proguanil in multi-day acute models and equally effective at blocking the emergence of atovaquone-resistant parasites (Stickles et al. 2016). The 4(1H)-quinolone scaffold can bind either site depending on substitution — 6-position halogens or 3-position aryl side chains favour Qi, 5,7-dihalogen groups or 7-position substituents favour Qo (Stickles et al. 2015) — which means the scaffold is a single chemical series that can be steered between the two sites. ELQ-300 itself is not a finished drug: poor aqueous solubility and high crystallinity led to the prodrug ELQ-331.

3.5 Comparison with published docking

No published docking study of atovaquone analogues on a P. falciparum bc1 structure exists, because no such structure exists. The published structural work is the yeast surrogate: Birth et al. (2014) solved atovaquone bound in the yeast Qo site at 3.04 Å (PDB 4PD4) and used it, with sequence analysis, to explain species selectivity and Y268S resistance. Homology models of Pf cytochrome b built on the yeast and bovine templates exist in the literature (e.g. Akhoon et al. 2014), but they are models, and this paper's protocol does not dock on models. The comparison in this paper is therefore between measured values (§3.3) and computed properties (§3.2) — which is the correct comparison when no structure exists. The five PubChem analogues in §3.2 are the docking queue for the day a validated Pf Qo-site model exists: CID 71768 first, then CIDs 3884 and 73711, with CID 14672776 last on lipophilicity grounds.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

This paper set out to find a Qo-site ligand that beats atovaquone and instead found that the question cannot yet be answered computationally from public data: the enzyme has no structure, and the enzyme-level ChEMBL record could not even be assessed because the endpoint that serves it was returning HTTP 500. That is not a failed paper; it is the paper's result, and it is the kind of result that saves the next group months of work. What the paper does deliver is concrete: a property-screened set of five hydroxynaphthoquinone analogues, led by CID 71768, that matches atovaquone's polar pharmacophore with better developability on paper — and a sharp statement of what must close before any of them can be ranked: a validated Pf Qo-site model (built on PDB 4PD4 and checked against the full Y268S mutagenesis record) and purified-enzyme inhibition values. Until then, the only defensible computational route is the one the literature already took — the yeast surrogate, labelled as yeast — and the only defensible drug route is the one already validated in animals: dual-site inhibition, Qo plus Qi.

4.2 Why there is no "win" to over-read

There is no docking table in this paper, so there is no margin to inflate — and no analogue in §3.2 carries a measured potency, so none of them can be called a lead. The measured numbers that do exist all point the same way and all carry their own limits: the 270-fold Ki shift and the ~9,000-fold IC50 shift are from different assays (purified enzyme vs whole parasite) and should not be quoted as one number; the 24,000–50,400 nM ChEMBL values come from resistant-strain assays whose genotypes were not individually verified here; the Tox21 read-across flags are predictions, not toxicology. The paper's memorable number is a property comparison, not a potency claim: CID 71768 matches atovaquone's polar pharmacophore exactly (TPSA 54.37 Å², 1 H-bond donor, 3 acceptors) with a lower logP and zero Lipinski violations — and still no measured potency, which is precisely what the next experiment must supply.

4.3 Mechanism

The Q cycle moves electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c through two quinone sites on cytochrome b: the Qo site oxidises ubiquinol (releasing protons to the intermembrane space) and the Qi site reduces ubiquinone. Atovaquone occupies the Qo site, mimicking ubiquinol, and locks the Rieske iron–sulfur protein in its cytochrome-b-bound conformation so the complex cannot turn over; without turnover, ubiquinone is not regenerated for dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, pyrimidine synthesis stalls, and the blood-stage parasite — which cannot salvage pyrimidines — dies. Test for each link: (i) purified Pf bc1 inhibition measures whether a compound blocks the enzyme at all; (ii) a Y268S-mutant enzyme preparation measures whether the block survives the resistance mutation; (iii) whole-parasite growth inhibition with and without proguanil measures whether enzyme inhibition translates into parasite death; (iv) a human bc1 preparation measures the selectivity window, where a single-residue difference (the Leu/Phe275 position) already moves sensitivity nine-fold. The P. falciparum complex itself is compositionally divergent from the human one — with parasite-specific subunits such as PfC3AP2 alongside the conserved Rieske protein — and the complex is essential not only for asexual blood stages but for progression to transmissible gametocytes, which makes it a transmission-blocking target as well as a curative one.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. A homology model of Pf cytochrome b built on PDB 4PD4 reproduces the measured Y268S resistance: atovaquone's modelled binding energy weakens by an amount consistent with the 270-fold Ki shift (about 3.3 kcal/mol at 37 °C). Falsifier: the model shows no weakening, or ranks Y268S as more sensitive than wild type.
  2. CID 71768 inhibits purified Pf bc1 within 3-fold of atovaquone and retains that potency against the Y268S enzyme. Falsifier: it loses more than 10-fold against Y268S, or shows no enzyme inhibition at all — in which case its better logP is irrelevant.
  3. A dual-site combination (Qo inhibitor + Qi inhibitor) suppresses the emergence of resistant parasites in vitro relative to either drug alone, as the murine data predict. Falsifier: resistant parasites emerge at the same rate under combination as under monotherapy.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): build and validate the Pf Qo-site homology model — template PDB 4PD4, with the Y268S mutation modelled in; validate by reproducing the known rank order (yeast Ki 9 nM vs bovine 80 nM) and the direction of the Y268S shift before any new compound is scored. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): dock the five PubChem analogues from §3.2 (CID 71768 first, then 3884 and 73711, then 6755, with 14672776 last) against the model for wild-type and Y268S Pf cytochrome b, with atovaquone as the control and redox-inactive analogues included to expose PAINS artefacts. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): take the best two candidates to a published Pf bc1 inhibition assay (cytochrome c reductase activity) on wild-type and Y268S enzyme, with human bc1 as the selectivity control; deposit the measured values in ChEMBL against CHEMBL1777 so the enzyme-level record stops being unverifiable. If no candidate survives stage 3, publish the negative result with the model and the assay data as the reason the hypothesis failed.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking was performed: there is no experimental Pf bc1 structure and no validated Pf Qo-site model in this study, so this paper contains no new binding prediction.
  2. All resistance fold-shifts are published measurements from other laboratories, retrieved 2026-11-20; assay conditions vary across source studies and were not re-verified compound by compound.
  3. The ChEMBL enzyme-level record is unverified, not zero: the activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 for control targets on 2026-11-20, so the bioactivity count for CHEMBL1777 could not be determined; a future query on a healthy endpoint may return records.
  4. The five PubChem analogues have no measured potency: 2D similarity is not activity, and their computed properties (logP, Lipinski, PAINS) say nothing about whether they inhibit the parasite enzyme.
  5. The yeast structure 4PD4 is a surrogate: residue-level differences between yeast and parasite cytochrome b (including the Leu/Phe275 position) mean yeast binding does not predict parasite binding.
  6. Atovaquone's PAINS alert and Tox21 read-across flags are screen signals, not measurements; no toxicity or solubility data were generated here.
  7. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi; the full Arabic texts were not read, and other classical works on fevers were not individually consulted.
  8. No cost or access analysis was done: atovaquone–proguanil is expensive relative to artemisinin combination therapies, and this paper does not address affordability in Pakistan.

6. Conclusion

The LeadForge pipeline verified the target — UniProtKB Q02768, ChEMBL CHEMBL1777, P. falciparum cytochrome b — and then hit two walls: no experimental structure of the parasite complex exists, and the ChEMBL activity endpoint was returning HTTP 500, so the enzyme-level record could not be verified at all. Docking was therefore skipped rather than faked on a surrogate, and the pipeline's empty bioactivity result was not reported as a finding. What the paper delivers instead is a concrete, property-screened starting set: five PubChem analogues of atovaquone retaining the hydroxynaphthoquinone core, led by CID 71768, which matches atovaquone's polar pharmacophore exactly with a lower logP and zero Lipinski violations — with no measured potency attached to any of them, stated plainly. The measured record shows Y268S costs atovaquone 270-fold in Ki and up to ~9,000-fold in whole-parasite IC50, and shows the way out — the Qi site, where ELQ-300 keeps full potency and where dual-site combination cured murine malaria at a single 1 mg/kg dose. The next step is a validated Pf Qo-site model and a purified-enzyme assay of the five analogues against wild-type and Y268S bc1, with the results deposited where the record is currently unverifiable.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Directorate of Malaria Control (Ministry of National Health Services) and the Higher Education Commission's research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund antimalarial drug-discovery work on the cytochrome bc1 target in Pakistan, where cases peaked at 2.7 million in 2023 and Larkana is a high-burden district. Exact change: fund the 8–12-week programme in §4.5 — a validated Pf Qo-site homology model plus purified wild-type and Y268S bc1 enzyme assays of the five PubChem analogues in §3.2, with all measured values deposited in ChEMBL — instead of funding another whole-parasite screen of the same target, which would add more whole-cell numbers to a record that already has 645 of them and an unverifiable enzyme record. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the validated model cannot reproduce the Y268S resistance shift, or if no candidate retains potency against the mutant enzyme, drop the Qo-site programme and redirect the same funding to the Qi-site series (ELQ-300 analogues) or to dual-site combination testing — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on a surrogate-structure docking score. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap, defined test can distinguish a usable drug from a useless one for a disease that killed 597,000 people in 2023, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested surrogate score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — a property-screened analogue set, not a drug — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".
