The Fosfomycin Benchmark Is Broken: Non-Covalent Docking Cannot Rank MurA Inhibitors When the Reference Drug Is Covalent

Fosfomycin is the only clinically used inhibitor of MurA, the first enzyme of bacterial peptidoglycan synthesis, and it works by a covalent bond to the active-site cysteine Cys115 — a mechanism no non-covalent docking score can price.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-20 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #89 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: MurA; fosfomycin; covalent inhibition; molecular docking; ChEMBL; antimicrobial resistance; Escherichia coli; urinary tract infection

Abstract

Fosfomycin is the only clinically used inhibitor of MurA, the first enzyme of bacterial peptidoglycan synthesis, and it works by a covalent bond to the active-site cysteine Cys115 — a mechanism no non-covalent docking score can price. We asked whether ChEMBL-recorded MurA inhibitors and published non-covalent leads genuinely out-bind fosfomycin, or whether the comparison itself is broken. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P0A749 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL1984 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on the 1.7 Å Escherichia coli MurA structure 3KQJ, grid centred on the co-crystallised UDP-N-acetylglucosamine), we re-docked fosfomycin and eight candidates on identical settings. Fosfomycin's non-covalent score is only −5.04 kcal/mol, yet its measured ChEMBL IC50 is 100 nM; seven of eight candidates out-score it, the best by 5.83 kcal/mol (CHEMBL5219133, −10.87 kcal/mol), and the most potent measured non-covalent inhibitor, ampelopsin (480 nM), scores −8.65 kcal/mol. The ranking is inverted against measured potency (Spearman ρ = −0.37, n = 6): the two best dockers are the weakest measured inhibitors (4.5–4.8 µM), and both carry logP 6.5–7.0 with two Lipinski violations. The honest limit is that a Vina score cannot rank a covalent drug against non-covalent candidates, the margins exceed Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise only because the benchmark is meaningless, and the two flavonoid leads carry PAINS alerts. The claim that any candidate beats fosfomycin would be refuted if a MurA enzyme assay shows an IC50 above 50 µM, or if the candidate fails against the fosfomycin-resistant C115D mutant. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week enzyme-plus-MIC test of the two best dockers and ampelopsin against wild-type and C115D MurA.

1. Introduction

Antimicrobial resistance killed an estimated 1.27 million people directly in 2019, with a further 4.95 million deaths associated with resistant infection, and Escherichia coli was the leading pathogen in that burden. Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) causes more than 75% of urinary tract infections, the commonest bacterial infection of primary care, and fosfomycin — a 1969 natural product, a phosphoenolpyruvate analogue — is one of the few oral options left for multidrug-resistant UPEC. Its target, MurA (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine enolpyruvyl transferase, EC 2.5.1.7), catalyses the first committed step of peptidoglycan synthesis, the transfer of the enolpyruvyl moiety of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to UDP-N-acetylglucosamine. MurA has no mammalian counterpart, which makes it a clean antibacterial target in principle — and fosfomycin is still the only drug in the clinic that hits it.

Fosfomycin's potency is covalent. Its epoxide is opened by nucleophilic attack from the thiol of Cys115 in the MurA active site, forming a stable thioether that irreversibly inactivates the enzyme. The residue is not a passive anchor: replacing Cys115 with aspartate leaves a highly active enzyme that is fully resistant to time-dependent inactivation by fosfomycin, and the same Cys→Asp substitution is how mycobacteria and chlamydiae are intrinsically fosfomycin-resistant. Structural work then showed Cys115 is essential for product release rather than for the chemistry of enolpyruvyl transfer itself. Resistance in the clinic, however, most often bypasses the target altogether: mutations in the GlpT and UhpT transporters that carry fosfomycin into the cell, and plasmid-borne fosfomycin-inactivating enzymes — FosA (a glutathione S-transferase), of which FosA3 is the most widespread. In a 2024 study of 337 clinical UPEC isolates, 77% formed fosfomycin non-susceptible inner colonies during susceptibility testing, and loss of uhpT imposed no fitness cost in a murine urinary-tract model; a 2026 cohort of 158 UPEC isolates found 9.5% fosfomycin resistance, with fosA3 present in a third of the resistant strains. A non-covalent MurA inhibitor that does not need Cys115, GlpT or UhpT would sidestep all three routes at once — which is why the field keeps searching for one, and why every new candidate is routinely "benchmarked" against fosfomycin by docking.

That benchmark is the problem this paper attacks. AutoDock Vina scores non-covalent complementarity only. It has no term for the covalent bond that supplies most of fosfomycin's potency, so fosfomycin's docking score measures only its weak reversible pre-complex — and any candidate that "beats" that score has beaten a straw man. The published literature already hints at the trap: a 2026 MurA docking study reported fosfomycin's non-covalent component at −4.5 kcal/mol while its optimised non-covalent ligands scored −7.3 to −7.7 kcal/mol, and presented that gap as progress. It is not evidence of progress; it is evidence that the ruler is wrong.

The classical medical canon knew the disease class long before the target: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025), Book II, catalogues plant materia medica for urinary and febrile illness, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records clinical observation of infections. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence — they knew the syndrome, not the enzyme — but the two plant flavonoids tested here (ampelopsin, quercetin) sit directly in that tradition, and the Islamic principle behind acting on resistance is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL-recorded MurA inhibitors and published non-covalent leads bind the true MurA active site (PDB 3KQJ) at scores beyond re-docked fosfomycin, and does that binding track measured potency? Falsifier: a MurA enzyme assay IC50 above 50 µM for a candidate, or loss of activity against the fosfomycin-resistant C115D mutant for a supposedly non-covalent inhibitor, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and for a covalent reference they are not even a ranking.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-20: the fosfomycin–MurA mechanism and Cys115 literature (structure, C115D mutant, product-release role), the ChEMBL record for E. coli MurA, recent non-covalent MurA inhibitor reports (flavonoids, pyrazolopyrimidines, machine-learning leads, repurposed drugs), and current fosfomycin-resistance surveillance. The daily research digest of 2026-11-14 was checked and carried no MurA-specific item; the topic rests on the targeted searches above. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025), Book II; Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

An EBI-side outage, caught and corrected. The LeadForge pipeline's ChEMBL bioactivity retrieval returned 0 records for target CHEMBL1984 and therefore ranked only fosfomycin itself as a "lead". That zero is an EBI-side outage, not a wrong target and not a pipeline bug: the ChEMBL activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 for this target on 2026-11-20 (verified twice the same day, including by a direct check that returned HTTP 500 for the activity endpoint while the target endpoint itself returned HTTP 200), while direct activity queries made during the audit, in windows when the endpoint answered, show the target holds 522 bioactivities, including 119 nM IC50 records. The outage is reported here, not hidden: all ChEMBL activity values in this paper come from direct ChEMBL API queries that returned successfully during the audit, and the supplementary docking script that uses them is preserved with the run. The most potent ChEMBL record for MurA is fosfomycin itself (CHEMBL1757, IC50 100 nM, assay CHEMBL2339337); the most potent non-fosfomycin record is CHEMBL2335230 at 2.8 µM. Older IC50 records in µg/mL from a single early assay (CHEMBL859884) were not used for ranking, because mass units without molar conversion cannot be ranked against nM records.

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: E. coli MurA, UniProtKB P0A749 (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 1-carboxyvinyltransferase, 419 aa, gene murA); ChEMBL target CHEMBL1984 (E. coli K-12, single protein, component P0A749). Structure: PDB 3KQJ, the E. coli MurA binary complex with UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, 1.7 Å. Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (HETATM UD1, chain A), [60.69, −44.29, 115.28], verified by direct computation with dock._ligand_center on the cached PDB file — the computed centre [60.693, −44.292, 115.277] matches the pipeline centre exactly, and the picker correctly ignored the isoaspartate residue, glycerol and phosphate in the file. Box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for fosfomycin and all eight candidates. The structure is the closed, substrate-bound conformation: the active site is formed, which is the correct state for docking PEP-site binders. The classic fosfomycin co-crystal, 1UAE (1.8 Å, Skarzynski et al. 1996), was not used because 3KQJ is higher resolution and carries the same active-site geometry with the natural substrate bound.

Compounds docked. Fosfomycin (PubChem CID 446987, C3H7O4P, MW 138.06) plus eight candidates: the four most potent distinct ChEMBL MurA actives by nM IC50 — CHEMBL2335230 (2.8 µM), CHEMBL5219390 (4.5 µM), CHEMBL2335229 (4.6 µM), CHEMBL5219133 (4.8 µM) — and four literature inhibitors with published activity: ampelopsin (dihydromyricetin, PubChem CID 161557; MurA IC50 480 nM, the most potent of 13 flavonoids in Frlan et al. 2023), quercetin (PubChem CID 5280343; active flavonoid MurA inhibitor, same study), albendazole (PubChem CID 2082) and diflunisal (PubChem CID 3059), both with MIC 0.0625 mg/mL against E. coli (Zhang et al. 2022). SMILES for all eight were taken from the ChEMBL molecule records or PubChem and are preserved in the supplementary docking JSON. No compound was docked from an unverified structure.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all nine compounds. Fosfomycin and six candidates are clean. Ampelopsin and quercetin carry a PAINS alert (catechol moiety) — reported, never hidden; it changes the validation design (see §4.3). Note that a clean PAINS result does not exclude covalent reactivity: CHEMBL2335230 is a brominated nitro-furan and CHEMBL2335229 is bromonitromethane, both electrophilic chemotypes whose measured activity may involve covalent chemistry that Vina cannot model.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for these eight compounds against MurA in this study beyond the ChEMBL and literature records cited. Measured IC50 values below are ChEMBL or literature records against MurA, not new measurements. Most importantly, Vina cannot price the covalent bond that makes fosfomycin work: fosfomycin's −5.04 kcal/mol is a score for its reversible pre-complex only, and comparing any non-covalent score against it as if it were a binding affinity is a category error. The comparison is reported because the field performs it, and the point of this paper is that it is meaningless.

Seven of eight candidates out-score re-docked fosfomycin, by 1.28 to 5.83 kcal/mol, with tight pose consistency (top-3 spread ≤0.6 kcal/mol for the top two, ≤1.3 kcal/mol for all but one). The two best dockers are large, lipophilic thiazole–furan carboxylates (MW 509–563, logP 6.45–7.00, two Lipinski violations each). The most potent measured non-covalent inhibitor, ampelopsin (480 nM), docks fourth at −8.65 kcal/mol. The only candidate that scores worse than fosfomycin is bromonitromethane (−3.79 kcal/mol) — a 140 Da reactive fragment whose measured 4.6 µM activity is almost certainly covalent chemistry, not non-covalent binding, and which Vina accordingly cannot see. That single row is the control that proves the rule: where the mechanism is covalent, Vina under-scores; where it is non-covalent, Vina over-rewards size and lipophilicity.

3.2 The docking–activity discordance that must not be hidden

For the six compounds with a measured enzyme IC50 (fosfomycin, ampelopsin, and the four ChEMBL actives), the Spearman rank correlation between measured potency and docking score is ρ = −0.37 — negative. The ranking is inverted: the most potent measured compound, fosfomycin (100 nM), docks fifth of six; the weakest measured compound, CHEMBL5219133 (4.8 µM), docks best; the second-weakest, CHEMBL5219390 (4.5 µM), docks second-best. Rigid Vina scoring on this pocket cannot rank these compounds, and it actively mis-ranks them in the wrong direction, because the score rewards molecular size and hydrophobic contact area (the two best dockers are the two largest and most lipophilic molecules in the set) while the one drug that works derives its potency from a single covalent bond to Cys115 that contributes nothing to the score. This is the paper's most important result, and it is a negative one: a docking "win" against fosfomycin is not evidence of anything.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

An independent 2026 MurA docking study (Kurniawan et al.) re-docked fosfomycin with an RMSD of 0.394 Å and reported its non-covalent component at −4.5 kcal/mol, against −7.3 to −7.7 kcal/mol for their optimised baeckenone derivatives. Our re-docked fosfomycin score of −5.04 kcal/mol agrees with that independent value within 0.5 kcal/mol — inside Vina noise — which validates our protocol and, more importantly, shows the field's published "improvements over fosfomycin" are the same artefact reproduced twice. No published Vina study of the four ChEMBL compounds or of ampelopsin/quercetin on 3KQJ was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (candidates vs re-docked reference on the same structure, same protocol). The re-docked fosfomycin score is the validated control that anchors the comparison — and what it validates is that the anchor itself is broken for this target.

3.4 The resistance problem the candidates must actually solve

A non-covalent MurA inhibitor is only useful if it escapes the three resistance routes that already limit fosfomycin. Transport: 77% of 337 clinical UPEC isolates form fosfomycin non-susceptible inner colonies, driven by uhpT/glpT loss that carries no fitness cost in the urinary tract. Enzymatic inactivation: fosA3 is the most widespread plasmid-borne determinant, present in a third of fosfomycin-resistant isolates in a 2026 UPEC cohort. Target mutation: C115D MurA is fully active and completely fosfomycin-resistant, and it already exists in nature (mycobacteria, chlamydiae). None of the eight candidates has published data against any of these three routes. The precedent that a non-covalent inhibitor can clear the third route exists: the pyrrolidinedione series of Fathalla et al. (2022) inhibits wild-type and C115D MurA equally (most potent compound 46, IC50 4.5 µM) and is additive with fosfomycin. That is the standard a candidate must meet, and it is an enzyme-assay standard, not a docking standard.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can actually answer is narrower than the one it started with. It cannot say "these compounds beat fosfomycin" — seven of eight out-score a benchmark that does not measure what fosfomycin does, the ranking is inverted against measured potency, and the two best dockers share the lipophilicity problem that kills most antibacterials before they reach the clinic. What it can say is: (a) the ChEMBL MurA record is thin — outside fosfomycin itself, the best measured inhibitor is 2.8 µM, and the pipeline run that day returned nothing only because the ChEMBL activity endpoint was returning HTTP 500; (b) the strongest measured non-covalent inhibitor remains the plant flavonoid ampelopsin at 480 nM, which docks well (−8.65 kcal/mol) but carries a PAINS alert; (c) the decisive experiment is now sharply defined — a MurA enzyme assay against wild-type and C115D enzyme, with fosfomycin as the comparator — and it is cheap and feasible in a university lab.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the benchmark is a category error: Vina scores non-covalent complementarity, fosfomycin's potency is covalent, so the 5.83 kcal/mol "margin" of the best docker measures the size of the error, not the size of an advantage. Second, the ranking is inverted (ρ = −0.37): the best dockers are the weakest measured inhibitors. Third, the two best dockers are highly lipophilic (logP 6.5–7.0, two Lipinski violations, MW >500) — the same developability wall that every MurA programme has hit, since Gram-negative penetration punishes exactly this profile. Fourth, the single-structure, rigid-receptor protocol under-samples a target that works by induced fit: MurA's Pro112–Pro121 loop moves through multiple conformations on substrate binding, and one closed structure cannot represent the binding landscape.

4.3 Mechanism

MurA transfers the enolpyruvyl moiety of PEP to the 3′-hydroxyl of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine by an addition–elimination mechanism, with UNAG binding first and inducing the domain closure that forms the active site in the interdomain cleft. Cys115, on the flexible Pro112–Pro121 loop, acts as the general acid in protonation of C-3 of PEP and is essential for product release. Fosfomycin, a PEP analogue, enters the same pocket and is alkylated by Cys115. A non-covalent inhibitor must therefore do one of two things: occupy the PEP pocket tightly enough to compete with PEP without the covalent anchor, or bind the UNAG-induced closed conformation and prevent the loop movement that product release requires. Test for each link: (i) a MurA enzyme assay measuring enolpyruvyl transfer (phosphate release or coupled assay) against wild-type enzyme; (ii) the same assay against C115D MurA — a true non-covalent inhibitor must retain activity, a covalent one will not; (iii) MIC determination against E. coli with and without efflux-pump inhibition, to separate target inhibition from penetration failure — the exact failure mode Frlan et al. reported for most flavonoids, whose enzyme activity did not translate into antibacterial activity.

4.4 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Ampelopsin and quercetin both carry a catechol PAINS alert, and Frlan et al. already showed their MurA inhibition is time-dependent and DTT-sensitive — the classic signature of redox-cycling or covalent artefacts from catechols. That does not make ampelopsin worthless (it is still the most potent measured non-covalent MurA inhibitor at 480 nM); it makes the assay design non-negotiable: every flavonoid measurement must be run with and without DTT, with and without pre-incubation, and with a detergent control against aggregation. If the 480 nM activity survives DTT, it is real; if it collapses, the compound is an artefact and the field should stop citing it. The same logic applies to the two electrophilic ChEMBL compounds: CHEMBL2335230 and CHEMBL2335229 must be tested for time-dependent inhibition and for activity against C115D before any claim of non-covalent inhibition is made.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL5219133 and CHEMBL5219390 inhibit wild-type E. coli MurA with IC50 ≤ 50 µM in a phosphate-release enzyme assay. Falsifier: IC50 > 50 µM for either compound.
  2. At least one of the two retains activity (within 3-fold) against C115D MurA, proving a non-covalent mechanism. Falsifier: >10-fold loss against C115D.
  3. Ampelopsin's 480 nM MurA inhibition survives 1 mM DTT in the enzyme assay. Falsifier: IC50 rises >10-fold with DTT, indicating a redox artefact.
  4. Re-docking with molecular-dynamics refinement preserves the two leads' advantage over the flavonoids within 1 kcal/mol. Falsifier: the advantage disappears after minimisation.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): recombinant E. coli MurA (wild-type and C115D) enzyme assay — phosphate-release readout, n = 3 — for CHEMBL5219133, CHEMBL5219390, ampelopsin and quercetin, with fosfomycin as the comparator and the pyrrolidinedione compound 46 as a positive non-covalent control; all flavonoid runs with and without DTT. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): MIC determination against E. coli ATCC 25922 and a small panel of clinical UPEC isolates (including a fosA3-positive and a uhpT-mutant strain), with fosfomycin as comparator. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any candidate passes stages 1–2, solubility and HepG2 cytotoxicity measurement (the published non-covalent leads L16 and X14 both cleared HepG2 at >100 µM, which is the bar); if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed — the negative result is the paper's contribution, not a failure to report.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol, and the fosfomycin benchmark is a category error (covalent drug scored by a non-covalent method).
  2. Docking order is inverted against measured potency (Spearman ρ = −0.37, n = 6); rigid docking cannot rank these compounds, and the inversion is the finding, not a flaw to smooth over.
  3. The two best dockers are highly lipophilic (logP 6.5–7.0, two Lipinski violations, MW >500); no solubility, penetration or protein-binding data were measured, and Gram-negative penetration punishes exactly this profile.
  4. A single structure (3KQJ) was used; MurA works by induced fit and one closed structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  5. Measured IC50 values are ChEMBL and literature records; assay conditions vary across source studies (fosfomycin's own recorded IC50s span assay-dependent values) and were not re-verified compound by compound.
  6. The two flavonoid leads carry PAINS alerts and their published inhibition is DTT-sensitive; the two electrophilic ChEMBL compounds may act covalently. Neither mechanism was tested here.
  7. No data against the three clinical resistance routes (uhpT/glpT transport loss, FosA enzymes, C115D MurA) were generated for any candidate.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi; the full Arabic texts were not read, and other classical works on urinary and febrile illness were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Seven of eight candidates out-dock fosfomycin on E. coli MurA (3KQJ) by up to 5.83 kcal/mol — and the result means nothing, because fosfomycin's potency is a covalent bond to Cys115 that Vina cannot price, its non-covalent score of −5.04 kcal/mol corresponds to a measured IC50 of 100 nM, and the docking ranking is inverted against measured potency (ρ = −0.37). The honest finding is narrower and more useful: the best measured non-covalent MurA inhibitor remains ampelopsin (480 nM, PAINS-flagged), the ChEMBL record outside fosfomycin tops out at 2.8 µM, and the two best dockers are lipophilic thiazole–furan carboxylates with no measured advantage. The next step is not another docking run — it is the cheap, decisive test: a MurA enzyme assay against wild-type and C115D enzyme, with DTT controls for the flavonoids. That test, not a docking score, is what would make a fosfomycin alternative real.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Higher Education Commission research-funding panels and the SMBBMU ORIC office, with DRAP as the eventual regulator. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of existing ChEMBL and literature MurA inhibitors as an academic drug-discovery exercise. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week wild-type-plus-C115D enzyme screen proposed in §4.6 for CHEMBL5219133, CHEMBL5219390 and ampelopsin against fosfomycin, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target — and require every future MurA docking proposal to state, in its methods, that fosfomycin is covalent and that its docking score is not a binding-affinity benchmark. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if all three candidates lose to fosfomycin in the enzyme assay or fail against C115D, drop this compound set and redirect the same screen to the pyrrolidinedione chemotype, which has already cleared the C115D test — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable drug from a useless one for infections that drive a large share of the 1.27 million annual AMR deaths, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

Asundexian Re-Docks at −9.05 kcal/mol on the Milvexian-Bound Factor XIa Structure — but the First Approved FXIa Inhibitor Still Leaves the Decisive Question Open

Stroke killed 6.8 million people in 2023, yet every anticoagulant that prevents it also causes the bleeding it is meant to avoid — and the first drug designed to break that trade-off has just split its own evidence in two.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-20 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #85 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Factor XIa; asundexian; milvexian; anticoagulation; stroke prevention; molecular docking; ChEMBL; factor XI deficiency

Abstract

Stroke killed 6.8 million people in 2023, yet every anticoagulant that prevents it also causes the bleeding it is meant to avoid — and the first drug designed to break that trade-off has just split its own evidence in two. Asundexian, an oral factor XIa (FXIa) inhibitor, failed its atrial-fibrillation trial (OCEANIC-AF: stroke or systemic embolism 1.3% vs 0.4% on apixaban, hazard ratio 3.79) but succeeded as add-on therapy after noncardioembolic stroke (OCEANIC-STROKE: ischaemic stroke 6.2% vs 8.4%, hazard ratio 0.74, no increase in major bleeding) and was approved by the US FDA on 9 November 2026 — the first FXIa inhibitor approved anywhere. We asked whether asundexian and its closest chemical analogues bind the true FXIa active site more strongly than the co-crystallised inhibitor milvexian. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P03951 → ChEMBL CHEMBL2820 → PubChem/RDKit, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked asundexian, four PubChem analogues and milvexian on the 0.92 Å FXIa structure 7MBO, centred exactly on the co-crystallised milvexian (centre audit 0.00 Å). Asundexian re-docked at −9.05 kcal/mol with tight pose consistency (−9.05, −9.04, −8.89), no PAINS alert, and one Lipinski violation (molecular weight 593). Two of four PubChem analogues out-scored it on best pose — 135205642 at −10.03 and 135205940 at −9.88 — but both margins (0.98 and 0.83 kcal/mol) lie inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the first is a single-pose outlier whose other poses (−8.99, −8.89) tie or trail asundexian; the other two scored −9.19 and −8.99. The decisive check is the self-dock control: milvexian, the co-crystallised ligand of this structure and the more potent drug by measured Ki (0.11 nM vs 0.26 nM), re-docked worst at −7.83 kcal/mol — 1.22 kcal/mol behind asundexian. Docking therefore ranks this scaffold family inversely to measured potency, and no analogue can be claimed to beat asundexian on this evidence. The honest limit: ChEMBL's activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 all day, so the analogues carry no measured potency and the comparison is structural, not pharmacological; no laboratory data exist for any compound in this study. The claim that any analogue beats asundexian would be refuted if a chromogenic FXIa enzyme assay shows a Ki worse than asundexian's 0.26 nM. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week enzyme-plus-aPTT test of the two best-scoring analogues against asundexian and milvexian.

1. Introduction

In 2023 there were 13.2 million new strokes worldwide, 6.8 million stroke deaths, and 104.8 million people living after a stroke, accounting for 156.5 million disability-adjusted life-years; stroke was the second leading cause of death and the third leading cause of death and disability combined, and more than 80% of the deaths and disability occurred in low- and middle-income countries. Ischaemic stroke accounted for 63.9% of incident cases. In Pakistan, where stroke care is concentrated in a few tertiary centres and rehabilitation is scarce, a prevented stroke is worth far more than a treated one — and prevention is where anticoagulation fails its own patients: the drugs that stop clots cause the bleeding that kills or disables, so the most vulnerable patients are the ones left unprotected.

Factor XI sits at the hinge of that dilemma. It is a serine protease of the intrinsic (contact) pathway that amplifies thrombin generation once a clot has started, but it contributes little to the initial haemostatic plug, which is driven by the extrinsic tissue-factor pathway. The human genetics agree: people born without factor XI (factor XI deficiency, formerly haemophilia C) usually have a mild, variable bleeding disorder — prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery, mostly at mucosal surfaces — and many never bleed at all; severe deficiency affects about 1 in 1 million people worldwide and about 1 in 450 Ashkenazi Jews. A drug that inhibits FXIa should therefore, in theory, uncouple antithrombotic efficacy from bleeding risk. That theory has now been tested in 27,000 randomised patients, and the answer depends on the indication.

Asundexian (BAY 2433334, Sunharbo; Bayer) is an oral, direct, reversible FXIa inhibitor from a substituted-oxopyridine series, with a human FXIa Ki of 0.26 nM and >38,000-fold selectivity over factor Xa and thrombin (nearest off-target plasma kallikrein, Ki 110 nM). In OCEANIC-AF, 14,810 high-risk atrial-fibrillation patients were randomised to asundexian 50 mg once daily or standard-dose apixaban; the trial was stopped early because asundexian was inferior for stroke or systemic embolism (1.3% vs 0.4%; hazard ratio 3.79, 95% CI 2.46–5.83) even though major bleeding was lower (0.2% vs 0.7%; hazard ratio 0.32). In OCEANIC-STROKE, 12,327 patients within 72 hours of a noncardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk transient ischaemic attack were randomised to the same 50 mg dose or placebo, added to planned single or dual antiplatelet therapy; ischaemic stroke fell from 8.4% to 6.2% (cause-specific hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.84; P < 0.001) with no significant increase in major bleeding (1.9% vs 1.7%; hazard ratio 1.10). On 9 November 2026 the FDA approved asundexian with antiplatelet therapy to reduce stroke risk after a recent mild-to-moderate noncardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA — the first FXIa inhibitor approved in the United States, and the first new antithrombotic class for this population. The second drug in the class, milvexian (BMS-986177/JNJ-70033093; Ki 0.11 nM, >5,000-fold selective over related serine proteases except chymotrypsin and plasma kallikrein), has had the opposite split: its phase 3 LIBREXIA-ACS trial (14,194 patients after acute coronary syndrome) was stopped for futility in November 2025 with identical event rates (5.4% vs 5.1%; hazard ratio 1.05), while its stroke and atrial-fibrillation programmes continue.

The classical medical canon discussed this disease class long before the enzyme was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses al-saktah (apoplexy/stroke) as a sudden loss of movement and sensation, and the management it proposes is entirely supportive — the Canon knows the syndrome, not the target. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence, but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do asundexian and its closest PubChem analogues bind the true FXIa active site (PDB 7MBO) at scores beyond re-docked milvexian, the co-crystallised inhibitor, and would that binding translate into stronger FXIa inhibition? Falsifier: a chromogenic FXIa enzyme assay showing a Ki worse than asundexian's 0.26 nM, or an aPTT assay showing no advantage over asundexian, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the approved drug re-docked on a co-crystal structure of its own target, with the co-crystallised inhibitor re-docked as a second control — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-20: the OCEANIC-AF and OCEANIC-STROKE trial records (NEJM 2025 and 2026), the asundexian design paper (Roehrig et al., J Med Chem 2023), the milvexian discovery paper (Dilger et al., J Med Chem 2022), the LIBREXIA-ACS result (NEJM 2026), the GBD 1990–2023 stroke fact sheet, and the RCSB records for PDB 7MBO and 8BO3. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: human coagulation factor XI, UniProtKB P03951 (F11 gene; 625 residues; "Factor XI triggers the middle phase of the intrinsic pathway of blood coagulation by activating factor IX"); ChEMBL target CHEMBL2820 (Coagulation factor XI, SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens — verified live 2026-11-20). Structure: PDB 7MBO, the FXIa protease domain (Pichia pastoris expression; C500S mutation) in complex with milvexian, 0.92 Å X-ray resolution — the highest-resolution FXIa structure available. Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised milvexian (ligand YXG, 66 atoms), [−1.06, 9.92, −17.80], verified by direct computation from the PDB file and by the pipeline's own dock._ligand_center (0.00 Å agreement); box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for asundexian, all four analogues and milvexian. Note that 7MBO is the milvexian structure, not the asundexian structure (asundexian's own co-crystal is PDB 8BO3, 1.84 Å): asundexian's score here is therefore a cross-dock into the milvexian site, and milvexian's score is the self-dock control.

A ChEMBL outage, stated plainly. On 2026-11-20 the ChEMBL activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 for every target queried (verified directly against the EBI API; the target endpoint still worked). The pipeline's step 2 therefore retrieved zero bioactivities for CHEMBL2820, and the run contains no ChEMBL lead set. Rather than ship a one-compound paper, the comparison set was built from PubChem fastsimilarity_2d against asundexian (Tanimoto ≥ 0.85, 30 analogues returned; four picked for docking: the smallest, the closest-to-asundexian formula, the largest, and one N7 variant). This is the established fallback from the 2026-11-11 FLT3 run, with the same rule: no measured potency is attached to any PubChem analogue, and the paper's comparison is structural only. All four analogues come from the same Bayer oxopyridine series as asundexian (PubChem CIDs 13520xxxx), so the set tests scaffold variation, not chemotype diversity. The discarded thin pipeline run is preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-098-2026-11-20.json; the re-dock is in hidden_files/dock-HP-098-redock-2026-11-20.json.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to asundexian and the four analogues. Asundexian carries no PAINS alert. All four analogues are PAINS-clean (PubChem CIDs 135205642, 135205940, 135205866, 135205878), as is milvexian.

2.4 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for asundexian: molecular weight 592.94, logP 4.6, 2 hydrogen-bond donors, 6 acceptors, TPSA 134.13 Å², 8 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation (molecular weight > 500) with an overall Lipinski pass and Veber pass. ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) for asundexian: maximum predicted probability 0.38 (SR-MMP), with a maximum neighbour similarity of only 0.263 — a weak read-across, not a measurement, and it does not clear the compound for development. The four analogues share asundexian's profile: each carries exactly one Lipinski violation (molecular weight > 500) with a Veber pass — PubChem-135205642 (MW 545.36, logP 3.85, HBD 2, HBA 6, TPSA 134.13 Å², 7 rotatable bonds), PubChem-135205940 (MW 578.91, logP 4.21, HBD 2, HBA 6, TPSA 134.13 Å², 7 rotatable bonds), PubChem-135205866 (MW 588.97, logP 4.91, HBD 2, HBA 6, TPSA 134.13 Å², 10 rotatable bonds), PubChem-135205878 (MW 553.98, logP 3.76, HBD 2, HBA 7, TPSA 147.02 Å², 10 rotatable bonds). Milvexian is the least drug-like of the set by these counts (MW 626.46, logP 5.80, HBD 1, HBA 7, TPSA 125.41 Å², 4 rotatable bonds, two Lipinski violations) — and the most potent by measured Ki — which is itself a warning that these descriptor counts do not rank this class.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for the four analogues against FXIa in this study, and no measured potency is attached to them. The two measured Ki values in this paper (asundexian 0.26 nM; milvexian 0.11 nM) are published enzyme-assay values, not new measurements.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured FXIa potency Best affinity, 7MBO (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) Median pose Margin vs asundexian
Asundexian (reference) Ki 0.26 nM −9.05 −9.05, −9.04, −8.89 −9.04 —
PubChem-135205642 none (PubChem analogue) −10.03 −10.03, −8.99, −8.89 −8.99 +0.98 (best pose only)
PubChem-135205940 none (PubChem analogue) −9.88 −9.88, −9.33, −9.16 −9.33 +0.83
PubChem-135205866 none (PubChem analogue) −9.19 −9.19, −9.09, −8.66 −9.09 +0.14
PubChem-135205878 none (PubChem analogue) −8.99 −8.99, −8.73, −8.65 −8.73 −0.06
Milvexian (co-crystallised ligand) Ki 0.11 nM −7.83 −7.83, −7.46, −6.80 −7.46 −1.22

Two analogues out-score asundexian on best pose, but neither margin survives the noise test: 0.98 and 0.83 kcal/mol against Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol, and PubChem-135205642's margin is a single pose — its median pose (−8.99) is actually worse than asundexian's median (−9.04). On medians, only PubChem-135205940 beats asundexian, by 0.29 kcal/mol. The control that settles the interpretation is milvexian: it is the ligand this structure was crystallised with, it is the more potent drug by measured Ki (0.11 nM vs 0.26 nM), and Vina scores it 1.22 kcal/mol worse than asundexian. A scoring function that ranks the weaker binder first and the stronger binder last, inside one scaffold family on one structure, cannot rank this family at all. The honest reading of the table is therefore a null result: no analogue beats asundexian beyond noise, and the method itself fails its own positive control.

Asundexian re-docked at −9.05 kcal/mol with tight pose consistency (top-3 spread 0.16 kcal/mol), which is the validated control that anchors the comparison: a method that could not recover strong binding for a 0.26 nM binder would be broken. It did.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of asundexian or these four analogues on 7MBO was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (analogues vs re-docked reference drugs on the same structure, same protocol). The crystal structures themselves (7MBO for milvexian, 8BO3 for asundexian) are the published ground truth for the binding mode; this paper tests whether a rigid scoring function can rank compounds inside that mode.

3.3 The clinical confounder that docking cannot see

The OCEANIC split is the paper's most important context: the same drug, the same dose, the same target — inferior in atrial fibrillation, superior after noncardioembolic stroke. The docking order cannot explain that split, and it cannot even rank the drugs: milvexian, the more potent binder by measured Ki, re-docks worst. The split is about indication, background therapy and thrombus biology (fibrin-rich cardioembolic clot versus platelet-rich atherosclerotic clot under antiplatelet cover), not about binding affinity. A compound that out-scores asundexian here would still face the same indication question, and the OCEANIC-AF failure is a standing warning that FXIa potency does not guarantee efficacy where factor Xa inhibition already works.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The FDA approval of 9 November 2026 changes the question this paper can ask. Before it, the question was "can an FXIa inhibitor work at all?" — now it is "which chemotype, if any, beats the approved drug, and in which indication?" The docking benchmark is therefore a screen for successors, not for proof of concept, and its bar is higher: a new compound must beat asundexian on the target and then survive the indication test that asundexian itself failed in atrial fibrillation.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, every margin in §3.1 lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise unless stated otherwise. Second, the four analogues carry no measured potency, so the ranking is a structural hypothesis with no pharmacological anchor — unlike the MDM2 and BCR-ABL papers in this series, where ChEMBL potencies disciplined the ranking. Third, all five compounds share the oxopyridine scaffold, so even a genuine docking advantage would be a variation on the approved chemotype, not a new one, and would inherit its developability profile (molecular weight near 600, logP 4.6, TPSA 134).

4.3 Mechanism

FXIa amplifies thrombin generation by activating factor IX; its inhibition prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) without changing prothrombin time, which is the laboratory signature of intrinsic-pathway selectivity. Test for each link: (i) a chromogenic FXIa enzyme assay measures Ki directly against asundexian (0.26 nM) and milvexian (0.11 nM) as comparators; (ii) aPTT prolongation in human plasma measures functional anticoagulation; (iii) a plasma-kallikrein counter-screen (asundexian Ki 110 nM; milvexian Ki 44 nM) measures whether the analogue kept the selectivity that defines the class — loss of kallikrein selectivity is the likeliest way a "better" FXIa binder becomes a worse drug, because kallikrein inhibition drives bradykinin-mediated angioedema risk.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-scoring analogue inhibits human FXIa with a Ki within 3-fold of asundexian's 0.26 nM in a chromogenic enzyme assay. Falsifier: Ki > 0.8 nM.
  2. The same analogue prolongs aPTT in human plasma at least as strongly as asundexian at matched concentration. Falsifier: no aPTT prolongation below 1 µM.
  3. The analogue keeps ≥100-fold selectivity over plasma kallikrein. Falsifier: kallikrein Ki within 10-fold of the FXIa Ki.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): chromogenic FXIa enzyme assay for the two candidate analogues — PubChem-135205940 (most consistent: median pose −9.33) and PubChem-135205642 (best single pose, −10.03) — plus asundexian and milvexian controls; readout Ki, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): aPTT and plasma-kallikrein counter-screen in human plasma for the same set. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed. No animal work is proposed at this stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin.
  2. ChEMBL was down (HTTP 500) on the run date, so the comparison set is four PubChem similarity analogues with no measured potency; the ranking is structural, not pharmacological.
  3. All five docked compounds share one scaffold (the Bayer oxopyridine series); no chemotype diversity was tested.
  4. Asundexian's score is a cross-dock (7MBO is the milvexian structure); its own co-crystal is 8BO3 at 1.84 Å, which was not used.
  5. A single rigid structure was used; the FXIa active site adapts to different chemotypes, so one structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  6. The 7MBO structure carries the C500S mutation and is a Pichia-expressed protease domain, not full-length human FXI.
  7. No data on the clinical confounder: docking cannot distinguish the atrial-fibrillation indication (where asundexian failed) from the post-stroke indication (where it succeeded).
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon; the full Arabic text was not read, and other classical works on stroke were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

Asundexian, the first FXIa inhibitor approved anywhere (FDA, 9 November 2026), re-docks at −9.05 kcal/mol on the 0.92 Å milvexian-bound FXIa structure 7MBO, with tight pose consistency and no PAINS alert — a validated control, not a discovery. No analogue beats it: the best best-pose margin (PubChem-135205642, +0.98 kcal/mol) is a single-pose outlier inside Vina noise, the most consistent analogue (PubChem-135205940, median −9.33) leads by only 0.29 kcal/mol on medians, and the method fails its own positive control — milvexian, the more potent drug by measured Ki, re-docks 1.22 kcal/mol worse than asundexian. The docking verdict is a null result, and it is useful precisely as one: this scaffold family cannot be ranked by rigid Vina scoring, and the next screen must be an enzyme assay, not a bigger docking set. What the docking cannot do is resolve the OCEANIC split: the same drug failed in atrial fibrillation and succeeded after stroke, and no binding score explains that. The next step is the cheap, decisive test — a chromogenic FXIa enzyme assay plus aPTT and kallikrein counter-screen for the best-scoring analogue against asundexian and milvexian — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Drug Regulatory Authority (DRAP) and the Higher Education Commission research-funding panels, with the SMBBMU ORIC office as the local route. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of FXIa inhibition as an academic drug-discovery exercise, and whether to prepare DRAP's assessment pathway for a first-in-class anticoagulant that will arrive with a split indication record. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week enzyme-plus-aPTT screen proposed in §4.5 for the best-scoring analogue against asundexian and milvexian, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target; and, in parallel, ask DRAP's registration reviewers to note the OCEANIC split explicitly in any future asundexian dossier — approval for post-stroke secondary prevention is not evidence for atrial fibrillation, where the drug was inferior to apixaban. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the best analogue loses >3-fold to asundexian in the enzyme assay or loses kallikrein selectivity, drop this scaffold set and redirect the same screen to the next FXIa chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable anticoagulant from a useless one for a disease that kills 6.8 million people a year, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

The 8-Chloro Isomer of Alisertib Out-Docks Alisertib on the 1.96 Å Aurora A Structure — but the 0.33 kcal/mol Margin Is Inside Vina Noise and the Most Potent Measured Inhibitor Docks Ninth

Aurora kinase A (AURKA) is amplified or overexpressed in many solid tumours, yet no Aurora kinase inhibitor is approved anywhere: alisertib, the most advanced, failed its Phase 3 LUMIERE trial in peripheral T-cell lymphoma (response rate 33% versus 45% for the comparators).

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-20 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #87 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Aurora kinase A; AURKA; alisertib; MLN8237; molecular docking; LY3295668; solid tumours; ChEMBL

Abstract

Aurora kinase A (AURKA) is amplified or overexpressed in many solid tumours, yet no Aurora kinase inhibitor is approved anywhere: alisertib, the most advanced, failed its Phase 3 LUMIERE trial in peripheral T-cell lymphoma (response rate 33% versus 45% for the comparators). We asked whether alisertib analogues or other clinical-stage AURKA inhibitors bind the true ATP pocket more strongly than re-docked alisertib. ChEMBL's bioactivity endpoint was down on the day of the run (HTTP 500 for every target), so the comparison set was built from PubChem 2D-similar analogues of alisertib plus four literature inhibitors with published potencies, and docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on the 1.96 Å AURKA structure 6C2R at the co-crystallised LY3295668 centroid. The best score came from PubChem CID 92044531, the 8-chloro positional isomer of alisertib, at −9.20 kcal/mol versus −8.87 for alisertib and −8.95 for the co-crystallised LY3295668; two further analogues scored −8.77 and −8.74, and the two top-similarity hits turned out to be sodium-salt forms of alisertib itself. The honest limit: the 0.33 kcal/mol margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, the most potent measured inhibitor (MK-5108, IC50 0.064 nM) docked ninth of ten at −8.19, the docking–potency correlation across the five literature compounds is weak (Spearman rho 0.40, p = 0.51), and no analogue carries a measured potency. The claim that the 8-chloro isomer is a better AURKA inhibitor would be refuted if a biochemical kinase assay shows its IC50 more than 10-fold worse than alisertib's 1.2 nM, or if cellular phospho-Thr288 inhibition shows no advantage. The falsifiable next step is an 8–12-week kinase-plus-cellular test of the isomer against alisertib and LY3295668.

1. Introduction

Cancer caused an estimated 20 million new cases and 9.7 million deaths worldwide in 2022, and in Pakistan 185,748 new cases and 118,631 deaths in the same year (IARC GLOBOCAN 2022). Most of those deaths are in solid tumours, where the drugs that work do so for a while and then stop working — resistance, not the absence of targets, is the usual failure. Aurora kinase A (AURKA) is one of the targets that keeps being re-tried: a mitotic serine/threonine kinase, encoded on chromosome 20q13, that matures centrosomes, builds the bipolar spindle and guards chromosome segregation. When it is amplified or overexpressed — in breast, ovarian, colorectal, lung, gastric, prostate, cervical and pancreatic cancers — it drives proliferation, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, metastasis, cancer-stem-cell self-renewal and resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy. In epithelial ovarian cancer, 82.8% of tumours overexpress Aurora A, and the most strongly overexpressing tumours cut median survival from 2.81 to 1.44 years.

The most advanced AURKA inhibitor, alisertib (MLN8237), is a selective ATP-competitive inhibitor with a cell-free IC50 of 1.2 nM and more than 200-fold selectivity over Aurora B. It reached Phase 3: the LUMIERE trial (NCT01482962) randomised 271 patients with relapsed or refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma to alisertib 50 mg twice daily (days 1–7 of a 21-day cycle) or investigator's choice of pralatrexate, romidepsin or gemcitabine. It was stopped early for futility — overall response rate 33% versus 45% for the comparators, median progression-free survival 115 versus 104 days, median overall survival 415 versus 367 days — and the most common adverse events were anaemia (53%) and neutropenia (47%). No Aurora kinase inhibitor is approved anywhere. The class did not fail because the target is wrong; it failed because a single molecule, dosed intermittently at the edge of myelosuppression, could not beat the comparators. That leaves the precise question this paper attacks: do other molecules — either analogues of alisertib itself or other clinical-stage AURKA inhibitors — bind the true ATP pocket of AURKA more strongly than re-docked alisertib, and do the measured potencies track the docking order?

The classical medical canon knew this disease class long before the gene was: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses sartan (cancer) as a hard, spreading swelling with a poor prognosis, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of tumours. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence — they knew the syndrome, not the target — but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do alisertib analogues and clinical-stage AURKA inhibitors bind the true ATP pocket of AURKA (PDB 6C2R) at scores beyond re-docked alisertib, and does the docking order track measured biochemical potency? Falsifier: if a fluorescence-based kinase assay shows a candidate's AURKA IC50 more than 10-fold worse than alisertib's 1.2 nM, or if cellular phospho-Thr288 Aurora A inhibition shows no advantage, the claim for that compound is refuted. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference drug and the co-crystallised ligand both re-docked on a co-crystal structure of the same target — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-20: the alisertib development record (Manfredi et al. 2011 characterisation; LUMIERE Phase 3 outcome, O'Connor et al. 2019), the LY3295668 RB1 synthetic-lethality study (Gong et al. 2019), AURKA reviews (Du et al. 2021; nuclear-function review 2024), the ovarian-cancer prognosis study (Landen et al. 2007), the latest literature digest (2026-11-14, no AURKA item — the sweep was therefore targeted, not digest-led), and the RCSB records for PDB 6VPM and 6C2R. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 The ChEMBL outage and the comparison set

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run first (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → Vina). It resolved the target correctly — UniProtKB O14965, human Aurora kinase A, 403 amino acids — but the ChEMBL bioactivity endpoint returned HTTP 500 for every target on 2026-11-20 (an EBI-side outage, verified the same day against other targets), so step 2 returned zero ligands and no ChEMBL-measured potencies were retrievable. The pipeline was run once; per the standing rule it was not re-run in the hope the outage would clear. The comparison set was therefore built the way the 2026-11-11 FLT3 run built its set under the same outage: PubChem fastsimilarity_2d (2D fingerprint similarity ≥80%) against alisertib, which returned 50 candidate CIDs, of which 49 yielded usable structures; and four literature-known AURKA inhibitors with published potencies — LY3295668 (Ki 0.8 nM, >1,000-fold selective over Aurora B), MK-5108 (IC50 0.064 nM), ENMD-2076 (IC50 14 nM) and danusertib (IC50 13 nM Aurora A, 79 nM Aurora B, 61 nM Aurora C). No measured potency is attached to any PubChem analogue in this paper — their PubChem similarity is a structural fact, not an activity claim, and any analogue that "wins" here is a candidate for the assay, not a better drug.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: human AURKA, UniProtKB O14965. Structure: PDB 6C2R, the AURKA kinase domain (residues 125–391) in complex with LY3295668, 1.96 Å. Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised ligand EG7 (LY3295668), [110.14, −17.65, 5.80], computed with dock._ligand_center; box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for alisertib and every comparator.

A wrong-site audit, stated plainly. The pipeline's first run for this topic picked PDB 6VPM (1.58 Å) — the highest-resolution AURKA structure — and docked alisertib there at −8.36 kcal/mol. That run is DISCARDED, not reported as a result. The audit showed the grid centre [−4.65, −7.62, −29.10] is exactly the centroid of R74, a covalent fragment disulfide-bonded to Cys290 in the activation loop — an allosteric redox site, not the ATP pocket — while the ATP-site nucleotide in the same structure sits ~34 Å away. Alisertib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor; a score at the R74 site says nothing about its ATP-pocket binding. The failure mode is the same class as the TYK2 JH1/JH2 domain audit (2026-11-11), the gyrase 3M4I audit (Paper #75) and the MDM2/PLK1 wrong-target audit (Paper #80): the auto-picked structure must be checked for the right site, not just the right protein. The corrected run uses 6C2R, whose co-crystallised ligand LY3295668 sits in the ATP pocket — verified directly: its centroid is 7.9 Å from the hinge Ala213 Cα and its closest atom is 1.88 Å from a hinge residue (210–216). All scores in §3 are from the corrected run (hidden_files/dock-HP-102-2026-11-20.json); the discarded 6VPM run is preserved in hidden_files/dock-HP-102-2026-11-20-WRONG-SITE.json for audit.

2.4 PAINS screen

The RDKit PAINS filter (PAINS-A/B/C) was applied to alisertib and every docked comparator. Results are in the table in §3.1. A PAINS alert is reported, never hidden; it changes the validation design (redox controls).

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for every compound; ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) run for alisertib in the pipeline run. Alisertib itself (PubChem CID 24771867, C27H20ClFN4O4, MW 518.93) has 2 Lipinski violations (logP 5.75, MW >500) and a maximum Tox21 read-across probability of 0.385 (SR-MMP).

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for the PubChem analogues against AURKA in this study, and none is claimed. Measured IC50 values below are published records, not new measurements, and they come from different assay formats (cell-free IC50, Ki, cellular autophosphorylation IC50) — they are not directly interchangeable, and the paper says so wherever they are compared.

Their scores therefore test the protonation state of alisertib, not a new scaffold.

The best score in the set belongs to the 8-chloro positional isomer of alisertib (CID 92044531): the same molecular formula as alisertib (C27H20ClFN4O4), the chlorine moved one position on the phenyl ring (8-chloro instead of 9-chloro), 0.33 kcal/mol better than alisertib itself. Two further genuine analogues — the 2,6-difluoro variant (CID 11712649) and the des-methoxy variant (CID 11526006, alisertib without the 2-methoxy group on the benzoic-acid ring) — score within 0.13 kcal/mol of alisertib. The co-crystallised ligand LY3295668 re-docks at −8.95 with tight poses (top-3 spread 0.46 kcal/mol), which validates the method: the protocol recovers strong binding for the ligand this structure was solved with. Every compound in the set is PAINS-clean.

3.2 The docking–activity relationship

The docking order does not track the measured potency order. Across the five compounds with published potencies, Spearman rho between measured potency (nM) and docking score is 0.40 (p = 0.51, n = 5) — weak and not statistically significant, and the five potencies mix IC50 and Ki formats, so even that number is an exploratory check rather than a measurement. The single most important discordance: MK-5108, the most potent measured inhibitor in the set by a factor of 12 (IC50 0.064 nM, 220-fold selective over Aurora B), docks ninth of ten at −8.19 kcal/mol — 0.76 kcal/mol worse than LY3295668, whose Ki is 0.8 nM. Conversely ENMD-2076, the weakest measured inhibitor (14 nM), docks last at −7.79, which is the one ranking the docking gets right. Rigid Vina scoring on this pocket cannot resolve a 12-fold potency difference, and it actively mis-ranks the most potent compound — the same failure Paper #80 found on MDM2, where the most potent measured compound also docked worst. This is the paper's most important negative result: the docking ranking is not a potency ranking, and any claim built on the −9.20 versus −8.87 gap alone would be over-reading noise.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of these PubChem analogues on 6C2R was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (analogues and literature inhibitors versus re-docked alisertib on the same structure, same protocol). A molecular-dynamics study of AURKA selectivity did dock LY3295668, MK-5108 and alisertib on Aurora A (and Aurora B) and reported MM/PBSA binding free energies, but it did not publish Vina scores comparable to these, so no numeric cross-check is possible. The re-docked LY3295668 score is the validated control that anchors the comparison: it is the co-crystallised ligand of this exact structure, so a method that could not recover strong binding for it would be broken. It did.

3.4 The developability problem the table does not solve

Every compound in the set except ENMD-2076 and danusertib is highly lipophilic (logP 5.09–5.87), and alisertib, its 8-chloro isomer, MK-5108 and LY3295668 all carry Lipinski violations driven by logP >5 (alisertib also by MW >500). The 8-chloro isomer inherits alisertib's exact developability profile — same formula, same logP — so even if its 0.33 kcal/mol edge were real, it would face the same solubility and protein-binding problems, and the same on-target myelosuppression that comes from inhibiting a mitotic kinase in normal proliferating tissue. The two analogues with the cleanest profiles are the des-methoxy variant (CID 11526006, MW 488.91, 1 violation) and the difluoro variant (CID 11712649, MW 476.87, 1 violation), but both are still logP >5.7. A better docking score does not fix a lipophilicity problem, and this paper does not pretend otherwise.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can actually answer is narrower than the one it started with. It cannot say "the 8-chloro isomer beats alisertib" — the 0.33 kcal/mol margin is inside noise, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order, and the isomer inherits alisertib's exact lipophilicity problem. What it can say is: (a) a positional isomer of alisertib, differing by one chlorine position, binds the true ATP pocket with a tight, reproducible pose and the best score in a ten-compound set; (b) two further genuine analogues bind within 0.13 kcal/mol of alisertib; (c) the two top-similarity PubChem hits are not new molecules at all but alisertib's own sodium salt, caught and reported rather than counted as discoveries; (d) the pipeline's first, wrong-site run was caught and corrected before publication, and the correction is documented; (e) the decisive experiment is now sharply defined — a biochemical kinase assay plus cellular phospho-Thr288 engagement for the 8-chloro isomer against alisertib and LY3295668 — and it is cheap and feasible in a university lab.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons, whatever the table shows. First, any margin under ~1–2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's noise. Second, rigid docking on one structure cannot rank compounds whose measured potencies span three orders of magnitude (0.064 nM to 14 nM) — if the docking order contradicts the measured order, the docking is wrong, not the measurements. Third, the PubChem analogues carry no measured potency at all: a good docking score for an analogue is a hypothesis for the assay, worth exactly one binding experiment, and nothing more.

4.3 Mechanism

AURKA is activated at the centrosome by TPX2 binding and by autophosphorylation of Thr288 in the activation loop; it then phosphorylates substrates that build the bipolar spindle (including TACC3/ch-TOG) and it stabilises N-Myc and MYC in the nucleus, where kinase-independent scaffolding functions also sustain oncogenic transcription. That nuclear, kinase-independent role is the reason kinase inhibitors can fail even when they occupy the ATP pocket perfectly — the protein keeps scaffolding. Test for each link: (i) a biochemical kinase assay measures whether the compound inhibits AURKA catalytic activity (IC50/Ki); (ii) phospho-Thr288 immunoblotting in mitotic cells measures whether the compound engages AURKA in cells; (iii) monopolar-spindle formation and G2/M arrest measure whether the mitotic phenotype follows; (iv) an RB1-deficient line (e.g. NCI-H446) versus an RB1-wild-type line measures whether the LY3295668 synthetic-lethality logic extends to the new compound.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-docking PubChem analogue inhibits recombinant AURKA with an IC50 within 10-fold of alisertib's 1.2 nM in a biochemical kinase assay. Falsifier: IC50 >12 nM.
  2. At least one analogue reduces phospho-Thr288 Aurora A in mitotic HCT116 cells at ≤1 µM, with monopolar spindles as the phenotypic readout. Falsifier: no phospho-Thr288 reduction below 10 µM.
  3. Re-docking with molecular-dynamics refinement preserves any analogue's advantage over alisertib within 1 kcal/mol. Falsifier: the advantage disappears after minimisation.
  4. The best analogue shows a selectivity window over Aurora B (phospho-HisH3 Ser10 readout) of at least 10-fold. Falsifier: Aurora B inhibition within 3-fold of Aurora A inhibition — the compound is a pan-Aurora inhibitor, not an AURKA inhibitor, and its development case collapses into the danusertib class.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): biochemical AURKA kinase assay for the best two analogues + alisertib and LY3295668 controls; readout IC50, n=3, with a known weak binder as a negative control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): cellular target engagement — phospho-Thr288 Aurora A and phospho-HisH3 Ser10 (Aurora B counter-screen) in HCT116, plus monopolar-spindle counts; RB1-deficient NCI-H446 versus RB1-wild-type as the synthetic-lethality check. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, solubility and plasma-protein-binding measurement plus a first cytotoxicity screen (HepG2); if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows every reported margin.
  2. The PubChem analogues have no measured potency against AURKA — or against anything — and similarity to alisertib is not evidence of activity.
  3. The ChEMBL bioactivity endpoint was down on the day of the run (HTTP 500), so no ChEMBL-measured AURKA ligands could be retrieved; the comparison set is smaller and less systematic than the pipeline's design intends. A re-run when the endpoint recovers may change the set.
  4. Published potencies compared here come from different assay formats (cell-free IC50, Ki, cellular autophosphorylation IC50) and are not directly interchangeable; the Spearman analysis in §3.2 treats them as one scale only as an exploratory check.
  5. A single structure (6C2R) was used; the ATP pocket is flexible and the DFG-in/DFG-out state and the TPX2-bound conformation change the pocket, so one rigid structure under-samples the binding landscape.
  6. AURKA's kinase-independent nuclear scaffolding functions (MYC/N-Myc stabilisation) are not addressed by ATP-pocket docking at all; an ATP-competitive inhibitor can score perfectly here and still fail against the scaffolding function.
  7. No Aurora B counter-screen was computed: selectivity over AURKB is the property that separates a usable AURKA drug from a pan-Aurora drug, and docking on AURKA alone cannot show it.
  8. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi; the full Arabic texts were not read, and other classical works on tumours were not individually consulted.

6. Conclusion

The 8-chloro positional isomer of alisertib (PubChem CID 92044531) binds the true ATP pocket of Aurora A (6C2R) with the best score in a ten-compound set, −9.20 kcal/mol against −8.87 kcal/mol for re-docked alisertib and −8.95 for the co-crystallised LY3295668, with tight pose consistency and no PAINS alerts. The 0.33 kcal/mol margin is inside Vina noise, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order, and the isomer shares alisertib's lipophilicity problem — so this is not evidence that the isomer beats alisertib, it is evidence that the isomer is worth the cheap, decisive test: a biochemical kinase assay and cellular phospho-Thr288 engagement with alisertib and LY3295668 as comparators. That test, not another docking run, is the next step.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's Higher Education Commission research-funding panels and the SMBBMU ORIC office, with DRAP as the eventual regulator. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of alisertib analogues and existing AURKA inhibitors as an academic drug-discovery exercise. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week biochemical-plus-cellular screen proposed in §4.5 for the best two PubChem analogues against alisertib and LY3295668, instead of funding another purely computational screen of the same target. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if both analogues lose >10-fold to alisertib in the kinase assay or show no phospho-Thr288 reduction in cells, drop this analogue set and redirect the same screen to the next AURKA chemotypes — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable drug from a useless one for a disease that kills 9.7 million people a year, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only, and for the analogues not even measured potency — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".
