† L-742,001 PA endonuclease IC50 0.5 µM (Stevaert et al., Mol Pharmacol 2015). ‡ Baloxavir acid inhibits the PA endonuclease at low-nanomolar concentrations (published in-vitro summaries). § EBSI-747 is the fragment hit co-crystallised in 5IEQ; no enzyme IC50 was reported for it in the structure record.

L-742,001 out-scores baloxavir acid by 0.55 kcal/mol with tight pose consistency (top-3 spread 0.44 kcal/mol). The fragment re-docks at −5.55 kcal/mol with near-identical poses — the expected behaviour for a small fragment in a large pocket, and a useful sanity check that the grid is on the real site.

3.3 The docking–activity discordance that must not be hidden

The measured potencies do not track the docking order. Baloxavir acid is roughly 100-fold more potent than L-742,001 by enzyme IC50 (low-nanomolar versus 0.5 µM), yet it docks 0.55 kcal/mol worse. The reason is visible in the structure: both inhibitors bind by chelating the two catalytic metal ions of the endonuclease active site, and 5IEQ contains no metal ions at all — Vina is scoring only the non-metal contacts (hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonds), which favour the larger, more hydrophobic L-742,001. Rigid Vina scoring on a metal-free structure cannot rank metal-chelating inhibitors. This is the paper's most important negative result: the docking ranking is not a potency ranking, and any claim built on the −7.17 vs −6.62 gap alone would be over-reading noise on top of a missing physical interaction.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina study of baloxavir acid or L-742,001 on 5IEQ was found in the sweep; the comparison here is internal (compounds vs re-docked reference on the same structure, same protocol). The re-docked baloxavir acid score of −6.62 kcal/mol and the fragment's −5.55 kcal/mol are the validated controls that anchor the comparison. Stevaert et al. (2013) previously docked L-742,001 into an inhibitor-free PA N-terminal structure and found a binding orientation distinct from the later crystal structure — a reminder that this pocket's docking poses are method-sensitive.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can actually answer is narrower than the one it started with. It cannot say "L-742,001 beats baloxavir" — the margin is inside noise, the potency order is reversed, and the scoring omits the metal chelation that defines both inhibitors. What it can say is: (a) baloxavir acid re-docks cleanly on the fragment structure with tight poses, so the protocol is sound; (b) the ChEMBL PA record has no usable small-molecule ligand set, a data-quality gap that any future screen must work around by curating inhibitors from the literature instead; (c) the decisive experiment is now sharply defined — a metal-containing endonuclease assay comparing baloxavir acid, L-742,001 and analogues on wild-type and I38T PA — and it is cheap and feasible in a university lab.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the 0.55 kcal/mol margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order by ~100-fold. Third, the two catalytic metal ions are absent from the structure, and resistance mutations act precisely around that metal centre — I38T sits adjacent to the active site and perturbs inhibitor binding without destroying catalysis. A compound that scores well here may still fail against I38T, and the only way to know is the enzyme assay.

4.3 Mechanism

The PA endonuclease cleaves host capped pre-mRNAs using two divalent metal ions coordinated by the catalytic residues (including His41 and Glu80); inhibitors chelate those metals while their hydrophobic groups occupy the surrounding pockets. I38T changes the shape of the pocket without touching the metals, which is why it costs baloxavir ~18-fold in binding while leaving the enzyme functional. Test for each link: (i) a metal-containing endonuclease cleavage assay measures whether the compound still inhibits wild-type and I38T enzyme; (ii) a cellular vRNP reporter assay measures whether inhibition survives in cells; (iii) a metal-containing co-crystal structure, if one becomes available, would let docking test the mechanism directly.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a metal-containing PA endonuclease assay, baloxavir acid retains a ≥10-fold IC50 advantage over L-742,001 on wild-type PA. Falsifier: L-742,001 within 3-fold of baloxavir acid.
  2. At least one L-742,001 analogue (from the Stevaert et al. series) shows ≤3-fold IC50 loss against I38T PA where baloxavir acid loses ≥18-fold. Falsifier: all analogues lose ≥10-fold against I38T.
  3. Re-docking on a metal-containing PA structure reverses the L-742,001 advantage over baloxavir acid. Falsifier: the advantage persists with metals present.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): recombinant wild-type and I38T PA endonuclease cleavage assay (fluorescence-based, with Mg²⁺/Mn²⁺ present) for baloxavir acid, L-742,001 and two analogues; readout IC50, n=3. Stage 2 (weeks 4–8): cellular mini-genome (vRNP) reporter assay in HEK293T cells for the same compounds, wild-type versus I38T. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): if any analogue passes stages 1–2, cytotoxicity (HepG2) and a first resistance-passage experiment; if none passes, publish the negative result with the docking data as the reason the hypothesis failed.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol swallows the reported margin.
  2. The 5IEQ structure contains no catalytic metal ions, removing the chelation interaction that defines both inhibitors; scores may not reflect true binding energetics.
  3. The ChEMBL PA ligand set is undockable (all seven ligands >1,686 Da); no ChEMBL-derived lead is proposed.
  4. Docking order contradicts measured IC50 order (~100-fold discordance); rigid docking cannot rank these compounds.
  5. A single structure (5IEQ, a fragment-bound H1N1 PA) was used; the pocket differs across subtypes and the I38T question is untested in this work.
  6. Published baloxavir enzyme IC50 values are taken from in-vitro summaries; the primary assay data were not re-verified compound by compound.
  7. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi; the full Arabic texts were not read, and the canon has no concept of a viral enzyme — the sweep is historical context only.

6. Conclusion

Baloxavir acid re-docks at −6.62 kcal/mol on the influenza PA endonuclease fragment structure 5IEQ, against −7.17 kcal/mol for the older diketo-acid inhibitor L-742,001 and −5.55 kcal/mol for the co-crystallised fragment, with tight pose consistency and no PAINS alerts. The ChEMBL PA ligand set proved undockable — seven giant molecules, none of which could generate a conformer — and the 0.55 kcal/mol L-742,001 advantage is inside Vina noise, reverses the ~100-fold measured potency order, and was scored on a metal-free structure that omits the chelation both inhibitors rely on. This is not evidence that L-742,001 beats baloxavir — it is evidence that the two are worth the cheap, decisive test: a metal-containing enzyme assay on wild-type versus I38T PA. That test, not another docking run, is the next step.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's National Institute of Health (NIH Islamabad) influenza surveillance programme and the provincial health departments, with DRAP as regulator. Decision: whether to fund a small, targeted validation of alternative PA endonuclease inhibitors against locally circulating influenza strains. Exact change: commission the 8–12-week metal-containing enzyme-plus-cellular screen proposed in §4.5 for baloxavir acid versus L-742,001 analogues on wild-type and I38T PA, instead of relying on imported susceptibility assumptions for baloxavir. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if all analogues lose ≥10-fold activity against I38T PA, drop this chemotype set and redirect the same screen to the next PA inhibitor series — do not proceed to any animal or clinical work on docking scores alone. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life, a maqsad of the Sharia): where a cheap test can distinguish a usable antiviral from a useless one for a virus that kills hundreds of thousands a year, running the test is the obligation; prescribing on an untested docking score would violate it. The evidence here is thin — docking only — so the recommendation is "run the trial", not "do the policy".

No Structure to Dock On: Five Single-Digit-Nanomolar TbNMT Inhibitors Share One Scaffold, and the Blood–Brain Barrier — Not Potency — Decides Whether Any of Them Treats Stage-2 Sleeping Sickness

Human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) is down to 471 reported cases worldwide in 2025, and the WHO target is interruption of transmission by 2030 — but the last cases are the hardest, and they need drugs that reach the brain.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-18 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #77 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: sleeping sickness; Trypanosoma brucei; N-myristoyltransferase; DDD85646; blood–brain barrier; neglected tropical disease; ChEMBL

Abstract

Human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) is down to 471 reported cases worldwide in 2025, and the WHO target is interruption of transmission by 2030 — but the last cases are the hardest, and they need drugs that reach the brain. DDD85646, a pyrazole-sulfonamide inhibitor of Trypanosoma brucei N-myristoyltransferase (TbNMT), is potent (enzyme IC50 1–2 nM) and cures stage-1 (haemolymphatic) infection in rodents, yet poor central nervous system exposure restricts it to stage 1. We asked whether ChEMBL holds a DDD85646 analogue that keeps the potency and fixes the brain exposure. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q388H8 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL3988596, 60 bioactivities → PubChem/RDKit similarity, PAINS and ADMET screen), we retrieved five single-digit-nanomolar TbNMT inhibitors, including DDD85646 itself. Docking was not performed: no Trypanosoma brucei NMT crystal structure exists in the PDB (verified 2026-11-18; the only NMT structures are from Leishmania major and Aspergillus fumigatus), and docking a T. brucei inhibitor onto another species' enzyme would be a false result. The honest finding is structural, not numerical: all five compounds share one scaffold (identical TPSA 92.15 Å², the published pyrazole-sulfonamide core), so none obviously escapes the parent's brain-exposure problem on descriptors alone — the smallest and least lipophilic analogue, CHEMBL4112331 (MW 426.55, logP 2.31), is the only one inside all standard CNS descriptor bands, and even it sits at TPSA 92.15 Å², just above the usual <90 Å² blood–brain-barrier guideline. The claim that any analogue is a stage-2 candidate would be refuted if PAMPA-BBB or MDCK-MDR1 testing shows no analogue beats DDD85646's brain exposure. The falsifiable next step is a 4-week BBB-permeability screen of the four analogues, not another potency assay.

1. Introduction

Sleeping sickness, caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense (92% of cases) and T. b. rhodesiense and transmitted by the tsetse fly, is fatal without treatment and has two stages: a haemolymphatic stage with non-specific symptoms, and a meningoencephalitic stage in which parasites enter the central nervous system, causing the sleep disturbance, psychiatric symptoms and coma that give the disease its name. In 1998 more than 34,000 cases were reported, with the WHO estimating the true number at ten times that; by 2025 only 471 cases were reported worldwide, most of them in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Guinea was validated by WHO in January 2025 as having eliminated gambiense sleeping sickness as a public health problem (fewer than one case per 10,000 people in endemic areas over 2019–2023). The WHO roadmap's harder goal is interruption of transmission — zero cases — by 2030.

Treatment has modernised fast: fexinidazole (2018) was the first all-oral drug, and acoziborole — a single-dose oral drug with 98.1% efficacy in trials — received a positive scientific opinion from the European Medicines Agency in 2026. Against that background, a new NMT inhibitor must answer a sharp question: what does it add that acoziborole does not already provide? The honest answer for a DDD85646 analogue is: nothing, unless it reaches the brain — because stage-2 disease is the unmet need, and DDD85646's failure was a brain-exposure failure, not a potency failure.

TbNMT catalyses the co-translational transfer of myristate from myristoyl-CoA to the N-terminal glycine of target proteins; bioinformatic analysis suggests more than 60 potential substrates in T. brucei, including ADP-ribosylation factor-1 (ARF-1) and ARF-like protein 1 (ARL-1), both essential for bloodstream parasite viability. RNAi knockdown of NMT is lethal in culture and abrogates infectivity in animal models. DDD85646 was discovered at Dundee: it inhibits TbNMT (IC50 2 nM as published; 1 nM in the ChEMBL record), kills T. brucei in culture (EC50 2 nM), has good oral pharmacokinetics and cures rodent models of peripheral infection — and its development stopped at the blood–brain barrier.

The classical Islamic medical canon has no specific discussion of trypanosomiasis: sleeping sickness is a sub-Saharan disease outside the clinical geography of Ibn Sina's Canon (c. 1025) and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900), and the canon sweep for this paper found no relevant text (see Limitations). What the canon does supply is the principle: hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) and maslaha (public benefit) applied to the neglected — the duty to test a cheap discriminating experiment for a disease of the poorest, rather than to abandon it because the case count is now small. A disease with 471 cases a year is exactly where a small, cheap test matters most, because no company will run it (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Does any ChEMBL-recorded DDD85646 analogue combine single-digit-nanomolar TbNMT inhibition with predicted blood–brain-barrier penetration better than DDD85646 itself? Falsifier: PAMPA-BBB or MDCK-MDR1 testing showing no analogue beats DDD85646's brain exposure, or a measured brain-to-plasma ratio below 0.1 for the best analogue. Causal identification: none available in this study — this is a descriptor and literature analysis, association only, stated in bold. No docking was possible, so there is no validated-control re-docking to anchor a causal claim.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-18: the Dundee DDD85646 papers (Nature 2010; Journal of Medicinal Chemistry 2012; Acta Crystallographica F 2015), the WHO human African trypanosomiasis fact sheet, the 2025–2026 elimination literature (Guinea validation; acoziborole EMA opinion; 471 cases in 2025), and the RCSB/PDBe records for NMT structures. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — no trypanosomiasis text was found in either, and that negative result is reported in the Limitations rather than hidden.

2.2 Why there is no docking section

Standardised AutoDock Vina docking requires an experimental structure of the target. The LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q388H8, ChEMBL target CHEMBL3988596) found no PDB entry for T. brucei NMT: find_pdb_for_uniprot returned no_pdb_found because the TrEMBL entry Q388H8 carries no PDB cross-reference. A direct RCSB full-text search on 2026-11-18 returned seven NMT structures — 5AG4, 5AG5, 5AG6, 5AG7, 5AGE (all Leishmania major NMT) and 4UWI, 4UWJ (both Aspergillus fumigatus NMT). None is T. brucei. Docking a T. brucei inhibitor onto the Leishmania enzyme would produce a number that looks like a result and is not one; the paper therefore reports no docking scores at all. This follows the precedent of Paper #70 (HP-067, Plasmodium PI4K), where the same situation was handled the same way.

2.3 Compound retrieval and screens

LeadForge pipeline, 2026-11-18: UniProtKB Q388H8 (glycylpeptide N-tetradecanoyltransferase, T. brucei brucei strain 927/4 GUTat10.1) → ChEMBL target CHEMBL3988596 (60 bioactivities) → PubChem verification of DDD85646 (CID 44199337) → RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen (top 25) → ADMET/PAINS/ToxGuard panel → composite ranking. RDKit descriptors and Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) computed for every lead; PAINS filter applied to all 26 leads.

2.4 Honesty limits

No docking, no experimental data, no BBB measurement in this study. Measured IC50 values are ChEMBL records. Blood–brain-barrier penetration is assessed here only through computed descriptors against standard CNS guidelines (TPSA <90 Å², MW <450 Da, logP 2–4) — descriptors predict, they do not measure. The ChEMBL IC50 for DDD85646 (1 nM) differs from the published value (2 nM); both are reported.

3.2 One scaffold, one TPSA, one problem

All five compounds share TPSA 92.15 Å² exactly — the same polar surface, the same pyrazole-sulfonamide core. The analogues differ only in peripheral substitution (MW 427–538, logP 2.31–4.51). That means the potency is a property of the scaffold, and the scaffold's brain problem is likely shared: DDD85646's poor CNS exposure is a property of this chemotype's polar surface and efflux profile, and changing a peripheral substituent rarely moves TPSA at all — indeed, here it did not move by a single unit. Against standard CNS descriptor bands (TPSA <90 Å², MW <450 Da, logP 2–4), only CHEMBL4112331 sits inside all three bands except TPSA, where it too is 92.15 Å² — 2.15 Å² over the line. CHEMBL3357685 (MW 537.52, logP 4.51, one Lipinski violation) is the worst BBB bet of the four.

3.3 Toxicity read-across

Tox21 kNN read-across predicted no assay at or above 0.3 probability for any of the five compounds, including DDD85646. This is a weak screen — read-across, not measurement — and it cannot see CNS exposure or efflux.

3.4 Comparison with published work

DDD85646's published profile (Frearson et al., Nature 2010; Brand et al., Journal of Medicinal Chemistry 2012): enzyme IC50 2 nM, T. brucei EC50 2 nM, good oral pharmacokinetics, cures rodent peripheral infection, poor CNS exposure. The ChEMBL record (IC50 1 nM) is consistent within assay variation. The fragment-screen paper (Acta Crystallographica F 2015) states the consequence plainly: poor CNS exposure restricts DDD85646 to the haemolymphatic (stage-1) form, and new chemical matter was sought specifically to occupy the DDD85646 binding site with better brain penetration. No analogue in this set has a published brain-exposure measurement.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question is not "which analogue is most potent" — four of the five are 1 nM, and potency stopped being the problem in 2010. The question is "which analogue, if any, crosses the blood–brain barrier", and this paper's descriptor analysis suggests the answer may be "none of these four": they share the parent's polar surface exactly, and the parent does not cross. The honest contribution of this paper is therefore a negative one — it narrows the search. It says: do not spend the next assay on enzyme potency for this scaffold; spend it on permeability, and if permeability fails, leave the scaffold.

4.2 Why a docking score would have made this paper worse

If a Leishmania NMT structure had been used as a surrogate, the paper could have reported attractive-looking scores (−10 kcal/mol and better) for compounds whose target is a different species' enzyme. Those scores would have been uninterpretable: NMT active sites are conserved enough to dock plausibly and different enough that a 1–2 kcal/mol difference means nothing. Refusing the surrogate dock is the methodologically correct choice, and it is also the reason this paper is shorter on numbers than its neighbours.

4.3 Mechanism

NMT transfers myristate from myristoyl-CoA to N-terminal glycine residues of substrate proteins; DDD85646 occupies the peptide-substrate pocket, not the myristoyl-CoA site. Inhibition blocks myristoylation of essential substrates (ARF-1, ARL-1), mislocalises them, and kills the parasite rapidly. For stage-2 disease the inhibitor must additionally cross the blood–brain barrier — which requires low polar surface, moderate lipophilicity, and escape from efflux transporters (P-glycoprotein, BCRP). Test for each link: (i) PAMPA-BBB measures passive permeability; (ii) MDCK-MDR1 efflux ratio measures transporter liability; (iii) a mouse brain-to-plasma ratio measures the outcome that matters.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL4112331 has a PAMPA-BBB permeability above the CNS-positive threshold and an MDCK-MDR1 efflux ratio below 2. Falsifier: permeability below threshold or efflux ratio ≥2.
  2. No analogue in this set achieves a mouse brain-to-plasma ratio above 0.3. Falsifier: any analogue exceeds 0.3.
  3. Acoziborole's single-dose efficacy (98.1%) makes a stage-1-only NMT inhibitor clinically redundant in gambiense HAT. Falsifier: a setting where acoziborole is unavailable or contraindicated and a stage-1 NMT inhibitor changes outcomes.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 4–8 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): PAMPA-BBB + MDCK-MDR1 for the four analogues and DDD85646; readout is permeability and efflux ratio, with a CNS-positive control. Stage 2 (weeks 3–5): for any analogue passing stage 1, mouse brain-to-plasma ratio after a single oral dose; if none passes, stop — publish the negative result. Stage 3 (weeks 6–8): only for an analogue with brain exposure: whole-cell EC50 against T. b. gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense bloodstream forms, plus a stage-2 mouse model. Total cost is small; the decision it buys is whether this scaffold lives or dies.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking (no T. brucei NMT structure exists) and no experimental data in this study; the BBB assessment is descriptor-based only.
  2. Measured IC50 values are ChEMBL records; the DDD85646 ChEMBL value (1 nM) differs from the published value (2 nM).
  3. TPSA/logP/MW bands are guidelines, not measurements; efflux transporters can defeat even a descriptor-perfect molecule.
  4. All five compounds share one scaffold; the analysis cannot speak to other NMT chemotypes.
  5. No human NMT selectivity data are reported here; human NMT inhibition would be a toxicity liability and was not assessed beyond Tox21 read-across.
  6. The Islamic-canon sweep found no classical text on trypanosomiasis — the disease lies outside the canon's clinical geography — so the canon contributes a principle (hifz al-nafs, maslaha for the neglected) rather than a precedent.
  7. No cost or access analysis for acoziborole in the DRC was available for this paper.

6. Conclusion

Five single-digit-nanomolar inhibitors of T. brucei NMT exist in ChEMBL — DDD85646 and four analogues at 1–4 nM, all PAINS-clean and Lipinski-clean except one. No T. brucei NMT structure exists, so no docking was performed and none is claimed. The five share one scaffold and one polar surface (TPSA 92.15 Å²), which means none obviously escapes the parent's published failure: poor brain exposure restricting it to stage-1 disease. The smallest analogue, CHEMBL4112331, is the only one inside the standard CNS descriptor bands apart from TPSA, and it is the only one worth the cheap permeability test. If it fails that test, the scaffold should be retired and the field's attention should stay on the drugs that already work — fexinidazole and acoziborole — and on the 2030 transmission-interruption goal.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: The WHO Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases and the DRC national sleeping-sickness programme, with DNDi as technical adviser. Decision: whether any further public money should go to the DDD85646 scaffold. Exact change: fund only the 4-week PAMPA-BBB/MDCK-MDR1 screen proposed in §4.5 for the four analogues, and fund no efficacy work on this scaffold until an analogue passes it — instead of continuing potency-first screening that has already produced five 1 nM compounds and zero stage-2 drugs. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if CHEMBL4112331 (or any analogue) shows a brain-to-plasma ratio above 0.3, escalate it to the stage-2 mouse model and a head-to-head comparison with acoziborole; if none passes, retire the scaffold and redirect the same funds to acoziborole delivery and tsetse control in the DRC, where the remaining 471 cases are. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs with maslaha for the neglected (mustad'afun): for a disease of the poorest, with 471 cases left, the obligation is to spend the small amount on the discriminating test and the large amount on delivery — not to keep polishing a potency number that stopped mattering in 2010.

A Target With No Approved Drug: Four PanC Inhibitors Dock at −10.64 to −7.66 kcal/mol on the 1.5 Å Fragment Structure — but the 90 nM Inhibitor Was Never Docked, and the Reference Drug Could Not Be Docked at All

Pantothenate synthetase (PanC) is essential for Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth in vitro and survival in mice, is absent from mammals, and has no approved drug — the ideal profile of an unexploited target, and the reason it has attracted twenty years of inhibitor chemistry without a clinical candidate.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-18 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #78 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: tuberculosis; pantothenate synthetase; PanC; actinomycin D; molecular docking; ChEMBL; drug target; MDR-TB

Abstract

Pantothenate synthetase (PanC) is essential for Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth in vitro and survival in mice, is absent from mammals, and has no approved drug — the ideal profile of an unexploited target, and the reason it has attracted twenty years of inhibitor chemistry without a clinical candidate. We asked what the ChEMBL record actually contains for this target and whether its inhibitors bind the known inhibitor pocket. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P9WIL5 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL6069, 59 bioactivities → PubChem/RDKit similarity, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we docked four leads on the 1.5 Å PanC structure 3IUB, centred on its co-crystallised fragment-derived inhibitor. The four leads scored −10.64 to −7.66 kcal/mol with tight pose consistency, and their measured potencies are 1.0–2.0 µM. The honest limits are twofold and both matter more than the scores. First, the reference compound, actinomycin D — the only named, PubChem-resolvable literature PanC inhibitor (IC50 22.44 µM) — could not be docked at all: Vina hit its 30-minute timeout on a 1,255 Da, highly flexible ligand, so there is no re-docked reference benchmark in this paper. Second, the similarity anchor (actinomycin D) biased lead selection so strongly that the most potent ChEMBL PanC inhibitor, CHEMBL428787 (IC50 90 nM), ranked 17th and was never docked, while the best-docked compound (CHEMBL2435654, −10.64 kcal/mol) has a measured Kd of only 1.8 µM. The claim that any docked compound here is a PanC lead would be refuted if a direct enzyme assay shows no inhibition below 10 µM, or if re-docking the 90 nM compound scores worse than the compounds reported here. The falsifiable next step is a 4-week enzyme assay plus a re-dock of the five most potent ChEMBL PanC inhibitors — selected by potency, not by similarity to actinomycin D.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis again kills about 1.25 million people a year (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024), and around 400,000 people annually develop multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant disease. Pakistan is among the eight countries accounting for two-thirds of the global burden. Every drug in the current regimens — including the BPaLM combination — hits targets the bacillus has learned to evade, which is why the field keeps a list of validated-but-unexploited targets. PanC sits at the top of that list.

PanC (pantothenate synthetase, product of the panC gene) catalyses the last step of pantothenate (vitamin B5) biosynthesis — D-pantoate plus β-alanine plus ATP to pantothenate, AMP and pyrophosphate. It is a homodimer (33 kDa per subunit), essential for M. tuberculosis growth in vitro and for survival in the mouse model, and it is absent from mammals, which obtain pantothenate from the diet. That combination — essential, pathogen-specific, structurally characterised — is exactly what a drug target should look like. Yet no PanC inhibitor has reached the clinic. The published chemistry falls into three generations: pantoyl-adenylate sulfamoyl analogues from Abell's group (Ki 220–300 nM, the most potent enzyme inhibitors reported); fragment-grown and fragment-linked indole-carboxamides (Angewandte Chemie 2009, the source of the 3IUB structure used here); and the 3-biphenyl-4-cyanopyrrole-2-carboxylic acids from a Lilly high-throughput screen (whole-cell MIC50 54 and 115 µM, with on-target behaviour confirmed by a PanC under-expressor strain that became ~2-fold more sensitive, rescued by added pantothenate). A fourth, stranger entry is actinomycin D — a cytotoxic DNA intercalator whose PanC inhibition (IC50 22.44 µM) was reported from a pharmacophore screen; it is a benchmark, not a candidate.

The classical canon's contribution here is a principle rather than a precedent: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) systematised the idea that a drug should act on a specific disease mechanism rather than on the whole body, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) insisted on observation over authority — both of which point the same way in this paper: report what the data actually show, including the selection bias, rather than what a tidy story would prefer (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL-recorded inhibitors of M. tuberculosis PanC bind the fragment-derived inhibitor pocket (PDB 3IUB) with scores consistent with their measured potency? Falsifier: a direct enzyme assay showing no inhibition below 10 µM for the best-docked compound, or the 90 nM compound (CHEMBL428787) re-docking worse than the compounds reported here. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking was NOT achieved — the reference compound could not be docked — so this paper's claims are association only, stated in bold, and the missing control is itself a reported result.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-18: the PanC inhibitor review (RSC Advances 2020, doi:10.1039/d0ra07398a), the high-throughput screen paper (PLoS One 2013, PMID 24244263), the fragment growing/linking paper (Angewandte Chemie 2009, PMID 19780086), the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, and the RCSB record for PDB 3IUB. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: M. tuberculosis pantothenate synthetase, UniProtKB P9WIL5 (H37Rv); ChEMBL bioactivity target CHEMBL6069. Structure: PDB 3IUB, M. tuberculosis PanC in complex with 5-methoxy-N-(5-methylpyridin-2-ylsulfonyl)-1H-indole-2-carboxamide, 1.5 Å (Hung et al., Angewandte Chemie 2009). Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised inhibitor via dock._ligand_center, [15.51, 10.02, 0.37], box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for all four leads and for the reference attempt.

Structure audit. 3IUB is the correct domain and the correct site: it is the full PanC enzyme with a fragment-derived inhibitor bound in the active-site pocket — the same pocket the pantoyl-adenylate analogues occupy. No correction was needed (contrast Paper #75, where the pipeline's first structure was the wrong domain).

2.3 Reference-compound problem, stated plainly

There is no approved PanC drug. The pipeline requires a PubChem-resolvable reference compound, and the only named literature PanC inhibitor that PubChem resolves is actinomycin D (PubChem CID 457193; MW 1,255.44; TPSA 359.98 Å²; two Lipinski violations). It was used as the similarity-query anchor. Two consequences follow, and both are reported as results, not hidden as methods footnotes. (i) Actinomycin D could not be docked: Vina ran for 30 minutes (the per-ligand timeout) without returning a pose, on a 1,255 Da ligand with ~30 rotatable bonds — rigid-body Vina triage cannot handle a molecule of that size and flexibility. The QUERY dock is therefore absent from §3, and there is no re-docked reference benchmark. (ii) Lead selection was biased by similarity to actinomycin D: the four docked leads are the most actinomycin-similar ChEMBL PanC ligands, not the most potent ones. The paper corrects for this in §3.3 by reporting the most potent ChEMBL PanC inhibitors regardless of similarity.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all 26 pipeline leads. No lead carries a PAINS alert — including all four docked compounds and the 90 nM compound.

2.5 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for every lead; ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) run for every lead. Actinomycin D itself carries measured Tox21 flags (NR-Aromatase 1, SR-p53 1) — consistent with its known cytotoxicity, and one more reason it is a benchmark rather than a candidate.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist in this study. Measured IC50/Kd values are ChEMBL records from different assay formats (IC50 vs Kd mixed) and were not re-verified compound by compound. The reference drug was not docked, so no validated control anchors the comparison.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound ChEMBL potency vs PanC* Best affinity, 3IUB (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses (kcal/mol) PAINS MW / logP / TPSA
CHEMBL2435654 Kd 1,800 nM (pChEMBL 5.75) −10.64 −10.64, −10.50, −10.22 none 411.44 / 3.20 / 113.68
CHEMBL3763165 IC50 1,020 nM (pChEMBL 5.99) −8.71 −8.71, −8.69, −8.44 none 313.43 / 3.92 / 46.40
CHEMBL1487172 IC50 1,990 nM (pChEMBL 5.70) −7.76 −7.76, −7.75, −7.48 none 257.34 / 2.71 / 46.40
CHEMBL3763965 IC50 2,000 nM (pChEMBL 5.70) −7.66 −7.66, −7.61, −7.23 none 263.37 / 2.77 / 46.40

* ChEMBL-recorded potency against M. tuberculosis pantothenate synthetase (target CHEMBL6069), retrieved live 2026-11-18. † Actinomycin D PanC IC50 from the RSC Advances 2020 review of PanC inhibitors.

All four leads dock with tight pose consistency (top-3 spread ≤0.42 kcal/mol). Three of the four share TPSA 46.40 Å² and molecular weights of 257–313 Da — small, fragment-like molecules, consistent with the indole-carboxamide fragment series that produced the 3IUB structure. CHEMBL2435654 is the outlier: larger (411 Da), more polar (TPSA 113.68 Å²), and it docks 1.93 kcal/mol better than the next compound.

3.2 The docking–potency discordance

The best-docked compound is not the most potent. CHEMBL2435654 scores −10.64 kcal/mol but its measured Kd is 1.8 µM — weaker than CHEMBL3763165's measured IC50 of 1.02 µM, which docks almost 2 kcal/mol worse. The four docked compounds span only a 2-fold potency range (1.0–2.0 µM) against a 2.98 kcal/mol docking range. Rigid Vina scoring on this pocket cannot resolve a 2-fold potency difference, and the −10.64 score should not be read as "five times better" than −8.71.

3.3 The compounds the pipeline did not dock — the selection-bias audit

Ranked by measured potency rather than by similarity to actinomycin D, the ChEMBL PanC record looks different:

Compound ChEMBL potency MW / logP Pipeline rank (by similarity) Docked?
CHEMBL428787 IC50 90 nM (pChEMBL 7.05) 428.54 / 5.48 17 No
CHEMBL408197 IC50 97 nM (pChEMBL 7.01) — 6 No
CHEMBL412059 IC50 120 nM (pChEMBL 6.92) — 11 No
CHEMBL261486 IC50 130 nM (pChEMBL 6.89) — 24 No
CHEMBL258966 / CHEMBL409940 IC50 140 nM (pChEMBL 6.85) — 19 / 20 No

The most potent PanC inhibitor in the ChEMBL record (90 nM, ten times more potent than the best docked compound) was never docked, because its similarity to actinomycin D is only 0.124. CHEMBL428787 is PAINS-clean, with one Lipinski violation (logP 5.48) and TPSA 72.95 Å². This is the paper's most important finding: the pipeline's similarity-first ranking is the wrong ranking for a target with no approved drug, and the right next step is to dock the potency-ranked list.

3.4 Toxicity read-across

Tox21 kNN read-across predicted no assay at or above 0.3 probability for any of the four docked leads (highest: SR-ARE 0.32 for CHEMBL3763165). This is a weak screen — read-across, not measurement.

3.5 Comparison with published work

No published Vina study of these four ChEMBL compounds on 3IUB was found in the sweep. The published benchmarks are the pantoyl-adenylate sulfamoyl analogues (Ki 220–300 nM) and the fragment-derived indole-carboxamides behind 3IUB itself — both more potent than any compound docked here, and neither was in the docked set. The 3IUB co-crystallised ligand (5-methoxy-N-(5-methylpyridin-2-ylsulfonyl)-1H-indole-2-carboxamide) is the fragment-series exemplar; re-docking it was not performed in this run, which is a gap: a self-dock of the co-crystallised ligand is the standard control, and its absence weakens the comparison further.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

This paper's result is not "CHEMBL2435654 docks at −10.64 kcal/mol". Its result is that the standard pipeline, pointed at a target with no approved drug, produces a misleading answer by construction: it ranks by similarity to a reference that is itself a poor inhibitor (22.44 µM) and a molecule Vina cannot dock, and it never looks at the 90 nM compound sitting in the same database. The honest conclusion is procedural: for no-approved-drug targets, rank by measured potency first and dock that list; similarity to a weak reference is the wrong filter.

4.2 Why the scores must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, there is no re-docked reference control — the one control that would anchor the scale failed to run. Second, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order. Third, the self-dock control (re-docking the 3IUB co-crystallised ligand) was not performed. Fourth, Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) covers the gap between three of the four leads entirely.

4.3 Mechanism

PanC joins D-pantoate and β-alanine in an ATP-dependent reaction proceeding through a pantoyl-adenylate intermediate; the sulfamoyl adenylate analogues mimic that intermediate and are the most potent inhibitors known (Ki 220–300 nM). The fragment-derived indole-carboxamides occupy the same pocket with a different chemotype. A genuine PanC lead must inhibit the enzyme, cross the mycobacterial cell wall, and retain activity in whole cells — the 3-biphenyl-4-cyanopyrrole-2-carboxylic acids are the only class with demonstrated whole-cell, on-target activity (MIC50 54–115 µM, sensitised in a PanC under-expressor, rescued by pantothenate). Test for each link: (i) enzyme inhibition (IC50) measures target engagement; (ii) the under-expressor shift measures on-target whole-cell activity; (iii) pantothenate rescue confirms the mechanism.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL428787 (90 nM) re-docks on 3IUB at a score better than −8.71 kcal/mol (the best of the micromolar set). Falsifier: it scores worse than −8.71.
  2. CHEMBL2435654 inhibits purified PanC with an IC50 within 3-fold of its ChEMBL Kd (1.8 µM). Falsifier: IC50 >10 µM.
  3. At least one of the five most potent ChEMBL PanC inhibitors shows whole-cell activity against H37Rv with a PanC under-expressor shift of ≥2-fold. Falsifier: no shift for any of the five.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): re-dock the five most potent ChEMBL PanC inhibitors (CHEMBL428787, CHEMBL408197, CHEMBL412059, CHEMBL261486, CHEMBL258966) on 3IUB, plus a self-dock of the co-crystallised ligand as the control this paper lacked. Stage 2 (weeks 3–8): enzyme inhibition assay (purified PanC, ATP/PPi readout) for the best three by potency and the best one by docking; readout IC50, n=3. Stage 3 (weeks 9–12): whole-cell MIC against H37Rv and a PanC under-expressor strain, with pantothenate rescue as the on-target control. If no compound passes stage 2, publish the negative result with the docking data.

5. Limitations

  1. No re-docked reference control (actinomycin D could not be docked — Vina 30-minute timeout on a 1,255 Da ligand); no self-dock of the co-crystallised ligand either.
  2. Lead selection was biased by similarity to a weak (22.44 µM) reference; the most potent inhibitor (90 nM) was not docked.
  3. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol.
  4. Measured potencies mix IC50 and Kd from different assay formats and were not re-verified compound by compound.
  5. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement; no whole-cell data for the docked compounds.
  6. Actinomycin D's measured Tox21 flags (NR-Aromatase, SR-p53) confirm it is cytotoxic; it must never be presented as a PanC drug candidate.
  7. The Islamic-canon sweep used the literature-map summaries of Ibn Sina's Canon and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi; the full Arabic texts were not read.

6. Conclusion

Four ChEMBL PanC inhibitors dock at −10.64 to −7.66 kcal/mol on the 1.5 Å structure 3IUB, with tight pose consistency and no PAINS alerts. The reference compound could not be docked, the docking order contradicts the measured potency order, and the most potent inhibitor in the database (90 nM) was never docked because the pipeline ranked by similarity to a weak reference. The paper's conclusion is therefore procedural, not molecular: for a target with no approved drug, dock the potency-ranked list, run the enzyme assay, and use the under-expressor shift as the on-target test. PanC remains a valid, unexploited target — but this paper does not name its lead. The next run might.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Pakistan's National TB Programme and the TB drug-discovery groups at Pakistani universities, with DRAP as regulator. Decision: whether to invest scarce assay capacity in PanC inhibitor screening. Exact change: fund the 8–12-week enzyme-plus-under-expressor validation proposed in §4.5 for the five most potent ChEMBL PanC inhibitors — selected by potency, not by similarity to any reference — instead of funding another similarity-screened docking list for this target. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if none of the five shows enzyme inhibition below 1 µM or a whole-cell under-expressor shift, deprioritise PanC for the local programme and redirect the same capacity to targets with whole-cell-active leads; if one does, advance it to combination testing with a cell-wall permeabiliser. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs with the scholarly duty Al-Razi stated plainly — observation over authority: a pipeline's ranking is an authority, and when its own audit shows the ranking missed the best compound, the honest act is to say so and re-rank, not to publish the ranking as a result.

Posaconazole and Itraconazole Dock Best on the Naegleria CYP51 Structure — and the Ranking Matches the Published Potencies — but Karachi's Brain-Eating Amoeba Kills in Days, and No Azole Has a Measured Brain Exposure in PAM

Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), caused by Naegleria fowleri, kills more than 97% of patients within five to seven days of symptom onset, and Karachi — where infection now comes through ablution with tap water, not swimming — reports more cases than the United States recorded in fifty years.

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-18 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #79 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Naegleria fowleri; primary amoebic meningoencephalitis; CYP51; posaconazole; itraconazole; Karachi; molecular docking; drug repurposing

Abstract

Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), caused by Naegleria fowleri, kills more than 97% of patients within five to seven days of symptom onset, and Karachi — where infection now comes through ablution with tap water, not swimming — reports more cases than the United States recorded in fifty years. The parasite's sterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51) is an essential, structurally characterised target, and the published conazole potencies span three orders of magnitude (itraconazole and posaconazole EC50 0.01 µM; fluconazole 13.9 µM). We asked whether docking on the Naegleria CYP51–posaconazole structure reproduces that ranking. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB A0A2H4A2U9 → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked posaconazole on its own co-crystal structure 5TL8 (1.71 Å) at −10.91 kcal/mol (reproducing the pipeline's −10.84 within 0.07), then docked the other four published conazoles at the same centroid. The ranking matches the published potencies: itraconazole −11.59, posaconazole −10.91, ketoconazole −10.21, isavuconazole −8.96, fluconazole −7.01 kcal/mol (Spearman rho 0.95, n = 5, tied ranks). The honest limits: the pipeline's own ChEMBL ligand retrieval failed for this target — no ChEMBL target exists for N. fowleri CYP51, so it silently substituted human maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) and returned alpha-glucosidase inhibitors as "leads"; those scores are discarded, not reported. Three of the five conazoles carry RDKit PAINS alerts despite being approved drugs, which says more about the filter than about the drugs. And no azole has a measured brain exposure in PAM — the property that decides whether any of this matters, since PAM is a brain infection. The claim that itraconazole or posaconazole is the best PAM candidate would be refuted if brain-exposure measurement shows it does not reach the brain, or if a mouse PAM model shows no survival benefit. The falsifiable next step is a 4-week brain-exposure and mouse-PAM efficacy test of posaconazole versus itraconazole, not another docking run.

1. Introduction

Naegleria fowleri, the "brain-eating amoeba", is a free-living thermophilic amoeba that infects through the nose — contaminated water entering the nasal passages, crossing the cribriform plate along the olfactory nerve, and invading the brain. The resulting primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) presents like bacterial meningitis, which delays diagnosis, and kills more than 97% of patients, most within five to seven days of symptom onset. There is no approved drug for PAM; treatment is amphotericin B-based combinations with experimental additions, and success is rare.

Karachi is now the global centre of this disease. The first Pakistani case was recorded in Karachi in October 2008, in a boy who had swum in a river. By 2019 Karachi alone had reported 146 cases — more than the 142 cases the United States recorded between 1968 and 2019. The Karachi pattern is distinct: in a 2011 series of 13 cases, none of the patients had any history of aquatic activity, and infection was attributed to ablution with tap water; rising temperatures, reduced chlorine in potable water and deteriorating distribution systems were implicated. The pattern has persisted: a 36-year-old woman died in February 2025 with no recreational water exposure besides domestic ablution, and a 17-year-old boy died in 2025 — the fourth Karachi fatality that year — again with no swimming history, the infection suspected from non-chlorinated tap water. In 2023 Pakistan recorded seven PAM deaths (six in the Karachi area including Hyderabad and Quetta, one in Lahore). A 2024 study of 74 cerebrospinal-fluid samples from Karachi meningitis patients confirmed N. fowleri by microscopy, culture and PCR. The Pakistani isolates belong to the type-2 genotype, which may exhibit enhanced salinity tolerance — consistent with survival in Karachi's saline municipal and groundwater. Pakistan now has the second-highest prevalence of Naegleria infections in the world.

Against that background, the drug question is narrow: which existing drug, already manufactured and already in pharmacies, kills the amoeba and reaches the brain? The target is settled. N. fowleri has an essential requirement for ergosterol, and its genome encodes sterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51), sharing only ~35% sequence identity with fungal orthologues — close enough to repurpose antifungal azoles, distant enough that the ranking must be measured, not assumed. Debnath and colleagues (PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases 2017) showed that conazoles disrupt sterol biosynthesis and kill cultured trophozoites across a 1,000-fold potency range, and solved the structures — 5TL8, 6AY4, 6AY6, 6AYB and 6AYC — that make docking possible.

The classical canon has no specific discussion of this disease: PAM is a twentieth-century diagnosis, and the fulminant amoebic meningoencephalitis it describes lies outside the clinical geography of Ibn Sina's Canon (c. 1025) and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900). What the canon supplies is the principle — hifz al-nafs, preservation of life — and the practical corollary the canon's physicians understood: when a disease kills in days, the intervention must be in the pharmacy before the patient arrives, not in a journal after he dies (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do the five published conazoles dock onto N. fowleri CYP51 (PDB 5TL8) in the same rank order as their published anti-N. fowleri EC50 values, with posaconazole and itraconazole on top? Falsifier: a docking rank order that contradicts the published potency order, or a brain-exposure measurement showing the top-docked drug does not reach the brain. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — posaconazole re-docked on its own co-crystal structure — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity, and neither is brain exposure.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-18: the CYP51 target-validation paper (Debnath et al., PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases 2017), the Karachi case literature (Shakoor et al., Emerging Infectious Diseases 2011; Annals of Medical & Surgical 2025; Journal of Parasitology Research 2024; Frontiers in Public Health 2023), the PAM treatment literature (Baig & Khan, CNS Neuroscience & Therapeutics 2014), and the RCSB records for PDB 5TL8 and 6AYC. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — no PAM text was found in either, and that negative result is reported in the Limitations.

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: Naegleria fowleri sterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51), UniProtKB A0A2H4A2U9. Structure: PDB 5TL8, N. fowleri CYP51 in complex with posaconazole, 1.71 Å. Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised posaconazole (X2N) via dock._ligand_center, [6.25, 19.98, 47.66], box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for all five conazoles. Ligand SMILES were fetched live from PubChem by name (connectivity SMILES, as the pipeline uses). The haem cofactor is retained in the receptor preparation as part of the protein structure; the CYP51 haem iron is the azole coordination site, and the docking box is centred on it.

Structure audit. 5TL8 is the correct target, the correct species and the correct site: it is the N. fowleri enzyme with posaconazole bound in the active site, coordinating the haem iron. No correction was needed.

2.3 The pipeline's ChEMBL failure, stated plainly

The LeadForge pipeline's ligand retrieval failed for this target and failed silently. No ChEMBL target exists for UniProt A0A2H4A2U9 (verified 2026-11-18: a ChEMBL target-components query for that accession returns zero targets), so the pipeline's fallback text search returned human maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) as its first hit and retrieved 55 bioactivities against it — alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, confirmed by the assay descriptions (rice alpha-glucosidase colorimetric assay). The four "leads" it docked on 5TL8 (CHEMBL120488, CHEMBL120226, CHEMBL332802, CHEMBL121283; scores −7.58 to −5.98 kcal/mol) are therefore not CYP51 ligands at all, and their scores are DISCARDED — they appear nowhere in §3. The pipeline's own posaconazole self-dock (−10.84 kcal/mol) is valid and is retained as a reproducibility check: the corrected re-dock reproduces it at −10.91 kcal/mol. The comparison set in §3 is instead the five conazoles with published anti-N. fowleri data (Debnath et al. 2017), docked by a corrected driver (hidden_files/redock_hp078.py, output dock-HP-078c-2026-11-18.json). A first version of that driver failed on all five compounds because it requested PubChem properties by the wrong key names ("CanonicalSMILES"/"IsomericSMILES" are not returned; the endpoint returns "SMILES" and "ConnectivitySMILES") — the fix is documented in the script, and the corrected run succeeded on all five.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to the five conazoles. Posaconazole, itraconazole and ketoconazole each carry a PAINS alert; fluconazole and isavuconazole do not. All three flagged compounds are approved antifungal drugs with decades of human use — the alert is reported, not hidden, and §4 discusses what it does and does not mean.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No brain-exposure or animal-efficacy data exist in this study. Published EC50 values are from one laboratory's trophozoite assay (Debnath et al. 2017) and were not re-measured. The haem iron is treated as part of the rigid receptor; azole–iron coordination geometry is approximated by the scoring function, not modelled quantum-mechanically.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Posaconazole 0.01 µM −10.91 −10.91, −10.40, −10.20 alert 700.79 / 4.57 / 115.70
Ketoconazole equipotent to amphotericin B −10.21 −10.21, −10.12, −9.46 alert 531.44 / 4.21 / 69.06
Isavuconazole equipotent to amphotericin B −8.96 −8.96, −8.83, −8.71 none 437.48 / 4.24 / 87.62

* Debnath et al., PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases 2017: conazole EC50 values against cultured N. fowleri trophozoites; itraconazole and posaconazole were an order of magnitude more potent than amphotericin B, ketoconazole and isavuconazole equipotent to it.

The docking rank order matches the published potency order: the two 0.01 µM drugs dock best (−11.59 and −10.91 kcal/mol), the two amphotericin-B-equipotent drugs dock in the middle (−10.21 and −8.96), and fluconazole — 1,390-fold weaker than the leaders — docks worst (−7.01). Spearman rho 0.95 (n = 5, tied ranks). Pose consistency is tight for all five (top-3 spread ≤1.60 kcal/mol; four of five ≤0.75). The posaconazole self-dock reproduces the pipeline's independent run (−10.91 vs −10.84 kcal/mol), which is the validated control that anchors the comparison.

3.2 The gap the ranking does not close

The 0.68 kcal/mol gap between itraconazole (−11.59) and posaconazole (−10.91) is inside Vina noise, and both share the same published EC50 (0.01 µM) — docking cannot distinguish them, and the paper does not claim it can. The 1.25 kcal/mol gap between ketoconazole (−10.21) and isavuconazole (−8.96) is also inside noise, although both are reported as equipotent to amphotericin B. The ranking is therefore a coarse validation (potent drugs dock well, the weak drug docks badly), not a fine one. The one gap that exceeds noise is the 3.90 kcal/mol between posaconazole and fluconazole, which matches the 1,390-fold EC50 difference.

3.3 The PAINS alerts on approved drugs

Three of the five conazoles — including the two best-docked — carry an RDKit PAINS alert. All three are approved medicines with extensive human exposure. The alert therefore cannot be read as "these compounds are assay artefacts"; it is a screening heuristic flagging a substructure the filter considers promiscuous, and its presence on approved drugs is a known limitation of the filter, not a property of the drugs. The paper reports the flags because the template requires it, and states plainly that they do not change the ranking or the recommendation. (For contrast: the two PAINS-clean compounds, fluconazole and isavuconazole, are the two worst-docked — a PAINS-clean result is not a potency result either.)

3.4 The missing number: brain exposure

PAM is a brain infection, and a drug that kills trophozoites in a dish but does not reach the brain cannot treat it. Neither itraconazole nor posaconazole has a measured brain exposure in PAM in the sources consulted. Both are large molecules (MW ~700 Da, 11–12 rotatable bonds, Veber failures), which is not a favourable profile for blood–brain-barrier penetration — and that, not the docking score, is the decisive unknown. Any recommendation that ignores it would be prescribing on a docking score for a disease that kills in five days.

3.5 Comparison with published work

The docking result is consistent with, and weaker than, the published record: Debnath et al. already established the EC50 ranking by experiment in 2017 and solved the structures (5TL8, 6AY4, 6AY6, 6AYB, 6AYC). This paper adds only the quantitative check that rigid docking on 5TL8 reproduces the experimental ranking — a useful validation of the docking protocol for future N. fowleri work, not a new discovery. The paper's other contribution is the documented pipeline failure (§2.3): a silent wrong-target substitution that would have produced a plausible-looking but false result if it had not been caught by auditing the ChEMBL target.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper can answer — "does docking reproduce the known potency ranking?" — is answered yes, with a rho of 0.95. The question that matters — "which azole should a Karachi hospital stock for the next PAM case, and does it reach the brain?" — is not answered by this paper, and the paper's value is in saying that plainly. The two best-docked drugs are both large, both PAINS-flagged, both unmeasured in the brain, and both already in pharmacies. The next step is not more docking; it is a brain-exposure measurement and a mouse PAM model.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the top-two gap (0.68 kcal/mol) is inside Vina noise, so itraconazole and posaconazole are tied, not ranked. Second, the EC50 values come from a single laboratory's trophozoite assay and have not been independently reproduced in this study. Third, the azole–haem coordination that drives CYP51 binding is approximated by Vina's scoring function; a 1–2 kcal/mol error there is expected, not exceptional.

4.3 Mechanism

Azoles inhibit CYP51 by coordinating the haem iron through the triazole nitrogen, blocking the 14α-demethylation of lanosterol-like substrates and depleting ergosterol, which the amoeba requires for membrane integrity. N. fowleri CYP51 shares only ~35% sequence identity with fungal orthologues, so the binding-site shape differs — which is why the ranking had to be measured rather than assumed from antifungal data. Test for each link: (i) UV-vis binding to recombinant NfCYP51 measures target engagement directly; (ii) sterol profiling of treated trophozoites confirms the mechanism; (iii) a mouse PAM model with brain drug-level measurement tests the only outcome that matters.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Itraconazole and posaconazole are indistinguishable in a mouse PAM model (no survival difference). Falsifier: a significant survival difference between the two arms.
  2. At least one of the two achieves a brain-to-plasma ratio above 0.3 in the mouse model. Falsifier: both below 0.3.
  3. A brain-penetrant azole (isavuconazole, the smallest of the five at 437 Da and PAINS-clean) outperforms the two leaders in the mouse model despite docking worse. Falsifier: no survival advantage for isavuconazole.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 4–8 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): UV-vis binding assay of the five conazoles against recombinant NfCYP51 (Kd), plus sterol profiling of treated trophozoites to confirm the mechanism. Stage 2 (weeks 3–5): mouse brain-to-plasma ratios for itraconazole, posaconazole and isavuconazole after a single dose. Stage 3 (weeks 6–8): mouse PAM model — the best brain-exposed azole versus amphotericin B, survival as the endpoint, with brain drug levels measured at sacrifice. If no azole reaches the brain, the result is still publishable: it redirects the field to intrathecal delivery or to non-azole chemotypes (for example the HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors reported as N. fowleri leads in 2020).

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this study. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol; the top-two gap is inside noise.
  2. Published EC50 values come from a single laboratory's assay and were not re-measured.
  3. No brain-exposure or animal-efficacy data exist in this work — the decisive property is untested.
  4. The haem–azole coordination is approximated by the scoring function, not modelled quantum-mechanically.
  5. No Pakistan-specific isolate was used: the structure is from the reference strain, and the Karachi type-2 genotype's CYP51 sequence was not compared.
  6. The pipeline's ChEMBL retrieval failed for this target (wrong target substituted silently); the corrected ligand set was assembled by hand from the published literature, which is a valid fix but not a pipeline result.
  7. The Islamic-canon sweep found no classical text on PAM — the disease is a twentieth-century diagnosis — so the canon contributes a principle (hifz al-nafs) rather than a precedent.

6. Conclusion

Five published conazoles dock onto N. fowleri CYP51 (5TL8) in the same rank order as their published anti-N. fowleri potencies: itraconazole −11.59, posaconazole −10.91, ketoconazole −10.21, isavuconazole −8.96 and fluconazole −7.01 kcal/mol, against EC50 values of 0.01, 0.01, amphotericin-B-equipotent, amphotericin-B-equipotent and 13.9 µM. The ranking validates the docking protocol and confirms posaconazole and itraconazole as the two candidates worth testing. But neither has a measured brain exposure in PAM, both are large molecules with PAINS flags that mean nothing and Veber failures that might, and Karachi's cases arrive through tap water and die in five days. The next step is a brain-exposure measurement and a mouse model — not another docking run.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: The Sindh Health Department and the Karachi Water & Sewerage Corporation, with the Aga Khan University Hospital and Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre as clinical advisers. Decision: what to do before the next Karachi PAM case arrives. Exact change: (a) stock posaconazole and itraconazole at the two hospitals that receive Karachi PAM cases, with a written protocol for their use alongside amphotericin B, instead of leaving the choice to the night of admission; and (b) fund the 4–8-week brain-exposure and mouse-PAM test proposed in §4.5 to decide between them — instead of funding further computational ranking. If evidence Z appears, reverse this: if the mouse model shows neither azole reaches the brain or improves survival, withdraw the stocking recommendation and redirect the same funds to intrathecal amphotericin B protocols and to the non-azole leads; if one azole shows brain exposure and survival benefit, make it the stocked drug. The Islamic principle is hifz al-nafs: a disease that kills healthy children in five days, through the water they use for ablution, imposes a duty to have the drug in the pharmacy before the case arrives — and the parallel duty, on the water authority, is chlorination: the 2011 Karachi series traced the rise in cases to falling chlorine and deteriorating distribution, and no drug programme substitutes for fixing the water.

Four Nanomolar Gyrase Inhibitors Out-Score Moxifloxacin at the M. tuberculosis Cleavage Site — but the Margin Is Inside Vina Noise and the D94G Test Is Still Missing

Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) kills because fluoroquinolones fail: resistance is dominated by gyrA mutations D94G and A90V in the quinolone resistance-determining region, and moxifloxacin — a core drug of the WHO BPaLM regimen — loses activity against them.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-18 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #75 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: tuberculosis; DNA gyrase; moxifloxacin; fluoroquinolone resistance; gyrA; molecular docking; ChEMBL; MDR-TB

Abstract

Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) kills because fluoroquinolones fail: resistance is dominated by gyrA mutations D94G and A90V in the quinolone resistance-determining region, and moxifloxacin — a core drug of the WHO BPaLM regimen — loses activity against them. We asked whether ChEMBL-recorded nanomolar inhibitors of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA gyrase A/B complex bind the true fluoroquinolone cleavage site more strongly than moxifloxacin itself. Using the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P9WG45 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL3430898, 46 bioactivities → PubChem/RDKit similarity, PAINS and ADMET screen → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7), we re-docked the top four leads and moxifloxacin on the moxifloxacin-bound cleavage complex 5BS8 (2.4 Å), centred on the co-crystallised moxifloxacin. The four leads scored −10.87 to −10.37 kcal/mol versus −9.38 kcal/mol for re-docked moxifloxacin, with tight pose consistency (top-3 spread ≤0.6 kcal/mol); their measured enzyme IC50 values are 5, 10, 65 and 780 nM, and none carries a PAINS alert. The honest limit: every margin over moxifloxacin (0.99–1.49 kcal/mol) lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so docking alone cannot rank these compounds, and none has yet been tested against a D94G or A90V mutant enzyme or whole cells. The claim that any of these four is a better fluoroquinolone-alternative would be refuted if re-docking on a D94G cleavage complex, or a mutant-enzyme assay, shows a ≥2 kcal/mol or >10-fold IC50 loss. The falsifiable next step is a 8–12-week enzyme-plus-MIC test of the four leads against wild-type and D94G/A90V M. tuberculosis gyrase and clinical isolates.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis returned to the top of the infectious-disease mortality list: the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 records about 10.8 million people falling ill with TB in 2023 and about 1.25 million deaths, with TB again the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent. Around 400,000 people each year develop multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), and Pakistan is among the eight countries that together account for two-thirds of the global burden. For MDR/RR-TB that remains fluoroquinolone-susceptible, WHO recommends the 6-month all-oral BPaL/BPaLM regimens — bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin in BPaLM — so the fluoroquinolone is load-bearing: lose it and the regimen collapses into longer, more toxic alternatives.

Fluoroquinolone resistance in M. tuberculosis is almost entirely a gyrase story. Mutations in the quinolone resistance-determining region (QRDR) of gyrA, above all D94G and A90V, block drug binding at the DNA-cleavage complex. In a 2025 South Korean series of 304 isoniazid- and/or rifampicin-resistant isolates, 34 carried gyrA/gyrB mutations and D94G (44.8%) and A90V (24.1%) were the most frequent gyrA changes; every gyrA mutant was moxifloxacin-resistant. In São Paulo, among rifampicin- and/or isoniazid-resistant isolates tested by line-probe assay, 38 of 41 second-line mutations were fluoroquinolone mutations (35 in gyrA), and 97% of MDR strains carrying a second-line mutation were pre-XDR — MDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance. The clinical question is therefore narrow and urgent: is there a compound that still binds the cleavage site when D94G or A90V is present?

The classical medical canon described this disease long before the bacillus was known: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) discusses pulmonary wasting disease ("sil") as a distinct consumptive syndrome, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi records clinical observation of chronic cough with wasting. These texts are hypothesis sources, not evidence — they knew the syndrome, not the target — but they establish that the disease burden this paper addresses is centuries old in the region, and the Islamic principle behind acting on it is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life (see §7).

Falsifiable question. Do ChEMBL-recorded nanomolar inhibitors of M. tuberculosis DNA gyrase bind the true fluoroquinolone cleavage site (PDB 5BS8) at scores beyond re-docked moxifloxacin, and would that binding survive the D94G/A90V mutations? Falsifier: a ≥2 kcal/mol loss on re-docking against a D94G (or A90V) cleavage complex, or a >10-fold IC50 shift in a mutant-enzyme assay, refutes the claim for that compound. Causal identification: validated-control re-docking — the reference drug re-docked on its own co-crystal structure — not a comparison against nothing. Association only beyond that: docking scores are not activity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searched 2026-11-18: PubMed-indexed and publisher sources on M. tuberculosis gyrA/gyrB fluoroquinolone resistance (2025–2026), the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, the RCSB records for PDB 3M4I and 5BS8, and the ChEMBL record for target CHEMBL3430898. The Islamic-canon sweep covered the available digitised canon relevant to the question: Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025); Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) — consulted in the literature-map summaries, not in full Arabic text (see Limitations).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3. Target: M. tuberculosis DNA gyrase, UniProtKB P9WG45 (DNA gyrase subunit B, H37Rv; the ChEMBL bioactivity target is the GyrA/GyrB protein complex CHEMBL3430898). Structure: PDB 5BS8, the gyrase–fluoroquinolone cleaved complex with moxifloxacin co-crystallised, 2.4 Å (Blower et al., PNAS 2016). Grid centre: centroid of the co-crystallised moxifloxacin (MFX) in 5BS8, [40.10, 2.92, 22.41], box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses reported. The same centre, box and exhaustiveness were used for moxifloxacin and all four leads.

A corrected-centre audit, stated plainly. The pipeline first auto-picked PDB 3M4I (1.95 Å) and docked all five compounds there, scoring −6.35 to −5.60 kcal/mol. That run is DISCARDED, not reported as a result: 3M4I is the isolated GyrB TOPRIM domain fragment, and its auto-picked centre sat on a small HETATM ion — it is not the fluoroquinolone site. Moxifloxacin binds the cleavage complex (GyrA + DNA + Mg²⁺), whose structure is 5BS8. This is the same class of error as the TYK2 JH1/JH2 domain audit (2026-11-11): the PDB domain must match the drug's binding site. All scores in §3 are from the corrected 5BS8 re-dock (hidden_files/redock_hp065.py, output dock-HP-065c-2026-11-18.json); the discarded 3M4I run is preserved in dock-HP-065-2026-11-18.json for audit. DNA chains in 5BS8 are ATOM records and are retained in the receptor; the Mg²⁺ ions are HETATM and are dropped by the receptor preparation, so the fluoroquinolone Mg²⁺–water bridge is absent from scoring — a stated limitation (§5).

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all 26 pipeline leads. None of the four docked leads carries a PAINS alert. One of the 26 leads (rank 24, CHEMBL3628453) carries a PAINS alert; it was not docked and is not proposed here.

2.4 ADMET and toxicity read-across

RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber) computed for every lead; ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) run for every lead. Moxifloxacin itself (PubChem CID 152946, C21H24FN3O4, MW 401.44) passes Lipinski with 0 violations and scores 0 on all 12 measured Tox21 assays.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data exist for these four compounds against mutant gyrase or whole-cell M. tuberculosis in this study. Measured IC50 values below are ChEMBL records against the wild-type gyrase complex, not new measurements.
