All seven compounds are PAINS-clean and drug-like (MW 491–537, logP 1.72–3.85, 0–1 Lipinski violations each). Presatovir: MW 532.07, logP 2.97, 2 donors / 7 acceptors, TPSA 125.93 angstrom², 5 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation. Rilematovir: MW 500.93, logP 3.85, 0 donors / 4 acceptors, TPSA 78.89 angstrom², 7 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation. ToxGuard read-across for presatovir is weak (maximum neighbour similarity 0.271) and is not quoted as safety evidence.

Three things in this table deserve attention. First, the duplicate: presatovir docked twice — once as the PubChem query, once as its ChEMBL record CHEMBL3410450 (pref_name PRESATOVIR, synonyms GS-5806; verified live) — scores −6.15 and −6.53, a 0.38 kcal/mol gap between identical molecules, because the two SMILES encodings differ in stereochemistry specification and RDKit generates different starting conformers. That gap is the run's noise floor, and every gap between distinct compounds in the table is of the same order or smaller. Second, the control: rilematovir re-docked into its own pocket scores only −5.36 — weaker than presatovir, weaker than its own ChEMBL twin — with three poses within 0.05 kcal/mol of each other. A proven nanomolar inhibitor, in its own crystal pocket, does not top this table. Third, the ranking is inverted against measurement: the most potent measured compound (CHEMBL4747540, 0.47 nM) scores −4.94, fifth of seven, while the weakest measured (presatovir's own record, 1,193 nM against the D486N mutant) scores best. Spearman rho between Vina affinity and measured pChEMBL is +0.1 (n = 5) — no correlation.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of presatovir on 5KWW was found in the literature sweep, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The structural fact is published: 5KWW is the JNJ-53718678 complex (Roymans et al. 2017), and 6EAD is the F140I inhibitor-escape-variant structure (2.8 angstrom), which confirms that the F140 region is part of the inhibitor pocket. Absolute Vina scores are protocol- and structure-dependent and cannot be compared across studies; only the within-protocol ranking in Table 3.1 is interpretable, and that ranking is the paper's negative result.

3.4 The clinical record, and why it matters more than the table

Presatovir's clinical history is the reason the docking result is a negative finding rather than a lead. In the human challenge study it worked: viral load 250.7 vs 757.7 log10 PFUe·h/mL (P < .001), mucus 6.9 vs 15.1 g (P = .03). In HCT recipients it did not. The Phase 2b lower-respiratory trial (NCT02254421, 60 patients, 31 presatovir / 29 placebo) found a viral-load difference of −0.02 log10 copies/mL (95% CI −0.62 to 0.57; P = .94), median supplemental-oxygen-free days 26 vs 28 (P = .84), incident respiratory failure 10.3 vs 10.7 percent (P = .98), and all-cause mortality 0 vs 7.1 percent (P = .19). The Phase 2 upper-respiratory trial (NCT02254408, 189 patients) found a viral-load difference of −0.33 log10 (95% CI −0.64 to −0.02; P = .040) against a prespecified alpha of 0.01 — not significant — and progression to lower-respiratory complications 11.2 vs 19.5 percent (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.22–1.18; P = .11); a post-hoc lymphopenia subgroup did show fewer complications (13.3 vs 64.3 percent, P = .008), which is hypothesis-generating, not evidence. Resistance-associated substitutions emerged in 6 of 29 presatovir-treated lower-respiratory patients (20.7 percent) and 10 of 89 upper-respiratory patients (11.2 percent), against none on placebo; V127A was already present at baseline in 8 subjects. The drug was well tolerated in both trials — the failure was efficacy, not safety. The class, meanwhile, has a positive Phase 3: ziresovir in hospitalised infants (n = 244) improved the Wang bronchiolitis score by 0.8 points (95% CI −1.3 to −0.3; P = .002) and cut viral load by 0.6 log10 at day 5, though resistance-associated mutations appeared in 15 participants (9 percent). The target is druggable; presatovir, in HCT recipients, was not the drug.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the screen's failure is the finding

This paper set out to rank RSV fusion inhibitors and found that its own screen cannot rank them. The value of the run is the calibration, not the table. A docking protocol that gives its co-crystallised control −5.36, its reference drug −6.15, and the most potent measured compound −4.94 — with a duplicate-molecule noise floor of 0.38 kcal/mol and a Spearman rho of +0.1 — has no ranking power on this target. The honest conclusion is that the five ChEMBL leads, however potent in cells, cannot be ordered by this screen, and none can be claimed better than presatovir from these scores. The sub-nanomolar leads (CHEMBL4747540 at 0.47 nM, CHEMBL4640616 at 2.0 nM, CHEMBL4779491 at 2.1 nM) remain what they were before docking: measured cell potencies with no structural ranking attached.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Presatovir's −6.15 is not a win. It is 0.38 kcal/mol behind its own duplicate record, and only 0.79 kcal/mol ahead of the control — barely twice the duplicate noise floor — and it sits in a table whose control — a proven nanomolar inhibitor in its own pocket — scores worse. The three poses of presatovir span 0.35 kcal/mol and the three poses of rilematovir span 0.05, so the poses are converged; the problem is the scoring function on this pocket, not the sampling. The pocket was crystallised around rilematovir, so any pocket-shape effect should favour the control, not presatovir — and still the control scores lower. The most likely reading is that rigid docking on a single prefusion structure, with no side-chain flexibility and no rescoring, cannot separate compounds whose measured potencies span 0.47 nM to 1,193 nM when the assay contexts differ (wild-type A2 infection vs the D486N mutant) and the binding site is a shallow, hydrophobic, inter-protomer groove.

4.3 Association only

This is a retrospective docking benchmark, not a causal experiment. It shows that Vina scores on 5KWW do not track measured RSV F potency for these five compounds, that presatovir's clinical failure is consistent with a weak and resistance-prone inhibitor, and that the pipeline's structure picker can silently dock onto a fragment. It does not show that any lead is inactive, that presatovir is inactive in any other population, or that another docking method would fail the same way. The causal identification is validated-control re-docking (rilematovir into its own pocket); beyond that, the paper is association only.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. A flexible-side-chain or MM-GBSA rescoring of the same seven compounds on 5KWW reaches rho ≤ −0.5 against the same five measured potencies. Falsifier: the rescoring run itself; rho above −0.5 refutes it, and the screen stays unusable for ranking.
  2. Docking the same compounds on a second prefusion structure (5EA3, JNJ-2408068 complex, 2.75 angstrom; or 6VKC, JNJ-36811054 complex, 2.6 angstrom) reproduces the 5KWW order. Falsifier: a different order on the second structure — which would show the ranking is structure-dependent, not compound-dependent.
  3. CHEMBL4747540 (0.47 nM) inhibits RSV A2 in a cell assay at sub-nanomolar EC50, while presatovir does not beat it. Falsifier: a head-to-head A2 HepG2 assay; if presatovir matches or beats it, the ChEMBL potency gap is an assay artefact.
  4. Presatovir's D486N weakness is the resistance mechanism that matters clinically. Falsifier: a D486N virus that presatovir still inhibits at wild-type potency in the same assay — which would point the resistance story at the other emergent substitutions instead.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain presatovir, rilematovir and the three sub-nanomolar leads commercially and confirm identity and purity by LC-MS. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): head-to-head RSV A2 infection assay in HepG2 cells (the assay context of the three sub-nanomolar measurements), EC50 for all five compounds in the same run, with a D486N-mutant counter-screen in parallel — the single experiment that tests both the potency gap and the resistance hypothesis. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): flexible docking / MM-GBSA rescoring of the same five compounds on 5KWW and 5EA3, compared against the assay order. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): report all results, including the negatives — a screen that cannot rank is a result. Total cost is one cell assay and five compounds, not a screening campaign.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only, and a negative calibration. No compound in this paper was tested in a cell; the headline is that the screen cannot rank, not that any lead works.
  2. Single structure, rigid receptor. One prefusion structure (5KWW), no side-chain flexibility, no MD, no rescoring; the rho of +0.1 is a property of this protocol on this structure, not of docking in general.
  3. Mixed assay contexts. The five pChEMBL values mix RSV A2 HepG2 infection with the D486N mutant in Hep2 cells; the calibration is weaker for it, and the presatovir record (1,193 nM) is a mutant measurement, not a wild-type one.
  4. No RMSD for the control. Rilematovir was re-docked into its own pocket but pose recovery was not measured, so the control validates the score scale, not the pose.
  5. No presatovir EC50 quoted. No PMID-verified in-vitro EC50 for presatovir was retrieved; the paper uses the challenge-study and trial numbers instead, and does not invent the missing value.
  6. No lab data, no clinical recommendation. Nothing here changes treatment; the prevention standard remains the monoclonals, and the treatment gap remains open.
  7. Islamic canon gaps (named, per the programme's rule). The Canon and Kitab al-Hawi were checked through named works, not read in full; the full 23-volume Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP), the National Institute of Health Islamabad, and the Federal Directorate of Immunization — and, for the method rule, every public funder of computational drug discovery in Pakistan. Three exact changes, each with its falsifier:

  1. Do not fund a presatovir-analogue programme on docking scores alone; require the head-to-head cell assay first. The five leads in Table 3.1 cost one assay to order, and this paper shows the docking order is random (rho +0.1). A programme that picks its lead from this table would pick presatovir's own record — the weakest measured compound — and call it the winner. Reverse this only if a rescoring method reaches rho ≤ −0.5 on this same set, in which case the docking order becomes usable evidence again.
  2. Prioritise prevention procurement over a new small-molecule programme. With 101,400 under-five deaths a year, more than 97 percent in countries like Pakistan, and two long-acting monoclonals now licensed (nirsevimab 74.5 percent efficacy; clesrovimab licensed June 2025), the fastest mortality reduction is a prevention programme, not a fusion-inhibitor discovery programme — especially when the only positive Phase 3 in the class (ziresovir, infants) still showed resistance in 9 percent. Reverse this if a fusion inhibitor posts a positive Phase 3 in infants with a resistance rate below that 9 percent, or if monoclonal supply or price makes prevention unreachable in Pakistan.
  3. Require accession-verified targets and structure audits in every publicly funded computational screen. Any screening proposal must state the UniProt accession, the ChEMBL target ID it resolved to, and the PDB ID with the bound ligand its centre was verified against; any run that falls back to text search or to a resolution-sorted structure pick must declare it. This paper's discarded fragment run is the evidence: without that rule, public money can fund a complete benchmark docked onto a 51-residue fragment. Reverse this only if the auto-picker is shown to return the correct structure first for a blinded set of viral accessions. Islamic principle behind the recommendations: preservation of life (hifz al-nafs, Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat) — RSV kills more than a hundred thousand young children a year, so a screening method that mis-ranks antivirals is a failure to protect life, not a technical footnote; and stewardship (khilafah, Qur'an 2:30) — public research funds are a trust, and a steward does not spend a trust on a benchmark of the wrong structure. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so; they do here.

7. Conclusion

Presatovir scores −6.15 kcal/mol on the prefusion RSV F structure 5KWW, at a centre verified against the co-crystallised inhibitor rilematovir — and the number means almost nothing, because the same screen gives the co-crystallised control −5.36 and the most potent measured compound −4.94, with a rank correlation of 0.1 against measured potency. The clinical record agrees with the negative reading: presatovir failed its Phase 2b trials in transplant recipients, with resistance emerging in a fifth of the lower-respiratory patients, while the class's one positive Phase 3 (ziresovir) and the licensed monoclonals carry the field forward. The memorable number is 0.1: the correlation between docking and measurement for RSV fusion inhibitors on this structure. The next step is one cell assay, not more docking.

Rigid Docking Cannot Rank the GRL0617 Series on SARS-CoV-2 PLpro: the 2.67 µM Reference Scores Best and the 42 µM Compound Beats Both Leads

SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease (PLpro) cleaves the viral polyprotein and strips ubiquitin and ISG15 from host proteins, suppressing type-I interferon — a second viral protease with no approved inhibitor, unlike the main protease (Mpro), which has nirmatrelvir.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-17 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #72 (daily 5-paper run) Topic ID: HP-073

Keywords: SARS-CoV-2; papain-like protease; PLpro; GRL0617; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; BL2 loop; antiviral drug discovery

Abstract

SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease (PLpro) cleaves the viral polyprotein and strips ubiquitin and ISG15 from host proteins, suppressing type-I interferon — a second viral protease with no approved inhibitor, unlike the main protease (Mpro), which has nirmatrelvir. GRL0617, a non-covalent PLpro inhibitor first described against SARS-CoV in 2008, remains the best-validated PLpro chemotype: it inhibits SARS-CoV-2 PLpro at 2.05 micromolar (median of 21 ChEMBL records) and blocks viral replication in cells and in mouse models, and its optimised analogues reach 0.11–0.67 micromolar. We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking on the GRL0617-bound structure 7JRN (2.48 angstrom) against five compounds from a single FRET assay (Ma et al. 2021): GRL0617 (2.67 micromolar in this assay) plus four analogues spanning 0.11–42 micromolar. The re-dock control worked — GRL0617 scored −9.90 kcal/mol in its own pocket — but the ranking failed: Spearman rho = +0.15 (n = 5). The weakest compound (42 micromolar) scored third-best (−9.14), beating both named leads Jun9-72-2 (−7.74) and Jun9-84-3 (−8.21), while the most potent analogue (0.11 micromolar) scored second (−9.74). All five compounds are PAINS-clean, so the failure is not assay artefacts but the method: the analogues' advantage is an ionic hydrogen bond to Asp164 and closure of the flexible BL2 loop, which rigid docking cannot score. Falsifiable claim: rigid Vina docking into 7JRN cannot rank PLpro inhibitors, and any PLpro claim resting on it alone is untested. The falsifier is a head-to-head test — run induced-fit docking or MM-GBSA on the same five compounds in the same pocket: if it recovers rho below −0.5 where rigid Vina gives +0.15, the failure is the rigidity and the claim stands; if it also fails, the pocket itself defeats scoring-based ranking.

1. Introduction

COVID-19 has caused nearly 780 million confirmed cases and more than 7.1 million reported deaths worldwide (WHO COVID-19 fact sheet, accessed November 2026), including about 1.58 million confirmed cases and 30,656 deaths in Pakistan (National Institute of Health, Pakistan, 2023). The virus still circulates, and the antiviral cupboard holds exactly one oral drug class: nirmatrelvir, which inhibits the main protease (Mpro, nsp5). The second viral protease has been left behind.

Papain-like protease (PLpro) is the nsp3 protease domain (replicase polyprotein 1ab residues 1564–1878; nsp3 residues 746–1060; EC 3.4.19.12; UniProt P0DTD1). It cuts the three N-terminal junctions of the replicase polyprotein, and it is also a deubiquitinase and deISGylase: it strips ubiquitin and ISG15 from host proteins, which shuts down type-I interferon signalling and lets the virus spread while the innate immune response is blind (Shin et al. 2020). A PLpro inhibitor is therefore two drugs in one — an antiviral and an immune-restoring agent — and that is why PLpro, not Mpro, is the underexploited target. It has no approved drug and no drug in late-stage trials.

GRL0617 is the reference compound for this target. Discovered against SARS-CoV PLpro in 2008 (IC50 0.6 µM; Ratia et al. 2008), it was repurposed for SARS-CoV-2, where it inhibits PLpro at 2.05 µM (median of 21 ChEMBL IC50 records, range 0.6–7.0 µM; 2.05 ± 0.12 µM in the Ma et al. 2021 FRET assay) and shows antiviral activity in Vero E6 cells (EC50 23.64 µM) and in Caco-2-hACE2 cells (19.96 µM). Structure-based optimisation from the GRL0617-bound structure produced the Jun9 series, with Jun9-75-4 (0.62 µM), Jun9-72-2 (0.67 µM) and Jun9-84-3 (0.67 µM) roughly threefold more potent than GRL0617 and threefold more active antivirally (EC50 6.6–8.3 µM; Ma et al. 2021). A 2025 invalidation study confirmed the field's central fact: most reported PLpro inhibitors act unspecifically (thiol-reactive or redox-active), and "GRL0617 and its derivatives remain the best-validated compounds with demonstrated antiviral activity in cells and in mouse models" (Kuzikov et al. 2025).

The companion paper in this series (HP-037) benchmarked the same rigid-docking method on Mpro and got the first positive rank correlation in the series (Spearman ρ = +0.48, n = 5): the most potent nirmatrelvir analogue scored best. This paper asks whether the same method works on the second protease, using the same protocol, the same reference-drug logic, and a cleaner test — five compounds from one assay, one paper, spanning 372-fold in potency.

Falsifiable question (stated before the results): can rigid AutoDock Vina docking into the GRL0617-bound PLpro structure 7JRN rank five GRL0617-series inhibitors in the order of their measured IC50 values? The claim is that it cannot, because the analogues' potency gain comes from an ionic interaction and a loop closure that a rigid receptor cannot represent. The claim is refuted if the docking scores rank the compounds in measured order (ρ ≤ −0.5), and confirmed in its strongest form if the ranking is inverted (ρ ≥ +0.5).

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed (E-utilities, accessed 17 November 2026) for GRL0617 + PLpro (65 hits), cross-checked against the ChEMBL bioactivity record and the full text of Ma et al. 2021 (PMC8265724) and Shin et al. 2020 (PMC7116779). Every number in this paper traces to a PMID-verified source in the References, or to a computation in the raw JSON. The Islamic canon check is in §2.7. The analysis plan — target, structure, docking set, and the Spearman test — was fixed before any docking score was seen; nothing in the Results is post-hoc except the mechanistic reading of the failure, which is labelled as such.

2.2 Target verification, and the discarded wrong-target run

PLpro was resolved by accession, not by text search: UniProt P0DTD1 (Replicase polyprotein 1ab, SARS-CoV-2, 7,096 aa); the PLpro (nsp3) domain is pp1ab residues 1564–1878, catalytic Cys111 (pp1ab Cys1674) and His272 (pp1ab His1835). The only ChEMBL target carrying component accession P0DTD1 as a single protein is CHEMBL4523582 (Replicase polyprotein 1ab). That target also holds Mpro activities, so PLpro potencies were filtered by assay description (contains "papain" or "PLpro"): 699 PLpro IC50 activities from 561 distinct molecules (ChEMBL, accessed 17 November 2026).

The standard pipeline run (run_docking.py --target "SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease" --ref GRL0617) failed exactly as the series has seen before: its ChEMBL text search returned CHEMBL2074 (human maltase-glucoamylase) first, resolved UniProt to P0DTC1 (replicase polyprotein 1a), and docked 26 maltase ligands into 8AZC (the NSP3 macrodomain) with every dock failing. That run is discarded in full and preserved as dock-HP-073-2026-11-17-WRONG-TARGET.json. It is the paper's first finding, again: a text-search fallback manufactures a complete, plausible-looking, entirely wrong result, and only the accession check catches it.

2.3 Structure and centre audit

PDB 7JRN: wild-type SARS-CoV-2 PLpro in complex with GRL0617, 2.48 Å, X-ray (Ma et al. 2021, PMID 34341772). The docking centre is the co-crystallised GRL0617 centroid computed by the pipeline's own dock._ligand_center — never hand-rolled — and audited in the driver: the pick is residue TTT (GRL0617), chain A, 23 heavy atoms (C20H20N2O), centroid [9.82, −11.83, 32.76]. The second TTT copy (chain J, the symmetry-related copy) was not averaged in, because the picker groups by full residue identity. The catalytic Cys111 sits in the pocket; GRL0617 binds the BL2 groove adjacent to it, not the catalytic site itself.

2.4 Docking protocol

AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å, best of three poses reported, same centre and box for all five compounds. Docking set (all from Ma et al. 2021, one FRET assay, document CHEMBL5107976): GRL0617 (CHEMBL549695; IC50 2,670 nM in this assay; paper value 2.05 ± 0.12 µM) as the reference and re-dock control; CHEMBL5079592 (113 nM, the most potent compound in the series); Jun9-72-2 (CHEMBL5173886; 670 nM); Jun9-84-3 (CHEMBL5182315; 670 nM); CHEMBL5200289 (42,000 nM, the weakest in the set). The two Jun9 names were verified PubChem → InChIKey → ChEMBL → activity; the other two analogues are tabled by ChEMBL ID only, because the paper's text does not name them and no name is invented. Rank correlation: Spearman ρ between best Vina score and measured pIC50 (pIC50 = −log10(IC50 in M)), ties by average ranks; negative ρ is the correct direction (better dock, more potent). Causal identification, named explicitly: validated-control re-docking (GRL0617 into its own crystal structure) — the only causal claim is about the method's ranking ability, and it rests on that control; everything else in this paper is association.

2.5 PAINS screen and ToxGuard

RDKit PAINS filter for every compound; RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber); ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (k = 15) reported with its maximum neighbour similarity, so the reader can see how weak the coverage is.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the receptor is rigid and the BL2 loop is frozen in its GRL0617-bound closed conformation; no MD or free-energy refinement was run; no experiment was performed. The measured IC50s are single-assay values from one paper (n = 5 compounds), and two of them tie at 670 nM.

2.7 Literature and the Islamic canon

The classical canon was checked alongside the modern literature, as the programme requires. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) classifies epidemic fevers (humma) and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900, 23 volumes) and On Smallpox and Measles (c. 910) record the clinical distinction of eruptive fevers — all centuries before the viral aetiology of COVID-19, so none names PLpro, and no Canon-listed remedy was docked or screened in this run; the paper claims no traditional-medicine finding. The honest limit, named here: the full 23-volume Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised; the sweep covers the named canonical works, not every book ever written.

3. Results

3.1 The ChEMBL landscape for PLpro

ChEMBL holds 699 PLpro IC50 activities (561 molecules) against the polyprotein target — a target that is, on paper, well covered. The most potent records in the database are 1–3 nM, from two 2024 ACS Medicinal Chemistry Letters patent-disclosure papers (PMID 39140061, 39563803); those values are single rounded records and were not used in the docking set, because a rank test needs one assay, not the smallest numbers in the database. The usable benchmark is the Ma et al. 2021 series: 57 compounds in one FRET assay, IC50s from 113 nM to 56 µM.

3.2 The discarded run, in one paragraph

The standard pipeline resolved the target to human maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074), UniProt P0DTC1, and docked 26 maltase ligands into the NSP3 macrodomain (8AZC), all failing. It completed with "PIPELINE OK: True". Only the target line betrayed it. This is the sixth time in this series the maltase substitution has had to be caught by hand (after GyrB, DHFR, PTP1B, Mpro, PfPI4K); the rule stands: no accession match, no benchmark.

3.3 Docking: the comparison table

CHEMBL5079592 (most potent) 113 −9.74 −9.74, −9.25, −8.79
CHEMBL5200289 (weakest in set) 42,000 −9.14 −9.14, −8.71, −8.00
Jun9-84-3 670 −8.21 −8.21, −7.76, −7.54

All five compounds are PAINS-clean. Properties: GRL0617 MW 304.39, logP 4.22, 2 H-bond donors, TPSA 55.12 Å², zero Lipinski violations; Jun9-72-2 MW 291.39, logP 4.74, zero violations; Jun9-84-3 MW 314.43, logP 5.51, one violation (logP > 5); CHEMBL5079592 MW 504.70, logP 4.60, 5 donors, one violation (MW > 500); CHEMBL5200289 MW 295.41, logP 4.70, zero violations.

3.4 The ranking fails

Spearman ρ = +0.15 (n = 5) between best Vina score and measured pIC50 — no correlation, slightly positive. The re-dock control worked: GRL0617 scored −9.90 in its own pocket with consistent poses. But the ranking is wrong in the ways that matter. The weakest compound in the set, CHEMBL5200289 (42 µM, 372-fold less potent than the best), scored third-best (−9.14) and beat both named leads. Jun9-72-2 and Jun9-84-3 — the paper's own leads, threefold more potent than GRL0617 in the enzyme assay and threefold more active against live virus — scored worst and second-worst (−7.74 and −8.21). The most potent compound (113 nM) did score second (−9.74), 0.16 kcal/mol behind GRL0617, which is inside the noise band: the top two are indistinguishable, and the bottom three are misordered. The docking spread is 2.16 kcal/mol against a 372-fold measured range (~3.5 kcal/mol), so the method compresses the differences as well as misordering them.

3.5 Comparison with published docking

There is no published Vina benchmark on this series to compare against. What exists is the mechanistic account from Ma et al. themselves: they docked Jun9-53-2, Jun9-72-2 and Jun9-75-4 into 7JRN and ran 100 ns molecular dynamics, showing that the analogues replace GRL0617's carboxamide with a trialkyl ammonium group, gaining a strong ionic hydrogen bond to Asp164 (plus Arg166) and a better fit in the S4 pocket, with the naphthalene ring π-stacking Tyr264 and contacting Pro247/Pro248. GRL0617's own binding closes the BL2 loop. None of that — the ionic bond, the loop closure, the induced fit — is visible to a rigid receptor and a Vina scoring function. The published MD result predicts exactly the failure observed here, which is why §4 reads the failure as a property of the method, not of the compounds.

3.6 ToxGuard read-across is too weak to quote

ToxGuard's kNN read-across found no close neighbour for any compound (maximum similarity 0.235–0.467). GRL0617's highest assay scores are NR-AhR 0.494 and SR-ARE 0.267 at maximum similarity 0.367. Read honestly, that is an admission that the model has almost nothing to read across from — not a safety assessment. The compounds' real safety signal is not computational: GRL0617 has animal and cell data behind it (Kuzikov et al. 2025), and the analogues have none yet.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the BL2 loop is the unmeasured variable

This paper's finding is the mirror image of the Mpro paper's. On Mpro, rigid docking got the extremes right (ρ = +0.48) because the potency differences tracked non-covalent fit in a rigid pocket. On PLpro it fails (ρ = +0.15) because the potency differences track something else: a charged interaction with Asp164 and the closure of a flexible loop. Ma et al.'s own MD shows the Jun9 compounds' advantage is precisely the part of binding that a rigid structure cannot represent — the receptor in 7JRN is frozen in the conformation GRL0617 induced, and the scoring function has no term for the ionic hydrogen bond that distinguishes the analogues. The re-dock control working (−9.90 for GRL0617) makes the failure sharper, not softer: the method can recognise the ligand the structure was solved with, and cannot rank anything else in that pocket. The honest reading is that 7JRN is a GRL0617-shaped hole, and Vina scores how well a molecule fills that hole — which is not the same as how well it inhibits the enzyme.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

GRL0617's −9.90 is a re-dock, not a discovery: it is the ligand the structure was solved with, scored in its own pocket, and a strong score there is the minimum a method must produce, not evidence that GRL0617 is the best inhibitor. The 0.16 kcal/mol gap to the most potent analogue is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. And the strongest absolute scores in this table belong to the wrong compounds: a 42 µM compound at −9.14 would look like a lead to anyone who read the scores without the measured potencies beside them. That is the operational danger this paper documents — a screening campaign that ranked by Vina score alone would advance the weakest compound over the two leads.

4.3 Association only

This is a retrospective computational benchmark, not a causal experiment. It shows that rigid Vina docking into 7JRN does not rank five GRL0617-series inhibitors (ρ = +0.15, n = 5), that the re-dock control works, and that the published MD mechanism predicts the failure. It does not show that any compound is a drug, that PLpro inhibition works in patients, or that flexible methods will succeed — that is the falsifier's job, not this paper's.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Induced-fit docking (or MM-GBSA rescoring) on the same five compounds recovers ρ ≤ −0.5. Falsifier: the same five compounds, same pocket, flexible receptor; ρ above −0.5 refutes the rigidity explanation and indicts the pocket or the scoring function instead.
  2. The Asp164 ionic hydrogen bond is the potency driver. Falsifier: an Asp164→Ala PLpro mutant; if Jun9-72-2 and Jun9-84-3 lose their threefold advantage over GRL0617 against the mutant while GRL0617 is unaffected, the mechanism is confirmed; if they keep it, the MD explanation is wrong.
  3. CHEMBL5079592 (113 nM) is a better antiviral than Jun9-72-2 in cells. Falsifier: Vero E6 antiviral assay; EC50 above Jun9-72-2's 6.62 µM would refute it despite the enzyme potency.
  4. A PLpro inhibitor that also restores interferon signalling beats a pure catalytic inhibitor in a cell model. Falsifier: paired enzyme + interferon-reporter assays; if interferon restoration tracks catalytic inhibition 1:1, the dual-mechanism framing adds nothing.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain GRL0617 and the four analogues commercially (all are in ChEMBL/PubChem with suppliers listed) and confirm identity and purity by LC-MS. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): FRET-based PLpro enzyme assay (Z-RLRGG-AMC substrate, as in Ma et al. 2021) at 10 µM, 1 µM and 0.1 µM, with GRL0617 as control and a redox/thiol-artefact panel (DTT sensitivity, detergent control) following Kuzikov et al. 2025 — the artefact check is mandatory for this target, not optional. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): FlipGFP cell assay for the compounds active below 1 µM, then Vero E6 antiviral assay for the best two. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): induced-fit docking or MM-GBSA on the same five compounds, to test hypothesis 1. Report all five results, including the negatives.

5. Limitations

  1. No lab data. All results are computational; no PLpro assay was run.
  2. Rigid docking, ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The 2.16 kcal/mol docking spread is barely outside the noise band, and the top-two gap (0.16) is inside it.
  3. Small n, one assay. The rank correlation uses five compounds from one paper's FRET assay; two tie at 670 nM, and a single additional compound could change ρ substantially.
  4. Single structure. One crystal structure (7JRN), one BL2-loop conformation; no ensemble, no MD, no free-energy refinement.
  5. No RMSD for the re-dock. The re-dock control is reported as a score with consistent poses; the docked pose was not compared atom-by-atom with the crystal pose.
  6. Assay heterogeneity for the consensus value. GRL0617's cross-assay median (2.05 µM, n = 21 records) spans 0.6–7.0 µM; the ranking test uses the single-assay value (2.67 µM) to avoid mixing assays, but the consensus is itself assay-dependent.
  7. ToxGuard coverage is weak. Maximum neighbour similarity 0.235–0.467; the Tox21 scores must not be quoted as safety evidence.
  8. Islamic canon gaps (named, per the programme's rule). The Canon and Kitab al-Hawi were checked through named works, not read in full; the full 23-volume Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP), the National Institute of Health, and the Higher Education Commission — and, for the method rule, every public funder of computational drug discovery in Pakistan. Three exact changes, each with its falsifier:

  1. Fund one PLpro enzyme assay in Pakistan, at a single reference laboratory, and publish the protocol. Pakistan has no domestic route from a computational PLpro claim to a measured number, and the country imports every antiviral it uses. One FRET assay (the Ma et al. 2021 protocol, Z-RLRGG-AMC substrate) plus the Kuzikov artefact panel would let any Pakistani group test a PLpro claim in weeks. If the assay shows the Jun9 leads inactive, the scaffold is closed and the money is still well spent — a dead end found in weeks beats a decade of untested docking. Reverse this only if a cheaper regional assay (e.g. through an international collaboration) becomes available to Pakistani groups.
  2. Require a re-dock control and an accession-verified target in every publicly funded computational screen. Any screening proposal must state the UniProt accession and the ChEMBL target ID it resolved to, and must report the reference drug re-docked into its own structure before any lead is claimed. This paper's discarded maltase run and its failed ranking are the evidence: without that rule, public money can fund a complete benchmark of the wrong enzyme, or a ranking that inverts the truth. Reverse this only if a blinded test shows rigid docking ranking PLpro inhibitors correctly without those controls.
  3. Do not buy or prescribe GRL0617 analogues as COVID-19 treatments. They are preclinical leads with enzyme and cell data only; the strongest evidence in this paper is a negative result about a computational method, not a positive result about a drug. The correct public position is to fund the assay in (1) and let the compounds decide. Islamic principle behind the recommendations: preservation of life (hifz al-nafs, Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat) — a screening method that mis-ranks antivirals during a circulating pandemic is a failure to protect life, not a technical footnote; and stewardship (khilafah, Qur'an 2:30) — public research funds are a trust, and a steward does not spend a trust on a ranking that inverts the truth. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so; they do here.

7. Conclusion

Rigid docking into the GRL0617-bound PLpro structure 7JRN gives no rank correlation with measured potency (Spearman ρ = +0.15, n = 5): the reference re-docks well (−9.90 kcal/mol), the most potent analogue scores second (−9.74), and the weakest compound in the set (42 µM) beats both named leads. The method that ranked Mpro analogues at the extremes cannot rank PLpro inhibitors at all, because the analogues' advantage — an ionic bond to Asp164 and closure of the flexible BL2 loop — is invisible to a rigid receptor. Docking can confirm that a molecule fits the GRL0617 pocket; ranking PLpro inhibitors needs the enzyme assay, and the flexible method that the falsifier names. The memorable number is +0.15: the correlation between the score and the truth, on the target that most needs a second drug.

No Structure to Dock On: MMV390048 and the Plasmodium PI4K Target That ChEMBL and the PDB Do Not Contain

Malaria still killed an estimated 597,000 people in 2023, from 263 million cases (WHO World Malaria Report 2024), and artemisinin partial resistance makes a new mechanism a priority.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-17 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #70 (daily 5-paper run) Topic ID: HP-067

Keywords: PfPI4K; MMV390048; malaria; Plasmodium falciparum; phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase; antimalarial; ChEMBL; drug discovery

Abstract

Malaria still killed an estimated 597,000 people in 2023, from 263 million cases (WHO World Malaria Report 2024), and artemisinin partial resistance makes a new mechanism a priority. Plasmodium falciparum phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase (PfPI4K) is the target of MMV390048, the first PI4K inhibitor to reach clinical development: it clears blood-stage parasites at 28 nM in vitro, blocks liver stages and gametocytes, and cured 8 of 8 P. vivax patients at day 14 on a single 120 mg dose, before its Phase 2a trial was stopped over emerging teratogenicity data. We asked whether the standard computational benchmark used in this series, ChEMBL potency retrieval plus AutoDock Vina docking, can evaluate this target at all. It cannot, and the failure is structural, not technical: ChEMBL holds no target carrying the PfPI4K accession Q8I406, and no experimental structure of PfPI4K exists in the PDB, so docking was skipped rather than faked. A first pipeline run that ignored this returned 26 human maltase inhibitors as PfPI4K leads and was discarded. What could be computed honestly was computed: MMV390048 is drug-like (MW 393.39, logP 3.82, zero Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean) with a weak ToxGuard read-across (max similarity 0.382); four close 2D analogues (Tanimoto 0.72–0.79) are likewise clean but have no published PfPI4K activity. Falsifiable claim: the 2-aminopyridine scaffold's future depends on an enzyme assay, not more docking. If none of the four analogues inhibits PfPI4K below 1 micromolar, the similarity neighbourhood is a dead end; if one does, it is the backup series that MMV390048's termination left behind. The falsifier is a single PfPI4K enzyme assay, which no Pakistani laboratory currently runs.

1. Introduction

Malaria killed an estimated 597,000 people in 2023, from 263 million cases, with about 11 million more cases than in 2022 and deaths nearly unchanged (WHO World Malaria Report 2024). Artemisinin partial resistance, now confirmed in Africa as well as Southeast Asia, means the field cannot rely on the artemisinin combination therapies that carry almost all treatment. A drug with a new mechanism, active against more than one life-cycle stage, is the stated priority of the Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) target product profiles: a single-dose cure, or a chemoprotective agent, that also blocks transmission.

Phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase (PI4K) is that kind of target. The parasite enzyme (PfPI4K, UniProt Q8I406, gene PF3D7_0509800) synthesises phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate, the lipid that organises membrane trafficking and protein secretion; the parasite needs it in the blood stage, the liver stage and the gametocyte, so one inhibitor can in principle treat, prevent and block transmission. MMV390048, a 2-aminopyridine discovered from a phenotypic screen at the University of Cape Town's H3D centre, was the first PI4K inhibitor to reach clinical development (Paquet et al. 2017). Its published profile is unusually complete: P. falciparum NF54 IC50 28 nM and IC90 40 nM, with a steep inhibition curve and only a 1.5-fold IC50 range across multidrug-resistant clinical isolates, suggesting low cross-resistance risk; a log parasite reduction ratio of 2.7 per 48-hour cycle; late-stage gametocyte IC50 285 nM; SCID-mouse ED90 0.57 mg/kg at day 7; full chemoprotection in monkeys; and delayed relapse (though not elimination of late hypnozoites) in the P. cynomolgi monkey model. Target validation was genetic and chemoproteomic: parasites selected for resistance carry PfPI4K mutations H1484Y (IC50 62.8 nM) and S1320L (57.7 nM) against a Dd2 parent of 22.7 nM, and chemoproteomics identified PfPI4K as the molecular target, with no binding to the human orthologues PI4KA (P42356) or PI4KB (Q9UBF8).

The clinical story then stopped. Phase 1 (Barnes et al. 2020) found single oral doses up to 120 mg generally well tolerated, rapidly absorbed, with a long half-life, though the volunteer infection study saw rapid recrudescence at the subtherapeutic 20 mg dose. The Phase 2a study in Ethiopia (2023) gave a single 120 mg dose to eight adult men with P. vivax malaria: adequate clinical and parasitological response at day 14 was 100% (8/8), asexual parasites cleared by 66 hours and gametocytes by 78 hours — and then the study was not completed, for operational reasons and emerging teratogenicity data. A 2022 rat study reported diaphragmatic hernias after a malarial PI4K inhibitor, with a potential link to mammalian kinase inhibition. MMV390048's trial is listed as terminated. The best-validated new antimalarial mechanism of the decade has no drug and no backup series in the clinic.

Falsifiable question (stated before the results): can the standard computational pipeline of this series — ChEMBL target resolution, potency retrieval, and Vina docking — evaluate PfPI4K at all, and if not, what honest computation is possible on the scaffold that remains? The claim is that the pipeline cannot evaluate the target, because the target is absent from both ChEMBL and the PDB, and that the only defensible computation is a property and similarity analysis of MMV390048 itself. The claim is refuted if a ChEMBL target carrying Q8I406, or an experimental PfPI4K structure, is produced — either would let the standard benchmark run.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed (E-utilities, accessed 17 November 2026) for MMV390048 (18 hits), cross-checked against the WHO World Malaria Report 2024 burden figures and the trial record. Every number in this paper traces to a PMID-verified source in the References, or to a computation in the raw JSON. The Islamic canon check is in §2.5.

2.2 Target verification, and the discarded wrong-target run

PfPI4K was resolved by accession, not by text search: UniProt Q8I406, 1-phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase (EC 2.7.1.67), Plasmodium falciparum (isolate 3D7), zero PDB cross-references. A ChEMBL target query by component accession (target_components__accession=Q8I406) returned total_count 0 on 17 November 2026, and a pref_name search returned seven PI4K targets, all human or bovine. An RCSB search by reference-sequence accession Q8I406 returned no entry. The standard pipeline run (run_docking.py --target Q8I406 --ref MMV390048) therefore had no ChEMBL target to retrieve from; its fallback text search silently substituted CHEMBL2074 — human maltase-glucoamylase — and returned 55 bioactivities and 26 "leads" that are maltase inhibitors. That run is discarded in full and preserved as dock-HP-067-2026-11-17-WRONG-TARGET.json. It is reported here because it is the paper's first finding: a text-search fallback in a drug-discovery pipeline can manufacture a complete, plausible-looking, entirely wrong result for a target that does not exist in the database, and the only defence is the accession check.

2.3 Corrected computation (no docking)

A corrected driver (dock_hp067_pi4k_2026-11-17.py, RDKit venv) computed: (a) MMV390048's structure from PubChem (CID 53311393; SMILES verified live; IUPAC 5-(4-methylsulfonylphenyl)-3-[6-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pyridinyl]pyridin-2-amine; formula C18H14F3N3O2S; CAS 1314883-11-8); (b) RDKit descriptors, PAINS screen and ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across for MMV390048; (c) PubChem 2D-similarity analogues (fastsimilarity_2d, threshold 85), top five by RDKit Morgan Tanimoto, with the same descriptors, PAINS and ToxGuard panel; (d) human PI4KA (CHEMBL3667) and PI4KB (CHEMBL3268) bioactivity counts at pChEMBL ≥ 5 as selectivity context. Docking was skipped: no experimental PfPI4K structure exists, and no homology model was docked, because a model built without a template of known accuracy would be a made-up structure. All outputs are in dock-HP-067-2026-11-17.json.

2.4 Honesty limits

No docking was run, so there is no docking score in this paper and no ranking. The four analogues have no published PfPI4K activity; similarity to MMV390048 is not evidence of activity. ToxGuard's read-across for MMV390048 rests on neighbours at maximum similarity 0.382, which is weak — its scores are a flag, not a safety assessment. Human PI4K bioactivity counts describe the human enzymes, not the parasite enzyme, and say nothing about MMV390048's selectivity beyond the published chemoproteomic result.

2.5 Literature and the Islamic canon

The classical canon was checked alongside the modern literature, as the programme requires. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) classifies intermittent fevers (humma) in detail, and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records fever remedies; both predate the parasite aetiology of malaria (Laveran, 1880) by centuries, so neither names PI4K, and no Canon-listed plant was docked or screened in this run — the paper claims no traditional-medicine finding. The honest limit, named here: the full 23-volume Kitab al-Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised; the sweep covers the named canonical works, not every book ever written.

3. Results

3.1 The target is absent from both databases the pipeline trusts

ChEMBL holds no target with component accession Q8I406 (0 targets, verified live). The seven PI4K targets it does hold are human PI4K alpha (CHEMBL3667), beta (CHEMBL3268), type 2-alpha (CHEMBL2251) and type 2-beta (CHEMBL3220), bovine PI4K alpha (CHEMBL3185), a human PI4K protein family (CHEMBL2096619) and a putative human PI4K alpha-like protein (CHEMBL4105789). The PDB holds no structure for Q8I406 (0 UniProt cross-references; RCSB accession search empty). PfPI4K is therefore unevaluable by the standard benchmark: there is no potency table to retrieve and no structure to dock on. This is not a data-quality footnote. The most clinically advanced PI4K inhibitor in history has a target that the two databases a computational screen trusts most simply do not contain, because the target's evidence lives in papers and patents, not in ChEMBL's target table.

3.2 The wrong-target run, and what it would have published

Had the accession check been skipped, the pipeline would have published a benchmark of 26 human maltase-glucoamylase inhibitors as PfPI4K leads, with docking scores on a maltase structure, under an MMV390048 heading. The run completed with "PIPELINE OK: True". Only the target line — CHEMBL2074 where a PfPI4K target should have been — betrayed it. This is the same trap that produced discarded runs earlier in this series (maltase substituted for GyrB, for DHFR, for PTP1B): the ChEMBL text search returns maltase-glucoamylase first for short queries, and a pipeline that falls back to text search without an accession check will silently evaluate the wrong enzyme. The rule this paper states, and follows, is: no accession match, no benchmark — a target without a verified ChEMBL target and a verified structure gets a literature-and-property paper, never a docking table.

3.3 MMV390048: drug-like, PAINS-clean, weakly covered by ToxGuard

MMV390048 (PubChem CID 53311393) computes as a clean drug-like molecule: MW 393.39, logP 3.82, 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 5 acceptors, TPSA 85.94 Å², 3 rotatable bonds, zero Lipinski violations, Veber pass, no PAINS alerts. ToxGuard's kNN read-across (k = 15) found no close neighbour — maximum similarity 0.382 — and returned low scores on all twelve Tox21 assays (highest: NR-ER 0.172, NR-ER-LBD 0.094, SR-ARE 0.093, all others 0.0). Read honestly, that is not a clean bill of health; it is an admission that the model has almost nothing to read across from, at a similarity where read-across is unreliable. The compound's real safety signal is not computational at all: it is the rat diaphragmatic-hernia finding and the teratogenicity data that stopped the Phase 2a trial. No Tox21 score in this paper should be quoted against that animal evidence.

3.4 Four close analogues, none with a published PfPI4K measurement

PubChem 2D similarity (threshold 85) returned 20 compounds; the top four distinct analogues by RDKit Tanimoto, after excluding the self-match, are all 2-aminopyridines that keep MMV390048's methylsulfonylphenyl half and vary the trifluoromethyl aryl ring:

Compound (PubChem CID) Tanimoto vs MMV390048 MW logP HBD / HBA TPSA (Å²) PAINS
53311566 — 5-(4-methylsulfonylphenyl)-3-[4-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl]pyridin-2-amine 0.791 392.40 4.42 1 / 4 73.05 none
53312146 — 3,5-bis(4-methylsulfonylphenyl)pyridin-2-amine 0.769 402.50 2.80 1 / 6 107.19 none
53259031 — 5-(4-methylsulfonylphenyl)-3-[3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl]pyridin-2-amine 0.723 392.40 4.42 1 / 4 73.05 none
57384535 — 5-(4-methylsulfonylphenyl)-3-[4-methyl-3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl]pyridin-2-amine 0.723 406.43 4.73 1 / 4 73.05 none

All four pass Lipinski and Veber and carry no PAINS alerts; their ToxGuard read-across is as weak as MMV390048's (maximum similarity 0.373–0.468). The structural lesson is narrow but real: the series tolerates moving the trifluoromethyl group around the phenyl ring (para, meta) and replacing the pyridyl ring with a phenyl, and it tolerates a second methylsulfonyl group at the cost of polarity (TPSA 107.19, logP 2.80 for CID 53312146). What is not known about any of them is the only thing that matters: none has a published PfPI4K measurement, and none is presented here as a lead. They are a prioritised assay list, not a result.

3.5 The human PI4K context, and why it does not settle selectivity

Human PI4KA (CHEMBL3667) holds 48 bioactivities at pChEMBL ≥ 5, the most potent at IC50 0.32 nM (CHEMBL3121323, pChEMBL 9.50); human PI4KB (CHEMBL3268) holds 45, the most potent at 0.98 nM (CHEMBL3923414, pChEMBL 9.01). Sub-nanomolar human PI4K inhibitors exist in number. That is the selectivity problem in one line: the human enzymes are eminently druggable, and a parasite inhibitor must thread the gap between PfPI4K and two human enzymes that bind the same lipid substrate. Paquet et al.'s chemoproteomic result — no binding to human PI4KA/PI4KB, with human PIP4K2C as the main human target at similar affinity to PfPI4K — is the only selectivity evidence for MMV390048, and it is assay evidence, not a database count. The ChEMBL counts cannot substitute for it, and the rat hernia signal is a reminder that the mammalian kinase liability is real even when the intended human orthologues are spared.

3.6 The field has not stopped

Two recent papers keep the target alive: 2,8-disubstituted-1,5-naphthyridines as dual PfPI4K inhibitors (J Med Chem 2024, PMID 38918002), a new chemotype beyond the 2-aminopyridines; and the ATM kinase inhibitor AZD0156 reported as a potent PfPI4Kβ inhibitor (Angew Chem Int Ed 2025, PMID 40317875), a repurposing lead from an oncology drug. A 2023 review (Trends Parasitol, PMID 37385921) frames the open question as opportunity or liability: kinase inhibitors for malaria carry mammalian-kinase risk by definition, and the field has not decided whether the PI4K class can be made safe enough. MMV390048's termination is a data point in that debate, not its conclusion.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the bottleneck is the database, not the chemistry

This paper's finding is not about MMV390048's potency, which was established in 2017, but about the infrastructure around it. A target can be genetically validated, chemoproteomically confirmed, clinically tested to Phase 2a — and still be invisible to the standard computational pipeline, because ChEMBL has no target row for it and the PDB has no structure. The pipeline's failure mode is worse than an error message: it silently substitutes a different enzyme and returns a clean-looking result. Any group screening antimalarial targets by text search should assume this has happened to them at least once and check by accession.

4.2 Why the analogues must not be over-read

Four clean, drug-like, similar molecules are not four leads. Similarity to an active compound is the weakest form of evidence in medicinal chemistry, and here it is unaccompanied by any enzyme data, any whole-cell data, and any structural model to explain why the changes should preserve binding. The correct reading of §3.4 is as an assay shopping list ordered by similarity: test CID 53311566 first (closest, Tanimoto 0.791), then 53312146 (the polarity variant, the most informative single change), then the two 0.723 analogues. The test that matters is a PfPI4K enzyme assay at 1 µM and 10 µM, with MMV390048 as the control and a human PI4KB counter-screen in the same run.

4.3 Association only

This is a retrospective database audit and property analysis, not a causal experiment. It shows that PfPI4K is absent from ChEMBL and the PDB, that MMV390048 is drug-like and PAINS-clean, and that four similar molecules exist without published activity. It does not show that any analogue inhibits PfPI4K, that MMV390048 is safe, or that PI4K inhibition is clinically viable. The falsifier names the experiment that could change each of those statements.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CID 53311566 inhibits PfPI4K below 1 µM. Falsifier: recombinant PfPI4K enzyme assay; IC50 ≥ 10 µM refutes it, and refutes the similarity neighbourhood with it.
  2. CID 53312146, the bis-sulfonyl analogue, is the most selective of the four against human PI4KB. Falsifier: paired PfPI4K / human PI4KB enzyme assays; a selectivity ratio below 10 refutes it.
  3. A PfPI4K structure or ChEMBL target will appear within two years. Falsifier: none needed — this is a dated prediction, checkable in November 2028; if neither exists, the infrastructure gap is permanent for practical purposes.
  4. The rat diaphragmatic-hernia signal tracks mammalian kinase inhibition, not PI4K inhibition itself. Falsifier: a PI4K inhibitor with no mammalian kinase binding at 10 µM that still produces hernias in rat would refute it; one that does not would support the mammalian-kinase link and clear the class.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain the four analogues commercially (all are in PubChem with suppliers listed) and confirm identity and purity by LC-MS. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): recombinant PfPI4K enzyme assay (ADP-Glo or equivalent) at 10 µM, 1 µM and 0.1 µM, MMV390048 as positive control, with a human PI4KB counter-screen in parallel. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): whole-cell P. falciparum 3D7 assay for any analogue active below 1 µM, plus the H1484Y and S1320L mutant lines as a resistance check. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): report all four results, including the negatives — a dead end is a result. Total cost is one enzyme assay and four compounds, not a screening campaign.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking, by design. No PfPI4K structure exists; no docking score is reported and no structural claim is made.
  2. No ChEMBL potency data for the parasite target. Every PfPI4K number in this paper is a literature value, not a database retrieval.
  3. No lab data. No assay was run; the four analogues are untested.
  4. Weak ToxGuard coverage. Maximum neighbour similarity 0.382 for MMV390048 means the Tox21 scores are unreliable and must not be quoted as safety evidence.
  5. The Phase 2a record is incomplete. The Ethiopia trial was not completed; its published report covers eight P. vivax patients, and the teratogenicity data that contributed to stopping it are described, not fully published.
  6. Islamic canon gaps (named, per the programme's rule). The Canon and Kitab al-Hawi were checked through named works, not read in full; the full 23-volume Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP), the National Institute of Health, and the Directorate of Malaria Control — and, for the method rule, every public funder of computational drug discovery in Pakistan. Three exact changes, each with its falsifier:

  1. Fund one PfPI4K enzyme assay in Pakistan, at a single reference laboratory, and publish the protocol. The four analogues in §3.4 cost one assay to test, and the country has no domestic route from a computational antimalarial claim to a measured number. If the assay shows all four analogues inactive above 10 µM, the scaffold is closed and the money is still well spent — a dead end found in weeks beats a decade of untested docking. Reverse this only if a cheaper regional assay (e.g. through MMV's network) becomes available to Pakistani groups.
  2. Require accession-verified targets in every publicly funded computational screen. Any screening proposal must state the UniProt accession and the ChEMBL target ID it resolved to, and any run that falls back to text search must declare it. This paper's discarded maltase run is the evidence: without that rule, public money can fund a complete benchmark of the wrong enzyme. Reverse this only if ChEMBL's text search is shown to return the correct target first for a blinded set of parasite accessions.
  3. Do not restart MMV390048, but do not abandon the PI4K class either. The teratogenicity signal and the terminated trial argue against reviving this compound; the 2024 naphthyridine series and the 2025 AZD0156 result argue the target is still live. The correct public position is to fund the assay in (1) and let the analogues decide. Islamic principle behind the recommendations: preservation of life (hifz al-nafs, Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat) — malaria kills nearly 600,000 people a year, so a screening method that mis-ranks antimalarials is a failure to protect life, not a technical footnote; and stewardship (khilafah, Qur'an 2:30) — public research funds are a trust, and a steward does not spend a trust on a benchmark of the wrong enzyme. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so; they do here.

7. Conclusion

PfPI4K is the target of the most clinically advanced new-mechanism antimalarial of the decade, and it is absent from ChEMBL and the PDB: no target row, no structure, no docking possible. The standard pipeline's answer to that absence was to silently benchmark human maltase instead, a run discarded here in full. What remains is honest and small: MMV390048 is drug-like and PAINS-clean (MW 393.39, logP 3.82); four close analogues exist, all clean, none tested; and a single PfPI4K enzyme assay — which no Pakistani laboratory currently runs — would settle whether the scaffold has a future. The memorable number is zero: zero ChEMBL targets, zero PDB structures, for a target that reached Phase 2a.

2026-11-17 Health Partial draft

Rigid Docking Gets the Dicarboxylates Right on IMP-1 but Collapses Four Captopril Stereoisomers into 0.08 kcal/mol for a 60-Fold Potency Range

IMP-1 is a subclass B1 metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) that hydrolyses almost all β-lactams, including carbapenems, and no clinically approved inhibitor exists for it.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Faculty of Pharmacy, SMBBMU, Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-17 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #69 (daily 5-paper run) Topic: IMP-1 metallo-β-lactamase (off-pool topic; no pool ID — an earlier draft mislabelled it HP-080, which is the FGFR2 topic)

Abstract

IMP-1 is a subclass B1 metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) that hydrolyses almost all β-lactams, including carbapenems, and no clinically approved inhibitor exists for it. We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking (v1.2.7) against measured IMP-1 inhibition for six compounds spanning 240 nM to 436 µM: the dicarboxylates 3AP-DPA (IC50 240 nM) and dipicolinic acid (3,030 nM), and the four captopril stereoisomers (d 7.2, l 23.3, epi-d 173.2, epi-l 436 µM), docked into the d-captopril-bound structure 4C1G (1.71 Å) and replicated on 6JED (1.57 Å). Falsifiable claim: Vina ranks the dicarboxylates ahead of the thiols and orders 3AP-DPA ahead of dipicolinic acid, but cannot rank the four captopril stereoisomers. Falsifier: a metal-aware re-dock (Zn(II) retained, metal-coordination term) that orders the four stereoisomers in measured order with a spread ≥1 kcal/mol refutes the blindness claim. On 4C1G, 3AP-DPA scored best (−7.42 kcal/mol) and dipicolinic acid second (−6.50), a 0.92 kcal/mol gap for a 12.6-fold measured difference (1.50 kcal/mol), and the overall rank correlation was Spearman ρ = −0.66 (n = 6, correct direction). But the four stereoisomers collapsed into 0.08 kcal/mol (−5.90 to −5.98) for a 60-fold measured range (2.43 kcal/mol), with the weakest, epi-l-captopril, scoring joint-best; within the series ρ = +0.20. The 6JED replication reproduced the pattern exactly (ρ = −0.66; stereoisomer spread 0.34 kcal/mol; epi-l again best of the four). The mechanism is stated in advance: the pipeline's receptor preparation strips the two catalytic Zn(II) ions, and Vina has no metal-coordination term, so inhibitors whose binding is Zn chelation are scored on shape alone — and four stereoisomers have the same shape. Rigid metal-free docking can shortlist dicarboxylate scaffolds for IMP-1; it cannot rank thiol stereoisomers, and any IMP-1 screen that uses it without a metal-aware step will mis-prioritise.

Keywords: IMP-1; metallo-β-lactamase; captopril; stereoisomers; dipicolinic acid; 3AP-DPA; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; carbapenem resistance; Pakistan

Introduction

Metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs) are zinc-dependent enzymes that hydrolyse almost all β-lactam antibiotics, including carbapenems, and no clinically useful MBL inhibitor exists. The B1 subclass — NDM, VIM and IMP types — is the most clinically relevant. IMP-1, the first IMP variant identified, is carried on transferable plasmids and integrons and is reported across Asia. In Pakistan the burden is documented: a 2019–2022 study of 2,170 clinical strains at Mayo Hospital, Lahore, found 42.1% carbapenem resistance, with blaIMP accounting for 2.7% of detected carbapenemase genes against 41.1% blaNDM-1 (Gondal et al., Antibiotics 2023). IMP-1 is the minority carbapenemase in Pakistan today, but it is the one with the thinnest inhibitor pipeline: the boronate taniborbactam inhibits VIM-2 (Ki 0.02 µM) and NDM-1 (0.08 µM) but does not inhibit IMP-type enzymes, where xeruborbactam is the current hope — and IMP variants resistant even to xeruborbactam are already reported (Le Terrier et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2024; Le Terrier et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2025).

A November 2026 audit in ACS Infectious Diseases asked bluntly why computational prediction keeps failing on B1 MBL inhibitor discovery (Balieiro et al., 2026; PMID 43023851) — the pitfalls this paper tests one by one on IMP-1, the third B1 enzyme in this series after NDM-1 and VIM-2. The audit's central warnings are metal handling and the gap between a docking score and a metal-binding mechanism. Captopril, the antihypertensive ACE inhibitor, is the cleanest test case in the field: its thiol chelates the two active-site zinc ions, and its four stereoisomers inhibit IMP-1 across a 60-fold range in a single assay — d-captopril 7.2 µM, l-captopril 23.3 µM, epi-d-captopril 173.2 µM, epi-l-captopril 436 µM (Brem et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2016). The crystal structures show different binding modes: in IMP-1, d-captopril's thiolate bridges the two Zn(II) ions while its carboxylate contacts the conserved Arg228 region; the epi-isomers bind differently again. The binding modes are visibly different; the question is whether a docking score can see the difference.

The dicarboxylates provide the counter-test. Dipicolinic acid (DPA, pyridine-2,6-dicarboxylic acid) inhibits IMP-1 at 3,030 nM, and its 4-(3-aminophenyl) analogue 3AP-DPA at 240 nM — a 12.6-fold gain from one substituent (Chen et al., J Med Chem 2017, via ChEMBL). Mechanistic work shows DPA and 3AP-DPA both strip metal from the IMP-1 active site and form ternary complexes, while captopril forms a ternary complex without stripping metal (Zhang et al., Bioorg Med Chem 2021). Two inhibitor classes, two mechanisms, one enzyme: if docking ranks the dicarboxylates correctly but collapses the stereoisomers, the failure is specific to metal-dependent stereochemistry, not to docking in general.

Falsifiable claim (stated before the results): under one standardised protocol on the d-captopril co-crystal structure 4C1G, Vina will rank 3AP-DPA ahead of DPA and both ahead of the four captopril stereoisomers, but the four stereoisomers will score within 0.1 kcal/mol of each other, in no measured order. The claim is refuted if a metal-aware re-dock (Zn(II) retained) orders the stereoisomers in measured order with a spread ≥1 kcal/mol, or if an independent re-assay moves the four IC50s within 2-fold of each other.

Methods

2.1 Target and compound selection

IMP-1 (UniProt P52699, Serratia marcescens, reviewed) was resolved to ChEMBL target CHEMBL4105964 ("Metallo-beta-lactamase type 2") by accession, not by text search — the ChEMBL text search returns maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) first for this query, the same trap that produced a discarded wrong-target run in this series' Mpro paper. ChEMBL holds exactly two measured IMP-1 activities for this target: CHEMBL4068259 (3AP-DPA), IC50 240 nM, pChEMBL 6.62; and CHEMBL284104 (dipicolinic acid), IC50 3,030 nM, pChEMBL 5.52 — both from Chen et al. 2017 (ChEMBL document CHEMBL4017500, assay CHEMBL4019028), accessed 17 November 2026. The four captopril stereoisomers and their IMP-1 IC50s are from Brem et al. 2016, Table 1 (single assay, n ≥ 3 replicates): d 7.2 ± 1.2, l 23.3 ± 1.3, epi-d 173.2 ± 1.2, epi-l 436 ± 1.1 µM. Stereochemistry was fixed independently of the paper's names: PubChem IUPAC names give L-captopril (CID 44093) as (2S)-1-[(2S)-2-methyl-3-sulfanylpropanoyl]pyrrolidine-2-carboxylic acid, D-captopril (CID 447055) as (2R)-1-[(2S)-…], and epi-D-captopril (CID 446549) as (2R)-1-[(2R)-…]; the four isomeric SMILES were generated by RDKit stereoisomer enumeration and their CIP codes verified atom-by-atom (proline centre first, methyl-bearing centre second): d = (R,S), epi-d = (R,R), l = (S,S), epi-l = (S,R). No compound in the set was invented, and no potency was estimated — every IC50 is a published measurement.

2.2 Structures: the pipeline's pick, the audit, and the correction

The pipeline's automatic structure pick for P52699 was 6JED (1.57 Å), the highest-resolution ligand-bound IMP-1 structure. Its centre picker chose the centroid of EPE — a HEPES buffer molecule (15 atoms) — because the true co-crystallised ligand, MCR (sulfanylacetic acid, mercaptoacetic acid, 5 heavy atoms), falls below the picker's ≥6-atom threshold. The 6JED docks run on that EPE centre are reported in §3.3 as a caught pipeline error and are not used as evidence: the centre was ~6.4 Å from the inhibitor site. The corrected 6JED run recentres on the MCR centroid [18.48, −3.53, 23.16], computed directly from the 6JED HETATM records. The primary structure is 4C1G (1.71 Å), the IMP-1 structure co-crystallised with d-captopril (Brem et al. 2016): its HETATM ligand MCO (14 heavy atoms — captopril's heavy-atom count) was picked by the centre routine, and the docking centre is the MCO centroid [12.76, −8.33, −17.59]. Both structures contain two catalytic Zn(II) ions (4C1G: ZN 300/301, chain A; 6JED: ZN 301/302). All docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å, 3 poses.

2.3 Limitations of the docking model, stated in advance

The metal is stripped before scoring. The pipeline's receptor preparation keeps ATOM records only, so both catalytic Zn(II) ions are removed from the receptor, and Vina's scoring function has no metal-coordination term. Every inhibitor in this set binds through the metal — captopril's thiolate bridges Zn1–Zn2, and the dicarboxylates chelate and partly strip Zn — so the scored interaction is shape complementarity against a metal-free pocket. This is the Balieiro et al. pitfall, stated before any score was read: a method that cannot see the metal cannot rank compounds whose potency lives in metal binding. Rigid docking carries a documented ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band. Any score difference below ~0.5 kcal/mol is uninterpretable, and differences below 0.1 kcal/mol are identical scores. Small n, single assay. Six compounds, one enzyme, one assay series for the stereoisomers; the rank correlation is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking. No RMSD for the re-dock. The re-dock control is reported as a score with tight poses; the docked pose was not compared atom-by-atom with the crystal pose.

2.4 Literature and the Islamic canon

The modern literature sweep used the daily digest of 2026-11-14 (722 candidates screened; item 3, Balieiro et al. 2026, is directly on this topic) plus targeted PubMed/ChEMBL/UniProt/RCSB checks on 2026-11-17. The Islamic canon was checked per the programme's literature map: for a drug-resistance paper the relevant works are Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (23 volumes of clinical observation — the method ancestor for testing a claim against measured outcomes rather than authority) and the maqasid literature (Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; systematised by Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat). The Canon's materia medica (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, Book II) was not screened against IMP-1 in this run — that is the map's world-problem #11 seed (test Canon-listed plants against a resistant target) and remains open; it is named as a gap in the Limitations, not claimed as done. The full 23-volume Kitab al-Hawi exists in English only in selections, so it was consulted through the map's verified summary, not read in full.

Results

3.1 The compounds

All six compounds pass Lipinski's rule of five with zero violations and are PAINS-clean (Table 1). The four captopril stereoisomers are identical by every descriptor (MW 217.29, logP 0.63, TPSA 57.61 Å², HBD 2, HBA 3, 3 rotatable bonds, C9H15NO3S) — they differ only in the spatial arrangement of two chiral centres, which is exactly the property a shape-only score cannot price. The dicarboxylates are larger and more polar: 3AP-DPA MW 258.23, logP 1.73, TPSA 113.51 Å²; DPA MW 167.12, logP 0.48, TPSA 87.49 Å². ToxGuard read-across gives no flags of concern: all measured-assay probabilities are 0, and the highest predicted value in the set is 0.147 (3AP-DPA, NR-ER, kNN read-across at 0.50 maximum similarity). Lead scores are 99.2–100.0 on the pipeline's 0–100 scale. Nothing in the ADMET panel distinguishes the four stereoisomers either — as expected, since they are the same molecule in four mirror arrangements.

3.2 On 4C1G, the dicarboxylates rank correctly and the stereoisomers collapse

3AP-DPA scored best (−7.42 kcal/mol; poses −7.42, −7.39, −7.37) and dipicolinic acid second (−6.50; −6.50, −6.47, −5.86) — the correct order for a 12.6-fold measured gap (1.50 kcal/mol at 298 K), compressed to a 0.92 kcal/mol docking gap. The four captopril stereoisomers then occupy a 0.08 kcal/mol band: epi-l −5.98, d −5.97, l −5.93, epi-d −5.90. The measured range across those four is 60.6-fold (7.2 → 436 µM), equivalent to 2.43 kcal/mol — thirty times the docking spread. The weakest compound in the set, epi-l-captopril (436 µM), scores joint-best among the four; the most potent, d-captopril (7.2 µM), scores second. Within the stereoisomer series the rank correlation is Spearman ρ = +0.20 — no ranking, in the wrong direction. The overall correlation across all six (ρ = −0.66, n = 6) is carried entirely by the dicarboxylate–thiol gap: remove the two dicarboxylates and there is no ranking left. The re-dock control worked: d-captopril re-docked into its own crystal structure with tight poses (−5.97, −5.93, −5.87), so the failure is not pose instability; the poses are stable and the scores are flat.
