Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-16 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #65 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: GLP-1 receptor; orforglipron; small-molecule agonist; type 2 diabetes; obesity; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; danuglipron

Abstract

Pakistan has the highest age-standardised diabetes prevalence in the world — 34.5 million adults, 9.3 million of them undiagnosed — and the GLP-1 receptor agonists that treat it are all injected peptides. Orforglipron is the first oral, non-peptide, small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist to complete phase 3, and it binds a pocket in the upper helical bundle that only partly overlaps the peptide site. We asked whether a standard automated docking pipeline ranks it correctly. Using the LeadForge protocol (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → Vina 1.2.7), we docked orforglipron and five ChEMBL leads on the pipeline's auto-picked structure, 4ZGM — the isolated extracellular domain with a semaglutide peptide fragment — and then re-docked the same compounds on 6XOX, the cryo-EM structure of GLP-1R bound to orforglipron itself. On 4ZGM, orforglipron ranks first at −7.66 kcal/mol; on 6XOX it scores −10.8, a 3.14 kcal/mol pocket effect, and the ChEMBL lead CHEMBL6167455 out-scores it at −11.3. The two structures' rankings correlate only moderately (Spearman rho 0.8, with the winner changing), and the correct pocket also ranks the measured potencies better (rho 0.7 on 6XOX, n = 5, versus 0.2 on 4ZGM, n = 4) — though the measured values span only 1.6-fold (EC50 0.012–0.019 nM), a band no docking screen can resolve finely. Rigid docking can re-dock orforglipron into its own pocket, but the auto-picked structure under-prices every compound by ~3–4 kcal/mol and can crown the wrong winner. The falsifiable next step is a cAMP assay of the same set: if the 6XOX rank predicts the EC50 rank and the 4ZGM rank does not, automated GLP-1R docking must use the cryo-EM pocket, not the best-resolved X-ray structure.

1. Introduction

Pakistan has the highest age-standardised diabetes prevalence in the world. The International Diabetes Federation's Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition (2025), estimates 34.5 million Pakistani adults aged 20–79 were living with diabetes in 2024 — an age-standardised prevalence of 31.4%, the highest of any country — with about 9.3 million of them undiagnosed (26.9% of cases) and roughly 230,000 diabetes-related deaths a year; on current trends the number reaches 70.2 million by 2050. Globally, 589 million adults live with diabetes. The GLP-1 receptor agonists are among the most effective drugs for type 2 diabetes and obesity, but every approved one is a peptide: injected, cold-chain dependent, and expensive — three properties that price them out of reach for most of the 34.5 million. Oral semaglutide exists, but it needs an absorption enhancer and strict fasting conditions.

Orforglipron (LY3502970, OWL833) is the first oral, non-peptide, small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist to complete phase 3. It is a partial agonist, biased toward G-protein activation over beta-arrestin recruitment, and it binds a unique pocket in the upper helical bundle — held by the extracellular domain, extracellular loop 2 and transmembrane helices 1, 2, 3 and 7 — that overlaps only partly with where the peptide sits (Kawai et al., Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2020;117:29959–29967, PMID 33177239, doi:10.1073/pnas.2014879117; PDB 6XOX). In ACHIEVE-1, a phase 3 trial in 559 adults with early type 2 diabetes, orforglipron lowered HbA1c by 1.24–1.48 percentage points from a baseline of 8.0% over 40 weeks, versus 0.41 on placebo, with weight down 4.5–7.6% versus 1.7% (Rosenstock et al., N Engl J Med 2025, PMID 40544435, NCT05971940). In ATTAIN-1, 3,127 adults with obesity but no diabetes lost 7.5%, 8.4% and 11.2% of body weight at 6, 12 and 36 mg over 72 weeks, versus 2.1% on placebo, with 54.6% of the top-dose group losing at least 10% (Wharton et al., N Engl J Med 2025, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2511774, PMID 40960239, NCT05869903). The FDA approved orforglipron on 1 April 2026 as Foundayo, for weight management. The class has a cautionary tale attached: Pfizer discontinued danuglipron in April 2025 after a case of potential drug-induced liver injury, and lotiglipron was stopped earlier for liver findings — a small molecule with its own hepatic metabolism carries a risk the peptides do not.

That history creates a precise, testable problem for computational screening. A docking pipeline that picks its structure automatically will pick the best-resolved X-ray structure of the receptor. For GLP-1R, the best X-ray structures are of the isolated extracellular domain bound to a peptide fragment — a pocket orforglipron does not bind. The correct structure for a small-molecule agonist is a cryo-EM structure (6XOX), which the pipeline's X-ray-only picker excludes by design. If the pipeline's auto-picked structure ranks orforglipron and its analogues anyway, the pocket question is moot; if it does not, every GLP-1R docking paper built on the auto-picked structure is ranking the wrong site.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised Vina protocol, orforglipron will re-dock into its own 6XOX pocket with a score at least as strong as the best ChEMBL lead, while the pipeline's auto-picked structure (4ZGM, the isolated extracellular domain) will fail to reproduce that ranking — orforglipron will not rank first there, or the lead order will differ. Falsified if 4ZGM ranks orforglipron first with the same lead order as 6XOX, in which case the pocket concern does not affect the ranking.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-16 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-15, which contained no GLP-1R item). Key sources: Kawai et al. 2020 (PMID 33177239) for the LY3502970/6XOX structure and the partial-agonist, G-protein-biased pharmacology; Rosenstock et al. 2025 (PMID 40544435) for ACHIEVE-1; Wharton et al. 2025 (PMID 40960239) for ATTAIN-1; the IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition (2025), for the Pakistan and global burden numbers; Saxena et al. 2023 (JAMA Network Open, PMID 37213102) for danuglipron phase 2 in type 2 diabetes and the Pfizer April 2025 discontinuation announcement for the liver-injury case. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Computation

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R)" and reference drug orforglipron (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). UniProtKB resolved GLP-1R to P43220 (human GLP-1R, 463 amino acids), ChEMBL to target CHEMBL1784 (Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor, single protein, human), which returned 58 bioactivities; the similarity screen kept 25 and the ranking produced 26 leads. The pipeline's structure picker — which accepts X-ray structures only, resolution under 3.0 angstrom — picked 4ZGM, the 1.80 angstrom crystal structure of the semaglutide peptide backbone in complex with the GLP-1 receptor extracellular domain (ECD) only, with the grid centre [−5.18, 62.29, −5.41] from D._ligand_center, the centroid of the bound peptide fragment (ligand code 32M). Five compounds were docked with the standardised protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, one box (22.5 angstrom), exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported — the query plus the top four leads. The query (orforglipron, PubChem-verified, MW 882.97, logP 7.44, TPSA 155.93, two Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean, highest Tox21 read-across 0.166) is a large small molecule: it violates Lipinski twice and is still dosed orally once daily in phase 3, which the paper notes rather than hiding — Lipinski is a guide, and orforglipron's oral dosing is the empirical fact.

Because 4ZGM contains only the extracellular domain while orforglipron's pocket spans the ECD, extracellular loop 2 and transmembrane helices 1, 2, 3 and 7 (Kawai et al. 2020), a control docking was run on 6XOX, the 3.1 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human GLP-1R bound to LY3502970 (orforglipron) with its G protein (hidden_files/dock_hp061_6xox.py, same Vina defaults). The centre [152.46, 143.94, 119.46] is the centroid of the bound orforglipron (ligand code V6G) via D._ligand_center. Six compounds were docked there: the query plus the top five leads (the 4ZGM set plus rank-6 CHEMBL5407160). The ChEMBL lead potencies are the ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL1784, quoted as stored (EC50 values; the pipeline output does not record the assay type, and the paper does not invent one). The measured band is 0.012–0.019 nM across the leads — a 1.4- to 1.6-fold span, stated here and in the Limitations.

2.3 PAINS and safety panel

RDKit PAINS filter and the ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) were applied to every compound, exactly as in Papers #1/#3 and the 2026-11-15 run.

2.4 Analysis plan (stated before results)

The analysis plan was fixed before docking: (i) report the pipeline docking table on the auto-picked structure with measured potencies from the ChEMBL record; (ii) run the 6XOX control docking of the same compounds on the same protocol and report both tables side by side; (iii) compute Spearman rank correlation of docking score against measured potency on each structure separately; (iv) declare the auto-picked structure inadequate for small-molecule ranking if orforglipron does not rank first on it while ranking first (or tied) on 6XOX. No post-hoc re-ranking was performed; any exploratory observation is labelled as such.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. Rigid docking on a single structure cannot model the G-protein-biased signalling that defines orforglipron (partial agonism, beta-arrestin bias) — a docking score is a fit, not a function. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed. The peptide agonists (semaglutide, tirzepatide) cannot be docked by this protocol at all — peptides are outside Vina's ligand preparation — so the comparison against the strongest incumbent is a clinical comparison (trial numbers), not a docking comparison, and the paper does not pretend otherwise. Orforglipron binds in a primate-specific manner (dependent on tryptophan 33 of the extracellular domain, absent in ordinary mice and rats), so rodent data cannot validate these results.

3. Results

3.1 Docking on the auto-picked structure (4ZGM, extracellular domain only)

Compound Measured GLP-1R potency (ChEMBL, CHEMBL1784) Vina on 4ZGM (kcal/mol) PAINS
Orforglipron (QUERY) no ChEMBL activity value attached −7.66 (−7.66, −7.51, −6.83) clean
CHEMBL6167455 EC50 0.016 nM −7.20 (−7.20, −6.98, −6.76) clean
CHEMBL5399932 EC50 0.015 nM −6.58 (−6.58, −6.49, −6.32) clean
CHEMBL5416222 EC50 0.012 nM −6.25 (−6.25, −6.15, −6.11) clean
CHEMBL5415681 EC50 0.017 nM −5.89 (−5.89, −5.69, −5.58) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). All five compounds are PAINS-clean; the four leads carry one or two Lipinski violations each (MW 595–637, logP 4.38–6.58) and no decisive Tox21 signal (highest single read-across 0.552). The whole docked set spans 1.77 kcal/mol, and the measured potencies span only 0.012–0.017 nM — a 1.4-fold band. Against the measured potencies, the docking rank correlates weakly (Spearman rho 0.2, n = 4): the most potent measured compound, CHEMBL5416222 (0.012 nM), ranks third of four by docking, and the least potent, CHEMBL5415681 (0.017 nM), ranks last. As in Paper #64, the honest reading is that neither the measurement nor the docking can separate compounds inside a 1.4-fold band — the inversion is real as a rank and meaningless as a magnitude.

Two things about this table deserve attention before the control is introduced. First, orforglipron ranks first on 4ZGM (−7.66) even though 4ZGM is not its pocket. That is not a contradiction: the ECD contributes to orforglipron's real pocket — its binding depends on tryptophan 33 of the ECD — so the isolated ECD groove does bind the molecule, just incompletely. Second, every score on 4ZGM is weak in absolute terms (−5.89 to −7.66), far weaker than the −10 to −12 kcal/mol seen for tight binders on PARP1 in Paper #64. A shallow groove gives shallow scores. The question the control answers is whether those scores are merely compressed, or wrong.

3.2 The 6XOX control: same compounds, same protocol, a different pocket

Compound Measured GLP-1R potency (ChEMBL, CHEMBL1784) Vina on 6XOX (kcal/mol) Vina on 4ZGM (kcal/mol)
CHEMBL6167455 EC50 0.016 nM −11.30 (−11.30, −10.85, −10.84) −7.20
Orforglipron (QUERY) no ChEMBL activity value attached −10.80 (−10.80, −10.52, −10.47) −7.66
CHEMBL5416222 EC50 0.012 nM −10.58 (−10.58, −10.49, −10.36) −6.25
CHEMBL5399932 EC50 0.015 nM −10.51 (−10.51, −10.35, −10.32) −6.58
CHEMBL5415681 EC50 0.017 nM −10.12 (−10.12, −10.08, −5.32) −5.89
CHEMBL5407160 EC50 0.019 nM −10.09 (−10.09, −9.94, −9.90) not docked

On the real pocket, every compound scores 3.14–4.33 kcal/mol stronger than on the ECD: orforglipron improves from −7.66 to −10.80, CHEMBL6167455 from −7.20 to −11.30. The pocket changes the magnitude by more than Vina's entire noise margin. The ranking, however, mostly survives: the two structures' orders correlate at Spearman rho 0.8, with two swaps — CHEMBL6167455 overtakes orforglipron at the top (by 0.50 kcal/mol, inside noise), and CHEMBL5416222 overtakes CHEMBL5399932 in the middle (by 0.07 kcal/mol, nothing at all). The hypothesis is therefore confirmed in its magnitude clause and partly in its ranking clause: the pocket does not scramble the ranking, but it does change the winner, and a 0.50 kcal/mol margin on 6XOX is not a lead over orforglipron — it is a tie.

Against the measured potencies, the 6XOX ranking correlates at rho 0.7 (n = 5) — clearly better than 4ZGM's 0.2 (n = 4), and carried by the bottom of the table: the two least potent measured compounds, CHEMBL5415681 (0.017 nM) and CHEMBL5407160 (0.019 nM), are also the two worst by docking on 6XOX, in the right order. The top of the table is still unresolved — CHEMBL6167455 (0.016 nM, third by measurement) leads the docking by 0.50 kcal/mol over orforglipron, inside noise. The control's real finding is therefore twofold: the correct pocket improves both the magnitude (by 3–4 kcal/mol) and the ranking (rho 0.2 → 0.7), while the measured band (0.012–0.019 nM, 1.6-fold) remains too narrow for any fine ranking. A docking programme that uses the auto-picked structure will report orforglipron at −7.66 and its leads at −6 to −7, and will conclude these are weak binders; the same programme on the correct structure reports −10 to −11 and ranks them in an order that tracks measurement. The structure choice, not the molecule, decides whether the compound looks worth pursuing.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina docking score for orforglipron on 6XOX was found to compare against, and the paper does not invent one. The reference point is the structure itself: Kawai et al. 2020 resolved orforglipron bound in this pocket at 3.1 angstrom, and our re-dock places it at −10.80 with tightly grouped poses (−10.80, −10.52, −10.47), consistent with re-docking into its own co-crystal pocket. The honest comparator is the clinical one: orforglipron lowered HbA1c by up to 1.48 points and body weight by up to 7.6% in ACHIEVE-1, and by 11.2% in ATTAIN-1 — numbers no docking score can predict, because docking cannot model partial agonism or G-protein bias, the properties that define this drug.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say that orforglipron re-docks into its own pocket at −10.80 kcal/mol with tightly grouped poses, and that the ChEMBL lead CHEMBL6167455 scores −11.30 there — a candidate worth the cAMP assay, not a verdict. It can say that the auto-picked ECD structure under-prices every compound by 3–4 kcal/mol, and that the ranking mostly survives the pocket change (rho 0.8) while the winner does not. It cannot say which of the four leads is most potent — the measured band is 1.4-fold, and both structures fail that test — and it cannot say anything about efficacy: orforglipron is a partial agonist, biased toward G-protein activation, and a docking score is a fit, not a function. A compound that docks at −11.3 and signals like a full agonist would be a different drug from one that docks at −11.3 and signals like orforglipron, and this screen cannot tell them apart.

4.2 Why the pocket matters more than the score

The pipeline's structure picker is not broken — it did exactly what it was built to do: take the best-resolved X-ray structure with a drug-like ligand. The failure is in the assumption behind it, that the best-resolved X-ray structure is the right pocket. For GLP-1R it is not: the small-molecule pocket was solved by cryo-EM, at 3.1 angstrom, in a structure the X-ray-only picker excludes by design. The same failure mode will recur for every target whose ligand pocket was solved by cryo-EM first — and cryo-EM now solves most GPCR structures. The fix is small and specific: the picker should accept cryo-EM structures when no X-ray structure contains the ligand chemotype, and it should prefer the structure crystallised or resolved with a ligand of the same class as the query (small molecule with small molecule, peptide with peptide). Until that fix lands, every GLP-1R docking result from this pipeline must carry the 6XOX control, and any paper that reports only the 4ZGM numbers is under-pricing its compounds by 3–4 kcal/mol.

4.3 The danuglipron warning, and what docking cannot see

The class's cautionary tale is not a docking failure — it is a metabolism failure. Danuglipron reached phase 2b with dose-dependent weight loss, then Pfizer ended the programme in April 2025 after a case of potential drug-induced liver injury; lotiglipron was stopped earlier for liver findings. Nothing in a docking score predicts hepatic metabolism, and nothing in the PAINS filter or the Tox21 read-across panel used here models drug-induced liver injury with any reliability. A screening programme that ranks GLP-1R small molecules by docking alone and then advances the winner without a hepatotoxicity screen is repeating the exact mistake the class has already made twice. The validation design below therefore puts a liver read-out (primary human hepatocytes, ALT/AST release) in stage 1, before any efficacy assay — the order matters, because a compound that fails the liver screen should never reach the efficacy screen.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Pocket hypothesis. In a cAMP accumulation assay in GLP-1R-expressing cells, the 6XOX docking rank reproduces the measured EC50 rank of the docked set, and the 4ZGM rank does not. Falsified if the 4ZGM rank predicts the EC50 rank — in which case the ECD is, unexpectedly, a usable surrogate pocket.
  2. Bias hypothesis. Orforglipron shows G-protein-biased signalling (higher cAMP efficacy relative to beta-arrestin recruitment) versus the peptide GLP-1, reproducing the Kawai et al. 2020 finding. Falsified if the bias factor is ~1 — in which case the partial-agonist claim does not hold in this assay system.
  3. Liver hypothesis. The best-scoring ChEMBL lead shows no hepatotoxicity signal in primary human hepatocytes at 10x its GLP-1R EC50. Falsified if ALT/AST release rises at or below that concentration — in which case the lead is dropped regardless of its docking score, as danuglipron was.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): primary human hepatocyte screen of the docked set (ALT/AST release, 10x EC50) — the danuglipron gate, run first. Stage 2 (weeks 3–5): GLP-1R cAMP assay (HEK293-GLP-1R) for the survivors, with orforglipron as control; report EC50 with 95% CI and the bias factor versus beta-arrestin recruitment. Stage 3 (weeks 6–9): glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in human islets or INS-1 cells for the best two compounds. Stage 4 (weeks 10–12): selectivity panel against related class B GPCRs (GIPR, GCGR). Success criterion: the 6XOX rank, not the 4ZGM rank, predicts the cAMP rank, and the winner passes the liver gate.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this paper. Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) is larger than several of the gaps reported.
  2. The pipeline's auto-picked structure is the isolated extracellular domain; the 6XOX control is a cryo-EM structure at 3.1 angstrom, with the G protein and nanobody present in the deposited coordinates.
  3. Rigid docking cannot model biased signalling, partial agonism, or the primate-specific Trp33 interaction; no MD or free-energy refinement was run.
  4. Peptide agonists cannot be docked by this protocol, so the incumbent comparison is clinical, not computational.
  5. Measured potencies mix sources (ChEMBL bioactivities and literature EC50 values); assay conditions differ between sources.
  6. The Islamic canon sweep covers the available digitised canon relevant to the question (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025; Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi, c. 900); the full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and many classical Arabic manuscripts remain undigitised — the sweep names this gap rather than claiming completeness.
  7. No Pakistan-specific data on GLP-1RA prices, availability, or prescribing are reported here; the burden numbers are national estimates (IDF Diabetes Atlas 2025).

6. Conclusion

Orforglipron re-docks at −10.80 kcal/mol in its own GLP-1R pocket, but only −7.66 on the pipeline's auto-picked extracellular-domain structure — a 3.14 kcal/mol pocket effect that exceeds Vina's noise margin — and the ChEMBL lead CHEMBL6167455 out-scores orforglipron on the correct structure at −11.30. The two structures' rankings correlate only moderately (rho 0.8), the winner changes, and the correct pocket ranks the measured potencies better (rho 0.7 on 6XOX versus 0.2 on 4ZGM) within a 1.6-fold band no screen can resolve finely. Automated docking must use the cryo-EM pocket for small-molecule GLP-1R agonists, not the best-resolved X-ray structure — and the next step is a cAMP assay of the same set, with a liver screen first, because the class has already lost one drug to hepatotoxicity.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) and the provincial health departments, with the Ministry of National Health Services as the diagnostics funder. Decision: whether to prioritise (a) registration and price negotiation for an oral small-molecule GLP-1RA, or (b) a national diabetes detection programme first. Recommendation: fund detection first — 9.3 million Pakistanis have diabetes and do not know it, and a drug that requires a diagnosis is useless to the undiagnosed. Negotiate the oral GLP-1RA price in parallel, but do NOT add it to the public formulary until the detection programme reports a measured diagnosis rate, and require a liver-safety registry for any small-molecule GLP-1RA on the formulary, given danuglipron's fate. Falsifier / reversal: if the detection programme stalls (diagnosis rate unchanged after two years) or if the negotiated price exceeds the per-patient cost of the current metformin-plus-insulin pathway without a measured outcome gain, reverse the formulary recommendation and keep the drug in the private market only. The principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) with maslaha (public benefit) as the weighing rule, in the tradition of Ibn Sina's Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025), whose first book puts regimen — diet and manner of living — before drugs: a health system that buys the pill before it finds the patient has the order backwards.

Four Captopril Stereoisomers Dock Within 0.07 kcal/mol on VIM-2 While Their Measured Potencies Span 76-Fold: Rigid Docking Is Blind to the Stereochemistry That Defines MBL Inhibition

VIM-2 is a B1 metallo-beta-lactamase that hydrolyses almost all beta-lactams including carbapenems, and no clinically useful inhibitor exists for it.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-15 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #61 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: VIM-2; metallo-beta-lactamase; captopril; stereoisomers; taniborbactam; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; carbapenem resistance

Abstract

VIM-2 is a B1 metallo-beta-lactamase that hydrolyses almost all beta-lactams including carbapenems, and no clinically useful inhibitor exists for it. The best measured inhibitor in the reference set, taniborbactam (Ki 0.02 µM), cannot be docked by AutoDock Vina at all because it contains boron, which Vina's PDBQT parser rejects — a tool limit the standard pipeline run for this paper hit and could not pass. The testable question that remains is whether rigid docking can resolve the potency gap between stereoisomers of the same molecule: D-captopril inhibits VIM-2 at 0.072 µM, L-captopril at 4.4 µM, and the two epi-isomers at 5.5 µM each, a 76-fold range from a single stereocentre flip, with crystal structures showing different binding modes. We docked all four stereoisomers with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on 4C1E, the 1.40 angstrom VIM-2 structure co-crystallised with D-captopril. The scores are minus 6.16, minus 6.19, minus 6.12 and minus 6.19 kcal/mol — a total span of 0.07 kcal/mol, thirty times smaller than Vina noise, with rank correlation against measured potency of 0.15. The screen cannot see the stereochemistry that defines this inhibition. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay IC50 comparison of the four stereoisomers on VIM-2 with a metal-aware rescoring of the same poses: if the measured 76-fold gap reproduces while every rescoring still ties them, the failure is confirmed as a scoring-function limit, not a pose-sampling error.

1. Introduction

Metallo-beta-lactamases (MBLs) are zinc-dependent enzymes that hydrolyse almost all beta-lactam antibiotics, including the latest cephalosporins and carbapenems, and no clinically useful MBL inhibitor exists. The B1 subclass — NDM, VIM and IMP types — is the most clinically relevant, and VIM-2, first described in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, is among the most widely disseminated: VIM-type enzymes are prevalent in India and across Asia, and NDM- and VIM-producing Enterobacterales are a documented and growing problem in Pakistan, where carbapenem resistance limits therapeutic options. A November 2026 review in ACS Infectious Diseases (PMID 43023851) audited exactly why computational prediction keeps failing on B1 MBL inhibitor discovery — the pitfalls this paper tests one by one. The clinical stakes are set by the newest boronate inhibitors: taniborbactam inhibits VIM-2 with a Ki of 0.02 µM and NDM-1 with 0.08 µM (Le Terrier et al. 2024), and cefepime-taniborbactam has shown efficacy in complicated urinary tract infection, but taniborbactam does not inhibit IMP-type enzymes, where xeruborbactam is the current hope — and IMP variants resistant even to xeruborbactam are already reported (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2025;69:e00297-25).

Captopril, the antihypertensive ACE inhibitor, is the cleanest test case in this field. Its thiol chelates the two active-site zinc ions, and its four stereoisomers inhibit VIM-2 across a 76-fold range in a single assay (Brem et al. 2016): D-captopril 0.072 µM, L-captopril 4.4 µM, epi-D- and epi-L-captopril 5.5 µM each. The crystal structures show why: D-captopril's carboxylate forms an electrostatic interaction with the conserved Arg228 at 2.9 angstrom, while L-captopril's carboxylate points away from Arg228 and interacts with Asn233 instead, and the L3 loop closes differently around the two. The binding modes are visibly different; the question is whether a docking score can see the difference. A screen that cannot distinguish stereoisomers cannot rank MBL inhibitors at all, because stereochemistry is where the potency lives in this chemotype.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol on the D-captopril co-crystal structure, docking rank will track the measured VIM-2 ranking (D first, the epi-isomers last), with D-captopril separated from L-captopril by more than Vina noise. Falsified if all four stereoisomers score within 0.1 kcal/mol of each other, in which case rigid docking is confirmed blind to the stereochemistry that defines MBL inhibition.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-15 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-14, which screened 722 candidates and selected 8 — item 3, the ACS Infectious Diseases audit of computational prediction on B1 MBLs (PMID 43023851), is directly on this topic). Key sources: Brem et al. 2016 (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 60:142–150, PMID 26482303, PMCID PMC4704194) for all measured IC50s, the MIC data and structures 4C1E/4C1D; Le Terrier et al. 2024 (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 68:e00991-23, doi:10.1128/aac.00991-23) for the taniborbactam Ki values; Silwal et al. 2025 (J Inorg Biochem 271:112975, PMID 40513263) for the VIM-20/VIM-31/VIM-15 structures and the D-captopril potency pattern; the 2026 Bioorganic Chemistry review of zinc-binding MBL inhibitors (doi:10.1016/j.bioorg.2026.110576); and Thomas et al. 2020 (J Inorg Biochem 210:111123, PMID 32622213) for the inhibition mechanisms of thiol MBL inhibitors including ANT431. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Pipeline failure and correction

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Verona integron-encoded metallo-beta-lactamase 2 (VIM-2)" and reference drug taniborbactam (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). It failed, and its numbers are DISCARDED (kept in hidden_files/dock-HP-064-2026-11-15.json for audit only). The ChEMBL target CHEMBL1255147 returned zero bioactivities, so the only "lead" was the query itself; and the single docking attempt failed because taniborbactam contains boron and Vina's PDBQT parser rejects it ("Atom type B is not a valid AutoDock type"). Boronates cannot be docked by this protocol at all. The pipeline's structure pick, 9CV3, is also wrong for the question: it is VIM-20 (a VIM-2-like variant from Enterobacter cloacae) with L-captopril, not VIM-2 itself.

The correction (documented fallback, HP-027 precedent; script health-papers-agent/dock_vim2_4c1e_correction.py) uses structure 4C1E — VIM-2 from Pseudomonas aeruginosa in complex with D-captopril, 1.40 angstrom (Brem et al. 2016) — with the centre from D._ligand_center, the centroid of the co-crystallised D-captopril. The centre [75.98, 6.89, 58.12] was audited: the two catalytic zinc ions sit 5.41 and 4.28 angstrom from the centre, with a Zn–Zn distance of 3.71 angstrom, matching the 3.7 angstrom reported on inhibitor binding. The four stereoisomers' SMILES were built by stereocentre inversion from the PubChem-verified L-captopril structure and checked by RDKit CIP assignment — D = (2S,2R), L = (2S,2S), epi-D = (2R,2R), epi-L = (2R,2S) — and each was confirmed against PubChem by isomeric-SMILES lookup (D: CID 447055; L: CID 44093; epi-D: CID 446549; epi-L: CID 688267, "Epicaptopril"). All four share the formula C9H15NO3S.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; one box (22.5 angstrom) and exhaustiveness 8 for every compound; best of three poses reported. Four compounds on 4C1E: D-captopril (re-dock control on its own structure), L-captopril, epi-D-captopril and epi-L-captopril. Taniborbactam was NOT docked (boron — see Section 2.2) and is carried as the measured reference only: Ki 0.02 µM against VIM-2 (Le Terrier et al. 2024). Measured potencies are all VIM-2 IC50s from Brem et al. 2016 Table 1 (same assay, same paper): D 0.072 µM; L 4.4 µM; epi-D 5.5 µM; epi-L 5.5 µM. A metal-aware caveat applies to every score here: Vina treats the two zinc ions as static point charges and cannot price thiol–zinc coordination, which is the dominant interaction for this chemotype.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All four are PAINS-clean. All four pass Lipinski and Veber outright (MW 217.29, logP 0.92, TPSA 83.90 for each — the stereoisomers share all descriptors except the stereochemistry).

2.5 Rank correlation

Spearman rank correlation was computed between the Vina scores and the measured VIM-2 IC50 values for the four stereoisomers (n = 4). The two tied measured values (5.5 µM, twice) and the two tied docking values (−6.19, twice) were assigned average ranks. A correlation on four points is reported as a descriptive check, not as a validated ranking — the paper's real test is the size of the docking span against the size of the potency span.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the entire docking span in this study (0.07 kcal/mol) is thirty times smaller than that. Vina cannot price thiol–zinc coordination or the carboxylate–Arg228 interaction that the crystal structures show distinguishing D- from L-captopril. D-captopril's score is a re-dock on its own co-crystal structure (4C1E). No molecular dynamics, covalent or metal-aware docking, or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed. The MIC data quoted are from Brem et al. 2016 and were not reproduced here.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured VIM-2 IC50 Vina on 4C1E (kcal/mol) PAINS
D-captopril (reference) 0.072 µM −6.16 (−6.16, −6.06, −5.95) clean
L-captopril 4.4 µM −6.19 (−6.19, −6.03, −5.94) clean
epi-D-captopril 5.5 µM −6.12 (−6.12, −6.05, −5.95) clean
epi-L-captopril 5.5 µM −6.19 (−6.19, −6.06, −5.88) clean
Taniborbactam (measured reference, not docked) Ki 0.02 µM — (boron; Vina rejects atom type B) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). Measured IC50s are VIM-2 values from Brem et al. 2016 Table 1; taniborbactam Ki from Le Terrier et al. 2024. "—" means not docked.

The four stereoisomers span 0.07 kcal/mol in docking — D −6.16, L −6.19, epi-D −6.12, epi-L −6.19 — against a 76-fold span in measured potency (0.072 to 5.5 µM). The most potent compound measured (D-captopril) does not even rank first by docking; it ranks third, behind two compounds 61- and 76-fold weaker. The docking span is not merely inside Vina noise: it is thirty times smaller than Vina noise. The screen is not noisy on this question. It is silent.

3.2 Rank correlation: none

Against the measured VIM-2 IC50s, Spearman rho is 0.15 (n = 4) — no correlation. The value is meaningless at this sample size, but its direction is not the point; the point is the span. A screening tool that returns the same number for four compounds whose potencies differ 76-fold has no discriminating power on this chemotype, whatever the correlation coefficient.

3.3 The crystal structures say what the scores cannot

The difference between D- and L-captopril is visible in the structures and invisible in the scores. In 4C1E (D-captopril, 1.40 angstrom) the carboxylate sits 2.9 angstrom from the conserved Arg228, the residue that binds the beta-lactam substrate carboxylate; in 4C1D (L-captopril, 1.20 angstrom) the carboxylate points away from Arg228 and interacts with Asn233 instead, and the L3 loop closes differently around the hydrophobic face. The thiol bridges both zinc ions in both structures. Vina's scoring function prices none of this: the zinc ions are static charges, the thiol–zinc bond is not a term, and the carboxylate–arginine salt bridge is worth the same in either orientation at this resolution of scoring. The structures are the ground truth here, and they contradict the scores — which is why the paper reports the structures as the finding and the scores as the failure.

3.4 The boronate gap

Taniborbactam, the most potent measured inhibitor in the reference set (Ki 0.02 µM, 3.6-fold more potent than D-captopril), cannot be docked by this protocol at all: Vina rejects the boron atom type. The same applies to xeruborbactam and every other boronate in the MBL pipeline. A screening programme built on Vina therefore cannot rank the single most important chemotype in current MBL inhibitor development. That is a tooling limit, not a scientific result, and it is stated here so that no future run silently drops the boronates and reports a ranking of everything else as if it were complete.

3.5 ADMET and safety panel

All four stereoisomers share identical descriptors (MW 217.29, logP 0.92, TPSA 83.90) and are PAINS-clean; they differ only in stereochemistry, which is the point. The safety story that matters is not in any panel: captopril is a clinically used antihypertensive, and the concentrations needed for MBL inhibition in vitro exceed the maximum used in treatment — a 2026 repurposing study (FEMS Microbiol Lett 2026;373:fnag064) concluded the repurposing objective could not be achieved for L-captopril on pharmacological grounds, while still reporting that imipenem and meropenem activity was restored for more than 80% and 60% of Enterobacterales strains respectively at 400 mg/L. The stereoisomers are research tools for the binding-mode question, not drug candidates.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say nothing about the relative potency of captopril stereoisomers on VIM-2. It cannot say that D-captopril is the best of the four — the measured record says that, and the screen ranks it third. It cannot say that the epi-isomers are equivalent to L-captopril — the measured record says they are (5.5 vs 4.4 µM), and the screen agrees by accident, returning the same number for all four. A paper that reported "all four stereoisomers dock at −6.1 to −6.2 and are therefore equivalent leads" would be reporting the screen's blindness as a finding. The honest conclusion is narrower and more useful: rigid docking with a static-zinc model has no discriminating power for thiol MBL inhibitors, and any ranking it produces on this chemotype should be discarded.

4.2 The metal-aware correction

The correct computational test for this chemotype prices the metal: a metal-aware docking protocol (with zinc coordination restraints or a metal-specific scoring term), or a free-energy comparison that includes the thiol–zinc interaction, or a QM/MM refinement of the docked poses. The crystal structures already exist for D- and L-captopril on VIM-2 (4C1E/4C1D), so the correction can be validated against known binding modes rather than against scores. The assay is the decisive step, because it also answers the question the docking cannot ask: whether the 76-fold gap is driven by the Arg228 interaction, the L3-loop closure, or the zinc geometry — the structures suggest all three, and only a designed experiment separates them.

4.3 Why this matters beyond VIM-2

The failure generalises. Any target whose binding is dominated by a metal interaction — MBLs, histone deacetylases, carbonic anhydrases, matrix metalloproteinases — will show the same pattern: a standard rigid-docking screen returning near-identical scores for compounds whose measured potencies differ by orders of magnitude, because the scorer cannot see the interaction that matters. The VIM-2 stereoisomer set is the cleanest demonstration available, because the four compounds are identical in every descriptor except stereochemistry, so there is no confounder to blame. Any screening programme that ranks metal-binding compounds on one Vina scale should first run this control: four stereoisomers, one target, known potencies. If the screen ties them, the screen is not measuring what it claims to measure.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Metal-aware hypothesis. Re-scoring the same four docked poses with a metal-aware protocol (zinc coordination restraints) restores the measured ranking (D first, epi-isomers last, with D separated from L by more than 1 kcal/mol). Falsified if the metal-aware scores still tie all four within 0.1 kcal/mol — in which case the failure is in pose sampling, not scoring.
  2. Arg228 hypothesis. A VIM-2 Arg228Ala mutant weakens D-captopril's IC50 by more than 10-fold while weakening L-captopril's by less than 3-fold. Falsified if both weaken equally — in which case the Arg228 interaction is not the driver of the 76-fold gap.
  3. Boronate hypothesis. A boron-capable docking protocol (e.g. a covalent or boron-parameterised scorer) docks taniborbactam on 4C1E with a score better than D-captopril's −6.16, matching its measured Ki advantage (0.02 vs 0.072 µM). Falsified if taniborbactam still scores worse — in which case the boronate's potency, like the thiol's, is invisible to docking.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain the four captopril stereoisomers and taniborbactam; confirm identity, stereochemistry and purity by LC-MS, NMR and chiral HPLC. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): IC50 assay on recombinant VIM-2 (nitrocefin hydrolysis), all five compounds on the same plates, in triplicate — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make, and the direct test of the 76-fold gap. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): metal-aware re-scoring of the docked poses for hypothesis 1, plus the Arg228Ala mutant assay for hypothesis 2. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if the metal-aware rescoring restores the ranking, apply it to a small library of thiol MBL inhibitors and synthesise the best two; if it does not, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency claim; the D-versus-L comparison needs the same, because a false "equivalent" call on a 61-fold gap is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Vina cannot price thiol–zinc coordination or the carboxylate–Arg228 salt bridge; the 0.07 kcal/mol span is the finding, not a defect to be averaged away.
  3. D-captopril's score is a re-dock on its own co-crystal structure (4C1E); the other three are cross-docked into a pocket shaped for D-captopril.
  4. The measured IC50s come from one paper (Brem et al. 2016) and were not re-measured on one plate here; the 0.072 µM value is at the sensitive end of the nitrocefin assay.
  5. Spearman rho is computed on four points with two ties; it is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking.
  6. Taniborbactam was not docked (boron); its Ki is quoted from Le Terrier et al. 2024, a different assay from Brem et al. 2016, so the 3.6-fold advantage over D-captopril is cross-assay.
  7. No molecular dynamics, metal-aware docking, or free-energy refinement was run — the methods that could actually price the zinc interaction.
  8. The 9CV3 (VIM-20) structure was not used; VIM-20 differs from VIM-2 by an active-site-adjacent residue, and the paper does not claim its results transfer to VIM-20.
  9. The captopril stereoisomers are research tools, not drug candidates; the concentrations needed for MBL inhibition exceed clinical use.
  10. No Pakistan-specific VIM-2 prevalence numbers are cited; the paper's relevance to Pakistan is the resistance context (NDM/VIM-producing Enterobacterales) and the methodological warning for local screening programmes.

6. Conclusion

On 4C1E, four captopril stereoisomers dock at −6.16, −6.19, −6.12 and −6.19 kcal/mol — a span of 0.07 kcal/mol, thirty times smaller than Vina noise — while their measured VIM-2 IC50s span 76-fold (0.072 to 5.5 µM), and the most potent measured inhibitor in the reference set, taniborbactam (Ki 0.02 µM), cannot be docked at all because Vina rejects boron. The screen is blind to the stereochemistry that defines MBL inhibition and to the chemotype that defines its future. The next step is the single-assay IC50 comparison in Section 4.5, with metal-aware rescoring of the same poses — and, as a standing rule, no docking screen on a metalloenzyme is trusted until it has passed the stereoisomer control: four stereoisomers, one target, known potencies, and a spread in the scores that matches the spread in the measurements.

Nintedanib Tops a PknB Docking Rank That Matches Measured Potency Exactly: Two Approved Cancer Kinase Inhibitors and the Mitoxantrone Caveat

PknB is an essential serine/threonine kinase of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and no PknB inhibitor has reached the clinic: the best published inhibitors are nanomolar in vitro and only micromolar against whole cells.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-15 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #62 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PknB; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; nintedanib; sunitinib; mitoxantrone; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; kinase inhibitor repurposing

Abstract

PknB is an essential serine/threonine kinase of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and no PknB inhibitor has reached the clinic: the best published inhibitors are nanomolar in vitro and only micromolar against whole cells. We docked five compounds with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on 3ORK, the 1.60 angstrom structure of the PknB kinase domain (L33D mutant) with an ATP-gamma-S analogue in the ATP site: nintedanib, two matched-pair aminopyrimidine/pyrazole inhibitors from the same series, sunitinib, and mitoxantrone, the literature PknB inhibitor. The docking rank matches the measured potency rank exactly (Spearman rho 1.0, n = 4): nintedanib, Kd 3.6 nM, docks at minus 9.70 kcal/mol; the matched pair, Ki 13 and 17 nM, at minus 8.66 and minus 8.30; sunitinib, Kd 87 nM, at minus 8.24. Mitoxantrone, which has no attached PknB potency number and is excluded from the correlation, docks worst at minus 7.19 and carries a PAINS alert with the maximum Tox21 read-across for the DNA-damage assays SR-ATAD5 and SR-p53. Two approved cancer kinase inhibitors top a tuberculosis kinase ranking, and the literature inhibitor is the weakest and the most toxic — a clean repurposing signal and a warning in the same table. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay PknB kinase comparison of the four ranked compounds with a whole-cell assay on Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv: if nintedanib again measures most potent on the enzyme but fails on whole cells, the gap is confirmed as permeability, not potency.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis killed more people than any other single infectious disease in 2024, and about 390,000 multidrug-resistant/rifampicin-resistant cases were estimated for that year (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025). The pipeline of new tuberculosis drugs is thin, and repurposing approved kinase inhibitors is one of the few routes that can move fast, because the safety data already exist. PknB is the most attractive kinase target in Mycobacterium tuberculosis: it is essential for survival, it regulates cell growth, cell shape and cell division through substrates including GarA, GlmU and EmbR, and it phosphorylates the proteasome alpha-subunit PrcA. Its sibling kinases PknA and PknB are essential, while PknG drives virulence and persistence — which is why multitarget PknA/B/G inhibition is the current design goal, and why a 2026 study reported structural insights into multitargeting the Pkn kinases (Pollaniemi et al., Microbiol Spectr 2026;14:e0004926).

The history of PknB inhibitor discovery is a cautionary tale. A screen of more than 50,000 compounds found ATP-competitive inhibitors that were nanomolar in vitro but only micromolar against whole cells, and none prevented mycobacterial growth at submicromolar concentrations (Lougheed et al., Tuberculosis 2011;91:277–286, PMID 21482481). Mitoxantrone was identified in 2006 as a PknB inhibitor capable of preventing mycobacterial growth (Wehenkel et al., FEBS Lett 2006;580:3018–3022, PMID 16674948), with a co-crystal structure (2FUM) — but mitoxantrone is a DNA intercalator with well-known cardiotoxicity, and no potency number was ever attached to its PknB inhibition in that paper. The question this paper tests is whether a standard rigid-docking screen can rank PknB inhibitors at all, and whether the approved cancer kinase inhibitors nintedanib and sunitinib — both in the ChEMBL bioactivity record for PknB — are worth carrying forward.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol on the 3ORK ATP site, docking rank will track the measured PknB potency rank (nintedanib first, sunitinib last), and mitoxantrone will score worst, because it is the literature inhibitor with the weakest evidence. Falsified if the docking rank disagrees with the measured rank on any pair, or if mitoxantrone scores within Vina noise of the best compound.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-15 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-14, which screened 722 candidates and selected 8 — none on PknB, so the digest's relevance here is methodological). Key sources: Lombana et al. 2010 (Structure 18:1667–1677) for the 3ORK structure; Wehenkel et al. 2006 (FEBS Lett 580:3018–3022, PMID 16674948, doi:10.1016/j.febslet.2006.04.046) for mitoxantrone as a PknB inhibitor and structure 2FUM; Lougheed et al. 2011 (Tuberculosis 91:277–286, PMID 21482481, PMCID PMC3158675) for the 50,000-compound screen; Pollaniemi et al. 2026 (Microbiol Spectr 14:e0004926, PMID 42446239) for the multitarget Pkn-kinase structural work; the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 for the 2024 MDR/RR-TB case estimate; and the 2025 SSRN in-silico PknB screen (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5954835) for the recent computational context. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Computation

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Mycobacterium tuberculosis serine/threonine protein kinase B (PknB)" and reference drug mitoxantrone (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). Unlike the KRAS and VIM-2 topics, this run was clean: UniProt P9WI81 (PknB, gene pknB, M. tuberculosis H37Rv, 626 amino acids) resolved to ChEMBL target CHEMBL1908385 (Serine/threonine-protein kinase PknB), which returned 57 bioactivities and 26 leads. The structure is 3ORK, 1.60 angstrom — the PknB kinase domain L33D mutant (crystal form 2) with the ATP-gamma-S analogue AGS in the ATP site (Lombana et al. 2010) — with the centre [13.05, 14.71, 12.04] from D._ligand_center, the centroid of the AGS analogue. The L33D mutation must be stated: every score in this paper is on the mutant kinase domain, not the wild type.

Five compounds were docked with the standardised protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, one box (22.5 angstrom), exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported. The four measured compounds: nintedanib (CHEMBL502835; approved 2014), CHEMBL4177445, CHEMBL4172982 and sunitinib (CHEMBL535; approved 2006). Their measured potencies are the ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL1908385: nintedanib Kd 3.6 nM; CHEMBL4177445 Ki 13 nM; CHEMBL4172982 Ki 17 nM; sunitinib Kd 87 nM. The two ChEMBL identifiers are a matched pair from one aminopyrimidine/pyrazole series — both MW 390.86, logP 2.79, TPSA 126.65, a 5-cyclopropyl-pyrazol-3-ylamino pyrimidine core, differing only in the sulfonamide phenyl substitution (meta vs para). Mitoxantrone (the query compound, PubChem-verified) carries no measured PknB potency number — Wehenkel et al. 2006 report it qualitatively as a PknB inhibitor that prevents mycobacterial growth — so it is excluded from the rank correlation and reported qualitatively.

2.3 PAINS and safety panel

RDKit PAINS filter and the ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) were applied to every compound. Four of the five are PAINS-clean; mitoxantrone carries a PAINS alert and fails Veber (TPSA 163.18, 12 rotatable bonds, 8 hydrogen-bond donors). Its Tox21 panel is in "measured" mode (maximum similarity 1.0 — the compound is in the Tox21 set) with the maximum values 1.0 for SR-ATAD5 and SR-p53, the two DNA-damage assays. Nintedanib and sunitinib show no decisive Tox21 signal (highest single values 0.239 for sunitinib NR-AhR and 0.084 for nintedanib SR-ARE).

2.4 Rank correlation

Spearman rank correlation was computed between the Vina scores and the measured PknB potencies for the four measured compounds (n = 4). The correlation mixes Kd and Ki values — two nintedanib/sunitinib Kd values against two matched-pair Ki values — which is stated here and in the Limitations rather than hidden. A correlation on four points is reported as a descriptive check, not as a validated ranking — the paper's real tests are the matched pair and the mitoxantrone negative control.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the gap between the first and last measured compounds (1.46 kcal/mol) is inside that noise, so the correlation is a rank match, not a magnitude match. The structure is the L33D mutant. The measured potencies mix Kd and Ki from the ChEMBL record, and the two matched-pair Ki values come from the same series while the two Kd values do not. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed, and no whole-cell data are reported here.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured PknB potency Vina on 3ORK (kcal/mol) PAINS
Nintedanib (CHEMBL502835) Kd 3.6 nM −9.70 (−9.70, −8.89, −8.72) clean
CHEMBL4177445 Ki 13 nM −8.66 (−8.66, −8.12, −7.77) clean
CHEMBL4172982 Ki 17 nM −8.30 (−8.30, −8.27, −8.16) clean
Sunitinib (CHEMBL535) Kd 87 nM −8.24 (−8.24, −7.94, −7.94) clean
Mitoxantrone (query) no PknB potency number −7.19 (−7.19, −7.14, −6.92) alert

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). Measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL1908385. Mitoxantrone is excluded from the rank correlation.

The ranking is exact. Nintedanib is first by 1.04 kcal/mol over the matched pair, and the matched pair is ordered correctly (13 nM before 17 nM, by 0.36 kcal/mol), and sunitinib is last among the measured compounds by 0.06 kcal/mol behind CHEMBL4172982 — a gap that is nothing, and which the paper does not pretend is a difference. Mitoxantrone, the literature inhibitor, docks worst at −7.19, a full 2.51 kcal/mol behind nintedanib.

3.2 Rank correlation: perfect, and carried by the extremes

Against the measured potencies, Spearman rho is 1.0 (n = 4). The value is carried by nintedanib sitting first and sunitinib sitting last in both rankings; the middle pair is ordered correctly but separated by only 0.36 kcal/mol in docking against a 1.3-fold measured gap. A correlation of 1.0 on four points, with the bottom two separated by nothing, is not a validated ranking — it is a screen that got the order right and cannot separate the bottom two. The honest reading is the same as in Paper #60 (KRAS G12D): the extremes are reliable, the middle is not.

3.3 The matched pair: the screen's sharpest test

CHEMBL4177445 and CHEMBL4172982 are the same molecule except for the sulfonamide phenyl substitution — meta in one, para in the other — with identical molecular weight (390.86), logP (2.79) and TPSA (126.65), and measured Ki values of 13 and 17 nM. Docking separates them by 0.36 kcal/mol, in the right direction. That is a real discrimination, but it is a small one: 0.36 kcal/mol is well inside Vina noise, and the 1.3-fold measured gap is itself within assay noise. The pair shows the screen can order a matched pair correctly; it does not show the screen can measure the gap. A screening programme that used the 0.36 kcal/mol difference to choose between them would be choosing on noise.

3.4 Mitoxantrone: the literature inhibitor that should not be the lead

Mitoxantrone is the only compound in this set with published evidence of preventing mycobacterial growth (Wehenkel et al. 2006), and it is the weakest by docking (−7.19), the only one with a PAINS alert, the only one that fails Veber, and the only one with maximum Tox21 values on the DNA-damage assays (SR-ATAD5 1.0, SR-p53 1.0 — measured, not read-across). The Tox21 values are consistent with its mechanism: mitoxantrone is a DNA intercalator, and its cardiotoxicity is well documented in its clinical use. The paper's conclusion is not that mitoxantrone does not inhibit PknB — Wehenkel et al. showed that it does, and structure 2FUM shows it in the ATP site. The conclusion is that it is a poor drug candidate for tuberculosis, and that a screen which ranks it last is ranking it correctly on the property that matters for a lead: it should not be the starting point.

3.5 ADMET and safety panel

Nintedanib (MW 539.64, logP 3.62, one Lipinski violation by molecular weight) and sunitinib (MW 398.48, logP 3.33, no violations) are both approved drugs with established human safety profiles — that is the point of repurposing them. The matched pair passes Lipinski and Veber outright. No decisive Tox21 signal appears for any of the four measured compounds. The safety story that matters is the one in Section 3.4: the literature inhibitor is the toxic one, and the approved drugs are the clean ones.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say that nintedanib is the best PknB binder in this set, by both measurement and docking, and that sunitinib is the weakest of the measured four, by both. It can say that the matched pair is ordered correctly. It cannot say that CHEMBL4172982 is worse than sunitinib — the 0.06 kcal/mol gap is nothing, and the measured gap (17 vs 87 nM, 5-fold) is real but invisible to the screen at this resolution. And it cannot say anything about mitoxantrone's potency, because there is no measured number to compare against; it can only say that mitoxantrone is the worst by docking and the most toxic by every other measure, which is a reason to stop, not a reason to test it first.

4.2 Why this is the clean win of the day

Papers #60 and #61 in this run are both docking failures — a rank inversion on KRAS G12D and a total blindness on VIM-2. This paper is the control that shows the same protocol can work: same Vina version, same box, same exhaustiveness, same PAINS and Tox21 panels, and the ranking comes out exact. The difference is the target, not the method: PknB's ATP site is a well-formed kinase pocket with a hydrophobic back pocket and a hinge, the kind of site rigid docking was built for, while VIM-2's zinc site and KRAS's switch-II pocket are the kinds it was not. The lesson is not that docking works or that it does not — it is that it works on some targets and fails on others, and the only way to know which is to run the control: a set of compounds with known potencies, ranked before the screen is trusted.

4.3 The repurposing question

Nintedanib and sunitinib are approved cancer drugs with known human pharmacokinetics. Nintedanib's Kd of 3.6 nM on PknB is the strongest measured value in this set, and its docking score of −9.70 is the best by more than a kilocalorie. The next step is not more docking — it is the enzyme assay and the whole-cell assay, because the 2011 screen's lesson is that nanomolar in vitro potency does not survive the mycobacterial cell wall. If nintedanib measures nanomolar on the enzyme and micromolar on whole cells, the project becomes a permeability problem, and the matched pair — smaller (MW 390.86) and more polar (TPSA 126.65) — is the more promising starting point for optimisation. If nintedanib fails on the enzyme, the docking rank is a false positive and the paper's conclusion is revised.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Enzyme hypothesis. In a single-assay PknB kinase comparison, nintedanib again measures most potent (IC50 below 10 nM) and sunitinib least potent (above 50 nM), with the matched pair between them. Falsified if any compound measures more than 5-fold from its ChEMBL value — in which case the ChEMBL record, not the screen, is the problem.
  2. Whole-cell hypothesis. Nintedanib's MIC against M. tuberculosis H37Rv is above 10 µM despite nanomolar enzyme potency, reproducing the 2011 pattern. Falsified if the MIC is below 1 µM — in which case nintedanib is a genuine repurposing candidate and the permeability problem does not apply to it.
  3. Mitoxantrone hypothesis. Mitoxantrone's PknB IC50, when measured, is above 1 µM — the weakest in the set, matching its docking rank. Falsified if it measures below 100 nM — in which case the docking rank is wrong and the literature inhibitor deserves a second look.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain nintedanib, sunitinib, the matched pair and mitoxantrone; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): PknB kinase assay (recombinant PknB, ATP-competitive format), all five compounds on the same plates, in triplicate — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make, and the direct test of hypothesis 1 and 3. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): MIC assay on M. tuberculosis H37Rv for the four measured compounds, plus cytotoxicity on a human cell line — the direct test of hypothesis 2 and the safety gate for any repurposing claim. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if any compound shows an MIC below 1 µM with a selectivity index above 10, dock its analogues and synthesise the best two; if all four are above 10 µM on whole cells, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 and per MIC determination is the minimum for a defensible potency claim; the nintedanib-versus-sunitinib comparison needs the same, because a false "nintedanib is best" call on a rank match is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. The structure is the L33D mutant kinase domain (3ORK); wild-type PknB may score differently, and the paper does not claim the ranking transfers to the wild type.
  3. The measured potencies mix Kd (nintedanib, sunitinib) and Ki (matched pair) from the ChEMBL record; the correlation treats them as one ranking, which is a stated approximation.
  4. Spearman rho is computed on four points; it is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking, and the bottom two compounds are separated by 0.06 kcal/mol — nothing.
  5. Mitoxantrone carries no measured PknB potency number and is excluded from the correlation; its docking rank is a hypothesis, not a result.
  6. No molecular dynamics, flexible-side-chain docking, or free-energy refinement was run.
  7. The 2011 screen's whole-cell data are quoted from the literature, not reproduced here; the permeability gap is a hypothesis, not a measurement in this paper.
  8. Nintedanib and sunitinib are approved for cancer, not for tuberculosis; repurposing requires the whole-cell and safety data in Section 4.5, and no clinical claim is made.
  9. No Pakistan-specific TB burden or PknB prevalence numbers are cited beyond the global MDR-TB count; the paper's relevance to Pakistan is the tuberculosis burden and the repurposing logic — approved drugs are the fastest route a resource-limited setting has.

6. Conclusion

On 3ORK, nintedanib docks at −9.70 kcal/mol against a measured Kd of 3.6 nM, the matched pair at −8.66 and −8.30 against Ki values of 13 and 17 nM, and sunitinib at −8.24 against a Kd of 87 nM — a docking rank that matches the measured rank exactly (Spearman rho 1.0, n = 4), while mitoxantrone, the literature PknB inhibitor, docks worst at −7.19 with a PAINS alert and maximum Tox21 values on the DNA-damage assays. Two approved cancer kinase inhibitors top a tuberculosis kinase ranking, and the literature inhibitor is the weakest and the most toxic. The next step is the single-assay kinase and whole-cell comparison in Section 4.5 — and, as a standing rule, the control that makes this paper trustworthy is the one Papers #60 and #61 lacked a clean result from: a set of compounds with known potencies, ranked before the screen is trusted.
