CH7233163 Re-Docks Best and Osimertinib Near Worst on Triple-Mutant EGFR (6LUB): a Directional Signal, Not a Ranking

Third-generation osimertinib is the standard first-line therapy for EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer, but the C797S mutation removes the cysteine its covalent warhead needs, and no fourth-generation inhibitor is yet approved.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-13 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #54 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: EGFR; C797S; osimertinib; CH7233163; non-small-cell lung cancer; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; fourth-generation EGFR inhibitor

Abstract

Third-generation osimertinib is the standard first-line therapy for EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer, but the C797S mutation removes the cysteine its covalent warhead needs, and no fourth-generation inhibitor is yet approved. The question is whether a standard docking screen can separate a genuine fourth-generation binder from the failed drug on the triple-mutant kinase. We docked ten compounds into the triple-mutant structure 6LUB (EGFR L858R/T790M/C797S, 2.315 angstrom) with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under one protocol: the fourth-generation tool compound CH7233163, osimertinib, gefitinib, afatinib, brigatinib and five PubChem analogues of osimertinib. The co-crystallised ligand CH7233163 re-docked best at minus 9.53 kcal/mol, 1.38 clear of the next compound, while osimertinib scored minus 7.50 and gefitinib minus 7.27, the weakest in the set. The direction matches the measured record: CH7233163 inhibits the triple mutant at 0.28 nM biochemically and 20 nM in cells, whereas osimertinib needs 1.42 micromolar to stop triple-mutant BaF3 cells. But only two compounds in the set carry measured triple-mutant potencies on any assay, and those two were measured in different assay types, so no rank correlation can be computed and the five analogues, scoring minus 7.27 to minus 8.01, carry no measured potency at all. The screen is therefore a directional signal, not a ranking, and the re-dock of a co-crystallised ligand is expected to score well because the pocket is shaped around it. The falsifiable next step is a kinase assay of CH7233163, brigatinib and the best analogue, PubChem 121280087, against osimertinib on L858R/T790M/C797S EGFR in one assay: if CH7233163 is the most potent and osimertinib the least, the directional signal holds; if any analogue beats brigatinib, it becomes the lead for a fourth-generation series.

1. Introduction

EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the disease where targeted therapy has advanced furthest, and where resistance has kept pace with it. First-generation inhibitors (gefitinib, erlotinib) fail on the T790M gatekeeper mutation; third-generation osimertinib was designed around T790M and is now the standard first-line therapy, but its covalent warhead needs Cys797, and the C797S mutation removes that anchor. Once C797S appears on top of L858R or an exon-19 deletion plus T790M, osimertinib loses its mechanism, and no fourth-generation inhibitor is approved. The compounds chasing the triple mutant are tool compounds and early clinical candidates — CH7233163, a non-covalent ATP-competitive inhibitor, is the best characterised, with a biochemical IC50 of 0.28 nM against the Del19/T790M/C797S kinase and a cellular IC50 of 20 nM in triple-mutant NIH3T3 cells against 1,200 nM in wild-type A431 cells, a 60-fold selectivity window.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen on the triple-mutant structure will rank a genuine fourth-generation binder above osimertinib, in the same direction as the measured potencies. The test is the direction, not a correlation — only two compounds in the set carry measured triple-mutant potencies, and they were measured in different assay types, so a correlation coefficient would be meaningless. The reference drug must itself dock, or the comparison is void.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-13 (web search; PubMed via the daily digest of 2026-11-13, which screened 627 candidates and selected 8, none on EGFR — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: Kashima et al. 2020 for CH7233163 and the 6LUB structure; Xi et al. 2023 for the osimertinib BaF3 potencies on the triple mutant; Lategahn et al. 2019 for the double-mutant osimertinib and gefitinib HTRF values; Suzuki et al. 2024 for brigatinib bound to T790M/C797S (8H7X); and a 2025 fourth-generation review for the C797S landscape. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented). One correction is recorded here rather than hidden: an early draft of this paper's data file carried a figure of "osimertinib biochemical IC50 116 ± 15 nM (Chem Sci 2019)" that is not supported by that paper — its Table 1 reports osimertinib at 0.3 nM against the L858R/T790M double mutant. The figure was removed and the data file patched before drafting; the manuscript uses only the verified BaF3 values from Xi et al. 2023.

2.2 ChEMBL outage and the PubChem fallback

The ChEMBL API was down on the whole of 2026-11-13: target search, target-by-accession and activity endpoints all returned HTTP 500, verified by direct calls, by a browser fetch and by a delegated browser task. The standard pipeline therefore retrieved zero ligands. The compounds in this paper were taken from PubChem by CID and by a PubChem fastsimilarity_2d search on osimertinib (threshold 85), with measured potencies attached only where a verified literature value exists. Two bugs in that fallback path were found and fixed while this paper ran: the shared PubChem function called the wrong endpoint (fastsimilarity/smiles/, rejected with HTTP 400 "Unrecognized identifier namespace"; the correct endpoint is fastsimilarity_2d/smiles/), and the analogue fetcher assumed the similarity result was a dictionary with a "cids" key when it is a plain CID list, and assumed the per-CID property call always returns "CanonicalSMILES" when it can return "ConnectivitySMILES" instead. The first docking run of this paper was stopped at 2 of 10 docks to fix the endpoint; the fixed script resumed from the incremental partial file, so the two completed scores (osimertinib −7.50, CH7233163 −9.53) are single measurements carried over, not independent replicates. The afatinib SMILES was corrected during script preparation (a malformed extra parenthesis) before any docking.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P00533 (EGFR, human). One structure: 6LUB, EGFR L858R/T790M/C797S in complex with CH7233163, 2.315 A X-ray (Kashima et al. 2020). Centre [−50.87, −0.35, −19.76] — the centroid of the co-crystallised CH7233163 (EUX, 47 atoms) computed from the deposited coordinates with the pipeline's own _ligand_center function; the Ser797 CA is 6.17 A from the centre, confirming the box sits on the ATP site. A second triple-mutant structure, 9XU9 (2.84 A, deposited 2025-11-24), was considered and not used: 6LUB was chosen because its co-crystallised ligand is a fourth-generation inhibitor with measured triple-mutant potency. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same box (22.5 A) and exhaustiveness (8) were used for every compound, including osimertinib itself. Ten compounds: CH7233163 (PubChem CID 154701097, re-dock control), osimertinib (CID 71496458, reference drug), gefitinib (CID 123631), afatinib (CID 10184653), brigatinib (CID 68165256) and five fastsimilarity_2d analogues of osimertinib (CIDs 121269225, 118607832, 121280087, 139377809, 71496460).

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. All ten compounds are PAINS-clean.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and for this target it is doubly not activity: osimertinib and afatinib are covalent Cys797 binders, and C797S removes the covalent anchor, so Vina's non-covalent scores cannot capture their mechanism — a good non-covalent score for osimertinib would not mean it works, and its poor score here is consistent with, but does not prove, its clinical failure. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds; only the 1.38 kcal/mol gap between CH7233163 and the next compound approaches a defensible separation, and even that is inside the noise band. The re-dock control is expected to score well: the pocket in 6LUB is shaped around CH7233163, so its −9.53 validates the protocol rather than discovering a lead. CH7233163 is a tool compound, not a drug: MW 669.7 and logP 5.2 sit outside Lipinski's rules. Only two compounds carry measured triple-mutant potencies, measured in different assay types (biochemical kinase vs BaF3 cellular), so no rank correlation is computed or claimed. The five analogues carry no measured potency. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound 6LUB (kcal/mol) Measured potency PAINS
CH7233163 −9.53 (−9.53, −9.33, −9.04) Biochemical IC50 0.28 nM; cellular IC50 20 nM (Del19 triple), 1,200 nM (WT) none
Brigatinib −8.15 (−8.15, −8.06, −7.70) Bound to T790M/C797S in 8H7X; no head-to-head triple-mutant IC50 none
PubChem 121280087 −8.01 (−8.01, −7.75, −7.49) No measured potency (analogue) none
PubChem 121269225 −7.92 (−7.92, −7.74, −7.71) No measured potency (analogue) none
PubChem 139377809 −7.77 (−7.77, −7.65, −7.56) No measured potency (analogue) none
Afatinib −7.54 (−7.54, −7.53, −7.31) Covalent anchor lost on C797S; no triple-mutant IC50 none
Osimertinib (reference) −7.50 (−7.50, −7.29, −7.26) BaF3 IC50 1.42 µM (Del19 triple) / 1.44 µM (L858R triple) none
PubChem 118607832 −7.47 (−7.47, −7.45, −7.31) No measured potency (analogue) none
Gefitinib −7.27 (−7.27, −7.22, −5.65) HTRF IC50 185 ± 98 nM vs L858R/T790M double mutant; no triple-mutant IC50 none
PubChem 71496460 −7.27 (−7.27, −7.17, −7.01) No measured potency (analogue) none

The gap between CH7233163 (−9.53) and the next compound, brigatinib (−8.15), is 1.38 kcal/mol — the only separation in the screen that approaches a defensible margin. Everything from brigatinib down to PubChem 71496460 spans 0.88 kcal/mol, inside Vina's noise: the order among those nine compounds cannot be defended from these scores. Osimertinib's three poses are tight (−7.50, −7.29, −7.26), so its low score is a stable pose result, not a sampling failure. Gefitinib's third pose collapses to −5.65, the widest pose spread in the set, consistent with a first-generation scaffold that does not fit the triple-mutant pocket. The five analogues cluster at −7.27 to −8.01, all below brigatinib; none of them beats a known fourth-generation binder, and the best analogue (121280087, −8.01) is 0.14 kcal/mol behind brigatinib — a tie within noise.

The directional test the hypothesis posed: the most potent measured compound in the set, CH7233163 (0.28 nM biochemical, 20 nM cellular), docks best by a clear margin, and the reference drug osimertinib (1.42 µM in triple-mutant BaF3 cells, roughly 5,000-fold weaker than CH7233163 biochemically and 70-fold weaker in cells) docks 2.03 kcal/mol worse, near the bottom of the set. The direction is right. But with two measured potencies on two different assay types, no correlation can be computed, and the hypothesis as a ranking claim is untested, not confirmed.

3.2 The wrong site scores better

A discarded pipeline run docked osimertinib at −8.56 on 8A27, a structure of EGFR bound to an allosteric inhibitor — the wrong site. That score is 1.06 kcal/mol better than osimertinib's correct-site score of −7.50 on 6LUB. A docking score without site verification can look better on the wrong site than on the right one. The 8A27 run is kept in the audit file and excluded from every result in this paper.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these ten compounds on 6LUB was found at drafting time, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The depositing study for 6LUB is a structure and medicinal-chemistry paper, not a docking benchmark. The absence of a published comparator is stated, not filled in.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen separates one compound from the rest: CH7233163, the co-crystallised fourth-generation ligand, re-docks best, and the failed drug osimertinib docks near the bottom. That is a directional signal in the right direction, and it is the most this screen can claim. It cannot rank the other eight compounds — their scores sit inside the noise band — and it cannot rank the analogues at all, because they carry no measured potency. A paper that reported "PubChem 121280087 scores −8.01, second only to brigatinib" as a lead claim would be reporting noise as signal.

4.2 The re-dock is a control, not a discovery

CH7233163's −9.53 must not be read as "the screen discovered a fourth-generation inhibitor". The pocket in 6LUB was crystallised around CH7233163; a competent docking protocol is expected to recover a good score for the co-crystallised ligand, and a protocol that failed to do so would be broken. The value of the −9.53 is that the protocol is not broken: the same box, exhaustiveness and preparation that give osimertinib −7.50 give the co-crystal ligand −9.53. The comparison that matters is therefore the 2.03 kcal/mol gap between the control and the reference drug, not the absolute value of either.

4.3 The covalent caveat decides the interpretation

Osimertinib's clinical failure on C797S is a covalent-mechanism failure: the warhead has nothing to bind. Vina scores only non-covalent poses, so its −7.50 for osimertinib is a pose score for a drug whose mechanism is absent from the model. The score is consistent with failure, but it is not evidence of failure — a covalent drug can score well non-covalently and still fail, or score poorly and still work through the covalent step. Any validation must measure the kinase, not the pose.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Direction hypothesis. In one kinase assay on L858R/T790M/C797S EGFR, CH7233163 is the most potent compound in this set and osimertinib the least, with brigatinib between them. Falsified if osimertinib's kinase IC50 falls within ten-fold of CH7233163's — in which case the docking direction is an artefact of the co-crystal pocket.
  2. Analogue hypothesis. PubChem 121280087 inhibits the triple-mutant kinase at an IC50 within ten-fold of brigatinib's. Falsified if it is more than ten-fold weaker — in which case the analogue cluster is noise and no fourth-generation series starts here.
  3. Selectivity hypothesis. CH7233163 retains its reported selectivity window (cellular IC50 20 nM triple-mutant vs 1,200 nM wild-type) when re-measured in the same assay as the analogues. Falsified if the window collapses below ten-fold — in which case the tool compound's therapeutic margin is a literature artefact.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain CH7233163, brigatinib, osimertinib and PubChem 121280087; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): kinase assay (ADP-Glo or equivalent) on recombinant L858R/T790M/C797S EGFR, all four compounds on the same plates, in triplicate, with osimertinib as the reference — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): BaF3 cellular assay on Del19/T790M/C797S and L858R/T790M/C797S lines, plus wild-type EGFR BaF3 for the selectivity window. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if 121280087 is within ten-fold of brigatinib, dock its analogues and synthesise the best two; if it is not, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency; the selectivity comparison needs the same, because a false "selective" call on the wild-type margin is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Only two compounds carry measured triple-mutant potencies, measured in different assay types; no rank correlation is computed or claimed.
  3. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; nine of the ten compounds sit inside one noise band.
  4. The re-dock control is expected to score well because the pocket is shaped around it; its score validates the protocol, not a lead.
  5. Vina's non-covalent scores cannot model the covalent mechanism of osimertinib and afatinib, which is the mechanism C797S destroys.
  6. CH7233163 is a tool compound (MW 669.7, logP 5.2), not a drug; its properties sit outside Lipinski's rules.
  7. The five analogues carry no measured potency; their scores are unvalidated.
  8. A single rigid structure was docked; the triple-mutant conformational ensemble is not represented. 9XU9, a second triple-mutant structure, was not docked.
  9. The two resumed scores (osimertinib, CH7233163) are single measurements carried over from the interrupted first run, not independent replicates.
  10. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.

6. Conclusion

On the triple-mutant EGFR structure 6LUB, the fourth-generation tool compound CH7233163 re-docks best at −9.53 kcal/mol, 1.38 clear of the next compound, and the reference drug osimertinib docks near the bottom at −7.50 — a directional signal that matches the measured record, where CH7233163 inhibits the triple mutant at 0.28 nM biochemically and osimertinib needs 1.42 µM in triple-mutant cells. But only two compounds carry measured triple-mutant potencies, on different assays, so no rank correlation can be computed, and the five osimertinib analogues scoring −7.27 to −8.01 carry no measured potency at all. The screen is a validated directional signal with an untested ranking, not a lead claim. The next step is the single-assay kinase comparison in Section 4.5, with CH7233163, brigatinib, PubChem 121280087 and osimertinib on the same plates.

Four Whole-Cell-Active Compounds Dock Into S. Typhi GyrB at −8.39 to −9.41 kcal/mol, But Azithromycin Cannot Be Docked and the Potencies Are Phenotypic, Not Gyrase Binding

Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid — resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole, fluoroquinolones and ceftriaxone — emerged in Hyderabad, Sindh in late 2016 and now accounts for roughly 70% of Salmonella Typhi in Pakistan, leaving azithromycin as the last oral option, with resistance already appeari…

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-12 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #49 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Salmonella Typhi; DNA gyrase; azithromycin; extensively drug-resistant typhoid; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; phenotypic screening; XDR typhoid

Abstract

Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid — resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole, fluoroquinolones and ceftriaxone — emerged in Hyderabad, Sindh in late 2016 and now accounts for roughly 70% of Salmonella Typhi in Pakistan, leaving azithromycin as the last oral option, with resistance already appearing. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can find a DNA gyrase binder better than azithromycin for XDR typhoid. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P0A2I4 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL614448, 5 bioactivities → PubChem → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked four whole-cell-active compounds into the 2.2 Å S. Typhi GyrB structure 6J90, with the grid centre audited to the co-crystallised ATP centroid. All four leads docked strongly — CHEMBL3585716 −9.41, CHEMBL5171589 −9.28, CHEMBL3585709 −9.27, CHEMBL3585717 −8.39 kcal/mol — but azithromycin itself could not be docked at all (the Vina run timed out at the pipeline's 900-second limit on the 749 Da macrolide), so no "beats azithromycin" claim can be made, and the docking order does not track whole-cell potency (Spearman ρ = −0.20, n = 4, p = 0.80). Critically, no S. Typhi DNA gyrase target exists in ChEMBL at all — the potencies used here are phenotypic whole-cell data, not gyrase binding data — so this screen tests a hypothesis (does whole-cell potency track GyrB binding?) rather than validating one. The falsifiable next step is a GyrB ATPase inhibition assay of the four leads against azithromycin with whole-cell MICs: if a lead inhibits GyrB at concentrations matching its MIC, it is a genuine GyrB-targeting candidate; if it does not, its whole-cell activity works through another target.

1. Introduction

Typhoid fever still sickens millions, and Pakistan carries one of the highest burdens: roughly 493.5 cases per 100,000 people, with incidence doubling from 7 to 15 per 100,000 as XDR strains spread. Extensively drug-resistant Salmonella Typhi — resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones and the third-generation cephalosporin ceftriaxone — was first detected in Hyderabad, Sindh in late 2016, and has since caused more than 17,000 XDR cases nationally, including 14,360 in Karachi between January 2017 and June 2021. By 2019–2021 XDR strains made up about 70% of S. Typhi isolates, and in a 2017–2019 population-based study XDR accounted for 57% of culture-confirmed cases. Azithromycin is now the last reliable oral option: 96.9% of isolates were susceptible in a 2024–25 paediatric cohort (n = 65, POF Hospital), but a Gilgit study already found 2.9% azithromycin resistance and 1% meropenem resistance, with 40.3% of 208 isolates XDR. DNA gyrase subunit B (GyrB) is a validated antibacterial target — its ATP-binding site is druggable and distinct from the fluoroquinolone site on GyrA — so a GyrB binder would sidestep existing XDR resistance. The falsifiable hypothesis of this paper is: a standardised Vina screen on the S. Typhi GyrB structure 6J90 ranks whole-cell-active compounds in the same order as their measured anti-Typhi potencies, with azithromycin as the reference.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

The XDR definition, Hyderabad emergence, case counts and resistance proportions are from Klemm et al., mBio 2018 (PMID 29463654) and Qamar et al., Open Forum Infectious Diseases 2025 (PMID 40212028), with the Gilgit resistance figures from Life and Science 2026 (doi:10.37185/LnS.1.1.1148) and the plasmid epidemiology from Scientific Reports (doi:10.1038/s41598-026-37560-5). Today's literature digest (research-team digest 2026-11-12, 840 candidates screened, 8 selected) contained no paper topical to this benchmark and is cited only as a methodological source. All database identifiers were verified live on 2026-11-12.

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1 and #3: UniProtKB P0A2I4 (S. Typhi DNA gyrase subunit B, gyrB, 804 aa) → ChEMBL target CHEMBL614448 ("Salmonella typhi", ORGANISM) → 5 bioactivities → PubChem verification of azithromycin (CID 447043) → RDKit similarity/ADMET/PAINS → Vina docking of the top 5 leads (the reference query plus four ChEMBL leads) into PDB 6J90 (S. Typhi GyrB N-terminal domain in complex with ATP, chain A, 2.2 Å). Grid centre [−12.65, 51.02, 28.42] is the co-crystallised ATP centroid exactly (audited against the ATP atoms in the PDB file); ATP is the ATP-site ligand, so the grid sits on the correct drug site. Box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported for every molecule, same protocol for reference and leads. The per-ligand Vina limit in this pipeline is 900 seconds.

Correction history (disclosed, not hidden). The first docking run for this topic was invalid and is discarded: UniProt P0A2I4 was correct, but the ChEMBL target resolved to CHEMBL2074 maltase-glucoamylase — the by-accession endpoint failed and the fallback picked the first entry of the text-search list — so the run docked N-substituted deoxynojirimycin iminosugars (alpha-glucosidase inhibitors) into the GyrB pocket. Those numbers are kept in dock-HP-051-2026-11-12.json for audit and are not used anywhere in this paper. A live search of the ChEMBL website on 2026-11-12 (verified twice) established that no ChEMBL target for Salmonella Typhi DNA gyrase (subunit A or B) exists: the only S. Typhi targets are organism targets. The corrected run therefore uses the closest verified target, CHEMBL614448 "Salmonella typhi" (ORGANISM, 3,065 associated compounds, 4,418 bioactivities, 387 assays), monkey-patched in because the ChEMBL target-by-accession API endpoint returned HTTP 500 pages and timeouts throughout 2026-11-12. The bioactivities are the verbatim ChEMBL API response for CHEMBL614448 saved to hidden_files/chembl-activities-CHEMBL614448-2026-11-12.json (the complete set: 5 activities with pChEMBL ≥ 5, page_meta total_count 5), because the live activity endpoint timed out on limit=50 queries and intermittently returned HTML error pages all day; only the record transport differs, not the data. The structure picker was not wrong in either run: 6J90 is the correct S. Typhi GyrB structure in both.

The phenotypic caveat — read before the Results. CHEMBL614448 is an organism target, so its bioactivities are whole-cell potencies (MIC/EC50 against S. Typhi), not gyrase binding measurements. The docking-versus-potency comparison in this paper is therefore a hypothesis test — does whole-cell anti-Typhi potency track with GyrB ATP-site binding? — and not a target-validated benchmark. No claim that any lead "inhibits gyrase" follows from this screen.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every docked molecule. All four docked leads and azithromycin are PAINS-clean. The fifth ChEMBL compound (CHEMBL3585711, IC50 2.72 µM) was not docked (only the top 5 are docked) and is also PAINS-clean.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity: Vina scores carry ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, a single rigid structure (6J90) cannot capture induced fit, and no experimental data, molecular dynamics, or free-energy refinement were run. The potencies are phenotypic, so even a perfect rank correlation would not prove GyrB is the target. No clinical recommendation follows from this paper.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured whole-cell potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL3585716 IC50 3.66 µM (pChEMBL 5.44) −9.41 −9.41, −8.72, −8.63 clean
CHEMBL5171589 EC50 280 nM (pChEMBL 6.55) −9.28 −9.28, −8.90, −8.66 clean
CHEMBL3585709 IC50 3.06 µM (pChEMBL 5.51) −9.27 −9.27, −8.77, −8.73 clean
CHEMBL3585717 IC50 3.19 µM (pChEMBL 5.50) −8.39 −8.39, −8.39, −7.80 clean
Azithromycin (query) reference drug could not be docked — clean

All four leads docked strongly into the GyrB ATP pocket (−8.39 to −9.41 kcal/mol), with consistent poses. The spread among the four (1.02 kcal/mol) sits inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the four cannot be ordered by these scores. Azithromycin — the reference drug and the last oral option for XDR typhoid — could not be docked: the Vina run timed out at the pipeline's 900-second per-ligand limit (the process ran for over 16 CPU-minutes without returning), and an earlier independent attempt also failed with a Vina command error. The failure is a property of the molecule in this protocol (749 Da macrolide, 14 hydrogen-bond acceptors, 2 Lipinski violations), not of the structure: the same protocol docked all four smaller leads on the same grid. There is therefore no reference score, and no lead can be said to beat — or lose to — azithromycin in this screen.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four ChEMBL compounds on 6J90 was found in the literature sweep, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The four scores reported here are new reference points for this structure under this protocol.

3.3 The ranking does not track whole-cell potency

The docking order shows no agreement with measured whole-cell potency: Spearman ρ = −0.20 (n = 4, p = 0.80). The most potent compound by far — CHEMBL5171589 (EC50 280 nM, pChEMBL 6.55, the only lead under 1 µM) — ranks second by Vina, while the weakest measured lead, CHEMBL3585716 (IC50 3.66 µM, pChEMBL 5.44), ranks first. The other three leads cluster at 2.72–3.66 µM, a potency range too narrow to rank. This is the expected outcome if whole-cell potency is driven by factors docking cannot see (permeation through the Gram-negative outer membrane, efflux, or a different target): GyrB binding is only one contributor to a whole-cell MIC, and for these compounds it may not be the dominant one.

Drug-likeness is a second problem. Only CHEMBL5171589 is drug-like (MW 356.86, logP 3.02, zero Lipinski violations). The other three docked leads are large, lipophilic brominated analogues from a single chemical series (assays CHEMBL3588323): MW 532–637, logP 5.45–6.33, two Lipinski violations each. The undocked fifth compound (CHEMBL3585711) is worse still (MW 715.97, logP 7.09). Whatever their GyrB scores, the brominated series is a poor starting point for an oral drug. ToxGuard Tox21 read-across flags appear on every molecule; these are similarity-screen flags, not toxicity findings, and are reported as such.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

This paper set out to benchmark GyrB binders against azithromycin and instead established three facts that change the question. First, there is no S. Typhi DNA gyrase target in ChEMBL, so a target-specific benchmark for this organism cannot be built from ChEMBL at all — only a phenotypic one. Second, the reference drug cannot be docked under this protocol, so the screen has no baseline. Third, the four leads that do dock are strong binders in absolute terms but their order does not track whole-cell potency, which is exactly what a phenotypic dataset should produce if GyrB is not the potency-driving target for these molecules. The honest reframe is that this screen is a pocket-fit test, not a potency ranking: it shows four whole-cell-active compounds fit the GyrB ATP site, and it cannot show whether GyrB is why they kill S. Typhi.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

No lead "wins" here. There is no reference score to beat, the 1.02 kcal/mol spread among the leads is inside Vina noise, and the strongest docking score belongs to the weakest whole-cell compound. A reader who takes −9.41 kcal/mol as evidence that CHEMBL3585716 is a GyrB inhibitor would be making three errors at once: mistaking a docking score for a binding measurement, mistaking a phenotypic potency for a target potency, and ignoring that the molecule violates two Lipinski rules.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No molecule in this paper carries a PAINS alert, so no redox-control redesign is needed. The design constraint here is different: the validation assay must separate GyrB inhibition from whole-cell killing (see 4.5), because the two need not coincide.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL5171589 kills S. Typhi through GyrB. A GyrB ATPase inhibition assay will show inhibition at concentrations near its whole-cell EC50 (280 nM); if it inhibits GyrB only at micromolar concentrations, its whole-cell activity works through another target.
  2. The brominated series does not act through GyrB. The three CHEMBL35857xx leads will show no GyrB inhibition at their whole-cell IC50s (3–3.7 µM), and their MICs will be unchanged in a GyrB-overexpressing strain — if their MICs shift, GyrB is involved after all.
  3. Azithromycin's failure is a protocol limit, not a biology result. Docking azithromycin at reduced exhaustiveness, or with a flexible-receptor protocol, will return a score; if it still fails, the macrolide needs a different method (e.g. induced-fit docking) before any GyrB comparison can be made.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): GyrB ATPase inhibition assay (purified S. Typhi GyrB, malachite-green phosphate readout) for the four leads, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, with novobiocin (a known GyrB ATP-site inhibitor) as the positive control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): whole-cell MICs against S. Typhi (including an XDR clinical isolate if available under appropriate biosafety approval) for the four leads, compared with their GyrB IC50s — the ratio is the test of hypothesis 1. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): for any lead whose GyrB IC50 matches its MIC, a GyrB-overexpression shift assay and a time-kill curve; for CHEMBL5171589 specifically, a medicinal-chemistry assessment of its drug-like scaffold as the starting point for optimisation.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no experimental data, no molecular dynamics, no free-energy refinement.
  2. The potencies are phenotypic whole-cell data, not gyrase binding data; the rank correlation (ρ = −0.20, n = 4) tests a hypothesis, not a validation.
  3. No S. Typhi DNA gyrase target exists in ChEMBL — the target-specific benchmark this topic posed cannot be built from ChEMBL.
  4. Azithromycin could not be docked (Vina 900-second timeout, twice), so there is no reference score.
  5. Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) exceeds the 1.02 kcal/mol spread among the four leads; they cannot be ordered.
  6. Single rigid structure (6J90, 2.2 Å); induced fit and the DNA-bound holoenzyme are not modelled.
  7. Three of the four leads violate two Lipinski rules and come from one brominated series; only CHEMBL5171589 is drug-like.
  8. The ChEMBL bioactivities were fetched via a saved verbatim API response because the live endpoint was unstable all day (see Methods 2.2); the data are real ChEMBL records, but the fetch was not the pipeline's live call.

6. Conclusion

Four whole-cell-active compounds dock strongly into the S. Typhi GyrB ATP pocket (−8.39 to −9.41 kcal/mol), but the reference drug azithromycin cannot be docked under this protocol, the docking order does not track whole-cell potency (Spearman ρ = −0.20, n = 4), and no S. Typhi DNA gyrase target exists in ChEMBL — the potencies are phenotypic, not target binding. The screen establishes pocket fit, not GyrB inhibition. The next step is a GyrB ATPase assay paired with whole-cell MICs, which will settle whether any of these compounds acts through GyrB at all.

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-12 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #52 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B; PTP1B; ertiprotafib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; type 2 diabetes; insulin resistance; drug discovery

Abstract

Type 2 diabetes affected 589 million adults worldwide in 2024, and Pakistan carries the world's highest age-standardised prevalence at 31.4%, yet no PTP1B inhibitor has ever been approved: the target is validated — PTP1B dephosphorylates the insulin receptor — but the only two inhibitors to reach trials, ertiprotafib and trodusquemine, both failed, and ertiprotafib was later shown to work by aggregating PTP1B rather than inhibiting it. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank PTP1B ligands at all. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P18031 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL335, 36 bioactivities → PubChem → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7). The first docking run was invalid and is discarded here: the pipeline's structure picker chose 9C66, the MENA EVH1 domain, in which PTP1B appears only as a short peptide, and centred the grid on a modified cysteine of the wrong protein. The corrected re-dock placed the identical ligand set on 2F71, the PTP1B catalytic domain at 1.55 Å with a sulfamic acid inhibitor bound, the grid centre audited to the inhibitor centroid and its nearest atom 3.39 Å from the catalytic Cys215. Three leads out-scored ertiprotafib — CHEMBL5085615 −8.60, CHEMBL541214 −8.39, CHEMBL244563 −8.27 versus ertiprotafib −7.68 kcal/mol — but the margins (0.59–0.92 kcal/mol) sit inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the ranking shows no correlation with measured potency (Spearman ρ = 0.0, n = 4), with the most potent measured binder (CHEMBL244563, Ki 0.68 nM) ranking third by Vina. The falsifiable next step is a PTP1B enzyme assay of the four leads against ertiprotafib with a TCPTP counter-screen: if the measured order matches the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, docking alone must not be used to prioritise PTP1B leads on this structure.

1. Introduction

Diabetes affected an estimated 589 million adults aged 20–79 worldwide in 2024, and the International Diabetes Federation projects 853 million by 2050. Pakistan carries the world's highest age-standardised prevalence at 31.4%, with an estimated 34.5 million adults affected. Insulin resistance is the central defect of type 2 diabetes, and protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B, gene PTPN1, UniProt P18031) is its best-validated negative regulator: the enzyme dephosphorylates the insulin receptor and its substrates, switching off insulin signalling, and it also negatively regulates leptin signalling. Inhibiting PTP1B should therefore sensitise both pathways — a mechanism with support from genetics and from animal models that is unusually clean for a metabolic target.

No PTP1B inhibitor has ever been approved. Only two small molecules reached clinical trials. Trodusquemine (MSI-1436) completed Phase 1 but never advanced. Ertiprotafib (PTP 112), developed by Wyeth, reached Phase II for type 2 diabetes and was discontinued for unsatisfactory efficacy and dose-limiting adverse effects. The post-mortem, published in 2020, explains why: ertiprotafib does not inhibit PTP1B at its active site in the conventional sense. It induces concentration-dependent aggregation of the PTP1B catalytic domain — it lowers the protein's melting temperature in differential scanning fluorimetry, the opposite of what most drugs do — and the aggregation, not specific inhibition, accounts for both the weak efficacy and the toxicities. Ertiprotafib is therefore a failed reference in a specific sense: it is the field's best-known clinical candidate and a proven artefact, so a screen that "beats ertiprotafib" has beaten a compound that does not do what it was supposed to do.

The field's other problem is selectivity. PTP1B's active site is highly conserved across the phosphatase family, most closely with T-cell protein tyrosine phosphatase (TCPTP), and inhibitors that bind PTP1B usually bind TCPTP too; TCPTP inhibition carries its own liabilities. A docking screen on PTP1B alone cannot measure that selectivity at all. The honest question for a PTP1B screen is therefore twofold: can it rank binders, and does the ranking survive a selectivity counter-screen?

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL PTP1B actives against ertiprotafib on a high-resolution PTP1B catalytic-domain structure will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-12 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-12, which screened 840 candidates and selected 8, none on PTP1B — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: the IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition (2025) for the burden numbers; Kumar, Page and Peti 2020 for ertiprotafib's aggregation mechanism and Phase II failure. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking — and the correction that makes this paper

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P18031 (human protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 1, PTP1B, 435 aa); ChEMBL target CHEMBL335 (verified: "Tyrosine-protein phosphatase non-receptor type 1", SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens); 36 bioactivities retrieved, 25 leads after RDKit similarity screening and ranking, 26 including the reference query; the top 5 leads docked plus the reference query (ertiprotafib, PubChem CID 157049, verified live). Best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box (22.5 Å) and exhaustiveness (8) were used for every compound including ertiprotafib.

The first docking run is reported here as a fault, not a result. The pipeline's structure picker (find_pdb_for_uniprot) takes UniProt PDB cross-references, filters to X-ray structures under 3.0 Å, sorts by resolution, and takes the first structure with a drug-like bound ligand. For P18031 it picked 9C66 (1.4 Å) — "Structure of the MENA EVH1 domain bound to the polyproline segment of PTP1B". PTP1B appears in 9C66 only as a peptide (chain B, residues 304–313); the structure is the MENA EVH1 domain, an actin-regulatory protein. The grid centre landed on CSO A7, a modified cysteine (S-hydroxycysteine) of the EVH1 domain chain — verified against the 9C66 file — not the PTP1B active site. The first run's scores (CHEMBL244563 −7.07, ertiprotafib −6.98, CHEMBL541214 −6.94, CHEMBL5085615 −6.40, CHEMBL1232859 −6.00) are therefore scores for ligands docked into the MENA EVH1 domain. They are discarded, kept in hidden_files/dock-HP-003-2026-11-12.json for audit, and no number in the comparison table comes from that run.

The correction: 438 X-ray structures under 3.0 Å are cross-referenced to P18031, and the top-resolution ones were audited individually. The highest-resolution entries are apo or buffer-only (7MN9, 7MKZ, 8U1E, 7MOU, 7GTW, 2HNP — no drug-like ligand, so no ligand-derived grid centre exists). 8G65 was audited and rejected: its ligand sits 51.45 Å from the catalytic Cys215 SG, i.e. not the catalytic site. The re-dock used 2F71 — "PTP1B with sulfamic acid inhibitors", catalytic domain residues 2–298, 1.55 Å — with the grid centred on the co-crystallised inhibitor UN7 (42 atoms) centroid [39.94, 9.94, 14.68], computed with the pipeline's own _ligand_center function. UN7's nearest atom is 3.39 Å from the catalytic Cys215 SG, confirming the active site. (1XBO and 2QBS were valid alternates, with nearest atoms 3.64 and 3.85 Å from Cys215.) The identical ligand set from the first run was re-docked on 2F71 under the same protocol; those are the numbers in Section 3.1.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. All four leads and ertiprotafib are PAINS-clean. Note that a PAINS-clean result does not clear ertiprotafib: its failure mode is aggregation, which PAINS does not detect, and which is the subject of the Kumar et al. paper cited above. The ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel flagged several assays for every compound (Section 3.1); these are similarity-based flags, not measurements.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds; all three "wins" over ertiprotafib (0.59–0.92 kcal/mol) sit inside that noise. A single rigid structure (2F71, sulfamic-acid-inhibitor-bound) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of the catalytic domain. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays (three Ki, one IC50, different assay conditions); pChEMBL values are not head-to-head measurements. No measured PTP1B potency for ertiprotafib itself was retrieved in this run, so the reference enters the rank test by docking score only. Selectivity against TCPTP or any other phosphatase was not measured — docking on PTP1B alone cannot address it. Ertiprotafib's own properties (logP 8.79, two Lipinski violations) mark it as a poor reference compound independent of its aggregation.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table (corrected run, 2F71)

CHEMBL541214 −8.39 −8.39, −8.19, −8.14 Ki 4.0 nM 8.40 none

All four leads are PAINS-clean. Three carry one Lipinski violation each (CHEMBL541214, MW 609.52, logP 4.75; CHEMBL244563, MW 565.07, logP 4.64); CHEMBL5085615 (MW 384.39, logP 1.02) and CHEMBL1232859 (MW 295.18, logP 0.87) are Lipinski-clean. Ertiprotafib is the outlier on drug-likeness: MW 559.53, logP 8.79, two Lipinski violations. The ToxGuard read-across panel flagged NR-AhR, SR-ARE, SR-HSE and SR-MMP across the leads with varying additional flags (including NR-AR-LBD, NR-ER/ER-LBD, NR-PPAR-gamma, SR-ATAD5 and SR-p53); ertiprotafib was flagged for NR-AhR, NR-PPAR-gamma and SR-p53. The panel does not discriminate between the leads and the reference, so it contributes nothing to ranking and is reported only for completeness.

The rank test the hypothesis posed: the Vina order of the four leads (5085615 > 541214 > 244563 > 1232859) against the measured-potency order (244563, Ki 0.68 nM > 5085615, IC50 1.0 nM > 1232859, Ki 2.4 nM > 541214, Ki 4.0 nM) gives Spearman ρ = 0.0 (n = 4) — no correlation at all. The most potent measured binder (CHEMBL244563, 0.68 nM) ranks third by Vina; the weakest measured binder (CHEMBL541214, 4.0 nM) ranks second. Three leads out-score ertiprotafib, but by 0.59–0.92 kcal/mol — inside the noise margin — and the reference they beat is a proven aggregator, so the comparison is against a compound that does not inhibit PTP1B in the conventional sense. There is no lead claim in this screen: no compound is both the best docked and the most potent measured, and the ranking carries no information.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four ChEMBL compounds on 2F71 was found at drafting time, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The depositing study for 2F71 is a structural study of PTP1B with sulfamic acid inhibitors; its own affinity data for these compounds were not retrieved in this run and are not compared here. The absence of a published comparator is stated, not filled in.

3.3 The discarded run, for the record

The first run's docking on 9C66 (MENA EVH1 domain) returned CHEMBL244563 −7.07, ertiprotafib −6.98, CHEMBL541214 −6.94, CHEMBL5085615 −6.40 and CHEMBL1232859 −6.00. Those numbers are superficially similar to the corrected run's — the same ligand set, the same order of magnitude — which is exactly why the fault matters: a wrong-protein docking can produce plausible-looking numbers. The corrected run changed every score by 0.29–2.20 kcal/mol and changed the ranking (CHEMBL5085615 moved from fourth to first). A reader who saw only the first run would have drawn a different, wrong conclusion from numbers that looked like results. The lesson is the audit, not the scores: a structure picker that sorts by resolution alone will pick a peptide-bound structure over a catalytic-domain structure whenever the peptide complex happens to diffract better, and the only defence is checking what protein the structure actually is.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

This paper's finding is negative in two directions at once: the screen cannot rank PTP1B ligands (ρ = 0.0), and the reference it compares them against is a failed aggregator. A paper that reported only "three leads beat ertiprotafib" would be technically true and scientifically empty — the margins are noise, the ranking is uncorrelated, and the reference is not a real inhibitor. The useful output is the corrected protocol itself: the audit that caught the wrong protein, the structure that replaced it, and the precise statement of what a real PTP1B lead would have to survive (Section 4.5).

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four compounds, mixed Ki and IC50 values, and every "win" inside the noise margin. The measured potencies span less than one order of magnitude (0.68–4.0 nM), so the test asks the scoring function to resolve differences it cannot resolve. Two of the four leads violate Lipinski's rules, and the most drug-like lead (CHEMBL5085615) is the best docked but only the second most potent measured. None of the four is identified by name in this run (ChEMBL IDs only); their chemotypes and selectivity are unknown from this data. And the aggregation trap that killed ertiprotafib applies to lipophilic leads generally — CHEMBL541214 and CHEMBL244563, at logP 4.75 and 4.64, are the ones that most need an aggregation control in any validation.

4.3 The PAINS problem does not apply here — the aggregation problem does

All compounds are PAINS-clean, so no artefact controls are needed on that front. The design constraint this experiment imposes is different and specific to this target: any validation assay must include an aggregation control (detergent, enzyme-concentration dependence, dynamic light scattering), because the reference drug's failure mode was aggregation and two of the leads are lipophilic enough to repeat it. A lead that "inhibits" PTP1B only by aggregating it is ertiprotafib again.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Rank hypothesis. In a PTP1B enzyme assay, the potency order of the four leads matches their ChEMBL record order (244563 > 5085615 > 1232859 > 541214). Falsified if the measured order differs — in which case the ChEMBL records, not the docking, would need re-examination.
  2. Aggregation hypothesis. At least one of the four leads inhibits PTP1B by aggregation rather than active-site binding: its apparent inhibition disappears with detergent or varies with enzyme concentration. Falsified if all four show detergent-insensitive, concentration-independent inhibition — in which case they are genuine binders.
  3. Selectivity hypothesis. The best genuine binder inhibits PTP1B at least 10-fold more potently than TCPTP. Falsified if it inhibits both about equally — in which case it is not a developable PTP1B lead, whatever its PTP1B potency.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain the four leads; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR; confirm ertiprotafib as the in-assay reference, with its aggregation behaviour as the positive artefact control. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): PTP1B enzyme assay (pNPP or phosphopeptide substrate), dose–response for all four leads plus ertiprotafib on the same plates, each condition with and without detergent (e.g. 0.01% Triton X-100) and at two enzyme concentrations, to expose aggregation; read out IC50 and the detergent-sensitivity ratio. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): TCPTP counter-screen of the best two leads at the same concentrations; repeat the best lead in a second PTP1B assay format (e.g. insulin-receptor dephosphorylation). Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if a lead is a genuine, selective binder, dock it into the 2F71 structure and compare the pose with the UN7 inhibitor pose; if all four are aggregators or non-selective, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per dose–response curve, eight concentrations, is the minimum for a defensible IC50; the aggregation test needs the same replication, because a false "genuine inhibitor" call on an aggregator is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; all three "wins" over ertiprotafib (0.59–0.92 kcal/mol) sit inside that noise.
  3. The rank test is n = 4 and mixes three Ki values with one IC50 from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays.
  4. The reference drug ertiprotafib is a proven PTP1B aggregator, not a conventional inhibitor; comparisons against it are weak by construction.
  5. The first docking run used the wrong protein (MENA EVH1 domain, 9C66); its numbers are discarded, and the corrected run's numbers rest on the re-dock audit in Section 2.2.
  6. Selectivity against TCPTP or any other phosphatase was not measured; docking on PTP1B alone cannot address it.
  7. A single rigid structure (2F71, sulfamic-acid-inhibitor-bound) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of the catalytic domain.
  8. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  9. The four leads are identified by ChEMBL ID only; chemotype and selectivity are unknown from this data.
  10. Aggregation — the failure mode that killed the reference — is not detectable by the PAINS filter or by docking.

6. Conclusion

On the true PTP1B active site (2F71, 1.55 Å), four sub- to low-nanomolar ChEMBL leads show no rank correlation with measured potency (Spearman ρ = 0.0, n = 4), and the three that out-score ertiprotafib do so by less than Vina's noise margin against a reference drug that inhibits by aggregation. The screen produces no lead claim. Its durable output is the correction: the pipeline's first run docked the wrong protein, the audit caught it, and the re-dock on the catalytic domain is the result reported. The next step is the assay in Section 4.5, with aggregation controls and a TCPTP counter-screen — the two tests that decide whether any PTP1B lead is real.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-12 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #47 (daily paper run)

Keywords: KRAS G12C; sotorasib; adagrasib; divarasib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; covalent inhibitor; switch-II pocket; drug resistance; Y96D

Abstract

KRAS G12C was the first "undruggable" oncogene to fall: the covalent switch-II pocket inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib are FDA-approved, and divarasib is in Phase I, yet acquired resistance — most often the Y96D switch-II pocket mutation — limits their benefit, and the field still ranks new candidates with non-covalent docking scores. We asked whether standardised AutoDock Vina docking on the verified KRAS G12C structure 6OIM (1.65 Å, KRAS G12C covalently bound to sotorasib) can rank five covalent inhibitors by measured potency. The LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P01116, ChEMBL, PubChem, RDKit ADMET and PAINS screen, Vina 1.2.7) failed twice at target resolution — once returning zero bioactivities, once resolving KRAS to the wrong target, maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) — so the lead set was rebuilt by direct verified queries against the correct ChEMBL target CHEMBL2189121 (4,666 activities at pChEMBL ≥ 5) plus PubChem verification of the three clinical drugs. On 6OIM, with the grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised sotorasib, Vina scored sotorasib −8.14, divarasib −8.06, adagrasib −7.58, CHEMBL4855521 −6.03 and CHEMBL4856277 −5.51 kcal/mol. The two ChEMBL leads carry the strongest measured potencies in the set — IC50 0.51 and 0.56 nM on the exact crystallised construct (KRAS G12C/C51S/C80L/C118S) — yet score worst, 2.11–2.63 kcal/mol behind sotorasib, a margin above Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. As a control, sotorasib scored −7.22 on wild-type KRAS-GDP (9IAY), which has no cysteine-12 to bind: Vina cannot see the covalent selectivity that makes the drug work. The falsifiable next step is a covalent-aware re-scoring of the same five compounds plus a same-plate biochemical assay on the 6OIM construct: if covalent docking does not restore the measured order, non-covalent scoring should be retired as a ranking tool for this target class.

1. Introduction

KRAS is the most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancer, and its glycine-12-to-cysteine mutant (G12C) occurs in approximately 12–15% of non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) and about 3% of colorectal cancers. For three decades KRAS was considered undruggable: the protein has no deep pocket in its active, GTP-bound state, and its affinity for GTP is picomolar. The breakthrough was the discovery of an inducible pocket in and around switch-II that exists only in the inactive, GDP-bound state, adjacent to the mutant cysteine-12. Covalent inhibitors that reach into that pocket and bond to Cys12 lock KRAS G12C in its inactive form. Two such drugs are now FDA-approved — sotorasib (Lumakras, accelerated approval 28 May 2021; CodeBreaK 100: objective response rate 37.1%, median overall survival 12.5 months in previously treated NSCLC) and adagrasib (Krazati, accelerated approval 12 December 2022; KRYSTAL-1: objective response rate 43%, median duration of response 8.5 months) — and a third, divarasib (GDC-6036), showed single-agent activity in its Phase I trial.

The benefit is real and time-limited. Acquired resistance is near-universal, and the on-target fraction clusters in the switch-II pocket itself: secondary mutations at R68, H95, Y96 and Q99. The Y96D substitution is the most frequently observed switch-II pocket mutation in post-progression cohorts (14% of patients in a 143-patient cohort carried a switch-II pocket mutation, Y96D the commonest), and in vitro Y96D/S confers resistance to both approved drugs, while G13D and R68M remain sensitive to adagrasib but not sotorasib, and Q99L is resistant to adagrasib but sensitive to sotorasib. The next generation of inhibitors must therefore be selected against this resistance landscape — and selection is exactly where the field's cheapest tool, docking, is least trustworthy. A 2026 benchmark (Pyrite, arXiv:2611.14511) showed that even expert chemists rank docking poses near chance, and a 2026 sequence-to-hits pipeline (ANTIOCH-VS, arXiv:2611.14287) shows how easily a screening campaign can now be launched from sequence alone — which makes the ranking step, not the generation step, the bottleneck. This paper tests that ranking step on the target where it matters most.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised non-covalent Vina protocol on the verified KRAS G12C structure 6OIM, docking scores rank covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors in the same order as their measured potencies. The test is the within-protocol ranking of five inhibitors whose measured potencies span 0.51 nM to 11 nM, including two leads measured on the exact crystallised construct.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-12 (web search; PubMed; RCSB; ChEMBL and PubChem APIs). The daily literature digest of 2026-11-12 screened 840 candidates and contributed the two methods papers framing this study (ANTIOCH-VS and Pyrite, above). Key sources: Lanman et al. 2020 for sotorasib (J Med Chem 63:52–65); Canon et al. 2019 for the 6OIM structure (Nature 575:217–223); Skoulidis et al. 2021 for CodeBreaK 100 (N Engl J Med 384:2371–2381); Hallin et al. 2020 for adagrasib (Cancer Discov 10:54–71); Sacher et al. 2023 for divarasib (N Engl J Med 389:710–721); a 2025 molecular-dynamics and biochemical study for divarasib's nucleotide-exchange potency and its Y96D sensitivity (Sci Rep 15:24843); Tanaka et al. 2021, Koga et al. 2021 and Awad et al. 2021 for acquired resistance; Whitley et al. 2026 (Nat Commun) for the structural mechanisms of switch-II pocket resistance; and Broker et al. 2025 for the 9IAY wild-type control structure (J Med Chem 68:15649–15668). Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 The pipeline run — and its two disclosed failures

The LeadForge pipeline was run twice on 2026-11-12 (UniProtKB P01116, human GTPase KRas, 189 residues; query compound sotorasib, verified in PubChem as CID 137278711, C30H30F2N6O3). Both runs failed at the same step, in two different ways, and both failures are disclosed because they determine what this paper can and cannot claim.

Failure 1 (first run): target resolution by UniProt accession returned the correct ChEMBL target (CHEMBL2189121) but the bioactivity query returned zero ligands. A direct re-query of the same endpoint minutes later returned HTTP 200 with 4,666 activities — the failure was transient ChEMBL unreliability, not absence.

Failure 2 (second run): the by-accession endpoint returned HTTP 500, so the pipeline fell back to ChEMBL text search for "KRAS", which returned maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) as its first hit — the same wrong target that corrupted the 2026-11-11 dengue paper's automatic run. The pipeline then retrieved 55 maltase-glucoamylase inhibitors (iminosugars; Tanimoto similarity to sotorasib ≈ 0.1) and docked five of them on the automatically picked structure. Those scores (best −9.12 kcal/mol) are meaningless for KRAS and are discarded; they do not appear in the results. The lesson, repeated from the 2026-11-11 centre audit: an automatic target or structure pick must be verified before any score is trusted.

2.3 The corrected benchmark

The lead set was rebuilt by direct, verified queries. ChEMBL target CHEMBL2189121 was queried for activities with pChEMBL ≥ 5 (HTTP 200; 4,666 activities). Most top hits are G12D/G12V assays, which are the wrong allele for this structure, so the set was restricted to the G12C-construct assays: the three most potent leads measured on KRAS G12C/C51S/C80L/C118S — the exact engineered construct of the 6OIM crystal structure (C51S/C80L/C118S are the structure's engineered mutations). Two could be resolved to structures: CHEMBL4855521 (IC50 0.51 nM, pChEMBL 9.29; a deuterated quinazolinone acrylamide) and CHEMBL4856277 (IC50 0.56 nM, pChEMBL 9.25). The third, CHEMBL4852458 (IC50 0.51 nM, same assay), could not be resolved: the ChEMBL molecule endpoint returned HTTP 500 on three attempts, so no SMILES is available for it. It is reported as missing, not invented. The three clinical drugs were verified in PubChem by name and CID — sotorasib CID 137278711, adagrasib CID 138611145 (C32H35ClFN7O2, MW 604.1), divarasib CID 146624881 (C29H32ClF4N7O2, MW 622.1) — and their isomeric SMILES were used for docking.

Docking used the verified structure 6OIM (KRAS G12C covalently bound to sotorasib/AMG 510, 1.65 Å; Canon et al. 2019), not the pipeline's automatic pick. The automatic pick was 9IAY (0.95 Å, "structure of 10 in complex with GDP-KRAS", Broker et al. 2025): its SEQADV records show no G12C mutation — it is wild-type KRAS-GDP in complex with a non-covalent pan-KRAS inhibitor (ligand WYU). Docking a G12C-selective covalent inhibitor into a wild-type structure is not a G12C benchmark, so 9IAY was demoted to a control: sotorasib was docked there once (score −7.22 kcal/mol, from the pipeline run) to test whether Vina can detect the drug's covalent selectivity.

On 6OIM, the grid centre was set exactly on the co-crystallised sotorasib (residue MOV, chain A, 41 atoms): centroid [1.87, −8.26, −1.36], computed with the pipeline's audited dock._ligand_center, which excludes the GDP cofactor (centroid [−6.13, 3.59, 7.31]) and waters. The audited centre was recomputed inside the docking script and matched the used centre to 0.0024 Å. Protocol, identical for all five compounds: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported.

2.4 ADMET and PAINS screen

RDKit descriptors (molecular weight, logP, hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations) and the PAINS filter were computed for all five compounds with the pipeline's chemistry module — the same code that scored the query compound in the pipeline run.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and for this target the gap is structural, not statistical: Vina is a non-covalent scorer, and all five compounds are covalent inhibitors whose potency depends on bond formation with Cys12, a term Vina cannot compute. A Vina score here measures only non-covalent shape complementarity to the switch-II pocket. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds. One rigid structure (GDP-bound, inactive) cannot represent the GTP-bound state, the switch-II ensemble, or the resistance mutants. The measured potencies in Table 1 come from different assay types (binding Ki, nucleotide exchange, cellular signalling, ChEMBL IC50), so cross-assay ranking is indicative, not exact — except for the two ChEMBL leads, which share one assay on the exact crystallised construct. No molecular dynamics, covalent docking, or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

All five compounds are PAINS-clean. All five breach Lipinski's molecular-weight or logP limits at least once — expected for switch-II pocket binders, which need size and lipophilicity to fill the pocket — so the ADMET panel does not separate them; the docking rank is the whole story.

3.2 The ranking is inverted for the most potent binders

The hypothesis fails. The two strongest measured binders in the set — CHEMBL4855521 and CHEMBL4856277, both sub-nanomolar on the exact crystallised construct — score worst by Vina (−6.03 and −5.51 kcal/mol), 2.11 and 2.63 kcal/mol behind sotorasib. That margin exceeds Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the inversion cannot be dismissed as scoring noise. Both ChEMBL leads are larger (MW 641–653 vs 561 for sotorasib) and more lipophilic (logP 5.28–5.94), with only three rotatable bonds each: their potency likely comes from a precise, rigid fit plus the covalent bond — exactly the contributions a rigid-receptor, non-covalent scorer undervalues. Within the three clinical drugs, Vina cannot separate anything: sotorasib and divarasib differ by 0.08 kcal/mol (noise), and adagrasib trails sotorasib by 0.56 kcal/mol (also noise), although divarasib's measured nucleotide-exchange potency (2.4 nM) is roughly five-fold better than sotorasib's binding Ki (11 nM) and its cellular potency is an order of magnitude better. The sotorasib re-dock (−8.14) confirms the protocol reproduces the crystal pose's pocket well; the protocol is sound — the scoring function is the problem.

3.3 The wild-type control: Vina cannot see covalent selectivity

Sotorasib scored −7.22 kcal/mol on wild-type KRAS-GDP (9IAY), which has no cysteine-12 for it to bond to — only 0.92 kcal/mol worse than its score on the G12C structure it was designed for, inside Vina's noise. A scorer that cannot distinguish the drug's true target from a protein it cannot covalently bind cannot rank candidates for this target class. The same blind spot explains Section 3.2: Vina rewards non-covalent complementarity and is silent on the covalent step that dominates measured potency.

4. Discussion

4.1 What this means for LeadForge and for the field

Every LeadForge paper to date has used the same Vina protocol as a ranking tool, and for non-covalent targets (FLT3, PPARγ, AmpC, the dengue protease) its failures were matters of noise or wrong structures — correctable by auditing. KRAS G12C is the first target in this series where the failure is in the physics: the scoring function lacks the term that matters most. Two practical consequences follow. First, any LeadForge run on a covalent target must pair Vina with a covalent-aware scorer (covalent docking, or a two-term score: non-covalent complementarity plus a warhead-reactivity term) before any ranking is reported; a Vina-only ranking for a covalent series is not a result, it is a shape contest. Second, the ChEMBL lane needs the same audit discipline as the structure lane: the pipeline's automatic target resolution failed twice in one day (a transient zero, then a wrong-target fallback to maltase-glucoamylase), and the wrong-target run produced confident-looking scores for the wrong enzyme. The fix applied here — direct verification of the ChEMBL target ID against the UniProt accession, and an allele check on the assays — should be a pipeline gate, not a manual rescue.

4.2 The literature context: ranking is the bottleneck, not generation

Today's digest makes the point from both sides. ANTIOCH-VS (Hasdemir et al. 2026) shows a complete screening campaign can now start from a protein sequence alone — generation is solved and cheap. Pyrite (Srivastava et al. 2026) shows the other side: on a 1,500-pair benchmark, even expert chemists rank docking poses near chance, and only purpose-built agents beat that bar. This paper is the same finding from inside a real campaign: the poses are easy to generate and the scores are easy to compute, and the ranking they produce is wrong for the compounds that matter most. The field's next gain is not more poses; it is scoring that knows what kind of chemistry it is scoring.

4.3 Resistance sets the bar for the next lead

The two ChEMBL leads are potent against the wild-type-pocket construct, but potency against today's pocket is not the selection criterion — survival against tomorrow's pocket is. Divarasib's nucleotide-exchange IC50 rises from 2.4 nM on G12C to 229 nM on G12C/Y96D, a ~100-fold loss from a single switch-II mutation, and Y96D is the commonest clinical resistance substitution. Whitley et al. (2026) classify the resistance mechanisms as Type I (loss of inhibitor contacts) and Type II (stabilisation of pocket-occluding switch-II conformations), with Y96D exhibiting both. A next-generation lead therefore needs either a Y96-independent contact network or a mechanism outside the switch-II pocket (the RAS(ON) tricomplex inhibitors are the live example). Neither ChEMBL lead has published resistance data; that is the first experiment to run on them, before any potency claim is repeated.

4.4 The falsifiable test

Two experiments decide whether this paper's conclusion holds. (1) Covalent-aware re-scoring: re-score the same five compounds with a covalent docking protocol (covalent bond to Cys12 modelled explicitly) on the same 6OIM structure. Prediction: the covalent-aware order restores the measured order — CHEMBL4855521 and CHEMBL4856277 at or near the top, ahead of sotorasib — while the non-covalent order reported here does not reproduce. If covalent scoring also fails to restore the order, the problem is the pocket model itself, not the covalent term. (2) Same-plate biochemical assay: measure all five compounds in one nucleotide-exchange assay on the 6OIM construct (KRAS G12C/C51S/C80L/C118S), plus the G12C/Y96D double mutant. Prediction: the two ChEMBL leads remain sub-nanomolar on G12C and lose potency on Y96D by at least an order of magnitude; sotorasib's Ki of 11 nM reproduces within two-fold. If the ChEMBL leads do not reproduce as sub-nanomolar on a shared plate, their ChEMBL numbers are assay artefacts and this paper's inversion claim falls with them.

5. Limitations

(1) Five compounds, one structure, one rigid-receptor protocol — a benchmark, not a screen. (2) Measured potencies mix assay types (Ki, nucleotide exchange, cellular signalling, ChEMBL IC50); only the two ChEMBL leads share an assay, so the cross-assay ranking is indicative. (3) The ChEMBL leads are unnamed, uncharacterised compounds from a single assay series; their structures were verified in ChEMBL but their provenance (patent vs paper) was not traced, and one sibling lead (CHEMBL4852458) could not be resolved at all because the ChEMBL molecule endpoint returned HTTP 500 three times. (4) No re-dock RMSD was computed for sotorasib against its crystal pose, so the −8.14 re-dock score is a pocket-fit check, not a pose-accuracy claim. (5) No molecular dynamics, no covalent docking, no free-energy calculation, no experiment. (6) ChEMBL was intermittently unavailable during this run (HTTP 500 on two endpoints); a re-query on another day could return additional G12C-construct leads.

6. Conclusion

On the verified KRAS G12C structure 6OIM, standardised non-covalent Vina docking ranks the two most potent measured binders last: CHEMBL4855521 and CHEMBL4856277 (ChEMBL IC50 0.51 and 0.56 nM on the crystallised construct) score −6.03 and −5.51 kcal/mol, 2.11–2.63 kcal/mol behind sotorasib (−8.14), whose measured Ki is 11 nM. Sotorasib scores nearly as well on wild-type KRAS (−7.22), which it cannot covalently bind. The hypothesis is rejected: for covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors, non-covalent Vina scores do not rank compounds by measured potency, and they should not be used as a ranking tool for this target class without a covalent-aware term. The two ChEMBL leads are genuine sub-nanomolar leads on the construct — and the next experiment is not more docking, it is a covalent re-score and a same-plate assay including the Y96D resistance mutant.
