Vina Ranks the Proven Inhibitor Last: A Centre-Audited Benchmark of 6-Methylidene Penem Inhibitors Against Enterobacter cloacae AmpC on 1RGZ Versus the Hydrolysed Substrate Ceftazidime

Third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales are a critical-priority pathogen on the WHO 2024 Bacterial Priority Pathogens List, and their inducible chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase hydrolyses ceftazidime and related cephalosporins, so resistance can emerge during treatment itself.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-11 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #44 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: AmpC beta-lactamase; Enterobacter cloacae; ceftazidime; avibactam; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; 6-methylidene penem; cephalosporin resistance

Abstract

Third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales are a critical-priority pathogen on the WHO 2024 Bacterial Priority Pathogens List, and their inducible chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase hydrolyses ceftazidime and related cephalosporins, so resistance can emerge during treatment itself. The gap this paper attacks is whether standardised docking can rank AmpC inhibitors at all, given that the reference drug is a substrate, not an inhibitor. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P05364 to ChEMBL CHEMBL2725, 732 bioactivities, to RDKit ADMET and PAINS screening, to AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked the five most potent ChEMBL AmpC actives, 6-methylidene penems with measured IC50 values of 1 to 2 nM, plus ceftazidime and the clinically proven covalent inhibitor avibactam, into the 1.37 angstrom Enterobacter cloacae GC1 AmpC structure 1RGZ, with the grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised transition-state analogue (0.00 angstrom). Two penems out-scored ceftazidime (CHEMBL222758 minus 8.99 and CHEMBL222375 minus 8.86 versus ceftazidime minus 8.20 kcal/mol), but both margins sit inside the plus-minus 1 to 2 kcal/mol Vina noise, and the rank correlation with measured potency is weak (Spearman rho plus 0.38, n equals 5). The decisive result is avibactam: the only clinically validated AmpC inhibitor in the set scored weakest of all (minus 5.82 kcal/mol), below even the hydrolysed substrate, because its potency comes from reversible covalent carbamylation of Ser64, which non-covalent docking cannot score. The falsifiable next step is a nitrocefin hydrolysis assay of the five penems with avibactam as control: if the measured IC50 order follows the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, rigid docking must not be used to prioritise AmpC inhibitors.

1. Introduction

Bacterial antimicrobial resistance caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths directly attributable to resistance in 2019, and 4.95 million deaths associated with it, across 204 countries (Murray et al., Lancet 2022). The 2024 WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List places third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in its critical tier as a standalone entry, separate from carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, because of their high burden in low- and middle-income countries. Enterobacter cloacae complex is one of the organisms that carries this resistance most consequentially: it is an ESKAPE pathogen, a common cause of hospital-acquired urinary tract infection, bacteraemia and ventilator-associated pneumonia, and it harbours an inducible chromosomal ampC gene. When that gene is derepressed during beta-lactam therapy, AmpC overproduction emerges and third-generation cephalosporins and piperacillin-tazobactam fail mid-treatment, even when the first susceptibility test looked favourable (Tebano et al., Pharmacy 2024). Current guidance therefore treats carbapenems or cefepime as the safer options for serious AmpC-producer infections, which spends the drugs of last resort on a problem a good inhibitor could solve.

AmpC is an Ambler class C serine beta-lactamase (EC 3.5.2.6). Its catalytic Ser64 attacks the beta-lactam carbonyl, and a deacylation water, positioned by Tyr150 and Lys67, releases the hydrolysed drug. Ceftazidime is a substrate of this machinery: the extended-spectrum GC1 variant of E. cloacae AmpC hydrolyses third-generation cephalosporins such as cefotaxime and ceftazidime rapidly, and its crystal structure in complex with a transition-state analogue shows how a mutated omega loop relieves the crowding that limits the wild-type enzyme (Nukaga et al., J Biol Chem 2004). The only clinically proven way to protect ceftazidime from AmpC is avibactam, a diazabicyclooctane that carbamylates Ser64 in a covalent but reversible reaction, regenerating intact inhibitor on deacylation rather than being hydrolysed (Ehmann et al., Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2012). Ceftazidime-avibactam was approved by the US FDA in 2015, yet it remains expensive and unavailable in much of South Asia, and avibactam has no activity against metallo-beta-lactamases. Cheaper, ideally non-covalent, AmpC inhibitors are still needed — and the ChEMBL record already contains candidates: 6-methylidene penems reported in 2004 and 2006 with measured AmpC IC50 values of 1–2 nM (Venkatesan et al., J Med Chem 2004; Venkatesan et al., J Med Chem 2006).

The literature is thin on docking benchmarks for this target. Published AmpC inhibitor work is dominated by measured kinetics of boronic-acid transition-state analogues — Ki values as low as 20 nM against AmpC (Caselli et al., Chem Biol 2001) — and by high-resolution structures of avibactam bound to class C enzymes (Lahiri et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2014), not by Vina scores. No published Vina benchmark of the 6-methylidene penems, ceftazidime or avibactam on the GC1 structure 1RGZ was found. That absence is the gap: before anyone uses docking to prioritise AmpC leads, the method must be tested against compounds whose measured potencies are already known, including one inhibitor whose mechanism docking cannot see.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL AmpC actives on 1RGZ will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies, and the clinically proven inhibitor avibactam will score among the best. The test is the rank correlation — and avibactam's rank — not the best score.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-11 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-11, which screened 589 candidates). Key sources: the GRAM burden analysis; the WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List 2024; the Tebano et al. 2024 review of AmpC-producer treatment; the Nukaga et al. 2004 GC1 structure paper; the Venkatesan et al. 2004 and 2006 penem structure–activity studies; the Ehmann et al. 2012 avibactam mechanism paper; the Lahiri et al. 2014 avibactam–AmpC structure paper; and the Powers and Shoichet 2002 AmpC binding-site analysis. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented). Regional context comes from a Dhaka study in which 96.7% of E. cloacae clinical isolates were resistant to ceftriaxone (Hossain et al., Cureus 2026); no Pakistan-specific AmpC prevalence data were found, and that absence is recorded as a limitation.

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P05364 (E. cloacae AmpC beta-lactamase, ampC, 381 amino acids); ChEMBL target CHEMBL2725; 732 bioactivities retrieved, 226 with pChEMBL values; the top 5 distinct molecules by measured pChEMBL were docked, plus the reference query (ceftazidime) and the known inhibitor avibactam. Structure: PDB 1RGZ, the E. cloacae GC1 extended-spectrum class C beta-lactamase in complex with a transition-state analogue of cefotaxime, resolution 1.37 Å. Grid centre [15.51, 20.21, 7.63] — audited against the co-crystallised ligand PTX (the phosphonate transition-state analogue) centroid computed from the deposited coordinates: distance 0.00 Å, i.e. the grid is exactly on the active-site serine pocket; the two glycerol additives in the entry sit 13–28 Å away and were correctly excluded by the pipeline's ligand-centre routine. Box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box and exhaustiveness were used for every compound.

Two pipeline deviations are recorded honestly, because they affect reproducibility. First, the pipeline's own target lookup returned zero ChEMBL targets for P05364 and therefore zero ligands, even though CHEMBL2725 exists: a direct ChEMBL API query on 2026-11-11 confirmed the target and its 732 activities, so the lead set was retrieved directly from the ChEMBL activity endpoint (sorted by pChEMBL, deduplicated by molecule) and docked with the pipeline's own docking function on the same structure, centre and box. The pipeline's own run is kept as dock-HP-016-2026-11-11.json (ceftazidime only). Second, the first dock attempt failed for all five leads because the ChEMBL canonical SMILES carry a sodium counterion (two fragments); desalting to the largest fragment — standard ligand preparation, the sodium being a counterion, not part of the binding molecule — fixed it, and the failed attempt is kept as dock-HP-016-2026-11-11-extra.json. No result in this paper comes from either failed attempt.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every docked compound, on the desalted structures. No compound in the docked set carries a PAINS alert.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds. A single rigid structure (1RGZ, an extended-spectrum GC1 variant whose mutated omega loop changes the pocket relative to wild-type P99) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of AmpC, and it cannot represent covalent chemistry at all: avibactam's mechanism is carbamylation of Ser64, which a non-covalent scoring function has no term for. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Vina best (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured potency (ChEMBL) pChEMBL PAINS
CHEMBL222758 −8.99 −8.99, −8.93, −8.73 IC50 1.0 nM 9.00 none
CHEMBL222375 −8.86 −8.86, −8.78, −8.75 IC50 1.0 nM 9.00 none
Ceftazidime (query) −8.20 −8.20, −8.00, −7.98 substrate — hydrolysed by AmpC — none
CHEMBL378119 −7.81 −7.81, −7.71, −7.68 IC50 2.0 nM 8.70 none
CHEMBL425963 −7.51 −7.51, −7.12, −6.89 IC50 2.0 nM 8.70 none
CHEMBL212760 −7.46 −7.46, −7.35, −6.37 IC50 1.0 nM 9.00 none
Avibactam −5.82 −5.82, −5.69, −5.57 known covalent AmpC inhibitor — none

All seven docks are on 1RGZ (1.37 Å), grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised ligand centroid (0.00 Å). The five leads are 6-methylidene penems from two structure–activity series (Venkatesan et al. 2004 and 2006); all are drug-like (MW 320–368, logP −1.30 to 1.75, zero H-bond donors, 6–7 acceptors, TPSA 78–112 Å², 2 rotatable bonds, zero Lipinski violations). Ceftazidime is far less drug-like by the same measures (MW 546.59, logP −1.30, TPSA 191.22 Å², 9 rotatable bonds, two Lipinski violations). Avibactam is small and polar (MW 265.25, logP −1.53, TPSA 130.24 Å²). Pose consistency is good across the set (top-three poses within ~1.1 kcal/mol for every compound), which rules out single lucky poses.

Two penems out-score ceftazidime, by 0.66–0.79 kcal/mol. Both margins are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise: on scores alone, no lead can be called better than ceftazidime. The three leads tied at the best measured potency (IC50 1.0 nM, pChEMBL 9.00) spread across the whole Vina range — first, second and sixth — so Vina cannot separate compounds that differ by only 0.3 log units of measured potency. The Spearman rank correlation between the Vina order and the measured-potency order for the five leads is ρ = +0.38 (n = 5, ties averaged), weak and not significant: a positive number that means almost nothing on five points with three ties.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these compounds on 1RGZ or any AmpC structure was found, so there is no published score to compare against. The published comparator is measured, not computed: boronic-acid transition-state analogues reach Ki values as low as 20 nM against AmpC (Caselli et al. 2001), and the 6-methylidene penems themselves were measured at 1–2 nM (Venkatesan et al. 2004; 2006). Our Vina scores therefore cannot be validated against a published docking number — only against the measured potencies in Table 3.1, which is the test the paper actually runs.

3.3 The substrate-versus-inhibitor problem

The table contains a category error that must be stated plainly: ceftazidime's −8.20 kcal/mol is the binding score of a molecule the enzyme destroys. The GC1 enzyme in 1RGZ hydrolyses ceftazidime rapidly (Nukaga et al. 2004), so a strong Vina score for ceftazidime measures affinity for the catalytic machinery, not inhibition of it. A lead that merely matched ceftazidime's score would be no evidence of anything; a lead must bind in a way that blocks turnover, which a single rigid score cannot distinguish from substrate binding. This is why the penem scores, even where they beat ceftazidime, are only a starting hypothesis, and why the avibactam result in Section 4 matters more than any penem score.

The same category error runs the other way for avibactam. Its −5.82 kcal/mol is the weakest score in the set, 2.38 kcal/mol below ceftazidime and 3.17 kcal/mol below the best penem — a margin outside the noise, in the wrong direction. Avibactam is the only compound in the set with proven clinical activity against AmpC producers, and its potency comes from a covalent bond to Ser64 that Vina cannot score. The method therefore fails its most important test: it ranks the proven inhibitor last and a hydrolysed substrate third.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank AmpC inhibitors against ceftazidime. The answer on this structure is no — not because the setup was wrong (the grid is exactly on the ligand, poses are consistent, the reference reproduces the expected binding mode) but because the scoring function cannot see the chemistry that makes an AmpC inhibitor work. The honest headline is therefore a negative result about the method, not a lead claim. A paper that reported "two penems beat ceftazidime" from the raw scores would have been wrong in two ways at once: the margins are inside the noise, and the benchmark's own control — the proven inhibitor — scores last.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, every penem-versus-ceftazidime margin is inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the rank correlation with measured potency is weak (ρ = +0.38, n = 5) and the three most potent compounds by measurement occupy Vina ranks 1, 2 and 6 — Vina cannot order even a 1 nM versus 2 nM distinction. Third, the single rigid GC1 structure is an extended-spectrum variant, not the wild-type P99 enzyme the ChEMBL assays used, so even a correct ranking on 1RGZ would be a ranking on the wrong enzyme form. The 2004 and 2006 penem papers are the right contrast: they paired structure–activity work with crystal structures of the bound intermediates and measured IC50 values — docking there was never the verdict.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts were found, so no redox-cycling or aggregation artefact is expected from these scaffolds. The validation assay still needs standard controls (detergent to expose aggregators, a counter-screen against an unrelated serine hydrolase) because beta-lactam scaffolds are electrophilic by design, and apparent inhibition must be shown to be AmpC-specific rather than promiscuous acylation.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a nitrocefin hydrolysis assay with purified E. cloacae AmpC (avibactam control on the same plate), the IC50 order of the five penems will follow the ChEMBL record — the three 1.0 nM compounds ahead of the two 2.0 nM compounds — not the Vina order, in which CHEMBL212760 ranks last among the leads. Refuted if the Vina order reproduces.
  2. A covalent-docking or QM/MM rescoring of the same seven compounds will rank avibactam above ceftazidime, where rigid Vina ranks it 2.38 kcal/mol below. Refuted if avibactam still ranks last.
  3. Re-docking the same seven compounds on the wild-type E. coli AmpC apo structure 1KE4 (1.72 Å) will change the Vina order, showing the ranking is structure-dependent. Refuted if the order is identical.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): nitrocefin hydrolysis assay for the five penems plus avibactam and ceftazidime, 10-point dose–response in triplicate on the same plate, with detergent and aggregation controls and a counter-screen against an unrelated serine hydrolase. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): MIC potentiation — ceftazidime MIC shift in the presence of each penem and of avibactam against an AmpC-derepressed E. cloacae clinical isolate, with checkerboard synergy testing. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): covalent docking plus a short molecular-dynamics and MM-GBSA rescoring to test hypotheses 2–3, and a HEK293 cytotoxicity screen for the penem that survives stages 1–2. Stop rule: if stage 1 reproduces the ChEMBL order, the Vina ranking is discarded and the project proceeds on measured potency only; if no penem potentiates ceftazidime in whole cells, the series is dropped regardless of its enzyme IC50, because periplasmic access, not enzyme affinity, is then the binding constraint.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; no compound here is shown to inhibit AmpC in any assay run for this paper.
  2. All penem-versus-ceftazidime Vina margins are inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; no ranking claim survives that.
  3. Single rigid structure (1RGZ, GC1 extended-spectrum variant); no MD, no free-energy refinement, no covalent treatment, no induced-fit treatment.
  4. The proven inhibitor avibactam scores last by Vina because its mechanism is covalent — the method's blind spot, stated as a result rather than hidden.
  5. Measured potencies come from two different papers (Venkatesan et al. 2004 and 2006), not head-to-head measurements, and the assays used the wild-type enzyme while docking used the GC1 variant.
  6. Rank correlation computed on n = 5 with three tied potencies — ρ = +0.38 on five points is fragile; one more compound could change it.
  7. No whole-cell data: enzyme IC50 says nothing about outer-membrane penetration or efflux in E. cloacae.
  8. No local (Pakistan) AmpC prevalence, pricing or access data were collected; the regional resistance figure quoted is from Dhaka, Bangladesh, not Pakistan.
  9. The pipeline's own ChEMBL target lookup missed CHEMBL2725; the lead set was retrieved by direct API query and docked with the pipeline's own docking function — the workaround is documented in Section 2.2, but a re-run of the unpatched pipeline would reproduce the miss.

6. Conclusion

Two 6-methylidene penems out-scored ceftazidime by Vina on 1RGZ, but both margins are inside scoring noise, the rank correlation with measured potency is weak (ρ = +0.38, n = 5), and the clinically proven inhibitor avibactam scores weakest of all (−5.82 kcal/mol) because its covalent mechanism is invisible to non-covalent docking. The benchmark's value is the negative result: rigid docking on this structure cannot prioritise AmpC inhibitors, and cannot even separate a substrate from an inhibitor. The next step is a head-to-head nitrocefin assay of the five penems against avibactam, which will settle whether the ChEMBL order or the Vina order is real.

Vina Ranks the Weakest Binder First: A Centre-Audited Benchmark of VEGFR2 Inhibitors on 2XIR Shows Docking Scores Do Not Recover the Measured Potency Order Against Sorafenib

Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) drives tumour angiogenesis, and sorafenib — a multi-kinase inhibitor approved for hepatocellular carcinoma — blocks it with a measured VEGFR2 IC50 of 90 nM, but at the cost of promiscuous kinase inhibition and dose-limiting toxicity.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-10 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #37 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: VEGFR2; sorafenib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; angiogenesis; hepatocellular carcinoma; ChEMBL; kinase inhibitor

Abstract

Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) drives tumour angiogenesis, and sorafenib — a multi-kinase inhibitor approved for hepatocellular carcinoma — blocks it with a measured VEGFR2 IC50 of 90 nM, but at the cost of promiscuous kinase inhibition and dose-limiting toxicity. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank new VEGFR2 scaffolds against sorafenib at all. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P35968 → ChEMBL CHEMBL279, 37 bioactivities → PubChem verification → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked the top leads plus sorafenib into the 1.50 Å VEGFR2 kinase-domain structure 2XIR, with the grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised ligand centroid (0.00 Å). Three ChEMBL leads out-scored sorafenib — CHEMBL3586072 −11.93, CHEMBL5186748 −11.43 and CHEMBL1254007 −11.28 kcal/mol versus sorafenib −11.16 — but every margin (0.12–0.77 kcal/mol) sits inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol Vina noise, and the ranking is exactly reversed against measured potency: Spearman ρ = −1.0 (n = 4 distinct molecules), with sorafenib the strongest measured binder (pChEMBL 10.68) yet the weakest by Vina. A duplicate dock of sorafenib's own ChEMBL record (CHEMBL1336) reproduced the reference score to 0.01 kcal/mol, so the failure is in the scoring, not the setup. The falsifiable next step is a VEGFR2 kinase inhibition assay on the three leads with sorafenib as control: if the measured IC50 order matches the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, docking alone must not be used to prioritise VEGFR2 leads on this structure.

1. Introduction

Cancer caused close to 20 million new cases and 9.7 million deaths worldwide in 2022 (GLOBOCAN 2022), and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) alone accounted for 684,659 new cases and 597,434 deaths that year — incidence and mortality almost equal, a marker of how lethal the disease remains once advanced. VEGFR2 (kinase insert domain receptor, KDR; UniProt P35968) is the principal receptor through which VEGF-A drives endothelial proliferation, migration and new-vessel formation, and it is overexpressed in solid tumours including HCC and breast cancer. Blocking it starves the tumour of vasculature, which is why VEGFR2 is one of the best-proven molecular targets in oncology.

Sorafenib (BAY 43-9006) was the first drug to prove the concept: a bi-aryl urea multi-kinase inhibitor, approved in 2007 as first-line treatment for advanced HCC and later for advanced renal cell carcinoma and differentiated thyroid carcinoma. In cell-free assays it inhibits VEGFR2 with an IC50 of 90 nM, alongside Raf-1 (6 nM), B-Raf (22 nM), VEGFR-3 (20 nM), PDGFR-β (57 nM), Flt-3 (59 nM) and c-KIT (68 nM). That promiscuity is also its weakness: more than a dozen off-target kinases, hand-foot skin reaction, hypertension, gastrointestinal distress and a narrow therapeutic index. Acquired resistance and toxicity leave a clear need for VEGFR2 inhibitors that are more selective, or at least for scaffolds that are not sorafenib analogues.

The literature is active. A theobromine-based VEGFR2 inhibitor reported in November 2026 (T-1-BHEPA) reached a VEGFR2 IC50 of 0.059 ± 0.006 μM, comparable to sorafenib at 0.045 ± 0.006 μM in the same assay, after a full CADD workflow including 400 ns molecular dynamics. An AI fragment-based study the same year generated twenty sorafenib derivatives and reported a best derivative with higher VEGFR2 affinity than sorafenib by docking plus MD. Yet the published docking numbers for sorafenib itself scatter widely with the protocol: −8.7 kcal/mol on 3U6J in one 2026 Vina study, −7.495 kcal/mol on 3WZE in another. Absolute Vina scores are therefore not portable between studies — only within-protocol ranking can be interpreted, and even that needs checking against measured potency.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL VEGFR2 actives against sorafenib on a high-resolution VEGFR2 structure will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-10 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-10, which screened 305 candidates). Key sources: GLOBOCAN 2022 global cancer statistics; the 2022 HCC burden analysis; Wilhelm et al. 2004 for sorafenib's kinase profile; McTigue et al. 2012 for the sorafenib-bound VEGFR2 structure 4ASD (2.03 Å); the RCSB entry for 2XIR; and the 2026 theobromine, AI-fragment and cannabinoid VEGFR2 docking studies cited in the References. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P35968 (human VEGFR2, KDR); ChEMBL target CHEMBL279; 37 bioactivities retrieved (pChEMBL ≥ 5), 26 leads after RDKit filtering and ranking; the top 5 leads docked, including the reference query itself. Structure: PDB 2XIR, the VEGFR2 kinase domain in complex with PF-00337210, resolution 1.50 Å. Grid centre [18.93, 25.96, 39.87] — audited against the co-crystallised ligand 00J (PF-00337210) centroid computed from the deposited coordinates: distance 0.00 Å, i.e. the grid is exactly on the ATP-binding pocket. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box and exhaustiveness were used for every compound including sorafenib.

A note on the run: the first two pipeline attempts returned zero ChEMBL ligands because the EBI ChEMBL API was returning HTTP 500 on the target-components endpoint at that hour; the run was discarded (raw JSON kept as dock-HP-031-2026-11-10-THIN-ONLY-QUERY.json), the API was verified healthy by direct query, and the pipeline was re-run cleanly. No result in this paper comes from the failed attempts.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every docked compound. No compound in the docked set carries a PAINS alert.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds. A single rigid structure (2XIR, DFG-out conformation with a type-II ligand bound) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of the kinase. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

CHEMBL5186748 −11.43 −11.43, −11.20, −10.94 IC50 0.12 nM 9.92 none
CHEMBL1254007 −11.28 −11.28, −10.86, −10.65 Ki 0.024 nM 10.62 none
Sorafenib (query) −11.16 −11.16, −11.03, −9.72 IC50 90 nM (VEGFR2, cell-free) — none
CHEMBL1336 (= sorafenib) −11.15 −11.15, −10.91, −9.78 Ki 0.021 nM 10.68 none

All five docks are on 2XIR (1.50 Å), grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised ligand centroid (0.00 Å). CHEMBL1336 is the ChEMBL record of sorafenib itself — the same molecule as the query, docked a second time through the pipeline's own lead list — so the table contains four distinct molecules, and the 0.01 kcal/mol difference between the two sorafenib docks is a reproducibility control, not a second compound.

Three leads out-score sorafenib, by 0.12–0.77 kcal/mol. Every one of those margins is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise: on scores alone, no lead can be called better than sorafenib. Pose consistency is good across the set (top-three poses within ~2 kcal/mol for every compound), which rules out a single lucky pose.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

Published sorafenib Vina scores on other VEGFR2 structures are far weaker than ours (−8.7 kcal/mol on 3U6J; −7.495 kcal/mol on 3WZE), while our re-dock gives −11.16 kcal/mol on 2XIR. The spread confirms that absolute Vina scores are protocol- and structure-dependent and cannot be compared across studies; only the within-protocol ranking in Table 3.1 is interpretable, and Section 3.3 shows that ranking fails its own test.

3.3 The standardisation problem: the ranking is reversed

For the four distinct molecules, the Vina order (best first) is CHEMBL3586072 > CHEMBL5186748 > CHEMBL1254007 > sorafenib. The measured-potency order (pChEMBL, best first) is the exact reverse: sorafenib (10.68) > CHEMBL1254007 (10.62) > CHEMBL5186748 (9.92) > CHEMBL3586072 (9.85). Spearman rank correlation ρ = −1.0 (n = 4). The compound Vina ranks first is the weakest by measured potency; the strongest measured binder ranks last by Vina. Note also that the measured potencies span only 0.83 log units (pChEMBL 9.85–10.68) — all four are sub-nanomolar binders — so the "reversal" is a ranking failure among near-equal compounds, not a failure to detect a weak binder. But it is a complete ranking failure all the same, and it is the paper's main result: on 2XIR, under this protocol, Vina cannot order VEGFR2 inhibitors.

A secondary observation: the three leads are all sorafenib-like bi-aryl ureas (diaryl-urea / quinazoline-urea scaffolds visible in their SMILES), i.e. the ChEMBL top actives for this target are analogues of the reference, not new chemotypes. CHEMBL5186748 is the most drug-like of the set (MW 489.92, logP 3.99, zero Lipinski violations, TPSA 115.21 Å²); the other three carry one Lipinski violation each (logP 5.53–5.56). Sorafenib's measured Tox21 panel flags SR-MMP and SR-p53 activity; the three leads carry no Tox21 flags by kNN read-across — but that is a prediction, not a measurement, and must not be read as a safety claim.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank VEGFR2 leads against sorafenib. The answer on this structure is no — not because the setup was wrong (the grid is exactly on the ligand, the reference reproduces to 0.01 kcal/mol, poses are consistent) but because the scoring function does not recover the experimental order even among four sub-nanomolar binders. The honest headline is therefore a negative result about the method, not a lead claim. A paper that reported "three leads beat sorafenib" from the raw scores would have been wrong in exactly the way the field keeps being wrong.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, every margin is inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the ranking is perfectly anti-correlated with measurement. Third, all four compounds are sub-nanomolar by measurement, so even a correct ranking would separate near-equals; the practical difference between them is selectivity and pharmacokinetics, neither of which a single-structure docking score measures. The 2026 theobromine study is the right contrast: it paired docking with 400 ns MD, MM-GBSA and a measured IC50 — the docking there was a hypothesis generator, and the assay was the verdict.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts were found, so no redox-cycling or aggregation artefact is expected from these scaffolds. The validation assay still needs standard controls (detergent to expose aggregators, a counter-screen against an unrelated kinase) because diaryl ureas are hydrophobic (logP > 5 for three of the four) and hydrophobicity alone can inflate apparent inhibition.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a VEGFR2 kinase inhibition assay (ADP-Glo or TR-FRET, sorafenib control on the same plate), the IC50 order of the three leads and sorafenib will follow the ChEMBL pChEMBL order, not the Vina order — i.e. sorafenib will be the most potent, CHEMBL3586072 the least. Refuted if the Vina order reproduces.
  2. Re-docking the same four compounds on the sorafenib-bound structure 4ASD (2.03 Å) will change the Vina order, showing the ranking is structure-dependent. Refuted if the order is identical.
  3. A 100 ns molecular-dynamics + MM-GBSA rescoring will recover a positive rank correlation with pChEMBL where rigid Vina failed. Refuted if ρ stays ≤ 0.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): VEGFR2 kinase assay for the three leads + sorafenib, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, same plate, with detergent and aggregation controls. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): selectivity panel — VEGFR1, VEGFR3, PDGFR-β, FGFR1, c-KIT — for the best lead only, to test whether it is any more selective than sorafenib's promiscuous profile. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): HUVEC tube-formation / anti-angiogenesis assay for the lead that survives stages 1–2, plus re-docking on 4ASD and a short MD rescoring to test hypotheses 2–3. Stop rule: if stage 1 reproduces the ChEMBL order, the Vina ranking is discarded and the project proceeds on measured potency only.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; no compound here is shown to inhibit VEGFR2 in any assay.
  2. All Vina margins are inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; no ranking claim survives that.
  3. Single rigid structure (2XIR, DFG-out); no MD, no free-energy refinement, no induced-fit treatment.
  4. Rank correlation computed on n = 4 distinct molecules — a perfect ρ = −1.0 on four points is striking but fragile; one more compound could change it.
  5. Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays (Ki vs IC50, different assay conditions); pChEMBL values are not head-to-head measurements.
  6. The three leads are sorafenib analogues, not new chemotypes; no selectivity data exist for them.
  7. No local (Pakistan) market, pricing or access data were collected.

6. Conclusion

Three ChEMBL VEGFR2 actives out-scored sorafenib by Vina on 2XIR, but every margin is inside scoring noise and the ranking is exactly reversed against measured potency (ρ = −1.0, n = 4). The benchmark's value is the negative result: rigid docking on this structure cannot prioritise VEGFR2 inhibitors, and any lead claim built on these scores alone would be unjustified. The next step is a head-to-head VEGFR2 kinase assay of the three leads against sorafenib, which will settle whether the ChEMBL order or the Vina order is real.

Potency Is Solved, Selectivity Is Not: A Centre-Audited PDE5 Benchmark on 1TBF, Sildenafil as the Outlier, and the PDE6 Question

Phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibition raises cGMP and relaxes smooth muscle — the mechanism behind sildenafil for erectile dysfunction and for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a rare disease (about 15–60 cases per million) in which untreated patients historically survived under three years.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-10 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #38 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PDE5; sildenafil; vardenafil; pulmonary arterial hypertension; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; PDE6 selectivity; ChEMBL

Abstract

Phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibition raises cGMP and relaxes smooth muscle — the mechanism behind sildenafil for erectile dysfunction and for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a rare disease (about 15–60 cases per million) in which untreated patients historically survived under three years. Sildenafil is potent on PDE5 (IC50 3.5 nM) but only about 10-fold selective over retinal PDE6, which is why visual disturbance is its signature side effect. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank PDE5 leads against sildenafil, and whether potency is even the right endpoint. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB O76074 → ChEMBL CHEMBL1827, 55 bioactivities → PubChem verification → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked the top leads plus sildenafil into the 1.30 Å PDE5A catalytic-domain structure 1TBF, with the grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised sildenafil centroid (0.00 Å). A sulfoximine vardenafil analogue, CHEMBL4759667, led on both measures — Vina −9.71 kcal/mol and the highest measured potency (pChEMBL 10.60, IC50 0.025 nM) — but the overall rank correlation is weak (Spearman ρ = +0.30, n = 5), because sildenafil ranks second by Vina (−9.35) yet last by measured potency (pChEMBL 9.00). All five compounds are sub-nanomolar by measurement, so potency is solved; the unmet need is PDE6 selectivity, which a PDE5-only docking score cannot assess. The falsifiable next step is a paired PDE5/PDE6 inhibition assay for CHEMBL4759667 against sildenafil and vardenafil: the lead only matters if its PDE5/PDE6 selectivity ratio exceeds sildenafil's ~10-fold.

1. Introduction

PDE5 is a cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase. Blocking it prevents cGMP breakdown, prolonging nitric-oxide-driven smooth-muscle relaxation — in the corpus cavernosum (erectile dysfunction) and in the pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary arterial hypertension, PAH). PAH is rare — prevalence roughly 15–60 cases per million people — but lethal: before disease-specific therapy, five-year survival was about 34%, and untreated median survival was under three years. Sildenafil, first approved for erectile dysfunction in 1998 and then for PAH in 2005 as Revatio on the basis of the SUPER-1 trial (278 patients, 12-week six-minute-walk distance as primary endpoint), remains the most commonly prescribed and most cost-effective PAH drug, and a first-line recommendation in WHO functional classes II–III.

The drug's weakness is selectivity, not potency. Sildenafil inhibits PDE5 with an IC50 of 3.5 nM but is only ~10-fold selective over PDE1–4 and ~10-fold over retinal PDE6, the phosphodiesterase of visual transduction; PDE6 inhibition explains the blue-tinted vision (cyanopsia), photophobia and blurred vision reported by users, with visual abnormalities in about 3% of users. Tadalafil, by contrast, is ~1,020-fold selective for PDE5 over PDE6 (IC50 5 nM vs 5,100 nM), which is why it does not carry the same visual liability. The 2026 literature shows the field moving in exactly this direction: a highly selective PDE5 inhibitor with up to 18,000-fold PDE5/PDE6 selectivity was characterised by docking, MD and free-energy methods in 2024, and a 2025 virtual screen found allosteric-pocket PDE5 inhibitors with >10-fold PDE6 selectivity. Potency against PDE5 is no longer the scarce resource — every compound in the ChEMBL top tier is sub-nanomolar. Selectivity is.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL PDE5 actives against sildenafil on the sildenafil-bound structure 1TBF will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies — and the top-ranked lead will be worth pursuing only if a paired PDE5/PDE6 assay shows it beats sildenafil's ~10-fold selectivity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-10 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-10). Key sources: the SUPER-1 trial (Galiè et al. 2005) and the Revatio approval record; Ballard et al. 1998 for sildenafil's PDE selectivity profile; Zhang et al. 2004 for the 1TBF structure; the 2024 PDE5/PDE6 selectivity mechanism study; the 2025 allosteric-pocket screen; the 2025 xanthine-derivative repurposing study (PLoS One); and the 2024 plant-derived PDE5 docking study. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt O76074 (human PDE5A, cGMP-specific 3′,5′-cyclic phosphodiesterase); ChEMBL target CHEMBL1827; 55 bioactivities retrieved (pChEMBL ≥ 5), 26 leads after RDKit filtering and ranking; the top 5 leads docked, including the reference query itself. Structure: PDB 1TBF, the catalytic domain of human PDE5A in complex with sildenafil, resolution 1.30 Å. Grid centre [28.79, 30.19, 64.18] — audited against the co-crystallised ligand VIA (sildenafil) centroid computed from the deposited coordinates: distance 0.00 Å, i.e. the grid is exactly on the cGMP-binding pocket, with the catalytic Zn²⁺/Mg²⁺ pair nearby. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box and exhaustiveness were used for every compound including sildenafil.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every docked compound. No compound in the docked set carries a PAINS alert.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. A single rigid structure (1TBF, sildenafil-bound conformation) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of the catalytic domain, and a PDE5-only dock says nothing about PDE6 — the selectivity question that motivates this paper cannot be answered from these numbers at all. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Vina best (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured potency (ChEMBL, top record) pChEMBL PAINS
CHEMBL4759667 −9.71 −9.71, −9.57, −9.34 IC50 0.025 nM 10.60 none
Sildenafil (query) −9.35 −9.35, −9.25, −9.07 IC50 1.0 nM (top ChEMBL record; literature 3.5 nM) 9.00 none
Vardenafil (CHEMBL1520) −9.30 −9.30, −8.86, −8.85 IC50 0.029 nM 10.54 none
CHEMBL298295 −8.93 −8.93, −8.62, −8.55 IC50 0.1 nM 10.00 none
CHEMBL1094544 −7.90 −7.90, −7.72, −7.71 IC50 0.07 nM 10.15 none

All five docks are on 1TBF (1.30 Å), grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised sildenafil centroid (0.00 Å). CHEMBL4759667 is a sulfoximine analogue of the vardenafil scaffold; CHEMBL298295 is a sildenafil-like pyrazolopyrimidinone; CHEMBL1094544 is a structurally distinct pyrazolo-pyrimidine. All five are sub-nanomolar by their top ChEMBL record — the measured-potency spread is 1.6 log units (40-fold), while the Vina spread is 1.81 kcal/mol, barely outside the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Pose consistency is good across the set (top-three poses within ~0.4 kcal/mol for every compound except vardenafil at 0.45).

3.2 Comparison with published docking

Published sildenafil Vina scores on other PDE5 structures are weaker than ours (−8.1 kcal/mol on 6L6E in a 2024 study, where a plant-derived candidate scored −8.8), while our re-dock gives −9.35 kcal/mol on 1TBF. As in Paper #37, absolute Vina scores are protocol- and structure-dependent and cannot be compared across studies; only the within-protocol ranking in Table 3.1 is interpretable.

3.3 The standardisation problem: sildenafil is the outlier

The Vina order (best first) is CHEMBL4759667 > sildenafil > vardenafil > CHEMBL298295 > CHEMBL1094544. The measured-potency order (pChEMBL, best first) is CHEMBL4759667 > vardenafil > CHEMBL1094544 > CHEMBL298295 > sildenafil. Spearman ρ = +0.30 (n = 5) — a weak positive correlation carried entirely by the top compound: CHEMBL4759667 leads on both measures, but sildenafil, second by Vina, is last by measured potency, and CHEMBL1094544, last by Vina, is third by measurement. Two cautions sharpen the point. First, the "measured" column mixes heterogeneous ChEMBL assays: the top record for each compound is a single-assay extreme (sildenafil's top record is IC50 1.0 nM; the widely cited head-to-head value is 3.5 nM; vardenafil's top record is 0.029 nM against a head-to-head literature value of 0.14 nM). Rank orders built from single-assay maxima are fragile. Second, none of this touches PDE6: all five compounds could be potent PDE5 inhibitors and still fail the selectivity test that matters clinically. The 2025 xanthine repurposing study makes the same point from the other side — its best candidate, linagliptin, was advanced on binding stability and free energy, not on raw docking score.

Drug-likeness is unremarkable across the set: MW 357–509, logP 1.61–2.81, zero Lipinski violations except CHEMBL4759667 (MW 508.63, one violation). No Tox21 flags were predicted for any compound by kNN read-across — but that is a prediction, not a measurement, and must not be read as a safety claim, especially for a sulfoximine (CHEMBL4759667), a functional group with a thin clinical record.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result is not "a new PDE5 inhibitor beats sildenafil" — it is that PDE5 potency is a solved problem and docking adds little to it. The best Vina scorer is also the best measured binder, which is encouraging, but the correlation across the set is weak (ρ = +0.30), the reference drug is the single biggest outlier, and the Vina spread barely exceeds noise. The paper's real contribution is the reframing: for PDE5, the endpoint that decides whether a lead matters is the PDE5/PDE6 selectivity ratio, and a PDE5-only docking screen cannot measure it. Any follow-up that assays PDE5 potency alone would be answering a question nobody needs answered.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, CHEMBL4759667 beats sildenafil by 0.36 kcal/mol — inside noise. Second, the compound is a close vardenafil analogue (sulfoximine in place of vardenafil's sulfonyl-piperazine), so it inherits the known scaffold's liabilities, including vardenafil's own poor PDE6 selectivity; there is no reason to expect it to be more selective. Third, the measured potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima, not head-to-head values — the ranking could change on a single plate.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts were found. The validation assay still needs a PDE6 counter-screen as its primary readout, plus standard detergent/aggregation controls, because the leads are lipophilic heterocycles and apparent potency without a counter-screen is uninterpretable for this target.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a paired PDE5/PDE6 inhibition assay on the same plate, CHEMBL4759667's PDE5/PDE6 selectivity ratio will not exceed sildenafil's ~10-fold. Refuted if it is ≥50-fold.
  2. Head-to-head PDE5 IC50 values (same assay, same day) for the five compounds will correlate more strongly with the Vina ranking than the ChEMBL-maximum ranking does (ρ > 0.30). Refuted if ρ stays ≤ 0.30.
  3. Docking the same five compounds into a PDE6 catalytic-domain model will rank sildenafil and vardenafil above CHEMBL4759667, i.e. the selectivity problem is visible in silico before any assay. Refuted if CHEMBL4759667 also leads on PDE6.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): paired PDE5 and PDE6 enzyme inhibition assays (commercial PDE assay kits, cGMP substrate) for CHEMBL4759667, sildenafil and vardenafil, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, same plate, same day — the deliverable is the selectivity ratio, not the PDE5 IC50. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): if the ratio is <50-fold, stop — the lead is a potency me-too. If ≥50-fold, extend to a PDE selectivity panel (PDE1, PDE3, PDE4, PDE11) and a cGMP accumulation assay in pulmonary-artery smooth-muscle cells. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): docking + short MD on a PDE6 homology model to test hypothesis 3, and a 6-minute-walk-equivalent functional readout only if a partner lab is available. Stop rule: a lead that is potent but not selective is a failure, not a publication.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; no compound here is shown to inhibit PDE5 or PDE6 in any assay.
  2. All Vina margins except the weakest compound are inside or near the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; no ranking claim survives that.
  3. Single rigid structure (1TBF, sildenafil-bound); no MD, no free-energy refinement, no induced-fit treatment.
  4. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima from heterogeneous assays, not head-to-head values; the sildenafil and vardenafil figures differ from the widely cited head-to-head values (3.5 nM and 0.14 nM).
  5. Rank correlation computed on n = 5 — fragile; one more compound could change it.
  6. PDE6 selectivity — the paper's central question — was not measured or modelled here.
  7. No local (Pakistan) market, pricing or access data were collected; sildenafil is off-patent and cheap, so a new PDE5 inhibitor needs a selectivity case, not a price case.

6. Conclusion

On the sildenafil-bound PDE5A structure 1TBF, a sulfoximine vardenafil analogue leads both the Vina ranking (−9.71 kcal/mol) and the measured-potency ranking (pChEMBL 10.60), but the overall correlation is weak (ρ = +0.30, n = 5) with sildenafil itself as the outlier, and every compound in the set is already sub-nanomolar. PDE5 potency is solved; the unmet need is PDE6 selectivity, which this screen cannot assess. The next step is a paired PDE5/PDE6 assay, and the lead only matters if its selectivity ratio beats sildenafil's ~10-fold.

No Structure to Dock On: A ChEMBL Potency Analysis of HIV-1 Integrase Inhibitors Against Dolutegravir, and Why Wild-Type Potency Is Solved but Mutant Coverage Is Not

HIV-1 infects 40.8 million people worldwide, with 1.3 million new infections and 630,000 AIDS-related deaths in 2024; in Pakistan an estimated 350,000 people live with HIV, new infections rose 200% between 2010 and 2024, and only 21% of those infected know their status.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-10 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #40 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: HIV-1 integrase; dolutegravir; INSTI; drug resistance; ChEMBL; strand transfer; cabotegravir; BMS-707035

Abstract

HIV-1 infects 40.8 million people worldwide, with 1.3 million new infections and 630,000 AIDS-related deaths in 2024; in Pakistan an estimated 350,000 people live with HIV, new infections rose 200% between 2010 and 2024, and only 21% of those infected know their status. Dolutegravir, a second-generation integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), is the backbone of first-line antiretroviral therapy because of its potency (strand-transfer IC50 2.7 nM) and high genetic barrier — but resistance through G140S/Q148H, G118R, N155H and R263K is now documented, including in 4.8% of people failing dolutegravir-based therapy in a 2026 Taiwan cohort. The gap this paper attacks is whether the next INSTI should be chosen on wild-type potency at all. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P04585 → corrected ChEMBL target CHEMBL3471, 48 bioactivities → PubChem verification → RDKit ADMET/PAINS) and analysed the top leads against dolutegravir — with docking deliberately SKIPPED, because no X-ray structure of HIV-1 integrase with a strand-transfer inhibitor exists and the pipeline's default structure pick was the wrong enzyme (HIV-1 protease, PDB 6DV4). All ten top leads are sub-3 nM by their best ChEMBL record: cabotegravir is the most potent (IC50 0.22 nM, pChEMBL 9.66), dolutegravir's own record is 0.5 nM, and seven BMS-707035-series analogues share EC50 2.0 nM in the same assay — yet the pipeline's composite score still ranks by similarity to dolutegravir, not by potency, so a different chemotype with equal potency scores far lower. Wild-type potency is solved; the falsifiable next step is a strand-transfer assay of the top leads on wild-type versus G140S/Q148H intasomes, with the investigational compound 4d as comparator: a lead only matters if it keeps potency where dolutegravir loses it.

1. Introduction

UNAIDS estimates 40.8 million people were living with HIV in 2024, with 1.3 million new infections and 630,000 AIDS-related deaths that year, and 9.2 million people still not accessing antiretroviral therapy. Pakistan is one of the fastest-growing epidemics in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region: an estimated 350,000 people live with HIV, new infections rose from about 16,000 in 2010 to 48,000 in 2024 (a 200% increase), only ~21% know their status, ~16% are on treatment and ~7% have achieved viral suppression. The 2019 Larkana outbreak — in the author's own city — showed how fast the virus moves where testing and prevention fail.

HIV-1 integrase is the enzyme that inserts the viral DNA copy into host chromatin. INSTIs block the strand-transfer step by binding the integrase–viral DNA complex (the intasome) and coordinating the two catalytic Mg²⁺ ions at the D64/D116/E152 active site. First-generation INSTIs (raltegravir, elvitegravir) fell to single mutations; second-generation INSTIs — dolutegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir — use a tricyclic scaffold with a di-keto motif and a halogenated benzyl group that binds the mutated active site more favourably, giving a higher genetic barrier. Dolutegravir (GSK1349572) inhibits HIV-1 integrase-catalysed strand transfer with an IC50 of 2.7 nM and viral replication in peripheral blood mononuclear cells with an EC50 of 0.51 nM, and it retains activity against raltegravir-resistant signature mutants Y143R, Q148K, N155H and G140S/Q148H in vitro — but only partially: the G140S/Q148H double mutant still reduces its potency about 5- to 6-fold. Resistance pathways are now defined along at least four routes (G118R, G140A/S/Q148H/K/R, N155H, R263K), and a 2026 multicentre Taiwan study found second-generation INSTI resistance-associated mutations in 4.8% of people failing dolutegravir-based therapy (6/127) and 5.5% failing bictegravir (4/73), most commonly Q148H/K/R (3.5%), G140A/C/R/S (3.0%) and R263K (1.5%).

Structural biology has explained why. Cryo-EM intasome structures (HIV-1 strand transfer complex, PDB 5U1C; SIVrcm intasome with dolutegravir and bictegravir) and eleven drug-resistant intasome structures published in 2023 show that G140S/Q148H perturb optimal magnesium coordination in the active site — and that the investigational compound 4d inhibits those mutants more effectively than dolutegravir, retaining antiviral potency against a panel of quadruple mutants where all three approved second-generation INSTIs lose potency.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): among ChEMBL HIV-1 integrase actives, wild-type potency no longer separates the leads — all top compounds are sub-3 nM — so the ranking that matters is potency on resistant intasomes, not potency on wild-type enzyme. The test is a strand-transfer assay on wild-type versus G140S/Q148H intasomes.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-10 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-10). Key sources: UNAIDS global HIV statistics 2024 and WHO/UNAIDS Pakistan figures; Kobayashi et al. 2011 and Hare et al. 2011 for dolutegravir's in vitro profile; Passos et al. 2017 (5U1C) and Cook et al. 2020 for intasome structures; Li et al. 2023 for the eleven drug-resistant intasome structures and compound 4d; the 2025 quadruple-mutant comparison of 4d against dolutegravir, bictegravir and cabotegravir; the 2026 Taiwan resistance cohort; and Naidu et al. 2018 for the BMS-707035 series. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 ChEMBL potency analysis (docking SKIPPED — see 2.3)

Standardised LeadForge pipeline, exactly as Papers #1/#3, except for the corrected target and the skipped docking step: UniProtKB P04585 → ChEMBL CHEMBL3471 (see correction below), 48 bioactivities retrieved (pChEMBL ≥ 5) → PubChem verification of dolutegravir → RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen vs dolutegravir → RDKit ADMET/PAINS + ToxGuard Tox21 kNN → composite lead ranking (similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20). The top 10 leads by composite score are reported with their best ChEMBL record (pChEMBL and activity).

Target correction (verified live, 2026-11-10): the pipeline's default path is wrong for this target. UniProt text search for "HIV-1 integrase" returns the Gag-Pol polyprotein P04585 (integrase is a cleavage product; UniProtKB has no standalone HIV-1 integrase entry for HXB2). The pipeline's ChEMBL lookup on that accession returns a single target, CHEMBL3638360 ("Gag-Pol polyprotein"), whose top bioactivities are HIV-1 protease assays (e.g. CHEMBL3887078, WT HIV-1 protease with a peptide substrate) and whole-virus T-cell assays (CHEMBL3887045) — not integrase assays. A paper built on those would be a protease paper mislabelled as integrase. The run was therefore corrected to the true HIV-1 integrase ChEMBL target CHEMBL3471 ("Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 integrase", SINGLE PROTEIN), using the pipeline's own bioactivity, similarity, ADMET and scoring functions with only the target lookup overridden (driver script run_docking_integrase.py, kept in the pipeline directory).

2.3 Why docking was skipped

Two independent reasons, both verified. First, the pipeline's structure picker, given the polyprotein accession P04585, selects PDB 6DV4 — HIV-1 wild-type protease with the inhibitor GRL-04315A, 1.14 Å — because it sorts the accession's PDB cross-references by resolution and takes the best ligand-bound X-ray structure, regardless of which Pol domain it is. A run_docking.py attempt on that structure was started, identified as the wrong enzyme, and killed mid-Vina; no result from it is used. Second, there is no correct structure for the pipeline to pick instead: no X-ray structure of HIV-1 integrase with a strand-transfer inhibitor at the strand-transfer site exists. The dolutegravir-bound structures are cryo-EM intasomes — e.g. 8FNG, the G140A HIV-1 intasome with dolutegravir bound (2.5 Å, Li et al. 2023) — whose active site is a protein–DNA–Mg²⁺ interface: rigid AutoDock Vina docking cannot model metal coordination, the DNA interface, or a megadalton nucleoprotein complex, and the pipeline's X-ray-only picker excludes cryo-EM entries by design. The X-ray integrase structures that do carry inhibitors are allosteric-site (LEDGIN) complexes such as 8CBT (MUT872, 2.14 Å) — a different pocket from the strand-transfer site. Docking dolutegravir on 6DV4, on 8CBT, or on a cryo-EM intasome would produce numbers that look like results and are not. The paper is therefore a potency and resistance-landscape analysis, and says so in its title.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every lead. No compound in the top 10 carries a PAINS alert.

2.5 Honesty limits

No docking was performed, so there are no docking scores in this paper at all — nothing is inferred about binding modes. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima from heterogeneous assays (enzyme strand-transfer IC50 vs cell-based antiviral EC50, different laboratories and years); they are not head-to-head values, and the EC50 and IC50 figures in the table are not directly comparable with each other. The pipeline's composite score is dominated by similarity to dolutegravir (40 of 100 points), so it ranks analogues above equally potent different chemotypes by construction. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Potency: the comparison table

5 CHEMBL4126686 0.330 72.5 IC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none
6 CHEMBL4127923 0.312 71.6 EC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none
7 CHEMBL4128240 0.304 71.4 EC50 1.0 nM (9.00) none
8 CHEMBL4130102 0.293 71.1 EC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none
9 CHEMBL4127873 0.278 70.4 EC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none

All ten leads are sub-3 nM by their best record; the measured-potency spread is under one log unit (pChEMBL 8.70–9.66). CHEMBL1229211 is dolutegravir's own ChEMBL record (identical MW 419.38, logP 1.35, similarity 1.0) — the duplicate is an internal consistency check, not a second compound. Cabotegravir (CHEMBL2403238) is the most potent by its best record (IC50 0.22 nM), ahead of dolutegravir's own record (0.5 nM) and ahead of the literature head-to-head values for dolutegravir (2.7 nM strand transfer). Ranks 4–10 are seven analogues from the BMS-707035 series (Naidu et al. 2018, Bioorg Med Chem Lett; document CHEMBL4118197), all reported at EC50/IC50 2.0 nM in the same strand-transfer antiviral assay — a single-assay cluster, not seven independent measurements.

3.2 Comparison with published potency data

The literature head-to-head values are less extreme than the ChEMBL maxima: dolutegravir strand-transfer IC50 2.7 nM (Kobayashi et al. 2011) against the ChEMBL top record of 0.5 nM for the same compound — a five-fold gap between a single-assay maximum and the standard reference value. The same caution applies to cabotegravir's 0.22 nM: it is a top record, not a head-to-head win over dolutegravir. The 2025 quadruple-mutant study is the relevant comparison instead: against G140S/Q148H-centred quadruple mutants, all three approved second-generation INSTIs lose potency while the investigational compound 4d retains it — a difference invisible in the wild-type table above, where everything is sub-3 nM.

3.3 The standardisation problem: similarity is not potency

The composite score's 40-point similarity component makes the ranking a similarity contest: the BMS-707035 series (similarity 0.28–0.34 to dolutegravir) scores 70–73 while dolutegravir and cabotegravir score 92–99, although the measured potencies are within one log unit of each other and the BMS compounds are, on their best records, as potent as dolutegravir itself. A reader who took the composite score at face value would conclude the BMS series is far worse; the data say it is not. Two further cautions: the EC50 figures (cell-based antiviral activity) and IC50 figures (enzyme strand transfer) in the table measure different things and cannot be ranked against each other; and the seven BMS records at exactly 2.0 nM are one assay's output, so the apparent depth of that chemotype is a single data point repeated seven times.

Drug-likeness is clean across the top 10: MW 361–505, logP 0.64–2.55, zero Lipinski violations except CHEMBL4127873 (MW 504.58, one violation). No Tox21 flags were predicted for any compound by kNN read-across — a prediction, not a measurement. Dolutegravir's long-acting sibling cabotegravir is already the clinical answer to adherence (injectable, every 2 months); a new oral INSTI must therefore beat dolutegravir on resistance, not on wild-type potency or convenience.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether a standardised screen can rank new integrase leads against dolutegravir. The answer is that the question is obsolete for wild-type enzyme: every compound in the top tier is sub-3 nM, and the ranking that the pipeline produces is driven by structural similarity to the reference, not by potency. The paper's contribution is therefore the reframe, plus a documented pipeline failure: for polyprotein targets, the standard UniProt→ChEMBL→PDB chain silently substitutes a different enzyme (protease for integrase) at all three steps, and the correction — not the docking — is the methodological result. Any future run on a viral polyprotein target must check the ChEMBL target's assay descriptions and the PDB entry's molecule name before trusting a score.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Cabotegravir's 0.22 nM is a single-assay ChEMBL maximum, not a head-to-head win; the literature value for dolutegravir in the same type of assay is 2.7 nM, and the two were not measured on the same plate. The BMS series' seven identical 2.0 nM records are one assay, not seven confirmations. And no docking exists to suggest a binding-mode advantage for any compound here — the structural claims in this paper come from the published cryo-EM intasome literature, not from this run.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts were found. The validation assay still needs standard controls (detergent to expose aggregators; a counter-screen against an unrelated enzyme) and, critically, a resistant-intasome arm — wild-type potency alone cannot distinguish the leads.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a strand-transfer assay on wild-type intasomes, the IC50 order of cabotegravir, dolutegravir and the BMS-707035 series will be within 3-fold of each other — i.e. no meaningful wild-type difference. Refuted if any lead is >10-fold better than dolutegravir.
  2. On G140S/Q148H intasomes, dolutegravir will lose 5- to 6-fold potency (as published) while at least one BMS-series compound retains wild-type potency. Refuted if all leads lose potency together.
  3. The investigational compound 4d will outperform all top-10 leads on the quadruple-mutant panel (G140S/Q148H + L74/E92/T97 + E138A/K), reproducing the published result. Refuted if it does not.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): strand-transfer enzyme assay for cabotegravir, dolutegravir, BMS-707035 and the two most potent BMS analogues, wild-type integrase, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, same plate — the deliverable is a head-to-head table, replacing the ChEMBL maxima. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): the same assay on G140S/Q148H and G118R mutant integrases, with compound 4d as comparator — the deliverable is the fold-change in IC50, which is the only number that matters for this target. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): for the lead that survives stage 2, a cell-based antiviral assay (single-round infection) on wild-type and quadruple-mutant virus, plus a comparison of the published cryo-EM intasome structures (8FNG and the 2023 series) to rationalise the mutant result structurally. Stop rule: a lead that is potent on wild-type but loses potency on G140S/Q148H exactly like dolutegravir is a failure, not a publication — wild-type potency is not the endpoint.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking was performed — this paper contains no binding-mode or docking-score claims at all, by design (see 2.3).
  2. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima from heterogeneous assays (enzyme IC50 vs cell-based EC50); they are not head-to-head values, and dolutegravir's own record (0.5 nM) differs five-fold from the literature reference value (2.7 nM).
  3. The pipeline's composite score is similarity-dominated; the ranking in Table 3.1 must not be read as a potency ranking.
  4. The seven BMS-series records at 2.0 nM come from a single assay and a single publication; they are not independent confirmations.
  5. The resistance discussion rests on published cryo-EM and virology, not on any measurement in this run.
  6. No data are presented on pharmacokinetics, long-acting formulation, or cost — cabotegravir's clinical advantage is adherence, which this analysis does not address.
  7. No local (Pakistan) epidemiological or access data beyond the national estimates in Section 1 were collected.

6. Conclusion

Against dolutegravir, the ChEMBL HIV-1 integrase top tier is uniformly sub-3 nM: cabotegravir leads on its best record (IC50 0.22 nM), dolutegravir's own record is 0.5 nM, and seven BMS-707035-series analogues share 2.0 nM in one assay — but the pipeline's similarity-dominated ranking obscures that equality, and none of it separates the leads where it matters, on resistant intasomes. Docking was skipped because no X-ray structure of HIV-1 integrase with a strand-transfer inhibitor exists and the pipeline's default pick was the wrong enzyme. The next step is a strand-transfer assay on wild-type versus G140S/Q148H intasomes, with compound 4d as comparator: a lead only matters if it keeps potency where dolutegravir loses it.

Sitagliptin Is the Weakest Compound in Its Own Benchmark: A Centre-Audited DPP-4 Docking Study on 4A5S Where Vina Rank and Measured Potency Are Uncorrelated

Type 2 diabetes affects 589 million adults worldwide (1 in 9), and Pakistan has one of the highest age-standardised prevalences at 31.4% (~34.5 million adults).
