The headline, stated honestly: no statin beats atorvastatin beyond noise. Atorvastatin scores best at −9.00 kcal/mol, the closest lead (atorvastatin itself in ChEMBL) trails by 0.40 kcal/mol, and the furthest by 1.12 kcal/mol — every margin inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The same molecule docked twice (atorvastatin as QUERY and as its ChEMBL record CHEMBL1487) scores −9.00 and −8.60, a 0.40 kcal/mol spread for an identical compound — which calibrates the protocol's run-to-run jitter on this site, and it is exactly the size of the "win" over the closest lead. The docking order also disagrees with measured potency: by IC50 the order is 0.23, 0.35, 0.57 and 1.8 nM, but by docking it is atorvastatin, then the 0.23 nM record, then the 1.8 nM analogue, then fluvastatin (0.35 nM), then the 0.57 nM analogue. The least potent measured inhibitor in the set (CHEMBL394937, 1.8 nM) scores third at −8.15 kcal/mol, ahead of two more potent compounds. The docking scores span only 1.12 kcal/mol while the measured potencies span 8-fold — Vina compresses the potency range on this site and ranks within it unreliably. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: every compound's three poses sit within 0.96 kcal/mol of its best score, so the scores are stable — stably wrong in potency order.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for atorvastatin or any of these leads on 2R4F was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for atorvastatin, fluvastatin and two statin analogues on the human structure are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the centre audit trail and the desalt correction. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: the four leads span measured HMGCR IC50 values of 0.23–1.8 nM, an 8-fold spread, while their docking scores span 1.12 kcal/mol in an order that disagrees with potency — the 1.8 nM compound third, fluvastatin fourth. Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and on this site it ranks them unreliably.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two things that could silently corrupt this result did not, and one did. The grid centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å and sits on the co-crystallised RIE inhibitor — the structure holds no cofactor, so the cofactor-centring fault is absent here. The pipeline's target resolution was also correct (P04035 HMGCR; CHEMBL402). What did fail was the screen's stated purpose: the topic asked for non-statin scaffolds for statin-intolerant patients, but the pipeline ranks by similarity to atorvastatin, and the most similar compounds to a statin are other statins. All four leads carry the 3,5-dihydroxyheptanoate pharmacophore — fluvastatin is a marketed statin, and the other three are statin analogues. A similarity screen cannot find a non-statin scaffold, because similarity to the query is the score. The second fault was minor and corrected: two leads' ChEMBL SMILES are sodium salts, which the ligand preparation rejects as two fragments; both were desalted to the parent drug and re-docked, and the salt forms are recorded in the data file so the fix is auditable.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a negative benchmark with a useful control — and a failed screen. There is no lead here: atorvastatin beats every statin in the set on its own site, the closest by 0.40 kcal/mol — inside noise, and the same size as the jitter between two dockings of the identical molecule. The durable findings are the benchmark values for atorvastatin on 2R4F (−9.00 kcal/mol, with full pose lists), the demonstration that Vina compresses an 8-fold potency range into 1.12 kcal/mol and orders it wrong, and the same-molecule control (−9.00 and −8.60 for atorvastatin twice), which calibrates the protocol's own reproducibility on this site at ±0.40 kcal/mol. The more important finding is the screen failure: a similarity-ranked pipeline cannot return non-statin scaffolds, so the clinical question — what to give a statin-intolerant patient — cannot be answered by this pipeline as configured. The next screen must rank by dissimilarity to statins, not similarity to atorvastatin.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the best margin here is 0.40. Second, the ranking must be checked against measured HMGCR IC50 values — the four leads span 0.23–1.8 nM, and a docking order that disagrees with that order is a measurement of the scoring function, not of the molecules. Third, the same-molecule control sets the floor: two dockings of atorvastatin differ by 0.40 kcal/mol, so a 0.40 kcal/mol "win" is indistinguishable from re-docking the reference. A docking "win" against atorvastatin on this site is not a discovery; it is a benchmark value awaiting an assay.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All leads are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 flags (NR-Aromatase 1.0 measured for atorvastatin and fluvastatin) are assay readouts, not clinical findings, and must not be reported as toxicity. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either. The validation assay must still include redox controls and a counter-screen, because a clean PAINS filter does not rule out assay interference. The larger safety question — muscle toxicity, the problem that motivates the search — is not addressed by PAINS at all and needs a dedicated muscle-cell model for any lead that advances.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-docking lead inhibits recombinant human HMG-CoA reductase with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value under identical assay conditions; a measured IC50 worse than atorvastatin's would confirm the noise interpretation, while a better one would refute it.
  2. A dissimilarity-ranked screen (Tanimoto < 0.3 to any statin) returns at least one non-statin HMGCR binder with a measured IC50 under 100 nM; failure to find one would show the target's known chemical space is statin-only.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised RIE inhibitor into 2R4F reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  4. Docking the same five ligands on the earlier HMGCR structure 1HWK (atorvastatin complex) gives the same ranking as on 2R4F; a different ranking would show the result is structure-dependent, not molecule-dependent.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): HMG-CoA reductase inhibition assay for the best-docking lead, fluvastatin and atorvastatin, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): a dissimilarity screen of the ChEMBL HMGCR bioactivities for non-statin scaffolds (Tanimoto < 0.3 to atorvastatin, no dihydroxyheptanoate), with the best three docked on 2R4F and assayed as in Stage 1. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): LDL-uptake assay in HepG2 cells for any compound that clears Stage 2, with atorvastatin as control, plus a muscle-cell toxicity screen, since muscle symptoms are the clinical problem a docking score cannot see. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as a real advantage — the best margin here is 0.40 kcal/mol. 3. Only one HMGCR structure (2R4F, one conformation) was docked; the earlier 1HWK atorvastatin complex was not scored. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking RMSD validation of the co-crystallised RIE pose was performed. 5. A single rigid receptor was used; the HMG-CoA binding pocket's flexibility is not modelled. 6. All leads are already-known HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, and all are statins — no non-statin scaffold was tested, so the paper cannot speak to the statin-intolerance question it was built around. 7. The same-molecule control (atorvastatin docked twice, −9.00 and −8.60) calibrates run-to-run jitter but was not repeated across days or Vina versions. 8. Muscle safety was not modelled for any lead. 9. LDL lowering was not measured for any lead.

6. Conclusion

No statin in this set beats atorvastatin on its own binding site: atorvastatin scores −9.00 kcal/mol on the human HMG-CoA reductase structure 2R4F, every lead trails it by 0.40–1.12 kcal/mol — inside Vina's noise — and the docking order disagrees with measured potency, with the 1.8 nM analogue third and fluvastatin fourth. The honest reading is that on this site, non-covalent docking cannot rank known inhibitors against atorvastatin — and the screen itself failed its purpose, returning only statins, so the next experiment is a dissimilarity-ranked search for a non-statin scaffold plus a head-to-head HMGCR assay with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, not more similarity docking.

Daclatasvir-Class NS5A Inhibitors Are All Picomolar and All Beyond the Rule of Five: A Corrected Ligand Screen, and Why Docking Was Skipped

Pakistan carries the world's largest hepatitis C burden — about 9 million people chronically infected in 2024, about 88,000 new infections that year, and about 48,700 hepatitis deaths — and genotype 3a, the hardest genotype to cure with first-generation regimens, accounts for roughly 55–80% of Pakistani infections.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-08 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #2 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: daclatasvir; NS5A; hepatitis C; Pakistan; genotype 3a; direct-acting antiviral; drug resistance; Y93H

Abstract

Pakistan carries the world's largest hepatitis C burden — about 9 million people chronically infected in 2024, about 88,000 new infections that year, and about 48,700 hepatitis deaths — and genotype 3a, the hardest genotype to cure with first-generation regimens, accounts for roughly 55–80% of Pakistani infections. Daclatasvir, the first-in-class NS5A inhibitor, blocks the viral NS5A protein at picomolar concentrations, but a single substitution, Y93H, raises its EC50 by thousands of fold, and the whole drug class is large and lipophilic. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET) against the verified hepatitis C NS5A target (ChEMBL CHEMBL3307224; 48 bioactivities) and ranked daclatasvir plus 25 known NS5A inhibitors. The top five leads are indistinguishable by potency — all EC50 0.010–0.013 nM — and indistinguishable by drug-likeness: every one carries two Lipinski violations and fails Veber's rules, exactly like daclatasvir itself. Docking was skipped, honestly and deliberately: the only NS5A domain I crystal structure (PDB 1ZH1, 2.5 Å) is apo, and no co-crystal of any daclatasvir-class inhibitor with NS5A exists, so there is no experimental binding site to dock into. The falsifiable next step is a defined docking run on 1ZH1 at the modelled dimer-interface site plus a genotype 3a replicon assay of the best-ranked lead against daclatasvir on wild-type and Y93H NS5A, with a pre-registered rule that a lead must keep picomolar potency on Y93H to count as an advance; a lead that loses potency on Y93H like daclatasvir would confirm that this class has no resistance advantage to offer.

1. Introduction

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infects about 47 million people worldwide, and Pakistan carries more of that burden than any other country: according to the World Health Organization's Global Hepatitis Report 2026, about 9.06 million Pakistanis — 3.6% of the population — were chronically infected with HCV in 2024, with about 88,199 new infections that year and about 48,715 deaths from hepatitis B and C combined. Only about 1.94 million Pakistanis had ever been diagnosed with hepatitis C by 2024, and about 2.47 million had ever started curative treatment — leaving roughly two thirds of the infected population untreated. Prevalence is highest in Punjab (8.9%), followed by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (6.5%), Sindh (6.2%) and Balochistan (5.2%), and transmission is driven largely by unsafe healthcare injections and unscreened blood.

The genotype mix makes the Pakistani problem harder than the global average. Genotype 3a is the dominant genotype in Pakistan — a 2023 meta-analysis of studies from 1996–2020 put genotype 3 at 65.35% of isolates and subtype 3a at 55.15%, and several large Pakistani series report 3a at 76–80%. Genotype 3a matters because it was the hardest genotype for first-generation direct-acting antivirals: it responds worse to daclatasvir than genotype 1b does, and its signature resistance substitution, Y93H, confers high-level resistance.

Daclatasvir (Daklinza, BMS-790052) was the first-in-class NS5A inhibitor, approved in 2014–2015. NS5A is a 447-amino-acid zinc-binding phosphoprotein, active as a homodimer organised into three domains, essential for viral RNA replication and virion assembly. Daclatasvir binds the N-terminal region of domain I and disrupts NS5A function at picomolar concentrations: the FDA label reports EC50 values of 0.001–0.009 nM against genotype 1b and 0.003–0.050 nM against genotype 1a. Its weakness is a low barrier to resistance: substitutions at M28, Q30, L31 and Y93 in the N-terminal 100 amino acids of NS5A. Y93H alone raises the genotype 1b EC50 from 0.009 nM to 24 nM (about 2,700-fold), and in genotype 3a Y93H raises it beyond 10,000 nM; the L31V + Y93H double mutant exceeds 14,000 nM. Because daclatasvir-class drugs are the backbone of the cheapest curative regimens available in Pakistan, a successor that keeps picomolar potency on Y93H — or a cheaper way to make the existing drugs — would matter more than a marginally more potent analogue.

The question this paper asks is methodological: can a standardised, automated pipeline rank known NS5A inhibitors against daclatasvir, and what can it honestly say when the target has no liganded structure to dock into? The falsifiable hypothesis is that the top-ranked leads will be indistinguishable from daclatasvir by measured potency and by drug-likeness, and that the only meaningful differentiator in this class is the resistance profile — which no docking score on an apo structure can measure.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 8 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-08.md (no HCV item that day), PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI), RCSB PDB and UniProtKB. Key sources: the WHO Global Hepatitis Report 2026 and WHO Pakistan hepatitis factsheet for burden figures; the 2023 meta-analysis of HCV genotypes in Pakistan (Infectious Medicine, DOI 10.1016/j.imj.2023.11.007) for the genotype 3a share; the daclatasvir FDA label for EC50 values and the resistance-substitution table; the NS5A domain I structure paper (Tellinghuisen et al., Nature 2005) for the docking decision; and the Barakat refined model of NS5A bound to daclatasvir for the proposed binding site. All ChEMBL potency values quoted were re-checked live against the ChEMBL API on 8 November 2026 for the target "Nonstructural protein 5A" (CHEMBL3307224).

2.2 Molecular docking — skipped, and why

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET). The first run was discarded after a target-resolution fault was caught and is documented here because it is part of the result.

Fault — wrong target. The pipeline's uniprot_target prefers human hits, so "Hepatitis C virus NS5A" resolved to human BTBD1 (UniProt Q9H0C5), and the ChEMBL side picked CHEMBL2074, human maltase-glucoamylase. Every "lead" in that run is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor (iminosugar), not an NS5A inhibitor. The file dock-HP-053-2026-11-08.json is discarded and must not be used.

Correction. HCV NS5A has no standalone reviewed UniProt entry (it is cleaved from the genome polyprotein), so the pipeline cannot resolve it. The corrected run forced the verified values: ChEMBL target CHEMBL3307224 ("Nonstructural protein 5A", Hepatitis C virus, SINGLE PROTEIN), confirmed live against the ChEMBL API, and the UniProt identifier of the HCV genotype 1b genome polyprotein P26662 (NS5A is residues ~1973–2420 of the polyprotein), used only as the target identifier. The corrected run retrieved 48 bioactivities and ranked 26 leads with the identical pipeline code (similarity, descriptors, PAINS, ToxGuard Tox21 kNN panel).

Docking was skipped. The only experimental structure of NS5A domain I is PDB 1ZH1 (Tellinghuisen et al., Nature 2005), 2.5 Å, and it is apo — no inhibitor bound. Daclatasvir binds at the NS5A domain I dimer interface, a site defined only by a computational model (Barakat et al.), and no co-crystal of any daclatasvir-class inhibitor with NS5A exists. Docking into the apo structure at a modelled site would produce a number with no experimental anchor, and the template rule for this series is explicit: if no experimental structure exists for the drug site, docking is skipped and the paper says so. No docking scores are reported in this paper. The proposed docking experiment is specified in §4.5 instead.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: daclatasvir and all 25 leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were SR-MMP 0.376 for CHEMBL4473049 and NR-AhR up to 0.26; daclatasvir itself scored highest on SR-p53 (0.077) and NR-AhR (0.084). These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: no docking was performed, so there is no structure-based ranking at all; no experimental data are presented; the potency values are ChEMBL replicon EC50/IC50 values measured by others, not by us, and they come from different assay formats (EC50 vs IC50) that are not strictly comparable; the leads are already-known NS5A inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed; the genotype coverage of the leads (in particular genotype 3a, which dominates in Pakistan) was not measured — the ChEMBL activities are mostly genotype 1b replicon data; and cost, the variable that decides whether a drug reaches a Pakistani patient, was not modelled.

3. Results

3.1 The ranked list: potency cannot separate the class

Compound Measured potency, ChEMBL MW logP Lipinski violations Veber PAINS Similarity to daclatasvir Composite score
Daclatasvir (reference, query) EC50 0.001–0.009 nM (GT1b, label) 738.9 6.22 2 fail clean 1.000 69.7
CHEMBL3765311 EC50 0.010 nM 778.9 6.97 2 fail clean 0.761 59.7
CHEMBL4466693 EC50 0.013 nM 788.9 6.25 2 fail clean 0.742 58.9
CHEMBL3360472 EC50 0.010 nM 780.9 5.81 2 fail clean 0.714 56.6
CHEMBL4787353 IC50 0.0116 nM 817.8 5.85 2 fail clean 0.671 56.4
CHEMBL4756850 IC50 0.012 nM 817.8 5.85 2 fail clean 0.671 56.4

Potencies are ChEMBL replicon values for the NS5A target (CHEMBL3307224), re-checked live on 8 November 2026; daclatasvir's EC50 is from the FDA label (genotype 1b replicon). Composite score: similarity×40 + Lipinski×20 + Veber×10 + PAINS×10 + tox×20, as in the LeadForge pipeline. All five leads are daclatasvir-class NS5A inhibitors (biphenyl-bis-imidazole analogues); none has a published common name in ChEMBL.

The headline, stated honestly: nothing separates the class. The top five leads span EC50 0.010–0.013 nM — a 1.3-fold range, smaller than the run-to-run variation of a replicon assay — and every one of them carries exactly the same drug-likeness profile as daclatasvir: molecular weight 769–818 Da, logP 5.8–7.0, two Lipinski violations, Veber fail (11 rotatable bonds, TPSA 174.6 Å² for daclatasvir). The composite ranking is therefore a ranking by structural similarity to daclatasvir, not by any property that would make a drug better: the most similar compound wins, and similarity to a drug is not an advantage. The whole class sits far outside the Rule of Five and succeeds anyway — daclatasvir is the proof that a 739 Da, logP 6.2 molecule can be a curative drug — which means the pipeline's Lipinski and Veber components actively penalise the exact chemistry that works on this target. A screen that ranks by drug-likeness would discard the class it is trying to improve.

3.2 Comparison with published work

No published Vina or Glide score for daclatasvir or any of these leads on NS5A domain I was found to benchmark against, because there is no liganded structure to dock into — which is the same reason this paper reports no docking. The nearest published structure-based work is the Barakat refined model of NS5A bound to daclatasvir, a molecular-dynamics model built on the apo 1ZH1 dimer that places the drug at the dimer interface and explains the resistance mutations (M28, Q30, L31, Y93) as contacts with the drug. That model is a hypothesis, not a structure, and it is the correct starting point for the docking experiment proposed in §4.5 — but it cannot be cited as a docking benchmark, because it reports no Vina score.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two things that could silently corrupt this result did occur, and one was caught. The pipeline's target-resolution fault did occur: left uncorrected, the paper would have been written about human maltase-glucoamylase inhibitors while claiming to target HCV NS5A, and the task brief's own suggested target string produced the fault. The same human-preferring ranking caused the same day's neuraminidase run to pick human ABL1 kinase. The deeper problem is structural, not procedural: the most useful number for a Pakistani clinician — the EC50 against genotype 3a, which causes most Pakistani infections — is the number the ChEMBL record does not contain. The potencies in the table are genotype 1b replicon values, and genotype 3a is precisely where daclatasvir is weakest (EC50 0.120–0.870 nM wild-type, and Y93H beyond 10,000 nM). A ranking built on genotype 1b numbers cannot answer the Pakistani question.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a negative benchmark with a useful control. There is no lead here: five compounds with EC50s of 0.010–0.013 nM are the same drug five times over by any measure that matters, and all five fail the same drug-likeness rules that daclatasvir itself fails. The durable findings are the corrected target record (CHEMBL3307224, with the BTBD1/maltase-glucoamylase fault documented so the next run does not repeat it), the demonstration that similarity-based ranking collapses when the class is uniformly potent, and the explicit statement that docking was skipped for lack of a liganded structure — a decision that protects the paper from a fabricated binding site. The most actionable negative is that the next experiment is not more similarity screening: it is a genotype 3a replicon assay against Y93H, the mutation that actually defeats the drug in the population that needs it.

4.2 Why the ranking must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the potency range (1.3-fold) is smaller than assay noise, so the ranking order is arbitrary. Second, the composite score is dominated by similarity to daclatasvir (40 of 100 points), so the ranking rewards being daclatasvir-like — and the resistance profile of a daclatasvir-like molecule is daclatasvir's resistance profile. Third, the potencies are genotype 1b numbers, while the Pakistani burden is genotype 3a, where the same molecules are 10- to 100-fold less potent and where Y93H is a treatment-ending mutation. A ranking that ignores genotype and resistance is a measurement of the scoring function, not of the molecules.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All leads are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (up to SR-MMP 0.376) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either. The validation assay must still include redox controls and a counter-screen, because a clean PAINS filter does not rule out assay interference. The larger safety question — drug–drug interactions through CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, which matter for daclatasvir-class drugs in patients on other medicines — is not addressed by PAINS at all and needs a dedicated interaction screen for any lead that advances.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-ranked lead inhibits a genotype 1b replicon with an EC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value under identical assay conditions; a measured EC50 worse than daclatasvir's would confirm that the ranking is only a similarity ranking, while a better one would refute it.
  2. A lead that ranks well on genotype 1b keeps picomolar potency on a genotype 3a replicon, where daclatasvir's EC50 is 0.120–0.870 nM; loss of potency on genotype 3a would show the ranking does not transfer to the Pakistani genotype.
  3. A lead that ranks well keeps its potency on Y93H NS5A (genotype 1b EC50 ≤ 1 nM on the mutant, versus 24 nM for daclatasvir); loss of potency on Y93H would show the lead shares daclatasvir's resistance profile and offers no advance.
  4. Docking the same six compounds on the 1ZH1 dimer at the Barakat modelled interface site, with the grid centred on the Y93 side chain, reproduces the resistance order (Y93H-sensitive compounds score worse on the mutant structure than on wild-type); failure to do so would show the modelled site cannot rank this class.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): genotype 1b replicon EC50 assay for the best-ranked lead and daclatasvir, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): the same assay on genotype 3a replicon and on Y93H mutant replicons (genotypes 1b and 3a) for any compound that clears Stage 1, to test whether the lead survives the mutation that defeats daclatasvir in the Pakistani genotype. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): docking on the 1ZH1 dimer at the Barakat modelled interface site (grid centred on Y93, 22.5 Å box, Vina 1.2.7) for any compound that clears Stage 2, plus a CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein interaction screen, since drug interactions are the safety question a replicon assay cannot see. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking was performed; no experimental data are presented. 2. The potency range of the top leads (1.3-fold) is smaller than replicon assay noise, so the ranking order is arbitrary. 3. Potencies are genotype 1b replicon values from ChEMBL; genotype 3a potency — the value that matters in Pakistan — was not measured and is not in the ChEMBL record. 4. EC50 and IC50 values from different assay formats are mixed in the table and are not strictly comparable. 5. The composite score rewards similarity to daclatasvir, which biases the ranking toward daclatasvir's own resistance profile. 6. All leads are already-known NS5A inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 7. The pipeline's target resolution picked the wrong protein (human BTBD1/maltase-glucoamylase) on the first run — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited. 8. Cost and access, the variables that decide whether a drug reaches a Pakistani patient, were not modelled. 9. The resistance analysis is literature-based: no mutant replicon was assayed and no EC50 was measured.

6. Conclusion

No NS5A inhibitor in this set separates from daclatasvir: the top five leads span EC50 0.010–0.013 nM, carry the same two Lipinski violations and the same Veber failure as daclatasvir, and the ranking among them is a ranking by similarity to daclatasvir, not by any property that would make a drug better. Docking was skipped because the only NS5A domain I structure is apo and no daclatasvir co-crystal exists — and the next experiment is a genotype 3a replicon assay against Y93H, the mutation that defeats daclatasvir in the genotype that causes most Pakistani infections, not more similarity screening.

No Lead Beats Letrozole Beyond Noise: A Vina Benchmark of Five Aromatase Inhibitors on the Human CYP19A1 Structure 3S79

Breast cancer was diagnosed in about 2.4 million women in 2024 and killed about 694,000; in Pakistan it is the commonest female cancer, with about 30,682 new cases and 15,552 deaths in 2022 and the highest incidence rate in Asia.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-08 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #1 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: letrozole; aromatase; CYP19A1; breast cancer; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; endocrine therapy; drug resistance

Abstract

Breast cancer was diagnosed in about 2.4 million women in 2024 and killed about 694,000; in Pakistan it is the commonest female cancer, with about 30,682 new cases and 15,552 deaths in 2022 and the highest incidence rate in Asia. Letrozole, a third-generation aromatase inhibitor, blocks CYP19A1 aromatase, the enzyme that converts androgens to oestrogens, and in the BIG 1-98 trial it cut the risk of recurrence by 18% versus tamoxifen (hazard ratio 0.82), but bone loss, arthralgia and acquired resistance limit its benefit, so new aromatase inhibitors are still wanted. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking) against the human aromatase structure in complex with androstenedione (PDB 3S79, 2.75 Å), with the grid centred on the co-crystallised androstenedione, and docked letrozole plus five known aromatase inhibitors with measured potencies of 0.02–0.21 nM, all under an identical AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol. No lead beat letrozole beyond noise: the best lead (CHEMBL197650, IC50 0.11 nM) scored −8.77 kcal/mol against letrozole's −8.74, a 0.03 kcal/mol margin, and the most potent measured inhibitor (letrozole itself in ChEMBL, Ki 0.02 nM) scored −8.71; every margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and the docking order disagrees with measured potency. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head aromatase inhibition assay of the best-docking lead against letrozole on wild-type and resistant-mutant enzyme, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage; a lead that keeps potency where letrozole loses it, or a measured IC50 advantage over letrozole, would refute the claim that the docking ranking is only a measurement of Vina's limits.

1. Introduction

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women worldwide: according to the World Health Organization fact sheet, about 2.4 million women were diagnosed in 2024 and about 694,000 died, and it was the most common cancer in women in 164 of 186 countries. In Pakistan the burden is the worst in Asia — GLOBOCAN 2022 records about 30,682 new cases and 15,552 deaths, the leading cause of cancer death among Pakistani women, with a lifetime risk of about one in nine women, and Karachi's incidence is reported as the highest in Asia. Late presentation is common, so systemic therapy carries much of the burden of care.

About two thirds of breast cancers are hormone-receptor positive and depend on oestrogen. In postmenopausal women almost all oestrogen comes from aromatase (CYP19A1, 503 amino acids, chromosome 15q21.1), the cytochrome P450 that converts androstenedione to oestrone and testosterone to 17β-oestradiol. Blocking aromatase starves the tumour of oestrogen, and third-generation aromatase inhibitors are the standard adjuvant endocrine therapy for postmenopausal hormone-receptor-positive disease.

Letrozole (Femara, 2.5 mg once daily) is a non-steroidal, reversible aromatase inhibitor. In the Breast International Group (BIG) 1-98 trial, 8,028 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer were randomised to letrozole or tamoxifen; in the monotherapy arms (4,922 women) at a median follow-up of 51 months, letrozole cut the risk of a disease-free-survival event by 18% (352 events on letrozole versus 418 on tamoxifen; hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.71–0.95, P = .007), and at a median follow-up of 74 months the inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted 5-year overall survival was 91.8% versus 90.4%. The price is the class toxicity of oestrogen deprivation: letrozole caused more bone fractures, arthralgia, low-grade hypercholesterolaemia and non-ischaemic cardiovascular events than tamoxifen. Acquired resistance also limits long-term benefit, and a drug that keeps letrozole's potency with less bone toxicity — or that works after letrozole failure — would still be valuable.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known aromatase inhibitors against letrozole on the true human structure, and what does an apparent docking "win" mean when the reference drug's own binding site is the grid? The falsifiable hypothesis is that any lead beating letrozole by less than 2 kcal/mol on Vina docking has no measurable potency advantage, and that the docking ranking will disagree with measured aromatase IC50 values on this target.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 8 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-08.md (no aromatase item that day), PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI), RCSB PDB and UniProtKB. Key sources: the WHO breast cancer fact sheet (2024 figures) and GLOBOCAN 2022 for burden figures; the BIG 1-98 trial reports (Coates et al., J Clin Oncol 2007; Colleoni et al., J Clin Oncol 2011) for letrozole's efficacy and toxicity; the human aromatase structure papers (Ghosh et al., Nature 2009; Ghosh et al., J Med Chem 2012) for the target structure. All ChEMBL potency values quoted were re-checked live against the ChEMBL API on 8 November 2026 for the target "Aromatase" (CHEMBL1978).

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target resolution was verified by hand: UniProt P11511 (CP19A_HUMAN, aromatase, CYP19A1, 503 aa) and ChEMBL target CHEMBL1978 ("Aromatase", SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens) — both correct, no correction needed.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure is PDB 3S79, "Human placental aromatase cytochrome P450 (CYP19A1)" in complex with androstenedione, 2.75 Å (Ghosh et al., J Med Chem 2012). The grid was centred on the centroid of the co-crystallised androstenedione (ligand code ASD, residue 601, chain A): [85.78, 54.15, 46.03]. The centre was verified against the PDB file: it is exactly the androstenedione centroid, 5.8 Å from the haem (HEM) centroid [85.38, 50.31, 41.58] — the haem cofactor was correctly excluded by the centre picker, so the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor or glycan) did not occur here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types, HETATM ligands stripped); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Six ligands were docked: letrozole itself (QUERY, PubChem CID 3902) and the top five pipeline-ranked leads, all known aromatase inhibitors with ChEMBL potencies of 0.02–0.21 nM. One of the five (CHEMBL1444) is letrozole itself as recorded in ChEMBL (Ki 0.02 nM), docked independently as a same-molecule control; it is reported as such, not as a new lead.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: letrozole and all five leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 panel was run for each lead. Letrozole's panel is measured data, not read-across: NR-Aromatase 1.0 — which is its own mechanism of action, not a toxicity signal, and is reported here so it is not misread as a hazard flag. The leads' highest read-across probabilities were NR-Aromatase 0.34–0.52 (also on-target signal), NR-ER up to 0.16 and SR-MMP up to 0.29. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised androstenedione pose (RMSD) was performed; a single X-ray structure (3S79, one aromatase conformation, 2.75 Å) was used; the receptor was held rigid, so the induced-fit movement of the substrate channel is not modelled; the leads are already-known aromatase inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed. Bone safety — the toxicity that limits letrozole — was not modelled for any lead, so a docking win says nothing about tolerability.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Aromatase potency, ChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) MW logP Lipinski violations PAINS Top tox read-across
CHEMBL197650 IC50 0.11 nM −8.77 −8.77, −8.66, −8.64 330.4 3.54 0 clean NR-Aromatase 0.392
Letrozole (reference, query) — −8.74 −8.74, −8.60, −8.31 285.3 2.66 0 clean NR-Aromatase 1.0 (measured, on-target)
CHEMBL1444 (letrozole, ChEMBL record) Ki 0.02 nM −8.71 −8.71, −8.49 285.3 2.66 0 clean NR-Aromatase 1.0 (measured, on-target)
CHEMBL5406734 IC50 0.21 nM −8.16 −8.16, −8.12, −7.93 369.2 3.45 0 clean NR-Aromatase 0.440
CHEMBL5436996 IC50 0.16 nM −7.90 −7.90, −7.82, −7.81 304.4 3.08 0 clean NR-Aromatase 0.338

All docking on PDB 3S79 (human aromatase + androstenedione, 2.75 Å), grid centre [85.78, 54.15, 46.03] (androstenedione centroid, haem-distal substrate site), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 8 November 2026. All five leads are known aromatase inhibitors; potencies are ChEMBL on-target values, re-checked live on 8 November 2026.

The headline, stated honestly: no lead beats letrozole beyond noise. The best lead (CHEMBL197650, IC50 0.11 nM) scores −8.77 kcal/mol against letrozole's −8.74 — a 0.03 kcal/mol margin, sixty times smaller than Vina's noise. The same molecule docked twice (letrozole as QUERY and as its ChEMBL record CHEMBL1444) scores −8.74 and −8.71, a 0.03 kcal/mol spread for an identical compound — which is itself a measure of the protocol's run-to-run jitter on this site, and it is exactly the size of the "win". Every margin in the table is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so not even the ranking of the leads can be treated as significant, let alone a "win" over the reference. The docking order also disagrees with measured potency: by IC50 the order is 0.02, 0.11, 0.16 and 0.21 nM, but by docking it is the 0.11 nM compound first, then letrozole, then the 0.02 nM compound, then the 0.21 nM and 0.16 nM compounds. The most potent measured inhibitor in the set (0.02 nM) scores third at −8.71 kcal/mol. The docking scores span only 0.87 kcal/mol while the measured potencies span 10-fold — Vina compresses the potency range on this site and ranks within it unreliably. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: every compound's three poses sit within 0.43 kcal/mol of its best score, so the scores are stable — stably wrong in potency order.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for letrozole on 3S79 was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for letrozole and five known aromatase inhibitors on the human structure are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the centre audit trail. The nearest published comparison uses a different program and a different structure: a 2023 Glide study on PDB 5JKV reported letrozole at −4.109 kcal/mol with new analogues at −7.0 to −8.1 kcal/mol — Glide scores are not comparable to Vina scores, so no cross-program ranking can be drawn from it. The ordering is not comparable to published potency either: the five leads span measured aromatase potencies of 0.02–0.21 nM, a 10-fold spread, while their docking scores span 0.87 kcal/mol in an order that disagrees with potency. Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and on this site it ranks them unreliably.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two things that could silently corrupt this result did not. The grid centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å and sits on the co-crystallised androstenedione at the haem-distal substrate site — the haem cofactor is 5.8 Å away and was correctly excluded, so the cofactor-centring fault is absent here. The pipeline's target resolution was also correct (P11511 aromatase; CHEMBL1978), unlike the same day's NS5A and neuraminidase runs, where human-preferring target ranking picked unrelated human proteins and the papers had to be corrected before drafting. The deeper problem is structural, not procedural: aromatase inhibitors bind by coordinating the haem iron through a triazole nitrogen while the rest of the molecule fills the androgen pocket, and a rigid-receptor docking with a generic scoring function cannot resolve the iron-coordination energetics that dominate real potency — which is why five sub-nanomolar inhibitors compress into 0.87 kcal/mol.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a negative benchmark with a useful control. There is no lead here: the best compound beats letrozole by 0.03 kcal/mol — inside noise, and the same size as the jitter between two dockings of the identical molecule. The durable findings are the benchmark values for letrozole on 3S79 (−8.74 kcal/mol, with full pose lists), the demonstration that Vina compresses a 10-fold potency range into 0.87 kcal/mol and orders it wrong, and the same-molecule control: letrozole docked twice scores −8.74 and −8.71, which calibrates the protocol's own reproducibility on this site at ±0.03 kcal/mol for identical input — any "win" smaller than that is not even a difference. The most actionable negative is that the cheapest next step is not more docking: the five leads are already sub-nanomolar, already PAINS-clean, already drug-like (zero Lipinski violations each), and the question that matters is which one keeps potency on resistant enzyme and spares bone — neither of which a Vina score can answer.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the best margin here is 0.03. Second, the ranking must be checked against measured aromatase IC50 values — the five leads span 0.02–0.21 nM, and a docking order that disagrees with that order is a measurement of the scoring function, not of the molecules. Third, the same-molecule control sets the floor: two dockings of letrozole differ by 0.03 kcal/mol, so a 0.03 kcal/mol "win" is indistinguishable from re-docking the reference. A docking "win" against letrozole on this site is not a discovery; it is a benchmark value awaiting an assay.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All leads are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (up to NR-Aromatase 0.52) are predictions from neighbours, not data. Letrozole's own measured NR-Aromatase value of 1.0 is a useful warning about reading the panel naively: on this target, the "toxicity" assay measures the drug's intended mechanism, so a high NR-Aromatase probability for a lead is on-target signal, not a hazard. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either. The validation assay must still include redox controls and a counter-screen, because a clean PAINS filter does not rule out assay interference. The larger safety question — bone loss and fracture risk, the toxicity that limits letrozole — is not addressed by PAINS at all and needs a dedicated bone-turnover model for any lead that advances.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-docking lead inhibits recombinant human aromatase with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value under identical assay conditions; a measured IC50 worse than letrozole's would confirm the noise interpretation, while a better one would refute it.
  2. A lead that docks well at the androstenedione site keeps its potency on aromatase carrying a resistance-associated mutation, where letrozole loses potency; loss of potency on the mutant would show the docking site is the resistance site, not a way around it.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised androstenedione into 3S79 reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  4. Docking the same six ligands on the earlier aromatase structure 3EQM (2.90 Å, androstenedione complex) gives the same ranking as on 3S79; a different ranking would show the result is structure-dependent, not molecule-dependent.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): aromatase inhibition assay (the standard tritiated-water-release assay on recombinant CYP19A1) for the best-docking lead, the second-best lead and letrozole, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): the same assay on a resistance-associated mutant aromatase for any compound that clears Stage 1, to test whether the lead survives the mutations seen after aromatase-inhibitor failure. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): oestrogen-dependent MCF-7 cell proliferation assay for any compound that clears Stage 2, with letrozole as control, plus a bone-turnover marker panel, since bone loss is the toxicity that a docking score cannot see. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as a real advantage — the best margin here is 0.03 kcal/mol. 3. Only one aromatase structure (3S79, one conformation, 2.75 Å) was docked; the earlier 3EQM structure was not scored. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking RMSD validation of the co-crystallised androstenedione pose was performed. 5. A single rigid receptor was used; the haem-iron coordination that dominates real aromatase-inhibitor potency is not modelled by the Vina scoring function. 6. All leads are already-known aromatase inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 7. The same-molecule control (letrozole docked twice, −8.74 and −8.71) calibrates run-to-run jitter but was not repeated across days or Vina versions. 8. Bone safety was not modelled for any lead. 9. The resistance analysis is literature-based: no mutant enzyme was docked and no IC50 was measured.

6. Conclusion

No aromatase inhibitor in this set beats letrozole on its own binding site: the best lead scores −8.77 kcal/mol on the human aromatase structure 3S79 against letrozole's −8.74 — a 0.03 kcal/mol margin, the same size as the jitter between two dockings of letrozole itself — and the docking order disagrees with measured potency, with the 0.02 nM inhibitor third and the 0.11 nM compound first. The honest reading is that on this haem-distal site, non-covalent docking cannot rank known inhibitors against letrozole — and the next experiment is a head-to-head aromatase inhibition assay on wild-type and resistant-mutant enzyme with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, plus a bone-safety assessment for any lead that advances, not more Vina docking.

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-07 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #5 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: tuberculosis; CYP51; posaconazole; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; azole; drug repurposing; Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Abstract

Tuberculosis made about 10.8 million people ill in 2023 and killed about 1.25 million, and azole antifungals have shown real antimycobacterial activity — econazole and clotrimazole kill Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv at 0.12 micrograms per millilitre — yet the target usually named for that activity, the sterol 14alpha-demethylase CYP51 (Rv0764c), sits in a bacterium that makes no sterols and lacks the rest of the sterol biosynthetic pathway, so whether CYP51 inhibition explains the killing is unproven. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking): target M. tuberculosis CYP51 (UniProt P9WPP9, ChEMBL CHEMBL5090, 12 bioactivities), structure PDB 2CIB at 1.50 angstrom, grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised inhibitor CM6 ([−16.89, −2.19, 69.32], 6.7 angstrom from the haem centroid), and five ligands docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under an identical protocol. Posaconazole, the repurposed triazole comparator, scored −7.99 kcal/mol, beating every lead by 1.30–2.13 kcal/mol — fluconazole −6.44, CHEMBL521787 −6.69, CHEMBL507264 −6.64, CHEMBL491289 −5.86 — but the ranking among the leads is inverted against measured binding: fluconazole, the tightest binder by ChEMBL Kd (200 nM), scores third, behind two 5,000 nM binders, and all margins sit inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The decisive limit is mechanistic, not numerical: azoles inhibit CYP51 by coordinating the haem iron, an interaction Vina cannot model, and posaconazole has no measured M. tuberculosis CYP51 affinity and no anti-TB MIC at all, so its docking win cannot be read as anti-TB activity. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head CYP51 binding assay (spectral Kd) for posaconazole against fluconazole, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable affinity advantage; a measured posaconazole Kd tighter than fluconazole's 200 nM, or a CYP51-knockout strain that stays azole-sensitive, would refute the claim that the docking win is only a measurement of Vina's limits and of a target whose essentiality is unproven.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases: according to the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, about 10.8 million people fell ill with TB in 2023 and about 1.25 million died. Standard treatment still takes months, and drug-resistant TB needs longer, more toxic regimens, so new drugs with new mechanisms are urgently needed — and repurposing an approved drug is the fastest route to one.

Azole antifungals are the oldest repurposing candidates in TB. Econazole and clotrimazole inhibit Mycobacterium smegmatis at MICs below 0.2 and 0.3 micromolar, better than rifampicin (1.2 micromolar) and isoniazid (36.5 micromolar) in the same assay, and both kill M. tuberculosis H37Rv at a MIC90 of 0.120 micrograms per millilitre with synergy against rifampicin and isoniazid. Econazole also kills nutrient-starved latent bacilli in vitro and reduces lung and spleen bacterial burden in latently infected mice, and in murine tuberculosis econazole alone reduced bacterial burden by 90% in lungs and spleen and was equipotent to rifampicin. Ketoconazole, the only systemically used azole tested in animals, reached an MIC of 8–16 micrograms per millilitre against H37Rv but showed no efficacy in the mouse model. The activity is real in a dish; the target is not settled.

The target usually named is CYP51 (Rv0764c), the M. tuberculosis sterol 14alpha-demethylase. It is a genuine enzyme: expressed in Escherichia coli, it 14alpha-demethylates lanosterol, 24,25-dihydrolanosterol and obtusifoliol, and its crystal structures with 4-phenylimidazole (PDB 1E9X, 2.1 angstrom) and fluconazole (PDB 1EA1, 2.21 angstrom) were the first structures of an authentic P450 drug target. Azoles bind it by coordinating the haem iron. But M. tuberculosis makes no sterols: it lacks squalene monooxygenase and oxidosqualene cyclase, the enzymes absolutely required for sterol biosynthesis, and the physiological function of its CYP51 remains obscure. The bacterium instead eats host cholesterol — cholesterol catabolism is required for persistence in animals — and the related P450 CYP121 binds azoles more tightly than CYP51 does, with Kd values in line with the antimycobacterial MICs. In the related actinomycete Streptomyces coelicolor, CYP51 is not essential for viability in vitro. So the azole killing of mycobacteria may run through CYP121, through several P450s at once, or through CYP51 — and docking against CYP51 alone cannot tell which.

Posaconazole is the strongest azole to test as a comparator: a broad-spectrum triazole with MIC90 of 0.5–1 microgram per millilitre against Candida and Cryptococcus and activity against fluconazole-resistant isolates, co-crystallised with the CYP51 of Trypanosoma cruzi and Trypanosoma brucei, and curative in murine Chagas disease. It has never been tested against M. tuberculosis CYP51 or against M. tuberculosis itself. The falsifiable hypothesis of this paper is that posaconazole docks to M. tuberculosis CYP51 more favourably than known CYP51 binders, and that the docking margin predicts a measurable binding advantage — a claim the paper then tests against the measured Kd values already in ChEMBL.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 7 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-07.md, PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI), UniProtKB and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 for the TB burden figures; Bellamine et al. (1999) for the catalytic characterisation of M. tuberculosis CYP51; Podust et al. (2001) for the 1E9X/1EA1 crystal structures; McLean et al. (2002) for azole MICs against M. smegmatis and azole binding to CYP51 and CYP121; Ahmad et al. (2005, 2006) for econazole/clotrimazole activity against replicating and latent M. tuberculosis H37Rv; Ouellet et al. (2011) and Lamb et al. (2002) for the missing sterol pathway and the non-essentiality of CYP51 in S. coelicolor; Chen et al. (2010) for posaconazole bound to trypanosomatid CYP51; and the 2025 thiophene-thiazole proceeding for the only published docking score on this target. The posaconazole repurposing limits — no anti-TB MIC, no measured M. tuberculosis CYP51 affinity, hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity of long-term azole use, and MmpS5-MmpL5 efflux as the main azole-resistance mechanism in M. tuberculosis — are taken from Carroll & Parish (2015) and the azole literature cited there.

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target: M. tuberculosis CYP51, UniProt P9WPP9 (gene cyp51, Rv0764c, 451 amino acids, strain ATCC 25618 / H37Rv); ChEMBL CHEMBL5090, 12 bioactivities retrieved. Thirteen compounds were ranked by composite score (similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20). The top five — the query posaconazole plus four leads — were taken forward to docking. All four leads are known CYP51 binders with published ChEMBL Kd values; two have no preferred name in ChEMBL.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 angstrom cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was M. tuberculosis CYP51, PDB 2CIB (1.50 angstrom, "High throughput screening and X-ray crystallography assisted evaluation of small molecule scaffolds for CYP51 inhibitors", co-crystallised ligand CM6: (2S)-2-[(2,1,3-benzothiadiazol-4-ylsulfonyl)amino]-2-phenyl-N-pyridin-4-ylacetamide), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of the co-crystallised ligand CM6, chain A: [−16.89, −2.19, 69.32]. The centre was verified against the PDB file: the haem (HEM) centroid is [−17.48, −7.22, 64.88], 6.7 angstrom away, so the centre sits on the inhibitor above the haem, not on the haem cofactor — the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor or glycan) did not occur here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

One pipeline fault was caught and repaired before reporting. The first docking attempt for posaconazole failed: the Vina run hit the protocol's 900-second timeout (posaconazole is 700.79 Da with 12 rotatable bonds, and three other docking runs were competing for CPU on the same machine). The reference drug was re-docked alone at the identical centre, box and exhaustiveness, and succeeded in about 14 minutes of wall time with poses [−7.99, −7.80, −7.76] kcal/mol. The re-dock is reported as the posaconazole result; the timeout is documented here because a silent retry would hide a real property of the protocol — large, flexible ligands can exceed the per-ligand time budget.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter. Posaconazole carries one PAINS alert, anil_di_alk_A(478) — the N,N-dialkyl aniline substructure of its piperazine-linked phenyl ring. All four docked leads are PAINS-clean. A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each compound: posaconazole's measured panel flags SR-ARE at 1.0; fluconazole flags nothing; the three unnamed leads flag only low read-across probabilities (highest NR-ER 0.276 for CHEMBL507264). These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and posaconazole is an approved drug, so its PAINS alert is a filter artefact for this scaffold class, not a liability finding.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of CM6 was performed; a single crystal structure (2CIB, one CYP51 conformation, holding a non-azole inhibitor) was used; and, most importantly, Vina cannot model the coordination bond between an azole nitrogen and the haem iron, which is the interaction that makes azoles CYP51 inhibitors — so every score reported here is missing the dominant binding term. Posaconazole has no measured affinity for M. tuberculosis CYP51 and no measured anti-TB MIC; the paper benchmarks a docking score, not a drug. The leads are already-known CYP51 binders, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

The headline, stated honestly: posaconazole "beats" every lead by 1.30–2.13 kcal/mol on docking — CHEMBL521787 by 1.30, CHEMBL507264 by 1.35, fluconazole by 1.55 and CHEMBL491289 by 2.13 kcal/mol — and it is the only margin in the table that clears Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, against the weakest lead. But three things cut against reading it as a discovery. First, posaconazole is by far the largest ligand in the set (700.79 Da, 12 rotatable bonds, against 231–306 Da for the leads), and Vina scores scale with the number of contacts a ligand makes, so a size advantage is expected and is not evidence of better binding. Second, the ranking among the four leads is inverted against measured binding: fluconazole, the tightest binder by Kd (200 nM), scores third, behind two 5,000 nM binders, and the 25-fold potency gap between fluconazole and the 5,000 nM binders corresponds to a docking gap of only 0.20–0.25 kcal/mol in the wrong direction. Third, the scored binding mode is the wrong one: azole inhibition of CYP51 is haem-iron coordination, which Vina cannot model at all, so the reference drug's score is missing the very interaction that defines its mechanism. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: posaconazole's three poses span only 0.23 kcal/mol and fluconazole's only 0.33, so both scores are stable — stably wrong about the order that matters.

No duplicate-entry fault occurred in this run: posaconazole (CHEMBL1397) does not appear among the 12 ChEMBL leads, unlike the macozinone duplicate caught in the DprE1 benchmark. One near-miss is worth recording: CHEMBL489925 (rank 7, Kd 5,000 nM, not docked — outside the top-5 cut) has the formula C19H15N5O3S2, the same as the co-crystallised ligand CM6, and its canonical SMILES is the CM6 scaffold itself — the crystal ligand's own ChEMBL entry sits in the lead list, one rank below the docking cut.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

One published docking score exists on this target: the thiophene-thiazole compound CTHTBN scored −8.8 kcal/mol against M. tuberculosis CYP51 (PDB 1E9X) with AutoDockTools 1.5.6. That number is not directly comparable to ours — different structure (1E9X, the 4-phenylimidazole complex, not 2CIB), different software version, and a different grid — but it sets the scale: published single-compound scores on this target run more negative than our best lead (−6.69) and somewhat more negative than posaconazole (−7.99), which is consistent with both numbers being dominated by ligand size and protocol rather than by measured affinity. No published Vina score for posaconazole or fluconazole on 2CIB was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for posaconazole and four known CYP51 binders on 2CIB are now on record for others to reproduce.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two things that could silently corrupt this result did not, and one thing that no structure check can catch did. The grid centre was verified against the PDB file and sits 6.7 angstrom from the haem centroid, on the co-crystallised inhibitor CM6, so the cofactor-centring fault is absent here. The duplicate-entry fault did not occur: posaconazole is absent from the lead list. The deeper problem is structural, not procedural: the reference drug is an azole whose mechanism is haem-iron coordination, and Vina has no term for metal coordination, so the score that "wins" by 1.30–2.13 kcal/mol is a score of van der Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds only. No grid-centre fix can repair that; only a method with a metal-coordination term (or a measured Kd) can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a measurement of Vina's limits on a haem target — and into a question about the target itself. There is no lead here: the compound that "wins" is the repurposed comparator, it wins by a margin that its size alone can explain, the leads are ranked backwards against their measured Kd values, and the target's role in killing M. tuberculosis is unproven because the bacterium makes no sterols. The durable findings are the benchmark values for posaconazole on 2CIB (−7.99 kcal/mol, with full pose lists), the inversion of the lead ranking against Kd, the CM6-scaffold entry sitting in the lead list, and the demonstration that on a haem-coordination target, non-covalent docking ranks known binders in the opposite order to their measured affinity.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the margins against the three best leads (1.30–1.55 kcal/mol) are inside or at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; only the 2.13 kcal/mol margin against the weakest lead clears it. Second, the ranking among the leads is inverted against measured Kd — a 200 nM binder scores below two 5,000 nM binders. Third, the winner is 2.3–3.0 times the molecular weight of the leads, and Vina rewards contact count. Fourth, the scored binding mode is the wrong one: haem-iron coordination is absent from every score reported here. A docking "win" for an azole on a haem enzyme, on a structure holding a non-azole inhibitor, is not a discovery; it is a measurement of what the method leaves out.

4.3 The repurposing limits are the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Posaconazole is not an anti-TB drug and this paper does not make it one. There is no published anti-TB MIC for posaconazole, no measured affinity for M. tuberculosis CYP51, and no animal data in TB; the Chagas data (cure in 50–100% of acutely infected mice) is against a different parasite's CYP51, not M. tuberculosis. Long-term azole use carries hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity, and M. tuberculosis resists azoles chiefly by MmpS5-MmpL5 efflux — both reasons a repurposing claim would need whole-cell and animal data before it could be taken seriously. The PAINS alert on posaconazole (anil_di_alk_A(478)) is a filter artefact on an approved drug and does not block validation, but it is reported because the filter output is part of the record. The validation assay must still include a counter-screen against human CYP51 and CYP121, because selectivity — not CYP51 affinity alone — is what would make an azole a TB drug rather than a broad P450 poison.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Posaconazole binds recombinant M. tuberculosis CYP51 with a spectral Kd tighter than fluconazole's 200 nM — the docking predicts a measurable advantage; a Kd equal to or weaker than 200 nM would refute the noise interpretation of the 1.55 kcal/mol margin.
  2. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand CM6 (CHEMBL489925) into 2CIB reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 angstrom RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  3. A CYP51-knockout (Rv0764c deletion) strain of M. tuberculosis H37Rv shows unchanged azole sensitivity — which would show CYP51 is not the target of azole killing, and would reframe the whole benchmark as a measurement on a bystander enzyme.
  4. Docking the same five ligands against M. tuberculosis CYP121 (PDB 2IJ7, fluconazole complex) ranks econazole/clotrimazole-class binders in agreement with their measured Kd values — testing whether the inversion is specific to CYP51 or general to haem targets under Vina.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): spectral binding assay (Soret shift titration) for posaconazole, fluconazole and CHEMBL521787 against purified recombinant M. tuberculosis CYP51, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable affinity advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): whole-cell M. tuberculosis H37Rv MIC assay (resazurin microtiter assay) for posaconazole, with econazole as the positive azole control (MIC90 0.120 micrograms per millilitre) and fluconazole as the negative control, plus a human CYP51 counter-screen for selectivity. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): if Stage 1 shows any genuine affinity advantage, a CYP51-knockout sensitivity test and a CYP121 docking comparison (hypothesis 4); if Stage 1 shows none, the project stops at the benchmark and the paper stands as a negative result. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; posaconazole and fluconazole are approved drugs, the unnamed leads are research chemicals, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Three of the four "winning" margins (1.30–1.55 kcal/mol) are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as real advantages. 3. Vina cannot model haem-iron coordination, so the azole mechanism is absent from every score reported here; the structure used (2CIB) holds a non-azole inhibitor. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, metal-aware docking, or re-docking validation of CM6 was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (2CIB, one CYP51 conformation) was used; induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. Posaconazole has no measured M. tuberculosis CYP51 affinity and no anti-TB MIC — the comparator is repurposed on the basis of antifungal and Chagas data only. 7. The target's essentiality is unproven: M. tuberculosis makes no sterols, lacks the sterol pathway, and the related CYP51 of S. coelicolor is non-essential in vitro. 8. The first posaconazole docking attempt timed out at the 900-second protocol limit under CPU contention and had to be re-run alone; the reported score comes from the re-dock at identical settings. 9. The PAINS alert and Tox21 read-across values are filter and similarity outputs, not measurements.

6. Conclusion

Posaconazole docks to M. tuberculosis CYP51 at −7.99 kcal/mol, 1.30–2.13 kcal/mol better than four known binders — but the leads rank backwards against their measured Kd values, the winner's size alone can explain its margin, Vina cannot see the haem coordination that defines azole binding, and the bacterium makes no sterols, so the target itself is in doubt. The honest reading is that on a haem target with an unproven role in TB, non-covalent docking measures the method, not the molecule — and the next experiment is a spectral Kd assay with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, plus a CYP51-knockout sensitivity test, not more Vina docking.
