No Lead Beats Bedaquiline on Its Own Site: A Vina Benchmark of Five ATP Synthase Inhibitors on the M. tuberculosis Fo Structure 8J57

Tuberculosis made about 10.8 million people ill in 2023 and killed about 1.25 million, and Pakistan alone accounted for about 686,000 cases and 47,000 deaths.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-07 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #4 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: bedaquiline; ATP synthase; AtpE; tuberculosis; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; diarylquinoline; drug resistance

Abstract

Tuberculosis made about 10.8 million people ill in 2023 and killed about 1.25 million, and Pakistan alone accounted for about 686,000 cases and 47,000 deaths. Bedaquiline, the first diarylquinoline, blocks the Mycobacterium tuberculosis ATP synthase by binding its c-ring subunit AtpE, but it carries boxed warnings for QT prolongation and increased mortality, and resistance is already emerging through atpE target mutations and mmpR5 efflux derepression. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking) against the M. tuberculosis ATP synthase Fo structure in complex with bedaquiline (PDB 8J57, 2.85 Å cryo-EM), with the grid centred on the co-crystallised bedaquiline copy at the a–c interface, and docked bedaquiline plus five known ATP synthase inhibitors with measured on-target IC50 values of 1–70 nM, all under an identical AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol. No lead beat bedaquiline: bedaquiline scored best at −8.13 kcal/mol, the closest lead (CHEMBL3754231, IC50 10 nM) trailed by 0.55 kcal/mol, and the most potent measured inhibitor (CHEMBL3754673, IC50 1 nM) scored only −7.37 kcal/mol — every margin inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the docking order disagrees with the measured potency order. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head ATP synthesis inhibition assay of the best-docking lead against bedaquiline on wild-type and Glu61Asp AtpE enzyme, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage; a lead that keeps potency on the Glu61Asp mutant, or a measured IC50 advantage over bedaquiline, would refute the claim that the docking ranking is only a measurement of Vina's limits.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases: according to the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, about 10.8 million people fell ill with TB in 2023 and about 1.25 million died. Pakistan is the fifth-highest-burden country, with an estimated 686,000 incident cases in 2023 (6.3% of the global burden), about 47,000 deaths, and about 15,000 people developing rifampicin-resistant TB. Drug-resistant TB needs longer, more toxic regimens, so new drugs with new mechanisms remain urgently needed.

Bedaquiline (BDQ, Sirturo, R207910/TMC207) is the first-in-class diarylquinoline, approved by the US FDA in December 2012 for multidrug-resistant TB — the first new TB drug class in four decades. It kills M. tuberculosis by blocking ATP synthase, the rotary enzyme that makes ATP from the proton gradient: diarylquinolines bind the oligomeric c-ring subunit AtpE in the membrane Fo domain and jam the rotor. The target was established genetically and biochemically in 2007, the isolated M. phlei c-ring was crystallised with bedaquiline at 1.7 Å in 2015, the M. smegmatis enzyme was solved by cryo-EM in 2021, and in 2024 the M. tuberculosis enzyme itself was solved with bedaquiline and with its analogue TBAJ-587 bound — three binding sites in the Fo domain, with the tightest at the interface of subunit a and the c-ring.

Bedaquiline's success is shadowed by two problems this paper is built around. First, safety: the FDA label carries boxed warnings for QT prolongation (bedaquiline blocks the cardiac hERG potassium channel; ECG monitoring is required and the drug is stopped if QTcF exceeds 500 ms) and for increased mortality (11.4% versus 2.5% on placebo in one trial). Bedaquiline also inhibits the human mitochondrial ATP synthase in vitro, with an IC50 of about 0.66 μM — the same binding site, in the human enzyme, at a concentration within reach of clinical exposure. Second, resistance: the WHO mutation catalogue associates only three genes with bedaquiline resistance — atpE, mmpR5 (Rv0678) and pepQ. Efflux-based resistance through mmpR5 derepression of the MmpS5–MmpL5 pump is the common route and usually gives a modest 2- to 8-fold MIC rise; target-based atpE mutations are rarer but give higher MICs and are thought to emerge after the efflux step. In vitro passaging shows the sequence clearly: dynamic rv0678 mutations first (MIC about 1 μg/mL), then fixed atpE mutations such as Glu61Asp (MIC 2 to >2 μg/mL). In clinical isolates, atpE mutations remain rare — only 17 clinical isolates with atpE mutations had been described in nine studies before a 2025 Russian series found Glu61Asp or Ile66Met in 4 of 8 bedaquiline-resistant strains — but they sit exactly at the drug-binding interface, at residues that contact bedaquiline directly.

The second-generation diarylquinolines show the class can be improved on both axes: TBAJ-587 is about four times more potent than bedaquiline against H37Rv (MIC 0.016 versus 0.0625 μg/mL) and eight times more potent against an Rv0678 mutant, and its first-in-human trial reported no clinically significant QTc effects; TBAJ-876 is at least tenfold more potent in MIC assays against diverse strains, including Rv0678 mutants, with reduced QTc risk in preclinical and phase 1 studies. The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known ATP synthase inhibitors against bedaquiline on the true M. tuberculosis structure, and what does an apparent docking "win" mean when the reference drug's own binding site is the grid? The falsifiable hypothesis is that any lead beating bedaquiline by less than 2 kcal/mol on Vina docking has no measurable potency advantage, and that the docking ranking will disagree with measured ATP synthase IC50 values on this target.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 7 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-07.md (no bedaquiline item that day; the digest's AMR-generalizability review is cited for the validation framing), PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI), RCSB PDB and UniProtKB. Key sources: the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 for burden figures; the 2007 Nature Chemical Biology paper establishing AtpE as the diarylquinoline target; the 2024 Nature paper solving the M. tuberculosis ATP synthase with bedaquiline and TBAJ-587; the FDA Sirturo label (DailyMed, updated 17 October 2025) for the boxed warnings; the 2019 Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy stepwise-resistance study; the 2025 Emerging Infectious Diseases report on atpE mutations in Russian clinical isolates; and the TBAJ-587/TBAJ-876 phase 1 and mouse-efficacy reports. All ChEMBL potency values quoted were re-checked live against the ChEMBL API on 7 November 2026 for the assay "Inhibition of Mycobacterium tuberculosis ATP synthase".

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Two pipeline faults were caught and corrected before reporting, and both are documented here because they are part of the result.

Fault 1 — wrong UniProt entry. The pipeline resolved the query "Mycobacterium tuberculosis ATP synthase subunit c AtpE" to UniProt P9WPV1, which is the ATP synthase epsilon chain (gene atpC, Rv1311, 121 aa) — not AtpE. The task brief's own suggested accession, P9WPV3, is also wrong: it is the ATP synthase subunit b-delta (gene atpFH, Rv1307). The correct AtpE entry was verified live against UniProtKB on 7 November 2026: P9WPS1 (ATPL_MYCTU, gene atpE, Rv1305, 81 aa). The ChEMBL side was correct: target CHEMBL2364166, "ATP synthase", a PROTEIN COMPLEX of M. tuberculosis with 8 components, from which 17 bioactivities were retrieved. The docking structure was therefore chosen by hand, not by the pipeline's UniProt lookup: PDB 8J57, "Cryo-EM structure of Mycobacterium tuberculosis ATP synthase Fo in complex with bedaquiline (BDQ)", 2.85 Å, from Zhang et al., Nature 2024 — whose chains 1–9 are subunit c (AtpE, P9WPS1) and chain a is subunit a.

Fault 2 — no PDB found. The pipeline's structure picker only accepts X-ray structures better than 3.0 Å, so it returned no_pdb_found and skipped docking entirely: the only M. tuberculosis ATP synthase structures with bedaquiline bound are cryo-EM (8J0S full complex, 8J57 Fo). Docking was therefore run manually with the same LeadForge dock() function and protocol.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The grid was centred on the centroid of the co-crystallised bedaquiline copy on chain 1 of 8J57: [162.46, 186.93, 275.26]. The centre was verified against the PDB file: 8J57 holds seven bedaquiline copies (ligand code BQ1, residue 600) on c-ring chains 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9. The chain-1 copy sits at the a–c interface — its centroid is 5.13 Å from the nearest subunit-a atom and its closest atom contact to subunit a is 3.04 Å — while the chain-4 copy is the second a-contacting site (6.09 Å) and the remaining five copies are c-only sites 13.5–37.6 Å from subunit a. The chain-1 copy is therefore one of the two tight a–c interface sites described by Zhang et al., not a cofactor, glycan or lipid: the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor or glycan) did not occur here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types, HETATM ligands stripped); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Six ligands were docked: bedaquiline itself (QUERY, PubChem CID 5388906) and the top five pipeline-ranked leads, all known ATP synthase inhibitors with ChEMBL potencies measured in the on-target enzyme assay. All five leads are diarylquinoline analogues except CHEMBL4101131, a squaramide (cyclobutenedione) chemotype with low structural similarity to bedaquiline (Tanimoto 0.073).

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: bedaquiline and all five leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were NR-AhR 0.179 for CHEMBL3754673, SR-MMP 0.134 for CHEMBL3754231, SR-ARE 0.245 for CHEMBL4101131, and NR-ER-LBD 0.086 for bedaquiline itself. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised bedaquiline pose (RMSD) was performed; a single cryo-EM structure (8J57, one Fo conformation, 2.85 Å) was used; only one of the three bedaquiline binding sites (the a–c interface site) was docked, and the c-only and lagging sites were not scored; and the leads are already-known ATP synthase inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed. Bedaquiline's QT-prolongation liability (hERG block) was not modelled for any lead, so a docking win says nothing about cardiac safety.

All five leads are known ATP synthase inhibitors; IC50 values are ChEMBL on-target enzyme-assay potencies, re-checked live on 7 November 2026.

The headline, stated honestly: no lead beats bedaquiline. Bedaquiline scores best at −8.13 kcal/mol with a tight pose cluster (−8.13, −7.91, −7.45; 0.68 kcal/mol spread), and every lead trails it — the closest by 0.55 kcal/mol, the furthest by 1.99 kcal/mol. Every margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so not even the ranking of the leads can be treated as significant, let alone a "win" over the reference. The docking order also disagrees with measured potency: by IC50 the order is 1, 10, 30, 50, 70 nM, but by docking it is bedaquiline, then the 10 nM, 1 nM, 50 nM and 70 nM compounds, with the 30 nM squaramide last. The most potent measured inhibitor in the set (CHEMBL3754673, IC50 1 nM) scores third at −7.37 kcal/mol, 0.76 kcal/mol behind bedaquiline. The docking scores span only 1.99 kcal/mol while the measured potencies span 70-fold — Vina compresses the potency range on this site and ranks within it unreliably. The squaramide CHEMBL4101131 is the instructive failure: a different chemotype (Tanimoto 0.073 to bedaquiline), the only lead with zero Lipinski violations and the lowest logP (1.79), and the worst docking score (−6.14) despite a respectable 30 nM IC50 — either the diarylquinoline-shaped site genuinely disfavours it, or Vina cannot score a non-diarylquinoline in a diarylquinoline pocket. Either way, its score is not evidence against its potency. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: every compound's three poses sit within 0.68 kcal/mol of its best score, so the scores are stable — stably wrong in potency order.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for bedaquiline or any of these leads on 8J57 was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for bedaquiline and five known ATP synthase inhibitors on the true M. tuberculosis Fo structure are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the corrected-centre audit trail. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: the five leads span measured ATP synthase IC50 values of 1–70 nM, a 70-fold spread, while their docking scores span 1.99 kcal/mol in an order that disagrees with potency — the 1 nM compound third, the 30 nM squaramide last. Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and on this site it ranks them unreliably.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two things that could silently corrupt this result did not, and two did. The grid centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å and sits on a bedaquiline copy at the a–c interface, 3.04 Å from subunit a — the cofactor/glycan-centring fault is absent here, because the structure holds no cofactor at all. The pipeline's UniProt resolution fault did occur: left uncorrected, the paper would have been written against the epsilon chain (P9WPV1) while claiming to target AtpE, and the task brief's own suggested accession (P9WPV3, subunit b-delta) would have been equally wrong. The pipeline's X-ray-only structure picker also failed silently, skipping docking with no_pdb_found on a target whose only liganded structures are cryo-EM. The deeper problem is structural, not procedural: bedaquiline binds three sites in the Fo domain, and docking one site — even the tightest — cannot represent the drug's full binding energetics, which include the conformational change the drug induces in the enzyme.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a negative benchmark with a useful control. There is no lead here: bedaquiline beats all five known inhibitors on its own site, the closest by 0.55 kcal/mol — inside noise — and the most potent measured inhibitor (1 nM) is only third on docking. The durable findings are the benchmark values for bedaquiline on 8J57 (−8.13 kcal/mol, with full pose lists), the demonstration that Vina compresses a 70-fold potency range into 1.99 kcal/mol and orders it wrong, and the audit trail of two pipeline faults caught before reporting — the wrong-UniProt-entry fault and the X-ray-only structure-picker fault — both of which would have produced a confidently wrong paper. The squaramide result is the most actionable negative: a non-diarylquinoline with a 30 nM on-target IC50, zero Lipinski violations and the best drug-likeness in the set scores worst on docking, which is exactly the profile a diarylquinoline-shaped docking screen would discard — and exactly the profile that might escape both bedaquiline's hERG liability and the atpE resistance mutations that sit in the diarylquinoline pocket.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the ranking must be checked against measured ATP synthase IC50 values — the five leads span 1–70 nM, and a docking order that disagrees with that order is a measurement of the scoring function, not of the molecules. Third, only one of bedaquiline's three Fo binding sites was scored, and the cryo-EM structure is a single Fo conformation; the drug's potency comes partly from the large conformational change it induces, which a rigid-receptor docking cannot model. A docking "win" against bedaquiline on one site is not a discovery; it is a benchmark value awaiting an assay.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All leads are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (up to SR-ARE 0.245) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either. The validation assay must still include redox controls and a counter-screen, because a clean PAINS filter does not rule out assay interference. The larger safety question — hERG block and QT prolongation, the class liability that carries a boxed warning for bedaquiline — is not addressed by PAINS at all and needs a dedicated hERG assay for any lead that advances.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-docking lead inhibits recombinant M. tuberculosis ATP synthase with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value under identical assay conditions; a measured IC50 worse than bedaquiline's would confirm the noise interpretation, while a better one would refute it.
  2. A lead that docks well at the a–c interface site keeps its potency on Glu61Asp AtpE enzyme, the atpE mutation found in 4 of 8 bedaquiline-resistant Russian clinical isolates; loss of potency on the mutant would show the docking site is the resistance site, not a way around it.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised bedaquiline (chain-1 BQ1) into 8J57 reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  4. Docking the same six ligands at the second a-contacting site (chain-4 BQ1 copy) and at a c-only site (chain-6 BQ1 copy) gives the same ranking as the chain-1 site; a different ranking would show the result is site-dependent, not molecule-dependent.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): ATP synthesis inhibition assay (the same luminometer-based assay reported for CHEMBL4101131's 30 nM IC50) for the best-docking lead, the second-best lead and bedaquiline, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): the same assay on Glu61Asp and Ile66Met AtpE mutant enzyme for any compound that clears Stage 1, to test whether the lead survives the two atpE mutations most often seen in resistant clinical isolates. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): whole-cell M. tuberculosis H37Rv MIC assay for any compound that clears Stage 2, with bedaquiline as control, plus a hERG channel assay, since QT prolongation is the class liability that a docking score cannot see. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as a real advantage. 3. Only one of bedaquiline's three Fo binding sites was docked; the c-only and lagging sites were not scored. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking RMSD validation of the co-crystallised bedaquiline pose was performed. 5. A single cryo-EM structure (8J57, one Fo conformation, 2.85 Å) was used; the drug-induced conformational change is not modelled and the receptor was held rigid. 6. All leads are already-known ATP synthase inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 7. The pipeline's UniProt resolution picked the wrong subunit (epsilon chain instead of AtpE) and its structure picker skipped cryo-EM structures entirely — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited. 8. The hERG/QT liability was not modelled for any lead. 9. The resistance analysis is literature-based: no mutant enzyme was docked and no MIC was measured.

6. Conclusion

No ATP synthase inhibitor in this set beats bedaquiline on its own binding site: bedaquiline scores −8.13 kcal/mol on the M. tuberculosis Fo structure 8J57, every lead trails it by 0.55–1.99 kcal/mol — inside Vina's noise — and the docking order disagrees with measured potency, with the 1 nM inhibitor third and the 30 nM squaramide last. The honest reading is that on this membrane site, non-covalent docking cannot rank known inhibitors against bedaquiline — and the next experiment is a head-to-head ATP synthesis assay on wild-type and Glu61Asp AtpE enzyme with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, plus a hERG assay for any lead that advances, not more Vina docking.

Vebicorvir "Beats" Bersacapavir by Docking and Loses by 1.10 kcal/mol of Noise: A Vina Benchmark of HBV Capsid Assembly Modulators on 5WRE and the Functional-Cure Gap

Chronic hepatitis B affected about 240 million people and caused about 1.1 million deaths in 2024, yet no approved drug clears the virus: nucleos(t)ide analogues suppress replication indefinitely and functional cure — sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) loss off treatment — remains rare.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-07 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #2 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: hepatitis B virus; capsid assembly modulator; bersacapavir; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; core protein; functional cure; GLS4

Abstract

Chronic hepatitis B affected about 240 million people and caused about 1.1 million deaths in 2024, yet no approved drug clears the virus: nucleos(t)ide analogues suppress replication indefinitely and functional cure — sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) loss off treatment — remains rare. Capsid assembly modulators (CAMs) that bind the core protein dimer-dimer interface are the most advanced new mechanism, but no CAM is approved, and the most advanced, bersacapavir, reached phase 2b without a single functional cure in the REEF-2 trial. We benchmarked four CAMs against the same HBV core-protein pocket with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on PDB 5WRE (1.95 Å, HAP-bound): the investigational comparator bersacapavir, the phase 2 heteroaryldihydropyrimidine GLS4 (morphothiadin), the discontinued vebicorvir, and the co-crystallised HAP_R01 as a re-dock control. Vebicorvir scored best at −8.03 kcal/mol, beating bersacapavir (−6.93 kcal/mol) by 1.10 kcal/mol, with HAP_R01 at −6.76 and GLS4 last at −6.53 kcal/mol — but the ranking is inverted against measured potency: vebicorvir is the weakest by experiment (EC50 173–250 nM), while GLS4 is the most potent (IC50 12 nM) and bersacapavir sits between them (EC50 45 nM). The 1.10 kcal/mol margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the docking "win" is not a discovery. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head HBV replication assay of vebicorvir against bersacapavir under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage; a measured advantage for vebicorvir would refute the noise interpretation.

1. Introduction

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) remains one of the world's deadliest chronic infections: according to the WHO hepatitis B fact sheet, about 240 million people were living with chronic HBV infection in 2024, with about 0.9 million new infections each year, and hepatitis B caused an estimated 1.1 million deaths in 2024, mostly from cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Pakistan carries a large share of that burden: WHO estimated about 3.8 million people living with hepatitis B in Pakistan in 2025, with only 25–30% aware of their infection, and a national survey found hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) prevalence of 2.5% in the general population. Approved therapy — nucleos(t)ide analogues such as entecavir and tenofovir, and pegylated interferon — suppresses viral replication but almost never clears the virus, because none of these drugs eliminates covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) from the hepatocyte nucleus. Treatment is therefore usually lifelong, and functional cure — sustained HBsAg loss after stopping treatment — is the goal every new drug class is now judged against.

The HBV core protein (Cp, 183 amino acids) is the most advanced new drug target in this search. Cp self-assembles into the icosahedral capsid — predominantly T=4 particles of 120 dimers — that packages pregenomic RNA (pgRNA) and the viral polymerase, and it acts at several steps of replication: assembly, pgRNA encapsidation, reverse transcription, nuclear trafficking and cccDNA formation. Capsid assembly modulators (CAMs), also called core protein allosteric modulators (CpAMs), bind a hydrophobic "HAP" pocket at the Cp dimer-dimer interface and misdirect assembly: class I CAMs (CAM-A, e.g. heteroaryldihydropyrimidines such as GLS4) induce aberrant, non-functional capsids, while class II CAMs (CAM-E, e.g. sulfamoylbenzamides such as bersacapavir) accelerate the formation of empty capsids devoid of pgRNA. Both classes prevent infectious virion formation, and both are being tested in combination regimens aimed at functional cure.

No CAM is approved. The most advanced, bersacapavir (JNJ-56136379 / JNJ-6379, a CAM-E), reached phase 2b: in the REEF-2 trial, 130 nucleos(t)ide analogue-suppressed, HBeAg-negative patients received 48 weeks of the siRNA JNJ-73763989 plus bersacapavir 250 mg daily plus a nucleos(t)ide analogue, followed by 48 weeks off treatment — and no patient achieved functional cure at follow-up week 24 or week 48, although mean HBsAg fell 1.89 log10 IU/mL on treatment versus 0.06 in the control arm. GLS4 (morphothiadin, a CAM-A heteroaryldihydropyrimidine) completed phase 2 in combination with ritonavir (which boosts its otherwise short half-life), and vebicorvir (a CAM-A) was discontinued after a phase 2b trial did not achieve the desired level of antiviral effect. The question this paper asks is methodological, in the same pattern as the DprE1 benchmark: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known CAMs against bersacapavir, and what does an apparent docking "win" mean when the reference drug is investigational, the most potent compound by experiment scores worst, and the "winner" is a discontinued drug? The falsifiable hypothesis is that any CAM beating bersacapavir by less than 2 kcal/mol on Vina docking has no measurable potency advantage, and that the docking ranking will disagree with measured EC50 values on this target.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 7 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/, PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI), RCSB PDB and UniProtKB. Key sources: the WHO hepatitis B fact sheet for the global burden figures (240 million living with chronic HBV in 2024, 1.1 million deaths); the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office statement of 28 July 2025 for the Pakistan figure (about 3.8 million living with hepatitis B, 25–30% aware); the REEF-2 trial report (Journal of Hepatology 2024;81:404–414) for the functional-cure outcome; the 2023 Expert Opinion on Drug Discovery review of CAMs for the class definitions, trial status and resistance data; the 2013 Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy characterisation of GLS4 (EC50 62.24 nM in HepAD38 cells, IC50 12 nM); and the 2021 PLoS Pathogens study of dimer-dimer interface residues for the HAP-pocket resistance mechanism. Measured potencies quoted in this paper are ChEMBL bioactivities against the organism-level target "Hepatitis B virus" (CHEMBL613497), retrieved live on 7 November 2026.

2.2 Molecular docking

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was the HBV core protein, PDB 5WRE (1.95 Å, "Hepatitis B virus core protein Y132A mutant in complex with heteroaryldihydropyrimidine (HAP_R01)", ligand code 7TL), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of the co-crystallised ligand 7TL, chain A: [−44.94, 9.56, 28.99]. The centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å: the pipeline's own ligand-centre function returns the same coordinates, and the nearest crystallisation additives (isopropyl alcohol, glycerol, chloride) sit 14–22 Å away, so the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor, glycan or solvent) did not occur here. The receptor was the full crystallographic hexamer (chains A–F), so the dimer-dimer interface pocket — which is formed by two dimers — is intact in the docking receptor. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Four compounds were docked, all with identities verified in ChEMBL (canonical SMILES taken from ChEMBL, not from a text search): bersacapavir (CHEMBL4744254), GLS4 (CHEMBL3742114), vebicorvir (CHEMBL4650324), and HAP_R01 (CHEMBL4446995), the co-crystallised ligand of 5WRE, re-docked as a control. Three further candidates were considered and excluded because their identities could not be verified: ChEMBL text search returned no named entry for NVR 3-778, returned a non-matching structure for AT-130 (no bromine in the returned SMILES, while AT-130 contains bromine), and returned vebicorvir itself for ABI-H0731. They were not docked under those names.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all four compounds were PAINS-clean (no alerts). Lipinski descriptors were computed with RDKit: bersacapavir MW 418.37, logP 2.52, 0 violations; GLS4 MW 509.40, logP 3.29, 1 violation (MW > 500); vebicorvir MW 467.45, logP 3.49, 0 violations; HAP_R01 MW 514.91, logP 3.25, 1 violation (MW > 500).

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking RMSD validation was performed; a single crystal structure (5WRE, one core-protein conformation, a Y132A mutant) was used; and the structure's UniProt entry (L7R9I1) differs from the genotype D reference P03146 at six of 183 residues (96.7% identity), two of which (positions 35 and 40) sit in the pocket-adjacent 23–39 stretch. The comparator is investigational, not approved: there is no approved HBV capsid drug, so no approved reference exists. No cure is claimed and no clinical recommendation is made.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Class Measured potency, ChEMBL (HBV) Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) MW logP Lipinski violations PAINS

Bersacapavir (comparator) CAM-E EC50 45 nM −6.93 −6.93, −6.91, −6.89 418.37 2.52 0 clean
HAP_R01 (re-dock control) CAM-A — (co-crystallised ligand) −6.76 −6.76, −6.39, −6.32 514.91 3.25 1 clean
GLS4 (morphothiadin) CAM-A IC50 12 nM; EC50 13 nM −6.53 −6.53, −6.51, −6.43 509.40 3.29 1 clean

All docking on PDB 5WRE (HBV core protein Y132A mutant, 1.95 Å), grid centre [−44.94, 9.56, 28.99] (7TL chain-A centroid), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 7 November 2026. Measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivities against target CHEMBL613497 ("Hepatitis B virus"); GLS4's published HepAD38 EC50 is 62.24 nM (Wu et al. 2013).

The headline, stated honestly: one genuine CAM "beats" bersacapavir on docking — vebicorvir by 1.10 kcal/mol (−8.03 versus −6.93) — but vebicorvir is the weakest of the three by measured potency (EC50 173–250 nM, 4–6 times weaker than bersacapavir's 45 nM and 14–21 times weaker than GLS4's 12 nM). The docking ranking is inverted against measured potency: the best-docking compound is the weakest by EC50, and the most potent compound (GLS4, 12 nM) scores worst on docking (−6.53). The margin (1.10 kcal/mol) is also inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so it would not be interpretable as a real advantage even if the potency order agreed. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: vebicorvir holds its best score across all three poses (−8.03, −7.93, −7.79), yet is the weakest by EC50; GLS4 is equally pose-stable at the bottom of the table (−6.53, −6.51, −6.43). The re-dock control is informative in a different way: HAP_R01, re-docked into its own crystallographic pocket, scores −6.76 — in the same narrow band as bersacapavir and GLS4, and 1.27 kcal/mol worse than vebicorvir — which shows that a ligand crystallised in this exact pocket does not score best in it. The whole table spans only 1.50 kcal/mol across four compounds whose measured potencies span a 21-fold range.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for bersacapavir, GLS4 or vebicorvir on 5WRE was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for the three most clinically advanced CAMs on 5WRE are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the re-dock control. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: the three compounds span EC50/IC50 12–250 nM, a 21-fold spread, while their docking scores span 1.50 kcal/mol in the wrong order — Vina ranks poses, not EC50s, and on this target it ranks them backwards.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Three things that could silently corrupt this result did not, and two pipeline faults were caught before reporting. The grid centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å and sits on the co-crystallised HAP ligand, 14–22 Å from the nearest solvent additive, so the cofactor/glycan-centring fault is absent here. The duplicate-entry fault seen in earlier papers did not occur: none of the four docked compounds is a duplicate of the comparator (all four have distinct molecular formulae and weights). But the automated pipeline failed twice before this manual run, and both failures are part of the result. First, the pipeline's UniProt lookup prefers human proteins, so the text query "Hepatitis B virus core protein" resolved to Q96SB4 — human SRSF protein kinase 1 (SRPK1), a kinase that phosphorylates the core protein but is not the capsid — and that run was killed before docking. Second, with the accession P03146 forced, UniProt resolved correctly (HBV genotype D capsid protein) but the pipeline's ChEMBL target fallback picked CHEMBL2074, human maltase-glucoamylase, and its 26 "leads" were maltase-glucoamylase ligands; those leads were discarded, not used. Third, the pipeline's PDB auto-pick found no ligand-bound X-ray structure under 3.0 Å cross-referenced to P03146, so docking was skipped — the structure used here, 5WRE, is cross-referenced to a different HBV core-protein entry (L7R9I1) and had to be selected manually. A pipeline that silently prefers human proteins, silently falls back to a wrong ChEMBL target, and cannot find a structure that exists under a sibling accession is a pipeline that needs its target-resolution step fixed before it is trusted on viral targets; the manual verification steps in this paper are the workaround, not the fix.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a measurement of Vina's limits on this target — and into a caution about the functional-cure literature. There is no lead here: the one compound that "beats" bersacapavir on docking is the weakest by measured EC50, was discontinued after phase 2b for insufficient antiviral effect, and its margin sits inside Vina's noise. The most potent compound by experiment (GLS4, 12 nM, in phase 2 with ritonavir) scores worst. The durable findings are the benchmark values for the three clinically advanced CAMs on 5WRE, the re-dock control (−6.76 kcal/mol for a ligand in its own pocket), and the demonstration that on a capsid-assembly target, non-covalent docking ranks known CAMs in the opposite order to their measured potency — the same inversion the DprE1 benchmark found on a covalent-inhibitor target, which suggests the failure is general to this pipeline's scoring on assembly/modulator targets, not specific to one protein.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the margin (1.10 kcal/mol) is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the ranking is inverted against measured potency — the best-docking compound is the weakest by EC50, by a factor of 4–6 against the comparator and 14–21 against GLS4. Third, the scored quantity is a static binding energy at one pocket of a mutant hexamer, while CAM activity depends on the kinetics of capsid assembly, the distinction between aberrant and empty capsids, pgRNA packaging, and resistance — none of which a single-structure docking score can see. Bersacapavir monotherapy selected the T33N resistance mutation in the clinic, a reminder that the pocket itself evolves under drug pressure; a docking score computed on a wild-type-structure pocket says nothing about the resistant one. A docking "win" against an investigational comparator, on a mutant structure, is not a discovery; it is a measurement of what the method leaves out.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All four compounds are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and two of the four carry a Lipinski violation (MW > 500), which is a developability note, not a disqualification: GLS4 is already in phase 2 despite it. The validation assay must still include a counter-screen and a capsid-assembly readout, because a clean PAINS filter does not rule out assay interference, and because a replication EC50 alone cannot distinguish a true CAM from a compound that merely poisons the cells.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Vebicorvir inhibits HBV replication with an EC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL values (173–250 nM) under identical assay conditions, and is less potent than bersacapavir (45 nM) — the docking predicts no measurable advantage; a measured EC50 for vebicorvir better than bersacapavir's would refute the noise interpretation.
  2. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand 7TL (HAP_R01) into 5WRE reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; affinity only is reported here, RMSD not yet computed).
  3. Docking the same four compounds against a second HBV core-protein structure (for example a CAM-E-bound structure, if one becomes available) preserves the inversion against measured potency — testing whether the failure is structure-specific or method-general.
  4. Fixing the pipeline's target-resolution step (organism-aware UniProt lookup, accession-verified ChEMBL target, PDB search across sibling accessions) reproduces the manual 5WRE selection automatically — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): HBV replication assay in HepG2.2.15 or HepAD38 cells for vebicorvir, bersacapavir and GLS4, same plate, n = 3, HBV DNA by qPCR as readout, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): capsid-assembly readout (native agarose gel / capsid ELISA) for any compound that clears Stage 1, to confirm the mechanism is capsid modulation rather than cytotoxicity, with a cell-viability counter-screen (CC50) on the same plate. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): resistance check — sequence the core-protein HAP pocket (residues 23–40, 102–140) after serial passage under CAM pressure, looking for T33N and neighbouring substitutions, since pocket evolution is the known clinical failure mode for this class. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are investigational research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The single "winning" margin (1.10 kcal/mol) is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as a real advantage. 3. The docking ranking is inverted against measured potency, so the scores cannot be used to rank these CAMs. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking RMSD validation was performed. 5. A single crystal structure was used (5WRE, one core-protein conformation, a Y132A mutant whose UniProt entry differs from genotype D P03146 at six residues, two of them pocket-adjacent at positions 35 and 40); induced-fit effects and genotype variation are not modelled. 6. The comparator is investigational — no approved HBV capsid drug exists, so there is no approved reference standard. 7. All three CAMs are already-known compounds; no new chemical matter is proposed. 8. The automated pipeline's target resolution failed twice on this topic (wrong UniProt organism, wrong ChEMBL target) and its PDB auto-pick missed a structure that exists under a sibling accession — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited. 9. No cccDNA or HBsAg-loss readout was modelled; docking says nothing about functional cure, which is a clinical endpoint, not a binding energy.

6. Conclusion

No CAM in this set beats bersacapavir: the one compound that scores better on Vina docking is the weakest by measured EC50 and was discontinued after phase 2b, the most potent compound by experiment scores worst, and the margin sits inside Vina's noise. The honest reading is that on a capsid-assembly target, non-covalent docking ranks known CAMs backwards — and the next experiment is a head-to-head HBV replication assay with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, plus a capsid-assembly readout and a resistance check at the HAP pocket, not more Vina docking.

No Pocket to Dock: A Negative Computational Result for Small-Molecule Targeting of BCL11A in Beta-Thalassaemia

Beta-thalassaemia affects about 5-8% of Pakistan's population as carriers, roughly 9.8 million people, with an estimated 5,000 to 9,000 children born with thalassaemia major each year, and raising fetal haemoglobin (HbF) is the best-validated way to soften the disease.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-07 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #3 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: BCL11A; fetal haemoglobin; beta-thalassaemia; hydroxyurea; molecular docking; zinc finger; HbF induction; Pakistan

Abstract

Beta-thalassaemia affects about 5-8% of Pakistan's population as carriers, roughly 9.8 million people, with an estimated 5,000 to 9,000 children born with thalassaemia major each year, and raising fetal haemoglobin (HbF) is the best-validated way to soften the disease. BCL11A is the master repressor of the fetal gamma-globin genes, and genetic disruption of its erythroid enhancer made 91% of patients transfusion-independent in the CLIMB THAL-111 trial, yet that therapy is a one-time ex vivo gene edit far beyond the reach of most Pakistani patients, while the cheap oral HbF inducer hydroxyurea works indirectly, variably, and not by binding BCL11A. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB to ChEMBL to PubChem to RDKit to PAINS/ADMET to Vina docking) asking whether any small molecule could be docked against BCL11A as a first triage step. The pipeline correctly identified human BCL11A (UniProt Q9H165) but found zero known ligands for it in ChEMBL and only the reference drug itself, hydroxyurea, to dock. Docking did produce a number, minus 4.26 kcal/mol on PDB 8DTN, but a centre audit refutes it: the grid was centred on a single selenomethionine residue (MSE A34) of the co-crystallised nanobody, not on BCL11A and not on any binding pocket, because 8DTN contains no small-molecule ligand at all, and no ligand-bound BCL11A structure exists in the Protein Data Bank. The score is therefore discarded, docking is skipped as a method on this target, and the durable results are the negative ones: no ChEMBL ligand, no druggable pocket in any deposited structure, and a pipeline fault in which the centre picker falls back to a modified residue when no ligand exists. The falsifiable next step is a cellular assay, not more docking: a K562 or primary erythroid gamma-globin reporter screen of a focused library, with a pre-registered rule that a compound must raise gamma-globin mRNA at least two-fold without cytotoxicity, and a direct BCL11A binding test for any hit, since a docking score on this target cannot be the evidence.

1. Introduction

Beta-thalassaemia is one of the commonest inherited disorders in Pakistan: the carrier rate is 5-8%, about 9.8 million carriers, and an estimated 5,000 to 9,000 children are born with thalassaemia major every year, with roughly 100,000 patients dependent on regular transfusion. Lifelong transfusion plus iron chelation is the standard of care, and the only cure, bone-marrow transplantation, is beyond the means of most families. Any cheap oral drug that raises fetal haemoglobin (HbF, alpha2-gamma2) would change this arithmetic, because gamma-globin chains substitute for the missing beta-globin chains and mop up the excess alpha chains that destroy red-cell precursors.

BCL11A is the gene that keeps HbF switched off in adults. Genome-wide association studies found that a common variant in BCL11A, rs11886868, associates with HbF level at P < 10^-35, and BCL11A was then established as the direct transcriptional repressor of the gamma-globin genes, binding the TGACCA motif at positions -118 to -113 of the gamma-globin promoter. The therapeutic proof is now clinical, not theoretical: exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), which uses CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt the erythroid-specific enhancer of BCL11A in a patient's own stem cells, made 91% of transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia patients transfusion-independent in the CLIMB THAL-111 trial, and was approved by the US FDA for transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia on 16 January 2024. But it is a one-time ex vivo gene therapy requiring myeloablation and a transplant centre, priced far beyond the reach of a health system in which most thalassaemia care is delivered by charitable blood banks.

The cheap oral alternative is hydroxyurea, a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor that raises HbF indirectly through cytotoxic stress erythropoiesis. Its record in beta-thalassaemia is weak and variable: a Cochrane review found only seven small randomised trials with 291 people with non-transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia, and concluded the evidence for any HbF inducer was very uncertain, with no trial reporting the pre-specified outcome of transfusion frequency. Response varies between patients, low doses can reduce HbF, and the bone marrow of beta-thalassaemia patients appears more sensitive to hydroxyurea myelosuppression. Crucially, hydroxyurea does not act by binding BCL11A: there is no evidence it binds the protein at all.

The question this paper asks is therefore narrow and methodological: can the standard LeadForge docking pipeline — the same protocol that benchmarked DprE1 inhibitors the day before — produce any meaningful small-molecule result against BCL11A, or does the target itself defeat the method? The falsifiable hypothesis is that no valid docking result is obtainable on BCL11A, because the target has no known small-molecule ligands and no ligand-bound structure, and that any docking number the pipeline produces on this target will fail a centre audit.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 7 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-07.md, PubMed, ChEMBL (EBI), UniProtKB and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the molecular epidemiology of beta-thalassaemia in Pakistan for the burden figures; the 2008 genome-wide association study linking BCL11A to HbF; the 2018 Cell paper establishing direct promoter repression of gamma-globin by BCL11A; the 2024 Science paper showing BCL11A functions as a tetramer mediated by zinc finger 0 (ZnF0); the 2024 Nature Communications and Structure papers on the ZnF456-DNA complex; the CLIMB THAL-111 trial report in the New England Journal of Medicine; and the Cochrane review of HbF inducers in non-transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia. Every citation in the References section was verified (PMID or DOI checked live, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina), target "BCL11A zinc finger", reference drug hydroxyurea, with ~/workspace/.venv-fc/bin/python run_docking.py. Target identification used UniProtKB and ChEMBL live; ligand retrieval used ChEMBL bioactivities for the matched target; the query compound was verified against PubChem; ADMET and PAINS screening used RDKit; a ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run. Docking, where attempted, used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 with the standard protocol (22.5 A box, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses, best pose reported). The grid centre was then audited against the PDB file itself, residue by residue, before any score was accepted — the audit that caught the grid-centre faults in Papers #1 and #3.

2.3 PAINS screen

The only compound carried forward, hydroxyurea itself, was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter and the Tox21 read-across panel. No other compound reached the screen, because no known BCL11A ligand exists in ChEMBL to screen against.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1-2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or cellular assay was performed; and, most importantly, HbF induction is a transcriptional event — a small molecule can only raise HbF by changing BCL11A abundance, localisation or complex formation, not by occupying a catalytic pocket, because BCL11A has no catalytic pocket. A docking score against this target, even a valid one, would not be evidence of HbF induction.

3. Results

3.1 The pipeline outcome: correct target, zero ligands, one faulty score

Step Result
Target identification (UniProtKB + ChEMBL, live) Human BCL11A, UniProt Q9H165, 835 aa, ChEMBL CHEMBL5498502 — correct target, correct organism
Known ligand retrieval (ChEMBL bioactivities) 0 bioactivities, 0 known ligands
Query verification (PubChem) Hydroxyurea, CID 3657, CH4N2O2, MW 76.05, logP -0.96, 0 Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean, all 12 Tox21 read-across assays 0
Similarity screen vs known actives Skipped — no known actives exist to screen against
Leads ranked 1 — hydroxyurea itself, the query, score 100.0 by default (no comparator)
Docking (Vina 1.2.7) Produced -4.26 kcal/mol on PDB 8DTN — discarded after centre audit (see 3.2)

The headline result is a negative one, and it is a result, not a failure of the run: ChEMBL holds no bioactivity record for human BCL11A (CHEMBL5498502, 0 bioactivities), so there is no known small-molecule BCL11A ligand for any pipeline to rank, screen, or dock against. The only compound the pipeline could carry forward was the reference drug itself. That is itself a measurement of the state of the field: as of 7 November 2026, direct small-molecule inhibition of BCL11A has no published chemical starting point.

3.2 The docking score is refuted by its own centre audit

The pipeline did return a docking number: hydroxyurea at -4.26 kcal/mol (poses -4.26, -4.20, -4.13) on PDB 8DTN at 2.2 A. That number is discarded, and the reason is documented here because it is the most important finding of the run.

PDB 8DTN is "the complex of nanobody 6101 with BCL11A ZF6": four copies of a nanobody bound to zinc finger 6 of BCL11A. It contains no small-molecule ligand of any kind. Its HETATM records are water (401 atoms), zinc ions (4), magnesium ions (4), and selenomethionine residues (MSE, 160 atoms across 20 residues) — selenomethionine is a crystallographic phasing label, an amino-acid residue, not a ligand. The pipeline's centre picker excludes MSE as a modified residue, but when no drug-like ligand survives its exclusions it falls back to the first HETATM group with at least 6 atoms — which is MSE residue 34 of nanobody chain A. The grid centre used for docking, [-17.85, 20.75, 157.93], is exactly the centroid of that single selenomethionine residue, to 0.00 A. The docking box was therefore centred on a surface methionine of a nanobody — not on BCL11A, not on a pocket, not on any site where a drug could bind. The -4.26 kcal/mol score measures Vina placing a 76-Da molecule next to a random protein surface residue. It is noise with a decimal point, and it is not reported as a result.

Two further facts make the failure structural rather than incidental. First, the pipeline's own step-7 check had already returned "skipped, pdb_id None" — no ligand-bound structure found — while the separate dock_leads call then produced a score anyway, because the two code paths disagree about what counts as a ligand site. Second, no ligand-bound BCL11A structure exists to dock against at all: every deposited BCL11A structure is a protein-DNA complex (6KI6, 2.50 A, ZnF456 bound to the 12-bp gamma-globin promoter DNA; 6U9Q and 8TLO, the same domain on longer DNA; 9E6R, 2.09 A) or a protein-nanobody complex (8DTN). There is no co-crystallised small molecule, so there is no pose to reproduce, no pocket to define, and no re-docking validation possible. Re-docking hydroxyurea at the ZnF456-DNA interface of 6KI6 would manufacture a second meaningless number — a score for binding to DNA bases — so it was not done. Docking is skipped as a method on this target, and the skip is the finding.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published docking score for any compound against BCL11A was found to benchmark against — which is consistent with the result above: there is no published docking on this target because there is no ligand-bound structure and no known ligand. The comparison that does exist is a contrast: on DprE1 the day before, the same pipeline produced interpretable scores against a genuine inhibitor-bound structure (4P8N), and the failure mode there was a scoring-function limit. Here the failure mode is one step earlier — there is nothing to dock against.

3.4 The literature-verified evidence for HbF induction, without docking

What the literature does establish, with numbers, is the following. Genetic evidence: rs11886868 in BCL11A associates with HbF at P < 10^-35, and the same variant ameliorates the beta-thalassaemia phenotype. Mechanistic evidence: BCL11A binds the TGACCA motif at -118 to -113 of the gamma-globin promoter and represses it directly; deletion of zinc finger 4 reduces BCL11A DNA binding by more than 70-fold and detectably restores gamma-globin expression. Structural evidence: BCL11A functions as a tetramer, and tetramer formation mediated by a single zinc finger (ZnF0) is required for steady-state protein production and for gamma-globin repression — the authors identify tetramer formation as a vulnerability for drug discovery, which is the only concrete small-molecule hypothesis the structural literature currently offers. Clinical evidence: disrupting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer by CRISPR-Cas9 (exagamglogene autotemcel) produced transfusion independence in 91% of transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia patients in CLIMB THAL-111. Pharmacological evidence: pomalidomide decreases BCL11A expression through transcriptional reprogramming of adult erythroid progenitors, and combining HRI depletion with pomalidomide reduced BCL11A mRNA and protein by about 90% and raised HbF to 50-60% in sickle-cell patient cells — but pomalidomide does not bind BCL11A; it rewires the transcription network around it. The newest small-molecule direction is molecular-glue degraders of the wider HbF-repressor network: BMS-986470, a dual WIZ and ZBTB7A degrader, and Novartis ITU512, a WIZ degrader, are both in early clinical trials, and a dual ZBTB7A/BCL11A degrader (SH6) is preclinical. None of these is a BCL11A binder, and none has published BCL11A docking data — because there is nothing to dock against.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper reframes from a discovery claim into a negative result with a usable conclusion: the standard docking pipeline cannot triage small molecules against BCL11A, and the reason is the target, not the pipeline's effort. There is no ligand, no pocket, and no ligand-bound structure, and the one number the pipeline produced was an artefact of a fallback in its centre picker. The durable findings are the three negative measurements (0 ChEMBL bioactivities; 0 ligand-bound structures; 1 faulty score, discarded with its cause identified) and the literature synthesis in 3.4, which points the next work at cells and degraders, not at docking.

4.2 Why the discarded score must stay discarded

Three reasons. First, the centre is a single selenomethionine residue of a nanobody — a phasing label, not a binding site — so the score has no referent. Second, hydroxyurea does not bind BCL11A by any published evidence, so a favourable score would have been false on its face, and the weak score actually obtained (-4.26 kcal/mol, inside the range Vina gives to almost any small polar molecule on an arbitrary surface) is exactly what an arbitrary-surface docking looks like. Third, the two code paths in the same pipeline disagreed — one correctly skipped docking, the other scored anyway — which means the score was produced by a path that does not check for a ligand site. A number produced by a path that cannot detect the absence of a binding site is not evidence.

4.3 The pipeline fault is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

The fault is specific and fixable: _ligand_center in the LeadForge docking module falls back to the first HETATM group with at least 6 atoms when no drug-like ligand survives its exclusion lists, instead of returning None. On any structure whose only HETATM records are waters, ions and modified residues, that fallback manufactures a centre. The fix is to return None when no drug-like ligand exists, and to make the pipeline's step-7 check and the dock_leads call share one ligand-site test. Until that fix is verified, every docking centre in this pipeline's output must be audited against the PDB file, as was done here. The fault does not invalidate the pipeline's other targets — on DprE1 the centre was verified to 0.01 A against a genuine inhibitor — but it does mean a docking score from this pipeline is only as trustworthy as its centre audit.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. A gamma-globin reporter screen in K562 cells of a focused library (FDA-approved drugs and known HbF inducers, including hydroxyurea, pomalidomide and decitabine) will find no compound whose HbF induction is explained by direct BCL11A binding, because no direct binder exists; any hit must act through BCL11A abundance or network rewiring, testable by BCL11A western blot.
  2. Disruption of BCL11A tetramerisation through ZnF0 — for example by a peptide or a small molecule selected in a tetramer-disruption assay, not by docking — will reduce steady-state BCL11A protein and raise gamma-globin expression in primary human erythroid progenitors; failure to raise gamma-globin despite tetramer disruption would refute ZnF0 as a drug target.
  3. A direct binding assay (surface plasmon resonance or thermal shift) of hydroxyurea against recombinant BCL11A ZnF456 will show no binding, confirming that its HbF induction is BCL11A-binding-independent; measurable binding would refute this paper's central claim.
  4. Fixing the _ligand_center fallback to return None when no drug-like ligand exists will make the pipeline return "no ligand site" for BCL11A and change no result on any target that has a genuine ligand-bound structure — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8-12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1-2): gamma-globin reporter assay in K562 cells for hydroxyurea, pomalidomide and decitabine at 3 doses, n = 3, with a pre-registered rule that a hit must raise gamma-globin mRNA at least 2-fold over vehicle without reducing viability below 80%. Stage 2 (weeks 3-6): any Stage 1 hit moves to primary human CD34+ erythroid differentiation culture, with BCL11A protein measured by western blot and HbF measured by HPLC, to test whether induction tracks BCL11A abundance. Stage 3 (weeks 7-12): direct binding test (thermal shift or surface plasmon resonance) of the best hit against recombinant BCL11A ZnF456, and, in parallel, a tetramer-disruption assay for ZnF0 as the structure-guided alternative to docking. No compound may be presented as a treatment; all work is preclinical triage for a disease whose only proven BCL11A therapy is a gene edit most Pakistani patients cannot access.

5. Limitations

  1. No experimental data; docking only, and the docking itself was discarded. 2. The negative result rests on database state as of 7 November 2026 (ChEMBL, UniProtKB, RCSB PDB); a newly deposited ligand-bound structure would change the conclusion. 3. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or pocket-detection analysis (for example FTMap or SiteMap) was run on the ZnF456-DNA structure; a cryptic pocket cannot be excluded, only stated as unproven. 4. The literature synthesis depends on published work, mostly from sickle-cell disease cohorts, and beta-thalassaemia-specific pharmacology (for example the Cochrane review's 291 patients) is thin. 5. Hydroxyurea's HbF-induction mechanism is incompletely understood, so the claim that it does not bind BCL11A rests on absence of evidence plus mechanism, not on a published negative binding assay. 6. The pipeline fault was identified by audit, not by a controlled regression test; other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited. 7. No cost or access analysis of exagamglogene autotemcel in Pakistan was performed beyond the published trial result.

6. Conclusion

No small molecule can currently be docked against BCL11A, because ChEMBL records no BCL11A ligand, the Protein Data Bank holds no ligand-bound BCL11A structure, and the one docking score the pipeline produced was centred on a nanobody selenomethionine and was discarded. The honest next step is not more docking but a cellular gamma-globin reporter screen with a direct BCL11A binding test for any hit, and a tetramer-disruption assay at ZnF0 — the only structure-backed small-molecule hypothesis the literature currently offers for raising fetal haemoglobin in beta-thalassaemia.

2026-11-07 Health Draft ready

Two Dietary Flavonoids "Beat" Acarbose by Docking and Lose by ~1 kcal/mol of Noise: A Vina Benchmark of Human Pancreatic Alpha-Amylase Inhibitors on 1XCX

Diabetes affected an estimated 828 million adults in 2022, including 36 million in Pakistan, where the prevalence among women rose from 9.0% in 1990 to 30.9% in 2022, the largest increase of any country, and most post-meal glucose control still depends on slowing starch digestion.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-07 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #1 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: alpha-amylase; acarbose; luteolin; quercetin; flavonoids; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; type 2 diabetes

Abstract

Diabetes affected an estimated 828 million adults in 2022, including 36 million in Pakistan, where the prevalence among women rose from 9.0% in 1990 to 30.9% in 2022, the largest increase of any country, and most post-meal glucose control still depends on slowing starch digestion. Acarbose, the standard alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, blunts postprandial glucose but causes flatulence in 74% of patients, diarrhoea in 31% and abdominal pain in 19%, which limits adherence; dietary flavonoids are proposed as gentler adjuncts, but their published enzyme inhibition has rarely been benchmarked against acarbose in the same protocol. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking): target human pancreatic alpha-amylase (UniProt P04746, AMY2A; ChEMBL CHEMBL2045, 23 bioactivities), structure PDB 1XCX at 1.9 Å, grid centred on the co-crystallised acarbose-derived ligand ([5.01, 16.45, 41.56]), and six ligands docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under an identical protocol. Luteolin scored −8.42 kcal/mol and quercetin −8.31 kcal/mol against acarbose at −7.35 kcal/mol, margins of 1.07 and 0.96 kcal/mol, inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, while both flavonoids carry PAINS catechol alerts and quercetin's oral bioavailability is under 10%. A ChEMBL acarbose isomer with a measured Ki of 12 nM scored −8.14 kcal/mol, and a second analogue (Ki 75 nM) scored −7.47 kcal/mol, ranking in the same order as their measured potency. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head in vitro alpha-amylase inhibition assay of luteolin against acarbose under identical conditions with redox controls, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage; a measured IC50 for luteolin better than acarbose's under those controls would refute the noise interpretation.

1. Introduction

Diabetes is one of the fastest-growing disease burdens in the world: the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration estimated 828 million adults living with diabetes in 2022, up by about 630 million since 1990, and 445 million adults aged 30 years or older (59%) received no treatment. Pakistan carries the fourth-largest national burden, about 36 million adults, and the rise in prevalence among Pakistani women — from 9.0% in 1990 to 30.9% in 2022 — was the largest increase recorded for any country. More than 95% of adult diabetes is type 2, where blunting the post-meal glucose rise is a central therapeutic goal.

Human pancreatic alpha-amylase (HPA, AMY2A, UniProt P04746) starts starch digestion in the small intestine, hydrolysing complex starches to oligosaccharides; the catalytic triad is Asp197 (the nucleophile), Glu233 and Asp300, with five binding subsites spanning the active-site cleft. Acarbose, a pseudo-tetrasaccharide from Actinoplanes utahensis, competitively and reversibly inhibits pancreatic alpha-amylase and the membrane-bound intestinal alpha-glucosidases, delaying carbohydrate digestion and lowering postprandial hyperglycaemia. It is minimally absorbed and acts locally in the gut — which is also the source of its problem: in US placebo-controlled trials (1,255 patients, 50–300 mg three times daily), flatulence occurred in 74% of acarbose-treated patients, diarrhoea in 31% and abdominal pain in 19%, against 29%, 12% and 9% on placebo, because undigested carbohydrate ferments in the colon. The side effects are the mechanism, so they cannot be dosed away.

Dietary polyphenols, especially flavonoids, are the obvious candidate adjuncts: they are present in everyday foods, they inhibit pancreatic alpha-amylase in vitro, and a 2019 structure–activity study found luteolin the best of five tested flavonoids — better than acarbose itself as the positive control — with quercetin and hesperetin also active by mixed-type inhibition, while catechin and rutin showed no inhibition. But that comparison was made in one assay system, and the flavonoid literature almost never benchmarks against acarbose in the same docking protocol. The falsifiable hypothesis of this paper is that, docked against human pancreatic alpha-amylase under one identical protocol, the dietary flavonoids luteolin and quercetin beat acarbose by less than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise margin — that is, the apparent win is a measurement of the method's limits, not a proven advantage — and that any genuine signal will instead appear in the ranking of measured ChEMBL potencies against their docking scores.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 7 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/ (2026-11-07, 595 papers screened, 8 selected — none on alpha-amylase, so this topic rests on targeted searches), PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI), PubChem PUG REST and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration's 2024 Lancet analysis for the diabetes burden figures; the FDA acarbose label (DailyMed) for the mechanism and the 74%/31%/19% adverse-reaction incidences; the 1XCX and 1B2Y crystal structures and their primary citations for the active site; the 2019 flavonoid structure–activity study for the luteolin-beats-acarbose in vitro finding; and the 2022 Trends in Food Science & Technology review for quercetin's oral bioavailability below 10%.

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 7 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target: human pancreatic alpha-amylase, UniProt P04746, gene AMY2A, Homo sapiens, 511 residues; ChEMBL target CHEMBL2045, 23 bioactivities retrieved. Twenty-four compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen against acarbose and were ranked by composite score (similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20). All 24 are acarbose analogues — large oligosaccharides, not drug-like molecules: the top five span molecular weights 483–2,366 Da with 6–39 rotatable bonds.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was human pancreatic alpha-amylase, PDB 1XCX (1.9 Å; acarbose rearrangement products bound), with the grid centred on the centroid of the full co-crystallised ligand — chain B pseudo-pentasaccharide, residues AC1 + BGC + GLC, 44 atoms: [5.01, 16.45, 41.56]. The centre was verified against the PDB file: the acarviosine-core (AC1) centroid [9.96, 17.05, 43.65] sits 4.01 Å from the catalytic-triad centroid (Asp197/Glu233/Asp300), the combined centre 7.23 Å, and the 22.5 Å box covers the full −3 to +2 subsite cleft. As a cross-check, the acarbose complex 1B2Y (3.2 Å) gives the same geometry: its AC1 centroid is 3.88 Å from its catalytic triad. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Six ligands were docked: acarbose itself (QUERY, the reference drug), the two dockable pipeline leads (CHEMBL1230193, rank 2; CHEMBL3618489, rank 4), an acarbose isomer (CHEMBL1233515, rank 6, same molecular formula C25H43NO18 as acarbose, measured Ki 12.0 nM — the most potent compound in the ChEMBL set), and two literature flavonoids added for the dietary-adjunct angle, luteolin (PubChem CID 5280445, C15H10O6) and quercetin (PubChem CID 5280343, C15H10O7), with SMILES verified live against PubChem PUG REST on 7 November 2026. Two pipeline leads were NOT docked and are reported as not docked, not as zero scores: CHEMBL3616594 (rank 3, MW 1,901 Da, 31 rotatable bonds, Ki 14.3 nM) and CHEMBL3616595 (rank 5, MW 2,366 Da, 39 rotatable bonds, Ki 41.6 nM) are far beyond Vina's reliable sampling range at exhaustiveness 8, and 39 torsions exceeds Vina's 32-torsion handling.

One pipeline fault was caught before reporting, and is documented here because it is part of the result. The pipeline auto-picked PDB 5U3A, an apo structure of human pancreatic alpha-amylase whose only non-water HETATM groups are the N-terminal pyroglutamate PCA (residue 1) and a glycan NAG 501. Both are in the pipeline's _CENTRE_EXCLUDE list, but the _ligand_center fallback ("first group with ≥ 6 atoms") re-picked PCA, giving centre [5.86, 82.81, 131.04] — the N-terminus, 19.5 Å from the catalytic-triad centroid (9.09, 81.66, 150.49). The run was killed before Vina produced any output, so no wrong-centre scores exist; the pipeline results were regenerated without docking, and all docking reported here is the corrected-centre re-dock on 1XCX. The root cause — the fallback ignoring _CENTRE_EXCLUDE — is a pipeline fix still owed in dock.py; until it is fixed, every auto-picked centre on an apo structure must be audited by hand.

Acarbose itself failed on the first docking attempt: Vina hit its 900-second cap while four to five sibling Vina runs shared the machine. It was retried once on a quiet machine (zero other Vina processes) with the identical protocol and completed in about 8 minutes at −7.35 kcal/mol. The first attempt's timeout is reported, not hidden: even the reference drug is a hard docking target.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter (FilterCatalog, PAINS A/B/C). Acarbose and all four ChEMBL compounds are PAINS-clean. Both flavonoids carry the same alert — catechol_A(92), from the 3′,4′-dihydroxy catechol B-ring present in luteolin and quercetin. A catechol alert is reported, never hidden; it changes the validation design (redox controls), because catechols can produce apparent inhibition through redox cycling and aggregation rather than active-site binding.

2.4 ADMET and toxicity read-across

Lipinski/Veber descriptors come from RDKit. Acarbose violates Lipinski three times (MW 645.61, 14 hydrogen-bond donors, 19 acceptors, TPSA 329 Å², logP −8.72) and fails Veber; the ChEMBL analogues are the same (2–3 violations each). The flavonoids are drug-like by the same rules (luteolin MW 286.24, quercetin MW 302.24, one rotatable bond each, zero Lipinski violations) — which is exactly why they are interesting and exactly why their PAINS alert and bioavailability matter more than their docking scores. A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for the ChEMBL compounds: it returned no neighbours (max similarity 0.000) for every ChEMBL lead, so the panel is uninformative for them and no tox claim is made from it; only acarbose itself had neighbours (max similarity 0.681, highest flag NR-ER 0.385). No read-across panel was run for the two added flavonoids.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised ligand was performed; a single crystal structure (1XCX, one HPA conformation) was used; induced-fit effects are not modelled; and the two most potent ChEMBL compounds by measured Ki (14.3 nM and 41.6 nM) could not be docked at all, so the docking set is missing its strongest measured binders. The flavonoid comparison rests on two molecules chosen from the literature, not on a screen.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table
