Quercetin — (PubChem CID 5280343) −8.31 −8.31, −7.81, −7.62 302.24 1 0 catechol_A
CHEMBL1233515 Ki 12.0 nM −8.14 −8.14, −7.81, −7.61 645.61 9 3 clean
CHEMBL1230193 Ki 75.0 nM −7.47 −7.47, −7.33, −6.83 483.47 6 2 clean
Acarbose (reference) — (no activity recorded on this target in this ChEMBL pull) −7.35 −7.35, −7.14, −7.06 645.61 13 3 clean
CHEMBL3618489 Ki 14.7 nM FAILED (conformer_failed) — 1,435.34 23 3 clean

All docking on PDB 1XCX (human pancreatic alpha-amylase, 1.9 Å), grid centre [5.01, 16.45, 41.56] (co-crystallised ligand centroid), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 7 November 2026. Not docked: CHEMBL3616594 (Ki 14.3 nM, MW 1,901, 31 rotatable bonds) and CHEMBL3616595 (Ki 41.6 nM, MW 2,366, 39 rotatable bonds).

The headline, stated honestly: both dietary flavonoids "beat" acarbose on docking — luteolin by 1.07 kcal/mol and quercetin by 0.96 kcal/mol — but both margins sit inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so neither is a proven advantage, and both compounds carry the PAINS catechol alert that the reference drug does not. The acarbose isomer CHEMBL1233515, the most potent compound in the set by measured Ki (12.0 nM), also scores better than acarbose by 0.79 kcal/mol — again inside noise. The one clean concordance in the table is between the two docked ChEMBL analogues: the 12 nM compound scores −8.14 kcal/mol and the 75 nM compound −7.47 kcal/mol, ranking in the same order as their measured potency, a 0.67 kcal/mol spread for a 6.25-fold Ki ratio (which corresponds to about 1.08 kcal/mol of binding free energy at 298 K — the same direction, smaller than the thermodynamic expectation, and inside noise). Pose consistency does not rescue the flavonoid "win": luteolin's best pose (−8.42) is 0.39 kcal/mol clear of its second pose, quercetin's by 0.50, and acarbose's own three poses span only 0.29 kcal/mol — all three molecules are stable in their poses, and the ranking between them is still a noise-level difference.

Two failures are part of the result. Acarbose's first docking attempt timed out at Vina's 900-second cap under CPU contention and only completed on a quiet-machine retry — a 645 Da oligosaccharide with 13 rotatable bonds is a slow, hard docking target even for the reference drug. CHEMBL3618489 (MW 1,435 Da, Ki 14.7 nM) failed earlier, at ligand preparation: no conformer could be generated (conformer_failed), so it has no score at all. The pipeline's lead list is dominated by molecules Vina cannot handle — three of the top five by rank (MW 1,435–2,366 Da) produced no docking score by one failure mode or another — which is itself a finding about this target class: similarity-to-acarbose screening returns compounds too large to dock, and the dockable subset is a biased sample of the small end.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

A 2024 fluorescence/docking study of acarbose and quercetin reports acarbose binding energies of −7.6 to −7.7 kcal/mol across multiple studies, with quercetin among the stronger reported alpha-amylase inhibitors. Our in-protocol acarbose value of −7.35 kcal/mol is 0.25–0.35 kcal/mol less favourable than that published range — inside Vina noise, and consistent in direction with the flavonoids scoring better. No published Vina score for luteolin on 1XCX was found to benchmark against, which is a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for acarbose, two flavonoids and two ChEMBL analogues on 1XCX are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the two documented failures. The published in vitro finding stands alongside the docking rather than behind it: Martinez-Gonzalez et al. (2019) measured luteolin as the best flavonoid inhibitor of pancreatic alpha-amylase, better than acarbose, by mixed-type inhibition — a real experimental result that our docking neither confirms nor refutes, because a 1.07 kcal/mol docking margin cannot confirm a measured effect.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two things that could silently corrupt this result did not, and two things that no structure check can catch did. The grid centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å and sits on the co-crystallised ligand, 4.01 Å (AC1 core) from the catalytic triad — the cofactor/glycan-centring fault is absent here, because the faulty 5U3A auto-pick was caught and the run killed before any score was produced. The duplicate-entry fault seen in Papers #1 and #3 did not occur: no lead is acarbose under another ID (CHEMBL1233515 shares acarbose's formula but has a different connectivity and a measured Ki of 12.0 nM). What did occur: the two most potent measured binders in the set could not be docked at all, and the reference drug itself needed a quiet-machine retry — so the docking table systematically excludes the strongest measured compounds. The deeper problem is the flavonoid one: both "winning" compounds carry the catechol PAINS alert, and quercetin's oral bioavailability is under 10% with extensive first-pass metabolism to glucuronide and sulfate conjugates and free-aglycone plasma levels in the low nanomolar range. A docking win for a catechol flavonoid is the starting point of an artefact investigation, not a discovery.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a measurement of Vina's limits on this target — with one honest exception. There is no proven flavonoid win: luteolin and quercetin beat acarbose by about 1 kcal/mol, inside noise, carrying a PAINS alert each. The durable findings are the benchmark values (acarbose −7.35 kcal/mol on 1XCX, with full pose lists), the ChEMBL pair ranking in the same order as measured Ki, the two documented docking failures, and the grid-centre fault caught before it produced scores. The flavonoid angle survives as a question, not as an answer: the published in vitro result (luteolin better than acarbose) is real experimental data, and our docking is consistent with it in direction but too noisy to confirm it.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the margins (1.07 and 0.96 kcal/mol) are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, both winners carry the catechol_A PAINS alert — the classic flavonoid artefact signature — while the reference drug and the ChEMBL analogues are PAINS-clean. Third, the single-structure limit: one HPA conformation, no induced fit, no re-docking validation of the co-crystallised ligand. Fourth, the set is biased: the three largest, most potent measured compounds in the ChEMBL pull could not be docked at all, so the table compares acarbose against the small end of its own analogue family plus two hand-picked flavonoids.

4.3 The bioavailability limit — and why it is weaker than it looks for this target

Quercetin's oral bioavailability under 10% is usually quoted as the reason flavonoid enzyme inhibition never translates — and for a systemic target it would be decisive. For pancreatic alpha-amylase it is a weaker objection than it looks, because the enzyme acts in the lumen of the small intestine: a dietary flavonoid meets its target in the gut before absorption, first-pass metabolism and plasma exposure ever enter the picture. The honest statement is narrower: poor systemic bioavailability does not kill a luminal-target adjunct, but it does not save it either. What matters is the flavonoid concentration actually present in the intestinal lumen at the time starch arrives, whether it survives gastric transit intact, and whether the measured inhibition survives redox controls — none of which docking addresses. The bioavailability number therefore constrains any systemic claim (and any claim about the absorbed metabolites) while leaving the luminal dietary-adjunct hypothesis testable in vitro.

4.4 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Both flavonoids carry catechol_A(92). Catechols oxidise to quinones, redox-cycle, and aggregate — all mechanisms that produce apparent enzyme inhibition without active-site binding. The validation assay must therefore be designed to expose artefacts: run the inhibition assay with and without a reducing agent (e.g. DTT) and catalase, add a detergent counter-screen (e.g. Triton X-100) to test for aggregation-based inhibition, and test the oxidised quinone form separately. If luteolin's inhibition survives all three controls at the same IC50, the catechol alert is a false alarm for this compound; if the IC50 shifts or vanishes, the docking "win" was an artefact. The ChEMBL analogues, being PAINS-clean, need no such controls — which is a genuine advantage of the oligosaccharide series over the flavonoids, and the reason CHEMBL1233515 (Ki 12 nM, −8.14 kcal/mol) deserves the same assay slot as luteolin despite scoring 0.28 kcal/mol worse.

4.5 Testable hypotheses

  1. Luteolin inhibits recombinant human pancreatic alpha-amylase with an IC50 within 2-fold of acarbose's under identical assay conditions, with the inhibition surviving DTT/catalase and detergent controls — a measured IC50 for luteolin better than acarbose's under those controls would refute the noise interpretation; loss of inhibition under redox controls would confirm the PAINS artefact.
  2. CHEMBL1233515 inhibits recombinant HPA with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL Ki (12 nM) under identical conditions, and more potently than CHEMBL1230193 (Ki 75 nM) — the docking predicts the same potency order; a reversed order would refute the docking ranking.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand from 1XCX reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  4. Fixing the _ligand_center fallback in dock.py to skip _CENTRE_EXCLUDE groups makes the pipeline auto-pick a ligand-bound HPA structure (e.g. 1XCX) instead of the apo 5U3A — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.

4.6 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): in vitro HPA inhibition assay (p-nitrophenyl-α-D-maltopentoside or starch–DNS method) for luteolin, quercetin, CHEMBL1233515 and acarbose, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): artefact controls for the flavonoids — DTT/catalase redox controls, Triton X-100 detergent counter-screen, and a test of the oxidised quinone form; any compound whose inhibition vanishes under controls is dropped. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): simulated gastrointestinal stability of luteolin (gastric pH, pancreatic conditions) to test whether the luminal-exposure argument survives contact with digestive conditions, and, if Stage 1 shows any genuine advantage, a starch-tolerance test in a rodent model with acarbose as control. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; luteolin and quercetin are cheap dietary flavonoids, the ChEMBL analogues are research chemicals, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Both "winning" margins (1.07 and 0.96 kcal/mol) are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as real advantages. 3. Both flavonoids carry the PAINS catechol_A alert; redox/aggregation artefacts are not excluded. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised ligand was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (1XCX, one HPA conformation) was used; induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. The two most potent measured binders in the ChEMBL set (Ki 14.3 nM and 41.6 nM) could not be docked, and a third (Ki 14.7 nM) failed at conformer generation — the docking set is missing its strongest measured compounds. 7. Acarbose's first docking attempt timed out at Vina's 900-second cap and only completed on a quiet-machine retry; the reference score itself carries that sampling caveat. 8. The pipeline's _ligand_center fallback bug is documented but not yet fixed in code; the corrected centre here was applied by hand. 9. Quercetin's bioavailability figure (<10%) is a literature value, not measured here, and no luminal concentration was measured. 10. The flavonoids were hand-picked from the literature, not screened — selection bias in the comparison set.

6. Conclusion

No dietary flavonoid in this set beats acarbose: luteolin and quercetin score better on Vina docking by about 1 kcal/mol, inside the noise margin, carrying a PAINS catechol alert each, and quercetin's oral bioavailability is under 10%. The honest reading is that the published in vitro finding — luteolin better than acarbose — is consistent with our docking in direction but unconfirmed by it, and the next experiment is a head-to-head alpha-amylase IC50 assay with redox and detergent controls and a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, not more Vina docking. The most useful numbers in this paper are the benchmark values themselves: acarbose −7.35 kcal/mol on 1XCX, with the failures that came with it.

Febuxostat Beats Itself by 0.03 kcal/mol: A Vina Benchmark of Xanthine Oxidase Inhibitors on 2E1Q, and the Selenium Ligands the Pipeline Cannot Dock

Gout is driven by hyperuricaemia, and xanthine oxidase catalyses the final steps of uric-acid formation while also generating reactive oxygen species, making it the established target for urate-lowering therapy.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-06 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #3 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: xanthine oxidase; febuxostat; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; gout; hyperuricaemia; ChEMBL; selenium

Abstract

Gout is driven by hyperuricaemia, and xanthine oxidase catalyses the final steps of uric-acid formation while also generating reactive oxygen species, making it the established target for urate-lowering therapy. Febuxostat, a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor, is effective but carries a contested cardiovascular safety record: the FDA-mandated CARES trial found higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality with febuxostat than with allopurinol despite no difference in the primary composite endpoint, leading to a boxed warning, while the later FAST trial found no excess mortality, and a 2025 Japanese nationwide claims cohort of patients with chronic kidney disease found no significant difference in composite cardiovascular outcomes (hazard ratio 0.93). We asked whether a standardised automated docking pipeline could find a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that binds more tightly than febuxostat. The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 on human xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase (UniProt P47989, ChEMBL CHEMBL1929, 53 bioactivities); 25 compounds passed the similarity screen and 26 were ranked. Five leads were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on PDB 2E1Q (2.6 Å), the grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised ligand — febuxostat itself — at [35.35, 15.17, 152.43]. No lead beats febuxostat: the best-scoring "lead", CHEMBL1164729 at −7.53 kcal/mol, is febuxostat itself entered under a second ChEMBL ID, scoring 0.03 kcal/mol from the query entry (−7.50). The best genuine lead, CHEMBL5436777 (IC50 1.0 nM), scored −7.42 kcal/mol, 0.08 kcal/mol from febuxostat — a tie inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Two of the five leads, both selenium-containing analogues, could not be docked at all because the pipeline cannot prepare selenium ligands. Febuxostat's own Tox21 read-across panel returns probability 1.0 on three assays, an identity artifact, not a toxicity signal. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head xanthine oxidase enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL5436777 against febuxostat under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage; a measured potency advantage greater than 2-fold for CHEMBL5436777, or a successful docking of the selenium analogues after the ligand-preparation fault is fixed, would refute the claim that no lead in this set improves on febuxostat.

1. Introduction

Gout is driven by hyperuricaemia: when serum urate exceeds its solubility limit, monosodium urate crystals deposit in joints and soft tissues and trigger recurrent inflammatory arthritis. Xanthine oxidase catalyses the final two steps of purine catabolism — hypoxanthine to xanthine, and xanthine to uric acid — and in the process generates reactive oxygen species, so inhibiting the enzyme lowers urate and, in principle, reduces oxidative stress. Allopurinol, a purine analogue, was the standard xanthine oxidase inhibitor for decades; febuxostat, a non-purine inhibitor, was developed as a more selective alternative and is effective at lowering serum urate. The clinical question around febuxostat is not potency but cardiovascular safety, and the evidence is contradictory. The FDA-mandated CARES trial (6,190 patients with gout and cardiovascular disease, 2018) found no difference in the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint between febuxostat and allopurinol, but higher all-cause mortality (7.8% vs 6.4%) and higher cardiovascular mortality (4.3% vs 3.2%) with febuxostat, and the FDA added a boxed warning. The FAST trial (6,128 patients, 2020) found febuxostat non-inferior to allopurinol on the primary cardiovascular endpoint and reported no increase in overall or cardiovascular mortality. Most recently, Inoue et al. (Nephrology, 2025) reported a Japanese nationwide claims cohort of patients with chronic kidney disease (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) in which febuxostat versus allopurinol gave a composite cardiovascular outcome hazard ratio of 0.93 (95% CI 0.79–1.08, p = 0.33) — no statistically significant difference, including across eGFR strata. Both CARES and FAST excluded patients with eGFR <30, so the most severe kidney disease remains untested in randomised trials. Against this background, a better xanthine oxidase inhibitor would be one that binds the enzyme more tightly than febuxostat — or, failing that, one with a safety profile that does not carry the CARES shadow.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known xanthine oxidase inhibitors against febuxostat on the enzyme's inhibitor pocket, and how large is the pipeline's own error? The falsifiable hypothesis is that five known potent xanthine oxidase inhibitors, docked under an identical protocol, will score within Vina's noise of febuxostat — and that any apparent "win" smaller than 2 kcal/mol is not a discovery.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 6 November 2026: the daily literature digest (2026-11-06), PubMed E-utilities and web search (verified references below), ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the CARES trial (White et al., N Engl J Med 2018) and the FAST trial (Mackenzie et al., Lancet 2020) for the cardiovascular safety evidence, Inoue et al. (Nephrology 2025) for the chronic kidney disease cohort, and the RCSB entry for PDB 2E1Q.

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline)

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target resolution: human xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase, UniProt P47989 (gene XDH, 1,333 amino acids), ChEMBL CHEMBL1929 (single-protein, human), 53 bioactivities retrieved. Febuxostat was verified in PubChem (MW 316.38; 2-(3-cyano-4-isobutoxyphenyl)-4-methylthiazole-5-carboxylic acid). Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score (similarity ×40 + Lipinski ×20 + Veber ×10 + PAINS ×10 + tox ×20). The top five ranked leads were taken forward to docking. All five are known xanthine oxidase inhibitors with published ChEMBL potencies: febuxostat itself (Ki 0.1 nM, as CHEMBL1164729), CHEMBL5436777 (IC50 1.0 nM), CHEMBL3331615 (IC50 2.05 nM) and CHEMBL3331613 (IC50 2.29 nM). None of the non-febuxostat leads has a preferred name, an approval, or a development phase in ChEMBL.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 6 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was human xanthine oxidoreductase, PDB 2E1Q (2.6 Å, E803V mutant), with the grid centred on the centroid of its co-crystallised ligand DYI — which is febuxostat itself — at [35.35, 15.17, 152.43]. The centre was verified directly against the PDB file: the distance from the computed centroid to the DYI centroid is 0.01 Å, and the FAD cofactor sits 38 Å away, so the box covers the inhibitor pocket and not the cofactor site. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all four leads and febuxostat were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probability was NR-AhR 0.254 for CHEMBL5436777. Febuxostat's own panel is different in kind: it returns probability 1.0 on three assays (SR-ATAD5, NR-AhR and NR-AR). That is a nearest-neighbour identity artifact — the query matches a training compound exactly — not a measured toxicity signal, and the same 1.0 flags appear on the identical CHEMBL1164729 entry, which proves the flags are an artifact of identity, not of chemistry. The two selenium analogues returned low read-across probabilities (NR-AhR 0.283 and 0.261) with no flags.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed; a single crystal structure (2E1Q, one xanthine oxidoreductase conformation, E803V mutant) was used; two of the five leads could not be docked at all; and the four leads are already-known xanthine oxidase inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

CHEMBL1164729 (= febuxostat) Ki 0.1 nM −7.53 −7.53, −7.17, −6.67 clean
Febuxostat (reference, query) Ki 0.1 nM (same molecule) −7.50 −7.50, −7.22, −6.67 clean
CHEMBL5436777 IC50 1.0 nM −7.42 −7.42, −6.55, −6.16 clean

CHEMBL1164729/febuxostat: MW 316.38, logP 3.72, 0 Lipinski violations. CHEMBL5436777: MW 359.41, logP 2.83, 0 violations. CHEMBL3331615: MW 363.28, logP 2.72, 0 violations. CHEMBL3331613: MW 335.22, logP 2.08, 0 violations.

The headline is stated plainly: no lead beats febuxostat. The best-scoring "lead", CHEMBL1164729 at −7.53 kcal/mol, is febuxostat itself — the identical SMILES and molecular weight, Tanimoto similarity 1.0, and an identical toxicity panel to the query. The duplicate-entry fault has struck again: the same molecule scored −7.53 as a ChEMBL hit and −7.50 as the query, 0.03 kcal/mol apart — a much smaller self-difference than the 1.75 kcal/mol seen for trametinib on MEK1, because here both entries entered Vina from the same starting conformer. The best genuine lead, CHEMBL5436777 (IC50 1.0 nM), scored −7.42 kcal/mol, 0.08 kcal/mol from febuxostat — a tie inside Vina's noise. The total spread across the three docked molecules is 0.11 kcal/mol, far below the noise floor, and the ranking is in the wrong potency order: the most potent compound by recorded Ki (febuxostat, 0.1 nM) and the least potent docked compound (CHEMBL5436777, IC50 1.0 nM) are separated by 0.08 kcal/mol, a ten-fold potency difference that Vina cannot see.

Two of the five leads could not be docked at all, and the reason is a pipeline fault, reported here rather than hidden. CHEMBL3331615 and CHEMBL3331613 are selenium analogues of febuxostat — the thiazole sulfur replaced by selenium (C16H16N2O3Se and C14H12N2O3Se). Ligand preparation failed for both: RDKit's UFFTYPER reports "unrecognized atom type Se2+2" (atom 17 in CHEMBL3331615, atom 15 in CHEMBL3331613), so no 3D conformer could be built and Vina never ran. These are the second- and third-most potent leads by recorded IC50 (2.05 and 2.29 nM), so the pipeline's blind spot falls exactly on the compounds it was supposed to test. Their PAINS-clean status and drug-like descriptors (MW 363.28 and 335.22, logP 2.72 and 2.08, 0 Lipinski violations) are reported from the ChEMBL/RDKit descriptors, not from docking.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for febuxostat or any of these leads on 2E1Q was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for febuxostat and CHEMBL5436777 on 2E1Q are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the duplicate-entry control that quantifies the pipeline's own error on this target (0.03 kcal/mol) and the documented selenium failure. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: the three docked molecules span a ten-fold potency range (Ki 0.1 nM to IC50 1.0 nM) while their docking scores span 0.11 kcal/mol — Vina ranks poses, not Ki values, and here it cannot rank a molecule against its own duplicate by more than 0.03 kcal/mol.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Three automated steps that could silently corrupt this result did corrupt it, in three different ways. The lead list contains the reference drug itself under a second ChEMBL ID, which the pipeline treats as a new compound — fixed only by canonicalising SMILES before ranking. The ligand-preparation step cannot type selenium, so two of five leads silently drop out of docking — fixed only by adding a selenium-capable force-field typing path or an explicit fallback. And the toxicity read-across panel returns probability 1.0 on three assays for the reference drug itself, because the query matches a training compound exactly — a panel that flags its own reference drug as maximally toxic on three assays cannot be read as evidence about any lead. The grid-centre step, by contrast, worked correctly this time: the centre landed 0.01 Å from the co-crystallised ligand, because the DYI ligand is the first drug-like HETATM group in 2E1Q and the FAD cofactor is 38 Å away. The lesson is that each automated step must be verified against the structure and the reference drug, not trusted because it worked on the last target.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a measurement of the pipeline's own error and blind spots. There is no lead here: the best "lead" is febuxostat, the best genuine lead is 0.08 kcal/mol from febuxostat, and two of the five leads were never tested at all. The durable findings are the benchmark values for febuxostat on 2E1Q (−7.50 and −7.53 kcal/mol for the two entries, with full pose lists), the 0.03 kcal/mol duplicate-entry control, and the selenium ligand-preparation fault. The clinical context sharpens the point: the unmet need in this field is not a marginally tighter binder but a xanthine oxidase inhibitor without febuxostat's contested cardiovascular record, and docking alone cannot speak to that need — a compound that scored 2 kcal/mol better would still need the CARES/FAST question answered in a trial.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the winner is the reference drug. Second, the 0.08 kcal/mol margin of the best genuine lead is smaller than the pipeline's own duplicate-entry error and far inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Third, potency and docking score disagree within the lead set: a ten-fold potency spread (Ki 0.1 nM to IC50 1.0 nM) collapses to a 0.11 kcal/mol docking spread, in no consistent direction.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts is good, but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the selenium analogues carry a different artifact risk: selenium is redox-active, so any future enzyme assay of CHEMBL3331615 or CHEMBL3331613 must include redox controls (e.g. catalase/superoxide dismutase counterscreens and a detergent control) to distinguish genuine xanthine oxidase inhibition from redox cycling. The Tox21 read-across panel is unusable as a discriminator here — it returns 1.0 on three assays for febuxostat itself — so safety claims for any lead must come from measured data, not from this panel.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL5436777 inhibits recombinant human xanthine oxidase with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (1.0 nM) under identical assay conditions, and inhibits it no more potently than febuxostat — the docking predicts no measurable advantage; a >2-fold advantage for CHEMBL5436777 would refute the noise interpretation.
  2. After the ligand-preparation fault is fixed, CHEMBL3331615 and CHEMBL3331613 dock on 2E1Q within 1 kcal/mol of febuxostat — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.
  3. Canonicalising the SMILES of all 26 ranked leads and re-running the pipeline removes the febuxostat duplicate and changes no other lead's rank — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.
  4. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand DYI (febuxostat) into 2E1Q reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant human xanthine oxidase enzyme inhibition assay (uric-acid formation, spectrophotometric) for CHEMBL5436777 and febuxostat, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): fix the selenium ligand-preparation fault (selenium-capable typing or manual conformer generation), dock CHEMBL3331615 and CHEMBL3331613 on 2E1Q under the identical protocol, and assay whichever selenium analogue docks within 1 kcal/mol of febuxostat, with redox controls (catalase/superoxide dismutase counterscreens, detergent control) to expose redox-cycling artifacts. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): urate-lowering comparison in a hyperuricaemic cell or animal model only for a compound that clears Stage 1 or Stage 2 with a measured >2-fold potency advantage; no compound advances to an animal model on a docking score alone. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The 0.08 kcal/mol margin of the best genuine lead is far inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and smaller than the pipeline's own duplicate-entry error. 3. Two of the five leads (both selenium analogues, IC50 2.05 and 2.29 nM) could not be docked because the pipeline cannot prepare selenium-containing ligands. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of DYI was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (2E1Q, one xanthine oxidoreductase conformation, E803V mutant) was used; the enzyme's molybdenum centre and induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. The Tox21 read-across panel is unusable as a discriminator here because it returns probability 1.0 on three assays for febuxostat itself (identity artifact). 7. All leads are already-known xanthine oxidase inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 8. The pipeline's lead deduplication and ligand preparation both failed silently and required manual reporting — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited. 9. The cardiovascular safety evidence (CARES, FAST, Inoue et al.) is summarised from the published trials; no new safety analysis was performed, and the eGFR <30 population remains untested in randomised trials.

6. Conclusion

No xanthine oxidase inhibitor in this set beats febuxostat: the best-scoring "lead" is febuxostat itself, the best genuine lead is 0.08 kcal/mol away — a tie inside Vina's noise — and two of the five leads could not be docked at all because the pipeline cannot prepare selenium ligands. The durable findings are the benchmark values for febuxostat on 2E1Q, the 0.03 kcal/mol duplicate-entry control, and the selenium fault. The next experiment is a head-to-head xanthine oxidase IC50 assay of CHEMBL5436777 against febuxostat, not more docking — and the next pipeline change is SMILES canonicalisation before ranking and a selenium-capable ligand-preparation path.

INCB13739 Still Leads by 1.05 kcal/mol — Inside the Noise: A Vina Benchmark of 11β-HSD1 Inhibitors on 4C7K and the Wrong-Target Run That Had to Be Discarded

Type 2 diabetes affected about 537 million adults worldwide in 2021, including about 33 million in Pakistan, and intracellular glucocorticoid excess is one of the metabolic drivers that existing therapies do not directly target.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-06 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #4 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: 11beta-HSD1; INCB13739; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; type 2 diabetes; glucocorticoid; metabolic syndrome; ChEMBL

Abstract

Type 2 diabetes affected about 537 million adults worldwide in 2021, including about 33 million in Pakistan, and intracellular glucocorticoid excess is one of the metabolic drivers that existing therapies do not directly target. The enzyme 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11beta-HSD1) converts inactive cortisone into active cortisol inside liver and adipose tissue, amplifying intracellular glucocorticoid action; its activity is elevated in the adipose tissue of obese rodents and humans and is linked to metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes. INCB13739, a selective 11beta-HSD1 inhibitor, showed a positive phase 2 result — 200 mg daily for 12 weeks lowered A1C by 0.6 percent, fasting glucose by 24 mg per decilitre and HOMA-IR by 24 percent versus placebo in 302 patients inadequately controlled on metformin — yet it was never approved, and no 11beta-HSD1 inhibitor has reached approval. We asked whether a standardised automated docking pipeline could rank known sub-nanomolar 11beta-HSD1 inhibitors against INCB13739. The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026; its first target query resolved to the wrong enzyme entirely (AKR1C3, not 11beta-HSD1) and was discarded, and its first structures failed receptor preparation or centred on a detergent molecule. On the corrected target (UniProt P28845, ChEMBL CHEMBL4235, 58 bioactivities) and the corrected centre — the centroid of the co-crystallised inhibitor DZL in PDB 4C7K (1.91 angstrom) — five ligands were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7. INCB13739 scored minus 11.32 kcal per mol; the best lead, CHEMBL3664636 (IC50 0.31 nM), scored minus 10.27 kcal per mol, with the remaining leads at minus 9.69, minus 9.36 and minus 8.55 kcal per mol. INCB13739 still leads on docking by 1.05 kcal per mol, inside Vina's plus-minus 1 to 2 kcal per mol noise, and all four leads are sub-nanomolar by measured IC50, so docking cannot separate them from the reference and the ranking is not a discovery. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head 11beta-HSD1 enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL3664636 versus INCB13739 under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal per mol predicts no measurable potency advantage; a measured potency difference larger than two-fold would refute that prediction.

1. Introduction

Diabetes affected approximately 537 million adults worldwide in 2021, including about 33 million in Pakistan (IDF Diabetes Atlas 2021). Most of that burden is type 2 diabetes, driven by insulin resistance in liver, muscle and adipose tissue. One amplifier of insulin resistance that standard glucose-lowering drugs do not directly target is intracellular glucocorticoid action: the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD1) converts inactive cortisone into active cortisol inside liver and adipose tissue, raising local glucocorticoid levels without raising circulating cortisol. Its activity is elevated in the adipose tissue of obese rodents and humans and is linked to metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, which makes selective 11β-HSD1 inhibition a mechanistically attractive target — lower cortisol where it does harm, without adrenal suppression.

INCB13739 is the most clinically advanced selective 11β-HSD1 inhibitor. In its phase 2 trial (Rosenstock et al., Diabetes Care 2010; 302 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin, 12 weeks, five doses versus placebo; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00698230), the 200 mg dose lowered A1C by 0.6%, fasting plasma glucose by 24 mg/dL and HOMA-IR by 24% versus placebo; total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides decreased significantly in hyperlipidaemic patients, and body weight fell by about 1 kg at the highest dose. The drug was well tolerated at all doses. Despite that positive result, INCB13739 was never approved, and to this day there is still no approved 11β-HSD1 inhibitor — a class-wide gap that makes the question of whether any known inhibitor is measurably better than INCB13739 worth asking properly.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known 11β-HSD1 inhibitors against INCB13739 on the inhibitor-bound structure, and how large is the pipeline's own error? The falsifiable hypothesis is that four known sub-nanomolar 11β-HSD1 inhibitors, docked under an identical protocol, will score within Vina's noise of INCB13739 — and that any apparent "win" smaller than 2 kcal/mol is not a discovery.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 6 November 2026: the daily literature digest, PubMed and web search (verified references below), ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the IDF Diabetes Atlas 2021 for diabetes burden; the Rosenstock et al. phase 2 trial report for INCB13739's clinical effects; and the RCSB entry for PDB 4C7K.

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline) — and a wrong-target fault caught

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Two faults were caught before any number was reported, and both are documented here because they are part of the result. The first target query, "11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1", resolved in UniProtKB to P42330 — AKR1C3 (aldo-keto reductase family 1 member C3), a different enzyme — and the pipeline docked on PDB 1S1P, the AKR1C3 structure. That whole run was discarded in full; its raw JSON is preserved for audit, and none of its scores is reported here as an 11β-HSD1 result. The run was repeated with the precise gene query "HSD11B1": UniProt P28845 (11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 1, Homo sapiens), ChEMBL CHEMBL4235 (single-protein, human), 58 bioactivities retrieved. INCB13739 was verified in PubChem (MW 467.53). Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score (similarity ×40 + Lipinski ×20 + Veber ×10 + PAINS ×10 + tox ×20). The top four ranked leads were taken forward to docking. All four are known 11β-HSD1 inhibitors with published ChEMBL potencies: CHEMBL3664636 (IC50 0.31 nM), CHEMBL4075869 (IC50 0.5 nM), CHEMBL4101787 (IC50 0.4 nM) and CHEMBL557417 (IC50 0.5 nM). None of the four has a preferred name, an approval, or a development phase in ChEMBL.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 6 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was human 11β-HSD1, PDB 4C7K (1.91 Å, "11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 in complex with inhibitor (DZL)"), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of its co-crystallised ligand DZL, chain A: [−21.30, −6.46, 34.49]. The centre was verified directly against the PDB file: the distance from the grid centre to the DZL chain-A centroid is 0.01 Å. The NADP+ cofactor centroid sits 11.12 Å away, so the centre is not on the cofactor. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Two further automated-pipeline errors were caught and corrected before reporting, and are documented here because they are part of the result. The pipeline's auto-picked structure 1XU9 (1.55 Å) fails RDKit receptor preparation — "pdb parse failed" — for all five ligands, so no docking on 1XU9 was possible at all. The next candidate, 1XU7, was rejected for the opposite reason: its grid centre lands on a CHAPS detergent molecule (CPS), not on an inhibitor, so a docking run there would have scored the detergent site. Only the third structure, 4C7K, passed both checks — a parseable receptor and a grid centre on a genuine co-crystallised inhibitor — and only the 4C7K numbers are reported. The raw JSON of every run is preserved (see Data availability), so the correction is auditable.

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: INCB13739 and all four leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were SR-ARE 0.515 for INCB13739, NR-ER 0.307 for CHEMBL3664636, SR-MMP 0.279 for CHEMBL4075869, NR-Aromatase 0.253 for CHEMBL4101787 and SR-MMP 0.207 for CHEMBL557417. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and the reference drug itself carries the highest flag in the panel, so a flag here does not distinguish a lead from the reference. No lead carries a PAINS alert that would require redox controls in validation.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed; a single crystal structure (4C7K, one 11β-HSD1 conformation) was used; the four leads are already-known 11β-HSD1 inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed; and no clinical inference can be drawn from docking scores — the phase 2 evidence for INCB13739 comes from the Rosenstock trial, not from this computation.

3. Results

The headline is stated plainly: INCB13739 still leads on docking, by 1.05 kcal/mol over the best lead — and that margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so it is not a significant lead. The ranking is also not a discovery in the other direction: all four leads are sub-nanomolar by measured IC50 (0.31–0.5 nM, a 1.6-fold spread), while their docking scores span 1.72 kcal/mol in the same order as potency only at the top — CHEMBL3664636 is both the most potent by IC50 and the best-scoring lead, but the remaining three are ranked by docking in the order −9.69, −9.36, −8.55 against IC50s of 0.5, 0.4 and 0.5 nM, which is no ordering at all. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking either: INCB13739 holds within 0.49 kcal/mol across its three poses and CHEMBL557417 within 0.22, so the poses are stable — the problem is that the scoring function itself cannot separate compounds whose measured potencies differ by less than two-fold. No lead beats INCB13739, and INCB13739 does not beat any lead by a margin this method can defend.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for INCB13739 or any of these leads on 4C7K was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for INCB13739 and four known 11β-HSD1 inhibitors on 4C7K are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the verified grid centre and the documented pipeline faults. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: all four leads are sub-nanomolar inhibitors, yet their docking scores span 1.72 kcal/mol — Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and here it cannot separate a 0.31 nM inhibitor from a 0.5 nM one.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Three automated steps that could silently corrupt this result did corrupt it. The UniProtKB free-text search for "11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1" returns AKR1C3 first — a different enzyme that also acts on steroids, so the error is easy to miss and the discarded run's scores would have looked plausible. The PDB picker then chose a structure (1XU9) that cannot be prepared at all, and a second structure (1XU7) whose centre is a detergent molecule. The first two are fixed by verification — check the accession, check that the receptor parses, check the co-crystallised ligand is an inhibitor and not a detergent or cofactor. The lesson generalises: a docking pipeline that reports a score without reporting its target accession, its structure's parse status, and the identity of the molecule its grid is centred on is not reporting a result, it is reporting a guess.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a negative benchmark with a useful control. There is no lead here: the reference drug leads by a margin the method cannot defend, and the most potent lead by measured IC50 (CHEMBL3664636, 0.31 nM) is the best-scoring lead by only 1.05 kcal/mol behind the reference. The durable findings are the benchmark values for INCB13739 on 4C7K (−11.32 kcal/mol, with full pose list) and the documented chain of three pipeline faults — wrong target, unparseable structure, detergent-centred grid — each caught by a verification step that any automated run should include. The class context sharpens the point: INCB13739 itself, despite a positive phase 2, was never approved, and no 11β-HSD1 inhibitor has been approved — so the field does not need a compound that docks 1 kcal/mol better than INCB13739; it needs a compound that is measurably more potent, more selective, or better tolerated in the laboratory and the clinic.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Two reasons. First, the 1.05 kcal/mol margin is smaller than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — the same protocol re-run from a different starting conformer could erase it or reverse it. Second, potency and docking score barely agree within the lead set: the measured IC50s span only 1.6-fold (0.31–0.5 nM) while the docking scores span 1.72 kcal/mol, and the three leads at 0.4–0.5 nM are ranked in no potency order. A docking "win" of this size, on compounds this close in measured potency, is noise wearing a ranking's clothes.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All five compounds are PAINS-clean, so no redox or aggregation controls are forced by the screen — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (SR-ARE 0.515 for INCB13739 itself) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either — least of all because the reference drug flags the same assays. The validation assay should still include a detergent control and a counter-screen against a related dehydrogenase (for example 11β-HSD2, which inactivates cortisol and must not be inhibited), because selectivity, not potency, is where an 11β-HSD1 programme most often fails.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3664636 inhibits recombinant human 11β-HSD1 with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (0.31 nM) under identical assay conditions, and is not more potent than INCB13739 by more than 2-fold — the docking predicts no measurable advantage; a >5-fold advantage would refute the noise interpretation.
  2. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand DZL into 4C7K reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  3. Re-running the pipeline with the precise gene query "HSD11B1" and the verified-centre check reproduces the 4C7K scores within 0.5 kcal/mol — a pipeline reproducibility check to be verified, not assumed.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant human 11β-HSD1 enzyme inhibition assay (cortisone-to-cortisol conversion, LC-MS or scintillation readout) for CHEMBL3664636, CHEMBL4075869 and INCB13739, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and a carbenoxolone positive control. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): selectivity counter-screen against 11β-HSD2 and AKR1C3 for any compound that clears Stage 1 — AKR1C3 is the enzyme the pipeline first mistook for the target, and cross-activity there would be a genuine liability. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): adipocyte cell-based assay (differentiated 3T3-L1 or human primary adipocytes) measuring intracellular cortisol generation for any compound that clears Stage 2, with INCB13739 as control. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The 1.05 kcal/mol margin between INCB13739 and the best lead is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and is not interpretable as a potency difference. 3. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of DZL was performed. 4. A single crystal structure (4C7K, one 11β-HSD1 conformation) was used; the enzyme's active site is flexible and induced-fit effects are not modelled. 5. The NADP+ cofactor was present in the structure but its 11.12 Å distance from the grid centre means cofactor interactions were not part of the scored pose. 6. All leads are already-known 11β-HSD1 inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 7. No clinical inference can be drawn: the phase 2 evidence cited for INCB13739 comes from the Rosenstock trial, and docking scores say nothing about A1C, weight, or tolerability. 8. The pipeline's automated target resolution, structure selection and grid-centre selection all failed silently and required manual correction — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited.

6. Conclusion

No 11β-HSD1 inhibitor in this set beats INCB13739: the reference leads by 1.05 kcal/mol on 4C7K, a margin inside Vina's noise, and all four leads are sub-nanomolar by measured IC50, so docking cannot separate them from the reference. The durable findings are the benchmark values for INCB13739 on 4C7K and the documented chain of pipeline faults — a wrong target, an unparseable structure, and a detergent-centred grid — each caught by verification. The next experiment is a head-to-head 11β-HSD1 IC50 assay of CHEMBL3664636 against INCB13739, not more docking — and the next pipeline change is to verify the accession, the parse, and the centred ligand before any score is reported.

No Lead Beats Roxadustat Beyond Noise: A Vina Benchmark of PHD2/EGLN1 Inhibitors on 6QGV and the Missing Metal Ion

Anaemia of chronic kidney disease is treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents that require injection and iron supplementation, and hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs) offer an oral alternative that raises endogenous erythropoietin and improves iron mobilisation.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-06 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #5 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PHD2; EGLN1; roxadustat; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; anaemia; chronic kidney disease; HIF prolyl hydroxylase

Abstract

Anaemia of chronic kidney disease is treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents that require injection and iron supplementation, and hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs) offer an oral alternative that raises endogenous erythropoietin and improves iron mobilisation. Roxadustat, the first HIF-PHI, is approved in China, Japan and the European Union but was refused approval in the United States in 2021 on benefit-risk grounds, and the search for a better PHD2 inhibitor continues. We asked whether a standardised, fully automated docking pipeline could rank known PHD2/EGLN1 inhibitors against roxadustat. The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026; its first target query resolved to the wrong enzyme entirely (P4HTM, not PHD2) and was discarded, and its first structure contained the HIF peptide sitting in the binding pocket, so every ligand scored positive and that run was discarded too. On the corrected target (UniProt Q9GZT9, ChEMBL CHEMBL5697, 57 bioactivities) and the corrected structure — PDB 6QGV (1.40 Å), grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised inhibitor J2H centroid [20.93, -0.43, 33.59] — five ligands were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7. The best-scoring lead, CHEMBL5572635, scored -8.38 kcal/mol against roxadustat's -7.50 kcal/mol, a margin of 0.88 kcal/mol that lies inside Vina's ±1-2 kcal/mol scoring noise. The most potent compound by measured IC50, CHEMBL3115307 (0.65 nM), scored -7.54 kcal/mol, effectively tied with roxadustat. No lead beats roxadustat beyond noise, and every score is metal-free because the pipeline's receptor preparation drops the active-site metal ion that roxadustat-class inhibitors chelate, so Vina cannot score the chelation interaction at all. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head PHD2 enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL5572635 against roxadustat under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage — a measured potency advantage greater than 2-fold for either compound, or a Fe-chelation-aware rescoring that reverses the ranking, would refute the claim that no lead here beats roxadustat.

1. Introduction

Anaemia is one of the most common complications of chronic kidney disease (CKD), driven by failing erythropoietin production and disordered iron metabolism, and it worsens fatigue, cardiovascular risk and quality of life. The established treatment is erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs), which require injection, need iron supplementation, and carry their own safety concerns at higher doses. Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs) are oral alternatives: by inhibiting the PHD enzymes (PHD1/2/3, encoded by EGLN2/1/3) that mark hypoxia-inducible factor alpha for degradation, they stabilise HIF, raise endogenous erythropoietin, improve iron absorption and mobilisation, and reduce hepcidin. Roxadustat (Evrenzo, FG-4592) was the first HIF-PHI: first global approval in China in December 2018, Japan in 2019 for dialysis patients and 2020 for non-dialysis patients, and the European Union in August 2021. In July 2021 the US Food and Drug Administration's Cardiovascular and Renal Drugs Advisory Committee voted 13-1 (non-dialysis) and 12-2 (dialysis) that the benefit-risk profile did not support approval — roxadustat is not approved in the United States. Daprodustat was approved by the FDA in early 2023 for dialysis patients. The phase III programme covered more than 8,000 patients. A 2025 network meta-analysis (searches through 1 May 2025, PROSPERO CRD420251066181) found that in non-dialysis CKD roxadustat gave the greatest haemoglobin rise versus placebo or ESA (mean difference 1.21 g/dL, 95% CI 0.72–1.71; SUCRA 88.6%) and in dialysis CKD 1.78 g/dL (95% CI 1.32–2.24; SUCRA 86.2%), but had the highest adverse-event incidence in non-dialysis CKD (SUCRA 18.4%); its major adverse cardiovascular event hazard ratio versus darbepoetin was similar. The clinical question is whether a better PHD2 inhibitor exists — one with a larger efficacy margin, a cleaner safety profile, or both.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known PHD2/EGLN1 inhibitors against roxadustat, and how large is the pipeline's own error? The falsifiable hypothesis is that five known sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar PHD2 inhibitors, docked under an identical protocol, will score within Vina's noise of roxadustat — and that any apparent "win" smaller than 2 kcal/mol is not a discovery.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 6 November 2026: the daily literature digest (2026-11-06), PubMed and web search (verified references below), ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the regulatory history of roxadustat (first approval China December 2018; EU August 2021; FDA advisory committee votes July 2021; daprodustat FDA approval early 2023) and the 2025 network meta-analysis of HIF-PHIs in CKD (PROSPERO CRD420251066181).

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline) — and a wrong-target fault caught

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Two faults were caught before any number was reported, and both are documented here because they are part of the result. The first target query, "Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase", resolved in UniProtKB to Q9NXG6 — P4HTM, transmembrane prolyl 4-hydroxylase, a different enzyme from the HIF prolyl hydroxylases (PHD1/2/3 = EGLN2/1/3) that roxadustat targets — and the pipeline docked on PDB 6TP5. That whole run was discarded; its raw JSON is preserved for audit. The run was repeated with the precise gene query "EGLN1": UniProt Q9GZT9 (hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase 2, PHD2/EGLN1, Homo sapiens), ChEMBL CHEMBL5697 (single-protein, human), 57 bioactivities retrieved. Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score (similarity ×40 + Lipinski ×20 + Veber ×10 + PAINS ×10 + tox ×20). The top four ranked leads were taken forward to docking, with roxadustat as the query reference. All four leads are known PHD2/EGLN1 inhibitors with published ChEMBL potencies: CHEMBL5572635 (IC50 1.0 nM), CHEMBL3115302 (IC50 1.5 nM), CHEMBL3115307 (IC50 0.65 nM) and CHEMBL4127286 (IC50 1.9 nM). None of the four has a preferred name, an approval, or a development phase in ChEMBL.

2.3 Molecular docking — and a peptide-blocked pocket caught

Docking was performed 6 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The first structure the pipeline auto-picked was PDB 7Q5V (1.17 Å, PHD2 in complex with N-oxalylglycine and the HIF-2α CODD peptide). That structure contains the HIF peptide sitting in the binding pocket: every ligand scored between +16.89 and +29.51 kcal/mol — positive scores, meaning clash, not binding — because the peptide physically occupies the site. That run was discarded in full; its raw JSON is preserved for audit. The re-dock used PDB 6QGV (1.40 Å, "HIF prolyl hydroxylase 2 (PHD2/EGLN1) in complex with a spiro[4.5]decanone inhibitor (JPHM-2-167, ligand code J2H)"), a single chain with no peptide in the pocket. The grid centre was placed exactly on the centroid of the co-crystallised inhibitor J2H — [20.93, −0.43, 33.59], verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

One systematic limitation of the receptor preparation is documented here because it bears directly on the result. The active-site metal ion in 6QGV (manganese, 5.48 Å from the grid centre) is dropped by the preparation step, so the docking is metal-free. Roxadustat is a 2-oxoglutarate-competitive inhibitor that chelates the active-site iron; Vina therefore cannot score the chelation interaction at all, and every score in this paper systematically undervalues roxadustat-class binders relative to a metal-aware method. This is not a small correction to be noted in passing — it is the single largest known bias in the comparison, and it works in the leads' favour.

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all four leads and roxadustat were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were NR-ER 0.219 for roxadustat itself, NR-ER 0.163 for CHEMBL3115302, NR-AhR 0.156 for CHEMBL3115307, SR-ARE 0.156 for CHEMBL5572635 and NR-ER 0.078 for CHEMBL4127286. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and roxadustat itself carries the highest flag in the panel, so a flag here does not distinguish a lead from the approved reference drug.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of J2H was performed; a single crystal structure (6QGV, one PHD2 conformation) was used; PHD1 and PHD3 were not docked (roxadustat inhibits all three PHD isoforms); the metal ion was dropped from the receptor, so the chelation interaction that defines roxadustat-class binding is unscored; and the four leads are already-known PHD2 inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound PHD2 potency, ChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL5572635 IC50 1.0 nM −8.38 −8.38, −8.31, −8.25 clean
CHEMBL3115302 IC50 1.5 nM −7.96 −7.96, −7.95, −7.82 clean
CHEMBL3115307 IC50 0.65 nM −7.54 −7.54, −7.32, −7.06 clean
Roxadustat (reference) — −7.50 −7.50, −7.48, −7.18 clean
CHEMBL4127286 IC50 1.9 nM −6.37 −6.37, −6.18, −6.09 clean

All docking on PDB 6QGV (human PHD2/EGLN1, 1.40 Å), grid centre [20.93, −0.43, 33.59] (J2H inhibitor centroid), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 6 November 2026. CHEMBL5572635: MW 418.46, logP 2.15, 0 Lipinski violations. CHEMBL3115302: MW 372.31, logP 0.65, 0 violations. CHEMBL3115307: MW 456.76, logP 2.03, 0 violations. Roxadustat: MW 352.35, logP 2.86, 0 violations. CHEMBL4127286: MW 220.18, logP −0.42, 0 violations.

The headline number is a near-tie, stated plainly: the best lead, CHEMBL5572635, beats roxadustat by 0.88 kcal/mol — inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The most potent compound by measured IC50, CHEMBL3115307 (0.65 nM), scores −7.54 kcal/mol against roxadustat's −7.50 kcal/mol, a difference of 0.04 kcal/mol — a tie. The total spread across the five molecules is 2.01 kcal/mol, and the only compound clearly separated is CHEMBL4127286, which scores 1.13 kcal/mol worse than roxadustat despite a measured IC50 of 1.9 nM — the ranking is not ordered by potency. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: CHEMBL5572635 holds within 0.13 kcal/mol across poses and CHEMBL3115302 within 0.14 kcal/mol, so the poses are stable — but a stable score inside noise is still inside noise. No lead beats roxadustat beyond the margin the method itself cannot resolve, and the metal-free preparation means the reference drug's defining interaction was never scored.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for roxadustat or any of these leads on 6QGV was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for roxadustat and four known PHD2 inhibitors on 6QGV are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the two discarded runs that document what the pipeline gets wrong. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: all four leads are sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar PHD2 inhibitors (IC50 0.65–1.9 nM, a 3-fold spread), while their docking scores span 2.01 kcal/mol in an order that does not track potency — Vina ranks poses, not IC50s.

3.3 The standardisation problem

Three automated steps that could silently corrupt this result did corrupt it, in two different runs. The UniProtKB free-text search for "Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase" returns P4HTM first — a different enzyme with a similar name — and the pipeline docked on it without complaint. The PDB picker then chose 7Q5V, a structure whose binding pocket is occupied by the HIF peptide, and reported positive clash scores as if they were results. The first two faults are fixed by verification — check the accession, check the co-crystallised ligand and any peptide in the pocket. The third fault, the dropped metal ion, is not fixed by verification: it is a property of the preparation step itself, and it biases every score against the very mechanism that makes roxadustat work. The fix is a metal-aware preparation or a rescoring method that models iron chelation — cheap to describe, not yet implemented in this pipeline, and not optional before any lead is claimed to beat roxadustat.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a measurement of the pipeline's own limits. There is no lead here: the best margin is 0.88 kcal/mol inside noise, the most potent compound ties the reference, and the reference drug's key interaction was never scored. The durable findings are the benchmark values for roxadustat on 6QGV (−7.50 kcal/mol, with full pose lists), the two discarded runs that document the pipeline's failure modes, and the metal caveat that any future PHD2 docking paper from this pipeline must address before claiming a win.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the 0.88 kcal/mol margin is smaller than Vina's nominal ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and smaller than the 2.01 kcal/mol total spread of the set. Second, potency and docking score disagree within the lead set: CHEMBL3115307, the most potent by recorded IC50 (0.65 nM), ties roxadustat at −7.54 versus −7.50, while CHEMBL4127286 (1.9 nM) scores a full 1.13 kcal/mol worse than the reference — a 3-fold potency spread against a 2.01 kcal/mol score spread, in no consistent direction. Third, the comparison is structurally unfair to roxadustat: the metal ion its class chelates was dropped from the receptor, so the best lead's margin was earned against a reference drug scored without its defining interaction.

4.3 The PAINS/tox picture is clean but thin

No PAINS alerts is good, but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (NR-ER 0.219 for roxadustat, NR-ER 0.163 for CHEMBL3115302) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either — least of all because the reference drug flags the same assay more strongly than any lead.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL5572635 inhibits recombinant PHD2 with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (1.0 nM) under identical assay conditions, and inhibits it more potently than roxadustat — the docking predicts no measurable advantage; a >2-fold advantage for either compound would refute the noise interpretation.
  2. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand J2H into 6QGV reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  3. Re-preparing 6QGV with the active-site metal ion retained, or rescoring with an Fe-chelation-aware method, improves roxadustat's score relative to the leads and reverses or erases the 0.88 kcal/mol margin — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant PHD2 enzyme inhibition assay (2-oxoglutarate competition, HIF peptide hydroxylation readout) for CHEMBL5572635, CHEMBL3115307 and roxadustat, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): iron-chelation assessment (spectrophotometric Fe(II) binding) for any compound that clears Stage 1, to test whether the metal-free docking systematically undervalued it. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): PHD1 and PHD3 inhibition assays for any compound that clears Stage 2, since roxadustat's clinical profile rests on pan-PHD inhibition and a PHD2-only compound is a different candidate. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The 0.88 kcal/mol best margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so no margin in this paper is interpretable as a potency advantage. 3. The active-site metal ion was dropped by the receptor preparation, so the iron-chelation interaction that defines roxadustat-class binding is unscored — the comparison is biased against the reference drug. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of J2H was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (6QGV, one PHD2 conformation) was used; the 2-oxoglutarate pocket is flexible and induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. PHD1 and PHD3 were not docked. 7. All leads are already-known PHD2 inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 8. The pipeline's automated target resolution and structure selection both failed silently and required manual correction — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited.

6. Conclusion

No PHD2 inhibitor in this set beats roxadustat: the best lead scores −8.38 kcal/mol against roxadustat's −7.50 kcal/mol, a 0.88 kcal/mol margin inside Vina's noise, and the most potent compound by measured IC50 ties the reference at −7.54 versus −7.50. The durable findings are the benchmark values for roxadustat on 6QGV and the two discarded runs that document the pipeline's failure modes — plus the metal caveat, which means this comparison was scored without the interaction that makes roxadustat work. The next experiment is a head-to-head PHD2 IC50 assay with Fe-chelation-aware rescoring, not more metal-free docking.

Two Leads "Beat" Macozinone by Docking and Lose by 1.23 kcal/mol of Noise: A Vina Benchmark of DprE1 Inhibitors on 4P8N and the Covalent Binding Vina Cannot See

Tuberculosis made about 10.8 million people ill in 2023 and killed about 1.25 million, and the search for shorter, safer regimens continues.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-06 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #2 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: DprE1; macozinone; tuberculosis; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; covalent inhibitor; benzothiazinone; ChEMBL

Abstract

Tuberculosis made about 10.8 million people ill in 2023 and killed about 1.25 million, and the search for shorter, safer regimens continues. Macozinone (PBTZ169), a benzothiazinone in phase 2 trials, covalently inhibits the Mycobacterium tuberculosis enzyme DprE1, blocking arabinan synthesis and cell-wall biogenesis, but its covalent binding cannot be modelled by standard docking, so a docking benchmark against it risks measuring the method rather than the molecule. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking): target DprE1 (UniProt P9WJF1, strain ATCC 25618 / H37Rv, ChEMBL CHEMBL3804751, 58 bioactivities), structure PDB 4P8N at 1.79 Å, grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised non-covalent inhibitor R57 ([16.51, −20.97, 1.7]), and five ligands docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under an identical protocol. Two known DprE1 actives "beat" macozinone on docking — CHEMBL4763381 at −12.05 kcal/mol and CHEMBL4752208 at −11.74 kcal/mol, against macozinone at −10.82 kcal/mol — margins of 1.23 and 0.92 kcal/mol, inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. But both leads are far weaker by measured potency: IC50 200 nM and 140 nM against macozinone's 10 nM, so the docking ranking is inverted against experiment, and a third "lead", CHEMBL3330226 at −10.96 kcal/mol, is macozinone itself entered twice, scoring −10.96 versus −10.82 as the query. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head DprE1 enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL4763381 against macozinone under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage; a measured potency advantage for the lead, or covalent docking showing macozinone binds Cys387 far more tightly than Vina suggests, would refute the claim that the docking win is only a measurement of Vina's limits.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases: according to the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, about 10.8 million people fell ill with TB in 2023 and about 1.25 million died. Standard treatment still takes months, and drug-resistant TB needs longer, more toxic regimens, so new drugs with new mechanisms are urgently needed. DprE1 (decaprenylphosphoryl-beta-D-ribose oxidase) is one of the most validated new TB targets: it catalyses a step in arabinan synthesis, and blocking it stops cell-wall biogenesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Macozinone (MCZ, PBTZ169) is a benzothiazinone that covalently inhibits DprE1 and is in phase 2 trials (NCT03334734); its minimum inhibitory concentration is 0.3 ng/mL by resazurin microtiter assay. It is not alone: BTZ043, the first benzothiazinone, is in phase 2b combination trials (NCT05926466, with bedaquiline and delamanid), and other DprE1 candidates in trials include TBA-7371 (an azaindole) and quabodepistat (a carbostyril). Macozinone also has a known human liability: human prostaglandin reductases PTGR1 and PTGR2 dearomatize it to H2MCZ, which loses antimycobacterial activity.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known DprE1 actives against macozinone, and what does an apparent docking "win" mean when the reference drug is a covalent inhibitor and the structure used holds a non-covalent inhibitor? The falsifiable hypothesis is that any lead beating macozinone by less than 2 kcal/mol on Vina docking has no measurable potency advantage, and that the docking ranking will disagree with measured IC50 values on this target.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 6 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/, PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 for the TB burden figures; the macozinone phase 2 trial record (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03334734) and the BTZ043 phase 2b combination trial record (NCT05926466); the 2025 Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy report of macozinone's MIC of 0.3 ng/mL by resazurin microtiter assay; and the 2026 Nature Communications paper showing that human PTGR1/PTGR2 dearomatize macozinone to inactive H2MCZ (DOI 10.1038/s44321-026-00526-1). The covalent mechanism of benzothiazinones — the nitroso moiety forming a semimercaptal with Cys387 of DprE1 — is the established mechanism for this class and is the reason standard non-covalent docking cannot represent macozinone's real binding mode.

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target: M. tuberculosis DprE1, UniProt P9WJF1, strain ATCC 25618 / H37Rv; ChEMBL CHEMBL3804751, 58 bioactivities retrieved. Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score. The top five ranked leads were taken forward to docking. All five are known DprE1 actives with published ChEMBL potencies; none has a preferred name in ChEMBL.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was M. tuberculosis DprE1, PDB 4P8N (1.79 Å, "M. tuberculosis DprE1 in complex with the non-covalent inhibitor QN118", ligand code R57), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of the co-crystallised ligand R57, chain A: [16.51, −20.97, 1.7]. The centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å. The FAD cofactor centroid is 12.75 Å away — the centre is not on the cofactor, so the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor or glycan) did not occur here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

One pipeline fault was caught before reporting, and is documented here because it is part of the result. The lead list contains macozinone itself: CHEMBL3330226 has the same molecular weight as macozinone (456.49), Tanimoto similarity 1.0 to the query, and an identical toxicity panel, and it scored −10.96 kcal/mol against macozinone-as-query at −10.82 kcal/mol — the same molecule, 0.14 kcal/mol apart. This is the duplicate-entry fault seen in earlier papers (Papers #1 and #3): the pipeline treats the reference drug as a new lead when it appears in ChEMBL under a different entry. CHEMBL3330226 is therefore not a lead; it is a duplicate-entry control, and it is reported as such.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all five leads and macozinone were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were SR-MMP 0.498 for CHEMBL4763381, SR-ARE 0.363 for CHEMBL4752208, SR-MMP 0.732 for CHEMBL3330226 and for macozinone (identical panels, as expected for the same molecule), and SR-MMP 0.551 for CHEMBL4868912. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and macozinone itself carries the highest flag in the panel (SR-MMP 0.732), so a flag here does not distinguish a lead from the reference drug.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or covalent docking was performed; a single crystal structure (4P8N, one DprE1 conformation, holding a non-covalent inhibitor) was used; and, most importantly, Vina cannot model covalent binding, so macozinone's real binding mode — a semimercaptal with Cys387 — is not represented in any score reported here. The leads are already-known DprE1 actives, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table
