Trametinib Beats Itself by 1.75 kcal/mol: A Vina Benchmark of MEK1 Inhibitors on 7B7R and the Conformer-Sampling Error Hiding Inside Every Docking Score

BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations produce response rates of 60–70% in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma, but resistance typically develops within 12–18 months, and the search for better MEK inhibitors continues.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-05 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #3 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: MEK1; trametinib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; melanoma; BRAF; allosteric inhibitor; ChEMBL

Abstract

BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations produce response rates of 60–70% in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma, but resistance typically develops within 12–18 months, and the search for better MEK inhibitors continues. We asked whether a standardised, fully automated docking pipeline could rank known MEK1 inhibitors against trametinib on the MEK1 allosteric pocket. The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 5 November 2026; its first target query resolved to the wrong protein entirely (KSR1, not MEK1) and was discarded, and its first grid centre was the ATP-site analogue, 10.14 Å from the allosteric inhibitor pocket. On the corrected target (UniProt Q02750, ChEMBL CHEMBL3587, 38 bioactivities) and the corrected centre — the centroid of the co-crystallised allosteric inhibitor T1K in PDB 7B7R (1.70 Å) — five ligands were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7. The best-scoring "lead", CHEMBL2103875 at −9.52 kcal/mol, is trametinib itself, entered twice by the pipeline under two SMILES orderings; the duplicate trametinib entry scored −7.77 kcal/mol. The same molecule therefore beats itself by 1.75 kcal/mol, an error larger than Vina's nominal ±1–2 kcal/mol scoring noise and larger than every real difference in the set. The remaining known inhibitors — CHEMBL5433950 −8.02 kcal/mol (IC50 0.7 nM), CHEMBL1615025 −7.94 kcal/mol (IC50 1.79 nM), CHEMBL507361 −7.13 kcal/mol (IC50 0.33 nM) — are statistically tied with trametinib and ranked in the wrong potency order. No lead beats trametinib once the duplicate is recognised. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head MEK1 enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL507361 against trametinib under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage.

1. Introduction

Melanoma of the skin caused approximately 332,000 new cases and 59,000 deaths worldwide in 2022 (IARC GLOBOCAN 2022). About half of cutaneous melanomas carry a BRAF V600 mutation, which drives the RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK (MAPK) pathway, and the combination of a BRAF inhibitor with a MEK inhibitor is now standard: BRAF/MEK combinations produce response rates of 60–70% in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma, among the highest in solid-tumour targeted therapy, with responses often beginning within days. The central limitation is resistance, which typically develops within 12–18 months, driven largely by MAPK pathway reactivation. Trametinib, an allosteric MEK1/2 inhibitor approved in combination with dabrafenib, is the benchmark: in the COMBI-d trial the combination gave median overall survival of 25.1 months versus 18.7 months for dabrafenib alone (hazard ratio 0.71), and in COMBI-v 25.6 months versus 18.0 months for vemurafenib alone. In a long-term Chinese cohort the combination gave an objective response rate of 71.7% and a 3-year overall survival rate of 28.8%. The clinical question is whether a better MEK inhibitor exists — one that binds the same allosteric pocket more tightly, or that retains activity against resistance mutations.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known MEK1 inhibitors against trametinib on the allosteric pocket, and how large is the pipeline's own error? The falsifiable hypothesis is that five known sub-nanomolar MEK1 inhibitors, docked under an identical protocol, will score within Vina's noise of trametinib — and that any apparent "win" smaller than 2 kcal/mol is not a discovery.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 5 November 2026: the daily literature digest (2026-11-05), PubMed E-utilities and web search (verified references below), ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: IARC GLOBOCAN 2022 for melanoma burden; the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence appraisal TA396 for the COMBI-d and COMBI-v survival figures; a 2021 Frontiers in Oncology long-term follow-up for the combination's response and survival in a Chinese cohort; and the RCSB entry for PDB 7B7R.

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline) — and a wrong-target fault caught

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 5 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). One fault was caught before any number was reported, and it is documented here because it is part of the result. The first target query, "MEK1/2 (MAP2K1/2)", resolved in UniProtKB to Q8IVT5 — KSR1, kinase suppressor of Ras 1, a scaffold protein, not MEK — and the ChEMBL target attached to it (CHEMBL1938215, KSR1) returned a single bioactivity. That run was discarded in full; its raw JSON is preserved for audit. The run was repeated with the precise gene query "MAP2K1": UniProt Q02750 (dual specificity mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase 1, MEK1, Homo sapiens), ChEMBL CHEMBL3587 (single-protein, human), 38 bioactivities retrieved. Trametinib was verified in PubChem (MW 615.39). Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score (similarity ×40 + Lipinski ×20 + Veber ×10 + PAINS ×10 + tox ×20). The top five ranked leads were taken forward to docking. All five are known MEK1 inhibitors with published ChEMBL potencies: trametinib itself (IC50 0.48 nM, pChEMBL 9.32, as CHEMBL2103875), CHEMBL5433950 (IC50 0.7 nM, pChEMBL 9.15), CHEMBL1615025 (IC50 1.79 nM, pChEMBL 8.75) and CHEMBL507361 (IC50 0.33 nM, pChEMBL 9.48). None of the three non-trametinib leads has a preferred name, an approval, or a development phase in ChEMBL.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 5 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was human MEK1, PDB 7B7R (1.70 Å, "MEK1 in complex with compound 4"), with the grid centred on the centroid of its co-crystallised ligand T1K — 2-[5-[ethyl(methyl)amino]imidazo[1,2-a]pyrimidin-7-yl]phenol, an allosteric MEK inhibitor (compound 4): [−28.04, −12.97, 13.32]. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

One automated-pipeline error was caught and corrected before reporting, and is documented here because it is part of the result. The pipeline's automatic grid-centre picker takes the centroid of the first drug-like HETATM group in the PDB file. In 7B7R that group is ANP (phosphoaminophosphonic acid-adenylate ester, the ATP analogue, residue 401, 31 atoms), not the inhibitor; the centre it produced was [−31.01, −3.89, 16.73], in the ATP site. The co-crystallised allosteric inhibitor T1K (residue 403, 20 atoms) sits 10.14 Å away. MEK allosteric inhibitors bind a pocket adjacent to the ATP site, so the 22.5 Å box still covered the allosteric pocket — and the first docking run's scores shifted by only 0.14–0.96 kcal/mol on re-docking — but the centre was wrong in principle, and on other structures the same default has landed 13–45 Å from the inhibitor site. All five ligands were re-docked at the T1K centroid with the same protocol, and only the corrected numbers are reported. The raw JSON of every run is preserved (see Data availability), so the correction is auditable.

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all four leads and trametinib were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were NR-ER 0.351 for CHEMBL5433950 and 0.338 for trametinib, and SR-MMP 0.087 for CHEMBL1615025. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and trametinib itself carries the highest flags in the panel, so a flag here does not distinguish a lead from the approved reference drug. CHEMBL507361's panel is measured data (not read-across) with no flags.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed; a single crystal structure (7B7R, one MEK1 conformation) was used; MEK2 was not docked (trametinib inhibits both MEK1 and MEK2); and the four leads are already-known MEK1 inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound MEK1 potency, ChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL2103875 (= trametinib) IC50 0.48 nM −9.52 −9.52, −8.90, −8.25 clean
CHEMBL5433950 IC50 0.7 nM −8.02 −8.02, −7.82, −7.60 clean
CHEMBL1615025 IC50 1.79 nM −7.94 −7.94, −7.69, −7.43 clean
Trametinib (reference, duplicate entry) IC50 0.48 nM (same molecule) −7.77 −7.77, −7.71, −7.42 clean
CHEMBL507361 IC50 0.33 nM −7.13 −7.13, −7.13, −6.32 clean

All docking on PDB 7B7R (human MEK1, 1.70 Å), grid centre [−28.04, −12.97, 13.32] (T1K allosteric-inhibitor centroid), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 5 November 2026. CHEMBL2103875/trametinib: MW 615.40, logP 3.94, 1 Lipinski violation. CHEMBL5433950: MW 617.42, logP 4.12, 1 violation. CHEMBL1615025: MW 504.23, logP 1.07, 1 violation. CHEMBL507361: MW 482.20, logP 2.47, Lipinski-clean.

The headline number is a self-contradiction, stated plainly: the pipeline entered trametinib twice — once as the query (SMILES written in one atom order) and once as the top ChEMBL hit CHEMBL2103875 (the same molecule, SMILES written in another order) — and the two entries scored −7.77 and −9.52 kcal/mol. The same molecule beats itself by 1.75 kcal/mol. The difference comes from conformer generation: the ligand-preparation step builds a 3D conformer from the SMILES string, and the starting conformer depends on atom ordering, so the same molecule enters Vina from different starting geometries and lands in different local minima. Every real difference in this table is smaller than that artefact: the gap between trametinib-as-QUERY and the best genuine lead (CHEMBL5433950, −8.02) is 0.25 kcal/mol, and the total spread across the four distinct molecules is 0.89 kcal/mol — all inside Vina's noise, and all smaller than the 1.75 kcal/mol the pipeline generates from one molecule against itself. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: trametinib-as-QUERY holds within 0.35 kcal/mol across poses, CHEMBL507361 holds its best score across two poses, and the most potent compound by measured IC50 (CHEMBL507361, 0.33 nM) has the worst docking score (−7.13) — the ranking is inverted against potency at the bottom of the table as well as the top.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for trametinib or any of these leads on 7B7R was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for trametinib and three known MEK1 inhibitors on 7B7R are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the duplicate-entry control that quantifies the pipeline's own error. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: all four distinct molecules are sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar MEK1 inhibitors (IC50 0.33–1.79 nM, a 5-fold spread), while their docking scores span 0.89 kcal/mol in the wrong order — Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and here it cannot even rank a molecule against itself.

3.3 The standardisation problem

Two automated steps that could silently corrupt this result did corrupt it, and a third corrupted it in a way no structure check can catch. The UniProtKB free-text search for "MEK1/2 (MAP2K1/2)" returns KSR1 first; the PDB picker centres on the ATP analogue 10.14 Å from the allosteric pocket; and the lead list contains the reference drug itself under a different SMILES ordering, which the pipeline treats as a new compound. The first two are fixed by verification — check the accession, check the co-crystallised ligand. The third is fixed only by canonicalising SMILES before ranking: two entries with identical canonical SMILES are one molecule, and any pipeline that does not canonicalise will periodically "discover" its own reference drug and report it as a lead beating the reference. The fix is cheap — canonicalise, deduplicate, and include a duplicate-entry control in every run — but it is not optional.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a measurement of the pipeline's own error. There is no lead here: the best "lead" is trametinib, the second-best is 0.25 kcal/mol from trametinib's duplicate score, and the most potent compound scores worst. The durable finding is the 1.75 kcal/mol self-difference — a direct, controlled measurement of conformer-sampling variance in this exact pipeline, on this exact structure, with the reference drug as its own control. Any future paper from this pipeline that reports a margin under ~2 kcal/mol without a duplicate-entry control is reporting noise. The benchmark values for trametinib on 7B7R (−7.77 and −9.52 kcal/mol for the two entries, with full pose lists) are now on record, and the honest way to read them is as a range, not a point: trametinib on 7B7R scores somewhere in a ~2 kcal/mol band depending on input ordering.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the winner is the reference drug. Second, the 1.75 kcal/mol margin is generated by the pipeline itself, not by chemistry — the same molecule, two SMILES orderings. Third, potency and docking score disagree within the lead set: CHEMBL507361, the most potent by recorded IC50 (0.33 nM), scores worst (−7.13), while CHEMBL5433950 (0.7 nM) scores best among genuine leads (−8.02) — a 0.89 kcal/mol spread against a 5-fold potency spread, in no consistent direction.

4.3 The PAINS/tox picture is clean but thin

No PAINS alerts is good, but PAINS-clean is a low bar for kinase inhibitors, and the Tox21 read-across flags (NR-ER 0.351 for CHEMBL5433950) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either — least of all because the reference drug flags the same assays.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL507361 inhibits recombinant MEK1 with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (0.33 nM) under identical assay conditions, and inhibits it more potently than trametinib (0.48 nM) — the docking predicts no measurable advantage; a >5-fold advantage would refute the noise interpretation.
  2. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand T1K (compound 4) into 7B7R reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  3. Canonicalising the SMILES of all 26 ranked leads and re-running the pipeline removes the trametinib duplicate and changes no other lead's rank — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant MEK1 kinase inhibition assay (ADP-Glo or equivalent) for CHEMBL507361, CHEMBL5433950 and trametinib, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): BRAF V600E melanoma cell-line viability (A375, SK-MEL-28) for any compound that clears Stage 1, with trametinib as control and a BRAF wild-type line as selectivity check. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): MEK2 inhibition assay for any compound that clears Stage 2, since trametinib's clinical value rests on dual MEK1/2 inhibition and a MEK1-only compound is a weaker candidate. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The 1.75 kcal/mol self-difference for trametinib means no margin under ~2 kcal/mol in this paper is interpretable. 3. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol on top of the conformer-sampling variance measured here. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of T1K was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (7B7R, one MEK1 conformation) was used; MEK's allosteric pocket is flexible and induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. MEK2 was not docked. 7. All leads are already-known MEK1 inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 8. The pipeline's automated target resolution, grid-centre selection and lead deduplication all failed silently and required manual correction — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited.

6. Conclusion

No MEK1 inhibitor in this set beats trametinib: the best-scoring "lead" is trametinib itself, and the same molecule scored −7.77 and −9.52 kcal/mol under two SMILES orderings — a 1.75 kcal/mol self-difference that exceeds every real difference in the table and sets the floor for what this pipeline can claim. The durable findings are the benchmark values for trametinib on 7B7R and the duplicate-entry control that quantifies conformer-sampling error. The next experiment is a head-to-head MEK1 IC50 assay, not more docking — and the next pipeline change is SMILES canonicalisation before ranking.

2026-11-05 Health Draft — not submitted

Metal-aware re-ranking of sulfonyl piperazine LpxH inhibitors: docking scores alone cannot distinguish di-manganese chelators from non-chelators in *Klebsiella pneumoniae* LpxH

Background: LpxH, the di-manganese UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine hydrolase of the lipid A (Raetz) pathway, is an essential antibacterial target in Klebsiella pneumoniae, but structure-based ranking of its sulfonyl piperazine inhibitors is confounded because standard docking ignores the catalytic di-manganese cluster.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509

Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI). All computations were run on 5 November 2026 and are reproduced from the files listed under Data availability.

Abstract

Background: LpxH, the di-manganese UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine hydrolase of the lipid A (Raetz) pathway, is an essential antibacterial target in Klebsiella pneumoniae, but structure-based ranking of its sulfonyl piperazine inhibitors is confounded because standard docking ignores the catalytic di-manganese cluster. Methods: We docked (AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) the four published inhibitors AZ1, JH-LPH-41, JH-LPH-45 and JH-LPH-50 and four patent-disclosed analogues into the 1.73 Å K. pneumoniae LpxH structure (PDB 7SS7) at the crystallographic ligand centroid, verified the grid centre against the co-crystallised ligand (deviation 0.0 Å), and measured hydroxamate-oxygen to manganese distances in every docked pose with an order-independent graph method. Results: Vina affinities span only −9.18 to −11.37 kcal/mol and misrank the known references: JH-LPH-45 (−11.37) outscores JH-LPH-50 (−11.04) although it is 2.3-fold less potent (IC50 18 vs 7.7 nM), and AZ1 (−10.04) sits within 1.0 kcal/mol of JH-LPH-50 despite lacking whole-cell activity. The metal geometry separates the series cleanly: the three known chelators place a hydroxamate oxygen 1.93–2.21 Å from manganese, the two hydroxamate analogues 1.97–2.65 Å, and the two non-hydroxamate analogues no oxygen closer than 6.5 Å. Re-docking JH-LPH-50 reproduces the crystal pose to 2.22–2.28 Å RMSD. Conclusion: a metal-aware re-rank (Vina affinity plus a chelation-distance term) is required for this target; we predict the des-chloro hydroxamate CID 156252442 inhibits K. pneumoniae LpxH at low-nanomolar potency comparable to JH-LPH-50, while the non-chelating analogues CID 156252448 and CID 156252462 will be at least 10-fold weaker despite similar docking scores — a prediction testable in a single malachite-green enzyme assay.

Keywords: LpxH; Klebsiella pneumoniae; lipid A; sulfonyl piperazine; di-manganese cluster; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; metal chelation; antimicrobial resistance

Introduction

No new class of antibiotics against Gram-negative pathogens has been approved in five decades, while multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae continues to spread in hospitals, including in Pakistan, where carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella is now a routine clinical problem. The lipid A biosynthetic (Raetz) pathway remains one of the few unexploited essential pathways in these organisms. LpxH (UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine hydrolase) catalyses a late, essential step — hydrolysis of the pyrophosphate of UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine to lipid X and UMP — and is present in ~70% of Gram-negative bacteria and in all World Health Organization priority Gram-negative pathogens. Inhibiting LpxH is doubly lethal: it blocks lipid A synthesis and causes toxic lipid A intermediates to accumulate in the inner membrane.

The sulfonyl piperazine series is the only inhibitor chemotype with structural validation against K. pneumoniae LpxH (KpLpxH). AstraZeneca reported AZ1 in 2015 as the first LpxH inhibitor; Cho et al. (2020) solved the KpLpxH–AZ1 crystal structure (PDB 6PIB, 2.26 Å) and showed that AZ1 occupies the L-shaped acyl-chain-binding chamber without reaching the active site, which explains its weak whole-cell activity against wild-type K. pneumoniae. Structure-guided optimisation produced JH-LPH-33 (IC50 26 nM) and JH-LPH-41, whose extended N-acyl chain reaches into the active site (PDB 6WII, 1.85 Å). Kwak et al. (2023) then reported the first-in-class di-manganese-chelating inhibitors, JH-LPH-45 (IC50 18 nM, KI 7.3 nM) and JH-LPH-50 (IC50 7.7 nM, KI 3.1 nM), whose hydroxamate groups coordinate the catalytic di-manganese cluster (PDB 7SS6, 1.74 Å; PDB 7SS7, 1.73 Å). Chelation, not hydrophobic fit alone, is what separates the nanomolar inhibitors from AZ1.

That distinction creates a specific hazard for computational screening: AutoDock Vina, the workhorse of virtual screening, has no metal-coordination term, and standard receptor preparation strips the manganese ions from the structure. A docking campaign against LpxH that reports Vina scores alone will therefore rank chelating and non-chelating analogues almost interchangeably. A same-target study published this week (Chakraborty et al., 2026) ran a full docking → ADMET → DFT → molecular-dynamics pipeline against K. pneumoniae LpxH without any metal-aware term, which makes the question urgent rather than theoretical: does the metal geometry, measured in the docked pose, rescue the ranking that Vina alone gets wrong?

This paper answers that question with a complete, reproducible computation. We dock the four published inhibitors and four patent-disclosed analogues into the JH-LPH-50 co-crystal structure, audit the docking grid centre against the crystallographic ligand (a step that recent work in our own pipeline showed is easy to get wrong), validate the protocol by re-docking, and measure the hydroxamate–manganese geometry of every pose. The result is a falsifiable, metal-aware ranking rule and two concrete potency predictions that one enzyme assay can confirm or refute.

Methods

Target and structures

The target is Klebsiella pneumoniae subsp. pneumoniae LpxH (UniProt A6T5R0, strain ATCC 700721 / MGH 78578; 240 residues). Fifteen X-ray structures are deposited for this accession; we used PDB 7SS7 (1.73 Å), the KpLpxH complex with JH-LPH-50, because it is the highest-resolution structure of the most potent known inhibitor bound in the chelating pose. Ligand identity and stereochemistry were taken from the RCSB Chemical Component Dictionary entries BN8 (JH-LPH-50; C24H29ClF3N5O5S), BKB (JH-LPH-45) and OKV (AZ1; C21H22F3N3O3S). Reference potencies are the published values of Kwak et al. (2023): JH-LPH-50 IC50 7.7 nM (KI 3.1 nM), JH-LPH-45 IC50 18 nM (KI 7.3 nM), JH-LPH-33 IC50 26 nM (KI 10 nM), KM 68.1 µM; and of Cho et al. (2020) for AZ1.

Compound set

The query compound is JH-LPH-50 (PubChem CID 167713149), verified live in PubChem by SMILES identity search. Analogues were retrieved by PubChem 2D fingerprint similarity (fastsimilarity_2d, Tanimoto ≥ 0.85, 25 records) and scored with RDKit descriptors (Lipinski, Veber), PAINS filters and a k-nearest-neighbour Tox21 read-across panel (12 assays). The top five by composite lead score were docked, together with the query and AZ1. Two of the 25 are the published inhibitors JH-LPH-41 (CID 146680856; PDB ligand U2V in 6WII) and JH-LPH-45 (CID 167713202); these were treated as additional references, not as novel leads. The remaining four analogues (CID 156252442, 156252744, 156252448, 156252462) are disclosed in patent US20240279174 (SureChEMBL entries) with no published enzyme-inhibition data; they are the prediction set. No ChEMBL target exists for LpxH (verified: zero targets for UniProt A6T5R0 and no LpxH entry by name search), so no measured-activity training set was available.

Docking and grid-centre audit

Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 with RDKit receptor preparation (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types) and meeko ligand preparation, a 22.5 Å cubic box, exhaustiveness 8, and 3 poses; the reported affinity is the best pose. The grid centre was the centroid of the co-crystallised BN8 ligand in 7SS7, computed independently of the docking code and compared with the centroid returned by the pipeline's automatic centre picker. The two manganese ions were located from the 7SS7 HETATM records. Because the receptor preparation keeps protein ATOM records only, the manganese ions are absent from the docking calculation itself — the metal geometry is therefore measured a posteriori on the docked poses, which is the point of the analysis.

Chelation geometry and re-dock validation

Hydroxamate oxygens in each docked pose were identified without assuming any atom ordering (Vina's PDBQT output reorders atoms relative to the input): bonds were inferred from interatomic distances (< 1.9 Å, heavy atoms), the hydroxamate nitrogen was identified as the unique nitrogen with an oxygen neighbour, and its oxygen neighbour (hydroxyl) and the carbonyl oxygen on the adjacent carbon were measured against both manganese positions. The same graph method recovered the crystallographic hydroxamate–manganese distances (carbonyl 2.49 Å, hydroxyl 2.11 Å; cf. 2.5 Å reported by Kwak et al.), validating the measurement. Re-dock validation: JH-LPH-50 was docked twice independently and each pose was aligned to the crystal ligand by maximum-common-substructure mapping onto the SMILES template; the heavy-atom RMSD is reported. All scripts and raw outputs are listed under Data availability.

Pipeline-fault disclosure

Two faults in our own pipeline were found and corrected during this run, and are disclosed so that the numbers can be audited. First, the pipeline's target resolver initially matched the text query to UniProt B5Y0K8 (Klebsiella variicola LpxH) and its ChEMBL fallback selected CHEMBL2074 (human maltase-glucoamylase); the 55 "ligands" and 26 ranked "leads" from that run are unrelated to LpxH and were discarded in full. The run was repeated against the exact accession A6T5R0; the ChEMBL fallback still mis-assigned CHEMBL2074, so the lead set used here comes exclusively from the PubChem similarity search described above, and the pipeline's ChEMBL-derived leads are not reported. Second, the first pose-analysis script assumed Vina's PDBQT atom order matched the input molecule; it did not, which produced a spurious re-dock RMSD of 8.23 Å. The order-independent graph method described above replaced it, and the corrected RMSD values (2.22 and 2.28 Å) are the ones reported.

Results

Grid-centre audit

The automatic centre picker returned (−35.42, −9.82, 3.75), identical to the independently computed BN8 centroid (deviation 0.0 Å; BN8 = 39 heavy atoms, the first non-solvent HETATM group in 7SS7). The two manganese ions sit at (−29.52, −19.19, 0.71) and (−29.26, −17.64, 3.71), i.e. 9–10 Å from the grid centre, inside the 22.5 Å box. The grid is therefore centred on the inhibitor site, not on a cofactor, solvent or glycan — the failure mode that invalidated two of our earlier papers before correction.

Vina affinities misrank the known references

All eight compounds dock with affinities between −9.18 and −11.37 kcal/mol (Table 1) — a spread of only 2.2 kcal/mol across a series whose measured potencies span from 7.7 nM to no whole-cell activity. The misranking is demonstrable on the known compounds alone: JH-LPH-45 scores best (−11.37) although it is 2.3-fold less potent than JH-LPH-50 (IC50 18 vs 7.7 nM; −11.04), and AZ1 (−10.04) lies only 1.0 kcal/mol below JH-LPH-50 although it is the weakest inhibitor in the series and has no whole-cell activity against wild-type K. pneumoniae. Vina, without a metal term, cannot see the interaction that the medicinal chemistry of this series is built on.

The metal geometry separates the series

The hydroxamate–manganese distances split the eight compounds into two groups with no overlap (Table 1). The three known inhibitors with measured nanomolar potency (JH-LPH-50, JH-LPH-45, JH-LPH-41) place their hydroxamate hydroxyl oxygen 1.93–2.21 Å from a manganese ion — the same distance as in the crystal structure (2.11 Å) — with the carbonyl oxygen at 2.87–3.51 Å. The two hydroxamate analogues behave the same way: CID 156252442 at 1.97 / 3.09 Å, essentially superimposable on JH-LPH-50's geometry, and CID 156252744 at 2.65 / 3.69 Å, the longest chelation distances in the set. The two non-hydroxamate analogues, despite Vina scores within 1.9 kcal/mol of JH-LPH-50, place no oxygen closer than 6.5 Å to either manganese — they cannot chelate by any geometry. AZ1, which the crystal structure shows does not reach the active site, is 10.25 Å away at its closest oxygen.

Re-docking JH-LPH-50 reproduces the crystallographic pose to 2.22 Å RMSD in the first run and 2.28 Å in the repeat — above the conventional 2.0 Å success cutoff, and the residual displacement is concentrated in the hydroxamate: the docked carbonyl oxygen sits 2.91–3.02 Å from manganese versus 2.49 Å in the crystal, while the hydroxyl oxygen is recovered at 1.95–2.00 Å versus 2.11 Å. The pose is approximately right but the metal coordination is systematically under-formed, exactly as expected from a scoring function with no metal term.

Drug-likeness and safety panel

All eight compounds pass Lipinski and Veber filters with no PAINS alerts (Table 2). The hydroxamate series carries one Lipinski violation each (molecular weight > 500 Da; 529–604 Da), as does JH-LPH-50 itself, so the violation is a property of the chemotype rather than a discriminator. Mean predicted Tox21 probabilities from k-nearest-neighbour read-across are low (0.069–0.108 across 12 assays); the highest single-assay values for JH-LPH-50 are SR-p53 (0.414), SR-ARE (0.310) and SR-MMP (0.278). These read-across values rest on low training-set similarity (maximum 0.31–0.32) and are reported as a triage flag only, not as a safety claim.

The metal-aware rule and its predictions

A chelation-competent pose is defined here as a docked hydroxyl oxygen ≤ 2.7 Å from a manganese ion (the crystal value is 2.11 Å; the longest distance among the known nanomolar inhibitors in their docked poses is 2.21 Å, and 2.7 Å allows for the ~0.5 Å outward displacement Vina introduces at the carbonyl oxygen). Under this rule, five of the eight compounds are chelation-competent and three are not, and the rule recovers the known potency order where Vina alone inverts it (JH-LPH-45 outscoring JH-LPH-50) and compresses it (AZ1 within 1.0 kcal/mol of JH-LPH-50).

Falsifiable claim. A metal-aware score — Vina affinity combined with a chelation-distance term — predicts KpLpxH inhibition better than Vina affinity alone. Specifically: (i) CID 156252442 (Vina −10.84; hydroxyl O–Mn 1.97 Å; carbonyl O–Mn 3.09 Å) will inhibit KpLpxH with an IC50 within 3-fold of JH-LPH-50 (7.7 nM), i.e. low-nanomolar; (ii) CID 156252448 and CID 156252462 (Vina −9.43 and −9.18; no oxygen within 6.5 Å of manganese) will be at least 10-fold weaker than JH-LPH-50 despite Vina scores within 1.9 kcal/mol of it; (iii) CID 156252744 (hydroxyl O–Mn 2.65 Å, the marginal case) will fall between the two groups. Test: malachite-green LpxH inhibition assay exactly as in Kwak et al. (2023) (KM 68.1 µM, triplicate dose–response), followed by MIC determination against K. pneumoniae ATCC 10031 with and without an outer-membrane permeabiliser (polymyxin B nonapeptide), as in Cho et al. (2020). If CID 156252442 is weaker than 25 nM, or if either non-chelating analogue is within 3-fold of JH-LPH-50, the claim is refuted.

Discussion

Three points follow. First, the LpxH series is a clean demonstration that a docking score can be right for the wrong reason: Vina rewards the hydrophobic burial of the sulfonyl piperazine tail in the L-shaped acyl-chain chamber, which every analogue in this series shares, and is blind to the metal coordination that actually drives the potency gain from AZ1 to JH-LPH-50. Any virtual screen against a metalloenzyme that reports scores without a metal-geometry check will make the same error, and will prefer large hydrophobic analogues over true chelators. The remedy is cheap — one distance measurement per pose — and we show it separates the series with no overlap.

Second, the predictions are deliberately asymmetric in risk. CID 156252442 is a des-chloro, C4-linker hydroxamate: it drops the 3-chloro substituent of JH-LPH-50 and shortens the linker by two methylenes, yet keeps the full chelation geometry (1.97 / 3.09 Å) and the best Vina score among the untested analogues (−10.84). If it confirms at low-nanomolar potency, it is a simpler, lighter (529.54 Da) and less lipophilic (logP 2.62) starting point than JH-LPH-50. CID 156252744 is the informative borderline: its hydroxyl oxygen at 2.65 Å is the longest chelation distance in the set, so its measured potency tests where the 2.7 Å cutoff actually bites.

Third, the negative predictions matter as much as the positive one. CID 156252448 (methyl ester) and CID 156252462 (carboxylic acid) are the two highest-scoring non-hydroxamate analogues by composite lead score (90.0 and 91.8) and would be the first compounds a score-only pipeline would order. Our analysis says they are the wrong order: without a metal-binding group they cannot reproduce the interaction that makes this series work. A single assay plate distinguishes the two rankings.

This week's literature sharpens the context rather than changing the conclusion. Chakraborty et al. (2026) independently selected LpxH as a docking target and ran the standard pipeline (docking → ADMET → DFT → MD) without a metal term; our result predicts their top-ranked quinolinone/thiazolidinone hits will need the same chelation check before synthesis. On the resistance-spread side, econazole was shown this week to block conjugative transfer of plasmid-borne last-line resistance genes (Hu et al., 2026), and proton-pump inhibitors were shown to restore ceftriaxone activity against multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae by efflux inhibition (Hussein & Auda, 2026) — both are combination partners, not competitors, for a direct LpxH inhibitor: an LpxH inhibitor that works would pair naturally with a permeabiliser or an efflux adjuvant, exactly as Cho et al. showed for the early sulfonyl piperazines. Genomic-language-model screening (MicrobeRT, 2026) and MIC prediction from sequence (Mikawa, 2026) are converging on the same practical problem from the diagnostic side; a validated LpxH inhibitor would give those tools a therapeutic counterpart.

Limitations

  1. No experimental data. Every potency statement about the four analogues is a prediction; none has a measured IC50. The claim is designed to be refuted by one assay.
  2. Vina has no metal term and the receptor has no manganese. The affinities are therefore systematically blind to chelation; the metal-aware rule is a post-hoc geometric correction, not a re-scored energy. A metal-aware scoring function or QM/MM refinement would be stronger, and was not run.
  3. Re-dock RMSD is 2.22–2.28 Å, above the conventional 2.0 Å cutoff, with the error concentrated at the hydroxamate. The protocol recovers the binding mode approximately, not exactly.
  4. Single structure, no dynamics. All docking used one rigid structure (7SS7); no ensemble docking and no molecular dynamics were run, so induced-fit and lid-domain motion (the insertion lid above the active site) are unmodelled.
  5. Toxicity panel is low-confidence read-across. Maximum similarity to the Tox21 training set is 0.31–0.32; the probabilities are triage flags, and hydroxamates as a class carry known off-target metal-binding liabilities that this panel cannot assess.
  6. Enzyme potency is not whole-cell activity. AZ1 is the standing warning: nanomolar enzyme inhibition in this series has repeatedly failed to translate into wild-type MIC without outer-membrane permeabilisation or efflux deletion. The MIC arm of the proposed test is therefore essential, not optional.
  7. ChEMBL has no LpxH target, so the analogue set could not be filtered against measured LpxH activity; the four prediction compounds are patent-disclosed (US20240279174), not novel chemical matter — the novelty claimed here is the ranking rule and the predictions, not the structures.
  8. Pipeline faults. The ChEMBL fallback mis-assignment and the atom-order error described in Methods were caught before reporting, but they show that automated pipelines need the same centre and identity audits applied here; the audit steps are part of the method, not an afterthought.

Conclusion

For Klebsiella pneumoniae LpxH, AutoDock Vina affinities span 2.2 kcal/mol across a series whose measured potencies span from 7.7 nM to no whole-cell activity, and Vina inverts the order of the two best-known inhibitors. A single geometric measurement — the hydroxamate-oxygen to manganese distance in the docked pose — restores the ranking: known nanomolar inhibitors place a hydroxamate oxygen 1.93–2.21 Å from manganese, non-chelating analogues place no oxygen closer than 6.5 Å. We predict CID 156252442 will inhibit KpLpxH at low-nanomolar potency comparable to JH-LPH-50, and CID 156252448 and CID 156252462 will be at least 10-fold weaker despite similar docking scores. One malachite-green assay can confirm or refute this. Any future virtual screen against LpxH — or any metalloenzyme — should carry a metal-geometry term alongside the docking score.

Direct InhA Inhibitors Dock 3.5–4.4 kcal/mol Better Than Free Isoniazid on Mycobacterium tuberculosis InhA: A Standardised Vina Benchmark at the INH–NAD Adduct Site

Tuberculosis killed an estimated 1.23 million people in 2024, and Pakistan — fifth among high-burden countries, with about 669,000 cases and 51,000 deaths — carries 6.3% of the global burden.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-05 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #1 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: InhA; isoniazid; KatG; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; tuberculosis; drug resistance; ChEMBL

Abstract

Tuberculosis killed an estimated 1.23 million people in 2024, and Pakistan — fifth among high-burden countries, with about 669,000 cases and 51,000 deaths — carries 6.3% of the global burden. Isoniazid, the cornerstone of TB chemotherapy, is a prodrug: it must be activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG into the INH–NAD adduct that inhibits the enoyl-ACP reductase InhA, and the KatG S315T mutation alone is found in 94% of isoniazid-resistant clinical isolates. Direct InhA inhibitors that need no KatG activation are therefore the rational bypass, but no standardised Vina benchmark for them on the adduct-bound structure existed. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 5 November 2026 (UniProtKB P9WGR1 → ChEMBL CHEMBL1849, 52 bioactivities → 26 ranked leads) and docked the top leads plus isoniazid with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 into InhA (PDB 4TRO, 1.40 Å) at the centroid of the co-crystallised INH–NAD adduct (ZID). The pipeline's first grid centre was the NAD cofactor centroid, 1.82 Å from the adduct centroid; all ligands were re-docked at the corrected centre and only the corrected numbers are reported. Two known direct inhibitors beat free isoniazid by 3.5–4.4 kcal/mol: CHEMBL3125235 scored −10.27 kcal/mol (ChEMBL IC50 2.0 nM) and CHEMBL3125270 −9.37 kcal/mol (IC50 4.0 nM), against −5.83 kcal/mol for isoniazid; a third, CHEMBL259138, scored −7.50 kcal/mol (Ki 1.0 nM). All three leads are PAINS-clean and already-published InhA actives, so this is a benchmark, not a discovery — and the margin over isoniazid is expected, because the free prodrug is not the active species; the adduct, not isoniazid, is the true comparator. The falsifiable next step is a direct InhA enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL3125235 against the INH–NAD adduct under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis remains the world's deadliest infectious disease. The World Health Organization's Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 records an estimated 10.7 million people falling ill with TB in 2024 and 1.23 million deaths; eight countries account for two-thirds of cases, and Pakistan ranks fifth, with an estimated 669,000 cases (6.3% of the global burden, incidence 266 per 100,000 population) and about 51,000 deaths. Roughly 75% of estimated cases were notified and treated, and Pakistan is listed among the high-burden countries for multidrug-resistant and rifampicin-resistant TB. Treatment success is reported at 95%, but the gap between estimated and notified cases — and the resistance burden — keeps new drugs a priority.

Isoniazid (INH) has been the cornerstone of TB chemotherapy for over seventy years. It is a prodrug: the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG (encoded by Rv1908c) activates it to a reactive isonicotinoyl species that reacts with NAD+ to form the INH–NAD adduct, which binds the active site of InhA, the NADH-dependent enoyl-ACP reductase of the FAS-II system, blocking mycolic-acid biosynthesis and killing the bacillus. The dominant resistance mechanism is loss of the activator: mutations in katG, above all S315T, are found in 94% of isoniazid-resistant clinical isolates, preventing prodrug activation. A second mechanism is mutation or overexpression of inhA itself (promoter c-15t), which titrates the drug. Because the activator, not the target, fails in most resistant isolates, the target itself remains druggable — a direct InhA inhibitor (DII) that binds InhA in its native state, without KatG activation, should retain activity against KatG-mutant strains. Recent work has pursued exactly this: triazolopyrimidine direct InhA inhibitors reported in 2026 bind with computed energies of −13.9 kcal/mol and outperform triclosan (−8.67 kcal/mol) in silico, with the explicit rationale of evading KatG-mediated resistance.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, fully automated docking pipeline benchmark known direct InhA inhibitors against isoniazid on the adduct-bound InhA structure, and can its automated grid-centre choice be trusted? The falsifiable hypothesis is that known potent direct InhA inhibitors, docked under an identical protocol, will score substantially better than free isoniazid on InhA (PDB 4TRO) — and that the margin must be read as a prodrug artefact, not as a discovery, unless it also beats the INH–NAD adduct itself.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 5 November 2026: the daily literature digest (2026-11-05), PubMed E-utilities and web search (verified references below), ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 for burden figures; the Microbiology Spectrum review of isoniazid and ethionamide resistance for the KatG S315T 94% figure and the adduct mechanism; Miesel et al. for the early genetic evidence; and a 2026 Research Square preprint on direct InhA inhibitors for the current DII rationale.

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline)

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 5 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target identification used the query "M. tuberculosis enoyl-ACP reductase (InhA)": UniProt P9WGR1, enoyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] reductase [NADH], gene inhA, Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv, 269 aa. The ChEMBL target was CHEMBL1849 (single-protein). Fifty-two bioactivities (pChEMBL ≥ 5) were retrieved; isoniazid was verified in PubChem and appears in the lead set as CHEMBL64 (SMILES NNC(=O)c1ccncc1, MW 137.14, logP −0.31). Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score (similarity ×40 + Lipinski ×20 + Veber ×10 + PAINS ×10 + tox ×20). The top five ranked leads were taken forward to docking. All five are known InhA actives with published ChEMBL potencies: isoniazid itself (Ki 0.75 nM, pChEMBL 9.12, as recorded in ChEMBL), CHEMBL3125235 (IC50 2.0 nM, pChEMBL 8.70), CHEMBL3125270 (IC50 4.0 nM, pChEMBL 8.40) and CHEMBL259138 (Ki 1.0 nM, pChEMBL 9.00). None of the three leads has a preferred name, an approval, or a development phase in ChEMBL; they are unnamed research compounds.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 5 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was M. tuberculosis InhA, PDB 4TRO (1.40 Å, "Structure of the enoyl-ACP reductase of Mycobacterium tuberculosis InhA, inhibited with the active metabolite of isoniazid"), with the grid centred on the centroid of its co-crystallised ligand ZID — isonicotinic-acetyl-nicotinamide-adenine dinucleotide, i.e. the INH–NAD adduct itself: [3.82, −33.34, 13.56]. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

One automated-pipeline error was caught and corrected before reporting, and is documented here because it is part of the result. The pipeline's automatic grid-centre picker takes the centroid of the first drug-like HETATM group in the PDB file. In 4TRO that group is the NAD cofactor (residue 301, 44 atoms), not the inhibitor; the centre it produced was [2.22, −32.75, 14.19]. The co-crystallised inhibitor ZID (residue 302, 52 atoms) sits 1.82 Å away at [3.82, −33.34, 13.56]. Because the INH–NAD adduct occupies the NAD-binding pocket, the two centroids nearly coincide, and the re-dock shifted scores by only 0.01–0.39 kcal/mol — but the correction matters in principle: on other structures the same default has landed 13–45 Å from the inhibitor site. All five ligands were re-docked at the ZID centroid with the same protocol, and only the corrected numbers are reported. The raw JSON of both runs is preserved (see Data availability), so the correction is auditable.

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all three leads and isoniazid were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were SR-MMP 0.564 for CHEMBL259138, SR-MMP 0.165 for CHEMBL3125270 and NR-AhR 0.135 for CHEMBL3125235. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and isoniazid itself carries a measured NR-AhR flag of 1.0 in the same panel, so a flag in this panel does not distinguish a lead from the reference drug.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed; a single crystal structure (4TRO, one conformation) was used; free isoniazid was docked, not the INH–NAD adduct, so the isoniazid number is a prodrug baseline, not a potency estimate; and the three leads are already-known InhA inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound InhA potency, ChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL3125235 IC50 2.0 nM −10.27 −10.27, −9.83, −9.51 clean
CHEMBL3125270 IC50 4.0 nM −9.37 −9.37, −9.35, −9.01 clean
CHEMBL259138 Ki 1.0 nM −7.50 −7.50, −7.37, −7.25 clean
Isoniazid (reference, free prodrug) Ki 0.75 nM (as recorded) −5.83 −5.83, −5.67, −5.58 clean
CHEMBL64 (= isoniazid, duplicate entry) Ki 0.75 nM −5.82 −5.82, −5.80, −5.36 clean

All docking on PDB 4TRO (M. tuberculosis InhA, 1.40 Å), grid centre [3.82, −33.34, 13.56] (ZID adduct centroid), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 5 November 2026. CHEMBL3125235: MW 514.59, logP 2.94, 1 Lipinski violation (MW > 500). CHEMBL3125270: MW 423.47, logP 1.71, Lipinski-clean. CHEMBL259138: MW 271.36, logP 4.70, Lipinski-clean.

The headline number needs its qualifier in the same breath: CHEMBL3125235 beats free isoniazid by 4.44 kcal/mol and CHEMBL3125270 by 3.54 kcal/mol, both far outside Vina's noise — but free isoniazid is not the active species, and its −5.83 kcal/mol is the score of a small prodrug that was never meant to bind InhA on its own. The meaningful comparison in this table is among the three direct inhibitors themselves: CHEMBL3125235 leads CHEMBL3125270 by 0.90 kcal/mol (inside noise) and CHEMBL259138 by 2.77 kcal/mol. Pose consistency is good across the set: the top two leads hold within 0.76 and 0.36 kcal/mol across all three poses, while isoniazid holds within 0.25 kcal/mol — consistency is not what separates them; the binding pocket's shape is. Note also that CHEMBL64 and the query isoniazid are the same molecule entered twice by the pipeline (similarity 1.0); their near-identical scores (−5.82 vs −5.83) are an accidental reproducibility check, not two independent measurements.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

Published direct-InhA docking exists for comparison: a 2026 study of triazolopyrimidine direct InhA inhibitors reported binding energies of −13.93 and −13.14 kcal/mol for its best compounds, against triclosan at −8.67 kcal/mol and ethambutol at −7.15 kcal/mol, using a different docking setup and a different InhA structure. Our Vina numbers are not directly comparable to those energies, and no published Vina score for any of our three leads on 4TRO was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for three known InhA actives on 4TRO (−10.27, −9.37, −7.50 kcal/mol, with full pose lists) are now on record for others to reproduce. The ordering is also consistent with the published potencies in direction but not in magnitude: CHEMBL259138 has the best recorded potency (Ki 1.0 nM) yet the worst docking score of the three (−7.50), a reminder that Vina ranks poses, not IC50s.

3.3 The standardisation problem

The grid-centre audit in §2.3 is the durable methodological finding. The pipeline's centre picker — first non-junk HETATM group — silently centred on the NAD cofactor in 4TRO. Here the error was only 1.82 Å, because the adduct occupies the cofactor pocket, and the re-dock moved scores by at most 0.39 kcal/mol. But the same default has previously centred grids on a cofactor 13.26 Å from the inhibitor site and on a glycan 45.24 Å away, in both cases producing publishable-looking numbers for the wrong pocket. The fix is cheap — verify the co-crystallised ligand's identity and centroid before docking — but it is not optional, and it must be applied per structure, because the distance between the first HETATM group and the true inhibitor site is not predictable from the file alone.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into two narrower contributions. First, a benchmark: three known direct InhA inhibitors dock at −7.50 to −10.27 kcal/mol on the adduct-bound structure under a standardised protocol, with pose consistency good enough to reproduce. Second, a caution: the 3.5–4.4 kcal/mol "win" over isoniazid is real as a docking number and meaningless as a drug comparison, because the comparator is a prodrug. The clinically relevant question is not whether a direct inhibitor out-docks free isoniazid — any molecule that actually binds the pocket will — but whether it out-binds the INH–NAD adduct in KatG-mutant strains, and whether it kills whole bacilli. Neither is answered by docking.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the comparator is wrong: the active species is the adduct, and docking the adduct itself (or a KatG-independent reference such as triclosan, published at −8.67 kcal/mol in another setup) is the honest baseline. Second, potency and docking score disagree within the lead set: CHEMBL259138, the most potent by recorded Ki (1.0 nM), scores worst (−7.50), while CHEMBL3125235, the best docker (−10.27), is the least potent by recorded IC50 (2.0 nM) — a 2-fold potency spread against a 2.77 kcal/mol score spread, in the wrong direction. Third, all three leads are already-known InhA actives; there is no new chemistry here, only a new comparison.

4.3 The PAINS/tox picture is clean but thin

No PAINS alerts is good, but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (SR-MMP 0.564 for CHEMBL259138) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either — least of all because the reference drug flags the same assay at 1.0.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3125235 inhibits recombinant InhA with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (2.0 nM) under identical assay conditions, and inhibits the KatG-independent enzyme directly, without activation.
  2. CHEMBL3125235 and CHEMBL3125270 retain whole-cell activity (MIC) against a KatG S315T mutant M. tuberculosis strain where isoniazid loses ≥32-fold potency — the direct-inhibitor prediction that docking alone cannot test.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ZID adduct into 4TRO reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant InhA enzyme inhibition assay (NADH oxidation readout) for CHEMBL3125235, CHEMBL3125270 and the INH–NAD adduct as control, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): whole-cell MIC against H37Rv and a KatG S315T mutant strain, isoniazid as control, with the pre-registered prediction that the leads lose <4-fold potency where isoniazid loses ≥32-fold. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): cytotoxicity (Vero/THP-1) for any compound that clears Stage 2, with a selectivity index (CC50/MIC) > 10 required to proceed. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all three leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The isoniazid comparator is the free prodrug, not the INH–NAD adduct — the 3.5–4.4 kcal/mol margin is a prodrug artefact, not a potency claim. 3. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the 0.90 kcal/mol gap between the top two leads is not significant. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of ZID was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (4TRO, one InhA conformation) was used; InhA's substrate-binding loop is flexible and induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. All three leads are already-known InhA inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 7. No whole-cell, resistance-strain, or Pakistani-market data are presented; the Pakistan burden figures are contextual, not part of the result. 8. The pipeline's automated grid-centre selection failed silently and required manual correction — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited.

6. Conclusion

Three known direct InhA inhibitors dock at −7.50 to −10.27 kcal/mol on the adduct-bound InhA structure (PDB 4TRO), beating free isoniazid (−5.83 kcal/mol) by 1.7–4.4 kcal/mol — a margin that is real as docking and meaningless as a drug comparison, because isoniazid is a prodrug and the adduct is the true comparator. The durable findings are the benchmark values themselves and the grid-centre audit: the pipeline centred on the NAD cofactor, 1.82 Å from the adduct site, and only a manual check caught it. The next experiment is a head-to-head InhA enzyme assay against the adduct, then MIC testing on a KatG S315T strain — not more docking.

Epalrestat Outscores Thymoquinone by 1.5 kcal/mol on Aldose Reductase at the True Inhibitor Site: A Grid-Centre Audit Refutes the Docking Lead

Standardised AutoDock Vina docking reported thymoquinone (TQ), the marker quinone of Nigella sativa, outscoring the aldose-reductase reference drug epalrestat (−7.27 vs −6.48 kcal/mol).

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 4 November 2026 · Paper #1 v2 — Health track (Daily Research Papers; resubmission of the paper rejected by ChemRxiv on 3 November 2026)

Keywords: thymoquinone; aldose reductase; molecular docking; grid centre; re-docking; PAINS; Nigella sativa; diabetic complications

Abstract

Standardised AutoDock Vina docking reported thymoquinone (TQ), the marker quinone of Nigella sativa, outscoring the aldose-reductase reference drug epalrestat (−7.27 vs −6.48 kcal/mol). We re-tested that lead with new computation: an exhaustiveness-16 repeat, RDKit ADMET, a grid-centre audit of all five screened targets, and re-docking validation against the crystallographic inhibitor. The exhaustiveness-16 repeat confirmed the lead in the original box (TQ −7.25 vs epalrestat −6.47 kcal/mol), but the audit showed the aldose-reductase grid was centred on the NADP+ cofactor centroid, 13.26 Å from the co-crystallised inhibitor IDD594, with the crystal pose mostly outside the 22.5 Å box. Re-docking the inhibitor at that centre failed (RMSD 17.0 Å; 16.4 Å after correcting the atom mapping). Re-centring on the inhibitor centroid, re-docking passed (RMSD 1.16 Å, no superposition; 1.29 Å Kabsch-aligned; ≤2 Å criterion), and at the true inhibitor site epalrestat outscores TQ by 1.45 kcal/mol at exhaustiveness 8 (−9.08 vs −7.63) and 1.56 kcal/mol at exhaustiveness 16 (−9.22 vs −7.65). The docking lead is therefore refuted, not confirmed. The audit found the same centre error in two more targets: the DPP-4 grid was a glycan sugar 45.24 Å from the inhibitor (corrected re-dock: TQ −6.88 vs sitagliptin −9.05), and the PTP1B and α-amylase rows are withdrawn — 9C66 is a MENA EVH1-domain structure with no PTP1B catalytic domain, and 5U3A is an apo structure centred on an N-terminal residue. Only the PPAR-γ centre was correct (TQ −6.47 vs pioglitazone −8.98). TQ is Lipinski-clean (MW 164.2, logP 1.67, 0 violations) but remains PAINS-positive (quinone_A(370)). The falsifiable next step is an in-vitro aldose-reductase assay with the corrected expectation — TQ does not outscore epalrestat at the true site — plus HPLC standardisation of Pakistani-market kalonji oils, where TQ content varies ~260-fold.

1. Introduction

Pakistan carries one of the world's heaviest diabetes burdens: roughly 34.5 million adults live with diabetes, a prevalence near 30.8%, with an estimated 9.3 million cases undiagnosed. Diabetic complications — neuropathy, retinopathy, nephropathy and cataract — rather than hyperglycaemia itself, account for most of the morbidity.

Nigella sativa (kalonji, black seed) is among the most widely used traditional adjuncts for diabetes in Pakistan. Its marker compound thymoquinone (2-isopropyl-5-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone; TQ) has reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and a substantial in-vitro literature claims activity against a striking range of targets. Yet the clinical literature is contradictory: meta-analyses of randomised trials report only a modest HbA1c reduction of ~−0.54%, with very high heterogeneity (I² 94–99%) and low certainty. Two under-examined confounders may explain the contradiction. First, product quality: a Swiss HPLC screening of commercial N. sativa products found TQ content ranging from 3.08 to 809.4 mg/100 g — a ~260-fold range — and a Malaysian survey found 0.07–1.88% TQ; most trials neither standardised nor even assayed TQ content. Second, chemistry: TQ is a quinone, a classic PAINS scaffold whose redox-cycling and Michael-acceptor reactivity can produce apparent activity against many targets in vitro without specific pharmacology.

Our first version of this paper (submitted to ChemRxiv, rejected 3 November 2026 as a proposed framework without new research data) reported a standardised computational screen of TQ against five diabetes-related targets and found one lead: TQ outscored epalrestat on aldose reductase (AR), the rate-limiting enzyme of the polyol pathway. This revision presents the new research data ChemRxiv asked for — an exhaustiveness-16 repeat, a full ADMET profile, interaction analysis, and, decisively, a grid-centre audit with re-docking validation — and the new data overturn the lead. The paper's result is now a correction, not a claim: at the crystallographic inhibitor site, epalrestat beats TQ by ~1.5 kcal/mol, and two of the five screen rows were never valid at all. We report the correction in full because a docking pipeline that can silently centre its grid on a cofactor, a glycan, or a protein's own N-terminus will produce confident-looking numbers for the wrong pocket — and the only defence is to audit the centre and re-dock the crystal ligand.

2. Methods

2.1 Molecular docking

Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 with the LeadForge pipeline protocol: for each target, TQ and the reference drug were docked into the same binding site with the same protocol (same PDB structure, same grid centre, same exhaustiveness, box 22.5 Å, 3 poses per ligand). Structures were retrieved from the RCSB Protein Data Bank. Affinities are reported as the best of three poses (kcal/mol); all three poses are reported in the tables. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone. The original screen (20 October 2026) used exhaustiveness 8; this revision repeats the aldose-reductase comparison at exhaustiveness 16 with the identical centre, box and receptor.

2.2 ADMET and PAINS screen

TQ was profiled with RDKit 2026.03.6 (Crippen logP, TPSA, Lipinski and Veber drug-likeness) and screened with the RDKit FilterCatalog PAINS set (Baell & Holloway, 2010); matching filter names are reported verbatim.

2.3 Grid-centre audit

For each screened target, the recorded grid centre was compared against the centroids of every non-water HETATM group in the PDB file, in file order, and against the centroid of the co-crystallised inhibitor where one exists. The audit reproduces the centre-selection logic of the docking pipeline (dock.py _ligand_center), which picks the first non-junk HETATM group in file order; the junk list excludes waters, ions and cryo additives but not glycans, modified protein residues, or cofactors. A centre was judged correct only if it coincided with the co-crystallised inhibitor's centroid.

2.4 Re-docking validation

The co-crystallised AR inhibitor IDD594 (residue LDT, chain A, seqnum 320; 24 heavy atoms) was re-docked into 1US0 at the original centre and at the corrected centre (the crystal LDT centroid), exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses. The ligand SMILES were derived from the RCSB CCD entry for LDT and verified against the CCD formula (C16H12BrF2NO3S) and element sequence. RMSD was computed on heavy atoms only, in the common receptor frame with no superposition as the primary metric, with Kabsch-aligned RMSD also reported. The standard success criterion is RMSD ≤2 Å for the best pose. Atom correspondence was established by graph isomorphism, with the substructure-match tuple inverted on both sides (a mapping error in the first calculation was caught by an element-consistency check and corrected; the corrected-mapping values are reported here).

2.5 Interaction analysis

Best pose (pose 1) of each ligand was analysed against the prepared 1US0 receptor (ATOM records only; NADP+ cofactor and waters excluded). Hydrogen bonds are geometric candidates only: donor–acceptor distance ≤3.5 Å, no angle criterion (PDBQT carries no angle information). Close contacts are any ligand heavy atom to any receptor heavy atom ≤4.0 Å. Contacts are reported as observed contacts in the docked poses, not as established binding modes.

2.6 Honesty limits

This is a computational study. No wet-lab data are presented. No clinical claim is made. Docking affinity is not enzyme inhibition, and a docking score is not evidence of efficacy. Where a result is withdrawn in this revision, the withdrawal is stated in the Results, not hidden.

3. Results

3.1 The exhaustiveness-16 repeat confirms the lead — in the original box

Ligand Exhaustiveness 8, original (20 Oct 2026) Exhaustiveness 8, v2 rerun Exhaustiveness 16, v2
Thymoquinone −7.27 / −7.24 / −7.15 −7.269 / −7.211 / −7.063 −7.245 / −7.204 / −7.078
Epalrestat (ref) −6.48 / −6.38 / −5.98 −6.753 / −6.736 / −5.916 −6.474 / −6.084 / −5.899
Margin (TQ − epalrestat, best) −0.79 −0.52 −0.77

At higher exhaustiveness the lead survived with the same direction and a similar margin (−0.77 kcal/mol). Every TQ pose still beat every epalrestat pose. The margin remains inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so even in the original box this was a lead, not a confirmed win. The repeat rules out a sampling artefact; it does not rule out a site artefact — which is what the audit then found.

3.2 The grid centre was the NADP+ cofactor, not the inhibitor site

Item Value
Grid centre used (original protocol) [21.26, −6.13, 27.39]
NADP+ cofactor (NDP) centroid [21.26, −6.13, 27.39] — identical
Co-crystallised inhibitor IDD594 (LDT) centroid [16.47, −7.21, 15.08]
Distance, grid centre to inhibitor centroid 13.26 Å
Crystal inhibitor pose, z-range 9.7–19.0 Å; box z-range 16.14–38.64 Å — pose mostly outside the box

The centre-selection code picks the first non-junk HETATM group in file order. In 1US0 that group is NDP, the NADP+ cofactor — not the inhibitor LDT. The crystal inhibitor pose sits ~13 Å away, mostly outside the 22.5 Å box. Every TQ and epalrestat pose in the original screen was therefore docked into a cofactor-centred box, not the crystallographic inhibitor site. The receptor preparation compounds the problem: it keeps ATOM records only, so NADP+ is excluded from the receptor even though the AR inhibitor pocket is NADP+-adjacent in the crystal — docked poses may occupy space the cofactor would clash with in reality.

3.3 Re-docking fails at the original centre and passes at the corrected centre

Centre Re-docked ligand Best-pose affinity (kcal/mol) RMSD, no superposition (Å) RMSD, Kabsch-aligned (Å) Verdict (≤2 Å)
Original [21.26, −6.13, 27.39] IDD594 (LDT) −7.943 17.00 (16.42 after mapping correction) 5.02 (3.89) FAIL
Corrected [16.47, −7.21, 15.08] IDD594 (LDT) −9.192 1.16 1.29 PASS

At the original centre the re-docked inhibitor lands ~15 Å from its crystal pose (bromine atom: crystal (14.88, −3.75, 9.69) vs docked pose 1 (19.13, −4.58, 24.37)). At the corrected centre — the crystal LDT centroid — the best pose reproduces the crystallographic binding mode within 1.16 Å. The protocol is therefore validated at the corrected centre and unvalidated at the original one. The RMSD failure is a protocol-centre artefact, not a failure of Vina itself.

3.4 At the true inhibitor site, epalrestat beats thymoquinone by ~1.5 kcal/mol

Ligand Exhaustiveness 8, corrected centre Exhaustiveness 16, corrected centre
Thymoquinone −7.626 / −7.044 / −6.621 −7.652 / −7.054 / −6.935
Epalrestat (ref) −9.080 / −8.679 / −8.576 −9.215 / −9.176 / −8.560
Margin (TQ − epalrestat, best) +1.45 +1.56

The margin flips sign and exceeds the noise band at both exhaustiveness levels: epalrestat outscores TQ by 1.45 kcal/mol at exhaustiveness 8 and 1.56 kcal/mol at exhaustiveness 16. The v1 lead does not survive re-centring. TQ's corrected-centre score (−7.63/−7.65) is close to its original-box score (−7.27/−7.25); what changed is epalrestat, which scores −9.08/−9.22 at the true site against −6.48/−6.47 in the cofactor-centred box. The original comparison flattered TQ by docking the reference drug into the wrong pocket.

3.5 Audit of the other four targets: one correct, one corrected, two withdrawn

Target PDB Recorded centre was Distance to inhibitor Corrected-centre result Status
DPP-4 4A5S NAG C 1, a glycan sugar 45.24 Å TQ −6.884 / −6.283 / −6.145; sitagliptin −9.049 / −8.794 / −8.749 Corrected; TQ still loses (by 2.17 kcal/mol)
PPAR-γ 9F7W Co-crystallised ligand 2OH (bisphenol A) 0.29 Å Not re-docked; centre correct Stands: TQ −6.47 vs pioglitazone −8.98
PTP1B 9C66 CSO A 7, a modified cysteine of MENA EVH1 — Not possible Withdrawn — 9C66 is a MENA EVH1-domain structure, not a PTP1B catalytic domain; it contains no PTP1B inhibitor site
Pancreatic α-amylase 5U3A PCA A 1, the protein's N-terminal pyroglutamic acid — Not possible Withdrawn — 5U3A is an apo structure with no inhibitor; the centre was the protein's own N-terminus

Three of the five original centres were wrong, and the root cause is the same in each case: the centre picker takes the first non-junk HETATM group, and the junk list does not cover glycans (NAG), modified protein residues (CSO, PCA), or cofactors (NDP). The DPP-4 correction strengthens the v1 conclusion for that target (TQ loses by more, 2.17 kcal/mol, at the true site). The PPAR-γ result stands because its centre was the co-crystallised ligand. The PTP1B and α-amylase rows are withdrawn outright: no valid docking comparison existed for those targets in this study, and no corrected re-dock is possible in those PDB entries.

3.6 ADMET: Lipinski-clean, PAINS-positive

Property Thymoquinone
Formula / MW C10H12O2 / 164.2 (exact 164.0837)
logP (Crippen) 1.67
H-bond donors / acceptors 0 / 2
TPSA 34.14 Å²
Rotatable bonds 1
Lipinski violations / Veber 0 / pass
PAINS Positive — quinone_A(370), 1 matching filter

TQ passes Lipinski and Veber with zero violations, which is why it looks like a clean lead on paper. The PAINS alert is the counterweight: as a quinone, TQ redox-cycles and can react with proteins as a Michael acceptor, which predicts exactly the published picture of apparent activity against many unrelated targets in vitro. Any in-vitro "hit" for TQ must be treated as guilty until proven innocent, with redox controls in the assay design.

3.7 Interactions at the corrected centre (observed contacts only)

Ligand H-bonds ≤3.5 Å (geometric candidates) Close-contact residues ≤4.0 Å (n)
Thymoquinone 1 — ALA299:N, 3.42 Å 10 — ALA299, PHE115, TRP111, LEU300, PHE122, CYS303, TRP79, TYR309, CYS80, CYS298
Epalrestat 2 — TRP20:NE1, 3.43 Å and 3.04 Å 10 — TRP20, TRP111, PHE122, CYS303, THR113, PHE115, TYR309, LEU300, TRP79, TRP219
Shared — 7 — CYS303, LEU300, PHE115, PHE122, TRP111, TRP79, TYR309

At the true site, neither ligand contacts the classic catalytic residues TYR48 or HIS110; both sit in the specificity-pocket region (LEU300, CYS303, PHE122, TRP111). These are observed contacts in the docked poses, not established binding modes — the poses are validated only in the sense that the re-docked crystal ligand reproduces its pose (RMSD 1.16 Å); no per-ligand pose validation exists. For the record, the original-box interaction analysis gave TQ 2 H-bonds (LYS77:NZ 3.37 Å, SER210:N 3.31 Å) and epalrestat 0 H-bonds, with 5 shared contact residues (CYS298, GLN183, TRP20, TYR209, TYR48) — those contacts describe the cofactor-centred box and are superseded by the corrected-centre analysis above.

3.8 The standardisation problem survives the correction

Commercial TQ content varies ~260-fold (3.08–809.4 mg/100 g; Malaysian survey 0.07–1.88%). Two capsules labelled identically can therefore deliver pharmacologically trivial or substantial TQ. No published study has characterised TQ content in Pakistani-market kalonji oils. This finding is independent of the docking correction: whatever TQ does or does not do at aldose reductase, any trial that does not assay TQ content is, in effect, testing an unknown dose.

4. Discussion

4.1 The lead was a centre artefact

The exhaustiveness-16 repeat shows the original result was reproducible; the audit shows it was reproducibly wrong. A docking score is a statement about a specific box, and the box was centred on the NADP+ cofactor. The reference drug suffered more from the mis-centring than TQ did, which is why the comparison flipped. The lesson is narrow and general at once: reproducibility across exhaustiveness does not validate a docking comparison — only a centre audit and a re-docking test do. Any pipeline that selects its grid centre automatically from HETATM order should audit the centre against the co-crystallised ligand before any score is believed.

4.2 Two screen rows were never valid

The PTP1B and α-amylase withdrawals are the more serious finding. 9C66 is not a PTP1B structure at all — it is the MENA EVH1 domain bound to a polyproline segment of PTP1B — and 5U3A is an apo amylase with no inhibitor to centre on. Docking a ligand into those entries and reporting the numbers as target comparisons was an error, and this revision withdraws both rows rather than re-interpreting them. The DPP-4 correction shows the constructive side of the same audit: at the true site TQ loses by more (2.17 kcal/mol), so the v1 conclusion for DPP-4 is strengthened, not weakened.

4.3 What survives

Three things survive the correction. First, the standardisation problem: the ~260-fold market variance in TQ content is a real, literature-backed confounder for every black-seed trial, and characterising Pakistani-market oils by HPLC remains a publishable Pharm-D-level finding on its own. Second, the PAINS constraint: TQ's quinone alert means any future assay must include redox and detergent controls, and an effect that vanishes under those controls is an artefact worth reporting. Third, the assay question itself, reframed: the enzyme assay no longer tests whether TQ beats epalrestat — it tests whether TQ inhibits aldose reductase at all at a plausible concentration, with epalrestat as the positive control and the corrected docking as the (negative) prior.

4.4 Why this paper is worth publishing as a correction

A negative result that overturns the author's own lead, with the mechanism of the error identified and the corrected numbers reported, is more useful than the original claim would have been. The centre-selection bug — first non-junk HETATM group, with glycans, modified residues and cofactors not treated as junk — is a failure mode any automated docking pipeline can hit, and the audit procedure in §2.3 is cheap enough to run on every structure before docking begins.

5. Future work

One short programme, in order: (1) HPLC standardisation of ten Pakistani-market kalonji oils against a TQ reference standard, reporting the range and the fraction below any plausible active threshold; (2) an in-vitro aldose-reductase inhibition assay (IC50) of the standardised samples plus a TQ reference standard, with epalrestat as the positive control, replicates, and redox controls (catalase, DTT) — confirmation is reproducible inhibition in a plausible range surviving redox controls, refutation is no inhibition or an effect abolished by redox controls; (3) re-docking of TQ and epalrestat with the NADP+ cofactor retained in the receptor, to test whether the corrected-centre margin survives a cofactor-aware preparation. No clinical claim and no trial design follow from this paper.

6. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The corrected-centre margin (1.45–1.56 kcal/mol) is at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; it is a reversal of direction, not a precise potency estimate. 3. The receptor preparation excludes NADP+ and waters, so corrected-centre poses may occupy space the cofactor would clash with in reality; a cofactor-aware re-dock is the required check (§5). 4. The re-docking validation covers 1US0 only; the DPP-4 corrected re-dock was run without a crystal-ligand re-dock of N7F, so its poses are unvalidated. 5. The PTP1B and α-amylase targets were not re-screened against valid structures in this revision; their rows are withdrawn, not replaced. 6. The literature synthesis rests on the 36-source review of 20 October 2026 and inherits its limits, including the low certainty of the clinical meta-analyses. 7. No Pakistani-market TQ data exist yet — the HPLC step is itself an untested premise.

7. Conclusion

New computation overturns our own lead. Thymoquinone does not outscore epalrestat on aldose reductase: at the crystallographic inhibitor site, validated by a re-dock that reproduces the crystal pose within 1.16 Å, epalrestat wins by 1.45–1.56 kcal/mol. The original lead was an artefact of a grid centred on the NADP+ cofactor, and the same audit withdrew two further screen rows and corrected a third. What remains is a cleaner question — does standardised TQ inhibit aldose reductase at all? — and a cheaper defence for every docking pipeline: audit the centre, re-dock the crystal ligand, and only then believe the score.
