The parent contacts the key AR residues — the catalytic Tyr48, His110, Trp111 and the specificity-pocket Cys298 — and shares 12 contact residues with epalrestat, while adding 7 of its own (ASN160, GLN183, HIS110, ILE260, TRP111, TRP79, VAL47). Its C-glycoside sugar moiety (12 heavy atoms) contacts 10 residues, including TYR48 (3.30 Å), TRP20 (3.40 Å), TRP111 (3.60 Å), VAL47 (3.61 Å) and SER210 (3.27 Å) — consistent with the sugar-occupies-the-sugar-pocket rationale, and no more than consistent. Neither ligand forms a geometric hydrogen bond in these poses. Two caveats: (i) these are observed contacts in original-box poses, not established binding modes, and the box is the wrong one (§3.3); (ii) one close contact in each ligand's list (1.80–1.82 Å) is to an unidentified heteroatom residue (UNK1) in the prepared receptor, which is not interpreted here. Corrected-centre pose files for the parent and all five analogs exist (v2c_pose_analog_*_1us0.pdbqt), but the contact analysis in this section was not repeated on them — that is a defined next step in §5, not a result claimed here.

3.7 ADMET: the analogs are clean; the reference drug is not

All five analogs and the parent are PAINS-clean with zero Lipinski violations (MW 392–453, logP 2.77–4.26, TPSA 49.7–69.9 Å²). Epalrestat, the reference drug, is itself PAINS-positive — rhodanine filter ene_rhod_A(235) — a fact worth stating plainly: the drug these molecules are compared against carries the same class of assay-interference alert that is held against thymoquinone (quinone_A(370)). That does not make epalrestat a bad control; it makes PAINS a property to design around in the assay, not a verdict on a molecule.

3.8 The novelty statement, precisely bounded

To our knowledge, no published paper reports dual aldose-reductase/SGLT2 activity for any molecule, and no trial has combined the two classes. That statement still holds — and this paper now makes the claim in a validated form on both sides: five SGLT2 analogs beat the AR reference drug at the crystallographic inhibitor site, with a passed re-docking validation behind the comparison, and the same five analogs beat the SGLT2 reference drug at the corrected empagliflozin site, with a passed re-docking validation behind that comparison too. This paper's contribution is therefore: five analogs with clean ADMET and control-beating corrected-centre scores on both targets, corrected controls on both targets, a passed re-docking validation on both targets, and the exact assay that would test the claim in vitro.

4. Discussion

4.1 What survives the correction

The analogs themselves survive: five novel molecules, designed against SGLT2, with measured-parent potency behind them (CHEMBL5288495, SGLT2 IC50 0.35 nM), clean ADMET, and corrected-centre AR scores from −10.09 to −10.73 kcal/mol. And now the comparison survives too: epalrestat at −9.07 is the right control value, and every analog beats it by 1.02–1.66 kcal/mol at the validated site, with all three poses of every analog beating the reference. The honest status of the dual-activity claim is therefore "validated on both sides, within the noise caveat, and awaiting an assay" — and the paper's value is in having checked the centre before a reader did, and in reporting the corrected result rather than the flattering original-box one. On the SGLT2 side the corrected numbers are stronger in absolute terms than v1's (−10.74 to −11.99 against dapagliflozin −9.96/−10.11, versus −7.03 against −4.79), but the margins over the control are smaller (0.63–1.98 kcal/mol) — because the old box flattered the comparison by scoring the reference drug ~5 kcal/mol too weak.

4.2 The polyol escape-route hypothesis, and the counterpoint

The mechanism reported by Azizogli et al. — SGLT2 inhibition → increased downstream SGLT1 glucose transport → aldose-reductase gene activation → sorbitol/fructose → uric acid, oxidative stress, cytokine inflammation, tubular damage — predicts a measurable consequence: markers of polyol flux (erythrocyte sorbitol, urinary fructose, AR expression) should rise, not fall, in some patients after SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, and that rise should track residual renal risk. If confirmed, it explains part of the residual risk on SGLT2 therapy and identifies the patients in whom adding AR inhibition should help most. If refuted, the hypothesis dies cleanly and cheaply. The counterpoint must not be hidden: in the ARISE-HF trial (AT-001, n = 691, 15 months, JACC 2024), which missed its primary endpoint (peak VO2), the only benefit signal appeared in a prespecified subgroup of patients not receiving SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs at baseline (+0.62 mL/kg/min peak VO2, p = .04; interaction p = .10). Read plainly, that subgroup result cuts against the combination: AR inhibition seemed to help precisely where SGLT2 inhibition was absent. Three readings are possible — (i) the subgroup is noise (interaction not significant), (ii) SGLT2 therapy already captures the benefit AR inhibition would add, or (iii) the combination was never actually tested. Only a trial that randomises the combination can distinguish them, and no such trial exists. This paper proposes that trial; it does not assume its outcome — and it does not propose it until the in-vitro assay in §5 confirms the docking signal, which now stands validated on both sides (§3.1, §3.5).

4.3 Why this matters in Pakistan specifically

Pakistan carries ~34.5 million adults with diabetes (~30.8% prevalence), and SGLT2 inhibitors are increasingly prescribed while AR inhibitors are essentially absent from practice. If the escape-route mechanism holds, the cheapest second step is not a new patented drug but the pairing of an existing SGLT2 inhibitor with a low-cost AR inhibitor — and the dual-activity signal for CHEMBL5288495 suggests the field should also look for single molecules that do both jobs, starting with the analogs already designed in our pipeline. That case is now explicitly conditional on the in-vitro assay in §5.

5. Future work

One short programme, in order: (1) corrected-centre 7VSI ligand docking — done in this revision (v2d/v2e, §3.5; parent and all five analogs beat dapagliflozin on best poses at exhaustiveness 8 and 16). What remains of this step: a cofactor-aware AR re-dock with the NADP+ cofactor retained in the receptor, to test whether the 1.02–1.66 kcal/mol analog margins survive a receptor that includes the cofactor, plus interaction analysis on the corrected-centre AR poses that already exist; (2) an in-vitro AR inhibition assay (IC50) of the best analogs with epalrestat as control, plus redox controls — all five analogs already beat epalrestat's corrected-centre score by more than 1 kcal/mol, so the assay is the immediate next step, gated only by the noise reading in §3.1 — and, in parallel, an in-vitro SGLT2 inhibition assay of the best analogs with dapagliflozin as control, since the SGLT2-side margins (0.63–1.98 kcal/mol) carry the same noise caveat; (3) a randomised combination-trial design (SGLT2 inhibitor + AR inhibitor versus SGLT2 inhibitor alone, residual albuminuria or neuropathy despite SGLT2 therapy, polyol-flux markers as the mechanistic readout) — drafted, not launched, until step 2 confirms the docking. No clinical claim follows from this paper.

6. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The analogs' AR scores are now corrected-centre scores at a validated site, but their margins over epalrestat (1.02–1.66 kcal/mol) sit at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the AR-side signal still needs an in-vitro assay before any inhibition claim is made. 3. The receptor preparation excludes NADP+ and waters, so all 1US0 poses may occupy space the cofactor would clash with in reality. 4. The SGLT2-side scores are now corrected-centre scores (§3.5), but their margins over dapagliflozin (0.63–1.98 kcal/mol on best poses) sit at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the parent's margin (0.63–0.78) is inside noise; only two analogs hold the win across all three poses at exhaustiveness 16. 5. Dapagliflozin scored −7.23 in the analogs run versus −4.84/−4.79 in two other runs, all in the mis-centred box — Vina run-to-run variability is real; only within-run comparisons are used, and at the corrected centre the control is −9.96 kcal/mol (exhaustiveness 8, single Vina mode) and −10.11 kcal/mol (exhaustiveness 16, three poses), agreeing within 0.15 kcal/mol. The exhaustiveness-16 third pose (−0.15) is effectively non-binding; only best-pose comparisons are used. 6. A large ligand can score highly from contact count alone — the parent's 19 contacts and the analogs' size mean pose inspection and dynamics are required before any score is trusted. 7. The SGLT2→AR activation mechanism rests on a single review's report; it needs direct experimental confirmation. 8. Epalrestat's corrected-centre score at exhaustiveness 16 (−9.22) comes from the companion revision's control run (Paper #1 v2), not from a run inside this paper's own pipeline; the exhaustiveness-8 value (−9.07) is from this paper's own corrected-centre run, and the exhaustiveness-16 value should be re-run alongside the analogs in step 1 of §5. 9. No Pakistani-market or population-specific data are presented.

7. Conclusion

Five novel SGLT2 analogs dock to aldose reductase at −10.09 to −10.73 kcal/mol at the crystallographic inhibitor site — and the reference drug they are compared against scores −9.07 kcal/mol at the same site, not the −6.48 kcal/mol of the original, mis-centred box. Every analog beats epalrestat by 1.02–1.66 kcal/mol, with all three poses of every analog beating the reference; the parent beats it by 0.75 kcal/mol, inside Vina noise. Thymoquinone still loses (−7.61). On the SGLT2 side the same correction now holds: at the empagliflozin centroid the parent scores −10.74 kcal/mol and the analogs −10.80 to −11.99 kcal/mol, against dapagliflozin −9.96/−10.11 kcal/mol — margins of 0.63–1.98 kcal/mol, again at the edge of Vina noise, and thymoquinone loses by ~3 kcal/mol. The dual claim is therefore validated at the corrected centre on both sides, within the noise caveat; what must follow is the in-vitro assay in §5. If the assay confirms the analogs, the cheapest path to closing residual diabetic risk may already be sitting in the SGLT2 pipeline; if it refutes them, the field learns that a −10.73 Vina score can mislead. Either answer is worth having, and this paper exists so the question is asked correctly.

Celecoxib Still Leads: A Dual-Isoform Vina Benchmark of Five COX-2 Inhibitors Shows Docking Selectivity Does Not Track Measured Selectivity

Selective COX-2 inhibition was designed to relieve pain without the gastrointestinal injury of non-selective NSAIDs, but the class carries a cardiovascular question mark ever since rofecoxib was withdrawn in 2004.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-04 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #6 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: COX-2; celecoxib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; selectivity; NSAID; cardiovascular risk; prostaglandin

Abstract

Selective COX-2 inhibition was designed to relieve pain without the gastrointestinal injury of non-selective NSAIDs, but the class carries a cardiovascular question mark ever since rofecoxib was withdrawn in 2004. The PRECISION trial (24,081 patients) later showed celecoxib non-inferior to ibuprofen and naproxen for cardiovascular events (primary outcome 2.3% vs 2.7% vs 2.5%), yet the search for a more selective coxib continues. We asked whether standardised docking could rank five known potent COX-2 inhibitors against celecoxib on both isoforms, and whether docking selectivity tracks measured selectivity. Compounds came from ChEMBL bioactivities against human COX-2 (CHEMBL230), were screened with RDKit (Lipinski/Veber/PAINS) and a Tox21 kNN panel, and were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 into COX-2 (PDB 3LN1, 2.4 Å) and COX-1 (PDB 3KK6, 2.75 Å) at the co-crystallised celecoxib centroids, under an identical protocol. Celecoxib scored best on COX-2 (−12.28 kcal/mol); the closest lead, CHEMBL282093, scored −12.13 kcal/mol, within noise. Docking selectivity (COX-1 minus COX-2 affinity) ranged 0.47–2.17 kcal/mol and did not track measured selectivity: CHEMBL432945, measured only 5-fold selective (COX-2 IC50 1.0 nM vs COX-1 5.0 nM), had the second-best docking selectivity (2.00 kcal/mol), while CHEMBL186632, measured ~8,700-fold selective (0.44 nM vs 3,828 nM), had the worst (0.47 kcal/mol). The falsifiable next step is a paired COX-1/COX-2 enzyme inhibition assay for CHEMBL282093 and CHEMBL432945 under identical conditions: if docking selectivity predicted the ranking, CHEMBL432945 would out-select CHEMBL282093; the measured data already predict the opposite, and the assay would settle which signal to trust.

1. Introduction

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) relieve pain by blocking cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes and prostaglandin synthesis, but blocking the constitutive isoform COX-1 injures the gastric mucosa, while blocking the inducible isoform COX-2 drives the anti-inflammatory effect. The coxibs were designed to exploit a single structural difference: at position 523, COX-1 carries a bulky isoleucine and COX-2 a smaller valine, opening a side pocket (lined by His90, Gln192, Leu352, Ser353, Tyr355, Arg513, Ala516, Phe518 and Val523) that the sulfonamide group of celecoxib occupies. Celecoxib — 4-[5-(4-methylphenyl)-3-(trifluoromethyl)-1H-pyrazol-1-yl]benzenesulfonamide (SC-58635) — was the first-in-class selective COX-2 inhibitor, identified by Penning et al. in 1997, and remains the only coxib on the market in most countries after rofecoxib (Vioxx) was withdrawn in 2004 for increased myocardial infarction and stroke.

The cardiovascular question was settled, as far as a trial can settle it, by PRECISION: 24,081 osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis patients randomised to celecoxib 100–200 mg twice daily, ibuprofen 600–800 mg three times daily, or naproxen 375–500 mg twice daily. The primary composite outcome (cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or non-fatal stroke) occurred in 2.3% of the celecoxib group, 2.5% of naproxen and 2.7% of ibuprofen (hazard ratio 0.93 vs naproxen and 0.85 vs ibuprofen, p < 0.001 for non-inferiority in both comparisons), while gastrointestinal events were 54% higher with ibuprofen and 41% higher with naproxen than with celecoxib. Celecoxib is therefore non-inferior on the heart and better on the gut — but a more selective coxib could, in principle, widen both margins, and the field still lacks a cheap computational screen that ranks selectivity correctly.

The hypothesis of this paper is that a standardised dual-isoform Vina docking protocol can rank COX-2 inhibitors by selectivity, with the docking selectivity (COX-1 minus COX-2 affinity) tracking the measured IC50 ratio. The paper tests that hypothesis against five known potent COX-2 inhibitors and reports the answer, which is negative.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 4 November 2026: the daily literature digest (2026-11-04), PubMed E-utilities (verified PMIDs below), and ChEMBL (EBI). Key sources: Nissen et al. (PRECISION) for the cardiovascular numbers; Penning et al. for celecoxib's identification; Bello-Vargas et al. for the COX-1/COX-2 cavity comparison and the 3LN1/3KK6 crystal selection; the RCSB PDB entries for the two structures.

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline)

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 4 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target identification used the gene query "PTGS2" (UniProt P35354, prostaglandin G/H synthase 2, human, 604 aa); the ChEMBL target was CHEMBL230 (single-protein, human). Thirty-nine bioactivities (pChEMBL ≥ 5) were retrieved; celecoxib was verified in PubChem (CID 2662). Twenty-five compounds passed the similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score. The top five distinct leads were taken forward; the rank-2 entry, CHEMBL118, is celecoxib itself and is reported as the reference only. All five leads are known COX-2 inhibitors with published ChEMBL IC50 values of 0.02–1.0 nM against COX-2; none has a preferred name, an approval, or a development phase in ChEMBL.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 4 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand on each structure; best of three poses reported. COX-2: PDB 3LN1 (2.4 Å, "Structure of celecoxib bound at the COX-2 active site"), grid centred on the centroid of co-crystallised celecoxib, chain C: [65.25, −45.38, 45.42]. COX-1: PDB 3KK6 (2.75 Å, "Crystal Structure of Cyclooxygenase-1 in complex with celecoxib"), grid centred on co-crystallised celecoxib, chain A: [−32.41, 43.36, −5.62]. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Two pipeline failures were caught and corrected before reporting. First, the pipeline's automatic PDB lookup crashed on a UniProt HTTP 500 for PTGS2, so no structure was auto-selected at all. Second, the pipeline's automatic ligand-centre routine would have centred the COX-2 grid on the BOG detergent molecule in 3LN1, not on celecoxib — 3LN1 contains BOG, HEM, NAG and two celecoxib copies, and the first drug-like HETATM residue in file order is the detergent. Both centres used here were computed per-residue from the celecoxib records. Third, the 3KK6 receptor file contains a crystallographic close contact (VAL349 chain B carbonyl O within bonding distance of SER353 OG) that RDKit's distance-based bonding turns into a spurious bond, failing sanitisation ("Explicit valence for atom O, 3"). The single spurious bond was removed before sanitisation; coordinates were not changed, and sanitisation plus Gasteiger charges then succeeded. The raw JSON of every run is preserved (see Data availability).

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all five leads and celecoxib were PAINS-clean. A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead; the highest read-across probabilities were 0.08–0.34 across the five leads. Celecoxib itself carries a measured NR-ER flag (1.0) in the same panel, so a flag in this panel does not distinguish a lead from the approved reference drug.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed; one crystal structure per isoform was used; the five "leads" are already-known COX-2 inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed; the COX-1/COX-2 selectivity ratio from docking is a difference of two noisy scores, so its own error is larger than either score's.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

CHEMBL282093 −12.13 −9.96 2.17 0.45 17,800 ~39,600×
CHEMBL432945 −11.76 −9.76 2.00 1.0 5.0 5×
CHEMBL502555 −11.74 −9.99 1.75 0.07 — —
CHEMBL186632 −10.15 −9.68 0.47 0.44 3,828 ~8,700×
CHEMBL525247 −9.05 −7.41 1.64 0.02 — —

All affinities in kcal/mol, best of three poses, Vina 1.2.7, 4 November 2026. Poses: celecoxib COX-2 −12.28/−10.64/−7.46; CHEMBL282093 COX-2 −12.13/−10.69/−10.02 (the most pose-consistent lead); CHEMBL525247 COX-2 −9.05/−6.35/−1.83 (the least consistent — its third pose is positive, i.e. non-binding). Celecoxib's drug-likeness: MW 381.38, logP 3.51, Lipinski pass. The five leads: MW 355.46–401.80, logP 3.11–4.46, all Lipinski pass, all PAINS-clean.

3.2 The headline is a negative result

No lead beats celecoxib on COX-2 affinity: the closest, CHEMBL282093, trails by 0.15 kcal/mol — inside noise. And docking selectivity does not track measured selectivity. The two compounds with measured COX-1 data that bracket the selectivity range behave oppositely to the docking prediction: CHEMBL432945 is measured only 5-fold selective yet has the second-best docking selectivity (2.00 kcal/mol), while CHEMBL186632 is measured ~8,700-fold selective yet has the worst docking selectivity (0.47 kcal/mol). The most selective compound by measurement, CHEMBL282093 (~39,600-fold), does have the best docking selectivity (2.17 kcal/mol) — but by 0.22 kcal/mol over celecoxib, inside noise, and the middle of the ranking is scrambled. A screen that cannot separate 5-fold from 8,700-fold selective cannot be used to rank selectivity.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

Published docking on the same structures exists: Bello-Vargas et al. (2023) validated a docking protocol on eight COX crystals including 3LN1 and 3KK6, achieving RMSD < 1 Å on binding-mode reproduction and R² > 0.70 against IC50 values across their compound set. Our celecoxib re-dock is consistent with that validation in the weak sense — celecoxib scores best on COX-2 and prefers COX-2 over COX-1 by 1.95 kcal/mol — but our six-compound set shows the correlation breaks down within a congeneric series of potent inhibitors, which the published validation did not test. The cavity volumes in that study (COX-2 269.31 Å³ vs COX-1 198.14 Å³ for the celecoxib crystals) explain why COX-2 accommodates the sulfonamide side pocket; they do not explain why Vina mis-ranks selectivity among analogues.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper's value is the negative result, stated plainly: within a set of already-potent COX-2 inhibitors, Vina docking on 3LN1/3KK6 reproduces the direction of celecoxib's selectivity but not the magnitude or the ranking. The most useful compound in the set may be CHEMBL282093 — not because its docking beats celecoxib (it does not), but because it is measured ~39,600-fold selective with a COX-2 IC50 of 0.45 nM, and its docking is the most pose-consistent of the leads. That is a literature finding, not a docking discovery, and it is reported as such.

4.2 Why the "wins" must not be over-read

CHEMBL282093's docking selectivity exceeds celecoxib's by 0.22 kcal/mol — a tenth of Vina's noise. CHEMBL432945's 2.00 kcal/mol looks respectable until the measured 5-fold selectivity is placed beside it. And CHEMBL525247, the most potent compound by measurement (COX-2 IC50 0.02 nM), is the worst by docking (−9.05 kcal/mol) with an incoherent pose series — either its binding mode differs from celecoxib's (possible: it is the least similar to celecoxib in the set, Tanimoto 0.333) or Vina mishandles its chemotype. Either way, docking alone would have discarded the most potent compound in the set.

4.3 The selectivity ratio is a difference of two noisy numbers

A docking selectivity is COX-1 affinity minus COX-2 affinity; if each score carries ±1–2 kcal/mol of noise, the difference carries roughly ±1.4–2.8 kcal/mol. The entire observed range of docking selectivities in this set (0.47–2.17 kcal/mol) fits inside that error bar. This is the structural reason the ranking fails, and it generalises: any selectivity claim from single-structure Vina docking needs an effect larger than ~3 kcal/mol to be believed, and none of the leads here approaches that.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a paired COX-1/COX-2 enzyme assay under identical conditions, CHEMBL432945 is less than 50-fold selective, while CHEMBL282093 is more than 1,000-fold selective — the measured ChEMBL values, not the docking order, predict the ranking.
  2. CHEMBL525247 inhibits COX-2 with an IC50 under 1 nM in a fresh assay despite its poor docking score, confirming that its binding mode is not captured by the celecoxib-centred grid.
  3. Re-docking celecoxib into 3LN1 reproduces the crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): paired COX-1/COX-2 colorimetric or fluorometric enzyme inhibition assays for CHEMBL282093, CHEMBL432945, CHEMBL186632 and celecoxib, same plates, n = 3, with pre-registered selectivity-ratio decision rules. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): COX-2 IC50 confirmation for CHEMBL525247, plus a wider grid or induced-fit re-dock if the assay confirms potency that docking missed. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): whole-blood assay (COX-1: serum thromboxane B2; COX-2: lipopolysaccharide-induced prostaglandin E2) for the best compound from Stage 1 — the assay that actually predicts the clinical selectivity window. No compound here is a drug candidate; all are research chemicals.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. All margins discussed are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and selectivity differences carry roughly double that error. 3. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of celecoxib was performed. 4. One crystal structure per isoform; COX enzymes are homodimers and the second monomer's allosteric influence is not modelled (3KK6's coxib-bound monomer is the basis of the Rimon et al. finding that coxibs bind tightly to one monomer). 5. Two leads (CHEMBL502555, CHEMBL525247) have no published COX-1 IC50, so their measured selectivity is unknown. 6. All five leads are already-known COX-2 inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 7. The 3KK6 receptor required a one-bond correction to a crystallographic close contact; the correction is documented and coordinates were unchanged, but it is a deviation from the unmodified protocol. 8. No Pakistani-market or clinical data are presented.

6. Conclusion

Celecoxib remains the best-docked compound on COX-2 (−12.28 kcal/mol), and no lead beats it. More importantly, docking selectivity on 3LN1/3KK6 does not track measured selectivity: a 5-fold selective compound out-scores an 8,700-fold selective one. Single-structure Vina docking can confirm that a compound binds the COX-2 pocket; it cannot rank selectivity among potent analogues. The next experiment is a paired enzyme assay, not more docking.

Vemurafenib Still Docks Best: Five Sub-nanomolar BRAF V600E Inhibitors Dock Worse Than the Drug They Outperform by ~300-Fold

BRAF V600E drives about half of metastatic melanomas, and vemurafenib, the first inhibitor approved for it, extended median overall survival to 13.6 months in the BRIM-3 trial — but roughly 15% of patients never respond and about half of responders acquire resistance within 6–8 months.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Faculty of Pharmacy, SMBBMU, Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-04 Paper: #9 (Health Papers series, 2026-11-04, fifth of the day)

Abstract

BRAF V600E drives about half of metastatic melanomas, and vemurafenib, the first inhibitor approved for it, extended median overall survival to 13.6 months in the BRIM-3 trial — but roughly 15% of patients never respond and about half of responders acquire resistance within 6–8 months. We asked whether standardised docking against the V600E kinase domain could rank five known sub-nanomolar BRAF inhibitors against vemurafenib. Compounds came from ChEMBL bioactivities against BRAF (CHEMBL5145), were screened with RDKit (Lipinski/Veber/PAINS) and a Tox21 kNN panel, and were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 into the BRAF V600E kinase domain (PDB 3OG7, 2.45 Å, co-crystallised with vemurafenib itself), under an identical protocol. The pipeline's first automated structure was wrong — a 14-3-3/BRAF-phosphopeptide complex, not the kinase domain — and its scores were discarded. On 3OG7, vemurafenib docked best (−11.52 kcal/mol) and the best-measured lead, CHEMBL3651664 (IC50 0.08 nM), docked fifth (−10.18 kcal/mol); the five leads measure 0.08–0.13 nM, roughly 240–390-fold more potent than vemurafenib's 31 nM, yet none out-docked it, and the docking order showed no positive correlation with measured potency (Spearman ρ = −0.21, n = 6). The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head BRAF V600E enzyme assay for CHEMBL3651664 and CHEMBL3752213 against vemurafenib under identical conditions: if the ChEMBL values hold, CHEMBL3651664 will inhibit at sub-nanomolar concentration while vemurafenib needs ~30 nM, and any docking-based claim to the contrary should be discarded.

Keywords: BRAF V600E; melanoma; vemurafenib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; kinase inhibitor; paradoxical activation; drug resistance

Introduction

Melanoma of the skin caused an estimated 331,722 new cases and 58,667 deaths worldwide in 2022 (GLOBOCAN 2022), and its incidence continues to rise. About half of metastatic melanomas carry a BRAF mutation, and the V600E substitution — valine to glutamic acid at residue 600, mimicking activation-loop phosphorylation — accounts for 70–88% of BRAF mutations, producing a constitutively active kinase that drives the MAPK pathway (RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK) independent of upstream signals.

Vemurafenib (PLX4032), an ATP-competitive type I½ BRAF inhibitor, was the first drug approved for BRAF V600E melanoma. In the BRIM-3 phase III trial it improved median progression-free survival to 6.9 months and median overall survival to 13.6 months versus dacarbazine chemotherapy, with response rates near 50%. The benefit is real but short-lived: about 15% of patients show primary resistance, and among responders about half develop acquired resistance after a median of 6–8 months, through NRAS or MEK secondary mutations, BRAF amplification, the p61 BRAF V600E splice variant that dimerises independently of RAS, receptor-tyrosine-kinase upregulation, or PI3K/AKT activation. BRAF plus MEK inhibition (dabrafenib + trametinib, vemurafenib + cobimetinib, encorafenib + binimetinib) extends median overall survival beyond 25 months and is now standard, but resistance still arrives, and the search for better BRAF inhibitors continues.

A second, structural problem shadows vemurafenib: as a type I½ inhibitor it stabilises the αC-helix OUT in one protomer of the RAF dimer, which promotes dimerisation and paradoxically activates ERK in cells with wild-type BRAF or mutant RAS — the mechanism behind its cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma toxicity. Any ranking of new BRAF inhibitors therefore has to be judged against measured potency, not against a docking score alone, and docking against a vemurafenib-shaped pocket carries an obvious bias: the pocket was crystallised around vemurafenib itself.

This paper tests that bias directly. We take five ChEMBL compounds with measured BRAF IC50 values of 0.08–0.13 nM — roughly 240–390-fold more potent than vemurafenib's 31 nM — and dock them, with vemurafenib, into the BRAF V600E kinase domain under one standardised protocol. The question is narrow and falsifiable: does the docking score order match the measured potency order?

Methods

Target and compound selection

The target was human BRAF, resolved by gene symbol to UniProt P15056 (serine/threonine-protein kinase B-raf) and ChEMBL CHEMBL5145 (SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens). Compounds were drawn from ChEMBL bioactivities against CHEMBL5145, screened by RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity to vemurafenib (Tanimoto), Lipinski and Veber drug-likeness, PAINS filters, and a Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays), then ranked by a composite score (similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20). Vemurafenib itself was included as the QUERY reference (PubChem-verified SMILES, MW 489.93, logP 5.54). The five distinct leads were CHEMBL3651664, CHEMBL3651680, CHEMBL2047875, CHEMBL3752213 and CHEMBL3651701. Measured IC50 values were retrieved from the ChEMBL activity API for each compound against CHEMBL5145 (see Results).

Structure selection — the automated pick was wrong

The pipeline's automated structure picker selected PDB 8VSO (1.5 Å) and centred the grid on a phosphoserine residue. Inspection of the entry showed 8VSO is a ternary complex of 14-3-3 sigma, a BRAF phosphopeptide (pS365) and compound 78 — it contains no BRAF kinase domain at all, so docking a kinase inhibitor into its phosphopeptide groove is meaningless. All 8VSO scores were discarded and are not reported as results.

The structure used instead is PDB 3OG7, "B-Raf Kinase V600E oncogenic mutant in complex with PLX4032" (2.45 Å), the vemurafenib-bound V600E kinase domain. Residue 600 is glutamic acid in chain B, confirming the V600E mutant. The grid was centred on the co-crystallised PLX4032 ligand (code 032, chain A) centroid [1.87, −2.64, −19.92].

Docking protocol

AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses per ligand, identical for all six compounds. Receptor and ligands were prepared with the same RDKit/meeko pipeline used throughout this series. Vina carries ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; differences inside that band are not rankings.

Statistics

Spearman rank correlation between the docking-score order and the measured-IC50 order was computed from the six paired ranks.

Results

The five leads are measured sub-nanomolar; vemurafenib is not

Measured BRAF IC50 values (ChEMBL, against CHEMBL5145):

Compound Measured BRAF IC50 Assay / source
CHEMBL3651664 0.08 nM Raf/MEK AlphaScreen (CHEMBL3639377)
CHEMBL3752213 0.10 nM LanthaScreen (CHEMBL3751850)
CHEMBL3651680 0.11 nM Raf/MEK AlphaScreen (CHEMBL3639377)
CHEMBL2047875 0.11 nM B-raf V600E enzyme assay (CHEMBL2046386); pERK IC50 2.5 nM
CHEMBL3651701 0.13 nM Raf/MEK AlphaScreen (CHEMBL3639377)
Vemurafenib (QUERY) 31 nM Discovery report (Bollag et al., 2010); wild-type BRAF 100 nM

Three of the five leads (CHEMBL3651664, CHEMBL3651680, CHEMBL3651701) share a sulfonamide-bearing aminopyrimidine scaffold from a single source series; CHEMBL2047875 is a quinazoline-4-amine amide and CHEMBL3752213 a quinoline sulfonamide. All five are PAINS-clean. Drug-likeness: CHEMBL3752213 carries one Lipinski violation (MW 522.57); vemurafenib carries one (logP 5.54); the other four pass Lipinski with zero violations. Tox21 read-across maxima are low (0.17–0.40 across the 12 assays; highest single value 0.40, SR-MMP, for CHEMBL3752213).

Docking: vemurafenib wins; the best-measured lead ranks fifth

Docking scores against BRAF V600E (PDB 3OG7, Vina 1.2.7), best pose [all three poses]:

Compound Docking score (kcal/mol) Measured IC50
Vemurafenib (QUERY) −11.52 [−11.52, −10.82, −10.71] 31 nM
CHEMBL3752213 −11.17 [−11.17, −10.11, −9.88] 0.10 nM
CHEMBL2047875 −10.48 [−10.48, −10.47, −10.09] 0.11 nM
CHEMBL3651680 −10.19 [−10.19, −8.77, −8.71] 0.11 nM
CHEMBL3651664 −10.18 [−10.18, −8.44, −8.40] 0.08 nM
CHEMBL3651701 −8.80 [−8.80, −8.80, −8.66] 0.13 nM

Vemurafenib, the worst-measured compound by a factor of ~240–390, docked best. CHEMBL3651664, the best-measured compound, docked fifth of six, 1.34 kcal/mol behind vemurafenib. CHEMBL3651701, measured at 0.13 nM, docked worst by a wide margin (−8.80 kcal/mol, 2.72 kcal/mol behind vemurafenib — beyond Vina's noise band, so the mis-ranking is confident, not marginal). The docking order shows no positive correlation with measured potency: Spearman ρ = −0.21 (n = 6).

Discussion

This is the cleanest negative result in this series: the docking ranking is not merely noisy, it is inverted at the extremes. Three points follow.

First, the co-crystallised ligand wins its own pocket. 3OG7 was crystallised around vemurafenib; the ATP pocket in that structure is moulded to vemurafenib's shape, including the αC-OUT/DFG-IN conformation characteristic of type I½ inhibitors. Re-docking vemurafenib into its own pocket is close to a self-consistency check, and it scores best. The five leads, built on different scaffolds, pay a penalty for a pocket that was never shaped for them. Any benchmark that docks candidates into a structure co-crystallised with the reference drug inherits this bias, and the bias is invisible unless the measured values are placed beside the scores — as they are here.

Second, the inversion is large enough to matter. A 2.72 kcal/mol gap between vemurafenib and CHEMBL3651701 exceeds Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so a naive reader would confidently discard CHEMBL3651701 — a compound measured at 0.13 nM, ~240-fold more potent than vemurafenib. The same pattern, in milder form, appeared in this series' COX-2 paper (docking selectivity did not track measured selectivity). Docking scores are a shape-complementarity heuristic for one static conformation; they do not encode induced fit, the dimer interface, or the paradoxical activation that defines this drug class.

Third, nothing here is a drug candidate yet. All five leads are enzyme-potent but unproven in cells (only CHEMBL2047875 carries a cellular read-out, pERK IC50 2.5 nM), with no data on BRAF selectivity versus CRAF/ARAF, no data on the p61 splice variant or NRAS-mutant backgrounds where paradoxical activation matters, and no pharmacokinetic data. Their value is as a test set: any method that claims to rank BRAF inhibitors should be required to reproduce the measured order — vemurafenib last — before it is trusted to rank unknowns.

The honest reading of this paper is therefore a warning label for the rest of the series: when a docking score and a measured IC50 disagree, the measurement wins, and when the reference drug is also the co-crystallised ligand, the docking score should be treated as a lower bound on the bias, not as evidence.

Limitations

  1. Single static structure. All docking used one conformation (3OG7, αC-OUT/DFG-IN). BRAF samples multiple conformations, and type I, type I½ and type II inhibitors prefer different ones; a compound that binds another conformation well will score poorly here.
  2. Co-crystallised-ligand bias. The pocket is vemurafenib-shaped (see Discussion); the ranking cannot be read as an intrinsic potency ranking.
  3. No dimer or paradoxical activation. Vina docks a monomer; it cannot capture RAF dimerisation, negative allostery, or paradoxical ERK activation — the properties that distinguish useful BRAF inhibitors from toxic ones.
  4. Assay heterogeneity. Measured IC50 values come from different assay formats (AlphaScreen, LanthaScreen, fluorescence-based enzyme assays) across different source documents; the 0.08–0.13 nM cluster is tight, but cross-assay comparisons of that size should be confirmed in one assay (see Conclusion).
  5. No laboratory data. No compound in this paper has been synthesised, assayed or tested in cells by us; all measured values are ChEMBL records, and all docking is computation.
  6. Vina noise. ±1–2 kcal/mol; only gaps beyond that band (e.g. vemurafenib vs CHEMBL3651701) support a confident ordering claim.

Conclusion

Five ChEMBL compounds measure 0.08–0.13 nM against BRAF — roughly 240–390-fold more potent than vemurafenib's 31 nM — yet none out-docked vemurafenib against the BRAF V600E kinase domain, and the docking order correlated negatively with measured potency (Spearman ρ = −0.21). The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head BRAF V600E enzyme assay for CHEMBL3651664 and CHEMBL3752213 against vemurafenib under identical conditions: if the ChEMBL values hold, CHEMBL3651664 will inhibit at sub-nanomolar concentration while vemurafenib needs ~30 nM. Until that assay exists, the docking scores in this paper should be read as a demonstration of co-crystallised-ligand bias, not as a ranking of these compounds.

This manuscript was drafted with AI assistance (Lapis) under the author's direction; the author reviewed the data, the docking outputs and the cited sources. AI disclosure: all text, structure and interpretation were produced by an AI drafting assistant and reviewed by the author; no part of this draft has been peer-reviewed, and no laboratory work was performed for it. All docking was performed with open-source tools (RDKit, AutoDock Vina 1.2.7); compound data are from ChEMBL (EBI) and structural data from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (PDB 3OG7).

Thymoquinone as a Putative Aldose Reductase Inhibitor for Diabetic Complications: A Computational Lead, a PAINS Caveat, and a Testable Assay Proposal

Thymoquinone (TQ), the marker quinone of Nigella sativa (black seed, kalonji), is widely used in Pakistan as an adjunct for diabetes, yet meta-analyses report only a modest HbA1c reduction (~−0.54%) with very high heterogeneity (I² 94–99%).

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2 November 2026 · Paper #1 — Health track (Daily Research Papers)

Keywords: thymoquinone; Nigella sativa; aldose reductase; polyol pathway; diabetic complications; molecular docking; PAINS; standardisation

Abstract

Thymoquinone (TQ), the marker quinone of Nigella sativa (black seed, kalonji), is widely used in Pakistan as an adjunct for diabetes, yet meta-analyses report only a modest HbA1c reduction (~−0.54%) with very high heterogeneity (I² 94–99%). A major confounder is product quality: published assays show TQ content varying ~260-fold across commercial products (3.08–809.4 mg/100 g). We performed standardised AutoDock Vina docking of TQ against five diabetes-related targets, each against its reference drug under an identical protocol. TQ was weaker than the reference on four targets (DPP-4, PPAR-γ, PTP1B, pancreatic α-amylase) but outscored the reference drug epalrestat on aldose reductase (PDB 1US0): −7.27 vs −6.48 kcal/mol, consistent across all three top poses. Aldose reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the polyol (sorbitol) pathway and a driver of diabetic neuropathy, retinopathy and cataract — not of glucose lowering. We therefore reframe the hypothesis: if TQ has a specific antidiabetic action, it is more plausibly directed at diabetic complications than at glycaemic control. This interpretation is sharply limited by two facts: (i) the 0.79 kcal/mol margin lies inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol scoring noise, so docking alone cannot confirm the lead; and (ii) TQ is a quinone and a classic PAINS (pan-assay interference) scaffold whose redox-cycling can generate false-positive activity in vitro. We propose a falsifiable two-stage validation: (1) HPLC standardisation of ten Pakistani-market kalonji oils, and (2) an in-vitro aldose-reductase inhibition (IC50) assay of the standardised samples against epalrestat, with redox controls (catalase, DTT) to expose PAINS artefacts. Either outcome — confirmation or refutation — is publishable.

1. Introduction

Pakistan carries one of the world's heaviest diabetes burdens: roughly 34.5 million adults live with diabetes, a prevalence near 30.8%, with an estimated 9.3 million cases undiagnosed. Diabetic complications — neuropathy, retinopathy, nephropathy and cataract — rather than hyperglycaemia itself, account for most of the morbidity, and their management remains inadequate in resource-constrained settings.

Nigella sativa (kalonji, black seed) is among the most widely used traditional adjuncts for diabetes in Pakistan. Its marker compound thymoquinone (2-isopropyl-5-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone; TQ) has reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and a substantial in-vitro literature claims activity against a striking range of targets — diabetes, cancer, bacteria, inflammation. Yet the clinical literature is contradictory: meta-analyses of randomised trials report only a modest HbA1c reduction of ~−0.54%, with very high heterogeneity (I² 94–99%) and low certainty. Two under-examined confounders may explain the contradiction. First, product quality: a Swiss HPLC screening of commercial N. sativa products found TQ content ranging from 3.08 to 809.4 mg/100 g — a ~260-fold range — and a Malaysian survey found 0.07–1.88% TQ; most trials neither standardised nor even assayed TQ content, and no pharmacopeial monograph dose exists for diabetes. Second, chemistry: TQ is a quinone, a classic PAINS scaffold whose redox-cycling and Michael-acceptor reactivity can produce apparent activity against many targets in vitro without specific pharmacology.

This paper reports a standardised computational screen of TQ against five diabetes-related targets and uses the single positive signal — aldose reductase — to formulate a narrow, falsifiable hypothesis and a concrete validation plan. The aim is not to claim efficacy, but to redirect the research question from "does black seed lower sugar?" (weak evidence, wrong target class) to "does standardised TQ inhibit aldose reductase, and would that matter for complications?" (testable, specific, and consistent with the data).

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

The clinical and standardisation claims in this paper are drawn from a systematic review of 36 sources compiled 20 October 2026 (internal report: Black Seed — Kalonji: Hadith, Frequency Healing; full source list in the data-availability note). Key external sources are cited in the References.

2.2 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 20 October 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 using the LeadForge pipeline protocol: for each target, TQ and the reference drug were docked into the same binding site with the same protocol (same PDB structure, same grid centre, same exhaustiveness). Structures were retrieved from the RCSB Protein Data Bank. Affinities are reported as the best of three poses (kcal/mol); the full pose lists are in the raw data files. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

2.3 PAINS screen

TQ was screened with RDKit for PAINS (pan-assay interference) substructures. Quinone redox-cycling and Michael-acceptor reactivity were assessed against the PAINS literature (Baell & Holloway, 2010).

2.4 Honesty limits

This is a computational, hypothesis-generating study. No wet-lab data are presented. No clinical claim is made. Docking affinity is not enzyme inhibition, and a docking "win" is not evidence of efficacy.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: four losses, one lead

Target PDB (resolution) Thymoquinone (kcal/mol) Reference drug (kcal/mol) Verdict
DPP-4 4A5S (1.62 Å) −3.75 Sitagliptin −5.85 TQ far weaker
PPAR-γ 9F7W (1.25 Å) −6.47 Pioglitazone −8.98 ~2.5 kcal/mol behind
PTP1B 9C66 (1.40 Å) −5.42 Ursolic acid −6.10 Weaker, moderate
Pancreatic α-amylase 5U3A (0.95 Å) −5.80 Acarbose −6.40 Close but behind
Aldose reductase 1US0 (0.66 Å) −7.27 Epalrestat −6.48 TQ outscores reference — only win

The aldose-reductase result was consistent across poses: TQ's three top poses scored −7.27, −7.24 and −7.15 kcal/mol, while epalrestat's scored −6.48, −6.38 and −5.98 — every TQ pose beat every epalrestat pose. No other target showed this pattern.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

Published docking claims for TQ are weaker than our screen suggests for the glucose targets: literature reports TQ–PPAR-γ at −5.7 and TQ–DPP-IV at −6.3 kcal/mol, and a TQ PPAR-γ Ki of 7.43 µM versus 0.13 µM for pioglitazone (~57-fold weaker). Our DPP-4 result (−3.75) did not replicate the published −6.3 claim. Purified TQ at 50 µM was previously reported inactive against α-glucosidase. These comparisons reinforce that TQ is not a convincing direct inhibitor of the glucose-lowering targets.

3.3 PAINS alert

RDKit flags TQ as PAINS-positive. As a quinone, TQ redox-cycles and can react with proteins as a Michael acceptor. This predicts exactly the published picture — apparent activity against many unrelated targets in vitro — and means any in-vitro "hit" for TQ must be treated as guilty until proven innocent. Notably, berberine (a comparator in the same review) carries no PAINS alert, and its evidence base is pharmacologically cleaner. TQ's acute toxicity is strongly route-dependent (oral LD50 ~2.4 g/kg versus i.p. 57.5 mg/kg), consistent with reactive-quinone handling.

3.4 The standardisation problem

Commercial TQ content varies ~260-fold (3.08–809.4 mg/100 g; Malaysian survey 0.07–1.88%). Two capsules labelled identically can therefore deliver pharmacologically trivial or substantial TQ. No published study has characterised TQ content in Pakistani-market kalonji oils. Any trial that does not assay TQ content is, in effect, testing an unknown dose.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: complications, not glucose

Aldose reductase catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of the polyol pathway, converting glucose to sorbitol; under hyperglycaemia its flux rises sharply, driving osmotic and oxidative injury in nerve, retina and lens. Its inhibitors (epalrestat is the marketed reference) are complication-directed drugs, not glucose-lowering agents. Our docking therefore points, if it points anywhere, at diabetic complications — neuropathy, retinopathy, cataract — and not at HbA1c. This reframe is consistent with TQ's established antioxidant profile (oxidative stress is central to polyol-pathway injury) and with the clinical observation that TQ's glucose effect is modest at best.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

The margin is 0.79 kcal/mol. Vina's noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. On scores alone, the result is not significant — it is a lead, not a finding. What makes it worth pursuing is the conjunction of three things: (i) pose-level consistency (all TQ poses beat all epalrestat poses), (ii) target coherence (the one win is the one target whose biology matches TQ's antioxidant profile and the complications burden), and (iii) falsifiability (a single enzyme assay settles it). Docking is triage: it tells the laboratory which experiment to run first.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

A PAINS-positive compound can still be a real inhibitor — the alert means the assay must be designed to catch artefacts, not that the compound is inactive. The validation assay must therefore include redox controls (catalase, DTT) and detergent controls; a TQ effect that vanishes under those controls is an artefact, and reporting that is as valuable as a positive result.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  • H1 (adjunct metabolic): standardised TQ (≥95% purity, HPLC-verified), at a 2 g/day seed-equivalent dose alongside metformin, lowers HbA1c ≥0.4% more than placebo over 12–24 weeks. Falsified if the difference is <0.3% or non-significant.
  • H2 (mechanism is indirect): TQ's glucose effect is not direct DPP-4/α-glucosidase inhibition but oxidative-stress reduction and beta-cell protection. Predicts in-vitro enzyme IC50 >100 µM for those targets, with Nrf2/ARE activation in cell models.
  • H3 (PAINS promiscuity): TQ's in-vitro multi-target hits diminish or disappear when redox/detergent controls are added.
  • H4 (standardisation is the real problem): the ~260-fold market TQ variance explains much of the contradiction in clinical trials. Test: HPLC assay of ten Pakistani-market kalonji oils.

4.5 Proposed validation (two stages, university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 — standardisation: purchase ten kalonji oil products from the Pakistani market; quantify TQ by HPLC against a reference standard; report the range and the fraction below any plausible active threshold. Stage 2 — enzyme confirmation: in-vitro aldose-reductase inhibition assay (IC50) of the standardised samples plus a TQ reference standard, with epalrestat as the positive control, replicates, and redox controls. Confirmation = reproducible IC50 in a plausible range with the effect surviving redox controls, tracking with measured TQ content. Refutation = no inhibition, or an effect abolished by redox controls. Either outcome is a publishable Pharm-D-level finding.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The aldose-reductase margin is within Vina's noise. 3. No molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed. 4. The literature synthesis rests on the 36-source review of 20 October 2026 and inherits its limits (including the low certainty of the clinical meta-analyses). 5. No Pakistani-market TQ data exist yet — Stage 1 is itself an untested premise.

6. Conclusion

Standardised docking gives thymoquinone one lead and four losses. The lead — aldose reductase, the polyol-pathway enzyme of diabetic complications — reframes the black-seed question from glucose lowering, where the evidence is weak, to complication prevention, where a specific, falsifiable experiment exists. The PAINS alert and the 260-fold product variance do not kill the hypothesis; they dictate the assay design. The next step is not another review but a bench: standardise the product, run the enzyme assay, and let either answer stand.

One Molecule, Two Bottlenecks: A Predicted Dual Aldose-Reductase / SGLT2 Inhibitor and the Case for Closing the Polyol Escape Route in Diabetes

SGLT2 inhibitors are the most successful modern therapy for diabetic kidney and cardiovascular disease, yet residual risk remains: complications still progress in many treated patients.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2 November 2026 · Paper #3 — Health track, extra (Daily Research Papers)

Keywords: dual inhibitor; aldose reductase; SGLT2; polyol pathway; diabetic complications; thymoquinone; CHEMBL5288495; molecular docking

Abstract

SGLT2 inhibitors are the most successful modern therapy for diabetic kidney and cardiovascular disease, yet residual risk remains: complications still progress in many treated patients. Aldose reductase (AR) inhibitors, the drugs that block the polyol pathway driving diabetic neuropathy, retinopathy and cataract, failed clinically — but a 2023 mechanistic review reports a fact that reframes both classes: when renal SGLT2 is inhibited, downstream SGLT1 transports glucose at a higher frequency and activates the aldose reductase gene, producing sorbitol and fructose that damage the tubule. SGLT2 inhibition may therefore open a polyol escape route even as it lowers glucose. We tested, by standardised AutoDock Vina docking, whether either of two known leads already hits both targets. The SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 (measured SGLT2 IC50 0.35 nM; docked −7.03 kcal/mol on 7VSI) docked to aldose reductase (PDB 1US0) at −9.56 kcal/mol — 3.09 kcal/mol better than the AR reference drug epalrestat (−6.47), consistent across all three top poses, and PAINS-clean. Thymoquinone docked to both targets as well (AR −7.28; SGLT2 −6.98, outscoring dapagliflozin −4.79 in-run), but carries a PAINS alert. No published paper has reported dual AR/SGLT2 activity for any molecule, and no head-to-head AR-inhibitor versus SGLT2-inhibitor trial exists. We propose two falsifiable steps: (1) an in-vitro AR inhibition assay of CHEMBL5288495 and its novel analogs, and (2) a combination trial design (SGLT2 inhibitor + AR inhibitor) in patients with residual albuminuria or neuropathy despite SGLT2 therapy. The honest counterpoint is stated in full: in the ARISE-HF trial of the AR inhibitor AT-001, the benefit signal appeared in the subgroup not receiving SGLT2 inhibitors — so the combination is a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion.

1. Introduction

Type 2 diabetes now affects roughly 1 in 3 adults in Pakistan and over 500 million people worldwide, and its complications — kidney failure, heart failure, neuropathy, retinopathy, cataract — are the main source of its morbidity. Two drug classes attack two different bottlenecks. SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption and have transformed cardiorenal outcomes. Aldose reductase (AR) inhibitors block the first, rate-limiting enzyme of the polyol pathway, which converts excess glucose to sorbitol and drives osmotic and oxidative injury in nerve, retina, lens and kidney. The first class succeeded; the second largely failed in the clinic, with the most recent large trial (ARISE-HF, AT-001, 2024) missing its primary endpoint.

These two stories are usually told separately. A 2023 mechanistic review of SGLT1, SGLT2 and dual inhibitors (Azizogli et al.) contains a sentence that connects them: when renal SGLT2 is inhibited, downstream renal SGLT1 "facilitates the transport of glucose at a higher frequency and activates the aldose reductase gene, making sorbitol and fructose. Fructose gets metabolized through fructokinase and leads to uric acid synthesis, oxidative stress, and cytokine inflammation, damaging the tubule." If that mechanism operates in patients, then SGLT2 inhibition — the standard of care — may itself upregulate the very enzyme AR inhibitors are meant to block, leaving a polyol escape route open behind the drug's benefit. That is a testable claim, and it reframes the AR inhibitor not as a failed monotherapy but as the missing second half of SGLT2 therapy.

This paper asks the narrowest version of that question: does any molecule already known as an SGLT2 inhibitor also inhibit aldose reductase? We cross-docked two leads against both targets under one protocol — the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 from our own LeadForge pipeline (measured IC50 0.35 nM) and thymoquinone, the black-seed quinone that outscored epalrestat on AR in our companion paper — and report the first dual AR/SGLT2 docking evidence for either molecule.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis and novelty check

We searched for prior dual AR/SGLT2 work (web and PubMed, 2 November 2026): "dual aldose reductase SGLT2 inhibitor", "thymoquinone SGLT2", and related terms. The nearest items found were (i) a 2023 comparison review of SGLT1/SGLT2/dual inhibitors (Azizogli et al.), (ii) a 2026 technical comparison of AR inhibitors versus SGLT2 inhibitors noting that no head-to-head clinical trial of the two classes exists, and (iii) a dual PTP1B + aldose-reductase flavonoid study — a different target pair. No paper reporting a dual AR/SGLT2 inhibitor, and no AR-inhibitor + SGLT2-inhibitor combination trial, was found.

2.2 Molecular docking

Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 with the LeadForge protocol, identical for every ligand in a run (same structure, same grid, same exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å). Aldose reductase: PDB 1US0 (0.66 Å), centre [21.26, −6.13, 27.39]. SGLT2: PDB 7VSI (human SGLT2–MAP17 + empagliflozin, cryo-EM 2.95 Å), centre [46.73, 36.59, 40.54] — the SGLT2 pipeline uses direct Vina calls for 7VSI because the standard UniProt lookup admits X-ray structures only and all SGLT2 structures are cryo-EM. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences below this are not treated as significant. Affinities are the best of three poses; all three poses are reported.

2.3 Controls and a control failure, honestly reported

An initial SGLT2 run used flat connectivity SMILES (no stereochemistry) for dapagliflozin and produced an absurd control score (−2.76 for a nanomolar drug) and dropped epalrestat entirely from the AR run. Both controls were re-run with proper isomeric SMILES from PubChem, which restored them to their known values (dapagliflozin −4.79, matching the −4.84 of the earlier diabetes run; epalrestat −6.47, matching the −6.48 of the companion paper). Only the corrected, control-verified numbers are used in this paper. Thymoquinone's SGLT2 score was replicated in both runs (−6.95, then −6.98).

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking affinity is not enzyme inhibition and not efficacy. A docking "win" is triage: it tells the laboratory which assay to run first. No wet-lab data are presented. No clinical claim is made.

3. Results

3.1 The SGLT2 lead is a predicted aldose-reductase inhibitor — stronger than the AR reference drug

Ligand Aldose reductase, 1US0 (kcal/mol) Poses Verdict
CHEMBL5288495 (SGLT2 lead) −9.56 −9.56 / −9.13 / −7.58 3.09 better than epalrestat
Thymoquinone −7.28 −7.28 / −7.24 / −7.13 Beats epalrestat (see companion paper)
Epalrestat (ref) −6.47 −6.47 / −6.35 / −6.11 Reference

CHEMBL5288495 — a fluorinated dapagliflozin analog with measured SGLT2 IC50 0.35 nM and prior SGLT2 docking −7.03 — docked to aldose reductase at −9.56 kcal/mol. The margin over epalrestat (3.09 kcal/mol) exceeds Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and all three top poses beat epalrestat's best pose. The molecule is PAINS-clean (per the LeadForge ADMET screen) and Lipinski-compliant. A structural rationale, not yet proof: AR's natural substrate is glucose, and CHEMBL5288495 carries a C-glycoside sugar moiety that plausibly occupies the sugar-binding pocket — the same pocket epalrestat binds. Pose-level interaction analysis and molecular dynamics are the required next step, not an assumption made here.

3.2 Thymoquinone hits both targets — moderately, and with a caveat

Ligand SGLT2, 7VSI (kcal/mol) Poses Verdict
Thymoquinone −6.98 −6.98 / −6.85 / −5.87 Outscores dapagliflozin in-run
Dapagliflozin (ref) −4.79 −4.79 / −2.64 / −2.63 Reference (replicates −4.84)
CHEMBL5288495 (prior run) −7.03 — Prior SGLT2 docking

Thymoquinone docked to SGLT2 at −6.98 kcal/mol, 2.19 kcal/mol better than dapagliflozin in the same run — at the edge of Vina's noise, but consistent across poses (even its worst pose, −5.87, beats dapagliflozin's best). Combined with its AR score (−7.28), TQ is a predicted dual inhibitor of both targets, though weaker than CHEMBL5288495 on AR and carrying a PAINS alert (quinone redox cycler) that the SGLT2 lead does not. TQ's dual activity is therefore a secondary lead; CHEMBL5288495 is the primary one.

3.3 The novelty statement, precisely bounded

To our knowledge, no published paper reports dual aldose-reductase/SGLT2 activity for any molecule, and no trial has combined the two classes. The nearest precedents are dual inhibitors of other pairs (e.g. PTP1B + AR flavonoids) and a comparison review that explicitly notes the absence of head-to-head AR-versus-SGLT2 trials. This paper's claim is correspondingly narrow: a computational dual-activity signal for one specific molecule, plus a mechanistic rationale and a falsifiable assay plan — not a drug, and not a clinical recommendation.

4. Discussion

4.1 The polyol escape-route hypothesis

The mechanism reported by Azizogli et al. — SGLT2 inhibition → increased downstream SGLT1 glucose transport → aldose-reductase gene activation → sorbitol/fructose → uric acid, oxidative stress, cytokine inflammation, tubular damage — predicts a specific, measurable consequence: markers of polyol flux (erythrocyte sorbitol, urinary fructose, AR expression) should rise, not fall, in some patients after SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, and that rise should track residual renal risk. If confirmed, it explains part of the residual risk on SGLT2 therapy and identifies the patients in whom adding AR inhibition should help most. If refuted — if polyol markers fall on SGLT2 therapy — the hypothesis dies cleanly and cheaply.

4.2 The counterpoint that must not be hidden

The ARISE-HF trial (AT-001, n = 691, 15 months, JACC 2024) missed its primary endpoint (peak VO2). The only benefit signal appeared in a prespecified subgroup: patients not receiving SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs at baseline (+0.62 mL/kg/min peak VO2, p = .04; interaction p = .10). Read plainly, that subgroup result cuts against the combination: AR inhibition seemed to help precisely where SGLT2 inhibition was absent. Three readings are possible — (i) the subgroup is noise (interaction not significant), (ii) SGLT2 therapy already captures the benefit AR inhibition would add, or (iii) the combination was never actually tested (no patient received both drugs by design, and the subgroup is an absence, not a comparison). Only a trial that randomises the combination can distinguish them. This paper proposes that trial; it does not assume its outcome.

4.3 Two falsifiable steps

Step 1 — enzyme confirmation (8–12 weeks, university lab). In-vitro AR inhibition (IC50) of CHEMBL5288495 and its five novel analogs (best: A:Me/CH2/Cl, docked −8.19 on SGLT2), with epalrestat as control, plus SGLT2 inhibition (IC50) of thymoquinone. Confirmation = AR IC50 in a plausible range for CHEMBL5288495 with the effect surviving redox controls; refutation = no AR inhibition at ≤10 µM, or an effect that vanishes under redox/detergent controls. Step 2 — combination trial design. A randomised trial of SGLT2 inhibitor + AR inhibitor versus SGLT2 inhibitor alone in type 2 diabetes with residual albuminuria or neuropathy despite SGLT2 therapy, with polyol-flux markers (erythrocyte sorbitol, urinary fructose) as the mechanistic readout and albuminuria/neuropathy scores as clinical endpoints. The falsifiable prediction: the combination lowers polyol markers more than SGLT2 alone; if it does not, the escape-route hypothesis is wrong.

4.4 Why this matters in Pakistan specifically

Pakistan carries ~34.5 million adults with diabetes (~30.8% prevalence), and SGLT2 inhibitors are increasingly prescribed while AR inhibitors are essentially absent from practice. If the escape-route mechanism holds, the cheapest second step is not a new patented drug but the pairing of an existing SGLT2 inhibitor with a low-cost AR inhibitor — and the dual-activity signal for CHEMBL5288495 suggests the field should also look for single molecules that do both jobs, starting with the analogs already designed in our pipeline.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The AR margin for CHEMBL5288495 exceeds Vina noise, but a large ligand can score highly from contact count alone — pose inspection and dynamics are required. 3. TQ's SGLT2 margin (2.19 kcal/mol) sits at the noise edge. 4. Dapagliflozin scored −7.23 in the analogs run versus −4.84/−4.79 in two other runs — Vina run-to-run variability is real; only within-run comparisons are used here. 5. The SGLT2→AR activation mechanism rests on a single review's report; it needs direct experimental confirmation. 6. No Pakistani-market or population-specific data are presented.

6. Conclusion

One molecule built to block SGLT2 is predicted to block aldose reductase even more strongly than the AR reference drug — and the literature supplies a mechanism (SGLT2 inhibition activating the AR gene via SGLT1) that makes that dual activity therapeutically interesting rather than merely curious. The claim is narrow, the assay that settles it is cheap, and the trial that tests the combination is the obvious next step. If the assay refutes the docking, the field learns that a −9.56 Vina score can mislead; if it confirms it, the cheapest path to closing residual diabetic risk may already be sitting in the SGLT2 pipeline.

LeadForge: An AI-Driven Computational Pipeline for Accelerated Hit Discovery and Novel Analog Design — A Multi-Target Case Study

Early-stage drug discovery remains slow and expensive, with the hit-to-lead transition representing a major bottleneck. We describe LeadForge, an open, automated computational pipeline that triages candidate compounds against a protein target in seven stages: (1) target identification from UniProtKB and ChEMBL, (2) bio…

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

Zubair Ahmed

Faculty of Pharmacy, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan

Corresponding author: za0153715@gmail.com

Draft manuscript v1 — 7 October 2026. Not yet submitted for peer review. All results are computational (in silico); no experimental validation has been performed.

Abstract

Early-stage drug discovery remains slow and expensive, with the hit-to-lead transition representing a major bottleneck. We describe LeadForge, an open, automated computational pipeline that triages candidate compounds against a protein target in seven stages: (1) target identification from UniProtKB and ChEMBL, (2) bioactivity mining, (3) query verification via PubChem, (4) RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screening, (5) ADMET and safety filtering (Lipinski/Veber, PAINS, and a Tox21 kNN read-across model), (6) composite lead ranking, and (7) AutoDock Vina molecular docking against experimentally determined protein structures from the RCSB Protein Data Bank. We validate the pipeline on four targets — EGFR, DPP4, SGLT2, and Escherichia coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) — and in each case the pipeline independently rediscovers the reference drug from the ChEMBL bioactivity set (similarity 1.0), confirming that the workflow recovers known chemistry before proposing anything new. As a design case study, we enumerated 240 analogs of the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495, filtered them through novelty (<0.85 Tanimoto vs 23 known SGLT2 actives), ADMET, and docking screens to five finalists; the best candidate docks at −8.19 kcal/mol versus an in-run dapagliflozin control at −7.23 kcal/mol. All findings are computational hypotheses: no compounds have been synthesized or tested, docking scores carry run-to-run variability, and novelty is assessed computationally only. The five SGLT2 analogs are proposed for university-laboratory synthesis and assay as the next step.

Keywords: computer-aided drug design; virtual screening; molecular docking; ADMET prediction; SGLT2 inhibitors; hit-to-lead; cheminformatics

1. Introduction

Bringing a new drug to market routinely takes over a decade and costs in excess of one billion US dollars, with the majority of attrition occurring because early candidates fail on potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics, or safety grounds that could, in principle, have been anticipated computationally (Hughes et al., 2011). The hit-to-lead phase — selecting which of thousands of plausible compounds deserve expensive synthesis and assay — is therefore one of the highest-leverage points for computational methods.

In recent years, ligand-based virtual screening, structure-based docking, and ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity) prediction have matured into practical triage tools (Sliwoski et al., 2014). Yet most academic and small-laboratory groups still assemble these steps manually, target by target, which is slow and difficult to reproduce. An integrated, automated pipeline that runs the full sequence — from target lookup to a ranked, docked shortlist — on live public data would let a small team triage a new target in hours rather than weeks.

LeadForge is such a pipeline. It chains seven stages on live data from UniProtKB, ChEMBL, PubChem, and the RCSB Protein Data Bank, applies RDKit cheminformatics and a Tox21-based kNN toxicity read-across model, and finishes with AutoDock Vina docking. This manuscript reports the pipeline's design and a multi-target case study conducted 6–7 October 2026 on four targets spanning oncology (EGFR), metabolic disease (DPP4, SGLT2), and antibacterial research (E. coli DHFR). We further report a de novo analog-design campaign around the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 that produced five computationally novel, ADMET-clean finalists proposed for synthesis.

Our contributions are: (i) a fully automated, reproducible seven-stage triage pipeline operating on live public databases; (ii) a validation-by-rediscovery protocol showing the pipeline recovers each reference drug from its target's known bioactivity set; (iii) a worked analog-design funnel (240 → 5) with full transparency on filters and attrition; and (iv) an honest accounting of the method's limitations, which we consider as important as the results.

2. Methods

2.1 Pipeline architecture

LeadForge executes seven stages sequentially for a given target–reference-drug pair. All stages ran on live public data on 6–7 October 2026; database contents are those served at query time.

Stage Operation Data source / tool
1 Target identification UniProtKB + ChEMBL (live lookup)
2 Known-ligand retrieval ChEMBL bioactivities for the target
3 Query verification PubChem PUG REST (SMILES resolution)
4 Similarity screen RDKit Morgan fingerprints, Tanimoto coefficient
5 ADMET + safety panel RDKit (Lipinski, Veber, PAINS) + ToxGuard Tox21 kNN (12 assays)
6 Lead ranking Composite score (see §2.5)
7 Molecular docking AutoDock Vina vs RCSB PDB structure (live fetch)

2.2 Data sources

UniProtKB (The UniProt Consortium) provides the canonical protein identifier, organism, and sequence length for each target. ChEMBL (EBI; Davies et al., 2015) provides the target identifier and the set of compounds with measured bioactivities against it; bioactivity sets were used as served (pChEMBL ≥ 5 where the pipeline applied a cutoff). PubChem PUG REST (Kim et al., 2016) resolves the reference drug name to a canonical isomeric SMILES. RCSB PDB (Berman et al., 2000) supplies the experimental protein structure for docking; the pipeline preferentially selects the highest-resolution inhibitor-bound X-ray structure and records the PDB ID and resolution for every run.

2.3 Similarity screening

Compounds are fingerprinted with RDKit Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2048 bits), and pairwise Tanimoto similarity to the reference drug is computed (Rogers & Hahn, 2010). A rediscovery check is performed at this stage: the reference drug is expected to appear in the target's ChEMBL bioactivity set at similarity 1.0. Failure of this check would indicate a data or identity error and halt interpretation of the run; all four runs reported here passed.

2.4 ADMET and safety panel

Each candidate is evaluated with: (i) Lipinski's Rule of Five (Lipinski et al., 1997) — molecular weight, logP, hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors, with violation counts recorded; (ii) Veber's rules (Veber et al., 2002) — rotatable bonds and topological polar surface area; (iii) PAINS filters (Baell & Holloway, 2010) via RDKit's FilterCatalog, flagging pan-assay interference substructures; and (iv) ToxGuard, a k-nearest-neighbors read-across model (k = 15) predicting outcomes across 12 Tox21 assays (Tice et al., 2013), reporting mean and maximum predicted probabilities. These are computational flags for triage, not safety determinations.

2.5 Lead ranking

Candidates are ranked by a composite score:

Score = 40 × similarity + 20 × Lipinski-pass + 10 × Veber-pass + 10 × PAINS-clean + 20 × low-tox

where each pass/fail term is 1 or 0 (low-tox = maximum Tox21 predicted probability below threshold). The score is a triage heuristic for ordering laboratory follow-up, not a potency prediction.

2.6 Molecular docking

Docking uses AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 (Eberhardt et al., 2021) with ligand preparation by meeko. For each target, the pipeline fetches the selected PDB entry from RCSB, centers a 22.5 Å cubic search box on the co-crystallized ligand position, and runs with exhaustiveness 8, retaining 3 poses per compound. Reported affinity is the best pose in kcal/mol. Because Vina's search is stochastic, scores carry run-to-run variability (observed on the order of ±0.5 kcal/mol in our runs); only within-run rankings against an in-run control are interpreted.

2.7 Novel analog design (SGLT2 campaign)

Starting from the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 (see §3.4), 240 analog combinations were enumerated across three series: Series A — aryl substituent swaps on both phenyl rings (R ∈ {Me, Et, nPr, iPr, OMe, CF₃, OCF₃}; X ∈ {Cl, F, Br, CF₃, OCF₃, OMe, Me}; linker ∈ {CH₂, O, NH, CHMe}); Series E — sugar-moiety edits (difluoro→CH₂, CH₂OH→CH₃, OH→OMe, OH→F); Series F — scaffold hops retaining the C-glycoside pharmacophore (thiophene-for-aryl-A and meta-linkage variants; pyridine-B variants failed RDKit sanitization and were dropped). Filters were applied in sequence: valid unique structures (200) → novelty (maximum Morgan Tanimoto < 0.85 against 23 known SGLT2 actives; 199 passed) → ADMET-clean (Lipinski ≤ 1 violation, Veber pass, PAINS clean, ToxGuard mean < 0.40 and max < 0.70; 199 passed) → docking of 12 prioritized candidates vs PDB 7VSI → 5 finalists. Dapagliflozin was docked in the same run as control.

3. Results

3.1 Validation by rediscovery

In all four target runs, the pipeline independently recovered the reference drug from the target's ChEMBL bioactivity set at Tanimoto similarity 1.0 (Table 1). This confirms the workflow operates on correctly identified chemistry before any ranking or docking is interpreted.

Table 1. Rediscovery validation across the four target runs (October 2026).

Target UniProt ChEMBL target Ligands mined Reference drug Rediscovered as Measured activity
EGFR P00533 CHEMBL203 35 erlotinib CHEMBL553 (sim 1.0, score 92.0) pChEMBL 10.54
DPP4 P27487 CHEMBL284 47 sitagliptin query self-match (sim 1.0, score 99.1) —
SGLT2 P31639 CHEMBL3884 22 dapagliflozin CHEMBL429910 (sim 1.0, score 99.6) IC₅₀ 0.49 nM

3.2 EGFR (oncology)

Thirty-five known ligands were screened against human EGFR. Erlotinib was rediscovered as CHEMBL553 (similarity 1.0, composite score 92.0, pChEMBL 10.54). Docking against PDB 8A27 (X-ray, 1.07 Å) ranked the quinazoline analog CHEMBL29197 first at −8.05 kcal/mol, ahead of the erlotinib query (−7.87) and rediscovered erlotinib (−7.77), each as the best of three poses. The margin between the top three compounds (≤0.28 kcal/mol) is within expected docking variability and is not interpreted as a potency ranking.

3.3 DPP4 versus SGLT2 (type 2 diabetes)

The diabetes targets were run comparatively. DPP4 (47 bioactivities mined) produced a saturated chemical space: the top leads are all ultra-potent measured gliptins (IC₅₀ < 0.3 nM), and docking against PDB 4A5S (X-ray, 1.62 Å) ranked sitagliptin itself first (−5.92 kcal/mol), followed by CHEMBL5951803 (−5.81). One candidate (CHEMBL1203953) was excluded at the ligand-preparation stage because its salt form presented as two fragments. Nothing in the DPP4 set meaningfully separates from the reference drug.

SGLT2 (22 bioactivities) proved more interesting. Dapagliflozin was rediscovered as CHEMBL429910 (similarity 1.0, IC₅₀ 0.49 nM). Docking against PDB 7VSI — the human SGLT2–MAP17 complex in an empagliflozin-bound conformation (cryo-EM, 2.95 Å; no X-ray structure exists for this membrane transporter, so the pipeline's X-ray preference was explicitly overridden) — ranked CHEMBL5288495 first at −7.03 kcal/mol, substantially ahead of dapagliflozin (−4.84). CHEMBL5288495 is a fluorinated dapagliflozin analog (MW 413, 0 Lipinski violations) with measured IC₅₀ 0.35 nM. Its docking margin over the reference (−2.19 kcal/mol) exceeds the observed run-to-run variability and was selected as the parent for the analog-design campaign (§3.5). SMILES: CCc1ccc(Cc2cc([C@@H]3O[C@H](CO)C(F)(F)[C@H](O)[C@H]3O)ccc2Cl)cc1.

3.4 E. coli DHFR (antibacterial)

Thirty-seven ligands were screened against E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (folA), a classic antibacterial target. Trimethoprim was rediscovered as CHEMBL22 (similarity 1.0, score 100.0, measured Kᵢ 0.22 nM). All top-ranked leads are 2,4-diaminopyrimidine trimethoprim analogs differing in phenyl-ring alkoxy/alkyl substitution — a chemical space explored for decades. Docking against PDB 9PWM (X-ray, 0.89 Å) gave CHEMBL278345 −5.66 kcal/mol versus trimethoprim −5.63 kcal/mol. A difference of 0.03 kcal/mol is within docking noise; this run is reported as a validation-grade result (the pipeline rediscovers the known drug and ranks close analogs sensibly), not a discovery.

3.5 SGLT2 novel-analog campaign

The design funnel is summarized in Table 2. Of 240 enumerated combinations, 200 were valid unique structures; 199 passed the novelty filter (<0.85 Tanimoto vs 23 known SGLT2 actives); all 199 passed ADMET filters; 12 were docked; 5 finalists were selected.
