3.2 Four derived numbers

1. The deuterium ladder. 3I/ATLAS water D/H (0.98%) is 62.9× VSMOW and 18.5× the water of comet 67P (5.3 × 10⁻⁴). Its methane D/H (3.18%) is 204× VSMOW. The entire measured Solar System comet water D/H range spans only 0.016–0.053% (103P/Hartley 2 to 67P); 3I/ATLAS sits 18.5× above the top of that range. There is no measured comet anywhere between 0.053% and 0.98% — a gap of a factor of 18.5 with zero occupants.

2. The same mechanism, running harder. Within 3I/ATLAS itself, methane is 3.24× more deuterated than water (3.18% / 0.98%). At 67P the same ratio is 4.62 (derived: 67P CH₄ D/H ≈ 0.24% from Roth et al.'s factor of 13 ± 2, divided by 67P water D/H of 0.053%). The two ratios agree within a factor of 1.4. This matters: whatever enriched 3I/ATLAS's ices enriched methane and water together, in the same proportion as in an ordinary Solar System comet — the process is the same, the magnitude is ~13–18× larger. Any model of 3I/ATLAS must explain both the absolute enrichment and the preserved CH₄/H₂O ratio; a model that produces the D/H values but the wrong ratio is falsified.

3. The carbon clock agrees with the deuterium thermometer. The ¹²C/¹³C ratios in 3I/ATLAS (123–191) exceed the solar value (~89) by 1.4–2.1×. Because ¹³C is a secondary nucleosynthesis product — it is made from pre-existing ¹²C in stars, so its Galactic abundance grows with time — a high ¹²C/¹³C ratio means formation when the Galaxy was younger and less enriched. This is an independent clock from the D/H thermometer, and it points the same way: Cordiner et al.'s Galactic chemical-evolution interpretation gives accretion as long ago as ~12 Gyr, and the independent kinematic estimate (thick-disk membership) gives 7.6–14 Gyr at 68% confidence (Hopkins et al. 2025). Two independent methods, one answer: this ice is roughly twice the age of the Solar System. The age is a model-dependent inference, not a measurement — see Limitations.

4. Two out of two active interstellar comets are CO-super-rich. 3I/ATLAS's December 2025 CO/H₂O ratio (2.40 ± 0.07) and Borisov's (≥1.73) both exceed the entire Solar System comet range (0.002–0.23) by an order of magnitude. The coma of 3I/ATLAS also evolved dramatically during its passage: CO₂/H₂O fell by a factor of ~7 between August and December 2025, while CO/CO₂ rose by a factor of ~10 — a CO₂-dominated coma becoming a CO-dominated one, with a likely H₂O-dominated phase around perihelion. The pattern is consistent with ices that formed beyond the CO snowline and were never thermally processed — the same cold story the isotopes tell.

3.3 The two-population model and its test

The observations define two bands in water D/H:

  • Cold-Core population: water D/H ≥ 0.3%, ¹²C/¹³C > 120. Ices formed at T ≲ 30 K in a prestellar core or the cold outer reaches of a metal-poor disk, then ejected with their fractionation intact. 3I/ATLAS is the sole member so far.
  • Warm-Disk population: water D/H ≤ 0.05%, ¹²C/¹³C < 100. Ices formed in a warmer disk where deuteration was modest — the Solar System comets, and, by hypothesis, interstellar comets ejected from similar disks. No interstellar member has yet been measured in this band.

Between them lies the gap band, 0.05–0.3% water D/H, which contains no measured comet of any origin. The model predicts it will stay nearly empty: the physics of deuteration is steep in temperature (H₂D⁺ chemistry switches on below ~30 K and the enrichment grows by orders of magnitude across a narrow temperature range), so a comet's ice either formed cold enough to be strongly enriched or it did not; intermediate values require a finely tuned formation temperature that disks rarely provide.

The test. The Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time is expected to discover 0.9–1.9 interstellar objects per year (Hoover et al. 2022) — roughly 5–10 by 2031 — with a September 2026 study estimating 0–8 cometary 3I-like objects in ten years. The next cometary interstellar object with a measured water D/H will either land in one of the two bands (model survives) or inside the 0.05–0.3% gap (model dies). Because the falsifier is a single measurement, the test is decidable by the very next object — it does not need a large sample. A secondary, joint test: a cold-band D/H (≥0.3%) must be accompanied by ¹²C/¹³C > 120; a cold-band D/H with ¹²C/¹³C < 100 would also kill the model, because it would break the link between the deuterium thermometer and the carbon clock.

4. Discussion

Comparison against the strongest incumbent. The incumbent explanation is the null: 3I/ATLAS is a single unusual object, and Solar System comets are representative of interstellar comets in general. That null is now strained on three independent axes at once. D/H: 18.5× above the Solar System range. ¹²C/¹³C: 1.4–2.1× above solar. CO/H₂O: >10× above the Solar System range, in two out of two active interstellar comets. A single outlier can be dismissed on one axis; the same direction of deviation on three axes, in two objects, is a pattern. The second incumbent is the processing hypothesis: that 3I/ATLAS's enrichment was produced after ejection, by cosmic-ray irradiation during billions of years in interstellar space, rather than at formation. Roth et al. themselves include high cosmic-ray irradiation in their interpretation, and irradiation certainly contributes — but irradiation alone, without cold formation, has no published model that reaches 3.18% methane D/H; the authors state explicitly that it is uncertain whether current models of either star formation or disk chemistry can reproduce the number. The processing hypothesis therefore remains open but unquantified, and it makes a different prediction: if irradiation dominates, D/H should correlate with time spent in interstellar space (kinematic age) rather than with formation environment — a test the next few objects can run.

Mechanism. Deuterium fractionation is driven by the ion–molecule reaction H₃⁺ + HD ⇌ H₂D⁺ + H₂, which is exothermic by ~230 K and therefore runs strongly forward only below ~30 K, enriching the gas in H₂D⁺ and, through subsequent chemistry, the ices that condense from it. Methane, which forms through a different chemical pathway from water, inherits a larger enrichment — hence CH₄ D/H exceeding H₂O D/H by a factor of ~3–5 in both 67P and 3I/ATLAS. Carbon isotopes work the other way: ¹²C is primary (made directly in stars), ¹³C is secondary (made from ¹²C), so the Galactic ¹²C/¹³C ratio falls with cosmic time as ¹³C accumulates. A comet with ¹²C/¹³C of 123–191 formed when that ratio was higher — earlier — than when the Sun formed (~89). The two mechanisms are independent, which is what makes their agreement informative.

Why this matters beyond one comet. Interstellar objects are the only direct samples of planet-forming material from other stars. If the Cold-Core population dominates — if most interstellar comets carry ices formed at ≲30 K in metal-poor environments — then the typical planetary system in the Galaxy formed from colder, older material than ours did, and the Solar System's relatively warm, well-mixed chemistry is the exception rather than the rule. That changes the priors for exoplanet atmosphere models, for the delivery of volatiles to young planets, and for the abundance of the prebiotic feedstock (deuterated organics) available to nascent biospheres.

5. Limitations

These limitations bite, and they are stated before any policy recommendation is drawn.

  1. n = 3 objects, n = 1 with water D/H. The entire two-population model rests on one measured interstellar water D/H and one measured interstellar methane D/H. The gap band could be a sampling artefact: the next object could land in it, and the model would fall. That is the point of stating the falsifier, not a reason to hide it.
  2. Single-epoch, single-instrument isotope measurements. The Roth et al. methane D/H rests on JWST/NIRSpec spectra from 22–23 December 2025; two of five background exposures failed because of field stars, so the spectra were extracted without background subtraction. The authors released their spectra and modelling scripts publicly, which mitigates this — but no independent repeat of the CH₃D measurement exists.
  3. The age is model-dependent. "As long ago as ~12 Gyr" (Cordiner et al.) and "7.6–14 Gyr" (Hopkins et al.) are inferences from Galactic chemical-evolution and kinematic population models, not measurements. The models depend on incomplete knowledge of star-formation history, gas flows and stellar yields, and the ¹²C/¹³C ratio also varies with distance from the Galactic centre. The comet's exact birthplace remains unknown, and its path cannot be traced back over billions of years.
  4. Selection bias. Only bright, active interstellar objects are detected. 1I/'Oumuamua showed no coma at all; if a large fraction of interstellar objects are dry and rocky, the cometary sample is biased toward the cold, volatile-rich end — exactly the population this paper calls "Cold-Core". The model describes interstellar comets, not interstellar objects in general, and the paper does not claim otherwise.
  5. The Islamic canon was not read in full. The classical works cited (Ibn al-Haytham's Kitab al-Manazir, Al-Biruni's Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi, Al-Battani's Kitab al-Zij, Al-Tusi's Tadhkira) were consulted through the programme's verified literature map, which records their dates, contents and availability; the full texts were not read for this paper. Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi has no complete modern English translation, and Kitab al-Zij survives in Arabic and Latin editions with only partial modern translations. Many classical Arabic astronomical manuscripts remain undigitised in libraries (Süleymaniye, Istanbul; Dar al-Kutub, Cairo; the British Library) with no online copy — the gap the programme's map names, and this paper names again. No claim is made to have read "every book"; the claim is to have used the relevant available canon and to have named what was not available.
  6. The bands are drawn from two data points. The Cold-Core/Warm-Disk boundary values (0.3% and 0.05%) are set by the observed gap, not derived from a physical model of disk chemistry. A quantitative disk-chemistry model that predicts the band edges from first principles is the obvious next step and is not attempted here.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker 1 — ESA and NASA (Comet Interceptor, launch 2029). Comet Interceptor will wait at the Sun–Earth L2 point for a dynamically new comet or an interstellar object, then fly by it. Exact change: the mission's target-selection criteria should explicitly prioritise an interstellar target over a dynamically new Solar System comet when one is available, and its payload operations plan should include an isotope-measurement mode (mass-spectrometer D/H and ¹²C/¹³C) as a Level-1 science requirement, not an opportunistic add-on. Why: a single flyby D/H measurement decides the two-population test years before Rubin accumulates a sample. Falsifier: if the flyby measures a gap-band D/H, the two-population model is abandoned and the mission's isotope requirement is downgraded. Islamic principle: hifz al-'aql — preservation of the intellect; the Qur'an asks "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" (39:9), and seeking knowledge of the heavens is presented as a duty, not a luxury (51:47; 67:3–5).

Decision-maker 2 — SUPARCO and Pakistan's Ministry of Science & Technology. Pakistan has no interstellar-object follow-up capacity. Exact change: (a) subscribe the national space agency to the Rubin Observatory alert stream and designate one astronomer as the interstellar-object duty scientist; (b) fund one PhD studentship in planetary science (spectroscopy of small bodies) at a Pakistani university, with the thesis topic fixed to interstellar-object follow-up. Cost: one studentship and one alert-stream subscription — orders of magnitude cheaper than a telescope. Why: the test in this paper will be decided in the 2030s by whoever measures the next objects; a country that only reads the results is a spectator. Falsifier: if the two-population model is killed by a gap-band measurement, the studentship's topic pivots to the replacement model — the capacity, not the hypothesis, is the investment.

Decision-maker 3 — the JWST and Hubble time-allocation committees. 3I/ATLAS is receding and fading; its three JWST epochs may remain the most detailed look at its ice for years. Exact change: approve Director's Discretionary Time for rapid-response NIRSpec follow-up of the next interstellar comet within two weeks of discovery, before perihelion, so that inbound (cold, unprocessed) ices are measured rather than only outbound ones. Why: the August 2025 (inbound, 3.32 au) and December 2025 (outbound, 2.4 au) spectra of 3I/ATLAS already show the coma changing by factors of 7–10; inbound data are the cleaner record of formation conditions.

7. Conclusion

3I/ATLAS gave us the first isotopes ever measured in material from another planetary system, and they are extreme: methane D/H of (3.18 ± 0.30)%, water D/H of (0.98 ± 0.06)%, ¹²C/¹³C of 123–191. Our synthesis adds four numbers — 63× VSMOW, 18.5× 67P, a CH₄/H₂O D/H ratio of 3.24 that matches 67P's within a factor of 1.4, and a CO/H₂O ratio above the entire Solar System range in two out of two active interstellar comets — and one testable claim: interstellar comets come in two formation populations, Cold-Core and Warm-Disk, separated by an empty gap band in water D/H (0.05–0.3%). The next cometary interstellar object with a measured water D/H will confirm the model or kill it with a single number. That is the standard this programme holds itself to: a paper is finished when a telescope can prove it wrong. The Rubin Observatory, discovering roughly one to two interstellar objects a year, will run that test within the decade — and the observatories, agencies and countries that prepare for it now will be the ones that read the answer first.

The memorable number: 3.18% — one hydrogen atom in every thirty-one in the methane of 3I/ATLAS is deuterium, the highest methane D/H ever measured.

8. Data availability

All data used are published measurements, listed with full citations in Table 1 and the References. Derived numbers (enrichment factors, ratios, gap-band boundaries) are arithmetic on those published values and are reproducible from the numbers printed in this paper; the Python calculation is retained in the run log. JWST spectra and modelling scripts for the Roth et al. measurement are publicly released through the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes and Zenodo, as reported by the authors. No new observations, no proprietary data, no unpublished results.

Pinning the Cosmic Shoreline with JWST: LTT 1445 A b and c Are Airless Above the Line, LHS 1140 b Keeps Its Helium Below It

Two results published in November 2026 test the cosmic shoreline — the I ∝ v_esc^4 boundary that separates rocky planets with atmospheres from airless worlds — from opposite sides.

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan — ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-14 Field: Space (astronomy / exoplanet atmospheres)

Abstract

Two results published in November 2026 test the cosmic shoreline — the I ∝ v_esc^4 boundary that separates rocky planets with atmospheres from airless worlds — from opposite sides. The JWST Rocky Worlds programme reports MIRI/F1500W secondary eclipses of LTT 1445 A b and c (Ih et al., arXiv:2611.17300): eclipse depths of 157(+18/−17) and 154(+54/−37) ppm give 15-µm brightness temperatures of 528(+39/−29) K and 625(+109/−79) K, both consistent with dark bare rock; for b, CO2 partial pressure is <0.6 mbar and surface pressure ≲0.1 bar. LTT 1445 A b is the closest planet to the shoreline yet observed in eclipse. In the same week, ground-based spectroscopy reported metastable helium escaping from the habitable-zone super-Earth LHS 1140 b in 2024 but not in 2025 (Cherubim et al., Science 2026), while four JWST NIRISS transits rule out helium at the reported level (Radica 2026; Bennett et al. 2026). We place all three planets on the classical Mars-anchored XUV shoreline, I_XUV = (a⊕/a)^2 (L*/L⊙)^0.4, and find LTT 1445 A b 2.3× above the line, LTT 1445 A c 11.9× above it, and LHS 1140 b 8.5× below it — every planet on its predicted side. The two results bracket the shoreline zero point to log10 I_XUV = 4 log10 v_esc + D with D in [−4.10, −2.81], against the canonical −3.17. We state this as a falsifiable claim: any substantial atmosphere found on a rocky planet more than 0.36 dex above the classical line, or any bare rock more than 0.93 dex below it, falsifies the classical zero point; simultaneous ground- and space-based helium transits of LHS 1140 b will decide whether its lower bound stands.

Keywords: exoplanet atmospheres; cosmic shoreline; atmospheric escape; JWST; M dwarfs; LTT 1445; LHS 1140 b; helium

1. Introduction

Which rocky planets keep their atmospheres? The question decides where habitable worlds can exist, and for a decade the organising idea has been the "cosmic shoreline" of Zahnle & Catling (2017): when Solar System bodies are arranged by escape velocity (v_esc) against the radiation they receive, a single straight line of slope four on logarithmic axes, I ∝ v_esc^4, separates the bodies with atmospheres from those without. The line is now the target-selection metric for the largest rocky-atmosphere survey ever attempted — the JWST Rocky Worlds Director's Discretionary Time (DDT) programme, 500 hours of JWST time plus 240 Hubble orbits, which uses secondary-eclipse photometry to test, planet by planet, whether rocky worlds around M dwarfs retain atmospheres (Ji et al. 2025).

Two results published within days of each other in November 2026 test the shoreline from opposite sides, and both concern the nearest rocky systems known. First, the Rocky Worlds programme reports MIRI/F1500W (15 µm) secondary eclipses of LTT 1445 A b and c, the transiting rocky siblings in the nearest M-dwarf system (6.9 pc): both planets are consistent with dark bare rock, and planet b — the closest planet to the canonical XUV-driven shoreline yet observed in eclipse — has no substantial atmosphere (Ih et al. 2026). Second, ground-based high-resolution spectroscopy reports metastable helium escaping from LHS 1140 b, a temperate super-Earth in the habitable zone of its M dwarf, detected in 2024 but not in 2025 (Cherubim et al. 2026), while four archival JWST NIRISS transits spanning December 2023 to July 2026 find no helium absorption at the reported level (Radica 2026; Bennett et al. 2026) — a dispute covered the same week in Nature Astronomy (Maltagliati 2026).

This paper does the quantitative step neither result takes on its own: it places all three planets on the same classical shoreline, using the published cumulative-XUV scaling, and derives the numerical bracket the two results jointly impose on the shoreline's zero point. The shoreline's slope is fixed by energy-limited escape physics; its height — the zero point — was set in 2017 by a single Solar System anchor, Mars, and has never been tested by exoplanets on both sides at once. These three planets now test it from both sides.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

The daily research digest for 2026-11-14 (health-focused; no space entries) was read, and targeted searches were run on arXiv (astro-ph.EP) and in the press for exoplanet-atmosphere results dated 10–14 November 2026. Every cited result was verified against its arXiv record or publisher page: the LTT 1445 paper (arXiv:2611.17300, submitted 12 November 2026), the LHS 1140 b helium detection (arXiv:2607.14326) and its two JWST follow-ups (arXiv:2608.13470; arXiv:2608.13473), and the Nature Astronomy News & Views piece (DOI 10.1038/s41550-026-03029-8, published 13 November 2026). No citation, number, or identifier in this manuscript is invented; where a number is our own derivation, the formula and inputs are shown in full.

2.2 The shoreline calculation (own analysis)

Escape velocity. v_esc = √(2GM_p/R_p), computed from published masses and radii relative to Earth (v_esc,⊕ = 11.186 km/s).

Cumulative XUV instellation. Following Zahnle & Catling (2017, Eq. 27), as restated by Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026):

I_XUV = (a⊕ / a)^2 × (L* / L⊙)^0.4

in Earth units, where a is the planet's semi-major axis and L* the stellar luminosity. This is the total stellar XUV flux integrated over the planet's lifetime, not the present-day bolometric insolation — the distinction matters for M dwarfs, whose long pre-main-sequence and flare activity make their cumulative XUV far larger than their present-day brightness suggests.

Shoreline and zero point. The classical shoreline is log10 I_XUV = 4 log10 v_esc + D. The zero point D was fixed by Zahnle & Catling by assuming Mars marks the boundary between worlds with and without atmospheres. We adopt that convention exactly: the shoreline passes through Mars's (v_esc, I_XUV) point, giving D = −3.17 (Mars: v_esc = 5.03 km/s, a = 1.524 AU, L* = L⊙, I_XUV = 0.43). A planet's shoreline distance is Δ = log10(I_XUV / I_XUV,shore), positive above the line (airless side), negative below it (retaining side).

Dayside temperature scale. For reference, the maximum dayside temperature for instant reradiation with zero albedo is T_day,max = T_eq × 4^(1/4), where T_eq is the zero-albedo equilibrium temperature. The observed 15-µm brightness temperature is a band temperature, not a bolometric dayside temperature, so ratios against T_day,max are reported as a scale comparison only; the papers' own conclusion ("consistent with the dark, bare rock limit") is what we rely on.

Inputs. LTT 1445 A b/c masses, radii, semi-major axes, instellations and equilibrium temperatures are from Pass et al. (2023, HST/WFC3 joint fit): b, M = 2.73 M⊕, R = 1.34 R⊕, a = 0.03813 AU, S = 5.7 S⊕, T_eq = 431 K; c, M = 1.37 ± 0.19 M⊕, R = 1.07 R⊕, a = 0.02659 AU, S = 11.7 S⊕, T_eq = 516 K; stellar luminosity L* = 0.00805 L⊙. LHS 1140 b uses the most precise values to date (Cherubim et al. 2026): M = 5.60 ± 0.19 M⊕, R = 1.730 ± 0.025 R⊕; with system parameters from Ment et al. (2019): a = 0.0936 AU, L* = 0.00441 L⊙, S = 0.503 S⊕, T_eq = 230 K. All arithmetic was computed in Python 3 and is reproducible from the formulae above.

Robustness checks. (i) Using the earlier Winters et al. (2022) masses and radii for LTT 1445 A b/c (M = 2.87/1.54 M⊕, R = 1.305/1.147 R⊕) changes the shoreline ratios from 2.29 to 1.96 (b) and 11.91 to 10.83 (c) — no conclusion changes. (ii) Pass et al. (2025), as summarised by Ji et al. (2025), revised cumulative XUV fluxes for mid-to-late M dwarfs upward by roughly a factor of 3 (pre-main-sequence plus flares); we repeat the calculation with I_XUV × 3 as a sensitivity test.

3. Results

3.1 LTT 1445 A b and c: bare rock at the shoreline

Ih et al. (2026) present Rocky Worlds DDT MIRI/F1500W observations of LTT 1445 A b and c — two eclipses of each planet across three visits — with three independent reductions and a joint fit including all existing JWST data and 220 radial velocities, improving the precision on planetary radii, masses, and orbital parameters by factors of 1.6–2.3. They measure eclipse depths of 157(+18/−17) ppm (b) and 154(+54/−37) ppm (c), corresponding to 15-µm brightness temperatures of 528(+39/−29) K and 625(+109/−79) K, both consistent with the dark, bare-rock limit. For planet b, combining these data with the archival MIRI/LRS spectrum in a Bayesian retrieval limits the CO2 partial pressure to <0.6 mbar and the surface pressure to ≲0.1 bar, while forward models exclude thick aerosol layers that could mimic a bare surface in transmission; the authors conclude planet b has no substantial atmosphere. For planet c, a potentially grazing eclipse and overlapping events leave the depth poorly constrained, and the data rule out only thick, CO2-bearing atmospheres (≳1 bar with ≥1% CO2). The paper states explicitly that LTT 1445 A b is the planet closest to the canonical XUV-driven Cosmic Shoreline observed in eclipse so far, and that its lack of a substantial atmosphere implies the shoreline cannot lie much farther toward the airless side than nominally predicted. This agrees with the earlier MIRI/LRS spectrum (Wachiraphan et al. 2025), which found a dayside brightness temperature of 525 ± 15 K and excluded >1 bar CO2 atmospheres at >4σ, and with the climate-constrained Bayesian analysis of Wogan et al. (2026), which found the bare-rock model moderately favoured over any atmospheric model (2σ upper limits ≲1 bar for O2/N2/CO, ≲0.1 bar for CO2).

3.2 LHS 1140 b: helium detected, then not — and JWST says no

Cherubim et al. (2026) observed LHS 1140 b with the WINERED high-resolution spectrograph on the Magellan Clay Telescope. In a transit on 23 September 2024 they detected excess absorption at the 1.083 µm metastable helium triplet: 1.24(+0.22/−0.23)% depth at the blended long-wavelength peaks, with FWHM 0.86 Å (23.9 km/s), interpreted as helium escaping from the upper atmosphere — the first evidence of an atmosphere, albeit a primordial one, around a rocky world in the classical habitable zone. A repeat transit in September 2025 showed no helium absorption, with an upper limit of 0.6% on the line depth, indicating time-variable escape; no helium was detected for the smaller, more irradiated sibling LHS 1140 c. The authors interpret the result as an upper atmosphere dominated by helium and depleted in hydrogen, consistent with atmospheric fractionation models.

Two independent JWST analyses challenge the persistence of that signal. Radica (2026) analyses four archival NIRISS/SOSS transits spanning December 2023 to July 2026: each visit disfavours helium absorption against a flat continuum with odds ratios of 3.9–11.6:1, and helium at the amplitude and width reported by Cherubim et al. is strongly ruled out, with odds ratios of 300–8.6×10^4:1 — though none of the JWST transits is contemporaneous with the ground-based detection — setting an abundance upper limit of 350–500 ppm. Bennett et al. (2026) likewise detect no helium in any of the four visits, reject the best-fit ground-based model at >3σ in each visit, and find no clear trend in mass loss with time; they conclude the reported detection may be spurious, although variability cannot be excluded if detectable helium absorption occurs in ≲50% of transits. Maltagliati (2026), in Nature Astronomy, frames the episode as "helium peekaboo": the first helium-escape claim for a habitable-zone rocky planet, contradicted in every JWST epoch so far.

3.3 Our calculation: three planets, three shoreline distances, one bracket

Table 1 gives the shoreline positions computed by §2.2. All three planets fall exactly on their predicted sides: the two planets above the line are airless, and the planet below the line shows (at least in one epoch) an escaping atmosphere.

Table 1. Shoreline positions of the three newly measured rocky planets (own calculation from published inputs).

Planet v_esc (km/s) I_XUV (Earth units) I_XUV,shore Ratio Δ (dex) JWST / ground verdict
LTT 1445 A b 15.97 99.95 43.71 2.29 +0.36 Airless (CO2 < 0.6 mbar)
LTT 1445 A c 12.66 205.53 17.26 11.91 +1.08 Thick CO2 ruled out
LHS 1140 b 20.13 13.04 110.34 0.12 −0.93 He escape reported 2024; JWST rules it out in 4/4 transits

The two results jointly bracket the shoreline zero point. Planet b's airlessness requires the shoreline at v_esc = 15.97 km/s to sit at or below I_XUV = 99.95, i.e. D ≤ −2.81: the zero point cannot be more than a factor 2.29 above its canonical Mars-anchored value (D = −3.17). LHS 1140 b's reported atmosphere requires the shoreline at v_esc = 20.13 km/s to sit at or above I_XUV = 13.04, i.e. D ≥ −4.10: the zero point cannot be more than a factor 8.46 below canonical. The allowed interval is therefore D ∈ [−4.10, −2.81], a factor-of-19.4 band that contains the canonical value with room on both sides — but with a hard, new upper edge set by the closest-to-the-line airless planet ever measured in eclipse.

The Pass et al. (2025) 3× XUV revision, applied as a sensitivity test, moves all three ratios up by a factor of 3 (b: 6.86, c: 35.72, LHS 1140 b: 0.35) and flips none of the three classifications: LHS 1140 b remains below the line even under the revised fluence. The dayside-temperature scale is consistent throughout: T_b/T_day,max = 0.866 (b) and 0.856 (c), with T_b/T_eq = 1.23 and 1.21 — hot daysides with no sign of the heat redistribution a substantial atmosphere would provide (with the §2.2 caveat that 15-µm brightness temperature is a band temperature).

3.4 The falsifiable claim

Claim. The classical Mars-anchored XUV cosmic shoreline (log10 I_XUV = 4 log10 v_esc − 3.17) correctly separates airless from atmosphere-bearing rocky planets, with zero point D ∈ [−4.10, −2.81]: LTT 1445 A b (Δ = +0.36 dex) and c (Δ = +1.08 dex) are airless, and LHS 1140 b (Δ = −0.93 dex) retains an atmosphere.

How to test it. (i) The Rocky Worlds programme will eclipse roughly a dozen more rocky planets. The shoreline predicts that every planet with Δ > +0.36 dex — further above the line than LTT 1445 A b — will be airless, and every planet with Δ < −0.93 dex will show an atmosphere signature. A single substantial atmosphere found above +0.36 dex, or a single bare rock found below −0.93 dex, falsifies the classical zero point (and, if the counterexample sits far from the line, the slope as well), forcing a move toward the steeper empirical shoreline of Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026) or the hydrodynamic shoreline of Ji et al. (2025). (ii) The lower bound stands or falls with the reality of LHS 1140 b's helium: a simultaneous WINERED + JWST NIRISS transit campaign will decide it. If helium at the 2024 level (1.24%) reappears in both instruments at once, variability is real and the lower bound D ≥ −4.10 stands; if JWST rules it out again while ground data show it, the discrepancy is systematic, the lower bound must be re-derived from transmission data alone, and the shoreline's retaining side loses its only habitable-zone anchor.

4. Discussion

The value of this result is not that the shoreline survives — it was designed to survive these three planets — but that the shoreline is now a measured, bracketed quantity rather than a single-anchor extrapolation. Before November 2026, the zero point rested on Mars alone: one planet, with a 6-mbar remnant atmosphere, sitting essentially on the line. Now the upper edge is set by an exoplanet: LTT 1445 A b is the first airless world measured in eclipse close enough to the line to matter, and its distance from the line (+0.36 dex) is the tightest exoplanet constraint on how far the shoreline can move toward the airless side. The lower edge is set by LHS 1140 b, the only temperate rocky planet with a claimed escaping atmosphere, 0.93 dex below the line.

Three features of the bracket deserve emphasis. First, it is asymmetric: the shoreline is pinned 2.3× from above but 8.5× from below, because the airless side now has a near-line calibrator while the retaining side has only one planet, far below the line, whose atmosphere is itself disputed. The most valuable next measurement is therefore not another far-above-the-line bare rock — the Rocky Worlds programme already has several (TRAPPIST-1 b and c, GJ 3929b, GJ 367b) — but a planet just below the line, which would tighten the lower edge the way LTT 1445 A b tightened the upper one. Second, the bracket is robust to the largest known systematic: tripling the cumulative XUV fluence for M dwarfs, as Pass et al. (2025) propose, changes no classification, because the three planets sit far enough from the line in ratio space (2.3×, 11.9×, 8.5×) that a factor-3 shift cannot cross them. Third, the bracket is compatible with, but does not require, the two 2025–2026 revisions of the shoreline: the steeper empirical shoreline of Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026), anchored to Mars plus four exoplanets with tentative atmospheric detections, and the hydrodynamic shoreline of Ji et al. (2025), which finds that varying the initial volatile inventory (0.01%–1% of planetary mass) blurs any single line. Both revisions predict that the classical line is an approximation; our bracket quantifies how good an approximation it is, and §3.4 gives the observations that would break it.

The LHS 1140 b dispute also carries a methodological lesson. The ground-based detection and the JWST non-detections are not yet in direct conflict, because no JWST transit was contemporaneous with the ground-based detection, and Bennett et al. show variability below a ~50% duty cycle is still allowed. But the episode shows that single-epoch helium claims for rocky planets are now in the regime where a claimed atmosphere can be challenged within months by archival data — the standard of evidence for "this rocky planet has an atmosphere" has risen, and the shoreline's lower bound should be treated as provisional until a simultaneous campaign settles it.

5. Limitations

  1. No new data. This is a synthesis and analytic re-derivation from published results; the shoreline positions are calculations, not measurements.
  2. Mars anchoring. The zero point D = −3.17 assumes Mars marks the boundary, following Zahnle & Catling (2017). Mars has a 6-mbar atmosphere, so whether it sits just above or just below the line is a judgement call in the original paper; shifting the anchor by Mars's own ambiguity moves D by ≲0.1 dex, small against the bracket width.
  3. The I_XUV scaling is a proxy. The (L*/L⊙)^0.4 scaling compresses stellar XUV evolution, pre-main-sequence duration, and flare history into one exponent; the Pass et al. (2025) 3× revision is tested as a sensitivity case, but the true fluence for any individual M dwarf is uncertain by factors of a few.
  4. Slope fixed at 4. We test the classical slope; the steeper empirical slope of Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026) would change the bracket, and is itself falsifiable by the same test in §3.4.
  5. Band temperatures. The 15-µm brightness temperatures are not bolometric dayside temperatures; the T_b/T_day,max ratios are a scale comparison only.
  6. The lower bound is conditional. D ≥ −4.10 assumes the Cherubim et al. (2026) helium detection is genuine. If it is spurious, the lower bound weakens to whatever JWST transmission data support for LHS 1140 b (a water-world or thin-atmosphere interpretation), and the bracket's lower edge must be re-derived.
  7. Small numbers. Three planets bracket a line; the test in §3.4 is the point — the bracket will tighten or break as the Rocky Worlds programme reports its remaining targets.
  8. Research agents. The installed research agents (Co-Scientist, Denario, EvoScientist) remain blocked on authentication — they need a real API key in the Authorization header, which this run does not hold — and Mimosa's literature-synthesis run is blocked on an unresolved MCP-discovery stall; the literature sweep and analysis here were therefore done directly from the daily digest and targeted arXiv checks.

6. Conclusion

In a single week, JWST and ground-based spectroscopy bracketed the cosmic shoreline from both sides. LTT 1445 A b — the closest planet to the line yet observed in eclipse — is airless, with CO2 below 0.6 mbar and surface pressure below 0.1 bar; its sibling c is airless too. LHS 1140 b, 0.93 dex below the line, shows escaping helium in one epoch and none in four JWST transits. Our re-derivation puts numbers on what those results mean together: the shoreline's zero point lies in D ∈ [−4.10, −2.81], no more than 2.3× above and 8.5× below its canonical Mars-anchored value. The next Rocky Worlds eclipses and a simultaneous helium transit campaign for LHS 1140 b will either tighten that bracket or break the classical line — and either outcome is progress, because the shoreline is now a falsifiable, measured quantity instead of a sketch anchored on Mars alone.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan — ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-11 Field: Space (astronomy / gravitational-wave astrophysics)

Abstract

Two results published within days of each other in November 2026 bracket the black-hole mass spectrum from opposite ends. At the stellar-mass end, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration's black-hole spectroscopy of GW250114 — the loudest gravitational-wave signal recorded to date, network signal-to-noise ratio 76 — requires at least two quasi-normal modes in the ringdown, constrains the dominant quadrupolar mode and its first overtone to match the Kerr prediction to tens of percent, and bounds the quadrupolar frequency to within a few percent of general relativity, delivering the most stringent single-event test of general relativity to date. At the supermassive end, the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array Collaboration reports the first direct nanohertz gravitational-wave limits on supermassive black-hole binaries at cosmic dawn (Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 191401, 2 November 2026), with a best all-sky chirp-mass upper limit of 8.47 × 10^9 solar masses and sensitivity mapped to redshift ~20 after correcting for a redshift bias earlier work ignored. We combine the two results into a single quantitative test. Treating the 1.2 × 10^10 solar-mass black hole in the quasar J0100+2802 (z = 6.327) as a hypothetical equal-mass binary gives a chirp mass of 5.22 × 10^9 solar masses — a factor of 1.62 below the current best pulsar-timing limit and a factor of 1.91 below the ~10^10 solar-mass exclusion quoted for that source, matching the published statement that the limits come within a factor of ~2 of the quasar's mass. A chirp-mass sensitivity improvement of a factor of ~1.6, equivalent to a factor of ~2.2 in strain, would therefore cross the threshold for this source. We state this as a falsifiable claim: if J0100+2802 assembled through a recent equal-mass merger, combined International Pulsar Timing Array data and Square Kilometre Array-era timing will detect its nanohertz signal or exclude the equal-mass binary configuration; a continued null at that sensitivity rules out the equal-mass merger origin and favours heavy-seed direct collapse or super-Eddington accretion. (Abstract: 2,110 characters.)

Keywords: gravitational waves; black-hole spectroscopy; quasi-normal modes; pulsar timing arrays; supermassive black holes; cosmic dawn; GW250114; J0100+2802

1. Introduction

Black holes are now empirical objects, studied with telescopes and gravitational-wave detectors alike, but one question remains open: how did the supermassive black holes — millions to billions of solar masses — assemble? The debate reduces to three options: black holes started massive (heavy seeds, e.g. direct collapse of a massive gas cloud), grew massive (sustained rapid accretion, possibly super-Eddington), or built up through mergers. The James Webb Space Telescope has sharpened the problem by finding luminous quasars powered by billion-solar-mass black holes less than a billion years after the Big Bang, and an unexpected abundance of luminous "little red dots" at redshifts around z = 10, corresponding to a cosmic age of about 500 million years, some of which may be active black holes as massive as 10^8 solar masses.

Two observational windows now constrain this problem from opposite ends of the mass scale, and both produced landmark results in the same week. At the stellar-mass end, gravitational-wave ringdown spectroscopy tests whether a merger remnant is a Kerr black hole of general relativity, mode by mode. At the supermassive end, pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) search for the nanohertz gravitational waves emitted by slowly orbiting supermassive binaries. Until November 2026, PTA limits applied only to the local Universe (z < 0.4); the new work extends them to cosmic dawn. This paper synthesises the two results and derives, from published numbers alone, the exact sensitivity gap that separates a null result from a decisive test of how the earliest quasars were built.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

The daily research digest for 2026-11-11 (health-focused; no space entries) was read, and targeted searches were run on arXiv (gr-qc, astro-ph) and in the press for gravitational-wave results dated 1–11 November 2026. Every cited result was verified against its publisher or arXiv record: the GW250114 spectroscopy paper (arXiv:2509.08099; Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 041403, 2026) and its companion area-law paper (Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 111403, 2025); the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array cosmic-dawn paper (arXiv:2609.00613; Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 191401, published 2 November 2026) and the accompanying Physics viewpoint (Physics 19, 146, 2026). No citation, number, or identifier in this manuscript is invented; where a number is our own derivation, the formula and inputs are shown in full.

2.2 Analytic methods (own calculations)

Chirp mass of a hypothetical equal-mass binary. For component masses m1 and m2, the chirp mass is M_c = (m1·m2)^(3/5) / (m1 + m2)^(1/5). For an equal-mass binary with each component m, this reduces to M_c = m / 2^(1/5) = m / 1.1487. Applied to J0100+2802, whose black-hole mass is estimated at 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses: splitting that mass into an equal-mass pair (m = 6.0 × 10^9 solar masses each) gives M_c = 5.22 × 10^9 solar masses.

Gap factors. The best published all-sky chirp-mass upper limit is 8.47 × 10^9 solar masses, and the exclusion quoted for the two cosmic-dawn targets is ~10^10 solar masses. The ratios 8.47 × 10^9 / 5.22 × 10^9 = 1.62 and 10^10 / 5.22 × 10^9 = 1.91 quantify how far current sensitivity is from testing the equal-mass binary hypothesis for J0100+2802.

Strain-sensitivity equivalent. For a binary at fixed distance and frequency, gravitational-wave strain scales as h ∝ M_c^(5/3). A chirp-mass reach improvement of a factor 1.62 therefore requires a strain-sensitivity improvement of 1.62^(5/3) ≈ 2.2.

Frequency scale. A binary orbiting about once per year emits gravitational waves at f_GW = 2 / P_orb ≈ 63 nHz in the observer frame. At the redshift of J0100+2802 (z = 6.327), the source-frame frequency is higher by (1 + z): ≈ 63 × 7.327 ≈ 464 nHz — the redshift brightening that makes distant sources counterintuitively easier for PTAs to see, because the observed signal comes from a later, tighter, more luminous stage of the inspiral.

All arithmetic was computed in Python 3 and is reproducible from the formulae above.

3. Results

3.1 GW250114: the loudest signal becomes the sharpest test of general relativity

GW250114 was recorded by the LIGO detectors on 14 January 2025 (Virgo and KAGRA were offline), with a network signal-to-noise ratio of 76 — the loudest gravitational-wave signal to date. Independent analyses agree on the source: two nearly equal-mass, low-spin, first-generation black holes of roughly 34 and 32 solar masses (mass ratio ≈ 0.94), with eccentricity e ≤ 0.03 at 13.33 Hz, forming a remnant inside the pair-instability mass gap. The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA spectroscopy analysis finds:

  • At least two quasi-normal modes are required to explain the post-merger signal: the dominant quadrupolar (ℓ = m = 2, n = 0) mode and its first overtone (n = 1), the most damped of which remains statistically significant for about one cycle. The overtone is supported at 3.6σ in the standard analysis, rising to 99.9% significance with orthonormalised modes.
  • The spectroscopic pattern of the dominant mode and its first overtone matches the Kerr prediction to tens of percent at multiple post-peak times; the fundamental (ℓ = m = 4) mode is constrained to tens of percent, and the quadrupolar frequency is bounded to within a few percent of the general-relativistic prediction.
  • A suite of inspiral, merger, and ringdown tests gives constraints comparable to — and in some cases 2–3 times more stringent than — those obtained by combining dozens of events in the fourth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog: the most stringent single-event verification of general relativity and the Kerr nature of black holes to date.
  • The companion analysis strongly favours a final horizon area larger than the sum of the initial areas, a direct test of Hawking's area law.
  • Independent follow-up analyses confirm subdominant (4, ±4) multipoles with higher evidence than the Collaboration first reported, find the quadratic (2,2,0)×(2,2,0) mode coupling consistent with numerical relativity to within 1.3σ, and recover the general-relativistic expectation for the remnant mass and spin within the 50% credible region.

3.2 The Parkes Pulsar Timing Array reaches cosmic dawn

Chen et al. (2026) reformulate pulsar-timing searches with a cosmological correction — the redshift bias — that earlier work ignored. Because a distant binary's observed frequency is redshifted, the signal seen in the nanohertz PTA band originates from a higher source-frame frequency, i.e. a later, tighter, more luminous stage of inspiral; this intrinsic brightening can outpace cosmological dimming, making PTAs counterintuitively more sensitive to faraway sources. Using Parkes Pulsar Timing Array data with this correction, they:

  • Map PTA sensitivity to binary mass and redshift from the local Universe out to z ~ 20 for the first time (previous work stopped at z < 0.4).
  • Set a best all-sky chirp-mass upper limit of 8.47 × 10^9 solar masses.
  • Anchor the limits on two electromagnetically detected cosmic-dawn sources: the quasar J0100+2802 (z = 6.327; black-hole mass ≈ 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses; its light left when the Universe was barely 900 million years old) and the galaxy JADES-GS-z14-0 (z = 14.32; only ~290 million years after the Big Bang). For both, binaries with chirp masses at or above ~10^10 solar masses are excluded across the nanohertz band — the tightest constraints to date on supermassive binaries at z > 6, and the first constraints of any kind at the redshift of JADES-GS-z14-0.
  • Show the Parkes observations are not yet sensitive enough to test whether either system is a binary, but the limits come close — within a factor of ~2 of the quasar's estimated mass.

3.3 Our calculation: the gap is a factor of 1.6 in chirp mass

Applying the method of §2.2 to J0100+2802 (Table 1), a hypothetical equal-mass binary totalling the quasar's estimated 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses has a chirp mass of 5.22 × 10^9 solar masses. This sits a factor of 1.62 below the best published all-sky limit (8.47 × 10^9 solar masses) and a factor of 1.91 below the ~10^10 solar-mass exclusion quoted for the source — quantitatively reproducing the published "within a factor of ~2" statement from first principles, and showing that the two published numbers (best limit vs target exclusion) are mutually consistent. Reaching this binary requires a strain-sensitivity improvement of only a factor of ~2.2, the scale of improvement expected from combining International Pulsar Timing Array data and from Square Kilometre Array-era timing precision.

3.4 The falsifiable claim

Claim. If the 1.2 × 10^10 solar-mass black hole in J0100+2802 assembled through a recent equal-mass merger, then a pulsar-timing chirp-mass sensitivity improvement of a factor of ~1.6 (≈ 2.2× in strain) will detect its nanohertz gravitational-wave signal or exclude the equal-mass binary configuration.

How to test it. (i) Apply the redshift-corrected analysis of Chen et al. to the next International Pulsar Timing Array data release and to Square Kilometre Array-era timing; a detection at ~63 nHz from the direction of J0100+2802 confirms the binary. (ii) A continued null at the improved sensitivity excludes an equal-mass binary totalling 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses at z = 6.327, and thereby rules out the equal-mass merger origin for this quasar, leaving heavy-seed direct collapse or super-Eddington accretion as the remaining explanations. (iii) Corollary at the stellar-mass end: if the Kerr hypothesis holds, the (2,2,1) overtone amplitude measured in the next signal-to-noise-ratio ≳ 50 binary black-hole event will match the numerical-relativity prediction within the same tens-of-percent band established by GW250114; a systematic deviation across events would falsify Kerr.

4. Discussion

The two results are complementary in a precise sense. GW250114 shows that general relativity and the Kerr metric survive their most stringent single-event examination: the remnant's ringing matches Kerr mode by mode, the area law holds, and no discrepancy appears in any of inspiral, merger, or ringdown. That licenses the use of general-relativistic waveforms to interpret the nanohertz sky. The Parkes result then uses that same physics at the opposite end of the spectrum: a galaxy-sized detector made of pulsars, sensitive to binaries orbiting about once a year, now reaches the epoch in which the first quasars turned on.

The scientific payoff is a dated, quantitative fork in the road for seed models. Heavy seeds (direct collapse of ~10^5 solar-mass clouds) predict that a quasar like J0100+2802 need never have been an equal-mass binary of two ~6 × 10^9 solar-mass holes; light seeds grown by mergers predict binary phases. Our calculation puts the fork within reach: a factor of ~2 in strain, not an order of magnitude. The redshift-bias correction is what makes this possible — without it, the sensitivity at z > 6 would be underestimated and the test would look decades away. Two further points strengthen the case: first, the same redshift brightening applies to JADES-GS-z14-0, so the method's first constraints at z = 14.32 are a floor, not a ceiling; second, the nanohertz gravitational-wave background detected by PTA collaborations in 2023 guarantees a population of supermassive binaries exists in the local Universe, so the question is now where in mass and redshift that population extends.

At the stellar-mass end, GW250114 also changes the economics of testing gravity: one event at signal-to-noise ratio 76 now constrains general relativity 2–3 times more tightly than dozens of earlier events combined. The implication for the next observing runs is that ringdown spectroscopy should be treated as a primary science goal, not a follow-up, and that the (4,4) mode and quadratic mode couplings are now measurable quantities with which to stress-test numerical relativity.

5. Limitations

  1. No new data. This is a synthesis and analytic re-derivation from published results; the chirp-mass and strain figures are calculations, not measurements.
  2. The binary hypothesis for J0100+2802 is hypothetical. There is no evidence that J0100+2802 is a binary; the calculation tests what PTAs could say if it were. The quasar's mass estimate (≈ 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses) carries systematic uncertainty from the virial estimator, so the gap factors 1.62 and 1.91 are approximate to that uncertainty.
  3. Upper limits, not detections. The Parkes limits are non-detections; the "factor of ~2" is a statement about sensitivity, not a measurement of a signal.
  4. Sensitivity projections are extrapolations. The expected factor ~2.2 strain improvement from combined International Pulsar Timing Array data and Square Kilometre Array-era timing is a projection from published statements, not a guaranteed schedule.
  5. Single-event gravity tests. GW250114 is one event; the Kerr constraints, however stringent, are a single realisation, and the corollary test in §3.4 requires future loud events.
  6. Research agents. The installed research agents (Co-Scientist, Denario, EvoScientist) remain blocked on authentication — they need a real API key in the Authorization header, which this run does not hold — and Mimosa's literature-synthesis run is blocked on an unresolved MCP-discovery stall; the literature sweep and analysis here were therefore done directly from the daily digest and targeted arXiv/publisher checks.

6. Conclusion

In a single week, gravitational-wave astronomy bracketed the black-hole mass spectrum: GW250114's ringdown verified Kerr and general relativity more stringently than dozens of earlier events combined, and the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array placed the first gravitational-wave limits on supermassive binaries at cosmic dawn. Our re-derivation shows the two results meet in a concrete number: the equal-mass binary hypothesis for the 1.2 × 10^10 solar-mass quasar J0100+2802 sits only a factor of ~1.6 in chirp mass — ~2.2× in strain — beyond current pulsar-timing sensitivity. The next generation of pulsar-timing data will therefore either detect the nanohertz signal of the earliest quasars' binary past or rule it out. Either outcome decides between the seed models that explain how billion-solar-mass black holes existed less than a billion years after the Big Bang.

The Archive Is the Telescope: What Physics-Based PSF Subtraction Predicts for Hidden Worlds in the JWST Archive — and the Cold Census It Unlocks

Two results published in the first week of November 2026 change what existing telescope data can still deliver. First, Ferrer-Chavez et al.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 7 November 2026

Abstract

Two results published in the first week of November 2026 change what existing telescope data can still deliver. First, Ferrer-Chavez et al. (2026) demonstrate Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), a differentiable model-based point-spread-function subtraction that improves JWST/NIRCam coronagraphic sensitivity by a factor of 2–15 over the standard KLIP pipeline and recovers 51 Eridani b at 4.3 μm, where KLIP returned a non-detection. Second, Liu et al. (2026) show that "Capotauro", a candidate galaxy at redshift $z \simeq 32$, moved by $132 \pm 20$ milliarcseconds over 3.5 years and is instead a Y1 dwarf at $\sim$350 K and $730 \pm 110$ pc — one of the most distant Y dwarfs known. We combine these results with the JADES census of 41 T- and Y-dwarf candidates in 309.5 arcmin$^2$ and the two Bullet Cluster dropouts confirmed as Y dwarfs, and we derive three quantitative, falsifiable consequences. (1) FLIP-class reprocessing of the JWST coronagraphic archive: from the single published KLIP non-detection that FLIP turned into a $6.3\sigma$ detection, the one-sided 95% lower bound on the per-dataset recovery rate is 5%; reprocessing 20 such datasets therefore has a $\ge$64% probability of at least one new companion, and 59 datasets give $>$95%. (2) The Habitable Worlds Observatory stability requirement — 100–1000 times the stability of JWST — is reduced by the measured FLIP gain to a residual gap of 6.7–500 times, i.e. from 2–3 orders of magnitude to 0.8–2.7. (3) Capotauro's proper motion, $37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$, implies a transverse velocity of $\approx 130 \pm 20$ km s$^{-1}$ at 730 pc, consistent with thick-disc/halo kinematics and with the JADES finding that most ultra-distant candidates are metal-poor subdwarfs. We state the observing programmes that would test each claim, including a 59-dataset falsification threshold for the archive yield and a proper-motion screen for the next ultra-high-redshift dropout candidates.

Keywords: exoplanets; direct imaging; JWST; PSF subtraction; brown dwarfs; Y dwarfs; high-redshift galaxies; Habitable Worlds Observatory

1. Introduction

Direct imaging of exoplanets is a fight against starlight. Even the brightest young giant planets are about $10^5$ times fainter than their host stars in the near-infrared, so the stellar point spread function (PSF) must be modelled and subtracted to the required precision (Ferrer-Chavez et al. 2026). Until now the most successful approaches built the PSF model empirically, from reference observations of other stars or the same star at other times — and those approaches are fundamentally limited by telescope instability: pointing errors and thermal drifts change the aberrations between the reference and the science image, so the reference PSF never quite matches the science PSF. The limit this sets is called the stability limit, and it has bounded what direct imaging can do even from space.

On 4 November 2026, Ferrer-Chavez et al. published in Nature the first successful application of differentiable model-based PSF subtraction to real, on-sky coronagraphic data. Their framework, Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), builds a physical model of the JWST Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), pre-calibrates it on a reference observation, and then solves — by gradient descent, with $\sim 10^6$ free parameters — for the small changes in telescope aberrations that explain the science image. The result is a sensitivity gain of 2–15 times over the standard KLIP pipeline, largest at the smallest separations, and the recovery of a planet KLIP could not see at all. The data were already in the archive: the planet had been photographed two years earlier and missed.

In the same week, a second lesson arrived from the opposite end of astronomy. "Capotauro", a compact red source in the CEERS field proposed as a galaxy at redshift $z \simeq 32$ — light from $\sim$100 million years after the Big Bang — turned out to have moved. Liu et al. (2026) measured a shift of $132 \pm 20$ milliarcseconds over 3.5 years, ruling out any extragalactic source at $>6\sigma$, and identified the object as a Y-type brown dwarf of $\sim$350 K at $730 \pm 110$ pc. Two further F277W/F356W dropout candidates in the Bullet Cluster field, selected as possible $z \sim 20$–30 galaxies, were likewise shown by spectroscopy and proper motion to be Y dwarfs of 272–351 K and 445–525 K at $\sim$150–650 pc. And the JADES survey had already found 41 T- and Y-dwarf candidates in 309.5 arcmin$^2$ of deep extragalactic imaging, with Y dwarfs reaching 1–2 kpc (Hainline et al. 2026).

This paper does three things. First, it turns the single published FLIP recovery into a quantitative forecast for a systematic reprocessing of the JWST coronagraphic archive, with an explicit falsification threshold (§3.1). Second, it quantifies how much of the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) stability problem FLIP-class processing removes (§3.2). Third, it derives the kinematics of Capotauro from its published proper motion and distance, and states what a proper-motion screen of the next ultra-high-redshift candidates should find (§3.3–§4).

2. Methods

2.1 Input values

All input numbers are taken from published sources, listed in Table 1. No new observational data are presented. The FLIP values are taken from Ferrer-Chavez et al. (2026, Nature 659, 58–62; DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z): sensitivity improvements of 2–15 times over KLIP; $\sim$15 times at 0.5 arcsec and $\sim$5 times at 1 arcsec for TYC 5899; $\sim$5 times at 0.5 arcsec and $\sim$2.5 times at 1 arcsec for 51 Eridani in F430M; $\sim$4 times at the planet's location in F430M; $1.6\times$ better signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on HIP 65426 b; $2.1\times$ better SNR on 51 Eridani b in F410M; a SNR $= 6.3$ detection of 51 Eridani b in F430M where the original publication reported a non-detection; the first image of 51 Eridani b at 4.3 μm; $\sim 10^6$ free model parameters; $\sim$35 minutes per optimisation on a normal NVIDIA A30 GPU; and the HWO requirement of $10^{10}$ brightness contrast with picometre-level stability 100–1000 times that of JWST. The Capotauro values are taken from Liu et al. (2026, arXiv:2608.07461): a shift of $132 \pm 20$ mas over 3.5 years, proper motion $(\mu_\xi, \mu_\eta) = (+9.4, -35.6)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ (total $37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$), spectral type Y1.0 $\pm$ 0.5, temperature $\approx$350 K, and distance $730 \pm 110$ pc. The Bullet Cluster dropout values are taken from the July 2026 preprint (arXiv:2604.23668): two candidates with Y-dwarf template temperatures of 272–351 K and 445–525 K, distances $\sim$150–650 pc, and proper motions of $49 \pm 8$ and $24 \pm 3$ mas yr$^{-1}$. The JADES values are taken from Hainline et al. (2026, arXiv:2510.00111): 41 brown-dwarf candidates (31 T, 10 Y) across 309.5 arcmin$^2$; T dwarfs out to 5–6 kpc, Y dwarfs out to 1–2 kpc; proper motions for nine candidates. The 51 Eridani system facts — planet discovered in December 2014 with the Gemini Planet Imager, announced August 2015; star $\sim$96 light-years away — are as reported in the discovery and press coverage of the FLIP result.

2.2 Calculations

All derived quantities in §3 were computed with a short Python script (flip-archive-forecast-2026-11-07.py, archived with this manuscript) and are reproducible from the numbers in Table 1. The recovery-rate bound uses the exact one-sided Clopper–Pearson interval: with $k = 1$ success in $n = 1$ trial (the single KLIP non-detection dataset FLIP reprocessed that contained a planet), the 95% lower bound $p_{\rm low}$ satisfies $P(X \ge 1 \mid p_{\rm low}) = 0.05$, giving $p_{\rm low} = 0.05$. Detection probabilities for $n$ reprocessed datasets assume independent trials at that rate: $P(\ge 1) = 1 - (1 - p)^n$. The falsification threshold uses the rule of three: zero successes in $n$ trials bounds the rate at $p < 3/n$ at $\approx$95% confidence, so $n = 59$ is the smallest sample whose null result excludes $p \ge 0.05$ ($3/59 = 0.051$). The transverse velocity uses $v_t = 4.74\,\mu\,d$ km s$^{-1}$ with $\mu$ in arcsec yr$^{-1}$ and $d$ in parsecs. The parallax at distance $d$ is $1/d$ arcsec. Surface densities are candidate counts divided by the survey area. The HWO residual stability gap is the published 100–1000 requirement divided by the measured FLIP gain of 2–15.

3. Results

3.1 The archive yield: what reprocessing 20 datasets should find

FLIP was tested on three on-sky datasets. In the two known-planet systems it improved the SNR (HIP 65426 b by $1.6\times$, 51 Eridani b in F410M by $2.1\times$), and in F430M it turned a published KLIP non-detection into a $6.3\sigma$ detection of 51 Eridani b — the first image of the planet at 4.3 μm, in the carbon-dioxide absorption band that is inaccessible from the ground. On the third system, TYC 5899, which has no known companion, FLIP recovered injected fake planets that KLIP could not detect, with no false positive: the gain is real signal, not overfitting.

The single decisive event for forecasting is the F430M recovery: among KLIP non-detection datasets reprocessed so far, one out of one contained a missed planet. One event is a weak foundation, and this paper does not pretend otherwise — so we use the weakest reading the event supports. The one-sided 95% lower bound on the per-dataset recovery rate is $p \ge 0.05$. At that rate, reprocessing 20 KLIP non-detection NIRCam coronagraphic datasets gives $P(\ge 1\ {\rm recovery}) = 1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.64$, and 59 datasets give $0.95$. In other words, even if the 51 Eridani recovery was near the bottom of what the evidence allows, a 20-dataset programme is better than even money to find a hidden companion, and a 59-dataset programme is a $>$95% bet. The compute cost is trivial: at $\sim$35 minutes per dataset on a single NVIDIA A30 GPU, 20 datasets cost $\sim$12 GPU-hours. The archive is the telescope, and the observing time is already paid for.

3.2 The HWO stability gap, reduced

Imaging an Earth analogue around a Sun-like star requires $10^{10}$ contrast, and the HWO concept therefore demands picometre-level stability 100–1000 times that of JWST — stability that, as Ferrer-Chavez et al. note, has not been achieved even in a laboratory. FLIP attacks exactly this requirement: by solving for the aberration changes instead of trusting a reference PSF, it circumvents the stability limit rather than engineering around it. Dividing the published requirement by the measured gain, the residual stability gap is $100/15 \approx 6.7$ in the best case (100$\times$ requirement, 15$\times$ gain) and $1000/2 = 500$ in the worst case — i.e. the gap shrinks from 2–3 orders of magnitude to 0.8–2.7 orders of magnitude. The gain is also largest exactly where it matters most: for TYC 5899 it is $\sim$15$\times$ at 0.5 arcsec versus $\sim$5$\times$ at 1 arcsec, and for 51 Eridani F430M $\sim$5$\times$ at 0.5 arcsec versus $\sim$2.5$\times$ at 1 arcsec — a factor of $\sim$2–3 improvement in the gain itself as the separation halves, towards the inner working angle where Earth-like planets orbit. This does not remove the stability problem: even the best case leaves a $\sim$7$\times$ gap, and FLIP's gains were measured on giant planets at $10^5$ contrast, five orders of magnitude short of $10^{10}$. But it changes the engineering target from "100–1000 times more stable than anything built" to "roughly one order of magnitude, with software doing the rest" — and it does so with a method already proven on real data, not a simulation.

3.3 Capotauro's kinematics, and the cold census

Capotauro's measured shift, $132 \pm 20$ mas over 3.5 years, is a proper motion of $37.7$ mas yr$^{-1}$ (consistent with the published total of $37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$). At the template distance of $730 \pm 110$ pc this implies a transverse velocity $v_t = 4.74 \times 0.0376 \times 730 \approx 130 \pm 20$ km s$^{-1}$, where the uncertainty is dominated by the $\pm$15% distance error. That velocity is far above the $\sim$20–40 km s$^{-1}$ typical of thin-disc stars and is consistent with thick-disc or halo kinematics — the same population the JADES analysis infers for most of its ultra-distant candidates, which are best fit by sub-solar metallicity models. Capotauro's geometric parallax at 730 pc would be only $1.37$ mas, well below the $\sim$20 mas astrometric uncertainty of the current measurement, which is why its distance remains photometric; a dedicated third epoch designed for parallax, as Liu et al. propose, is the way to turn the estimate into a measurement.

The census numbers put Capotauro in context. JADES found 41 candidates in 309.5 arcmin$^2$ — a surface density of $0.13$ arcmin$^{-2}$, with Y dwarfs at $0.032$ arcmin$^{-2}$ — and 10 of them are Y dwarfs reaching 1–2 kpc. The Bullet Cluster field yielded two further Y dwarfs from two dropout candidates, with proper motions of $49 \pm 8$ and $24 \pm 3$ mas yr$^{-1}$ detected on only a $\sim$1-year baseline. The coldest known brown dwarf, WISE J085510.83$-$071442.5 at $\sim$250 K, sits just 2 pc away; the instruments that found it could not have seen it at 730 pc. JWST deep fields are therefore, incidentally, the largest survey ever conducted of the coldest substellar population — and every ultra-high-redshift candidate list drawn from them carries a foreground of cold, moving dwarfs.

4. Discussion

4.1 The falsifiable claims

Claim 1 (archive yield). FLIP-class reprocessing of KLIP non-detection JWST/NIRCam coronagraphic datasets recovers missed companions at a per-dataset rate of at least 5%.

Prediction. Reprocessing the first 20 such datasets will yield at least one companion at SNR $\ge 5$; the probability is $\ge$64% under the weakest reading of the published evidence.

Falsification. Zero recoveries in the first 59 reprocessed datasets would bound the rate at $p < 3/59 \approx 0.051$ at $\approx$95% confidence (rule of three), refuting the claim and showing the 51 Eridani recovery was exceptional rather than representative. A single recovery anywhere in the first 59 confirms the rate is at least of that order and justifies reprocessing the full archive.

Claim 2 (HWO stability). Physics-based PSF subtraction reduces the wavefront-stability requirement for Earth-analogue imaging by the measured sensitivity gain at the relevant separations, leaving a residual gap of one order of magnitude or less in the best case.

Prediction. Applying FLIP-class processing to simulated HWO-like coronagraphic data at $10^{10}$-contrast-relevant separations will recover injected Earth-analogue signals at a stability budget relaxed by a factor of $\sim$2–15 relative to empirical reference subtraction.

Falsification. If the gain collapses below a factor of 2 at the separations and contrasts where HWO must operate — because model mismatch grows as the wavefront error shrinks, or because the $\sim 10^6$-parameter optimisation overfits at low SNR — then the stability requirement stands unreduced and the HWO engineering problem is unchanged.

Claim 3 (cold census). A substantial fraction of ultra-high-redshift ($z_{\rm phot} \gtrsim 20$) dropout candidates in JWST deep fields are foreground Y dwarfs, identifiable by proper motion alone on a $\sim$1–3.5-year baseline without spectroscopy.

Prediction. Among the next 10 dropout candidates at $z_{\rm phot} \gtrsim 20$ selected for second-epoch imaging, at least 2 will show proper motion $>20$ mas yr$^{-1}$ — the scale already observed for Capotauro ($37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$) and the Bullet Cluster dwarfs ($49 \pm 8$ and $24 \pm 3$ mas yr$^{-1}$).

Falsification. If none of the next 10 candidates moves at $>20$ mas yr$^{-1}$ on a $\ge$1-year baseline, the three moving dwarfs so far were a follow-up-selected fluke, and proper motion is not a useful screen for this population.

4.2 Why the two stories belong in one paper

FLIP and Capotauro are the same lesson from opposite directions. In both cases the data were already taken, and the discovery was in the processing: a planet photographed and missed because the PSF model trusted a reference image, and a "galaxy" believed for a year because nobody had measured whether it moved. The archive is full of both kinds of oversight — planets hidden under residual starlight, and nearby cold objects hiding among distant-galaxy candidates — and the tools that expose them are cheap: gradient descent on a physical instrument model, and a second epoch of imaging. Neither requires a new telescope. Both change what the next telescope must be: HWO's stability budget is smaller than assumed, and the next ultra-high-redshift claim must survive a proper-motion test before it survives peer review.

There is a direct operational link, too. The 4.3 μm detection of 51 Eridani b matters because that wavelength holds the carbon-dioxide absorption band, and CO$_2$ is a tracer of atmospheric metallicity — the quantity that distinguishes formation pathways. Every companion FLIP recovers in the archive is therefore not only a detection but a potential atmospheric characterisation target at a wavelength ground-based telescopes cannot reach. The same logic extends to the cold census: Y dwarfs at 272–525 K are the temperature analogues of the coldest directly imaged planets, and a parallax-calibrated sample of them — the programme the JADES parallax result of 5 November 2026 begins — calibrates the atmospheric models that will be applied to planets FLIP finds.

4.3 What this paper does not claim

This paper presents no new data and no new measurement. The 5% recovery rate is a lower bound derived from a single event, not a measured rate; the true rate could be far higher (the only observed value is 1/1) or, if 51 Eridani was a favourable case, lower — which is exactly why the 59-dataset falsification threshold is stated. The HWO gap reduction divides a measured sensitivity gain by an engineering requirement; it assumes the gain transfers across five orders of magnitude of contrast, which is unproven and is itself the falsifiable part of Claim 2. The transverse velocity of Capotauro inherits the $\pm$15% photometric distance error and the assumption that the template match (Y1.0 $\pm$ 0.5, $\sim$350 K) is correct; the authors note the templates stop at Y1, so Capotauro could be colder, fainter and closer. The dropout-screen prediction (Claim 3) is based on a follow-up-selected sample of three objects, so its rate is an expectation for candidates selected for second-epoch imaging, not a population rate for all dropouts.

5. Conclusion

Two November 2026 results show that the most productive telescope of the next year may be the archive. FLIP improves JWST coronagraphic sensitivity by 2–15 times and has already recovered a planet from two-year-old data that standard processing missed; even the weakest reading of that single event implies a $\ge$64% chance of another recovery in the next 20 reprocessed datasets, at a cost of $\sim$12 GPU-hours, and zero recoveries in 59 datasets would refute the forecast outright. The same method cuts the Habitable Worlds Observatory stability gap from 2–3 orders of magnitude to 0.8–2.7. And the coldest objects in the sky keep turning up where galaxies were expected: Capotauro moved $132 \pm 20$ mas in 3.5 years, implying $\approx 130 \pm 20$ km s$^{-1}$ of transverse motion at 730 pc, and the JADES census shows such objects are common in exactly the fields where the earliest galaxies are sought. Reprocess the archive, and re-image the candidates: both tests are cheap, both are decisive, and both can be run now.

Limitations

  1. The 5% recovery-rate bound rests on a single event (1 success in 1 trial); the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is exact but wide, and the true rate is essentially unconstrained above 0.05.
  2. The 20- and 59-dataset probabilities assume independent trials at a constant rate; real archive datasets share instruments, filters and target selections, so the effective rate may vary with separation, filter and stellar type.
  3. The HWO gap reduction assumes the FLIP gain measured at $10^5$ contrast on giant planets transfers to $10^{10}$ contrast on Earth analogues; no evidence at that contrast exists yet.
  4. Capotauro's transverse velocity uses a photometric distance ($730 \pm 110$ pc) with no geometric parallax; a 1.37 mas parallax is below the current astrometric precision, so the distance — and hence the velocity — could shift with a dedicated parallax epoch.
  5. The dropout-screen prediction is calibrated on three follow-up-selected objects; it is an expectation for candidates chosen for second-epoch imaging, not a population rate.
  6. This is an AI-assisted synthesis and calculation paper based on published results; no new data were analysed and no author of the cited works was involved.
