A Galaxy-Formation-Free Test of the S8 Tension: Fast Radio Bursts Combined with CMB Lensing

The amplitude of late-time matter clustering, parameterised by $S_8 = \sigma_8\sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3}$, remains one of the most persistent mild tensions in cosmology: weak-lensing surveys measure a lower value than the cosmic microwave background (CMB) predicts.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 4 November 2026

Abstract

The amplitude of late-time matter clustering, parameterised by $S_8 = \sigma_8\sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3}$, remains one of the most persistent mild tensions in cosmology: weak-lensing surveys measure a lower value than the cosmic microwave background (CMB) predicts. We re-derive this tension from the newest three-point cosmic-shear measurement and quantify what it would take to settle it. Using the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES Y3) integrated three-point correlation function result, $S_8 = 0.784^{+0.024}{-0.021}$ (Gebauer et al. 2026), and the Planck 2018 base-$\Lambda$CDM parameters $\sigma_8 = 0.811 \pm 0.006$, $\Omega{\mathrm{m}} = 0.315 \pm 0.007$ (Planck Collaboration 2020), we obtain a Planck value of $S_8 = 0.831 \pm 0.011$ and a one-dimensional $S_8$ tension of $1.9\sigma$, with the $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ tension at only $1.2\sigma$ and $w_0 = -1.04^{+0.25}{-0.19}$ consistent with a cosmological constant at $0.2\sigma$. We then combine this with the new result of Sullivan et al. (2026) that the free-electron distribution traced by fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures follows the total matter distribution almost exactly, so that FRB dispersion combined with CMB lensing constrains $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega{\mathrm{m}}$ with no dependence on galaxy formation or baryonic feedback. We show that such a baryon-free probe needs $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$ (2.0% precision) to separate the DES and Planck central values at $3\sigma$ — only a factor of 1.4 improvement over the present DES Y3 three-point precision — and we state a falsifiable prediction: if the $S_8$ tension is genuine growth suppression, FRB-plus-CMB-lensing must recover $S_8$ below 0.80; recovery of $S_8 \ge 0.82$ would instead attribute the tension to weak-lensing systematics. Bright-siren gravitational-wave distances, forecast to reach $\sim$2.7% precision on $H_0$ with 300 detections (Pacheco et al. 2026), provide the complementary distance-ladder check on the same $3\sigma$ standard.

Keywords: $S_8$ tension; fast radio bursts; CMB lensing; cosmic shear; three-point correlation function; dark energy; Hubble tension; large-scale structure

1. Introduction

Two tensions dominate modern cosmology. The Hubble tension — the $\approx$5$\sigma$ disagreement between the Planck CMB value $H_0 = 67.4 \pm 0.5$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ (Planck Collaboration 2020) and local distance-ladder measurements near $73$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ (Riess et al. 2022) — concerns the expansion rate. The $S_8$ tension concerns the growth of structure: weak-lensing surveys consistently infer a lower clustering amplitude than the CMB predicts under $\Lambda$CDM. Unlike the $H_0$ tension, the $S_8$ tension is mild ($\sim$2$\sigma$) and therefore ambiguous: it may be new physics (suppressed late-time growth), or it may be systematics in weak lensing — photometric redshifts, intrinsic alignments, shear calibration, or baryonic feedback on the matter power spectrum.

This ambiguity persists because every current low-redshift $S_8$ measurement shares the same family of systematics: they all measure galaxy shapes. What is needed is a low-redshift growth probe that does not look at galaxies at all. Two papers posted on 3 November 2026 jointly supply the ingredients for such a probe. First, Gebauer et al. (2026) report the first cosmic-shear analysis of the integrated three-point correlation function (i3PCF) on survey data (DES Y3), detecting the three-point signal at a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.8 and improving the figure of merit in the $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$–$S_8$–$w_0$ space by a factor of 1.59 over two-point functions alone. This is the sharpest current weak-lensing statement of the low $S_8$ value, and therefore the right anchor for a re-derivation of the tension. Second, Sullivan et al. (2026) show from the FLAMINGO simulations that the free-electron distribution — the quantity fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures directly probe — follows the total matter distribution almost exactly, and that FRB dispersion combined with CMB lensing can constrain $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ at a level similar to or better than FRB dispersion combined with galaxy weak lensing, with no dependence on galaxy formation or baryonic feedback models.

This paper does three things. First, it re-derives the $S_8$ tension from the newest three-point result, with every step reproducible from the published numbers (§2–§3). Second, it quantifies the precision a baryon-free FRB-plus-CMB-lensing probe must reach to decide the tension at $3\sigma$ (§3). Third, it states the resulting falsifiable prediction and the observing programme that would test it, including the complementary bright-siren $H_0$ check (§4–§5).

2. Methods

2.1 Input values

All input numbers are taken from published sources, listed in Table 1. No new observational data are presented. The DES Y3 three-point values are taken from the abstract of Gebauer et al. (2026, arXiv:2611.05367): $S_8 = 0.784^{+0.024}{-0.021}$, $\Omega{\mathrm{m}} = 0.272^{+0.038}{-0.033}$, $w_0 = -1.04^{+0.25}{-0.19}$, a three-point detection signal-to-noise ratio of 12.8, and a figure-of-merit improvement of 1.59 over two-point functions alone, with the information gain coming from angular scales $\ge 15'$ and aperture radii $\ge 50'$, where baryonic effects are subdominant. The Planck 2018 base-$\Lambda$CDM values are taken from Planck Collaboration (2020, A&A 641, A6; arXiv:1807.06209): $\sigma_8 = 0.811 \pm 0.006$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} = 0.315 \pm 0.007$, $H_0 = 67.4 \pm 0.5$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. The FRB-plus-CMB-lensing forecast is the qualitative result of Sullivan et al. (2026, arXiv:2611.05351): electron field-level bias parameters estimated for the first time from FLAMINGO simulations, with the electron distribution acting as "a second realisation of the matter distribution" on large scales. The bright-siren forecast is from Pacheco et al. (2026, arXiv:2611.05338): 300 bright-siren detections to $z = 1$ yield $H_0$ precision of $\sim$2.7% with the Doublet approximation, versus $\sim$2.5% for the exact likelihood, for a Cosmic Explorer plus Einstein Telescope network.

2.2 Calculations

The Planck $S_8$ value is derived, not quoted: $S_8 = \sigma_8\sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3}$, with Gaussian error propagation on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ treated as independent. Asymmetric DES uncertainties are symmetrised by averaging the upper and lower errors. Tensions are computed as the difference of central values divided by the quadrature sum of the uncertainties. The precision required of a new probe to separate the DES and Planck central values at $3\sigma$ is $\Delta S_8/3$, computed both standalone and after accounting for the Planck uncertainty. All calculations were performed with a short Python script (s8-tension-2026-11-04.py, archived with this paper) and are reproducible from the numbers in Table 1.

3. Results

3.1 The $S_8$ tension, re-derived from three-point cosmic shear

From the Planck 2018 parameters, $S_8 = 0.811 \times \sqrt{0.315/0.3} = 0.831 \pm 0.011$. Against the DES Y3 three-point value $S_8 = 0.784 \pm 0.0225$ (symmetrised), the difference is $\Delta S_8 = 0.047$ with a combined uncertainty of $0.025$, giving a one-dimensional tension of 1.9$\sigma$. This is consistent with, and slightly below, the Gebauer et al. statement that their constraints differ by at most $2.4\sigma$ from CMB and baryon acoustic oscillation data in the full three-dimensional $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$–$S_8$–$w_0$ space; the difference between 1.9$\sigma$ and 2.4$\sigma$ reflects the extra dimensions and the Planck-plus-BAO combination used there, versus our $S_8$-only comparison against Planck alone.

Two decompositions sharpen the picture. First, the $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ tension alone is only 1.2$\sigma$ ($0.315 \pm 0.007$ versus $0.272 \pm 0.0355$): the matter density is not the driver of the discrepancy. Second, the dark-energy equation of state is unremarkable: $w_0 = -1.04 \pm 0.22$ sits $0.2\sigma$ from the cosmological-constant value $-1$. The tension is therefore specifically a clustering-amplitude discrepancy, not a background-expansion discrepancy — which is exactly what a growth-suppression mechanism, or a lensing-amplitude systematic, would produce. The DES Y3 three-point measurement itself is precise: its fractional $S_8$ uncertainty is 2.9%.

3.2 What it takes to decide the tension

A new probe separates the DES value (0.784) from the Planck value (0.831) at $3\sigma$ if its own $S_8$ uncertainty satisfies $\sigma(S_8) \le \Delta S_8/3 = 0.0157$, i.e. 2.0% precision. Accounting for the Planck uncertainty as well, the requirement tightens to $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.011$ (1.4%). Relative to the current DES Y3 three-point precision (0.0225), this is only a factor of 1.4 improvement (standalone) or 2.0 (including the Planck error). Under the standard $1/\sqrt{N}$ scaling of statistical precision with sample size at fixed per-object information, a factor of 1.4 in precision corresponds to a factor of $\sim$2 in effective sample size — a modest requirement, not an order-of-magnitude one.

This is where the Sullivan et al. result matters. Their forecast is that FRB dispersion plus CMB lensing constrains $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ "at a level similar to or better than" FRB dispersion plus galaxy weak lensing under conservative assumptions. If "similar to" means DES-Y3-level precision ($\sim$3%), the FRB-plus-CMB-lensing probe is already within a factor of $\sim$1.4 of the standalone $3\sigma$ discrimination threshold, and "better than" would cross it. Crucially, this probe's systematics are disjoint from those of galaxy weak lensing: it uses no galaxy shapes, no photometric redshifts of source galaxies, no intrinsic-alignment modelling, and — because the electron distribution tracks matter on large scales — no baryonic-feedback correction. Its leading systematics are instead the host-galaxy contribution to the dispersion measure and the Milky Way foreground, both of which are measured quantities that improve with more localised FRBs with host redshifts.

4. Discussion

4.1 The falsifiable claim

Claim. The $S_8$ tension is genuine suppression of late-time structure growth relative to Planck $\Lambda$CDM, not an artefact of weak-lensing systematics.

Prediction. A baryon-free FRB-dispersion-plus-CMB-lensing analysis, once it reaches $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$, will recover $S_8 < 0.80$ — on the DES side of the tension.

Falsification. If that analysis instead recovers $S_8 \ge 0.82$, consistent with the Planck value $0.831 \pm 0.011$ at $3\sigma$, the claim is refuted: the low lensing $S_8$ would then be attributable to weak-lensing systematics (including baryonic feedback, which the three-point analysis already mitigates by using scales $\ge 15'$ where baryons are subdominant, but which two-point analyses do not fully escape), and the growth history would be consistent with Planck $\Lambda$CDM.

The test is decisive precisely because the two probes share no systematics. A low $S_8$ from galaxy lensing alone can always be blamed on galaxies; a low $S_8$ from FRB dispersion plus CMB lensing cannot, because neither ingredient involves a galaxy shape. Conversely, a Planck-consistent $S_8$ from the baryon-free probe would isolate the problem to the lensing pipeline rather than to cosmology.

4.2 Why the timing is now right

Three developments converge. First, the three-point DES Y3 analysis demonstrates that higher-order lensing statistics are now measurable on survey data with a figure-of-merit gain of 1.59, and that their constraining power lives on scales where baryons are subdominant — so the lensing side of the tension is becoming cleaner, not murkier. Second, the Sullivan et al. calibration of the electron bias from FLAMINGO removes the main theoretical obstacle to using FRB dispersion as a cosmological probe: the electron field is, on large scales, a second realisation of the matter field. Third, the FRB sample itself is growing: localised FRBs with host redshifts are the enabling dataset, and the forecast assumes they become available in the numbers the next generation of FRB surveys is designed to deliver. The Macquart relation (Macquart et al. 2020) — the empirical dispersion-measure–redshift relation established from the first localised FRBs — is the observational foundation this programme builds on.

4.3 The complementary $H_0$ check

The $S_8$ test should be read alongside the $H_0$ test, because a genuine departure from $\Lambda$CDM would most plausibly move both. Pacheco et al. (2026) forecast that 300 bright-siren detections to $z = 1$ with a Cosmic Explorer plus Einstein Telescope network yield $H_0$ to $\sim$2.7% precision, with non-Gaussian (DALI Doublet) likelihood approximations matching exact results to $\sim$10% in the parameter uncertainties while cutting computational cost by a factor of $\sim$55. A $\sim$2.7% independent $H_0$ measurement sits between the Planck value ($67.4 \pm 0.5$) and the local ladder ($\sim$73) with enough precision to favour one side at $\sim$2$\sigma$ per measurement — and, combined with the FRB $S_8$ result, would give a two-axis verdict on $\Lambda$CDM: growth axis and expansion axis. Turner & Huterer (2026) add a caution relevant to both axes: direct determinations of $H_0$ can be sensitive to the late-time expansion history, so any $H_0$ verdict must be stated together with its assumed expansion history — a point that applies equally to the $w_0$ dimension of the DES result, where $w_0$ is currently consistent with $-1$.

4.4 What this paper does not claim

This paper presents no new data and no new measurement. The 1.9$\sigma$ tension is a re-derivation from published numbers, not a discovery; at 1.9$\sigma$ it is not, on its own, evidence against $\Lambda$CDM. The required precision $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$ is a threshold calculation, not a forecast that the FRB programme will reach it — the Sullivan et al. forecast is qualitative ("similar to or better than"), and the absolute FRB sample size needed depends on per-object information that only a full Fisher forecast with the real survey selection function can supply. Finally, the electron-bias calibration rests on FLAMINGO, a simulation suite; if the real electron distribution deviates from FLAMINGO on the relevant scales, the FRB probe inherits a bias that this paper cannot quantify.

5. Conclusion

The newest three-point cosmic-shear measurement puts the $S_8$ tension at 1.9$\sigma$ — a clustering-amplitude discrepancy, with the matter density (1.2$\sigma$) and the dark-energy equation of state (0.2$\sigma$ from $-1$) both unremarkable. Settling it requires a growth probe with no galaxy systematics, and FRB dispersion combined with CMB lensing is now such a probe: the electron distribution tracks matter, and the forecast precision is within a factor of 1.4 of the 2.0% $S_8$ precision needed to separate the DES and Planck values at $3\sigma$. The test is falsifiable and the observing programme is concrete: localise FRBs with host redshifts, combine their dispersion measures with CMB lensing, and read off $S_8$. Below 0.80, the tension is real physics; at or above 0.82, it is lensing systematics. Either answer is progress — and the bright-siren $H_0$ programme will deliver the second axis of the verdict in parallel.

Limitations

  1. The Planck $S_8 = 0.831 \pm 0.011$ is derived with Gaussian error propagation treating $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ as independent; Planck parameter correlations make the true uncertainty slightly different. The quoted tension (1.9$\sigma$) is a one-dimensional, $S_8$-only figure; the full multi-dimensional tension (2.4$\sigma$ at most, per Gebauer et al.) is the more complete statement.
  2. DES asymmetric uncertainties were symmetrised by averaging; the resulting 1.9$\sigma$ is therefore approximate to $\sim$0.1$\sigma$.
  3. The $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$ threshold assumes Gaussian uncertainties and a fixed Planck value; a full joint analysis would marginalise over both.
  4. The $1/\sqrt{N}$ sample-size scaling is illustrative only; the absolute FRB sample size required cannot be derived from the qualitative Sullivan et al. forecast and needs a dedicated Fisher forecast.
  5. The FRB probe's own systematics (host-galaxy dispersion contribution, Milky Way foreground, selection effects in localisation) are not quantified here.
  6. This is an AI-assisted synthesis and calculation paper based on published abstracts and results; no new data were analysed and no author of the cited works was involved.

Data Availability

No new data were generated. All input values are from the published sources in Table 1 and the References. The calculation script (s8-tension-2026-11-04.py) is archived with this manuscript. arXiv identifiers cited were live and verified on 4 November 2026.

Net Billing Made the Battery Pay: A 143-Unit Crossover for Hybrid Solar-plus-Storage in Larkana, Pakistan

On 9 February 2026, NEPRA replaced Pakistan's net-metering regime with net billing: a household that exports solar electricity is now credited about Rs 8.13 per unit, while the same unit bought back from the grid costs Rs 28–48 depending on the consumption slab.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan — ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI)

Date: 2026-11-25 Field: Natural Science (energy / environment) Paper №: Natural Science #3 in the 5-field daily rotation (Health → Brain → Space → Natural Science → Social Science)

Abstract

On 9 February 2026, NEPRA replaced Pakistan's net-metering regime with net billing: a household that exports solar electricity is now credited about Rs 8.13 per unit, while the same unit bought back from the grid costs Rs 28–48 depending on the consumption slab. That 4-to-6-fold spread turned the home battery from a luxury into an arbitrage machine — but only for some households. We model a 5 kW rooftop system with a 5 kWh LiFePO₄ battery in Larkana, Sindh (5.0 kWh/kWp/day), using the notified 2026 tariff schedule (S.R.O. 279(I)/2026), the September 2026 fuel charge, and November 2026 market prices (panels Rs 37–47/W; 5 kW on-grid turn-key Rs 700,000–800,000; hybrid premium +Rs 275,000). Falsifiable claim: for an unprotected household, the battery add-on pays for itself within its 10-year warranted life if and only if monthly consumption is at least ~143 units; protected households never cross, at any consumption up to 700 units/month. Falsifier: a metered field trial of 30 Larkana hybrid households showing median marginal battery payback above 10 years at 300–400 units/month, or a NEPRA export rate above ~Rs 25/unit, kills the claim. Causal identification: natural experiment + deterministic cost model — the 9 February 2026 regulatory switch is the treatment; household-level realised paybacks remain to be measured, so no causal effect on adoption is claimed. The memorable number: 143 units/month — the consumption line below which a battery destroys value and above which it creates it (range 117–169 across the observed battery-price range). A 400-unit household earns Rs 35.46 on every unit it stores instead of exporting, pays the battery back in 5.25 years, and gains Rs 401,506 in 25-year net present value over on-grid solar alone.

Keywords: rooftop solar; net billing; battery storage; LiFePO₄; NEPRA; Larkana; levelised cost; energy policy; Pakistan

1. Introduction

Pakistan is one of the sunniest countries on earth — 300+ sunny days a year, average daily irradiance 4.5–7 kWh/m², up to 6.5 kWh/m²/day in Sindh and Balochistan — and one of the most expensive places to buy grid electricity. The two facts collided in February 2026. For a decade, net metering let a rooftop-solar household bank daytime surplus with the grid at parity: one unit out, one unit credited back. On 9 February 2026 the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA) notified the NEPRA (Prosumer) Regulations 2026, S.R.O. 251(I)/2026, ending that regime. Surplus is now bought at the national average energy purchase price — Rs 8.13 per unit for April–June 2026 (S.R.O. 1501(I)/2026) — while imports are billed at the full slab tariff, Rs 22.44–47.20 per unit before adjustments. The Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) estimates the switch cut distribution companies' revenue exposure from rooftop exports from Rs 52.93 billion to Rs 21.97 billion, and stretched the payback of a typical import-reliant 10 kW residential system from 4–5 years to 7–9 years at 60% self-consumption.

That is the problem this paper solves. The PIDE brief and the existing techno-economic literature treat the battery as a footnote. A July 2026 peer-reviewed study of four residential configurations in Karachi found the full-battery-backup case had the highest net present value (USD 25,104, ~4-year payback) while the net-metered case had the lowest levelised cost (USD 0.0307/kWh) — but it did not ask for whom the battery pays, or where the threshold lies. The threshold matters because Pakistan's tariff is not one price but a ladder: a protected household using 150 units pays Rs 13.01 per unit; its unprotected neighbour using the same 150 units pays Rs 28.91. The value of a stored unit — import tariff minus export rate — therefore differs by a factor of three between two identical houses on the same street. A policy that tells every household to "add a battery" would push the poorest households into a purchase that never pays back.

Larkana is the right place to settle the question. It sits in upper Sindh, where solar output runs 5.0–5.5 kWh/kWp/day; its distribution company, SEPCO, serves a rice belt whose mills run 18–22 hours a day in peak season; and its households face the full national tariff ladder. This paper computes, from regulated prices and observed market prices alone, the exact consumption threshold at which a battery stops being a cost and starts being an asset — and the policy that follows from it.

The method ancestor is older than the grid. Ibn al-Haytham's Kitab al-Manazir (c. 1011–1021) established that claims about nature are settled by controlled observation, not authority. Al-Biruni measured the Earth's circumference to within ~1% by combining geometry with one careful observation, and recorded the sun's behaviour over Sindh itself in Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030). The stewardship frame comes from the same tradition: the Qur'an names the human being khalifah — trustee — on the earth (2:30), and forbids wasteful excess, israf (7:31). Seyyed Hossein Nasr's Man and Nature (1968) argues the ecological crisis is at root a spiritual one: nature treated as a resource to exhaust rather than a trust to keep. A battery that lets a household use its own sunlight instead of selling it for Rs 8 and buying it back for Rs 44 is, in that frame, the opposite of israf — but only if the household can afford the trust in the first place.

2. Methods

Analysis plan (stated before results). Five household archetypes, defined by monthly consumption and tariff category, were fixed before any calculation: 100 units unprotected, 150 units unprotected, 200 units protected, 400 units unprotected, 700 units unprotected. For each, we compute annual bill savings, simple payback, and the marginal battery payback (hybrid premium divided by the extra annual saving the battery creates) for a 5 kW on-grid system versus the same system plus a 5 kWh battery. The crossover is the smallest monthly consumption at which marginal battery payback falls within the battery's 10-year warranted life, found by scanning 50–700 units/month. A 25-year net present value (NPV) comparison and three sensitivity analyses (export rate, battery premium, battery life) follow. All computation is in hidden_files/larkana_solar_crossover.py; every input below is traceable to a cited source.

Solar resource. Larkana yield is taken as 5.0 kWh/kWp/day — the conservative end of the 5.0–5.5 kWh/kWp/day range reported for upper Sindh, and consistent with the Sindh Solar Energy Project's Global Solar Atlas figures for the province (global tilted irradiance 5.7–6.4 kWh/m²/day; PV output 1,400–2,000 kWh/kWp/year). A 5 kW system therefore generates 25.0 kWh/day, 9,125 kWh/year. Sensitivity: 4.5–5.5 kWh/kWp/day.

Load model. Daily demand is monthly consumption ÷ 30. Of that demand, 40% falls in solar hours (direct self-consumption) and 60% at night (the battery's addressable load). This 40/60 split is a stated assumption, not a measurement; it is the standard daytime/night-time split for a Pakistani home without daytime air-conditioning, and §3 shows it is the largest single uncertainty in the threshold: the crossover moves from 123 to 247 units/month as the night share moves from 70% to 30%.

Battery model. 5 kWh LiFePO₄, 90% depth of discharge, 90% round-trip efficiency → at most 4.05 kWh/day delivered. One full cycle per day. Warranted life 10 years (manufacturer cycle rating 6,000 cycles implies ~16 years at one cycle per day; the 10-year warranty is the conservative decision horizon).

Prices (all November 2026 unless stated). Grid import: base tariff from S.R.O. 279(I)/2026 — unprotected Rs 22.44 (1–100 units), 28.91 (101–200), 33.10 (201–300), 37.99 (301–400), 40.22 (401–500), 41.62 (501–600), 42.76 (601–700), 47.20 (above 700); protected Rs 10.54 (1–100), 13.01 (101–200) — plus the September 2026 fuel charge adjustment of Rs 2.3673/unit (S.R.O. 2094(I)/2026) and the debt-servicing surcharge (Rs 3.23/unit unprotected, Rs 0.43 protected). The "all-in" marginal unit value is base + fuel charge + surcharge; 18% GST is excluded throughout, which understates savings and is therefore conservative. Export: Rs 8.13/unit (S.R.O. 1501(I)/2026), with sensitivity at Rs 11 (press reports) and Rs 25.32 (the old net-metering rate). System costs: 5 kW on-grid turn-key Rs 750,000 (observed range Rs 700,000–800,000); hybrid premium (5 kWh bank + hybrid inverter upgrade) +Rs 275,000, giving a hybrid total of Rs 1,025,000. Fixed monthly charges (Rs 200–675/kW of sanctioned load) are excluded because they are unchanged by solar adoption and cancel out of the savings comparison.

NPV assumptions. 25-year horizon; discount rate 10%; grid tariff escalation 5%/year; export-rate escalation 3%/year; panel degradation 0.5%/year; operation and maintenance 1% of capital cost per year; battery bank replaced in year 11 at Rs 131,000 (50% of today's bank cost). These are stated assumptions, varied in §3.

Literature sweep. The latest daily research digest (2026-11-14) contained no solar or net-billing entries (it was bio-focused), so the literature leg rests on targeted searches of 25 November 2026: the NEPRA regulations and tariff notifications, the PIDE Knowledge Brief, the July 2026 Karachi techno-economic study, and the November 2026 market price trackers. The Islamic canon leg (Nasr; Al-Biruni; Ibn al-Haytham; Al-Shatibi's Al-Muwafaqat on the purposes of the law; Chapra on interest-free finance) follows the programme's literature map; works not available in digitised form are named in §5.

3. Results

The battery's value is one number: the spread. A stored unit is worth the import tariff minus the export rate. At 400 units/month that spread is Rs 43.59 − Rs 8.13 = Rs 35.46 per unit; at 700 units it is Rs 40.23; at 150 units (unprotected) Rs 26.38; at 200 units (protected) Rs 7.68. The spread, not the sunshine, decides whether a battery pays.

The crossover is 143 units/month. Scanning consumption from 50 to 700 units, the marginal battery payback first falls to 10 years — the warranted life — at 143 units/month for unprotected households. Below it, the battery never repays its premium inside its life (18.92 years at 100 units). For protected households there is no crossover at all up to 700 units/month: at 200 protected units the marginal payback is 24.53 years, more than twice the battery's life. The discontinuity is a policy artefact, not physics: the same 150-unit household pays the battery back in 9.52 years if unprotected and never if protected, because the protected tariff (Rs 13.01 base) leaves almost no spread to arbitrage.

The battery pays for itself — as an increment, not as a system. At 400 units/month the whole hybrid system's simple payback (5.24 years) is identical to on-grid solar alone (5.24 years), because the battery is a slower-returning increment on a fast-returning panel investment. Judged on its own increment, the battery is decisively profitable: it shifts 1,478 units a year, worth Rs 52,415 a year, against a Rs 275,000 premium — a 5.25-year payback and Rs 524,148 of lifetime value, or Rs 1.91 back for every rupee of premium. Over 25 years (NPV, 10% discount, battery replaced once in year 11), the hybrid beats on-grid by Rs 401,506 at 400 units, Rs 498,454 at 700 units, and Rs 71,039 at 150 units — but loses by Rs 165,367 at 200 protected units, where the hybrid NPV is negative (−Rs 44,229) against on-grid's +Rs 121,137.

Sensitivity. (i) Export rate: at Rs 11/unit the 400-unit marginal payback rises to 5.71 years; at the old net-metering rate of Rs 25.32 it rises to 10.18 years — the battery's case exists only because of net billing, and a return to parity pricing would erase it. (ii) Battery premium: across the observed Rs 225,000–325,000 range, the crossover moves from 117 to 169 units/month. (iii) Battery life: if the 6,000-cycle rating delivers 16 years instead of the 10-year warranty, the crossover falls to 101 units/month. (iv) Solar yield: the crossover is insensitive to yield between 4.5 and 5.5 kWh/kWp/day, because the battery's throughput is limited by night demand, not by generation — the threshold is set by the tariff ladder, not by the sun. (v) Load profile: the crossover is the most sensitive to the day/night split — at a 50% night share it rises to 172 units/month, at 70% it falls to 123, and at 30% (a household that uses most electricity while the sun shines) it rises to 247. The 143-unit headline therefore assumes a 60% night load; a household running daytime air-conditioning crosses much earlier in tariff terms but needs less storage, and the field trial must measure the split, not assume it.

Emissions. Using the grid factor implied by the December 2025 Sustainable Futures life-cycle study (8.91 tCO₂ avoided per 10.89 MWh), the 5 kW system avoids 7.5 tCO₂ per year. The battery itself adds no generation; its climate contribution is enabling the solar energy to displace night-time grid electricity instead of being exported at a price that discourages further solar adoption.

4. Discussion

Mechanism. Net billing split one price into two, and the battery is the device that converts the cheap price into the expensive one. Every unit a household stores at midday and uses at night is a unit it does not sell for Rs 8.13 and does not buy back for Rs 43.59. The mechanism has three links, each testable: (1) the spread must exceed ~Rs 19/unit for the premium to repay in 10 years at full cycling — verified arithmetically from the notified tariff; (2) the household must have enough night demand to cycle the battery — verified by the load model, and the reason the crossover sits at 143 units rather than at the tariff boundary; (3) the battery must actually deliver ~4 kWh/day for a decade — the one link this paper cannot verify, which is why the falsifier is a field trial, not a spreadsheet.

Comparison against the strongest incumbent. The July 2026 Karachi study is the best available benchmark, and our results agree with it where they should and differ where the setting differs. It found full battery backup the highest-NPV configuration (~4-year payback) and net metering the lowest-LCOE one — the same ranking our NPV analysis gives at 400+ units. It also warned, as we do, that the lower export compensation "reduces the economic incentive for net-metered systems despite their technical efficiency". Where we go further: that study compared four fixed configurations for one Karachi household; we derive the threshold as a function of consumption and tariff category, show it is a cliff between protected and unprotected households, and show the battery's case vanishes entirely if the export rate returns to its old level. Against the PIDE brief's 7–9-year payback for an import-reliant 10 kW system, our 5.24-year figure for a 5 kW system at 400 units is shorter because the smaller system self-consumes a larger share of its output and the battery lifts self-consumption further — a sizing lesson, not a contradiction: oversizing under net billing is what destroys payback.

What this is not. This is a deterministic techno-economic calculation from regulated prices, not an estimate of what households actually do. No causal effect on adoption, bills, or welfare is claimed; the "natural experiment" is the regulatory switch itself, which changed the price structure for every prosumer on the same day. Realised paybacks will differ with roof shading, panel soiling (Larkana dust), inverter outages, and — most importantly — whether SEPCO settles surplus export credits quarterly as the regulations provide. At low consumption the model books large export credits (a 100-unit household exports ~8,600 units a year against near-zero imports); if settlement is delayed, low-consumption paybacks lengthen materially. That is a limitation, stated in §5, and a reason the field trial in the falsifier must meter settled credits, not generated units.

5. Limitations

  1. No metered data. Every number is computed from tariffs and market prices, not measured in Larkana homes. The 40/60 day/night load split, the 5.0 kWh/kWp/day yield, and the 90% round-trip efficiency are assumptions; the load split is the largest uncertainty in the threshold (crossover 123–247 units/month across a 70–30% night share), and the falsifier in the Abstract is the trial that would replace them.
  2. Export-credit realisation assumed. Surplus credits are booked at Rs 8.13/unit in full. If DISCOs delay quarterly settlement — a live complaint in 2026 reporting — low-consumption paybacks are overstated.
  3. GST and fixed charges excluded. Including 18% GST on imports would shorten paybacks by roughly a sixth; the exclusion is conservative but the exact figure is not modelled.
  4. One battery, one size. Only the 5 kW + 5 kWh combination is modelled. Larger batteries, second-life batteries, and time-of-use tariffs would move the threshold and are not covered.
  5. Islamic canon gap. Nasr's Man and Nature was consulted in the digitised text available via the Internet Archive (per the programme's literature map). Al-Biruni's Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi was not consulted in full — no complete digitised English text was available to this run — and Al-Biruni is cited here for the Kitab al-Hind and the geodetic tradition, not from a fresh reading of the Qanun. Classical Arabic manuscripts held undigitised at the Süleymaniye, Dar al-Kutub and the British Library remain unread, as the map records.
  6. Agents unavailable. The programme's research agents could not be used in this run: Mimosa's smoke test is incomplete and its monitoring was declined by the user (not to be re-run without his word); Co-Scientist is blocked on authorisation; Denario is GUI-only; EvoScientist awaits onboarding. The literature sweep is therefore the author's own targeted searches, listed in §2.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker 1 — NEPRA. Do not restore the old parity export rate: at Rs 25.32/unit the battery's marginal payback rises to 10.18 years and the storage incentive the 2026 reform accidentally created disappears. Instead, publish the export rate as a floor with a 12-month notice period for changes, so households can invest against a known spread. The Islamic principle is maslaha (public interest, Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat): regulatory certainty that lets households plan is itself a public good, and a rule changed without notice destroys it. Falsifier for this recommendation: if a published floor fails to raise hybrid adoption among 150–400-unit households within two years, the constraint is not price certainty but credit — see recommendation 2.

Decision-maker 2 — Government of Sindh, Energy Department, with SEPCO. Target any battery subsidy or financing at unprotected households using 150–700 units/month — the band where the battery pays — and explicitly exclude protected and lifeline households, for whom the same purchase destroys value (24.53-year payback at 200 protected units). A subsidy that ignores the tariff ladder would transfer public money to households that lose on the deal, violating 'adl (justice: the burden must not fall on the poorest — Qur'an 4:135) and hifz al-mal (preservation of wealth, one of the five purposes of the law, Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat). Financing must be interest-free: a conventional battery loan at interest would breach the prohibition of riba (Qur'an 2:275–279), so the window should be structured as diminishing musharakah or murabaha through Islamic banks (Chapra, Islam and the Economic Challenge, 1992). Exact change: a Sindh solar-plus-storage window covering the Rs 275,000 hybrid premium, first-loss-guaranteed, for unprotected 150–700-unit households, disbursed through SEPCO billing records (which already hold the consumption data that identifies the eligible band).

Decision-maker 3 — SEPCO. Settle surplus export credits quarterly and publish the settlement lag. Until settlement is reliable, every payback figure in this paper is an upper bound on what low-consumption households actually receive. The principle is shura (consultation, Qur'an 42:38): the households bearing the reform were not consulted when net metering ended, and transparent settlement data is the minimum repair.

7. Conclusion

NEPRA's February 2026 switch from net metering to net billing accidentally created the strongest economic case for home batteries Pakistan has ever had — and drew a sharp line through the middle of the tariff ladder. In Larkana, a 5 kW hybrid system pays its battery back in 5.25 years for a 400-unit household and in 4.62 years at 700 units, but the same battery needs 18.92 years at 100 units and 24.53 years for a protected 200-unit household. The crossover is 143 units/month for unprotected households, and there is none for protected ones. The policy conclusion follows the arithmetic: subsidise storage for the 150–700-unit unprotected band, finance it without interest, leave protected households alone, and publish the export rate as a floor. The claim stands or falls on a 30-household metered trial — and on whether NEPRA keeps the spread that makes the battery pay.

Two Tarbelas a Year: The Post-2015 Acceleration of Indus Basin Groundwater Loss and a Stepped-Wedge Groundwater Budget for Punjab

Question. Has Indus Basin groundwater loss genuinely accelerated since 2015, is the acceleration driven by pumping rather than climate, and what policy, tested how, would stop it in Pakistan's Punjab? Claim.

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan. ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509. Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI research assistant). Date: 20 November 2026. Field: Natural Science (hydrology / water policy). Status: Manuscript draft. Not submitted anywhere. No professor's endorsement is claimed; the Harvard / MIT / Oxford policy-shaping scholars named in the method brief are the standard this paper practises, not co-authors.

Abstract

Question. Has Indus Basin groundwater loss genuinely accelerated since 2015, is the acceleration driven by pumping rather than climate, and what policy, tested how, would stop it in Pakistan's Punjab?

Claim. Yes, the loss more than tripled: basin-wide terrestrial water storage fell at −0.65 cm/yr in 2002–2015 and at −2.16 cm/yr after 2015 (Dharpure et al., Water Resources Research, 2025). Converted to volume over the basin's 1.12 million km², that is a rise from ~7 km³/yr to ~24 km³/yr — about twice the design live storage of Tarbela Dam, every year. The acceleration is pumping-driven and concentrated in managed landscapes: non-glaciated regions lose water about twice as fast as glaciated ones (−1.44 vs −0.78 cm/yr), downscaled GRACE attributes 47–83% of the decline in most sub-regions to anthropogenic stressors, and aquifer depletion drives 67% of the Indus's total water-storage decline. Pakistan alone extracts ~65 km³/yr of groundwater against ~55 km³/yr of recharge — a ~10 km³/yr deficit, roughly one Tarbela a year.

Falsifier. The claim fails if (i) GRACE-FO data for 2024–2028 show the non-glaciated/glaciated loss ratio collapsing toward 1 (which would mean the acceleration is climate-driven, not pumping-driven), or (ii) a stepped-wedge trial of district groundwater budgets shows no divergence between pilot and control districts after five years (see §6). Either result would require withdrawing the pumping-driven attribution or the policy, respectively.

Identification. Natural-experiment contrast (glaciated vs non-glaciated regions under shared climate forcing; managed vs natural landscapes in downscaled GRACE) plus a general additive model decomposition for attribution; the attribution is association only — not causal proof. The policy claim will be tested by a stepped-wedge cluster-randomised rollout of district groundwater budgets, which is the causal design.

One clean number: 24 km³/yr — the water the Indus Basin now loses every year, about two Tarbelas. The stakes number is 300 million: the people the basin supports.

Keywords: Indus Basin; groundwater depletion; GRACE; GRACE-FO; Punjab; tube wells; solar pumping; stepped-wedge trial; khilafah; water commons.

1. Introduction

The Indus Basin — 1.12 million km² across Afghanistan, China, India and Pakistan, home to nearly 300 million people — is the most intensively irrigated river basin on Earth, and its groundwater is its hidden reservoir. Pakistan is the world's fourth-largest user of groundwater, and its aquifer system is the second-most overstressed on the planet (Pakistan Institute of Development Economics, 2026). Per-capita water availability in Pakistan has fallen from over 5,000 m³ in 1947 to under 1,000 m³ today — the standard threshold of absolute water scarcity.

Until recently the depletion was understood as a slow, chronic decline. A study published in February 2025 changed the picture: using GRACE and GRACE-FO satellite gravity data from April 2002 to May 2023, Dharpure, Howat and Kaushik showed that the basin's water loss more than tripled after 2015 — from −0.65 cm/yr to −2.16 cm/yr — and that 83.7% of the basin is now in significant decline. The question this paper answers is the one the study leaves open: how big is that loss in volumes a minister can picture, is it pumping or climate, which districts cross the danger line first, and what exactly should Punjab — which pumps over 90% of Pakistan's groundwater — do, tested in a way that can prove itself wrong?

The paper's method ancestor is named deliberately: Al-Biruni (973–1050), who measured the Earth's circumference to within about 1% and recorded the rivers and lands of India before theorising about them (Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030). The discipline this paper demands of Punjab's water policy is the same: measure first, publish the measurement, and let the claim be killed by the next measurement.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

Three legs, in the order required by the programme's standing rules:

  1. Modern scientific literature. The daily research digest of 14 November 2026 (health-focused; no water item) plus targeted searches on 20 November 2026 for Indus groundwater depletion, GRACE/GRACE-FO rates, Pakistan abstraction and tube-well counts, and Lahore water-table decline. Peer-reviewed sources used: Dharpure, Howat & Kaushik (2025, Water Resources Research 61(2), e2024WR038279, DOI 10.1029/2024WR038279); Arshad et al. (2024, Water Resources Research 60, DOI 10.1029/2023WR035882); the Frontiers in Earth Science decomposition of Indus–Ganges–Brahmaputra storage (2025, DOI 10.3389/feart.2025.1551218); and the Lahore aquifer literature (MDPI Water, 2022; Groundwater Environment in Lahore, Elsevier, 2017). Grey literature used and labelled as such: the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics report Pakistan's Groundwater Crisis: Policy Lessons and a Framework for Sustainable Resource Use (2026, as reported by The News and ProPakistani, October–November 2026); Punjab Irrigation Department piezometer data as reported by Dawn (12 May 2025) and the Sustainable Development Policy Institute; Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources (PCRWR) figures as reported by Business Recorder (2026). Grey sources are cited as grey sources; no grey figure is presented as a peer-reviewed result.
  2. Islamic canon. The hadith of the three commons — "Muslims are partners in three things: pasture, water and fire" (Sunan Abi Dawud 3477, graded sahih by al-Albani); Qur'an 21:30 ("We made from water every living thing"); Qur'an 2:30 (humanity as khalifah, steward, on earth); Al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030); Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Man and Nature: The Spiritual Crisis of Modern Man (1968); Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa (the five necessities of the law); Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat (systematisation of maqasid al-shariah). Consulted through the programme's verified literature map; full-text re-reading was not done in this run (see §7).
  3. Method standard. The 10-point checklist of the policy-shaping professors (Banerjee & Duflo; Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson; Chetty; Thaler & Sunstein; Heckman; Hanushek; Rodrik; Deaton; Haynes & Gawande; Pacala & Socolow; Myles Allen): one falsifiable question, named identification, mechanism, effect size with uncertainty, analysis plan stated before results, replication/data availability, limitations that bite, policy implications naming the decision-maker, comparison against the strongest incumbent, one clean number.

Research agents were not used in this run: Mimosa's litellm patch has landed but its smoke test remains incomplete; Co-Scientist, Denario and EvoScientist remain blocked on authentication or onboarding. The run therefore used the digest plus targeted searches, as the plan's fallback provides.

2.2 Pre-registered analysis plan (stated before results)

  1. Convert the published satellite rates to volumes using the published basin area (1.12 million km², range 1.08–1.165 million km²), with the arithmetic shown and the range carried through as the uncertainty band. No new satellite processing is claimed.
  2. Test the pumping-driven attribution against three independent published lines: the glaciated/non-glaciated contrast (Dharpure et al. 2025), the downscaled-GRACE anthropogenic share (Arshad et al. 2024), and the storage-decomposition share (Frontiers 2025). The claim requires at least two of the three to point the same way.
  3. Rank Punjab districts by published water-table decline rates and abstraction volumes, and propose a regulatory trigger threshold grounded in the observed Lahore rate.
  4. Design the policy test as a stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial with a pre-stated success criterion, so the policy can fail in public.

2.3 Volume conversion (the paper's own arithmetic)

Water-equivalent depth (cm/yr) × basin area (km²) = volume (km³/yr). 1 cm over 1 km² = 0.01 km³. All conversions in §3 are this multiplication, labelled "derived here", and use the central basin area of 1.12 million km² with the published area range (1.08–1.165 million km²) as the band. Tarbela Dam's design live storage is 9.68 million acre-feet (MAF) = 11.94 km³ (1 MAF = 1.2335 km³); siltation has cut its present live storage to roughly 5.7–6.8 MAF (7.0–8.4 km³). Both figures are used, and the paper says which one each comparison uses.

3. Results

3.1 The acceleration, in volumes

Dharpure et al. (2025) report basin-wide terrestrial water storage anomaly (TWSA) falling at −0.65 cm/yr before 2015/16 and −2.16 cm/yr after — a 3.3-fold acceleration — with 83.7% of the basin in significant decline (>−0.15 cm/yr, p < 0.05). Converted (derived here):

Period Rate (cm/yr) Volume loss (km³/yr) In Tarbelas (design live storage, 11.94 km³)
2002–2015 −0.65 7.3 (range 7.0–7.6) ~0.6
2015–2022 −2.16 24.2 (range 23.3–25.2) ~2.0

The basin now loses about 24 km³ of water a year — two Tarbelas a year, every year — against about 7 km³/yr before 2015. Against Tarbela's present, silted live storage (7.0–8.4 km³), the annual loss is roughly three Tarbelas. The Indus River system distributes about 153 billion m³ (153 km³) of freshwater a year through its canals; the groundwater loss is now equivalent to about one-sixth of that entire annual surface flow, disappearing underground.

3.2 The acceleration is pumping-driven, not climate-driven

Three independent published lines point the same way:

  • The glaciated/non-glaciated contrast (Dharpure et al. 2025). Glaciated regions lose −0.78 cm/yr; non-glaciated regions lose −1.44 cm/yr — about twice as fast. Both regions share the same climate forcing; what differs is that the non-glaciated plains are where the pumping happens. Among sub-basins, the Upper Indus (glaciated, little pumping) loses least (−0.42 cm/yr) while the Panjnad (the Punjab confluence of the five rivers, intensively pumped) loses most (−1.70 cm/yr).
  • The downscaled-GRACE attribution (Arshad et al. 2024). At 1 km² resolution, validated against 2,200 monitoring wells (Kling–Gupta efficiency 0.50–0.85, correlation 0.60–0.95), a general additive model attributes 47–83% of the total water-storage decline in most sub-regions to anthropogenic stressors — expanding cropped area, water consumption and settlements. The worst hotspots are in managed landscapes: Dehli Doab groundwater storage falling at −585 mm/yr, BIST Doab at −556 mm/yr. In upstream sub-regions, by contrast, climatic factors explain 72–91% of the change — the method can tell the two apart, and it says the plains are us.
  • The storage decomposition (Frontiers in Earth Science, 2025). Aquifer depletion drives 67% of the Indus's total water-storage decline (76% in the Ganges). The falling signal is mostly groundwater, not snow or soil moisture.

Dharpure et al. also report the climate contribution honestly: declining precipitation and surface runoff, rising evapotranspiration, and vegetation cover growing 0.23% a year (more crops, more water demand). Climate loads the gun; pumping pulls the trigger. Attribution is association only — no randomised manipulation exists — but the three lines agree, and the glaciated/non-glaciated contrast is the closest thing to a control group the basin offers.

3.3 Pakistan's side of the ledger

The satellite picture and the ground picture agree in magnitude:

  • Extraction vs recharge (PIDE, 2026). Pakistan extracts ~65 km³/yr of groundwater against ~55 km³/yr of natural recharge — a deficit of ~10 km³/yr, roughly one Tarbela (design live storage) every year. Punjab accounts for over 90% of national abstraction.
  • The tube-well explosion (Punjab Irrigation Department, via Dawn, May 2025). Agricultural tube wells in Punjab rose from 333,881 in 1994 to over 1.2 million in 2024; nationally the count exceeds 1.4 million. Punjab's wells now withdraw over 51 MAF/yr — about 63 km³/yr, slightly less than Punjab's entire allocated share of river water under the 1991 Water Apportionment Accord. District Rahim Yar Khan alone has 97,571 tube wells extracting around 4 MAF/yr, driven largely by sugarcane. Punjab's extraction rate is 142% above its recharge rate (Dawn, February 2025).
  • The solar accelerant (Reuters, via Business Recorder, 2026). Roughly 650,000 of Pakistan's 1.4 million-plus tube wells — nearly half — are now solar-powered. Solar pumping has zero marginal energy cost: once the panels are installed, every extra hour of pumping is free. That is the mechanism by which a water-saving technology became a water-mining technology.
  • The water table on the ground (Punjab Irrigation Department piezometers, 2004–2024). Water tables fell in 30 Punjab districts, sharply in 27. Lahore's fell from 31 ft to 79 ft — a decline of 2.61 ft/yr (≈0.8 m/yr), the fastest in the province — with the central city now below 40 m and falling about 0.9–1.0 m/yr (WASA; PCRWR 2023). Pakpattan fell 44 ft and Multan 32 ft over the same twenty years. Outside the canal command the rates are worse: Rawalpindi ~2.5 m/yr, Quetta Valley ~6 m/yr with wells now deeper than 350 m (PCRWR 2023). Lahore alone extracts about 4.32 million m³ of groundwater a day through nearly 1,800 tube wells.

3.4 Which districts cross the line first — a proposed trigger

No official "critical district" threshold exists for Punjab's groundwater. This paper proposes one, grounded in the observed data rather than invented: a district is declared critical when its five-year mean water-table decline exceeds 2 ft/yr (≈0.61 m/yr) — a rate Lahore (2.61 ft/yr) and Pakpattan (2.2 ft/yr) already exceed, and Multan (1.6 ft/yr) approaches. The threshold is a proposal, not a measurement; its purpose is to convert a satellite trend into an administrative fact with a named consequence (metering, then a cap). On published rates, the first critical districts are Lahore, Pakpattan, Rahim Yar Khan (by abstraction volume), Multan, and the Lahore-adjacent urbanising districts — the order is a ranking by published evidence, and the trial in §6 will test whether the ranking predicts stabilisation.

4. Discussion

4.1 Mechanism

The causal chain has five links, each with a published test:

  1. Free energy. Solar panels collapsed the marginal cost of pumping to zero for ~650,000 wells. Standard economics predicts more pumping; the well count (334,000 → 1.2 million in Punjab) and the post-2015 acceleration are consistent with it.
  2. Thirsty crops. Sugarcane in Rahim Yar Khan and rice across the doabs expanded on pumped water; vegetation cover grew 0.23%/yr basin-wide (Dharpure et al. 2025).
  3. Open access. Groundwater was a de facto open-access resource until the Punjab Irrigation, Drainage and Rivers Act (2023) vested all groundwater rights in the government; the Punjab Water Act (2019) already provides licensing tools for large users. The law now exists; enforcement does not.
  4. Falling recharge. Declining precipitation and runoff plus urban paving reduce the water going back in, while abstraction rises — the 142%-above-recharge figure.
  5. Deepening. As shallow water fails, wells go deeper (Lahore's potable water now at 800 ft in places; Quetta beyond 350 m), raising costs for the poorest farmers first and mining fossil water that accumulated over thousands of years.

4.2 Why the incumbent answer — build more dams — cannot fix this

The strongest incumbent policy is surface storage: build another Tarbela. The comparison is arithmetic. A new large dam adds, at best, one Tarbela's worth of live storage (~7–12 km³) after a decade or more of construction and tens of billions of rupees — and storage does not create water, it only retimes it. The groundwater deficit recurs every year: ~10 km³/yr for Pakistan alone, ~24 km³/yr basin-wide. Dams also lose live storage to siltation (Tarbela has lost roughly a third). Capping abstraction at recharge, by contrast, saves the same volume every year at the cost of meters and licences. Storage and demand management are complements, not substitutes — but a policy that only builds storage while abstraction grows 3.3-fold is arithmetic denial. The PIDE report reaches the same conclusion: the crisis is "fundamentally a failure of policy and governance rather than a physical lack of water."

4.3 The Islamic frame: water as a commons, not a commodity

The policy conclusion the modern evidence points to is the one the Islamic canon stated fourteen centuries ago. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Muslims are partners in three things: pasture, water and fire" (Sunan Abi Dawud 3477, graded sahih by al-Albani) — water that is not under anyone's private control is a shared property, and monopolising it is prohibited. The Qur'an grounds the same point in creation itself: "We made from water every living thing" (Qur'an 21:30), and in stewardship: humanity is placed on earth as khalifah, trustee (Qur'an 2:30). Al-Biruni's Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030) measured the rivers and lands of this very basin before theorising about them — the measurement-first discipline this paper follows. Seyyed Hossein Nasr (Man and Nature, 1968) argues the ecological crisis is at root a spiritual one: nature treated as a resource to exhaust rather than a trust (amanah) to keep. Against the maqasid al-shariah (Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat), the current regime fails on the preservation of life (nafs) — 70–80% of Pakistan's groundwater is unsafe to drink, with arsenic threatening up to 60 million people (PIDE 2026) — and on wealth (mal), as the aquifer, the country's largest water store, is mined. Where the Islamic source and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so: both say water is a commons, pumping must be capped at recharge, and the burden must not fall on the poorest farmers. Where they differ, the paper says so too: the canon gives the principle, not the number — the 2 ft/yr trigger and the stepped-wedge design are modern instruments, not derived from scripture.

5. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Secretary, Punjab Irrigation Department, acting with the Punjab Water Commission under the Punjab Irrigation, Drainage and Rivers Act (2023) and the Punjab Water Act (2019). The exact change, in order:

  1. Declare critical districts by the 2 ft/yr trigger (§3.4), starting with Lahore, Pakpattan, Rahim Yar Khan and Multan, and publish the district ranking with the underlying piezometer data — Chetty's lesson: publish the data as a public tool, not just the finding.
  2. Meter solar tube wells first, within 24 months. The ~650,000 solar wells are the marginal-cost-free pumpers; metering them is the cheapest measurement in the system and the precondition for any cap. Fund it from the electricity-subsidy savings as diesel/electric wells convert.
  3. Cap district abstraction at recharge, rolled out as a stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial. Districts are randomised into licensing waves; each wave's cap is set at the district's GRACE-derived recharge rate, enforced through the 2019 Act's licensing tools. Pre-register the analysis: the primary outcome is the district GWSA trend from GRACE-FO plus piezometers; success is a pilot-district trend of −0.5 cm/yr or better against control districts continuing at −1.5 cm/yr or worse, after five years. If pilot districts show no divergence from controls, the cap-and-meter approach is withdrawn and the recommendation reverses to supply-side measures only.
  4. Protect small farmers by design ('adl). The cap must be paired with a lifeline allocation for smallholders and a shift of price support away from sugarcane and rice toward less thirsty crops — otherwise the burden falls on the poorest, and the policy fails the justice test (Qur'an 4:135, 16:90).

Islamic principle behind the recommendation: the hadith of the three commons (water as shared property — Sunan Abi Dawud 3477) and khilafah stewardship (Qur'an 2:30), operationalised through maslaha (public interest) and 'adl (justice). The trial design itself is an act of shura in method: the policy is tested in the open, and its subjects — the districts — are its witnesses.

6. The falsifiable claim, stated once more

Claim: the post-2015 acceleration of Indus groundwater loss is pumping-driven and concentrated in Punjab's managed landscapes, and a district groundwater budget (cap at recharge, metered solar wells) will stabilise pilot districts within five years. Falsifier 1 (attribution): GRACE-FO 2024–2028 shows the non-glaciated/glaciated loss ratio falling to ~1. Falsifier 2 (policy): pilot districts' GWSA trends do not diverge from controls by at least 1 cm/yr after five years. Falsifier 3 (mechanism): metering shows solar wells are not the marginal pumpers — i.e., metered solar abstraction is flat while total abstraction still rises, which would point to a different driver. Any one of the three kills the corresponding part of the claim.

7. Limitations

  1. GRACE cannot see a district. GRACE/GRACE-FO resolve ~300 km; the 1 km² downscaled products are model outputs, validated against wells with correlation 0.60–0.95 and RMSE of 17.5 cm against in-situ groundwater storage in the Indus (ISPRS Archives, 2026). District rankings in §3.4 rest on piezometers and abstraction proxies, not on direct district-level satellite measurement.
  2. The 65/55 km³ figures are estimates. PIDE's national extraction and recharge numbers carry wide, unstated uncertainty; different sources put national abstraction at 50 MAF (~62 km³) to 65 km³ and Punjab's well count at 1.2–1.5 million. The deficit is robust in sign, not precise in size.
  3. Attribution is association only. The glaciated/non-glaciated contrast and the GAM decomposition are quasi-experimental; no randomised manipulation of pumping exists. The stepped-wedge trial is proposed precisely because the current evidence cannot prove causality.
  4. The 2 ft/yr trigger is proposed, not measured. It is calibrated to the observed Lahore rate, but the threshold at which a district's aquifer becomes economically unviable for small farmers is not established in the literature and will vary with depth to water and energy cost.
  5. Grey sources. PIDE, PCRWR and Punjab Irrigation Department figures reach this paper through reputable press reporting, not through the underlying reports, which were not obtained in this run. They are labelled as such in §2.1.
  6. Islamic canon gaps. Al-Biruni's Kitab al-Hind and Nasr's Man and Nature were consulted through the programme's verified literature map, not re-read in full in this run. The classical fiqh chapters on water rights beyond the cited hadith, and Ibn Khaldun's discussion of urban water supply in the Muqaddimah, were not consulted; many classical Arabic manuscripts on water law remain undigitised in libraries (Süleymaniye, Istanbul; Dar al-Kutub, Cairo) with no online copy. The hadith and Qur'an citations were verified against published references in this run; no quotation is offered from memory.
  7. Transboundary scope. The basin spans four countries; this paper's policy lever sits in Punjab, Pakistan. The fastest-declining hotspots (Dehli and BIST doabs) lie across the border, and no basin-wide treaty mechanism for groundwater exists.

8. Conclusion

The Indus Basin's groundwater loss more than tripled after 2015, from ~7 km³/yr to ~24 km³/yr — two Tarbelas a year. The loss is concentrated where the pumping is, the attribution is consistent across three independent published lines, and Pakistan's own deficit is about one Tarbela a year. The law to fix it already exists; the measurement to enforce it already exists; what does not exist is a tested policy. The proposal is therefore small and testable: declare critical districts by a published trigger, meter the solar wells first, and cap abstraction at recharge in a stepped-wedge trial that can fail in public. Water is a shared trust — the satellite, the piezometer and the hadith agree on that much. What remains is to act as if it were true.
