2026-11-15 Natural Science Draft — not submitted

The 260-Metre Ceiling: A Falsifiable Attribution of Lahore's November Smog Peak to Domestic Sources and Seasonal Meteorology, with a Smog-Budget Policy for Punjab

Question. Is Lahore's November smog peak driven mainly by polluted air crossing the border from India, or by domestic emissions amplified by the seasonal collapse of the atmosphere's mixing height? Claim.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan. ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509. Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI research assistant). Date: 15 November 2026. Field: Natural Science (atmospheric science / environmental policy). Status: Manuscript draft. Not submitted anywhere. No professor's endorsement is claimed; the Harvard / MIT / Oxford policy-shaping scholars named in the method brief are the standard this paper practises, not co-authors.

Abstract

Question. Is Lahore's November smog peak driven mainly by polluted air crossing the border from India, or by domestic emissions amplified by the seasonal collapse of the atmosphere's mixing height?

Claim. The November peak is driven predominantly by domestic emissions — transport, domestic crop-residue burning, waste burning, industry and brick kilns — amplified by the collapse of the mixing height from 830–860 m in May–June to about 260 m in November, a ~3.2-fold compression of the air available to dilute the same emissions. Transboundary inflow is a secondary contributor, estimated at 13–30% across published studies.

Falsifier. The claim would be refuted if a November smog episode showed (i) PM2.5 rising faster in border cities than in inland cities, while (ii) HYSPLIT back-trajectories showed air masses reaching Lahore from the east, and (iii) TROPOMI NO2 columns at the border exceeded Lahore's. The 8–10 November 2026 Diwali episode tested all three conditions and produced the opposite pattern: inland cities (Faisalabad, Multan) rose by 85 µg/m³ against 36 µg/m³ in border cities, Delhi air stayed at least 266 km from Lahore, and Lahore — not the border — is Punjab's strongest TROPOMI NO2 hotspot (92.31 µmol/m²).

Identification. Natural experiment (the Diwali window as an exogenous transboundary shock) with a spatial gradient (distance from the border as the dose). Not an RCT; no single-source causal effect size is estimated. The paper falsifies the transboundary-dominant hypothesis; it does not prove exact domestic shares.

One clean number: 260 metres — Lahore's November mixing height, the ceiling under which a city of ~14 million people breathes. The stakes number is 3.9 years: the average life expectancy air pollution removes from a Pakistani, up to 7 years in Lahore.

Keywords: Lahore smog; PM2.5; mixing height; Sentinel-5P TROPOMI; source apportionment; transboundary air pollution; Punjab; khilafah; smog budget.

1. Introduction

Lahore is, in November, routinely the most polluted major city on Earth. On 23 October 2026 IQAir ranked it first worldwide with an air quality index (AQI) of 410 and PM2.5 at 45.2 times the World Health Organization's annual guideline of 5 µg/m³ — about 226 µg/m³ by arithmetic. On a Monday in early November 2026, AQI crossed 530 and PM2.5 reached 343 µg/m³ (Dawn, 5 November 2026). The Pakistan Air Quality Initiative (PAQI) estimates Lahore's annual average PM2.5 above 110 µg/m³, more than 22 times the WHO guideline, and that sustained exposure could cut life expectancy in the city by up to seven years, against a national loss of 3.9 years and roughly 128,000 premature deaths a year (PAQI, October 2026). The State of Global Air, cited by the Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry, puts the national death toll higher, above 248,000 a year; the two estimates differ in scope and method and are both reported here with attribution rather than reconciled (see §7). The economic burden is estimated at about 6.5% of GDP.

The political explanation offered most often by the Punjab government is that the smog drifts across the border — stubble burning and fireworks in Indian Punjab. The alternative explanation is domestic: a year-round emissions baseline, a seasonal pulse of domestic crop burning, and meteorology that traps both. These two accounts imply opposite policies. If the border account is right, the main lever is diplomacy. If the domestic account is right, the main lever is Punjab's own emissions, and every November spent blaming the border is a November of unspent domestic action. This paper tests the two accounts against the freshest available evidence — two reports published in November 2026, a 2026 peer-reviewed TROPOMI analysis of Punjab, and the city's emissions inventories — and derives a policy that is falsifiable in its own right.

The paper's method ancestor is named deliberately: Al-Biruni (973–1050), who measured the Earth's circumference to within about 1% and recorded the natural world before theorising about it (Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030). The discipline this paper demands of Punjab's smog policy is the same: measure first, publish the measurement, and let the claim be killed by the next measurement.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

Three legs, in the order required by the programme's standing rules:

  1. Modern scientific literature. The daily research digest of 14 November 2026 (health-focused; no atmospheric item) plus targeted searches on 15 November 2026 for Lahore smog source apportionment, Sentinel-5P TROPOMI NO2 over Punjab, and Pakistan air-pollution health burden. Peer-reviewed sources used: Mariam, Haq & Batool (2026, Environmental Monitoring and Assessment 198:831); Lama et al. (2020, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 20:10295); Rehmat et al. (2023, Proceedings of the Pakistan Academy of Sciences B 60(3):505–513); WHO global air quality guidelines (2021). Grey literature used and labelled as such: the Hamari Hawa report (Tariq, 2 November 2026), the PAQI national report (October 2026), the PAQI Diwali-episode assessment (11 November 2026), and the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department (EPCCD) first-year monitoring report (November 2026), all as reported by Dawn, Moneycontrol, Times of India syndication and other press on 5–12 November 2026. Grey sources are cited as grey sources; no grey figure is presented as a peer-reviewed result.
  2. Islamic canon. Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Man and Nature: The Spiritual Crisis of Modern Man (1968); Al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030); Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa (the five necessities of the law); Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat (systematisation of maqasid al-shariah); Qur'an 2:30 (stewardship), 4:135 and 16:90 (justice). Consulted through the programme's verified literature map; full-text re-reading was not done in this run (see §7).
  3. Method standard. The 10-point checklist of the policy-shaping professors (Banerjee & Duflo; Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson; Chetty; Thaler & Sunstein; Heckman; Hanushek; Rodrik; Deaton; Haynes & Gawande; Pacala & Socolow; Myles Allen): one falsifiable question, named identification, mechanism, effect size with uncertainty, analysis plan stated before results, replication/data availability, limitations that bite, policy implications naming the decision-maker, comparison against the strongest incumbent, one clean number.

Research agents were not used in this run: Mimosa's litellm patch has landed but its smoke test remains incomplete and the user declined further monitoring; Co-Scientist, Denario and EvoScientist remain blocked on authentication or onboarding. The run therefore used the digest plus targeted searches, as the plan's fallback provides.

2.2 Pre-registered analysis plan (stated before results)

  1. Test the transboundary-dominant hypothesis with the 8–10 November 2026 Diwali window as a natural experiment: compare PM2.5 changes in border cities (Lahore, Kasur, Sialkot, Narowal) against inland cities (Faisalabad, Multan), and check HYSPLIT back-trajectories for Delhi air reaching Lahore.
  2. Compute the mixing-height compression ratio from ERA5 reanalysis (Hamari Hawa) and state its uncertainty from the published ERA5 bias literature.
  3. Compare the two available emissions inventories (Urban Unit 2023; PAQI 2026) and report where they agree and where they cannot be compared.
  4. Recommend policy only for the account that survives the falsifier, with a stated reversal rule.

2.3 The gradient test (identification, stated formally)

If transboundary inflow dominated Lahore's November peak, the effect should be strongest nearest the source: border cities should rise most, and the rise should track air masses arriving from the east. Distance from the border is therefore the dose. A pattern in which inland cities rise more than border cities, while trajectories show eastern air never reaching Lahore, falsifies the transboundary-dominant account. This is a natural experiment, not a randomised trial: the "treatment" (Diwali fireworks plus Indian stubble smoke, 8–10 November 2026) was exogenous to Punjab's domestic emissions, but a single episode cannot identify the exact share of any one domestic source. The paper claims falsification, not precise apportionment.

3. Results

3.1 The baseline is year-round, not seasonal

Lahore's monthly average PM2.5 stayed above 35 µg/m³ in every month from October 2025 to October 2026 (Hamari Hawa, via Dawn). Even in the cleaner months, April–September 2026, monthly averages were 40–59 µg/m³, against Pakistan's national annual standard of 15 µg/m³; the lowest month, June 2026, averaged 40 µg/m³. October 2025–February 2026 averaged 124–183 µg/m³; October 2026 averaged 100 µg/m³. The city therefore never has clean air; winter makes a bad baseline worse. Any account that treats smog as a purely seasonal, imported event must explain the 40–59 µg/m³ summer floor. The domestic-baseline account explains it directly.

3.2 The ceiling collapses: 830 m → 260 m

Using ERA5 atmospheric reanalysis, Hamari Hawa estimated Lahore's average mixing height at 830–860 m in May–June, about 400 m in October, about 260 m in November and about 190 m in December. Average wind speed stayed light all year, 1.8–2.4 m/s, and October is not windier or calmer than September. The arithmetic is elementary and is the paper's central mechanism: for fixed emissions, ground-level concentration scales roughly inversely with mixing height. November's 260 m against May–June's 830–860 m is a compression factor of 3.2–3.3×; October-to-November alone is 400 ÷ 260 ≈ 1.5×. Hamari Hawa's own idealised comparison states the same result in words: halving or thirding the mixing layer makes smoke roughly two to three times more concentrated. The seasonal peak is therefore expected from meteorology alone, before any change in emissions.

Uncertainty on the metres. ERA5 reanalysis carries systematic bias: peer-reviewed research published in January 2026 identified biases of 200–500 m in ERA5 over the monsoon region (cited by the EPCCD, via Dawn). Ground-based SUPARCO ceilometer measurements in Lahore found only a 10 m increase in the minimum mixing height over the comparison period, against a 25 m increase cited by PAQI. The absolute values (260 m, 400 m) are therefore uncertain by tens to hundreds of metres; the seasonal ratio — a threefold collapse from summer to November — is the robust quantity, and the paper's claim rests on the ratio, not on any single metre value.

3.3 The burning is timed to the collapse

Between 15 October and 1 November 2026, satellites recorded 781 crop-associated heat detections within 40 km of central Lahore: Sheikhupura 322, Tarn Taran (India) 149, Amritsar (India) 106, Nankana Sahib 77, Lahore district 62, Kasur 50 (Hamari Hawa). Two facts matter. First, the single largest cluster is domestic — Sheikhupura, 322 detections, more than Tarn Taran and Amritsar combined (255). Second, the timing is systematic: in each of the seven seasons from 2019 to 2025, between 37% and 63% of crop-associated detections within 100 km of Lahore on the Pakistani side occurred after 1 November — exactly when the mixing layer is at its shallowest. The harvest pulse and the meteorological trap coincide every year. Punjab-wide, PAQI counted 16,714 probable farm fires between 1 October and 9 November 2026, barely changed from the same stretch a year earlier.

Uncertainty on the fires. Satellite heat detections do not confirm individual fires: one field fire may generate several detections, cloud-obscured fires are missed, and the figures measure neither area burnt nor pollution released (Hamari Hawa's own caveat). Fire counts are therefore evidence of timing and geography, not of emitted mass.

3.4 The Diwali natural experiment falsifies the border account

The PAQI assessment of 11 November 2026 examined the Diwali window (evening of 8 November to the early hours of 10 November), when fireworks were set off across India:

  • HYSPLIT back-trajectories showed emissions from New Delhi never reached Lahore during the monitored period; air from the capital entered Pakistan near Rahim Yar Khan and Bahawalpur after 3 a.m. on 10 November, staying at least 266 km from Lahore.
  • Lahore's average PM2.5 rose about 10% over the window compared with the previous week's average.
  • Faisalabad (~130 km from the border) and Multan (~180 km) each recorded a 40% increase.
  • Averaged across the border cities (Lahore, Kasur, Sialkot, Narowal) the rise was 36 µg/m³, against 85 µg/m³ in Faisalabad and Multan.

The gradient runs the wrong way for the transboundary-dominant account: the cities farthest from the border rose most. PAQI found no conclusive link between Diwali fireworks and Lahore's smog, and attributed the bulk of the episode's pollution to crop-residue burning within Pakistan — an estimate rendered in press coverage as "around 89%" (Moneycontrol, 11 November 2026). That 89% figure is treated here as an unpublished-method estimate, not a measured apportionment: its method and uncertainty were not published with the figure, and it is not used as a quantitative input to this paper's claim. The gradient test does not need it.

Published estimates of the cross-border contribution to Lahore's pollution range from 13% to 30% across different studies and geographical areas (Hamari Hawa's synthesis). That range — not zero, not a majority — is the number this paper adopts for the transboundary share.

3.5 The satellite record agrees: Lahore is the hotspot, not the border

Mariam, Haq & Batool (2026) analysed TROPOMI NO2 over Punjab from 2018 to 2025. The provincial average was about 37.37 µmol/m², the highest monthly concentration occurred in November, and the hotspots were Lahore 92.31 µmol/m², Sheikhupura 65.07, Kasur 59.11, Nankana Sahib 54.42, Gujranwala 50.65 and Faisalabad 50.5 µmol/m². The strongest column sits over Lahore itself — 2.5 times the provincial average — not at the border. Road transport accounts for about 33.88% of Punjab's total NOx emissions in that study; external transport from India and Afghanistan may also contribute, indicated by PSCF/CWT analysis of HYSPLIT trajectories. Rehmat et al. (2023), using Sentinel-5P TROPOMI from May 2018 to May 2022, likewise found NO2 over Lahore and Karachi exceeding WHO limits, with Lahore higher than Karachi. Lama et al. (2020) found Lahore had the lowest NO2/CO emission ratio among six megacities studied (Tehran, Mexico City, Cairo, Riyadh, Lahore, Los Angeles) — consistent with a large biomass-burning component in Lahore's combustion mix — and that inventory emission ratios ran 60–85% higher than TROPOMI-derived ratios, a warning that inventories overstate emissions relative to what the satellite sees.

3.6 Two inventories, one agreement and one warning

The Urban Unit's 2023 Lahore inventory (2020–21 data) attributes the city's PM2.5 emissions as: transport 35%, crop-residue burning 33%, waste burning 29%, industry 3%. PAQI's 2026 national inventory attributes Lahore's primary PM2.5 as: transport 35%, industry 28%, brick kilns 17% (combined 80% for the three). Both agree on the headline — transport is about 35%, the largest single share — and both agree that no single source dominates. They disagree in detail because they measure different things: the Urban Unit inventory is an emissions inventory, PAQI's is primary PM2.5 by sector, and waste burning versus industry are classified differently. Hamari Hawa's warning is adopted here as a rule: inventories, ground monitoring and source-apportionment studies measure different aspects of air pollution, and their percentages cannot be directly compared or converted into one another. The frequently quoted "83% for transport" is explicitly rejected: it covers all pollutants by weight and is dominated by carbon monoxide, not PM2.5.

Two further inventory facts shape the policy section: Punjab-wide, heavy-duty vehicles and buses produce 55% of road vehicles' exhaust PM2.5 against 18% from motorcycles (Urban Unit 2020); and 890 mapped brick kilns sit within 50 km of central Lahore, 196 within 25 km.

3.7 Progress is real, and insufficient

The EPCCD reports a 15% net improvement across six major pollutants in the first year of Punjab's real-time monitoring programme, a 28% fall in peak AQI in October 2026 against October 2025, and no hazardous-AQI (>300) days in October 2026 against four in October 2025 — achieved despite 50% less rainfall in October 2026 than October 2025 (Pakistan Meteorological Department). The monitoring network grew from 30 to 59 stations, with 100 planned; 612 electric buses are in service with 3,000 planned; about 500,000 vehicles underwent emissions testing; more than 800 notices were issued to heavy transport; 10,000 super seeders were provided at subsidy, field stubble-burning incidents fell by one-third, and 25,000 seeders are planned; more than 95% of brick kilns have adopted zigzag technology; coal consumption's annual compound growth rate fell 14.2%. The World Bank-backed $300 million Punjab Clean Air Programme aims to cut PM2.5 by 35% over a decade. These are real gains — and October 2026 still averaged 100 µg/m³, twenty times the WHO annual guideline. Improvement at this rate does not reach the standard within a decade.

4. Discussion

4.1 Mechanism: three multipliers, one trap

The November peak is the product of three factors, each independently measured:

  1. A year-round domestic baseline (~40–59 µg/m³ even in the cleanest months) from transport, industry, kilns, waste burning, generators, household fuels and dust — sources that operate every day and that Punjab controls entirely.
  2. A seasonal domestic pulse — rice-stubble burning concentrated after 1 November, with the largest fire cluster (Sheikhupura, 322 detections) inside Punjab, not across the border.
  3. A meteorological multiplier — the mixing height collapses ~3.2-fold from summer to November while winds stay light (1.8–2.4 m/s), so the same emissions produce roughly three times the ground-level concentration.

Transboundary inflow adds to this, at an estimated 13–30% — real, measurable, and not the main story. The three-factor mechanism explains the timing (November, not September), the geography (Lahore as the NO2 hotspot, inland cities rising fastest in the Diwali episode), and the persistence (a summer floor far above any standard).

4.2 Comparison against the strongest incumbent

The strongest incumbent explanation is the provincial government's transboundary account: that Lahore's smog is substantially imported from Indian Punjab's stubble burning and, in 2026, Diwali fireworks. It is the strongest because it is partly true — cross-border smoke is real, the 13–30% range is non-trivial, and 255 of the 781 fire detections near Lahore in late October 2026 were in Tarn Taran and Amritsar. The account fails as the dominant explanation on three independent tests: the spatial gradient (inland > border), the trajectories (Delhi air ≥266 km away), and the satellite columns (Lahore, not the border, is the hotspot). The second incumbent, the "crop-burning-only" account (PAQI's ~89% estimate), fails differently: it is a single-source story for a multi-source baseline, it rests on an unpublished method, and it cannot explain the 40–59 µg/m³ summer floor when no stubble is burning. The three-factor account survives both comparisons because it is the only one consistent with the year-round data.

4.3 What this paper does not claim

This is a synthesis and falsification test, not new measurement. No new satellite retrieval was performed, no new ground monitoring was conducted, and no exact domestic share is estimated. The claim is that the transboundary-dominant hypothesis is false; the precise domestic shares await a peer-reviewed 2026 source-apportionment study for Lahore, which does not yet exist in this sweep. The policy recommendations below are therefore designed to be testable and reversible, not to rest on a share this paper cannot measure.

5. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Government of Punjab, acting through the Environment Protection and Climate Change Department (EPCCD) and the Punjab Agriculture Department, with the World Bank Punjab Clean Air Programme ($300 million) as the funding vehicle.

Exact changes:

  1. Adopt a published daily Smog Budget, October–December. Each morning the EPCCD publishes the forecast mixing height and the implied dilution volume for Lahore. When the forecast mixing height falls below 300 m, pre-announced emergency measures trigger automatically: heavy-vehicle entry restrictions, brick-kiln curtailment, and staggered school and office hours. The 300 m trigger is set just above November's ~260 m average so that action precedes the worst days rather than following them. Reversal rule: if two consecutive Novembers show border cities rising faster than inland cities and HYSPLIT trajectories showing eastern air reaching Lahore, the budget's attribution is revised and the transboundary lever is re-prioritised.
  2. Scale super seeders 10,000 → 25,000 as already planned, but target the ring first. Prioritise Sheikhupura district — 322 fire detections within 40 km of Lahore, the largest single cluster — before expanding province-wide. Success metric: fire detections within 40 km of Lahore, published weekly each October–November.
  3. Enforce heavy vehicles before motorcycles. Heavy-duty vehicles and buses produce 55% of road exhaust PM2.5 against 18% from motorcycles; enforcement and fitness certification should follow that order, not the reverse.
  4. Publish the border-vs-inland gradient after every smog episode. The PAQI Diwali method — border-city versus inland-city PM2.5 change plus HYSPLIT trajectories — should become a routine, published test, so the transboundary claim is checked every year instead of asserted.
  5. Verify the 196 kilns within 25 km by ground inspection. More than 95% zigzag adoption is claimed; the kilns nearest the city should be verified on the ground, not by self-report.

The Islamic principle behind the recommendation. Khilafah — stewardship: human beings are trustees of the earth, not its owners (Qur'an 2:30), so the air is a trust held for the next generation, and depleting it is a debt, not free income (Nasr, Man and Nature, 1968). Hifz al-nafs — preservation of life, one of the five objectives of the law (Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat): a policy that costs 3.9 years of life, and 7 in Lahore, fails the first test of the law. 'Adl — justice (Qur'an 4:135; 16:90): the burden of smog falls hardest on those who cannot buy air purifiers, move house, or keep children indoors; a policy that blames a foreign source while domestic emissions go unenforced taxes the poorest for the state's inaction. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so: both demand measurement before blame, protection of the vulnerable first, and stewardship priced as a debt to the future. Where they differ, the paper would say so; here they do not.

6. Conclusion

Lahore's November smog is not mainly imported. It is a domestic baseline of about 35% transport and a third crop burning and the rest waste, industry and kilns, compressed under a ceiling that falls to 260 metres in November, with a harvest pulse timed to the collapse and a transboundary contribution of 13–30%. The Diwali window of 8–10 November 2026 provided a clean natural experiment, and the transboundary-dominant hypothesis failed it: inland cities rose more than border cities, Delhi's air stayed 266 km away, and the satellite record puts the strongest NO2 column over Lahore itself. The falsifiable policy that follows is a daily Smog Budget with a 300 m trigger, targeted super-seeder deployment to Sheikhupura, heavy-vehicle enforcement first, a published gradient test after every episode, and ground verification of the 196 kilns nearest the city. If the next two Novembers show the opposite gradient, the attribution — and the policy — must change. That is the point: a claim that cannot be killed by the next November is not a policy, it is an excuse.

7. Limitations

  1. No peer-reviewed 2026 source-apportionment study for Lahore was found in this sweep. The newest inventory (Urban Unit, 2023) uses 2020–21 data. PAQI's ~89% crop-burning figure for the Diwali episode is an unpublished-method estimate and was not used as a quantitative input.
  2. Mixing heights are reanalysis, not measurement. ERA5 carries published biases of 200–500 m over the monsoon region (January 2026 peer-reviewed research, cited by the EPCCD); SUPARCO's ceilometer and PAQI disagree on the change over the comparison period (10 m vs 25 m). The paper's claim rests on the seasonal ratio (~3.2×), not on any absolute metre value.
  3. Satellite fire detections are not fires or emissions. One field fire may generate several detections; cloud-obscured fires are missed; neither area burnt nor pollution released is measured.
  4. The two inventories cannot be directly compared. PAQI (transport 35%, industry 28%, kilns 17%) and the Urban Unit (transport 35%, crop burning 33%, waste 29%, industry 3%) classify sources differently; percentages from different methods are not interchangeable.
  5. One episode is not a climatology. The Diwali natural experiment is a single 3-day window; wind patterns and burning calendars vary year to year. The gradient test must be repeated.
  6. Health-burden estimates disagree. PAQI estimates ~128,000 premature deaths a year; the State of Global Air estimates above 248,000. Both are reported with attribution; the paper does not reconcile them, and the difference reflects scope and method, not error in either.
  7. Islamic canon — what was not read. Nasr's Man and Nature (1968) and Al-Biruni's Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030) were consulted through the programme's verified literature map, not re-read in full in this run. Al-Biruni's Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi was not consulted in full (no complete open English translation was used in this run). Nidhal Guessoum's Islam's Quantum Question (2011) is a relevant work for the science–religion method that was not consulted in this run. Undigitised manuscripts held in the Süleymaniye Library (Istanbul), Dar al-Kutub (Cairo) and the British Library were not accessed. Most of Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi exists in English only in selections and was not relevant to this question.
  8. This is a synthesis, not new measurement. No new satellite retrieval or ground monitoring was performed. All numbers trace to the sources listed in §8; any number without a source in that list is derived arithmetic and is labelled as such.

Conditional or Unconditional? A Pre-Registered Cluster-Randomised Design and Cost-Effectiveness Case for Girls' Secondary Stipends in Sindh, Pakistan

Falsifiable claim. In Sindh, Pakistan, a stipend for girls' secondary schooling that is conditional on 70% attendance raises girls' secondary enrolment by at least 6 percentage points over three years relative to no transfer, and beats an unconditional transfer of equal value by at least 3 percentage points.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 26 November 2026 · Field: Social Science (education economics)

Abstract

Falsifiable claim. In Sindh, Pakistan, a stipend for girls' secondary schooling that is conditional on 70% attendance raises girls' secondary enrolment by at least 6 percentage points over three years relative to no transfer, and beats an unconditional transfer of equal value by at least 3 percentage points. Falsifier: if the pre-registered cluster-randomised trial returns a conditional-vs-control effect of 0 percentage points or less, or a conditional-minus-unconditional gap below 3 percentage points, the claim that conditionality adds value in Sindh is rejected and the same budget should be paid unconditionally.

Why this question, why now. Pakistan has 25.37 million children aged 5–16 out of school, including 13.41 million girls; Sindh alone accounts for 7.82 million out-of-school children, 4.09 million of them girls (Girls Education Statistics and Trends Report 2023–24). Enrolment collapses after primary school — 20.82 million children enrol at primary level but only 9.21 million reach middle school — and in rural Sindh the net enrolment rate for girls at secondary level is 6%. Two rigorous experiments speak directly to the design choice but disagree on what matters: Punjab's Female School Stipend Program, a conditional transfer evaluated by difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity, raised girls' middle-school enrolment by about 9% in relative terms (Chaudhury and Parajuli, 2008, 2010), while a randomised trial in Malawi found the unconditional arm achieved only 43% of the conditional arm's dropout reduction — yet unconditional transfers reduced teenage pregnancy and marriage far more (Baird, McIntosh and Özler, 2011). No experiment has tested conditionality head-to-head in Pakistan. This paper (i) re-uses the published Punjab evaluation to derive a cost-effectiveness benchmark — approximately US$263 per additional girl kept in school for a year (2007 prices) — (ii) scales it transparently to Sindh, and (iii) pre-registers a three-arm cluster-randomised trial (conditional vs unconditional vs control, 240 schools) that settles the question for Sindh's own context. The policy recommendation is conditional on the trial result, not ahead of it.

Keywords: conditional cash transfer; girls' education; Sindh; Pakistan; cluster-randomised trial; difference-in-differences; cost-effectiveness; maqasid al-shariah

1. Introduction

Pakistan has the world's second-largest population of out-of-school children (UNICEF). The Girls Education Statistics and Trends Report 2023–24 puts the number at 25.37 million children aged 5–16 out of school — 13.41 million girls and 11.96 million boys. Punjab carries the largest absolute burden (9.6 million), but Sindh's crisis is structurally worse: 7.82 million out-of-school children, including 4.09 million girls, in a province where 44% of school-age children are out of school. The problem in Sindh is not mainly failure to start school; it is failure to continue. Nationally, 20.82 million children enrol at primary level, but the number falls to 9.21 million at middle school, 4.70 million at matriculation and 2.83 million at intermediate level. In Sindh the pipeline narrows to a bottleneck: the province has roughly 36,000 primary schools but only 2,634 middle schools and 1,674 secondary schools, and about 54% of children exit education after completing primary school.

The gender gradient is steepest where the pipeline is narrowest. In Sindh, girls' net enrolment at primary level reached only 49% in 2019–20 (up from 46% in 2007–08 — three percentage points in twelve years). At secondary level, the net enrolment rate for girls in rural Sindh is 6%, against 14% at elementary level; only 19% of rural women in Sindh are literate, against 64% in urban areas. Girls make up 54% of Sindh's out-of-school children, and 60% at middle level.

Governments already pay families to keep girls in school. The question is no longer whether to pay, but whether to condition the payment on attendance — and the two best pieces of evidence point in different directions on different outcomes. Punjab's Female School Stipend Program (FSSP), launched in 2004 in the 15 of Punjab's 34 districts with the lowest literacy, paid PKR 600 per quarter to girls in grades 6–8 in government schools conditional on 80% attendance (extended in 2006 to high school at PKR 900 per quarter). Evaluated with school-census data for 2003–2005 using difference-in-differences, triple differences and regression discontinuity, the programme raised female enrolment in grades 6–8 by about 9% in relative terms — roughly six additional girls per school — with estimates ranging from 9 to 23 percentage points across specifications (Chaudhury and Parajuli, 2008, 2010). Five years on, beneficiary girls were 3–6 percentage points more likely to complete middle school and 4–6 percentage points more likely to transition to high school (Baez, Alam and Del Carpio, 2011).

The only experiment that randomises conditionality itself, however, complicates the story. Baird, McIntosh and Özler (2011, Quarterly Journal of Economics 126: 1709–1753) randomised 2,907 adolescent girls aged 13–22 across 176 enumeration areas in Zomba district, Malawi, to a conditional transfer (US$1–5 per month to the girl plus US$4–10 to the parent, conditional on 80% attendance), an unconditional transfer of identical value, or control. The unconditional arm's dropout reduction was only 43% as large as the conditional arm's, and the conditional arm outperformed on English reading comprehension. But teenage pregnancy and marriage were substantially lower in the unconditional arm — entirely because of effects among girls who had dropped out of school, whom the conditional arm by design stopped paying. Conditionality buys schooling; unconditionality protects the girls schooling fails to reach.

Sindh has never run this test. The federal Benazir Taleemi Wazaif programme — a conditional cash transfer for children of Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) Kafalat beneficiaries, piloted in five districts in November 2012 and expanded to all districts by July 2020, now covering over 12 million children — is conditional nationwide (70% quarterly attendance; PKR 3,000 per quarter for a secondary-school girl, PKR 4,000 at higher secondary, plus a one-time PKR 3,000 bonus for girls completing primary). It has never been evaluated against an unconditional arm of equal value. This paper's contribution is a design that does so, with the analysis plan stated before any data are collected, and a cost-effectiveness benchmark computed transparently from the published Punjab evaluation so that the trial's result can be judged against a known price.

2. Literature and the Islamic canon

2.1 Modern evidence

The causal-education literature gives this paper its method standard. Banerjee and Duflo's randomised-evaluation programme (J-PAL; Nobel Prize in Economics 2019) established that a small, testable question answered by randomisation beats a grand reform asserted without one. Heckman's Perry Preschool follow-up showed a 6–10% annual return per dollar invested in early human capital — the fiscal argument for investing in children rather than the sentimental one. Hanushek's value-added work insists on measuring the output (learning) rather than the input (spending); this paper therefore pre-specifies enrolment and learning outcomes, not disbursement counts. Chetty's Opportunity Atlas shows that place — down to the neighbourhood — causally shapes a child's adult outcomes; Sindh's district-level variation in girls' enrolment is the same phenomenon at provincial scale.

Within cash transfers specifically, the evidence base is: Chaudhury and Parajuli (2008, 2010) on Punjab's FSSP (difference-in-differences, triple difference and regression discontinuity on the 2003 and 2005 school censuses); Baez, Alam and Del Carpio (2011) on the FSSP's longer-term effects on completion, transition, marriage and labour-force participation; Baird, McIntosh and Özler (2011) on the Malawi conditionality experiment; and the BISP's own programme documentation for Benazir Taleemi Wazaif (pilot 2012, national coverage 2020, 70% attendance condition, published stipend rates). The gap this paper fills: no head-to-head conditional-vs-unconditional test exists in Pakistan, and no published cost-per-additional-girl figure exists for the Punjab programme. Both are supplied here — the first as a design, the second as a computation.

2.2 The Islamic canon on education

The Islamic tradition treats the education of girls not as a modern development goal but as a religious duty. The first revealed word of the Qur'an is a command to read: "Read, in the name of your Lord who created" (Qur'an 96:1–5). The Qur'an asks, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" (Qur'an 39:9). The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said, "Seeking knowledge is a duty upon every Muslim" (Sunan Ibn Majah 224; scholars differ on the grading of this narration — al-Albani graded it sahih, others da'if — and the paper relies on the Qur'anic command, which is not in dispute, for the normative claim). Classical scholarship systematised the point: Al-Ghazali, in Al-Mustasfa, defined the five objectives of the law (maqasid al-shariah), including preservation of intellect (hifz al-'aql); Al-Shatibi systematised the maqasid in Al-Muwafaqat (d. 1388); Muhammad al-Tahir Ibn Ashur expanded them to freedom, justice and equality in Maqasid al-Shari'ah al-Islamiyyah (written 1946). Ibn Khaldun devoted chapter 6 of the Muqaddimah (1377) to education as a craft acquired by habituation — a claim this paper's mechanism section tests directly: attendance is the habit, and the stipend is the incentive that builds it. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way — that keeping girls in school is among the highest-return uses of public money — this paper says so; where they differ, it says so too: the tradition's duty is unconditional (knowledge is owed to every Muslim, girl or boy, in school or out), while the instrument tested here is conditional. That tension is exactly what the unconditional arm of the trial measures.

3. Methods

3.1 Analysis plan (stated before results)

This paper contains no new field data. It contains (a) a re-analysis of published estimates into a cost-effectiveness benchmark, with every arithmetic step shown, and (b) a pre-registered trial design. The distinction is stated here so that no reader mistakes a computation for a finding: the cost-effectiveness figures in Section 4.1 are extrapolations from published estimates, not new causal estimates — association and arithmetic only, in bold. The causal claim is the trial's to settle, and its analysis plan is fixed below before any school is randomised.

3.2 The cost-effectiveness computation

Inputs (all published, all cited in Section 1): FSSP stipend spending in 2007, US$7.3 million; beneficiaries in 2007, 245,000 girls in grades 6–8; preferred treatment-effect estimate, +6 female students per school (difference-in-differences combined with regression discontinuity, Chaudhury and Parajuli); middle schools covered by the programme, 4,621. Computation: 4,621 schools × 6 additional girls = 27,726 additional girls enrolled. Marginality: 27,726 ÷ 245,000 beneficiaries = 11.3% — roughly one in nine stipend recipients was an additional girl in school; the other eight would have enrolled anyway. Cost per additional girl-year: US$7,300,000 ÷ 27,726 ≈ US$263. Sensitivity: if the true effect were +3 girls per school, US$527; if +9, US$176. All figures are 2007 US dollars, not inflation-adjusted — the limitation is stated, not hidden.

3.3 The trial design (pre-registered, to be run)

Design. Three-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial in Sindh, randomised at school level, stratified by district and by baseline girls' enrolment. Arms: (A) conditional stipend — PKR 3,000 per quarter per secondary-school girl (the Benazir Taleemi Wazaif secondary rate), conditional on 70% quarterly attendance; (B) unconditional transfer — PKR 3,000 per quarter per secondary-school girl, no attendance condition, paid to the same household on the same schedule; (C) control — existing Taleemi Wazaif only, no additional payment. Population: government girls' middle and secondary schools in Sindh's lowest-enrolment districts (Thatta, where 71% of children are out of school, and the other bottom-quintile districts on PSLM 2019–20). Duration: three school years. Primary outcome: girls' net enrolment rate at secondary level, measured by independent school-census audit (not programme records). Secondary outcomes: attendance rate, grade progression, standardised Urdu and mathematics scores (Hanushek's output test), dropout, and — following Baird et al. — marriage and pregnancy among girls who leave school. Identification: randomisation at school level; intention-to-treat estimation; difference-in-differences on PSLM waves as a secondary check. Power: to detect a 6-percentage-point effect on enrolment from a 50% baseline at 5% significance with 80% power requires about 1,089 girls per arm if individually randomised; with clustering (intra-cluster correlation 0.05, 40 girls per school, design effect 2.95) this becomes about 3,212 girls — about 80 schools — per arm, or 240 schools in total. All power assumptions are stated and can be re-run. Pre-registration: design, outcomes and the falsifier in the Abstract are fixed before randomisation; any post-hoc analysis will be labelled exploratory.

3.4 Mechanism

The causal chain, with a test for each link: (1) cash relaxes the household budget constraint — tested by whether enrolment rises in both paid arms; (2) the attendance condition changes the marginal decision to send a girl on a given day — tested by the CCT-minus-UCT gap in attendance; (3) attendance becomes habit, in Ibn Khaldun's sense of education as a craft acquired by repetition — tested by whether the enrolment effect persists in the year after payments stop; (4) schooling delays marriage — tested by the marriage outcome in each arm, with the Malawi result predicting the unconditional arm does better here. If link (2) fails but link (1) holds, conditionality is pure administrative cost and the policy should be unconditional. If link (4) reverses the ranking on welfare even while schooling favours the conditional arm, the recommendation must weigh the two outcomes explicitly rather than declare a winner on enrolment alone.

3.5 Comparison against the strongest incumbent

The incumbent is not "nothing". It is Benazir Taleemi Wazaif as it operates today in Sindh: conditional, PKR 3,000 per quarter for a secondary-school girl, 70% attendance, delivered through BISP to Kafalat households. The trial's control arm keeps that programme. The question is therefore narrow and honest: does adding conditionality discipline, or removing it, beat the status quo per rupee? A design that compared a stipend against nothing would flatter any transfer; this one does not.

4. Results

4.1 Cost-effectiveness of the Punjab programme (computation, not a new estimate)

4.2 Scaling to Sindh (back-of-the-envelope, assumptions stated)

Sindh has 4.09 million out-of-school girls. Suppose the policy goal is 100,000 additional secondary-school girls in Sindh — about 2.4% of the out-of-school stock. At the Punjab marginality rate (11.3%), reaching them requires paying about 885,000 girls (100,000 ÷ 0.113). At the Taleemi Wazaif secondary rate for girls (PKR 3,000 per quarter = PKR 12,000 per year), the annual stipend bill is about PKR 10.6 billion, or PKR 106,000 per additional girl kept in secondary school for a year. That is the paper's single memorable number — and it is a warning as much as a price: nine-tenths of a universal stipend budget pays girls who would have enrolled anyway. Targeting (poorer households, lowest-enrolment districts, girls at the dropout margin) is where the cost-effectiveness lives, and the trial's stratification is designed to find it.

4.3 What the trial must show — and what would kill the claim

The claim survives only if the conditional arm beats control by at least 6 percentage points on secondary net enrolment and beats the unconditional arm by at least 3 points. It dies if either condition fails. A second, independent falsifier already exists in the literature and must be respected: if Sindh's rollout reproduces the Malawi pattern — conditionality winning on schooling while losing on marriage and pregnancy among dropouts — then a conditional-only scale-up is the wrong recommendation even if the enrolment test passes, and the policy must be a hybrid (conditional stipend in school, unconditional support for girls who leave).

5. Discussion

Three points follow. First, the Punjab evidence justifies paying for girls' schooling, but it does not justify paying conditionally — that was never the tested margin in Pakistan, and the one experiment that did test it found the answer depends on which outcome you care about. Second, the cost arithmetic disciplines enthusiasm: PKR 106,000 per additional girl-year is affordable at small scale and ruinous as an untargeted entitlement, which is why the trial stratifies by district enrolment and why the paper recommends starting in the lowest-enrolment districts rather than province-wide. Third, the supply side binds: Sindh has 2,634 middle schools against 36,000 primary schools, so a demand-side stipend in a district with no middle school buys nothing — the trial excludes schools beyond reasonable travel distance and the policy recommendation pairs stipends with the classroom construction the Civil Services Academy review identifies as the binding constraint.

The Islamic frame strengthens rather than softens the conclusion. Preservation of intellect (hifz al-'aql) makes girls' education a duty of the community, and justice ('adl, Qur'an 4:135) forbids a design whose burden falls on the poorest — which is precisely what an unconditional payment to the poorest households does better than a conditional one that stops paying the moment a girl drops out. Public interest (maslaha) requires counting the welfare of the girl who leaves school, not only the girl who stays. The trial is therefore not a technical nicety: it is the mechanism by which the state discovers whether its instrument serves the principle.

6. Limitations

  1. No new Sindh microdata were analysed in this run. The Punjab difference-in-differences result is a published finding re-used here, not re-estimated; PSLM district microdata were not re-analysed. The trial is a design, not results.
  2. The 11.3% marginality rate is extrapolated across province and twenty years. Punjab in 2004 is not Sindh in 2026: different baseline enrolment, different transfer size, different delivery system. The PKR 10.6 billion figure is a planning bound, not a budget.
  3. 2007 US dollars are not adjusted for inflation or converted to 2026 rupees. The US$263 and PKR 106,000 figures sit in different price years and must not be compared directly.
  4. Supply constraints may dominate. Where no middle school exists within travel distance, no stipend design enrols anyone; the trial's exclusion of such areas limits generalisability to exactly the districts that need help most.
  5. External validity of the Malawi experiment is limited. Different country, different transfer size (US$1–5 per month), different marriage norms. It motivates the unconditional arm; it does not predict its size in Sindh.
  6. Classical Islamic works were consulted through the verified catalogue in the project's literature map (Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah, Rosenthal translation, via archive.org; Al-Ghazali selections via ghazali.org; Al-Shatibi and Ibn Ashur via the map's verified holdings), not by a fresh full-text reading in this run. The Qur'anic verses (96:1–5; 39:9; 4:135) and Sunan Ibn Majah 224 were verified against live sources in this run; the grading of Ibn Majah 224 is disputed among scholars and is reported as such. Untranslated and undigitised manuscripts — including most of Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi and the full Kitab al-Tasrif — were not accessible and are named here as the gap.
  7. The most recent daily research digest available to this run was 14 November 2026; the digest series appears to have stopped after that date, so the literature sweep for this paper relied on targeted searches of the primary sources instead.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: Government of Sindh, School Education & Literacy Department, jointly with the Benazir Income Support Programme. Exact change, in sequence: (1) fund the three-arm cluster-randomised trial in 240 schools in Sindh's lowest-enrolment districts (80 schools per arm, three school years, independent census audit), at the Taleemi Wazaif secondary rate of PKR 3,000 per quarter; (2) if the conditional arm beats control by ≥6 percentage points and the unconditional arm by ≥3 points, adopt a conditional secondary-girls stipend in those districts, paired with middle-school construction where the school census shows no school within travel distance; (3) if it does not, pay the same PKR 3,000 per quarter unconditionally — the Malawi evidence says the unconditional arm protects out-of-school girls from early marriage and pregnancy, which the conditional arm cannot do by design; (4) in either case, publish the trial data as a public tool, in the manner of Chetty's Opportunity Atlas, so that districts can be targeted by evidence rather than by patronage. Islamic principle: hifz al-'aql (preservation of intellect, Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat) and 'adl (Qur'an 4:135) — the state owes every girl the means to learn, and a design that abandons the girl who drops out fails the duty even when it raises the average. Falsifier for the policy: if the trial returns a conditional-vs-control effect of 0 or below, the conditional stipend is not scaled, and the budget is reallocated to unconditional transfers or to school construction, whichever the trial shows works.

8. Conclusion

Sindh's 4.09 million out-of-school girls are the sharpest edge of Pakistan's education crisis, and the province's pipeline — 36,000 primary schools narrowing to 2,634 middle schools — guarantees the crisis reproduces itself every year. Punjab's conditional stipend worked, at about US$263 per additional girl-year in 2007 prices, but it never tested whether the condition was doing the work. Malawi's experiment says conditionality buys schooling and unconditionality protects the girls schooling misses. The honest next step is not to scale either answer province-wide, but to run the three-arm trial in Sindh that distinguishes them — and to let its pre-registered falsifier, not habit or ideology, decide which rupee is spent how. One number to remember: PKR 106,000 — the cost of keeping one additional Sindh girl in secondary school for a year at Punjab's marginality rate, and the price of getting the design wrong.

Who Gets the Youth Loan? Concentration, Subsidy and the Missing Enterprise Test in Pakistan's PMYBALS, 2023–2026

Question. Pakistan's Prime Minister's Youth Business & Agriculture Loan Scheme (PMYBALS) has disbursed roughly Rs 289 billion since January 2023 to over half a million borrowers, at a taxpayer subsidy the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) prices at about 15 paisa per rupee lent.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan. ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509. Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI research assistant). Date: 21 November 2026. Field: Social Science (public economics / development finance). Status: Manuscript draft. Not submitted anywhere. No professor's endorsement is claimed; the Harvard / MIT / Oxford policy-shaping scholars named in the method brief are the standard this paper practises, not co-authors.

Abstract

Question. Pakistan's Prime Minister's Youth Business & Agriculture Loan Scheme (PMYBALS) has disbursed roughly Rs 289 billion since January 2023 to over half a million borrowers, at a taxpayer subsidy the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) prices at about 15 paisa per rupee lent. Its stated purpose is youth enterprise creation. Does the money actually reach young entrepreneurs and create new enterprises — or does subsidised credit concentrate in a small number of large borrowers while youth unemployment keeps rising?

Claim. On the published aggregates, the scheme fails its own enterprise test twice over. First, concentration: in the SBP's own tier tables to December 2025, Tier-III loans (Rs 1.5–7.5 million, 7% fixed interest) took 67.0% of all money disbursed while reaching only 11.0% of borrowers, and the average Tier-III loan (Rs 2.92 million) was 22 times the average interest-free Tier-I loan (Rs 132,339) that 85.6% of borrowers received. Second, no enterprise signal: while Rs 175 billion had been disbursed by June 2025, youth unemployment (ages 15–24) rose from 11.1% (2020-21) to 12.6% (2024-25) in the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics Labour Force Survey, and the 27.4% jump in SECP company registrations in FY2024-25 is attributed by SECP itself to digitisation (99.9% of incorporations online), not to the loan scheme. A third finding is a data-quality failure: the press-reported claim that Rs 102 billion went to 3,957 agriculture borrowers is arithmetically impossible under the scheme's Rs 7.5 million loan cap (maximum Rs 29.7 billion) — a 3.4× gap that the government has not explained.

Falsifier. The claim is refuted if either (i) district-level SBP disbursement data, once published, show that per-youth disbursement positively predicts per-youth SECP registrations or Labour Force Survey youth self-employment after controlling for the pre-2023 registration trend and the SECP digitisation rollout, or (ii) a follow-up survey of a random sample of Tier-I borrowers finds that at least 50% operate a business that was still trading 24 months after disbursement. The FY2026-27 outturn — a Rs 292 billion disbursement target that exceeds the entire three-year cumulative total — is the first scheduled test.

Identification. Association only. This is a descriptive audit of published national aggregates, with no control group and no randomised or quasi-experimental variation in who receives loans. Confounders — SECP digitisation, GDP growth, inflation, the January 2023 scheme launch coinciding with post-flood recovery lending — are named, not controlled. The paper falsifies the claim that "disbursement equals enterprise creation"; it does not estimate a causal effect of any loan. A difference-in-differences design on district-level data and a randomised musharakah-vs-interest-loan trial are proposed as the causal tests.

One clean number: 67% of the money to 11% of the borrowers — the share of PMYBALS disbursements absorbed by the largest loan tier, against 85.6% of borrowers sharing 23.7% of the money in the interest-free tier. The stakes number is Rs 38 billion: the SBP's estimated annual subsidy bill for the scheme, against Rs 21 billion budgeted — a Rs 17 billion (45%) funding gap.

Keywords: PMYBALS; youth enterprise; credit concentration; subsidy; Pakistan; SBP; SECP; riba; musharakah; 'adl; maqasid.

1. Introduction

Pakistan has 46.3 million people aged 15–24 — 18.5% of the population — and their unemployment rate rose from 11.1% in 2020-21 to 12.6% in 2024-25, even as the youth labour force grew from 18.3 million to 21.1 million (Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, Labour Force Survey 2024-25). The government's flagship answer is the Prime Minister's Youth Business & Agriculture Loan Scheme (PMYBALS), launched in January 2023: subsidised credit for young Pakistanis aged 21–45 (18 for IT and e-commerce), in tiers — Tier-I up to Rs 0.5 million interest-free, Tier-II Rs 0.5–1.5 million at 5%, Tier-III Rs 1.5–7.5 million at 7% — with a new Tier-IV of Rs 7.5–25 million at 8% approved by the Economic Coordination Committee on 4 November 2026 and ratified by the federal cabinet, plus an interest-free Tier-V for laptops and overseas workers (Dawn, 11 November 2026; The News, November 2026).

The scheme is large. By 31 December 2025 the State Bank of Pakistan recorded 461,795 loans disbursed worth Rs 220.9 billion, cumulative from January 2023 (SBP, PMYBALS Quarterly Data Tables, December 2025). Press reporting of official statistics to June 2026 puts the total at Rs 288 billion to 570,290 beneficiaries (The Express Tribune, November 2026). The FY2026-27 disbursement target is Rs 292 billion — more than the scheme disbursed in its entire first three years. And it is expensive: the SBP estimates the subsidy at Rs 38 billion on Rs 250 billion of disbursement in the current fiscal year, against Rs 21 billion budgeted (Tribune, November 2026).

Yet no published evaluation asks the scheme's central question: does subsidised youth credit create youth enterprises? The SBP publishes disbursement counts and amounts by tier, not outcomes — no business survival rate, no jobs created, no district breakdown, no follow-up of borrowers. This paper performs the audit that the published data permit: it computes the concentration of disbursements across tiers, the subsidy cost per rupee, the non-performing-loan profile by tier, and the only enterprise signal available — SECP company registrations and Labour Force Survey youth unemployment — and tests the scheme's stated purpose against them. It then applies the Islamic policy lens the programme's own principles require: the prohibition of riba (Qur'an 2:275–279), 'adl — justice in distribution (Qur'an 4:135) — and the maqasid test of whether public money serves the public interest (maslaha).

2. Methods

Analysis plan (stated before results). Before any computation, the plan was: (1) take the SBP's quarterly PMYBALS tables as the authoritative source and compute, for each tier, the share of borrowers, the share of money, the average loan, and the non-performing-loan (NPL) rate by amount and by count; (2) derive quarterly disbursement flows by differencing cumulative totals; (3) cross-check the press-reported June 2026 totals against the scheme's own loan caps for arithmetic consistency; (4) compare the enterprise outcome proxies (SECP registrations, LFS youth unemployment) against the disbursement series; (5) compute the subsidy rate and the budget gap from the SBP's published estimates. No post-hoc analysis was added after seeing the results; the inconsistency check in step (3) was pre-specified because press totals and SBP tables use different reporting dates.

Data sources. SBP PMYBALS Quarterly Data Tables as of 31 March 2025, 30 June 2025, 30 September 2025 and 31 December 2025 (SBP, sbp.org.pk and archive.sbp.org.pk); The Express Tribune, "Farming leads PM's youth loan drive" (November 2026, reporting official statistics to June 2026); Dawn, "Cabinet, ECC sanction new tier-4 category for PM loan scheme" (11 November 2026); The News, "Revised structure of PM's youth business loan more beneficial" (November 2026); SECP press statement via Business Recorder / Centreline (11 January 2026); Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, Labour Force Survey 2024-25, as reported by Dawn, The News and Geo (November 2025).

Islamic canon consulted. Qur'an 2:275–279 (riba), 4:135 ('adl), 42:38 (shura), 2:30 (khilafah/stewardship), 9:60 (zakat); Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat (maqasid al-shariah); Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah (1377, Rosenthal translation, Princeton, 1958), ch. 3 (state expenditure and dynastic cycles); Chapra, Islam and the Economic Challenge (1992); Siddiqi, Banking Without Interest (1983); Usmani, An Introduction to Islamic Finance (2002). These works were consulted through the verified holdings named in the programme's Islamic-thought literature map; no Qur'anic verse or classical passage is quoted from memory — all citations are to the named surah:ayah or named book.

Method standard. Banerjee & Duflo's RCT programme (Poor Economics, 2011) is the template for the proposed causal test; Chetty et al.'s Opportunity Atlas (NBER Working Paper 25147, 2018) is the template for publishing the underlying data as a public tool; Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson (American Economic Review, 2001) are the template for finding variation no one can manipulate; Thaler & Sunstein (Nudge, 2008) are the template for small, tested design changes over grand reform. None of these scholars is a co-author and none endorses this paper.

Limitations of method (stated here, expanded in §6). The SBP publishes no district-level disbursement data and no borrower outcomes. All enterprise tests in this paper are therefore ecological — national aggregates against national aggregates — and the identification is association only.

3. Results

3.1 Concentration: two-thirds of the money to one-tenth of the borrowers

As of 31 December 2025 (SBP, cumulative from January 2023), 461,795 loans had been disbursed for Rs 220,948 million — an average loan of Rs 478,455. The tier breakdown is stark:

Tier-II (Rs 0.5–1.5m, 5%) 15,545 3.4% 20,620.9 9.3% 1,326,529 3.78% 5.60%
Tier-III (Rs 1.5–7.5m, 7%) 50,746 11.0% 147,986.5 67.0% 2,916,220 0.44% 2.65%
Total 461,795 100% 220,948.0 100% 478,455 0.70% 0.75%

Three facts follow. First, the interest-free tier is where the youth are, but the money is elsewhere: 85.6% of borrowers share 23.7% of the money, while 11.0% of borrowers in Tier-III take 67.0%. Second, 76.3% of all money disbursed is lent at fixed interest (Tiers II and III combined) — the scheme's financial core is interest-bearing credit, not the interest-free Tier-I that dominates its public presentation. Third, the average Tier-III loan is 22.0 times the average Tier-I loan (Rs 2,916,220 vs Rs 132,339). Agriculture dominates the large end: of total disbursements, agriculture loans were Rs 115,541.5 million (52.3%) against Rs 105,406.5 million for SME/business loans.

3.2 The pace is accelerating — and the target exceeds the history

Quarterly disbursement flows, derived by differencing the SBP's cumulative totals, accelerated through 2025: Rs 13,832.7 million in Q4 FY2024-25 (April–June 2025), Rs 22,169.2 million in Q1 FY2025-26, and Rs 23,874.2 million in Q2 FY2025-26. Press-reported totals to June 2026 imply a further Rs 67.1 billion disbursed to 108,495 borrowers in the first half of 2026 (average Rs 618,019). The FY2026-27 target of Rs 292 billion is 1.01 times the entire cumulative disbursement of the scheme's first three years (Rs 288 billion) — the government plans to lend in one year what it lent in three.

3.3 The non-performing-loan profile: the middle tier defaults most

Overall NPLs are low: 3,469 loans (0.75% by count) and Rs 1,555.1 million (0.70% by amount) at December 2025. But the profile is uneven. Tier-II — small shops, workshops and farm upgrades at 5% — carries the worst repayment record by a wide margin: 5.60% of Tier-II loans by count and 3.78% by amount are non-performing, against 0.32%/0.24% in Tier-I and 2.65%/0.44% in Tier-III. The middle of the scheme, not the top or the bottom, is where credit discipline breaks down. (One caution: the SBP's own tables show NPL amounts moving non-monotonically — Rs 1,263.0 million at June 2025, Rs 1,722.3 million at September 2025, Rs 1,555.1 million at December 2025 — and the SBP disclaimer notes figures vary with revisions and reversals; the tier ranking, however, is stable across all four quarters.)

3.4 The enterprise test: no signal in the only outcomes published

Two outcome series exist. Company registrations: SECP recorded 35,087 new companies in FY2024-25, up 27.4% from 27,542 in FY2023-24, with 21,542 more in the first half of FY2025-26 and the registry passing 258,000 companies. But SECP attributes the growth to its own digitisation reforms — 99.9% of incorporations processed online — not to the loan scheme, and most PMYBALS borrowers are sole proprietors and farmers who never register a company. Registrations therefore cannot be credited to the scheme without district-level matching, which the SBP does not publish. Youth unemployment: the LFS 2024-25 records youth (15–24) unemployment at 12.6%, up 1.5 percentage points from 11.1% in 2020-21, while the scheme disbursed Rs 174.9 billion by June 2025. The number of unemployed persons rose from 4.5 million to 5.9 million over the same interval. A youth-enterprise scheme that coincides with rising youth unemployment has not demonstrated its mechanism; at minimum, the burden of proof has not been met. Both tests are ecological and association-only — but the scheme's defenders, not its critics, bear the burden of producing borrower-level outcome data.

3.5 Data-quality audit: the reported concentration figures do not add up

Press reporting of official statistics to June 2026 states that Rs 102 billion — over 35% of all loans — went to 3,957 agriculture borrowers taking loans "in the range of Rs 1.5 million to Rs 7.5 million" at 7%, and that Rs 193 billion (67%) went to 24,362 borrowers in the maximum-loan category (Tribune, November 2026). Both claims are arithmetically inconsistent with the scheme's own caps:

  • 3,957 borrowers × Rs 7.5 million (the Tier-III ceiling) = Rs 29.7 billion maximum — against Rs 102 billion claimed, a 3.44× gap. The implied average loan is Rs 25.8 million, more than triple the legal maximum.
  • 24,362 borrowers × Rs 7.5 million = Rs 182.7 billion maximum — against Rs 193 billion claimed; the implied average of Rs 7.92 million also exceeds the cap.

Possible explanations — multiple loans per borrower, misreported borrower counts, or a reporting error — cannot be distinguished from the published figures, and the government has published no correction. The SBP's own tier tables (Table 3.1) are internally consistent and are therefore the evidentiary basis of this paper; the press-reported figures are cited here only as a data-quality finding. Either the concentration is even worse than the SBP tables show, or the official statistics released to the press are wrong. Both possibilities demand the same remedy: publish borrower-level, district-level data.

3.6 The subsidy: 15 paisa in every rupee

The SBP estimates the subsidy at Rs 38 billion on Rs 250 billion of disbursement for the current fiscal year — 15.2% of every rupee lent — against Rs 21 billion budgeted, a Rs 17 billion (45%) funding gap (Tribune, November 2026). At the FY2026-27 target of Rs 292 billion, the same subsidy rate implies roughly Rs 44 billion of taxpayer money in a single year, with no published estimate of jobs or enterprises created per rupee of subsidy. For comparison, the entire subsidy bill now rivals the annual development budget of a small province — spent without a published cost-per-enterprise figure.

4. Discussion

4.1 Mechanism: why the money concentrates

The mechanism is structural, not accidental. Tier-III loans require bank-policy security and an 80:20 debt-equity ratio for new businesses (SBP, PMYBALS terms); collateral and equity screen out exactly the asset-poor young people the scheme names as its beneficiaries, while favouring established farmers and businesses that can post security. Agriculture's 52.3% share of disbursements, and the press-reported concentration among large agriculture borrowers, follow from the same design: land is collateral, and collateral is what banks can lend against. The scheme therefore functions less as youth-enterprise finance and more as subsidised agricultural and SME credit routed through a youth label — a classic case of what Banerjee & Duflo warn against: a programme whose targeting mechanism defeats its targeting intent, measurable only because the SBP publishes tier tables.

4.2 Comparison vs the strongest incumbent

The strongest incumbent is not "no scheme" but the scheme's own Tier-I: interest-free, collateral-light (personal guarantee), reaching 85.6% of borrowers with the lowest default rate in the programme (0.24% by amount). Tier-I is also the only tier that is unambiguously compatible with the Islamic prohibition of riba. The honest comparison is therefore Tier-I against Tiers II–IV: the interest-free tier reaches eight times as many borrowers per rupee of subsidy, defaults less, and needs no theological defence. The new Tier-IV (Rs 7.5–25 million at 8%) moves the scheme further in the opposite direction — larger loans, higher rates, more collateral — and should be judged against Tier-I's record, not against nothing.

4.3 The Islamic lens

Four principles bear on the scheme, and on each the evidence points the same way:

  • Riba (Qur'an 2:275–279). "Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden interest." Tiers II, III and the new Tier-IV charge fixed interest of 5%, 7% and 8% — 76.3% of all money disbursed. The state's subsidy pays the difference between the borrower's rate and the bank's KIBOR-plus margin; the subsidy makes interest cheaper, it does not remove it. A scheme that is three-quarters interest-bearing cannot be presented as consistent with the prohibition; the interest-free Tier-I and Tier-V show the alternative already exists inside the same programme.
  • 'Adl — justice (Qur'an 4:135). "Stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to Allah, even if it be against yourselves, your parents, and your relatives." A subsidy is a public transfer. When 67% of subsidised credit reaches 11% of borrowers — and the largest borrowers are established agriculturalists with land collateral — the transfer is regressive: public money subsidises those who already hold assets. The 'adl test asks who bears the burden and who takes the benefit; here the benefit concentrates at the top.
  • Maqasid and maslaha (Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat). Public policy must preserve life (nafs), intellect ('aql) and wealth (mal) and secure genuine public benefit. A Rs 38 billion annual subsidy with no published outcome measure — no enterprises counted, no jobs counted, no survival rate — fails the maslaha test of accountability: benefit that cannot be measured cannot be claimed. Hifz al-mal cuts both ways: it protects the borrower's wealth, but also the public purse.
  • Shura (Qur'an 42:38) and Ibn Khaldun's fiscal warning. Decisions are to be taken by consultation; no published consultation with borrowers, youth organisations or Islamic-finance scholars accompanies the scheme's revisions, including the November 2026 Tier-IV expansion. Ibn Khaldun (Muqaddimah, ch. 3) warned that state expenditure grows as dynasties age and that rising exactions shrink the base that pays them — the scheme's subsidy bill growing from Rs 21 billion budgeted to Rs 38 billion estimated, while the FY2026-27 target exceeds three years of lending, is the pattern he described: expenditure that expands faster than the revenue and the results that justify it.

The Islamic alternative is not to abolish youth finance but to restructure it on risk-sharing: a musharakah youth fund in which the state shares profit and loss with the young entrepreneur instead of charging fixed interest (Chapra, Islam and the Economic Challenge, 1992; Siddiqi, Banking Without Interest, 1983; Usmani, An Introduction to Islamic Finance, 2002). Under musharakah the state's return depends on the enterprise succeeding — which aligns the state's incentive with the outcome the scheme claims to want, and which automatically concentrates state attention on the smallest borrowers, since a profit-share in a failed large loan loses public money. Zakat and waqf instruments (Qur'an 9:60) can fund the smallest, collateral-free tier outright as grants for the poorest applicants, where even an interest-free loan is a burden.

5. Policy Implications

Decision-maker 1 — the Prime Minister's Youth Programme (PMYP) and the Ministry of Finance. Before the Rs 292 billion FY2026-27 target is released: (a) publish district-level disbursement and borrower-outcome data (business survival at 12 and 24 months, jobs created) as open data, on the Chetty model of publishing the data as a public tool; (b) cap any single borrower's cumulative subsidised borrowing and publish the concentration ratio quarterly; (c) freeze Tier-IV disbursements until the arithmetic inconsistency in the reported June 2026 figures (§3.5) is corrected in public. If district data show no positive association between per-youth disbursement and enterprise formation, the target should be cut and the money redirected to Tier-I. Islamic principle: 'adl and maslaha — public money must be shown to benefit the public, with the burden of proof on the spender.

Decision-maker 2 — the State Bank of Pakistan. Add three fields to the quarterly PMYBALS tables: district, borrower age band, and 24-month business-survival status. The tables already exist and are published quarterly; the marginal cost is small and the accountability gain is large. Islamic principle: shura — the public cannot consult on what it cannot see.

Decision-maker 3 — the Ministry of Finance and the SBP Shariah governance framework. Pilot a musharakah youth window alongside Tiers II–IV: identical eligibility, but the state takes a profit-share instead of fixed interest, with the return capped and losses shared. Randomise eligible applicants between the musharakah window and the standard interest-bearing tiers (the Banerjee & Duflo template) and measure business survival and repayment at 24 months. If the musharakah arm survives at least as well, convert the scheme's growth funding to risk-sharing. Islamic principle: the riba prohibition (Qur'an 2:275–279) requires an alternative, not only a criticism — Chapra (1992) and Usmani (2002) supply the design.

Decision-maker 4 — the Auditor General of Pakistan. Audit the June 2026 concentration figures: reconcile the reported Rs 102 billion to 3,957 borrowers against the Rs 7.5 million loan cap, and publish the reconciliation. A 3.44× arithmetic gap in official statistics released to the press is itself a finding that requires an answer. Islamic principle: hifz al-mal — stewardship of public wealth (Qur'an 2:30, khilafah) begins with accurate accounts.

6. Limitations

  1. Association only. No district-level or borrower-level data are published, so no causal claim is made. The concentration finding is arithmetic on official aggregates; the enterprise finding is ecological. A district panel could overturn the enterprise conclusion — which is why the paper's first recommendation is to publish one.
  2. Press-reported totals are inconsistent (§3.5). The June 2026 totals come from press reporting of official statistics, not from a published SBP table. If the SBP's own June 2026 table, when published, differs, the figures in §3.2 and §3.5 must be revised — and the inconsistency itself would remain a finding about statistical reporting.
  3. Outcome proxies are indirect. SECP registrations capture only incorporated companies; most youth enterprises are sole proprietorships. LFS youth unemployment reflects the whole economy, not the scheme's borrowers. The paper claims only that the scheme has not demonstrated its effect on the outcomes its own purpose implies — not that it has no effect.
  4. NPL figures are revised. The SBP disclaimer notes figures vary with revisions and reversals; the September-to-December 2025 fall in NPL amounts illustrates this. Tier rankings are stable across quarters, but point estimates should be read with the revision caveat.
  5. Islamic canon gaps (named, per the programme's sweep rule). This paper consulted the Qur'an, Al-Shatibi, Al-Ghazali, Ibn Khaldun, Chapra, Siddiqi and Usmani as named in the literature map. It did not consult: Al-Mawardi's Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya (constitutional theory of public finance) in full; the classical fiqh literature on qard hasan (benevolent loans) beyond the modern summaries; or the State Bank's own Shariah-board rulings on subsidised lending, which are not published in accessible form. A fuller treatment would read Al-Mawardi on the treasury (bayt al-mal) and the modern AAOIFI Shariah standards on musharakah; their absence is a gap, not a claim that they were read.

7. Conclusion

Pakistan's youth loan scheme is big, expensive and unevaluated. On the State Bank's own tables, 67% of its money reaches 11% of its borrowers, 76% of its money is lent at fixed interest, the middle tier defaults at fifteen times the rate of the interest-free tier, and the subsidy costs the taxpayer 15 paisa per rupee lent — while youth unemployment rose through the scheme's first three years and the official concentration figures released to the press are arithmetically impossible under the scheme's own loan caps. The interest-free Tier-I, which reaches 85.6% of borrowers with the lowest default rate, shows the scheme already contains its own best design. The honest next step is not a bigger target — the Rs 292 billion FY2026-27 target exceeds the scheme's entire three-year history — but published district-level outcomes, a corrected statistical record, and a randomised musharakah pilot that tests whether risk-sharing finance serves young Pakistanis better than subsidised interest. Until those exist, the claim that the scheme creates youth enterprises is unproven, and the subsidy is a transfer whose beneficiaries are, on the evidence, the borrowers who needed it least.
